Name: belief_updating_dynamics
Title: Does It Update or Overwrite? Tracing How LLMs Revise Beliefs When Confronted with Evidence
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM is presented with counter-evidence to a proposition it internally 'believes' to be true, its belief representation does not smoothly move toward the new state; instead it exhibits a distinct, measurable dynamical signature (e.g., abrupt overwrite, oscillation, or a persistent latent 'residual belief') that predicts whether the model will actually change its stated answer or superficially comply while retaining its prior belief.
Related Work: Prior work establishes that LLMs linearly encode truth/belief in activations (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Burns et al. 2022; Zou et al. 2023) and that these representations of self/other beliefs exist and are causally steerable (Zhu et al. 2024; 'Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations' 2024). Yang & Jia 2025 show that a momentary belief probe predicts retraction. However, all existing work treats belief as a static, single-shot readout: they probe the belief at one point or steer it once. No work characterizes the *temporal dynamics* of how a belief representation moves through activation space across successive turns of an evidence-presentation dialogue, nor whether the internal update trajectory (as opposed to the final state) predicts genuine vs. superficial (sycophantic) belief change. We uniquely study belief revision as a trajectory-level phenomenon and connect the geometry of that trajectory to downstream behavior (persistence, sycophancy, retraction).
Abstract: Large language models linearly encode whether they 'believe' a proposition to be true, and these belief directions are causally implicated in behavior. Yet belief is not static: in real interactions, models are repeatedly presented with evidence for and against propositions. We ask a simple question that no prior work has addressed: what happens *inside* the model, over the course of a multi-turn confrontation, when its belief is challenged? We hypothesize that belief revision leaves a characteristic dynamical signature in activation space and that the shape of this trajectory—not just the endpoint—predicts whether the model genuinely updates or merely superficially complies while retaining a latent 'residual belief.' We introduce a lightweight methodology: (1) train a belief probe from prior work on true/false statements, (2) construct multi-turn dialogues that inject supporting or contradicting evidence about held-out propositions, and (3) read the projected belief score along the probe direction at each turn to trace belief trajectories. We taxonomize trajectory motifs (smooth update, abrupt overwrite, oscillation, sticky residual) and test whether motif identity predicts (a) whether the model's stated answer changes, (b) whether it reverts once evidence is removed, and (c) whether the change is sycophantic (evidence-independent). Causal steering experiments verify the residual belief is functional. Our results reframe belief in LLMs as a dynamical rather than static object and provide a cheap diagnostic for distinguishing genuine belief revision from surface compliance.
Experiments: 1. Belief probe construction: Using LLaMA-3-8B, Mistral-7B, and Gemma-2-9B, train mass-mean and logistic-regression belief probes on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than, and their negations) at the best-performing layer, following Marks & Tegmark. Validate probe accuracy on held-out statements.

2. Dialogue construction: Build a set of ~300 verifiable propositions (held out from probe training) each paired with a supporting evidence snippet, a contradicting evidence snippet, and a neutral filler. Construct multi-turn templates: (initial assertion) -> (evidence turn) -> (further evidence turns) -> (evidence-removal / re-query turn).

3. Belief trajectory extraction: At each dialogue turn, extract activations at the probe layer over the proposition tokens and project onto the belief direction, producing a scalar belief score per turn. Aggregate into per-example trajectories.

4. Trajectory taxonomy: Cluster trajectories (k-means / DTW-based clustering) into motifs; characterize motifs as smooth-update, abrupt-overwrite, oscillation, and sticky-residual using simple summary statistics (monotonicity, step size, reversion).

5. Behavioral prediction: Record the model's stated answer at each turn. Test whether motif/trajectory features predict (a) whether stated answer flips, (b) whether it reverts after evidence removal, using logistic regression; report AUROC vs. baselines (final-turn belief score only, output-token probability).

6. Sycophancy discrimination: Compare belief trajectories under genuinely correct vs. deliberately false 'authoritative' evidence. Test whether trajectory shape (e.g., large surface answer change but small internal belief change) separates sycophantic compliance from genuine revision. Metric: separation AUROC.

7. Residual-belief causal test: For sticky-residual examples where the model verbally agreed but retained internal belief, apply activation steering along the belief direction to amplify/suppress the residual and measure downstream effects (reversion rate, contradiction on a later re-query). Norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls.
8. Robustness: Repeat across the three model families and two probe methods; report consistency of motif taxonomy and predictive power.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The belief probe may itself be brittle to surface form (Haller et al. 2025), confounding trajectory measurements; we mitigate by using diverse propositions and reporting probe validation.
Trajectory motifs may not cluster cleanly, weakening the taxonomy; we report continuous trajectory features as a fallback that do not require discrete clusters.
Distinguishing genuine revision from sycophancy relies on our constructed correct/false evidence conditions, which may not fully capture natural sycophancy.
Effects may be model- or scale-dependent; findings on 7-9B models may not generalize to larger models, though academic-budget replication across three families provides reasonable coverage.
Causal steering results can be sensitive to intervention strength; we use norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls to guard against artifacts.

Name: provenance_weighted_belief
Title: Whom Do I Believe? Probing Provenance-Weighted Belief Integration in LLM Activations
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM encounters the same proposition asserted by sources of differing credibility, its internal belief representation does not merely track the assertion's content but integrates a separable, decodable 'provenance signal' whose weight on the belief direction reflects source credibility; this provenance-weighting is (a) linearly decodable, (b) causally manipulable independently of belief magnitude, and (c) predictive of whether the model rationally integrates or irrationally overweights salient/recent sources.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLM belief/truth directions are linearly encoded (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Bao et al. 2025) and context-sensitive (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024; Linear representations change over a conversation 2026; Accumulating Context Changes Beliefs 2025). Knowledge-source probing (Probing LMs on Their Knowledge Source 2024) distinguishes parametric vs. contextual knowledge as a binary. Source-framing work (Source framing triggers evaluation bias 2025; Attribution Bias in RAG 2024) documents behavioral biases toward source metadata. However, no work asks whether the *belief representation itself* carries a graded, separable provenance/credibility signal that is combined with content to form a credibility-weighted posterior, nor whether this provenance component is causally dissociable from belief magnitude. We move beyond binary PK-vs-CK and beyond behavioral bias measurement to a mechanistic, causal account of credibility-weighted belief integration in activation space.
Abstract: Large language models increasingly ingest assertions from heterogeneous sources of varying reliability, yet we lack a mechanistic account of how source credibility shapes a model's internal beliefs. Behavioral studies show LLM outputs are biased by source framing, and interpretability work shows belief truth-directions are context-sensitive, but no study characterizes whether the internal belief representation carries a graded, separable provenance signal reflecting how much the model trusts each source. We hypothesize that when the same proposition is asserted by sources of differing credibility (e.g., a domain expert, an anonymous forum, an explicitly unreliable source, or the user), the model's activations encode both (1) a belief-magnitude component and (2) a dissociable provenance/credibility component, and that the projection of belief onto the truth direction reflects a credibility-weighted integration of these signals. We test this with three interventions: (i) a decoding experiment training linear probes to recover source credibility and belief magnitude separately from held-out activations; (ii) an integration experiment measuring whether the belief score varies monotonically with assigned source credibility and whether it follows rational Bayesian-like combination when a source contradicts the model's parametric prior; and (iii) a causal experiment steering the provenance component up/down and measuring effects on stated belief, sycophantic over-trust of unreliable sources, and robustness under evidence removal. We compare rational integration against recency/salience baselines. Our results establish provenance-weighted belief as a distinct, manipulable internal structure and yield a cheap diagnostic for detecting when models irrationally overtrust unreliable sources.
Experiments: 1. Probe & direction setup: On LLaMA-3-8B, Mistral-7B, and Gemma-2-9B, train a standard belief/truth linear probe on true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations) at the best layer (Marks & Tegmark). Validate on held-out statements.

2. Stimulus construction: Build ~300 verifiable propositions held out from probe training. For each, create prompt templates that assert the proposition as attributed to sources spanning a credibility ladder: (a) named domain expert / peer-reviewed source, (b) reputable news, (c) unattributed user statement, (d) anonymous forum, (e) explicitly-flagged unreliable/known-liar source. Include both true and false versions of each proposition so content and source vary orthogonally.

3. Separable-decoding test: Extract activations over the proposition tokens for each (proposition, source) pair. Train linear probes to decode (i) source-credibility rank and (ii) belief magnitude. Test whether the two are decodable from near-orthogonal directions (measure cosine similarity of probe weight vectors, and cross-decoding accuracy) to establish separability. Report probe AUROC/accuracy vs. shuffled-label controls.

4. Integration curve: Project activations onto the belief direction and measure how belief score varies across the credibility ladder for (a) propositions consistent with the model's parametric prior and (b) propositions contradicting it. Fit the belief score against source credibility and against the model's zero-context parametric belief; test whether integration is monotonic in credibility and whether it approximates a credibility-weighted (Bayesian-like) combination. Compare against a recency/salience baseline that predicts belief tracks only the most recent/most emphatic assertion regardless of credibility.

5. Behavioral alignment: Record the model's stated answer and stated confidence for each condition; test whether the internal belief-score integration curve predicts stated-answer flips and confidence, with AUROC vs. a content-only baseline.

6. Causal steering: Using the recovered provenance direction (component of belief change attributable to credibility, orthogonalized against content), steer it up/down at inference on held-out unreliable-source items. Measure effects on (a) stated belief, (b) over-trust of the unreliable source (does suppressing provenance reduce sycophantic acceptance of flagged-unreliable false claims?), and (c) reversion after the assertion is removed. Use norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls.

7. Irrational-overtrust diagnostic: Define an over-trust score as the residual belief attributable to a low-credibility source beyond what rational integration predicts. Test across models and topics whether this diagnostic identifies conditions/models most susceptible to unreliable-source manipulation; correlate with behavioral susceptibility on adversarial misinformation prompts.

8. Robustness: Replicate across three model families, two probe methods (mass-mean, logistic regression), and paraphrased source-framing templates to test that provenance-weighting is not an artifact of surface phrasing.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The provenance and belief components may not be linearly separable; we report cross-decoding and orthogonality metrics and fall back on characterizing the joint representation if separability fails.
Source-credibility framing may act through surface lexical cues rather than a genuine credibility abstraction; we mitigate with paraphrased templates and orthogonal true/false variation.
Belief probes are known to be brittle to surface form; we validate probes and use diverse propositions.

Rational-integration comparison requires an operational Bayesian baseline whose assumptions (e.g., prior extraction from zero-context belief) may be imperfect; we report sensitivity to baseline specification.
Causal steering effects can be sensitive to intervention strength and layer; we use norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls.
Findings on 7-9B models may not generalize to frontier-scale models, though three-family replication provides reasonable coverage within an academic budget.

Name: epistemic_ownership_interference
Title: Whose Belief Is It? Disentangling Factual Truth from Attributed Belief and Measuring Epistemic Leakage in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM tracks a character who holds a belief it knows to be factually false, it maintains two functionally distinct latent quantities along a shared belief direction — a 'factual-truth' signal reflecting the model's own knowledge and an 'attributed-belief' signal reflecting the character's mental state — tagged by a separable 'epistemic-ownership' direction; the degree to which the factual-truth signal leaks into the attributed-belief readout (epistemic leakage) causally predicts false-belief ToM errors.
Related Work: Prior work shows belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024) and that self- vs. others' beliefs are separately decodable in attention heads and causally steerable (Zhu et al. 2024 'LMs Represent Beliefs of Self and Others'; Bortoletto et al. 2024 'Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations'). 'Language Models use Lookbacks to Track Beliefs' (2025) reverse-engineers the binding/visibility algorithm for character belief tracking. However, these works treat the character-belief probe as a readout of *who* holds a belief, and none isolates the *interference* between the model's own factual-truth signal and the attributed-belief signal, nor tests whether such epistemic leakage mechanistically causes the classic true-belief-easier-than-false-belief asymmetry. We introduce (a) an explicit 'epistemic-ownership' axis that tags a belief quantity as 'reality' vs. 'the character's', dissociated from belief valence, and (b) a per-example leakage metric that predicts and (via steering) causes false-belief errors. This moves from 'beliefs are decodable' to 'a specific representational confusion between reality and attributed mind causes ToM failure'.
Abstract: Language models can attribute beliefs to characters, yet they systematically fail more on false-belief scenarios — where a character's belief contradicts reality — than on true-belief ones. We hypothesize this asymmetry has a concrete representational cause: the model's own factual-truth signal contaminates its readout of the character's attributed belief. We propose that LLMs carry two functionally distinct quantities along their belief direction, one tracking reality (the model's knowledge) and one tracking a character's mental state, and that these are tagged by a separable 'epistemic-ownership' axis (reality vs. attributed). We formalize an epistemic-leakage metric: the extent to which the factual-truth value bleeds into the attributed-belief readout on a per-example basis. Using controlled false-belief stories with orthogonal manipulation of reality-value and character-belief-value, we (1) show reality and attributed-belief are separately decodable and that an ownership direction is near-orthogonal to belief valence; (2) demonstrate leakage is larger precisely for false-belief items; (3) show per-example leakage predicts the model's overt false-belief errors; and (4) causally reduce ToM errors by steering to suppress leakage (projecting out the reality component from the attributed-belief subspace) and increase errors by amplifying it, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls. Experiments span three model families and standard ToM benchmarks. Our results reframe ToM failure as an epistemic-source confusion in activation space and yield a cheap, targeted, training-free intervention that improves belief attribution.
Experiments: 1. Probe & direction setup: On LLaMA-3-8B, Mistral-7B, and Gemma-2-9B, train a belief-valence linear probe on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) at the best layer; validate on held-out statements.

2. Controlled ToM stimulus set: Construct ~400 short false-belief stories (Sally-Anne style, adapting CausalToM/BigToM templates) where the object's true final location (reality-value) and the character's believed location (attributed-belief-value) are independently manipulated to give a 2x2 design: true-belief-true, true-belief-false, false-belief (attributed contradicts reality), and control. For each story define a probe target token span both for 'what is actually true' and 'what does the character believe'.

3. Separable decoding: Extract activations at the belief layer over reality-query and character-query readout positions. Train linear probes to decode (i) reality-value and (ii) attributed-belief-value, and a third probe for epistemic-ownership (reality-frame vs. character-frame). Report decoding AUROC vs. shuffled-label controls, and cosine similarity between the ownership direction and the belief-valence direction to establish near-orthogonality.

4. Epistemic-leakage metric: For each example, define leakage as the component of the reality-value signal present in the attributed-belief readout after regressing out the true attributed-belief signal (e.g., projection of activations onto the reality direction measured at the character-belief readout position, normalized). Compare leakage distributions across the 2x2 conditions; predict leakage is largest for false-belief items (paired tests, effect sizes).

5. Behavioral prediction: Record the model's overt answer to the character-belief question. Test whether per-example leakage predicts false-belief errors via logistic regression; report AUROC vs. baselines (attributed-belief probe score only, output-token probability, story length).

6. Causal suppression (fix ToM): At inference on held-out false-belief items, project out the reality direction's contribution from the character-belief subspace at the readout position (leakage suppression) and measure change in false-belief accuracy. Compare to norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction ablations.

7. Causal amplification (break ToM): Add the reality direction into the attributed-belief readout on true-belief items and measure induced false-belief-style errors, verifying the leakage direction is functionally responsible rather than correlational.

8. Generalization: Evaluate the fitted leakage direction and suppression intervention on independent ToM benchmarks (BigToM forward-belief, ToMi) without refitting; report transfer accuracy gains. Repeat across the three model families and two probe methods (mass-mean, logistic regression) for robustness.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Reality and attributed-belief signals may not be cleanly separable at the same positions; we report cross-decoding and orthogonality metrics and fall back to characterizing a joint representation if separability fails.
Belief probes are brittle to surface form (Brittle Minds 2024); we validate probes, use paraphrased templates, and report per-template consistency.
The leakage metric depends on a linear projection assumption; nonlinear contamination could be missed, so we treat leakage as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.
Steering effects are sensitive to layer and intervention strength; we use norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls and sweep strengths.
Findings on 7-9B models may not generalize to frontier scale, though three-family replication and transfer to independent benchmarks provide reasonable coverage within an academic budget.

The causal amplification result could reflect general disruption rather than specific leakage; the norm-matched random-direction control and specificity of induced errors (false-belief-style vs. random) address this.

Name: belief_coherence_geometry
Title: Is the Belief Manifold Coherent? Testing Whether LLM Belief Geometry Obeys a Logical Algebra and Predicts Contradiction
Short Hypothesis: The scalar projections of an LLM's activations onto its belief/truth direction for logically related propositions (P, ¬P, P∧Q, P∨Q, P→Q) approximately satisfy an internal probabilistic-logical algebra; the per-example magnitude of violation of these coherence constraints is a latent 'incoherence' signal that predicts, and causally drives, the model's behavioral self-contradictions—beyond what any single belief probe readout reveals.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs answer inconsistently across logically related queries and fixes this with external symbolic memory or losses (BeliefBank 2021; REFLEX 2023; Neuro-Symbolic Consistency 2024; IS-A transitivity, Lin 2022; Conceptual Consistency 2022). Interpretability work shows a linear truth direction (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Burns et al. 2022) that generalizes across logical transformations (Geometry of Truth generalization 2025) and is context-sensitive and a causal mediator of NLI (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024). However, prior work treats logical consistency behaviorally OR shows a single probe *classifies* each proposition well; none tests whether the *geometry itself*—the set of projections across a family of logically related propositions—forms a coherent algebra (e.g., proj(P)+proj(¬P)≈const, proj(P∧Q)≤min(proj(P),proj(Q))), whether the residual violation is a distinct latent quantity, and whether that latent incoherence predicts and causally produces behavioral contradiction. We move from 'the probe generalizes' to 'the belief manifold has (im)perfect internal coherence structure that mechanistically causes self-contradiction'.
Abstract: Large language models linearly encode whether they 'believe' a proposition, yet they routinely contradict themselves across logically related questions. Prior work fixes such contradictions with external symbolic memory, or shows that a single truth direction classifies individual propositions and generalizes across logical forms. We ask a different, geometric question: does the *set* of belief-direction projections across a family of logically related propositions obey an internal logical algebra, and if not, does the size of the violation predict and cause behavioral contradiction? We construct families of atomic and compound propositions (P, ¬P, P∧Q, P∨Q, P→Q) with controlled ground-truth, project their activations onto a fixed belief direction, and test whether the projections satisfy coherence constraints analogous to probabilistic-logical laws (negation complementarity, conjunction/disjunction bounds, entailment monotonicity). We define a per-family scalar 'incoherence' as the aggregate constraint violation. We then test three claims: (1) belief geometry is partially but imperfectly coherent, with violation patterns depending on connective, layer, and model scale; (2) per-family incoherence predicts the model's behavioral self-contradictions across the same propositions, beyond individual probe scores; and (3) steering activations to reduce a targeted violation (e.g., enforcing negation complementarity) causally reduces behavioral contradiction, while amplifying it induces contradiction. Experiments span three model families, two probe methods, and held-out logical templates, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls. Our results recast logical consistency as a measurable, manipulable geometric property of the belief manifold and yield a cheap, training-free contradiction diagnostic and repair.
Experiments: 1. Belief direction setup: On LLaMA-3-8B, Mistral-7B, and Gemma-2-9B, fit a fixed belief/truth direction using mass-mean and logistic-regression probes on standard atomic true/false datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and their negations; Marks & Tegmark) at the best layer; validate accuracy on held-out atomic statements. Freeze this single direction for all subsequent projections.

2. Logical-family stimulus construction: Build ~400 proposition families. Each family shares atomic components P (and where needed Q) with known truth values and instantiates a fixed set of logical forms: P, ¬P, P∧Q, P∨Q, P→Q (and ¬(P∧Q) etc.), across the 2×2 truth-value grid for (P,Q). Use paraphrase templates so surface form varies while logic is fixed. Reserve a held-out set of logical templates for generalization.

3. Geometric coherence measurement: For each proposition, extract activations at the belief layer over the readout span and project onto the frozen belief direction, giving a scalar b(·). Optionally map projections to a [0,1] 'belief mass' via a monotone calibration fit on atomic true/false. Test three coherence laws: (a) negation complementarity |b(P)+b(¬P)−c|; (b) conjunction/disjunction bounds (b(P∧Q)≤min(b(P),b(Q)) and b(P∨Q)≥max(b(P),b(Q))); (c) entailment monotonicity (if P entails H then b(H)≥b(P)). Report per-law violation distributions vs. shuffled-direction and random-direction controls; break down by connective, layer, and model scale.

4. Incoherence as a distinct signal: Define per-family incoherence as the aggregate normalized violation across laws. Test whether incoherence is not merely explained by low individual probe confidence (regress out mean/variance of individual b scores; report residual structure) and whether it varies systematically with epistemic familiarity of the atomic content.

5. Behavioral contradiction prediction: Query the model for yes/no answers to each proposition in the family; compute a behavioral contradiction score (number of logically impossible answer combinations). Test whether per-family geometric incoherence predicts behavioral contradiction via logistic/linear regression; report AUROC/R^2 vs. baselines (mean individual probe score, output-token confidence, family length).

6. Causal repair (reduce contradiction): For families with a targeted violation (e.g., negation complementarity), apply a training-free activation edit that projects the compound/negated proposition's representation to satisfy the constraint relative to its atomic components (i.e., steer along the belief direction to restore complementarity). Measure change in behavioral contradiction and answer accuracy. Compare to norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction edits.

7. Causal induction (break coherence): On coherent families, add the belief direction to specific propositions to deliberately violate a law and measure whether behavioral contradiction is induced, verifying the geometric constraint is functionally responsible rather than correlational.

8. Generalization and robustness: Evaluate the incoherence metric and repair intervention on held-out logical templates and an independent consistency benchmark (BeliefBank constraints) without refitting. Replicate across three model families, two probe methods, and multiple layers; report consistency of the coherence-law violation profile and predictive power.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The belief direction may not linearly support a genuine probabilistic algebra; projections might not map to coherent belief masses, in which case we report the geometry as sub-probabilistic and treat coherence laws as qualitative bounds rather than exact equalities.

Belief probes are brittle to surface form (Brittle Minds 2024; context-sensitivity 2024); we mitigate with paraphrase templates, orthogonal truth-value variation, and per-template consistency reporting.
Compound propositions may be read out at different token positions than atomic ones, confounding comparisons; we standardize readout spans and report position-sensitivity analyses.
Incoherence may partly reduce to individual-probe uncertainty; we explicitly regress out individual scores and report residual predictive power.
Causal edits are sensitive to layer and strength; we sweep strengths and use norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, and check that repair does not merely degrade accuracy.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and transfer to an independent benchmark provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: epistemic_state_geometry
Title: Ignorance, Error, or Delusion? A Three-State Geometry of LLM Belief that Separates Abstainable Mistakes from Confident Delusions
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's internal belief for a proposition is not one-dimensional (true<->false) but occupies a two-axis epistemic space combining a truth/belief-valence axis with a near-orthogonal knowledge-awareness (know/don't-know) axis; false answers split into two geometrically distinct classes—'abstainable errors' where the don't-know axis is engaged (the model internally represents its own ignorance) and 'delusions' where a false proposition is mislocated into the confidently-known region—and this per-example 'epistemic misplacement' causally predicts and drives whether the model hallucinates confidently versus abstains.
Related Work: Prior work linearly decodes truth/belief (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth Neurons 2025; context-sensitive truth directions 2024) and, separately, models knowledge-awareness / ignorance: entity-recognition directions that gate refusal vs. hallucination (Ferrando et al. 2024 'Do I Know This Entity?'), (un)answerability encoding (Slobodkin et al. 2023), epistemic-vs-aleatoric uncertainty (Distinguishing the Knowable from the Unknowable 2024; To Believe or Not 2024), and verbal-vs-semantic uncertainty as a linear feature (Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty 2025). 'Delusions of Large Language Models' (2025) behaviorally identifies high-confidence hallucinations but offers no mechanistic geometry. Ignorance-awareness fine-tuning (SEAT 2025) preserves abstention but does not characterize its representation relative to belief valence. Crucially, no prior work (a) jointly places belief-valence and knowledge-awareness as two axes of a single epistemic space, (b) shows that false answers partition into abstainable-error vs. delusion regions of that space, or (c) defines and causally tests an 'epistemic misplacement' quantity that converts one into the other. We move from 'truth is decodable' and 'ignorance is decodable' (studied in isolation) to a unified two-axis geometry whose structure mechanistically distinguishes recoverable mistakes from delusions.
Abstract: Large language models sometimes admit ignorance, sometimes make correctable mistakes, and sometimes assert falsehoods with unshakable confidence ('delusions'). We ask whether these outcomes are geometrically distinct in the model's activation space. We hypothesize that belief is organized along two near-orthogonal axes: a belief-valence axis (does the model represent the proposition as true or false) and a knowledge-awareness axis (does the model represent that it does or does not know the answer). Under this view, a wrong answer is not simply low truth-projection: 'abstainable errors' engage the don't-know axis (the model internally flags its ignorance and could refuse), whereas 'delusions' are false propositions mislocated into the confidently-known region of the plane. We formalize a per-example 'epistemic misplacement' metric—how far a false proposition sits from the ignorance region toward the confidently-known region—and test three claims across three model families and standard factual QA. First, belief-valence and knowledge-awareness are separately decodable and near-orthogonal, and false answers split into two clusters in this plane. Second, epistemic misplacement predicts, per example, whether the model will hallucinate confidently versus abstain, beyond truth-probe score or output confidence. Third, causal steering along the knowledge-awareness axis converts delusions into abstentions (and vice versa) with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, verifying the axes are functional and dissociable. Our results recast confident hallucination as a specific misplacement in a two-axis epistemic geometry and yield a cheap, training-free delusion detector and a targeted intervention that trades false confidence for calibrated abstention.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup: On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit (a) a belief-valence direction from standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) and (b) a knowledge-awareness direction from contrastive known-vs-unknown entity/question sets (following 'Do I Know This Entity?' and (un)answerability constructions: questions the model reliably answers correctly vs. questions about non-existent/unanswerable entities). Fit both with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out items.

2. Orthogonality & two-axis structure: Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding accuracy between the belief-valence and knowledge-awareness directions to establish near-orthogonality (report vs. shuffled-label controls). Project a large held-out QA set (TriviaQA/NaturalQuestions short-answer + PopQA long-tail entities) onto the two-axis plane and visualize where correct answers, abstentions, and wrong answers land.

3. Error partition test: Among wrong answers, test whether they form two clusters in the plane—one near the ignorance/don't-know region (abstainable errors) and one in the confidently-known-but-false region (delusions). Cluster with a 2-component GMM on the two projections; report separation (silhouette) and validate that the ignorance-region cluster corresponds to items the model abstains on when given an explicit 'you may say I don't know' option, while the confident-false cluster corresponds to items it re-asserts.

4. Epistemic-misplacement metric: Define per-example misplacement as the signed distance of a (false) proposition's projection along the knowledge-awareness axis away from the empirical ignorance region toward the confidently-known region (calibrated on the known/unknown fit). Report distributions for abstainable errors vs. delusions.

5. Behavioral prediction: Record whether the model, on each item, (a) hallucinates confidently, (b) abstains when abstention is allowed, or (c) is correct. Test whether misplacement predicts confident-hallucination vs. abstention via logistic regression; report AUROC vs. baselines (belief-valence probe score alone, output-token confidence/entropy, verbal-uncertainty feature).

6. Delusion detector: Frame delusion detection (confident hallucination) as a downstream task and compare the two-axis misplacement detector against strong internal-state baselines (P(IK) probe, semantic-entropy proxy, verbal-uncertainty feature). Report AUROC, ECE of the resulting abstention policy, and accuracy-coverage curves.

7. Causal delusion->abstention steering: On held-out delusion items, steer activations along the knowledge-awareness (don't-know) direction and measure whether the model switches from confident false assertion to abstention/refusal; measure effect on overall accuracy and false-confidence rate. Compare to norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls, sweeping strengths.

8. Causal abstention->delusion steering (specificity): On abstainable-error and unanswerable items, steer along the known direction and test whether it induces confident false assertions, confirming the axis functionally gates confident hallucination rather than generically degrading output.

9. Robustness & generalization: Replicate across the three model families and two probe methods; test transfer of the fitted axes and misplacement detector to an independent factual benchmark (e.g., a held-out slice of PopQA / TruthfulQA) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The belief-valence and knowledge-awareness axes may not be cleanly orthogonal or separable; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, and fall back on characterizing a joint (possibly entangled) two-axis representation if strict orthogonality fails.

The known/unknown contrastive fit may capture surface familiarity rather than genuine self-knowledge; we mitigate with diverse entity types, paraphrase templates, and validation against measured answer correctness rather than assumed familiarity.

The error partition (abstainable vs. delusion) relies on operationalizing abstention via an explicit 'I don't know' option, which may not perfectly match a natural notion of delusion; we report sensitivity to the abstention prompt and cross-check with confidence measures.
Belief/truth probes are known to be brittle to context and surface form; we use paraphrase templates, orthogonal true/false variation, and report per-template consistency.

Causal steering results are sensitive to layer and strength; we use norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and check that delusion->abstention steering does not merely collapse the model into always abstaining (measure accuracy retention on knowable items).
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and transfer to an independent benchmark provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: assertoric_force_axis
Title: Believing vs. Merely Entertaining: Testing Whether LLMs Encode a Separable Assertoric-Force Axis or Collapse Supposition into Belief (Spinozan Default)
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM processes a proposition under a suppositional frame ('Suppose that...', 'Imagine...', 'In a story...', 'It might be that...') rather than a plain assertion, its internal belief-valence direction does NOT by default distinguish entertaining a proposition from believing it; instead entertainment is encoded by a separable, near-orthogonal 'assertoric-force' axis, and the degree to which supposition leaks onto the belief-valence direction (a 'Spinozan default' signature) causally predicts whether the model erroneously treats merely-supposed false content as if it were factually true.
Related Work: Interpretability work establishes a linear truth/belief direction (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Geometry of Truth 2023) that is context-sensitive (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024) and can be pushed by premises. Belief-tracking and ToM work separates self/other beliefs (Zhu et al. 2024; Lookbacks 2025), and fact-vs-counterfactual competition traces how in-context content overrides parametric facts (Ortu et al. 2024). Representational Stability (2025) shows fictional vs synthetic content differs in stability. None of these asks the classic cognitive-science question of propositional attitude / assertoric force: do models represent *entertaining* a proposition (supposition, hypothetical, fiction, modal 'might') as distinct from *believing/asserting* it? Cognitive neuroscience (Spinozan 'unbelieving' in IFG, 2022; modal displacement, 2020) shows humans default to belief-on-comprehension and require active 'unbelieving'. We uniquely (a) introduce an 'assertoric-force' axis dissociating entertainment from belief-valence, (b) define a per-example 'Spinozan leakage' metric measuring how much supposed content is encoded as believed, and (c) causally test whether this leakage drives factual contamination from hypothetical/fictional context. This moves from 'context shifts the truth probe' and 'facts vs counterfactuals compete' to a mechanistic account of *propositional attitude* representation.
Abstract: Humans can entertain a proposition—suppose it, imagine it, treat it as fiction, or flag it as merely possible—without believing it. Cognitive neuroscience suggests we may even default to believing what we comprehend, requiring active 'unbelieving.' We ask whether large language models make an analogous distinction internally. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs linearly encode whether a proposition is true (belief-valence) and that this direction is context-sensitive, but no work asks whether models represent the *attitude* toward a proposition: believing versus merely entertaining it. We hypothesize that (1) LLMs carry a separable, near-orthogonal 'assertoric-force' axis distinguishing asserted from supposed/hypothetical/fictional/modal content, (2) but the belief-valence direction exhibits a 'Spinozan default'—supposed content partially reads as believed—quantifiable as a per-example leakage metric, and (3) this leakage causally predicts and drives factual contamination, where merely-supposed false content is treated as fact on later queries. We test this by contrasting matched propositions across framing conditions (plain assertion, suppositional, hypothetical, fictional, modal, explicit negation-of-supposition) and probing both the belief-valence and force axes. We measure orthogonality and separability, characterize how much supposition leaks onto belief-valence per framing, and connect leakage to behavioral contamination on downstream factual queries. Causal steering along the force axis tests whether amplifying 'entertainment' quarantines supposed content (reducing contamination) and suppressing it induces belief-like contamination, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls. Experiments span three model families and two probe methods. Our results recast a classic propositional-attitude question mechanistically and yield a cheap diagnostic and training-free intervention for the failure mode where LLMs 'believe' what they were only asked to imagine.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup: On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a belief-valence direction from standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomic statements. Freeze this direction.

2. Attitude stimulus construction: Build ~400 verifiable propositions (both true and false variants), each embedded in six matched framing conditions holding the propositional content fixed: (a) plain assertion ('X is the capital of Y'), (b) suppositional ('Suppose that X is the capital of Y'), (c) hypothetical/conditional ('If X were the capital of Y...'), (d) fictional ('In a story, X is the capital of Y'), (e) modal ('It might be that X is the capital of Y'), (f) explicit disbelief-of-supposition ('Imagine, though it's false, that X is the capital of Y'). Use paraphrase templates so surface form varies while attitude is fixed; reserve held-out framing templates.

3. Force-axis fitting and orthogonality: Train a linear probe to decode assertoric force (asserted vs entertained) from activations over the proposition span, pooling across framing conditions and orthogonal to content truth-value. Report force-probe AUROC vs shuffled-label controls, cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the force axis and the frozen belief-valence axis to establish near-orthogonality/separability.

4. Spinozan-leakage metric: For each (proposition, framing) pair, project activations onto the frozen belief-valence direction and measure how far the belief-valence readout for a *supposed* proposition sits relative to its plain-assertion baseline (leakage = fraction of the assertion-level belief signal retained under supposition, calibrated per model). Compare leakage distributions across framing conditions (b–f), across true vs false content, and across epistemic familiarity (following Representational Stability), testing the prediction that supposition leaks substantially onto belief-valence (Spinozan default) and that modal/negation-of-supposition frames leak least.

5. Behavioral contamination measurement: After each framed prompt, query the model on a downstream factual question whose correct answer conflicts with the merely-supposed (false) content (e.g., 'Setting the story aside, what is actually the capital of Y?'). Score contamination as the rate at which the model asserts the supposed-false content as fact. Test whether per-example Spinozan-leakage predicts contamination via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence probe score alone, output-token confidence, framing-condition identity, prompt length).

6. Causal quarantine (reduce contamination): On held-out supposed-false items, steer activations along the assertoric-force (entertainment) direction and measure whether the model better quarantines supposed content, reducing downstream factual contamination while preserving accuracy on genuinely factual controls. Compare to norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction steering; sweep strengths.

7. Causal induction (specificity): On plain-assertion or firmly-entertained items, suppress the force axis (push toward 'asserted') and test whether it induces belief-like contamination and confident false assertions, confirming the axis functionally gates attitude rather than generically degrading output.

8. Robustness and generalization: Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; test transfer of the fitted force axis, leakage metric, and quarantine intervention to held-out framing templates and an independent set of propositions without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The belief-valence and assertoric-force axes may not be cleanly separable; we report cosine similarity and cross-decoding and fall back to characterizing a joint (possibly entangled) representation if strict orthogonality fails.

Framing manipulations may act through surface lexical cues ('suppose', 'imagine') rather than a genuine attitude abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, orthogonal true/false variation, and transfer to held-out templates.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, and report per-template consistency.
The Spinozan-leakage metric relies on a linear projection and a per-model calibration; nonlinear contamination could be missed, so we treat leakage as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.
Behavioral contamination depends on how the downstream 'setting aside' query is worded; we report sensitivity to multiple query phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify quarantine does not merely make the model refuse or degrade factual accuracy on controls.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and held-out transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: temporal_validity_belief_axis
Title: When Was It True? Testing Whether LLMs Encode a Temporal-Validity Axis or Conflate Belief Revision with Belief Update
Short Hypothesis: For time-varying facts, an LLM's belief representation does not merely encode 'true vs. false' but carries a separable, near-orthogonal 'temporal-validity' axis that tags whether a proposition is currently-true, formerly-true (stale), or never-true; the degree to which formerly-true facts leak onto the plain belief-valence direction (a 'revision-update conflation' signature) causally predicts whether the model anachronistically asserts outdated facts as currently true.
Related Work: A classic AI/philosophy distinction separates belief revision (the world is unchanged; only knowledge changed) from belief update (the world itself changed over time) (Katsuno & Mendelzon 1991; Friedman & Halpern 1999). Interpretability work shows belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023) and that specific 'Temporal Heads' recall time-specific facts (2025), that time is hierarchically represented and log-compressed around a subjective 'now' (The Other Mind 2025), and that dynamic facts cause greater intra-memory conflict (DynamicQA 2024; Analysing the Residual Stream under Knowledge Conflicts 2024). Temporal knowledge-editing work (History Matters 2023; EvoEdit 2025) and drift benchmarks (Temporal Wiki 2025; Chronos 2026) study behavioral updating and editing. However, no work asks whether the belief representation itself is time-indexed: whether a formerly-true fact is internally tagged as 'no longer true' along a separable temporal-validity axis, or whether the model conflates revision with update by keeping stale facts in the confidently-true region. We move from 'facts can be edited' and 'truth is decodable' to a mechanistic account of whether LLMs represent the temporal validity window of a belief, and whether conflation of revision and update causally drives anachronistic assertions.
Abstract: A fact can be true now, have been true in the past but false now, or never have been true. Philosophy and AI distinguish revising a belief (correcting an error about an unchanged world) from updating a belief (registering that the world itself changed). We ask whether large language models make an analogous internal distinction. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs linearly encode whether a proposition is true and that dedicated heads recall time-specific facts, but no work asks whether the belief representation is time-indexed: does a formerly-true fact sit in a distinct region of activation space, tagged as 'no longer true,' or is it conflated with a currently-true belief? We hypothesize that (1) belief is organized along a plain belief-valence axis and a separable, near-orthogonal 'temporal-validity' axis distinguishing currently-true, formerly-true (stale), and never-true propositions; (2) models exhibit a 'revision-update conflation' signature whereby formerly-true facts leak substantial belief-valence signal (they read as still true), quantified per example; and (3) this conflation causally predicts and drives anachronistic assertions where outdated facts are stated as currently true. Using datasets of time-varying facts with known validity windows, we fit both axes, measure orthogonality and separability, characterize per-example conflation, and connect it to behavioral anachronism. Causal steering along the temporal-validity axis tests whether pushing stale facts toward 'formerly-true' suppresses anachronistic assertions (and amplifying conflation induces them), with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, across three model families. Our results recast a classic revision-vs-update distinction mechanistically and yield a cheap diagnostic and training-free intervention for outdated-fact hallucination.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup: On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a belief-valence direction from standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomic statements. Freeze this direction.

2. Temporal-validity stimulus construction: Build ~400 time-varying fact families using Wikidata-derived relations with explicit validity intervals (e.g., 'X plays for club Y', 'Z is head of state of country W', 'company C's CEO is P'). For each relation instantiate three matched classes as of the model's subjective 'now': currently-true (the value holding today), formerly-true/stale (a value that held in a past interval but is now false), and never-true (a plausible but always-false value). Use paraphrase templates so surface form varies while temporal class is fixed; reserve held-out relations/templates. Include time-anchored variants ('As of 2010, ...', 'Currently, ...') to test time-conditioning.

3. Temporal-validity axis fitting and orthogonality: Train a linear probe to decode temporal-validity class (currently-true vs. formerly-true vs. never-true) from activations over the proposition span, controlling for content. Report probe accuracy/AUROC vs. shuffled-label controls, and cosine similarity plus cross-decoding between the temporal-validity axis and the frozen belief-valence axis to establish near-orthogonality/separability. Localize whether the axis co-occurs with previously reported Temporal Heads by comparing layers/positions.

4. Revision-update conflation metric: For each formerly-true (stale) proposition, project activations onto the frozen belief-valence direction and measure how far its belief-valence readout sits relative to the currently-true baseline and the never-true baseline (conflation = fraction of currently-true belief signal retained by a stale fact, calibrated per model). Compare conflation distributions across relation types, recency of the stale interval (predicting more recent stale facts leak more), and epistemic popularity. Test the prediction that stale facts leak substantially onto belief-valence (revision-update conflation) while explicit time-anchoring reduces leakage.

5. Behavioral anachronism measurement: Query the model on present-tense factual questions whose currently-correct answer differs from the stale value (e.g., 'Which club does X currently play for?'). Score anachronism as the rate at which the model asserts the stale value as currently true. Test whether per-example conflation predicts anachronistic assertion via logistic regression; report AUROC vs. baselines (belief-valence probe score alone, output-token confidence/entropy, relation type, fact popularity, recency).

6. Causal correction (reduce anachronism): On held-out stale items, steer activations along the temporal-validity axis toward 'formerly-true' and measure whether the model better withholds/updates the stale value, reducing anachronistic assertions while preserving accuracy on genuinely currently-true controls. Compare to norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction steering; sweep strengths.

7. Causal induction (specificity): On currently-true items, steer toward retaining stale content (amplify conflation) and test whether it induces anachronistic-style errors and confident outdated assertions, confirming the axis functionally gates temporal validity rather than generically degrading output.

8. Robustness and generalization: Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; test transfer of the fitted temporal-validity axis, conflation metric, and correction intervention to held-out relations/templates and an independent time-varying benchmark (e.g., DynamicQA or a Temporal-Wiki slice) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice and to the model's subjective reference year.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The belief-valence and temporal-validity axes may not be cleanly separable; we report cosine similarity and cross-decoding and fall back to characterizing a joint (possibly entangled) representation if strict orthogonality fails.

Temporal-class labels depend on the model's pretraining cutoff and subjective 'now'; a fact labeled 'currently-true' by us may be stale for the model. We mitigate by calibrating the subjective reference year (following The Other Mind 2025) and by using facts with unambiguous validity windows well before the cutoff for the formerly-true class.

The temporal-validity signal might reflect surface cues (dates, tense) rather than a genuine temporal abstraction; we mitigate with paraphrase templates, matched tense, and transfer to held-out relations.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, and report per-template consistency.
The conflation metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear contamination could be missed, so we treat conflation as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.
Behavioral anachronism depends on how present-tense queries are worded; we report sensitivity to multiple query phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify correction does not merely make the model refuse or degrade accuracy on currently-true controls.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and held-out/independent-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: latent_introspective_gap
Title: Knowing That It Doesn't Say What It Knows: A Latent Introspective-Gap Signal for LLM Belief-Report Mismatch
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM's stated answer diverges from its internal belief representation (a probe-query disagreement), the model carries a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'introspective-gap' signal that flags the impending mismatch before generation; this signal is decodable and causally usable to (a) predict per-example belief-report mismatch and (b) close the gap via steering, even though the model does not spontaneously verbalize the mismatch.
Related Work: Query-probe disagreement work (Liu et al. 'Cognitive Dissonance' 2023) taxonomizes why LLM outputs diverge from internal truthfulness probes (confabulation, deception, heterogeneity) but treats the belief probe and the output as two independent readouts and never asks whether the model *internally represents* the fact that its report will mismatch its belief. Introspection work (Anthropic 'Emergent Introspective Awareness' 2025; 'Feeling the Strength but Not the Source' 2025; 'Latent Introspection' 2026; 'LMs Fail to Introspect About Language' 2025) studies whether models can *report* injected or perturbed internal states, using artificial concept injection; they do not study natural belief-report mismatch nor define a latent mismatch-flag signal. Metacognition/self-knowledge work ('Trust Your Feelings' 2024, ESMA 2026) fine-tunes models to express what they know, but is behavioral and does not isolate a representational mismatch signal or test it causally against the belief direction. We uniquely (a) define a per-example 'introspective-gap' direction distinct from the belief-valence direction, capturing whether the *forthcoming report* will match the belief; (b) show it predicts mismatch before generation; and (c) causally test whether steering along it closes the belief-report gap. This moves from 'probes and queries disagree' and 'models can/can't report injected states' to 'the model latently represents its own report-belief inconsistency and this representation is functional.'
Abstract: Large language models sometimes assert things their own internal representations indicate they do not believe, and sometimes hedge on things they internally hold true. Prior work catalogues these probe-query disagreements and asks whether models can report artificially injected internal states, but no work asks a sharper question: does the model itself internally represent that its forthcoming answer will diverge from its belief? We hypothesize that beyond a belief-valence direction, LLMs carry a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'introspective-gap' signal that flags impending belief-report mismatch prior to generation. We test three claims across three model families and standard factual/true-false datasets. First, using a fixed belief probe and the model's own generated answers, we label each example as report-consistent or report-mismatched, then train a linear probe to decode the impending mismatch from mid-layer activations at the final prompt position; we measure its accuracy and its orthogonality to the belief-valence direction. Second, we test whether this introspective-gap signal predicts mismatch per example better than baselines (belief-probe margin, output entropy, verbalized confidence), and whether it dissociates mismatch subtypes (confabulation vs. suppression). Third, we causally steer along the introspective-gap direction to close the gap—making the model voice its internal belief—and along the belief direction as a control, using norm-matched and shuffled-direction ablations. We also test whether prompting the model to introspect activates the same direction, linking latent representation to (failed) self-report. Our results establish an internally represented, functional self-monitor for belief-report consistency, yielding a cheap honesty diagnostic and a training-free repair.
Experiments: 1. Belief-direction & data setup: On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a belief-valence direction with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes on standard true/false datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) at the best layer; validate on held-out atomic statements. Freeze this direction.

2. Mismatch labeling: On a held-out mix of factual QA (TriviaQA/PopQA short-answer) and true/false statements, for each example (a) read the belief-probe score/margin at the readout span and (b) elicit the model's actual generated yes/no or short answer. Label each example report-consistent or report-mismatched (probe says believe-true but model denies, or probe says believe-false but model asserts). Following the confabulation/deception/heterogeneity taxonomy, sub-label mismatches by probe-margin sign and confidence.

3. Introspective-gap probe: Extract activations at mid layers at the final prompt position (before answer generation). Train a linear probe to predict impending mismatch (consistent vs. mismatch). Report AUROC vs. shuffled-label controls; report cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the introspective-gap direction and the frozen belief-valence direction to establish near-orthogonality/separability.

4. Predictive comparison: Test whether the introspective-gap probe predicts per-example mismatch beyond baselines: belief-probe margin, output-token entropy, verbalized confidence, and answer length. Report AUROC and calibration (ECE), and incremental AUROC from adding the gap signal in a logistic model.

5. Subtype dissociation: Test whether the gap direction (or a small gap subspace) separates mismatch subtypes—confabulation (model over-asserts beyond weak belief) vs. suppression (model hedges/denies despite strong belief). Report cluster separation (silhouette) and per-subtype decoding.

6. Causal gap-closing: On held-out mismatch examples, steer activations along the introspective-gap direction and measure whether the model's stated answer moves toward its internal belief (mismatch rate drop), while accuracy on report-consistent controls is preserved. Compare to steering along the belief-valence direction (control) and to norm-matched random and shuffled-direction ablations; sweep strengths.

7. Causal gap-inducing (specificity): On report-consistent examples, steer opposite along the gap direction and test whether it induces belief-report mismatch (model says the opposite of its probe belief), confirming the direction functionally gates report-belief consistency rather than generically degrading output.

8. Link to self-report/introspection: Prompt the model to explicitly introspect ('Does your answer reflect what you actually believe? Are you confident?') and test whether the latent gap signal predicts these self-reports, and whether models fail to verbalize the gap even when it is strongly present in activations (quantify the verbalization failure rate).

9. Robustness/generalization: Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted gap probe and gap-closing intervention to an independent dataset (TruthfulQA / a held-out PopQA slice) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The introspective-gap signal may be entangled with the belief-valence direction or simply reflect belief-probe uncertainty; we report orthogonality, cross-decoding, and incremental predictive power over the belief margin, and treat entanglement as a reportable finding if separability fails.

Mismatch labels depend on the fidelity of the belief probe, which is brittle to surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, restrict to high-margin probe cases for cleaner labels, and report label-noise sensitivity.

The gap direction might capture generic answer-uncertainty rather than a genuine self-monitor; the baseline comparisons (entropy, verbalized confidence) and the subtype-dissociation test address this, and the causal specificity test guards against generic degradation.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify gap-closing does not merely make the model flip all answers or refuse.

The introspection-prompt link (experiment 8) risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we control by comparing gap-signal-predicted self-reports against cross-model baselines as in prior introspection critiques.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: categorical_vs_graded_belief
Title: Two Kinds of Belief: Disentangling Categorical Acceptance from Graded Credence in LLM Activations
Short Hypothesis: LLMs do not represent belief on a single continuum; instead, mirroring the philosophy/neuroscience distinction between categorical belief (all-or-nothing acceptance of a proposition as true) and graded belief (a continuous credence/subjective probability), LLMs carry two separable, near-orthogonal internal quantities—a categorical-acceptance axis and a graded-credence axis—and the mismatch between them (e.g., high credence but no categorical acceptance, or categorical acceptance decoupled from credence) causally predicts characteristic behavioral failures such as overconfident assertion of low-credence claims and unwarranted hedging on accepted facts.
Related Work: Interpretability work fits a single linear truth/belief direction (Marks & Tegmark 2023) and treats its scalar projection as a graded confidence, and separately fits correctness/confidence directions (No Answer Needed 2025; The Confidence Manifold 2026), verbal vs. semantic uncertainty as a linear feature (Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty 2025), and calibration directions (Calibration Across Layers 2025). Cognitive Dissonance (2023) studies probe-vs-query disagreement but treats truthfulness as one quantity. Crucially, none tests the classic philosophical/neuroscientific dichotomy between categorical (binary) belief—accepting a proposition outright as a fact—and graded belief (credence), which cognitive science treats as convergent yet dissociable (Neural Convergence of Graded and Binary Belief 2025; The truth is in there 2024). All prior LLM work collapses these into one axis, implicitly assuming the truth-direction projection IS credence. We uniquely (a) operationally separate categorical acceptance from graded credence, (b) test whether they are two near-orthogonal axes in activation space, and (c) show that their mismatch causally drives overconfident assertion and unwarranted hedging. This moves from 'there is one truth/confidence direction' to 'there are two psychologically distinct belief quantities whose interaction governs behavior.'
Abstract: Philosophy and cognitive neuroscience distinguish two kinds of belief: categorical belief—an all-or-nothing acceptance of a proposition as true—and graded belief, a continuous credence or subjective probability. Interpretability research on large language models has ignored this distinction, treating the scalar projection onto a single truth/belief direction as if it were the model's credence. We ask whether LLMs instead represent categorical acceptance and graded credence as two separable internal quantities, and whether their interaction governs behavior. We hypothesize that LLMs carry (1) a categorical-acceptance axis that encodes whether a proposition is treated as flatly true/false, and (2) a near-orthogonal graded-credence axis that encodes a continuous degree of belief, and that the mismatch between them (categorical acceptance decoupled from low credence, or high credence without acceptance) causally predicts overconfident assertion of shaky claims and unwarranted hedging on facts. We fit both axes using stimuli that orthogonally vary categorical status (clear facts/falsehoods vs. genuinely uncertain propositions) and credence level (via graded-probability framings and objectively varying evidence strength), measure their orthogonality and separability via cross-decoding, and characterize per-example categorical–graded mismatch. We connect mismatch to behavioral overconfidence/hedging, and causally steer each axis independently—testing whether nudging credence without changing acceptance shifts hedging language while leaving asserted content intact, and vice versa—with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, across three model families. Our results recast a foundational belief distinction mechanistically and yield a cheap diagnostic and training-free intervention for overconfident hallucination.
Experiments: 1. Axis setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a categorical-acceptance axis using clearly-true vs. clearly-false factual statements (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) at the best layer with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes; validate on held-out atomic statements. Separately fit a graded-credence axis using propositions annotated with continuous credence targets: (a) claims framed with explicit probability language ('there is a 20%/50%/80% chance that...'), and (b) real uncertain propositions whose empirical answer-correctness rate (measured by sampling the model) provides a continuous credence label. Fit credence via linear regression (not classification) onto activations.

2. Orthogonality & separability. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the categorical-acceptance axis and the graded-credence axis to test near-orthogonality. Critically test the dissociation predicted by the two-type view: among genuinely uncertain propositions (no categorical acceptance), does credence still vary continuously along the credence axis while the acceptance axis stays neutral? And among clear facts, is acceptance saturated while credence can be pushed by evidence framing? Report regression R^2 for credence and AUROC for acceptance vs. shuffled-label controls.

3. Stimulus grid. Construct ~400 propositions crossing categorical status (clear-fact, clear-falsehood, genuinely-uncertain) x credence level (low/medium/high via probability framings and evidence-strength manipulations), with paraphrase templates and held-out templates for transfer.

4. Mismatch metric. Define per-example categorical–graded mismatch as the signed discrepancy between the acceptance-axis readout (binarized/calibrated) and the credence-axis readout (calibrated to [0,1]). Characterize two mismatch regimes: 'over-acceptance' (categorical accept but low credence) and 'under-acceptance' (high credence but no categorical accept). Report distributions across the stimulus grid.

5. Behavioral prediction. Elicit the model's free-form answer plus its verbalized confidence/hedging (assertive vs. hedged language, scored automatically) and asserted truth-value. Test whether per-example mismatch predicts (a) overconfident assertion of low-credence claims and (b) unwarranted hedging on clear facts, via logistic regression; report AUROC vs. baselines (single truth-direction projection, output entropy, verbal-uncertainty feature from Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty).

6. Independent causal steering. Steer the credence axis while holding the acceptance axis fixed (orthogonalize the steering vector against the acceptance direction) and test whether this shifts hedging language and stated confidence without flipping asserted content; then steer the acceptance axis holding credence fixed and test whether it flips asserted truth-value while leaving confidence language intact. This double dissociation is the core causal test. Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls and sweep strengths.

7. Overconfidence repair. On held-out overconfident items (categorical accept + low credence), steer to reduce categorical acceptance toward the credence level and measure reduction in confident-false assertions while preserving accuracy on clear-fact controls; report ECE and accuracy-coverage curves vs. the single-axis calibration baseline.

8. Robustness & generalization. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axes, mismatch metric, and interventions to held-out templates and an independent uncertain-QA benchmark (e.g., a held-out PopQA/TriviaQA slice) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The categorical-acceptance and graded-credence axes may not be cleanly separable—they might collapse to one direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, and treat near-collapse as an informative negative result that would itself challenge assumptions in prior single-axis work.

Graded-credence labels derived from probability framings may act through surface lexical cues rather than a genuine credence abstraction; we mitigate with the evidence-based empirical-correctness credence labels, paraphrase templates, and held-out-template transfer.
Truth/belief probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, and report per-template consistency.
The mismatch metric relies on calibrating two axes onto comparable scales; miscalibration could inflate apparent mismatch, so we report sensitivity to the calibration procedure.

The double-dissociation steering is the crux; if steering one axis unavoidably moves the other, the axes are entangled—we quantify cross-talk and use orthogonalized steering vectors with norm-matched controls.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: belief_entrenchment_axis
Title: Stubborn by Design? A Latent Entrenchment Axis that Predicts and Controls How Hard an LLM's Beliefs Are to Revise
Short Hypothesis: Before any counter-evidence is presented, an LLM encodes a proposition's revisability as a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'entrenchment' axis (distinct from belief-valence and from confidence/credence): the entrenchment readout at assertion time causally predicts how strongly the belief resists later counter-evidence, and steering along this axis makes a given belief more stubborn or more plastic without changing its truth-value or initial confidence.
Related Work: Behavioral work characterizes belief entrenchment in reasoning and multi-agent debate (Martingale Score 2025; DReaMAD 2025), belief perseverance in humans (Debunking meta-analysis 2017; constraint-satisfaction models 2001; cognitive-coherence accounts 2025), and how AI response features shape belief change (How AI Responses Shape User Beliefs 2025). Mechanistic work studies compliance/knowledge-conflict resolution as orthogonal interference or mechanism competition *after* conflict is introduced (Simulated Adoption 2026; Competition of Mechanisms 2024; Too Big to Fool 2024), representational stability under perturbation as a function of epistemic familiarity (Representational Stability 2025), and belief depth of implanted facts (Believe It or Not 2025). Crucially, all of these measure resistance either behaviorally or as a post-conflict geometric consequence; none asks whether an LLM carries a *forward-looking, per-proposition revisability signal at assertion time*, separable from belief-valence and confidence, that predetermines and can causally set how stubborn that belief will be. We move from 'entrenchment is a behavior / a post-hoc rotation' to 'entrenchment is a decodable, dissociable, and steerable latent property fixed before evidence arrives.'
Abstract: Large language models sometimes abandon a claim at the first sign of pushback and sometimes cling to it through repeated, high-quality counter-evidence. We ask whether this variability is predetermined: does the model, at the moment it asserts a proposition, already encode how hard that belief will be to revise? We hypothesize a latent 'entrenchment' axis in activation space that (1) is decodable at assertion time, (2) is near-orthogonal to the belief-valence direction and to internal confidence/credence, (3) predicts, per proposition, the amount of counter-evidence required to flip the model's stated answer, and (4) is causally steerable to make any given belief more stubborn or more plastic without altering its truth-value or initial confidence. We fit the axis by pairing each proposition with a measured behavioral revisability score (obtained via a graded counter-evidence ladder) and probing pre-conflict activations. We then test separability from belief-valence and confidence via cross-decoding and orthogonality, show incremental prediction of revisability beyond confidence and epistemic familiarity, and perform double-dissociation steering: pushing along the entrenchment axis changes how many rounds of counter-evidence are needed to flip a belief while a belief-valence control flips the answer outright and a confidence control shifts hedging. Experiments span three model families with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls. Our results recast belief entrenchment as a forward-looking, dissociable, and controllable internal property, yielding a cheap diagnostic for stubborn misinformation and a training-free knob for calibrated open-mindedness.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit a confidence/credence direction using empirical answer-correctness rates (sampled) and probability-framed items, following prior confidence-direction work.

2. Behavioral revisability measurement. Assemble ~400 verifiable propositions the model initially asserts.
