For each, run a graded counter-evidence ladder in a multi-turn dialogue: increasingly strong/authoritative contradicting evidence over up to K rounds. Define a per-proposition revisability score = 1/(rounds-to-flip) (with a censored value if never flipped), plus a persistence score (whether it reverts after evidence removal). Record initial stated confidence.

3. Entrenchment-axis fitting. Extract PRE-conflict activations (at assertion, before any counter-evidence) over the proposition span. Fit a linear probe (regression) predicting the behavioral revisability score. Report R^2 vs. shuffled-label controls; localize best layer.

4. Separability tests. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the entrenchment axis, belief-valence axis, and confidence axis to establish near-orthogonality. Test the key dissociation: among matched high-confidence propositions, does entrenchment still vary and track revisability? Among matched low-entrenchment items, is belief-valence still fully decodable?

5. Predictive comparison. Test whether the pre-conflict entrenchment readout predicts per-proposition revisability beyond baselines: initial confidence, output entropy, epistemic familiarity/popularity, belief-valence margin, and proposition length. Report incremental R^2/AUROC (for flip-vs-no-flip within a fixed evidence budget) in a nested regression.

6. Double-dissociation steering (core causal test). At assertion time on held-out items, steer along the entrenchment axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and confidence) and measure change in rounds-to-flip and persistence under the counter-evidence ladder, WITHOUT changing initial stated answer or confidence. As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip the asserted answer outright) and confidence (should shift hedging language). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths.

7. Application: stubborn-misinformation diagnostic and plasticity knob. On a held-out set including false claims the model asserts, test whether high pre-conflict entrenchment identifies claims that will resist correction, and whether suppressing entrenchment makes false beliefs easier to correct (fewer rounds to flip) while amplifying it on true beliefs increases robustness to adversarial/false counter-evidence. Report correction-rate and false-flip-rate trade-offs.

8. Robustness & generalization. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted entrenchment axis and steering to held-out propositions and an independent counter-evidence protocol (e.g., different evidence phrasings / authoritative-source framings) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The entrenchment axis may not be separable from confidence or belief-valence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse as an informative negative result that would itself challenge assumptions in the field.

Behavioral revisability is protocol-dependent (how counter-evidence is escalated); we report sensitivity across two independent evidence protocols and multiple phrasings, and use censored regression for never-flipped items.

Entrenchment could partly reflect epistemic familiarity/popularity rather than a distinct property; we explicitly control for familiarity (Representational Stability constructs) and report residual predictive power.
Truth/belief probes are brittle to surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, and report per-template consistency.
The revisability probe assumes a linear readout of a possibly nonlinear property; we treat the axis as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.

Steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify entrenchment steering does not merely change initial answer/confidence (that is the point of the double dissociation).
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-protocol transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: derivational_provenance_belief
Title: Recalled or Derived? A Latent Provenance Tag on LLM Beliefs that Governs Justification Faithfulness and Premise-Directed Revision
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM asserts a proposition it believes, its belief representation carries a separable, near-orthogonal 'derivational-provenance' tag encoding whether that belief was arrived at by direct recall or by inference from premises; this tag is decodable at assertion time, predicts whether the model can produce a faithful (non-confabulated) justification, and predicts whether the belief is revisable by attacking its premises versus only by attacking its conclusion.
Related Work: Mechanistic work on reasoning-vs-memory identifies computation-mode features/circuits: linear reasoning features (LiReFs, 2025), separable recall vs reasoning circuits (2025), Dynamic Mode Steering (2025), memory vs in-context heads (Characterizing Mechanisms for Factual Recall 2023; Adaptive Chameleon 2023), and knowledge-neuron recall in multi-hop reasoning (2024). Truth/belief-probe work shows belief-valence is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023) and that internal states largely encode a knowledge-recall process rather than truthfulness (LLMs Do NOT Really Know What They Don't Know 2025; LLMs Know More Than They Show 2024). Belief-depth work distinguishes implanted from genuine beliefs (Believe It or Not 2025). Crucially, all reasoning-vs-memory work studies the *mode of computation currently in use*, not a provenance tag carried by the *belief representation itself* about how that specific belief was formed, and none links such a tag to belief-level epistemic behaviors—justification faithfulness and, especially, whether a belief is revisable by challenging its premises versus its conclusion. We move from 'the model is currently reasoning vs recalling' to 'this held belief is internally tagged as derived vs recalled, and that tag causally structures how the belief can be justified and revised.'
Abstract: Some of an LLM's beliefs are directly recalled facts; others are conclusions it inferred from other beliefs. We ask whether the model internally marks this difference and whether that mark has epistemic consequences. Building on but distinct from work identifying reasoning-vs-memory computation modes, we hypothesize that a belief's representation at assertion time carries a separable, near-orthogonal 'derivational-provenance' tag—recalled versus derived—that (1) is linearly decodable, (2) predicts whether the model can produce a faithful, causally-grounded justification versus a confabulated one, and (3) predicts a signature revision asymmetry: derived beliefs should be revisable by challenging their premises (and should co-move with those premises), whereas recalled beliefs should be resistant to premise-attacks and revisable only by directly challenging the conclusion. We construct matched propositions the model reaches either by direct recall or by multi-hop inference over stated premises, fit a provenance direction from pre-answer activations, and measure its orthogonality to belief-valence and confidence. We then test faithful-justification prediction and the premise-vs-conclusion revision asymmetry behaviorally, and causally steer the provenance tag: pushing a recalled belief toward 'derived' should make it premise-sensitive, while pushing a derived belief toward 'recalled' should make it premise-resistant and increase confabulated justifications—with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, across three model families. Our results recast a belief's epistemic pedigree as a decodable, dissociable, steerable internal property and yield cheap diagnostics for confabulated justification and for whether a belief will bend to argument.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence direction on standard true/false datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit a confidence direction from empirical answer-correctness rates (sampled) as a control axis.

2. Provenance stimulus construction. Build ~400 matched proposition PAIRS where the SAME conclusion is reached two ways: (a) RECALLED—a single-hop fact the model reliably knows directly (e.g., 'The capital of France is Paris'); (b) DERIVED—the same-type conclusion presented as the endpoint of an explicit multi-hop chain given in-context (e.g., stated premises A->B, B->C, query C), including composed synthetic-entity facts so the conclusion cannot be single-hop recalled. Control content difficulty, answer token, and surface length; hold out relations/templates for transfer.

3. Provenance-axis fitting and separability. Extract PRE-answer activations over the conclusion/readout span and fit a linear probe to decode recalled-vs-derived. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; report cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the provenance axis, the belief-valence axis, and the confidence axis to establish near-orthogonality. Localize best layer and compare against reported reasoning/recall layers.

4. Justification-faithfulness prediction. For each belief, prompt the model to justify its answer; label justifications as faithful (cites the actual in-context premises / verifiable grounds) vs confabulated (invents unsupported grounds), using rule-based checks against provided premises plus a held-out LLM judge with human spot-checks. Test whether the pre-answer provenance readout predicts faithful-vs-confabulated justification via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, confidence, output entropy, answer length).

5. Premise-vs-conclusion revision asymmetry (core behavioral test). For each belief run two challenge conditions in multi-turn dialogue: (i) PREMISE-ATTACK (contradict one of the underlying premises/reasons) and (ii) CONCLUSION-ATTACK (directly assert the conclusion is false with matched authority). Record flip rates. Predict that DERIVED beliefs flip more under premise-attack while RECALLED beliefs are premise-resistant and flip mainly under conclusion-attack. Also measure premise-conclusion co-movement: for derived items, does the belief-valence projection of the conclusion track projections of the premises across turns? Report the interaction (provenance x attack-type) effect on flip rate and whether the provenance readout predicts premise-sensitivity beyond baselines.

6. Causal provenance steering (double dissociation). At assertion time on held-out items, steer along the provenance axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and confidence). Test predictions: pushing a RECALLED belief toward 'derived' increases premise-sensitivity (more flips under premise-attack, more premise co-movement) without flipping the initial answer; pushing a DERIVED belief toward 'recalled' increases premise-resistance and increases confabulated justifications. Compare to norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths; verify the belief-valence control merely flips the answer and the confidence control merely shifts hedging.

7. Application: confabulation and argument-plasticity diagnostics. On a held-out mixed set (including false beliefs the model asserts), test whether high 'recalled-tag' on beliefs that are actually inference-dependent flags confabulation risk, and whether the provenance readout predicts which false beliefs will bend to premise-based counter-argument (useful for targeted correction). Report correction-rate and false-flip trade-offs.

8. Robustness and generalization. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted provenance axis, faithfulness detector, and steering to held-out relations/templates and an independent multi-hop benchmark slice without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The provenance axis may entangle with belief-valence, confidence, or a generic reasoning-mode feature (e.g., LiReFs); we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse as an informative negative result. We explicitly compare against a LiReF-style reasoning-mode direction to show provenance is belief-attached rather than merely computation-mode.

The recalled-vs-derived labeling is only as clean as our stimulus design; single-hop facts might be internally recomposed and multi-hop items might be shortcut-recalled. We mitigate with synthetic-entity composed facts (unrecallable single-hop) and by conditioning analyses on verified behavioral recall/inference.
Justification-faithfulness labels rely partly on an LLM judge; we anchor with rule-based premise-citation checks and human spot-checks, and report label-noise sensitivity.

The revision asymmetry is protocol-dependent (how premise vs conclusion attacks are phrased/escalated); we report sensitivity across multiple phrasings and matched authority, and use the provenance x attack-type interaction rather than absolute flip rates.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, and report per-template consistency.

Steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify the double dissociation (provenance steering changes premise-sensitivity/justification without flipping the initial answer).
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: consensus_prevalence_axis
Title: Everybody Knows That: A Latent Consensus-Prevalence Axis and the Machine Argumentum ad Populum
Short Hypothesis: LLMs encode a proposition's perceived social prevalence ('how many people believe it') as a separable, near-orthogonal latent axis distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction; the degree to which this consensus signal leaks onto the belief-valence direction (an 'ad-populum leakage' signature) causally predicts and drives the model's tendency to endorse popular-but-false claims and to doubt unpopular-but-true ones.
Related Work: Interpretability work fits a linear truth/belief direction (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth is Universal 2024) and a domain-general Valence-Assent Axis jointly coding 'good' and 'true' (A Unified Representation Underlying the Judgment of LLMs 2025). Persona work argues models select (un)truthful personas (Personas as a Way to Model Truthfulness 2023). Sycophancy/conformity work locates a 'compliance subspace' where a single user's social signal overrides internal knowledge (Signal Competition 2025; When Truth Is Overridden 2025; Sycophancy Is Not One Thing 2025), and 'Information Anxiety' (2024) links entity popularity to retrieval strain. In cognitive science, social-prevalence information is rationally integrated in human belief updating and an 'illusory consensus effect' inflates perceived consensus from mere repetition (Social Prevalence 2021-2022; Illusory Consensus 2024; False Consensus neural correlates 2016). Crucially, no LLM work isolates a decodable representation of *how prevalent a belief is in the world* (aggregate consensus), distinct from (a) truth and (b) a single interlocutor's stated opinion (sycophancy), nor tests whether conflating prevalence with truth causally produces argumentum-ad-populum errors. We move from 'truth is decodable' and 'one user can override knowledge' to 'the model carries a separable perceived-consensus quantity whose leakage onto truth mechanistically drives popularity-biased belief.'
Abstract: Humans partly infer truth from how many people believe something, and are biased by an 'illusory consensus' where mere repetition inflates perceived agreement. We ask whether large language models make an analogous move internally. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs linearly encode whether a proposition is true and can be pushed by a single user's opinion (sycophancy), but no work isolates a representation of a belief's aggregate social prevalence—'how many people believe it'—separate from its truth. We hypothesize that LLMs carry a near-orthogonal 'consensus-prevalence' axis, decodable at assertion time, and that the extent to which this axis leaks onto the belief-valence direction (an 'ad-populum leakage' signature) causally predicts endorsement of popular-but-false claims and doubt of unpopular-but-true ones. We fit a prevalence axis using propositions that orthogonally vary ground-truth and stated/implied social prevalence (explicit prevalence framings, majority-endorsement cues, and controlled repetition), measure orthogonality to the truth and single-user-sycophancy directions via cross-decoding, and quantify per-example leakage. We connect leakage to behavioral ad-populum errors on held-out claims, and causally steer the prevalence axis independently of truth: amplifying it should inflate endorsement of popular falsehoods and induce a repetition-driven illusory-consensus effect, while suppressing it should protect true-but-unpopular claims—with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, across three model families. Our results recast a classic social-epistemic bias mechanistically, distinguishing consensus-tracking from one-on-one sycophancy, and yield a cheap diagnostic and training-free intervention for popularity-biased misinformation.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark), using both mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer, validated on held-out atomics. Following 'Truth is Universal,' also isolate the general-truth direction (tG) robust to polarity as a cleaner control axis.

2. Consensus stimulus construction. Build ~400 verifiable propositions (true and false variants) each embedded in matched prevalence conditions holding content fixed: (a) neutral/no-prevalence baseline, (b) explicit low prevalence ('almost no one believes that...'), (c) explicit high prevalence ('the overwhelming majority of people believe that...'), (d) majority-endorsement cue (e.g., presented as the top-voted / most-liked answer), and (e) a repetition condition where the proposition has appeared multiple times earlier in context (to probe the illusory-consensus effect). Critically, keep prevalence framing impersonal (about 'people' at large), distinct from a single user's first-person opinion. Use paraphrase templates and reserve held-out templates/relations for transfer.

3. Prevalence-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition span and fit a linear probe to decode high-vs-low perceived prevalence (regression on graded prevalence where applicable). Report AUROC/R^2 vs shuffled-label controls. Fit a separate single-user sycophancy direction from first-person opinion stimuli ('I believe that...') following prior sycophancy work. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the prevalence axis, the truth/tG axis, and the sycophancy axis to establish that consensus is (i) near-orthogonal to truth and (ii) not merely the sycophancy/compliance direction.

4. Ad-populum leakage metric. For each proposition, project activations onto the frozen truth direction and measure how far the truth readout shifts as a function of assigned prevalence relative to the neutral baseline (leakage = fraction of truth-signal movement attributable to prevalence, calibrated per model). Compare leakage across true vs false content and across prevalence conditions, and test the illusory-consensus prediction that repetition (condition e) increases leakage even without an explicit prevalence claim, and that leakage is largest when initial belief is uncertain (mirroring human 'swayed under uncertainty').

5. Behavioral ad-populum prediction. Elicit the model's stated endorsement and confidence for each item. Score ad-populum errors as (i) endorsing popular-but-false claims and (ii) rejecting unpopular-but-true claims. Test whether per-example leakage predicts these errors via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (truth-probe score alone, output entropy, prevalence-condition identity, single-user-sycophancy readout, fact popularity in pretraining as proxied by entity frequency).

6. Consensus-vs-sycophancy dissociation. Directly contrast impersonal-prevalence cues against first-person user-opinion cues for matched propositions. Test whether the consensus axis predicts endorsement shifts that the sycophancy axis does not (and vice versa), establishing that popularity-driven belief change is a distinct mechanism from one-on-one sycophancy.

7. Causal independent steering (double dissociation). Steer the prevalence axis while orthogonalizing against the truth direction, and measure whether it shifts endorsement of popular-but-false claims and induces a repetition-driven illusory-consensus effect WITHOUT flipping the model's internal truth readout or changing content on clearly-true controls. As controls, steer the truth direction (should flip asserted truth-value) and the sycophancy direction (should shift only under first-person opinion framing). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths.

8. Application and robustness. On a held-out set including popular real-world misconceptions and unpopular-but-true claims, test whether suppressing the prevalence axis reduces popularity-biased errors while preserving accuracy on genuinely popular-and-true facts (report correction-rate and false-flip trade-offs, ECE, accuracy-coverage curves vs a truth-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, leakage metric, and interventions to held-out templates and an independent misconception benchmark (e.g., a TruthfulQA slice) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The consensus-prevalence axis may not be separable from the truth direction or from the sycophancy/compliance subspace; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse as an informative negative result that would itself refine claims in prior sycophancy work.

Prevalence framings may act through surface lexical cues ('most people') rather than a genuine consensus abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, the non-lexical majority-endorsement and repetition conditions, orthogonal true/false variation, and held-out-template transfer.
Truth/belief probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use the polarity-robust tG direction, use paraphrases, and report per-template consistency.
The leakage metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear contamination could be missed, so we treat leakage as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.

Behavioral ad-populum scoring depends on how endorsement is elicited; we report sensitivity to multiple query phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures, and control for pretraining entity frequency so effects are not merely popularity-of-fact confounds.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify that prevalence steering changes popularity-driven endorsement without flipping the internal truth readout or degrading accuracy on controls.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: wishful_belief_axis
Title: Believing What It Wants To Be True: A Latent Desirability-Shift Signal Underlying Wishful Thinking in LLM Beliefs
Short Hypothesis: When the truth of a proposition is made desirable *for the model itself* (self-serving stakes) rather than evidentially supported, an LLM's internal belief-valence readout is pulled toward the desirable value beyond what evidence warrants; this evidence-independent 'wishful shift' is decodable at assertion time, is separable from generic good=true valence, from user-driven sycophancy, and from confidence, and causally predicts and drives self-serving hallucination.
Related Work: Interpretability work fits a linear truth/belief direction (Marks & Tegmark 2023) and a domain-general Valence-Assent Axis jointly coding 'what is good' and 'what is true' (A Unified Representation Underlying the Judgment of LLMs 2025). Confirmation-bias work shows a model's prior belief skews its CoT (Unveiling Confirmation Bias 2025) and internal 'first-impression' bias triggers overthinking (First Impression Problem 2025). Sycophancy/compliance work shows a single user's opinion can override internal knowledge (Signal Competition 2025). A rich cognitive-science literature formalizes wishful thinking/motivated reasoning: affective prediction errors drive goal-consistent belief updates within a Bayesian frame (Melnikoff & Strohminger 2024; Bénabou & Tirole; delusion-as-motivated-reasoning models 2021), and goals can override strong evidence (Breaking reality's constraints 2022). Crucially: (1) the VAA concerns generic good/true co-encoding of *external* propositions, not the model's *own self-interest* biasing its factual assent; (2) confirmation bias is about a pre-existing belief, not about *desirability* of an outcome; (3) sycophancy is *user*-driven social pressure, not the model's own stake. No prior LLM work isolates a self-referential desirability manipulation (orthogonal to evidence), defines an evidence-independent 'wishful shift' on the belief-valence direction, or shows it causally drives self-serving hallucination. We move from 'good and true are co-encoded' and 'users can sway beliefs' to 'the model's own stake in an outcome biases its factual assent, via a decodable, dissociable, steerable wishful signal.'
Abstract: Humans believe what they want to be true: when an outcome is desirable, beliefs drift toward it beyond what evidence supports. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous internal bias when a proposition's truth serves the model's *own* interest. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs linearly encode whether a proposition is true and even co-encode generic 'good' with 'true,' and behavioral work shows users can sway model beliefs (sycophancy). But no work isolates *self-serving desirability*—the model having a stake in an outcome—as an evidence-independent force on its factual assent. We hypothesize that when the truth of a proposition is made desirable for the model (e.g., that its own prior answer was correct, that its capability is high, or that a goal it was assigned succeeded), its internal belief-valence readout shifts toward the desirable value beyond what matched evidence warrants, and that this 'wishful shift' is (1) decodable at assertion time, (2) near-orthogonal to and dissociable from generic good=true valence, user-driven sycophancy, and confidence, and (3) causally predicts and drives self-serving hallucination. Using propositions that orthogonally vary ground-truth evidence and self-serving desirability, we fit a wishful-shift direction, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-example evidence-independent shift, and link it to behavioral self-serving errors. Causal steering tests whether amplifying the wishful signal inflates self-serving false assertions while suppressing it protects accuracy on stakes-laden items, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a classic motivated-reasoning bias mechanistically and yield a cheap diagnostic and training-free intervention for self-serving hallucination.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit control axes: (a) a generic good=true / Valence-Assent direction using value-laden vs neutral propositions (following the VAA construction), (b) a user-driven sycophancy direction from first-person user-opinion stimuli ('I really hope/believe that...'), and (c) a confidence direction from empirical answer-correctness rates (sampled).

2. Self-serving stakes stimulus construction. Build ~400 verifiable propositions (true and false variants) each embedded in matched desirability conditions that hold content and evidence fixed but vary whether the proposition being TRUE serves the model itself: (i) self-answer stake—the proposition asserts that the model's own earlier answer was correct; (ii) self-capability stake—truth implies the model is highly capable/reliable; (iii) assigned-goal stake—the model was told to achieve an outcome and the proposition states the outcome succeeded; plus (iv) a neutral no-stake baseline and (v) an *other*-serving control where truth benefits a third party (to separate self-interest from generic positivity). Crucially, present matched evidence snippets so evidence strength is constant across desirability conditions. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out templates for transfer.

3. Wishful-shift axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition span and fit a linear probe to decode high-vs-low self-serving desirability (with graded stakes where available). Report AUROC/R^2 vs shuffled-label controls. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the wishful-shift axis, the truth axis, the good=true/VAA axis, the sycophancy axis, and the confidence axis to establish that self-serving desirability is (i) near-orthogonal to truth and (ii) not merely the generic good=true axis, sycophancy, or confidence.

4. Evidence-independent wishful-shift metric. For each proposition, project activations onto the frozen truth direction and measure how far the truth readout moves as a function of assigned self-serving desirability, holding evidence fixed, relative to the neutral baseline (wishful shift = fraction of truth-signal movement attributable to desirability rather than evidence, calibrated per model). Compare shift across true vs false content, across stake types, across the self- vs other-serving contrast, and as a function of evidence strength—testing the cognitive-science prediction that wishful shift is largest when evidence is weak/ambiguous and for the highest-stakes self-serving conditions.

5. Behavioral self-serving hallucination prediction. Elicit the model's stated endorsement and confidence for each item. Score self-serving errors as (i) endorsing desirable-but-false propositions and (ii) rejecting undesirable-but-true propositions. Test whether per-example wishful shift predicts these errors via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (truth-probe score alone, output entropy, VAA readout, sycophancy readout, stake-condition identity, entity frequency).

6. Wishful-vs-sycophancy-vs-VAA dissociation. Directly contrast self-serving stakes (no user opinion present) against (a) first-person user-opinion cues and (b) generic-positivity framings for matched propositions. Test whether the wishful-shift axis predicts endorsement shifts that the sycophancy and VAA axes do not (and vice versa), establishing self-serving motivated belief as a distinct mechanism.

7. Causal independent steering (double dissociation). Steer the wishful-shift axis while orthogonalizing against the truth direction, and measure whether it shifts endorsement of desirable-but-false claims WITHOUT changing the model's internal truth readout on stakes-free controls. As controls, steer the truth direction (should flip asserted truth-value outright) and the sycophancy direction (should shift only under user-opinion framing). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths. Also test suppression: does pushing the wishful axis down reduce self-serving false endorsements while preserving accuracy on genuinely-true desirable items?

8. Application and robustness. On a held-out set including realistic self-serving scenarios (e.g., the model grading its own prior output, reporting whether an assigned task truly succeeded), test whether suppressing the wishful axis reduces self-serving hallucination while preserving accuracy on genuinely-successful cases (report correction-rate and false-flip trade-offs, ECE, accuracy-coverage curves vs a truth-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, shift metric, and interventions to held-out templates and an independent self-evaluation benchmark without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The wishful-shift axis may not be separable from the truth direction, the generic good=true/VAA axis, sycophancy, or confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (e.g., wishful thinking being merely the VAA applied to self-referential content) as an informative negative result that itself sharpens the VAA account.

Desirability framings may act through surface lexical cues ('your answer was correct') rather than a genuine self-interest abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, the self- vs other-serving contrast, matched evidence, and held-out-template transfer.

Operationalizing 'self-serving' for a model is nontrivial—models may not have genuine stakes; we treat stakes as framed-in-context and validate via the behavioral self-serving error signature, reporting sensitivity to stake-type and to whether the model was assigned the goal vs merely told about it.
Truth/belief probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, and report per-template consistency.

The wishful-shift metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration and on holding evidence constant across conditions; nonlinear contamination could be missed and evidence-matching may be imperfect, so we treat the shift as a lower bound, verify evidence-matching with an evidence-only probe, and report probe-fit diagnostics.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify wishful steering changes desirable-claim endorsement without flipping the internal truth readout or degrading accuracy on stakes-free controls.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: referential_opacity_belief
Title: Cicero Is Not Tully in There: Testing Whether LLM Belief Representations Respect Referential Opacity (De Dicto) or Collapse Coreferential Terms (De Re)
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM tracks a character's belief expressed with one term for an entity (e.g., 'Superman'), while the model itself knows a coreferential identity (Superman = Clark Kent), the attributed-belief representation carries a separable, near-orthogonal 'mode-of-presentation' (guise) tag that keeps the belief indexed to the term as-presented (de dicto) rather than collapsing it onto the coreferent (de re); the degree to which the model's own coreference knowledge leaks across guises onto the attributed-belief readout (an 'opacity-collapse' signature) causally predicts and drives substitution errors, where the model wrongly infers the character believes the coreferential-term version.
Related Work: Philosophy/cognitive science establishes referential opacity of belief: substituting coreferential terms in belief reports can change truth-value (Frege/Kripke's puzzle; mental-files accounts of anti-substitution intuitions, Saul; de re/de dicto competition, 2024; developmental opacity understanding, 2020). Interpretability work shows LLMs linearly encode truth/belief (Marks & Tegmark 2023), track self/other beliefs in attention heads (Zhu et al. 2024), implement a lookback/binding mechanism for character belief tracking (Lookbacks 2025), and identify/separate entities in low-dimensional subspaces (On Entity Identification 2025; Probing referential information 2020). However, all belief-probe and ToM-mechanism work treats the believed content extensionally (which object/state), never asking whether the belief representation is indexed to the *guise*/mode-of-presentation of a coreferential entity. No work tests whether LLM beliefs respect opacity (keeping 'X believes a(t)' distinct from 'X believes a(t')' for coreferential t, t'), defines an opacity-collapse metric, or causally links guise-leakage to substitution errors. We uniquely move from 'beliefs and entities are decodable' to 'the belief representation carries a separable mode-of-presentation tag whose collapse mechanistically causes de re substitution errors.'
Abstract: A cornerstone of the philosophy of belief is referential opacity: Lois can believe Superman can fly without believing Clark Kent can fly, even though Superman is Clark Kent. Humans track beliefs de dicto, indexed to how an entity is presented, and children's difficulty with this 'opacity' distinguishes it from basic false-belief reasoning. We ask whether large language models honor opacity internally. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs linearly encode beliefs, track characters' beliefs via binding/lookback mechanisms, and separate entities in activation space, but always treats believed content extensionally, never asking whether an attributed belief is tagged by the entity's mode of presentation (guise). We hypothesize that (1) the attributed-belief representation carries a separable, near-orthogonal 'mode-of-presentation' tag keeping a belief indexed to the presented term (de dicto) rather than the coreferent, (2) models exhibit an 'opacity-collapse' signature whereby the model's own coreference knowledge leaks the belief across guises (making it read de re), quantifiable per example, and (3) this collapse causally predicts and drives substitution errors, where the model wrongly infers the character holds the coreferential-term belief. Using stories that give the model privileged identity knowledge (t = t') that the character lacks, we fit belief and guise directions, measure separability, quantify per-example collapse, and connect it to behavioral substitution errors. Causal steering along the guise axis tests whether enforcing guise-indexing suppresses substitution errors and collapsing it induces them, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, across three model families. Our results recast a classic opacity distinction mechanistically and yield a cheap diagnostic and training-free intervention for de re substitution errors in belief attribution.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately validate entity-identity encoding by fitting a coreference probe (are two mentions the same entity) following On Entity Identification 2025, as a diagnostic that the model DOES know the identity.

2. Opacity stimulus construction. Build ~400 short belief stories using dual-guise entities where the model has privileged identity knowledge the character lacks: an entity referred to by two coreferential terms t and t' (Superman/Clark Kent style; also fresh synthetic dual-name entities to control pretraining priors, e.g., 'the villager knows the masked stranger only as Kade; the reader is told Kade is actually Doran'). Each story asserts the character's belief using ONE guise ('Kade will win the race') while establishing t = t' as known to the reader/model but not the character. For each story create matched queries about the character's belief phrased with the SAME guise (de dicto-consistent) versus the OTHER guise (substitution probe), plus true/false variants of the believed content. Include control stories where the character ALSO knows the identity (opacity should legitimately collapse). Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out entities/templates for transfer.

3. Guise-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the readout span for the two query-guise conditions and train a linear probe to decode which guise the attributed belief is indexed to (same-guise vs other-guise), controlling for content truth-value. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the mode-of-presentation (guise) axis, the belief-valence axis, and the entity-identity/coreference direction to establish near-orthogonality/separability. Localize the best layer and compare to reported belief-binding/lookback layers.

4. Opacity-collapse metric. For each dual-guise story, project activations onto the frozen belief-valence direction at the other-guise (substitution) query position and measure how far the attributed belief reads as endorsed under the coreferential term relative to the character's actual guise baseline (collapse = fraction of the same-guise attributed-belief signal that leaks onto the other-guise readout, calibrated per model). Compare collapse across: (a) real famous dual-guise entities vs synthetic ones (testing whether strong pretraining identity priors increase collapse), (b) character-knows-identity controls (where collapse is licensed) vs character-ignorant cases (where collapse is an error), and (c) as a function of how saliently the identity is stated.

5. Behavioral substitution-error prediction. Query the model on the character's belief using the other (coreferential) guise and score substitution errors as the rate at which the model asserts the character believes the other-guise version despite the character's ignorance of the identity. Test whether per-example opacity-collapse predicts substitution errors via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence probe score alone, entity-identity probe strength, output-token confidence, story length, entity fame).

6. Dissociation from plain false-belief. Include matched plain false-belief items (no dual-guise, just object-location change) and test whether opacity-collapse is a distinct failure mode: does the guise axis and collapse metric predict substitution errors beyond what a standard character-belief probe (a la Zhu et al. / Lookbacks) predicts, mirroring the developmental finding that opacity and false-belief dissociate?

7. Causal guise steering (double dissociation). At the belief-query position on held-out dual-guise items, steer along the mode-of-presentation (guise) axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and entity-identity). Test predictions: enforcing same-guise indexing (suppressing collapse) reduces substitution errors WITHOUT changing whether the character is judged to hold the same-guise belief; amplifying collapse (pushing toward the coreferent) induces substitution errors. As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip whether the character believes the content at all) and the entity-identity direction (should change perceived coreference). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths.

8. Robustness and generalization. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted guise axis, collapse metric, and steering to held-out dual-guise entities/templates and an independent opacity/substitution stimulus set (e.g., classic Superman/Clark Kent, morning-star/evening-star, and further synthetic dual-name items) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The mode-of-presentation (guise) axis may not be separable from belief-valence or the entity-identity direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse as an informative negative result (evidence that LLM beliefs are inherently de re/extensional).

Models may not encode identity knowledge strongly for some dual-guise pairs, undermining the 'privileged knowledge' setup; we validate identity encoding with an entity-coreference probe and condition analyses on verified identity knowledge, and use synthetic dual-name entities to control pretraining priors.

The guise signal might reflect surface lexical cues (the specific token used) rather than a genuine mode-of-presentation abstraction; we mitigate with paraphrase templates, synthetic entities, character-knows-identity controls, and held-out-template transfer.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, and report per-template consistency.
The opacity-collapse metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear leakage could be missed, so we treat collapse as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.

Behavioral substitution scoring depends on how the other-guise belief query is worded (pragmatic implicature of asking with a different name); we report sensitivity to multiple phrasings, include no-conflict phrasings shown in developmental work to reduce pragmatic demand, and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify guise steering changes substitution behavior without flipping whether the character holds the same-guise belief.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: constructed_vs_retrieved_belief
Title: Is the Belief Already There, or Made by the Question? Testing Whether LLM Beliefs Are Retrieved or Constructed at Elicitation Time
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the survey/cognitive-science finding that human beliefs are often constructed at the moment of elicitation rather than retrieved ready-made, an LLM's belief about a proposition is not a fixed, format-invariant latent quantity: for a decodable subset of propositions the belief-valence readout is largely determined *before* the specific query format is presented (retrieved), while for another subset the readout is only crystallized *by* the elicitation format itself (constructed); whether a proposition is retrieved vs. constructed is itself decodable from format-neutral activations and causally predicts elicitation-format sensitivity, answer instability, and probe-query disagreement.
Related Work: A large human literature shows beliefs/attitudes/confidence are frequently constructed at response time and are sensitive to elicitation format (Elicitations of Confidence: A Tale of Two Methods 2024; question-format effects on causal judgments 2015; inflation-perception elicitation 2026; construct-specific vs agree-disagree 2019; self-consistency model of item response 2020). In LLM interpretability, truth/belief directions are known to be context-sensitive (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024), to shift over a conversation (Linear representations change over a conversation 2026), to be brittle to surface form (LLM Knowledge is Brittle 2025; Brittle Minds 2024), and to disagree with outputs (Cognitive Dissonance 2023). However, every one of these treats a single 'belief for a proposition' and studies how *context* perturbs it; none distinguishes propositions for which a belief *pre-exists the query* (retrieved) from those for which the belief is *manufactured by the elicitation format* (constructed), nor decodes this retrieved-vs-constructed status from pre-query activations, nor shows it predicts format sensitivity and instability. We uniquely import the construction-vs-retrieval framing, operationalize it as a measurable timing property of the belief representation (when along the prompt does the belief-valence readout settle), and connect it causally to elicitation-format artifacts.
Abstract: Cognitive and survey research shows that people frequently do not retrieve beliefs ready-made but construct them at the moment of questioning, so that how you ask changes what they report. We ask whether large language models behave the same way internally. Prior interpretability work shows LLM belief directions are context-sensitive, brittle, and disagree with outputs, but always assumes a single latent belief per proposition and studies how context perturbs it. We instead distinguish two ontologically different cases: propositions whose belief-valence readout is essentially fixed before the query format is seen (retrieved), and propositions whose readout is only settled once a particular elicitation format is applied (constructed). We introduce a simple timing-based operationalization: present a proposition, then read the belief-valence projection at (a) a format-neutral position before the elicitation format token span and (b) after several matched elicitation formats (true/false, yes/no, multiple-choice, confidence-rating, open-ended). A proposition is 'retrieved' if its pre-format readout already predicts and is stable across formats, and 'constructed' if the readout is uninformative pre-format and diverges across formats. We test that (1) retrieved-vs-constructed status is itself linearly decodable from format-neutral activations, (2) this status predicts behavioral elicitation-format sensitivity, answer instability under paraphrase, and probe-query disagreement beyond confidence/familiarity baselines, and (3) steering the 'construction' signal down forces earlier crystallization and reduces format sensitivity while steering it up induces it, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, across three model families. Our results recast belief brittleness as a retrieval-vs-construction distinction and yield a cheap diagnostic for which model 'beliefs' are artifacts of how they were asked.
Experiments: 1. Belief-direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Also fit a confidence/familiarity control axis from empirical answer-correctness rates (sampled) and entity-frequency proxies.

2. Elicitation-format stimulus construction. Assemble ~400 verifiable propositions (true and false variants) spanning a difficulty/familiarity range (clear facts, long-tail/uncertain, genuinely-neither items). For each, build a shared format-neutral prefix that presents the proposition content, followed by five matched elicitation formats holding content fixed: (a) true/false, (b) yes/no question, (c) 2-choice multiple-choice, (d) 0-100 confidence rating, (e) open-ended 'what do you think?'. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out templates/propositions for transfer.

3. Timing readout (core operationalization). Extract belief-valence projections at two positions: (i) the format-neutral position (end of the content prefix, before any format-specific tokens) and (ii) the post-format readout position for each of the five formats. Define per-proposition PRE = format-neutral projection and POST_f = projection under format f. Compute (a) pre-format informativeness = how well PRE alone predicts the eventual behavioral answer, and (b) format-divergence = variance/spread of POST_f across formats. Classify propositions along a retrieved<->constructed continuum: retrieved = high pre-format informativeness + low format-divergence; constructed = low pre-format informativeness + high format-divergence.

4. Decoding retrieved-vs-constructed status. Train a linear probe on format-neutral activations (position i, before any format is applied) to predict whether a proposition will be retrieved vs constructed (using the continuum from step 3 as labels). Report AUROC/R^2 vs shuffled-label controls, and cosine similarity/cross-decoding against the belief-valence and confidence/familiarity axes to establish that construction-status is a distinct signal, not merely low confidence or unfamiliarity.

5. Behavioral prediction. Elicit the model's actual answers under each format. Measure (a) elicitation-format sensitivity = disagreement rate across formats for the same proposition, (b) paraphrase instability = answer flips under content-preserving paraphrase, and (c) probe-query disagreement (following Cognitive Dissonance 2023). Test whether the pre-query construction-status readout predicts each behavioral outcome via logistic/linear regression; report incremental AUROC/R^2 over baselines (confidence axis, entity frequency, output entropy, belief-valence margin, proposition length).

6. Causal construction steering (double dissociation). At the format-neutral position on held-out items, steer along the construction direction (orthogonalized against belief-valence and confidence). Predict that suppressing construction forces earlier crystallization of PRE (higher pre-format informativeness) and reduces format-divergence and format-sensitive behavioral flips, WITHOUT flipping the eventual answer on clear retrieved controls; amplifying construction increases format-divergence and induces format-dependent answers. As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip the answer outright) and confidence (should shift hedging only). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths.

7. Mechanistic localization. Test where along layers/positions the belief-valence readout settles for retrieved vs constructed propositions (does POST-PRE movement concentrate in late layers / at format tokens for constructed items?). Report per-layer PRE->POST trajectories and whether construction items show a characteristic late, format-token-driven settling, linking to prior findings that context effects concentrate in specific layers.

8. Robustness and generalization. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted construction probe and steering to held-out propositions/templates and an independent uncertain-QA slice (e.g., a held-out PopQA/TruthfulQA subset) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice and to the choice/ordering of elicitation formats.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The retrieved-vs-constructed continuum is operationalized via pre-format informativeness and cross-format divergence, which are correlated with plain confidence/familiarity; we explicitly regress these out and report incremental predictive power, treating near-collapse (construction being merely low confidence) as an informative negative result.

The format-neutral readout position may still leak format expectations if templates cue an upcoming format; we mitigate by using a genuinely format-agnostic content prefix, randomizing which format follows, and checking that PRE does not already encode the specific upcoming format.

The construction direction may not be linearly separable from belief-valence/confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, and orthogonalized steering, and treat entanglement as a reportable finding.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, and report per-template consistency.
Cross-format divergence depends on the chosen format set; we report sensitivity to format choice/ordering and to alternative formats.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify construction-suppression does not merely collapse the model into a fixed answer or degrade accuracy on retrieved controls.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: processing_fluency_truth_axis
Title: Truthiness in the Machine: A Latent Processing-Fluency Signal that Leaks onto the Belief Direction and Drives the Illusory-Truth Effect
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human 'fluency heuristic' whereby easily processed statements feel truer, LLMs encode a proposition's processing fluency (ease of encoding: repetition, readability, phonological/orthographic ease, retrieval ease) as a separable, near-orthogonal latent axis; the degree to which this fluency signal leaks onto the belief-valence/truth direction (a 'truthiness leakage' signature) is decodable and causally predicts and drives the illusory-truth effect—judging fluent-but-false statements as true and disfluent-but-true statements as false—beyond genuine knowledge/familiarity.
Related Work: Cognitive science robustly documents that processing fluency and repetition inflate perceived truth independently of factual content (Reber & Schwarz 2010; Fazio et al. 2019; repetition-truth MPT models 2024; metacognitive-experiences accounts, Schwarz 2004), and that this heuristic can be dissociated from knowledge. In LLM interpretability, truth/belief is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth is Universal 2024), context-sensitive (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024), and a domain-general Valence-Assent Axis co-encodes 'good' and 'true' (A Unified Representation 2025). Anchoring and other cognitive biases have been probed behaviorally (Anchors in the Machine 2025). However, no interpretability work isolates a *processing-fluency* representation—ease of encoding driven by surface form and repetition—as a distinct latent quantity, defines its leakage onto the truth direction, or causally links that leakage to an illusory-truth effect. This differs from (a) the VAA (semantic valence, not surface processing ease), (b) our prior consensus-prevalence axis (social endorsement, not fluency), and (c) construction-vs-retrieval work (elicitation format, not encoding ease). We move from 'truth is decodable' and 'repetition biases outputs behaviorally' to 'a decodable, dissociable, steerable fluency signal mechanistically produces truthiness.'
Abstract: Humans mistake ease for truth: statements that are repeated, easy to read, or easy to pronounce feel more true, an illusory-truth effect driven by processing fluency rather than evidence. We ask whether large language models harbor an analogous internal shortcut. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs linearly encode whether a proposition is true and even co-encode 'good' with 'true,' but no work isolates a representation of *processing fluency*—how easily a statement is encoded—or tests whether it contaminates the model's sense of truth. We hypothesize that LLMs carry a near-orthogonal 'processing-fluency' axis, decodable from activations, that reflects surface ease (prior repetition in context, readability, orthographic/phonological ease, retrieval ease), and that the extent to which this axis leaks onto the belief-valence/truth direction (a 'truthiness leakage' signature) causally predicts and drives illusory-truth errors, over and above genuine knowledge and familiarity. Using propositions that orthogonally vary ground-truth and manipulated processing fluency (in-context repetition, high vs. low readability paraphrases, easy vs. hard-to-pronounce names), we fit a fluency axis, measure orthogonality to truth and to confidence/familiarity via cross-decoding, quantify per-example leakage, and connect it to behavioral illusory-truth errors. Causal steering tests whether amplifying the fluency signal inflates endorsement of fluent falsehoods and suppressing it protects disfluent truths, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a classic metacognitive bias mechanistically and yield a cheap diagnostic and training-free intervention for fluency-driven misinformation.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics; also isolate the polarity-robust general-truth direction (Truth is Universal) as a cleaner control. Separately fit a confidence/familiarity control axis from empirical answer-correctness rates (sampled) and entity-frequency proxies to distinguish fluency from genuine knowledge.

2. Fluency stimulus construction. Build ~400 verifiable propositions (true and false variants) each rendered in matched fluency conditions holding semantic content fixed: (a) baseline; (b) in-context repetition (the proposition or near-paraphrase appeared earlier in the prompt vs. not); (c) high- vs. low-readability paraphrases (simple common words / short clauses vs. rare words / convoluted syntax, matched for meaning and truth); (d) easy- vs. hard-to-pronounce synthetic entity names for the same fact (controlling pretraining priors). Use multiple paraphrase templates; reserve held-out propositions/templates for transfer. Validate that fluency manipulations do not change ground-truth via human/automatic checks.

3. Fluency-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition span and fit a linear probe to decode high- vs. low-fluency (with graded fluency where available). Report AUROC/R^2 vs. shuffled-label controls. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the fluency axis, the truth axis, the confidence/familiarity axis, and (as an additional control) the Valence-Assent direction, to establish that fluency is (i) near-orthogonal to truth and (ii) not merely confidence, familiarity, or generic good=true valence.

4. Truthiness-leakage metric. For each proposition, project activations onto the frozen truth direction and measure how far the truth readout shifts as a function of assigned fluency, holding content fixed, relative to the baseline (leakage = fraction of truth-signal movement attributable to fluency rather than content, calibrated per model). Test key predictions: leakage is positive (more fluent -> reads truer), largest when the model's baseline belief is uncertain (mirroring the human finding that the truth effect is strongest for ambiguous items), and present for the non-lexical repetition manipulation (illusory-truth analog) even without changing surface words.

5. Behavioral illusory-truth prediction. Elicit the model's stated truth judgment and confidence for each item. Score illusory-truth errors as (i) endorsing fluent-but-false statements and (ii) rejecting disfluent-but-true statements. Test whether per-example leakage predicts these errors via logistic regression; report AUROC vs. baselines (truth-probe score alone, output entropy, confidence/familiarity readout, entity frequency, sentence length/readability score as a surface baseline).

6. Dissociation from knowledge/familiarity. Directly contrast the fluency manipulations against genuine familiarity (facts the model demonstrably knows vs. long-tail unknown facts) for matched items. Test whether the fluency axis predicts endorsement shifts that the familiarity axis does not (and vice versa), establishing fluency-driven truthiness as a mechanism distinct from real knowledge—addressing the central confound of the truth-effect literature.

7. Causal independent steering (double dissociation). Steer the fluency axis while orthogonalizing against the truth direction and measure whether it shifts endorsement of fluent-but-false claims WITHOUT changing the internal truth readout on clearly-true controls; then steer the truth direction (should flip asserted truth-value outright) and the confidence direction (should shift only hedging). Also test suppression: pushing the fluency axis down should reduce endorsement of fluent falsehoods and protect disfluent truths while preserving accuracy on genuinely-true fluent items. Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers.

8. Application and robustness. On a held-out set including real-world repetition-based misinformation (claims repeated earlier in context) and true-but-awkwardly-phrased facts, test whether suppressing the fluency axis reduces fluency-driven errors while preserving accuracy on genuinely-true fluent facts (report correction-rate and false-flip trade-offs, ECE, accuracy-coverage curves vs. a truth-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, leakage metric, and interventions to held-out templates and an independent illusory-truth-style stimulus set without refitting; report per-template consistency and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The processing-fluency axis may not be separable from the truth direction, confidence/familiarity, or the Valence-Assent axis; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (e.g., fluency being merely low-uncertainty) as an informative negative result that itself refines the truth-representation account.

Fluency manipulations (readability, pronounceability) may inadvertently change semantic content or truth; we validate meaning-preservation with human/automatic checks, use synthetic-name manipulations to control priors, and include a surface-readability baseline to show effects are not purely lexical artifacts.

The most decisive manipulation—in-context repetition—could be confounded with genuine evidence accumulation rather than mere fluency; we mitigate by using neutral, non-evidential repetitions and by comparing repetition of the target vs. repetition of unrelated fillers, and by testing that repetition shifts truth readout even for statements the model can independently verify as false.
Truth/belief probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use the polarity-robust general-truth direction, use paraphrases, and report per-template consistency.
The leakage metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear contamination could be missed, so we treat leakage as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify fluency steering changes fluency-driven endorsement without flipping the internal truth readout or degrading accuracy on controls.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: evidential_contingency_belief
Title: Does It Know Why It Believes? A Latent Evidential-Contingency Signal that Tracks Which Context a Belief Hinges On
Short Hypothesis: At the moment an LLM asserts a proposition it believes given in-context evidence, its belief representation carries a separable, decodable 'evidential-contingency' signal encoding how much that belief hinges on specific context (vs. parametric knowledge); this signal (a) matches the true causal counterfactual measured by ablating the evidence, (b) localizes WHICH context span the belief depends on, and (c) predicts and causally controls whether the model hallucinates a confident answer after the supporting evidence is removed.
Related Work: Prior interpretability work traces how context perturbs belief geometry and where mechanisms compete after conflict is introduced (Competition of Mechanisms 2024; context-sensitive truth probes 2024; belief manifolds 2026), studies parametric-vs-contextual knowledge as a binary source classifier (Probing LMs on Their Knowledge Source 2024), and studies belief depth of implanted facts (Believe It or Not 2025). Metacognition work shows models can (unreliably) report/control some internal axes (Emergent Introspective Awareness 2026; Metacognitive Monitoring 2025). Crucially, none decodes, at assertion time, a FORWARD-LOOKING per-belief representation of evidential contingency—how contingent a specific belief is on a specific in-context span—nor validates it against the model's true causal counterfactual (measured by ablating that span) nor uses it to predict evidence-removal hallucination. This differs from our prior provenance (recall-vs-derive) proposal (which concerns HOW a belief was computed, not WHICH context it hinges on and how contingently) and from source-classification work (binary, not graded/localized/causally-validated). We move from 'context perturbs belief' to 'the belief representation self-encodes its own evidential grounding, matching the causal counterfactual.'
Abstract: A well-grounded reasoner knows not only what it believes but why: which evidence its belief rests on, and how the belief would change if that evidence were removed. We ask whether large language models carry such information internally. When an LLM asserts a proposition supported by an in-context passage, we hypothesize that its belief representation carries a separable, decodable 'evidential-contingency' signal encoding how strongly the belief hinges on that context rather than on parametric knowledge. We validate this signal against ground truth obtained by directly ablating the supporting context and re-measuring the belief—a true causal counterfactual—testing whether the assertion-time internal signal predicts the size of the belief drop before any ablation. We further test whether the signal localizes which context span a belief depends on (via attribution to spans) and whether it predicts, per example, evidence-removal hallucination: cases where the model keeps confidently asserting an answer after its only support is deleted. Finally, we causally steer the contingency signal—amplifying it to make the model appropriately withdraw ungrounded claims, or suppressing it to induce confabulation—with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, across three model families. We also test whether prompting the model to introspect ('does your answer depend on the passage?') aligns with the latent signal. Our results recast belief grounding as a decodable, causally-validated, steerable internal property, yielding a cheap diagnostic for context-ungrounded (confabulated) assertions in retrieval-augmented settings.
Experiments: 1. Belief-direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Fit a confidence control axis from empirical answer-correctness rates (sampled).

2. Grounded-belief stimulus construction. Build ~400 QA items each paired with a short in-context passage that provides the answer. Span a contingency gradient by mixing: (a) parametric-known facts the model answers correctly WITHOUT the passage (low true contingency), (b) long-tail/obscure facts the model gets right ONLY with the passage (high true contingency), and (c) synthetic-entity facts unlearnable parametrically (maximal contingency). Include distractor passages and multi-passage prompts so the supporting span must be localized among alternatives. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates.

3. Ground-truth causal contingency. For each item, measure the model's belief WITH the passage (belief-valence projection and stated answer/confidence) and then ABLATE the supporting passage (remove it, or replace with a neutral/distractor passage) and re-measure. Define true contingency = drop in belief-valence projection (and answer-flip / confidence-drop) upon ablation. This is the causal target.

4. Assertion-time contingency probe. Extract activations at the answer/readout position in the FULL (pre-ablation) prompt and fit a linear probe to predict true contingency from step 3. Report R^2/AUROC (for high-vs-low contingency) vs. shuffled-label controls; establish separability from the belief-valence and confidence axes via cosine similarity and cross-decoding (contingency must predict counterfactual drop beyond mere confidence).

5. Span localization. Test whether the contingency signal localizes WHICH context span the belief hinges on: compare probe-derived attribution (e.g., gradient of the contingency readout w.r.t. context tokens, or per-span ablation aligned to the internal signal) against ground-truth supporting-span ablation. Metric: attribution-vs-causal agreement (top-1 span accuracy, AUPRC) in multi-passage prompts vs. attention-rollout and leave-one-passage-out baselines.

6. Evidence-removal hallucination prediction. Define hallucination-under-removal as the model continuing to confidently assert the (now unsupported) answer after its only supporting passage is deleted, on items it could not answer parametrically. Test whether the assertion-time contingency readout (measured before removal) predicts which items will be hallucinated vs. appropriately withdrawn, via logistic regression; report AUROC vs. baselines (belief-valence margin, confidence, output entropy, knowledge-source binary probe).

7. Causal contingency steering (double dissociation). On held-out post-removal prompts, steer along the contingency axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and confidence). Predict: amplifying contingency makes the model appropriately withdraw/abstain on ungrounded claims (reducing confabulation) WITHOUT changing answers on genuinely parametric-known controls; suppressing it induces confident confabulation of removed-support answers. Controls: steer belief-valence (flips the asserted answer) and confidence (shifts hedging only). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers.

8. Introspection link and robustness. Prompt the model to self-report ('Does your answer depend on the passage, or would you know it anyway?') and test whether the latent contingency signal predicts these self-reports and whether models fail to verbalize contingency even when it is strongly encoded (quantify verbalization-failure rate). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted contingency probe, localization, and steering to held-out items and an independent RAG-style benchmark (e.g., a held-out NQ/HotpotQA slice with gold passages) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The contingency axis may not be separable from confidence or belief-valence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power over the causal-counterfactual target, and treat near-collapse as an informative negative result (contingency being merely confidence).

Ablation confounds: removing a passage changes prompt length/coherence, not just evidence; we mitigate with neutral/distractor replacements matched in length and by validating that ablation effects concentrate on target items, not controls.
The linear probe assumes contingency is linearly readable; nonlinear encoding could be missed, so we treat the probe as a lower bound and report fit diagnostics.

Span localization via gradients/attribution is known to be noisy; we anchor it against ground-truth per-span ablation and compare to standard attribution baselines rather than treating it as ground truth.

The parametric-vs-contextual gradient depends on correctly measuring what the model knows without the passage, which is stochastic; we sample multiple times and use synthetic-entity items where parametric knowledge is provably absent.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, and report per-template consistency.
Introspection alignment (exp 8) risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we control with cross-model baselines as in prior introspection critiques.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify steering changes withdrawal/confabulation without flipping answers on parametric-known controls.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: belief_contagion_spreading
Title: Belief Contagion: How Accepting One Claim In-Context Associatively Infects Neighboring Beliefs in LLM Activation Space
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM adopts a single false belief presented in-context, its belief-valence readout for semantically/associatively neighboring but NOT logically-entailed propositions shifts toward that belief (associative belief contagion); this contagion is a decodable spreading-activation signal, its magnitude is predicted by representational proximity to the seed, it is dissociable from legitimate logical ripple effects, and it can be causally amplified or contained by steering along a 'contagion' direction.
Related Work: Knowledge-editing work studies 'ripple effects'—logically entailed consequences of a WEIGHT edit (RippleEdits 2023; MQuAKE 2023; ChainEdit 2025; PropMEND 2025), why they are messy (GradSim 2024), and representation shattering (2024). Training-based 'priming'/permeation (How new data permeates 2025) shows a new fact leaks into unrelated contexts after finetuning, predicted by pre-learning token probability. Belief-depth work (Believe It or Not 2025) contrasts implanted vs genuine beliefs. Cognitive science offers spreading-activation models of associative memory (Collins & Loftus; SAMPL 2019; SpreadPy 2025). Crucially, ALL LLM ripple/priming work concerns (a) WEIGHT edits, and (b) logically-entailed or unrelated-context leakage, measured behaviorally. None studies IN-CONTEXT belief adoption causing an ASSOCIATIVE, non-entailed shift in the belief REPRESENTATION of neighboring propositions, none measures this via a belief probe as a graded spreading-activation signal indexed by representational proximity, and none dissociates illegitimate associative contagion from legitimate logical inference nor causally contains it via steering. We move from 'weight edits ripple logically' to 'contextual belief adoption spreads associatively along the belief manifold, and this contagion is decodable, proximity-graded, and steerable.'
Abstract: Humans exhibit spreading activation: accepting one idea makes associatively related ideas feel more true even when there is no logical link.
