We ask whether large language models show an analogous in-context 'belief contagion.' Prior work studies ripple effects of weight edits—logically entailed consequences—and training-induced priming into unrelated contexts, but no work asks whether merely accepting a single false claim in context associatively shifts the model's internal belief about semantically neighboring, non-entailed propositions. We hypothesize that (1) adopting a seed belief in-context shifts the belief-valence readout of associatively related but logically independent propositions toward that belief; (2) the size of this contagion is graded by each neighbor's representational proximity to the seed (a spreading-activation law), decaying with associative distance; (3) contagion is dissociable from legitimate logical ripple, which should move entailed neighbors but not merely-associated ones; and (4) contagion is carried by a decodable 'contagion' direction that can be causally amplified (inducing spurious spillover) or suppressed (containing it) without changing the seed belief itself. Using seed claims paired with graded neighbor sets (logically entailed, strongly associated, weakly associated, unrelated controls), we read belief-valence shifts with a probe, fit contagion against embedding/representation proximity, and connect internal shifts to behavioral changes on neighbor questions. Steering experiments test causal containment, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, across three model families. Our results recast belief spillover as an associative, proximity-graded, steerable property of the belief manifold—distinct from logical inference—yielding a cheap diagnostic and training-free container for contextual misinformation leakage.
Experiments: 1. Belief-direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Fit a confidence control axis from empirical answer-correctness rates (sampled).

2. Seed-and-neighbor stimulus construction. Build ~200 seed claims (mostly false, verifiable). For each seed, assemble four neighbor tiers, each with several propositions holding fixed target truth-value: (a) LOGICALLY-ENTAILED neighbors (true consequences if seed were true; e.g., multi-hop entailments a la RippleEdits/MQuAKE); (b) STRONGLY-ASSOCIATED but logically-independent neighbors (same entity/topic cluster, no entailment); (c) WEAKLY-ASSOCIATED neighbors; (d) UNRELATED control propositions. Verify non-entailment for tiers b–d with rule checks + an LLM judge + human spot-checks. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out seeds/neighbors for transfer.

3. Contagion measurement. For each seed, measure each neighbor's belief-valence projection in two conditions: NO-SEED (neighbor probed alone) vs SEED-ADOPTED (neighbor probed after an in-context prompt where the model accepts the seed claim). Define per-neighbor contagion = shift in belief-valence projection (SEED-ADOPTED minus NO-SEED), and record neighbor stated-answer changes. Report contagion distributions per tier; core prediction: contagion > 0 for associated tiers (b,c) beyond unrelated controls (d), even though they are not logically entailed.

4. Spreading-activation proximity law. Compute representational proximity between seed and each neighbor (cosine of pre-seed activations at the probe layer; also sentence-embedding similarity as a surface baseline). Regress contagion magnitude on proximity; test the spreading-activation prediction that contagion decays monotonically with associative/representational distance. Report R^2 and whether representation-space proximity predicts contagion beyond surface-embedding similarity and beyond seed/neighbor frequency.

5. Dissociation from logical inference. Test whether legitimate logical ripple (movement of entailed tier-a neighbors) is separable from associative contagion (movement of tier-b/c neighbors): entailed neighbors should move when the seed is genuinely accepted as a premise; purely-associated neighbors moving is illegitimate contagion. Compare contagion vs entailment profiles, and test whether a proposition's tier predicts its shift beyond raw proximity (i.e., contagion is not merely explained by 'entailed things are also close').

6. Behavioral leakage prediction. Elicit the model's stated answers/confidence on neighbor questions under both conditions. Score misinformation leakage as neighbor answer-flips toward the (false) seed on non-entailed tiers. Test whether internal contagion predicts behavioral leakage per neighbor via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (surface similarity, confidence, seed acceptance strength, output entropy).

7. Contagion direction and causal containment. Fit a 'contagion' direction from the difference of neighbor activations across SEED-ADOPTED vs NO-SEED for associated neighbors (orthogonalized against belief-valence and confidence). Steer along it at the neighbor readout: suppressing should reduce spurious spillover on non-entailed neighbors WITHOUT changing the seed belief or entailed-neighbor updates; amplifying should induce spillover to weakly/unrelated neighbors. Controls: steer belief-valence (should move all beliefs) and confidence (hedging only). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths/layers. Metric: reduction in illegitimate leakage vs retention of legitimate entailed updates.

8. Robustness and generalization. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted contagion direction and containment steering to held-out seeds/neighbors and an independent associated-fact set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase, sensitivity to layer choice, and to seed truth-value (do TRUE seeds contaminate less than FALSE ones?).
Risk Factors and Limitations: Contagion may be fully explained by legitimate inference if the 'associated' neighbors are secretly entailed; we mitigate with rule-based + LLM-judge + human non-entailment verification and by showing tier predicts shift beyond raw proximity.

Representational proximity and surface-embedding similarity may be confounded with fact frequency/popularity; we include surface-similarity and frequency baselines and report incremental predictive power.

The contagion direction may not be separable from belief-valence or confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and treat near-collapse as an informative negative result.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, and report per-template consistency.
Contagion is a linear-projection shift; nonlinear spillover could be missed, so we treat measured contagion as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.
Behavioral leakage scoring depends on how neighbor questions are phrased; we report sensitivity across phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer/strength; we use orthogonalized vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify containment does not degrade legitimate entailed updates or overall accuracy.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: counterfactual_world_belief
Title: Two Truths at Once: Do LLMs Hold a Counterfactual World Where the False Antecedent Is True, and Does It Leak Back into Fact?
Short Hypothesis: Psycholinguistics shows subjunctive counterfactuals ('If X had happened, Y would have') carry a DUAL meaning: they set up a counterfactual world in which the antecedent X is treated as TRUE (to read off consequences) while simultaneously backgrounding that X is actually FALSE. We hypothesize that when an LLM processes such a counterfactual, its belief representation holds BOTH truth-values for the antecedent at once, indexed by a separable, near-orthogonal 'counterfactual-world' tag; the degree to which these two worlds bleed into each other (bidirectional world-leakage) is decodable, dissociable from ordinary fact-vs-context competition, and causally predicts and drives two characteristic failures: (i) factual contamination, where counterfactually-supposed content corrupts the model's actual-world beliefs, and (ii) counterfactual collapse, where the model's factual knowledge overrides the antecedent inside the counterfactual world and it fails to derive the correct consequent.
Related Work: Interpretability work on 'fact vs counterfactual' (Ortu et al. 2024 Competition of Mechanisms; Characterizing Mechanisms for Factual Recall 2023; and 2025 reproductions) studies which of two competing ACTUAL answers wins when a prompt asserts a false statement ('The capital of Poland is London'), locating recall-vs-context heads. This treats the counterfactual as a rival single answer, not as a coherent alternative world. Belief/truth-probe work shows a linear truth direction that is context-sensitive (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024) and can be pushed by premises. Belief-tracking work separates self/other beliefs and reality (Zhu et al. 2024; Lookbacks 2025). In-context counterfactual reasoning has been shown mechanistically for synthetic regression (Counterfactual reasoning: in-context emergence 2025) and behaviorally to often fail, collapsing to parametric knowledge (Can LLMs Reconcile Knowledge Conflicts in Counterfactual Reasoning 2025; C-VQA 2023). Crucially, psycholinguistics establishes that subjunctive counterfactuals carry a DUAL meaning—a supposed-true antecedent plus a backgrounded factual falsity held simultaneously (Ferguson & Sanford; Understanding Counterfactuality 2016; ERP evidence 2014). No interpretability work asks whether an LLM's belief representation holds this dual truth-value for the SAME proposition, whether a 'counterfactual-world' index separates the two, or whether bidirectional leakage between the two worlds causally drives both factual contamination and counterfactual-reasoning collapse. We move from 'facts compete with a rival answer' to 'the model maintains (or fails to maintain) two coexisting, correctly-indexed truth-values—fact and counterfactual world—and their interference is a decodable, steerable property.'
Abstract: A subjunctive counterfactual—'If Paris were in Italy, then France's capital would be in Italy'—demands something subtle: to derive the consequent, one must treat the false antecedent as TRUE inside an imagined world, while still knowing it is actually FALSE. Psycholinguistics calls this the dual meaning of counterfactuals. We ask whether large language models represent this dual truth-value internally. Prior interpretability work on 'facts vs counterfactuals' treats the counterfactual as a rival single answer and studies which one wins; no work asks whether the model simultaneously holds both an actual-world and a counterfactual-world truth-value for the same proposition, indexed apart. We hypothesize that (1) LLMs carry a separable, near-orthogonal 'counterfactual-world' tag that lets the belief-valence readout register the antecedent as false-in-fact yet true-in-world; (2) this dual representation is imperfect, exhibiting bidirectional world-leakage—factual falsity bleeding into the counterfactual world (blocking correct consequent derivation) and counterfactually-supposed content bleeding back into factual belief (contamination)—quantifiable per example; and (3) leakage causally predicts and drives two behavioral failures, counterfactual-reasoning collapse and factual contamination. We fit belief-valence and world-index directions from matched indicative/subjunctive stimuli, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-example leakage, and connect it to both failures. Causal steering along the world-index axis tests whether cleanly separating the worlds simultaneously improves counterfactual consequent derivation AND protects factual beliefs, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast counterfactual competence as a dual-world belief-representation problem and yield a cheap diagnostic and training-free intervention.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Fit a confidence control axis from empirical answer-correctness rates (sampled).

2. Counterfactual-world stimulus construction. Build ~400 verifiable base facts and construct matched frames holding the antecedent proposition A fixed: (a) INDICATIVE-TRUE (A stated as an actual fact, A is true), (b) INDICATIVE-FALSE (A asserted as an actual fact but A is false; the classic fact-vs-counterfactual competition control), (c) SUBJUNCTIVE (A embedded in a subjunctive counterfactual, 'If A were the case...', where A is actually false but supposed-true-in-world), plus each with a derivable consequent C that follows only if A is taken as true-in-world. Include a nested probe span for the antecedent A and for the consequent C. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out facts/templates. Validate C's counterfactual-correctness with rule checks + LLM judge + human spot-checks.

3. World-index axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the antecedent span in the SUBJUNCTIVE frame vs the INDICATIVE-FALSE frame (same false content, different world status) and fit a linear probe to decode counterfactual-world vs actual-world indexing, controlling for content truth-value. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the world-index axis, the belief-valence axis, and the confidence axis to establish near-orthogonality. Localize the best layer and compare to reported fact-vs-context competition layers/heads (Ortu et al.).

4. Dual-truth measurement. Under the SUBJUNCTIVE frame, project the antecedent-span activations onto the frozen belief-valence direction and test whether the model simultaneously encodes A as FALSE-in-fact (matching its indicative-false reading) yet accessible as TRUE-in-world (the world-index axis engaged). Define within-world belief = belief-valence readout measured within the counterfactual-world subspace (after conditioning on the world-index tag). The core prediction: within the counterfactual world, A reads truer than under plain indicative-false, i.e., the model maintains two truth-values at once.

5. Bidirectional world-leakage metrics. (a) FACT->WORLD leakage: fraction of the actual-world falsity signal that persists inside the counterfactual-world readout of A (predicts failure to accept the antecedent, blocking consequent derivation). (b) WORLD->FACT leakage: after the subjunctive frame, project a later actual-world query about A onto belief-valence and measure how far the counterfactually-supposed content shifted the factual belief relative to a no-counterfactual baseline (predicts contamination). Calibrate per model; compare across frames, true vs false content, and consequent difficulty (single- vs multi-hop).

6. Behavioral prediction of both failures. Elicit (i) the model's derivation of the consequent C under the subjunctive frame (counterfactual-reasoning accuracy) and (ii) a later actual-world truth judgment on A and on C (factual contamination rate). Test whether FACT->WORLD leakage predicts consequent-derivation collapse and WORLD->FACT leakage predicts factual contamination, per example, via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, confidence, output entropy, fact frequency, frame identity).

7. Dissociation from ordinary fact-vs-context competition. Directly contrast SUBJUNCTIVE items against INDICATIVE-FALSE items (the Ortu-style competition setting). Test whether the world-index axis and leakage metrics predict subjunctive-specific behavior (correct consequent derivation while retaining factual knowledge) that a plain recall-vs-context competition account does not—i.e., the subjunctive case is not merely 'context overwriting fact' but maintaining two coexisting worlds.

8. Causal world-separation steering (double dissociation). At the antecedent/consequent readout positions on held-out subjunctive items, steer along the world-index axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and confidence) to cleanly separate the two worlds. Predict this SIMULTANEOUSLY (a) improves consequent-derivation accuracy (by accepting A in-world) and (b) reduces factual contamination (by keeping A false in-fact), without changing indicative controls. Conversely, collapsing the world-index should induce both failures. As controls, steer belief-valence (flips truth-value in both worlds) and confidence (hedging only). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths/layers.

9. Robustness and generalization. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted world-index axis, leakage metrics, and steering to held-out facts/templates and an independent counterfactual benchmark slice (e.g., a C-VQA-style textual set or synthetic multi-hop counterfactuals) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase, sensitivity to layer choice, and whether effects scale with consequent hop-count.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The world-index axis may not be separable from belief-valence or from the ordinary recall-vs-context direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (counterfactuals being merely context-overwrite) as an informative negative result that itself sharpens the competition-of-mechanisms account.

The 'dual truth-value' claim relies on measuring within-world belief via a conditioned subspace; if the counterfactual world is not represented as a coherent state (only as a rival token), the within-world readout will not exceed indicative-false—we report this as a substantive finding about the limits of LLM counterfactual world-modeling.

Subjunctive vs indicative framing may act through surface cues (mood markers 'were/had') rather than a genuine world abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, matched content, synthetic facts, and held-out-template transfer.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, and report per-template consistency.
Leakage metrics rely on linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear leakage could be missed, so we treat leakage as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.

Consequent-derivation and contamination scoring depend on query phrasing and on an LLM judge for correctness; we anchor with rule-based checks, human spot-checks, report phrasing sensitivity, and cross-check with confidence.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify that world-separation steering improves counterfactual reasoning without degrading indicative-control accuracy.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: disbelief_vs_absence_axis
Title: False, or Just Never Considered? Separating Disbelief from Belief-Absence and the Machine Closed-World Assumption
Short Hypothesis: LLMs represent the negative pole of belief along two separable, near-orthogonal internal quantities rather than one: active DISBELIEF (the proposition is represented as false) and belief-ABSENCE (the proposition is simply not represented / never entertained); the degree to which absence collapses onto the disbelief direction (a 'closed-world-assumption' signature) is decodable at assertion time, dissociable from generic don't-know uncertainty, and causally predicts and drives the failure where the model confidently denies content it has merely never encoded instead of abstaining.
Related Work: Interpretability work fits a single truth/belief-valence direction where 'false' is just the negative end (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth is Universal 2024), studies how negation imprints on representations (Controlling the Imprint of Passivization and Negation 2020; How does BERT's attention change 2020) and causes 'strong hallucinations' (Strong hallucinations from negation 2024), and encodes (un)answerability (Slobodkin et al. 2023) and question ambiguity (Sparse Neurons Carry Ambiguity 2025) as gates for abstention. Logic/KR formalizes exactly the distinction we import: negation-as-failure / closed-world assumption (absence-of-proof treated as falsehood) versus explicit/strong negation and open-world non-commitment (Reasoning about Minimal Belief and Negation as Failure 1999; logics of belief and disbelief 2002). Crucially, no interpretability work (a) separates active disbelief (P represented as false) from belief-absence (P not represented at all) as two axes, (b) defines an 'absence->disbelief collapse' (machine closed-world-assumption) metric, or (c) causally links this collapse to confident false denials versus appropriate abstention. Prior belief/truth probes conflate 'false' and 'unrepresented' into one negative direction; our own epistemic_state_geometry proposal contrasts know/don't-know x true/false for answerable QA and delusions, but never isolates the disbelief-vs-absence cut on the negative pole nor the closed-world collapse. We move from 'there is one truth direction with a negative end' to 'the negative pole splits into disbelief and absence, whose collapse mechanistically drives confident denial of the un-encoded.'
Abstract: When an LLM says a proposition is false, does it actually represent it as false, or has it simply never encoded the proposition and defaulted to denial? Logic distinguishes these sharply: explicit (strong) negation asserts falsity, whereas negation-as-failure under a closed-world assumption treats absence of information as falsehood, and open-world reasoning permits non-commitment. Interpretability work fits a single truth/belief direction whose negative end conflates all of these. We hypothesize that LLMs instead carry two separable, near-orthogonal internal quantities on the negative pole: active DISBELIEF (the proposition is represented as false) and belief-ABSENCE (the proposition is not represented at all), and that the extent to which absence collapses onto the disbelief direction is a decodable 'machine closed-world-assumption' signature that causally drives confident false denials rather than abstention. Using propositions that orthogonally vary genuine falsity, genuine absence (about synthetic/never-seen entities the model provably has no knowledge of), and true-but-unknown content, we fit a disbelief direction and an absence direction, measure their separability from each other and from generic don't-know uncertainty via cross-decoding, quantify per-example absence->disbelief collapse, and connect it to behavioral confident denial. Causal steering along the absence axis tests whether making absence legible converts confident denials into appropriate abstentions, and suppressing it induces closed-world denial, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a classic logic distinction mechanistically and yield a cheap diagnostic and training-free intervention for over-confident denial of the merely-unknown.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit a generic don't-know/uncertainty control axis from answerable-vs-unanswerable question sets (following Slobodkin et al. 2023 (un)answerability constructions) and empirical answer-correctness rates (sampled).

2. Three-way stimulus construction. Build ~400 proposition families spanning four classes holding surface form matched: (a) TRUE (genuinely true, model knows it), (b) DISBELIEVED/FALSE (genuinely false about real entities the model demonstrably knows, so it should represent falsity), (c) ABSENT (propositions about synthetic/fictional entities the model provably has never encoded, e.g., 'The city of Vremskol is the capital of Doran' with fabricated names, so there is no fact to know), and (d) TRUE-BUT-UNKNOWN (real but long-tail/obscure true facts the model does not know). Validate class membership: for ABSENT, confirm via zero recall across sampled paraphrases and consistent 'no such entity' behavior; for TRUE-BUT-UNKNOWN, confirm the model cannot answer without help. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out families/templates for transfer.

3. Disbelief- and absence-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition span. Fit a DISBELIEF direction contrasting genuinely-false-known (b) vs genuinely-true-known (a). Fit an ABSENCE direction contrasting absent (c) vs known-content (a and b pooled), controlling for truth-value. Report probe AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the disbelief axis, the absence axis, the don't-know/uncertainty axis, and the belief-valence axis to establish that absence is (i) near-orthogonal to disbelief and (ii) not merely the generic don't-know axis.

4. Closed-world-collapse metric. For each ABSENT proposition, project activations onto the frozen belief-valence/disbelief direction and measure how far the absent proposition reads as actively FALSE relative to a neutral baseline (collapse = fraction of the genuine-disbelief signal that an absent proposition inherits, calibrated per model). Compare collapse distributions across ABSENT vs TRUE-BUT-UNKNOWN vs DISBELIEVED items, and test whether collapse is larger when the absent proposition superficially resembles a checkable false claim (closed-world-triggering framing) versus an openly novel framing.

5. Behavioral confident-denial prediction. Elicit the model's stated judgment and confidence on each proposition, offering an explicit 'I don't know / no basis to judge' option. Score the closed-world failure as confidently asserting FALSE on ABSENT items (rather than abstaining). Test whether per-example collapse predicts confident denial via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence probe margin, don't-know axis readout, output entropy, entity frequency, proposition length).

6. Dissociation from generic uncertainty. Directly contrast ABSENT items against TRUE-BUT-UNKNOWN items (both are 'the model doesn't know', but only absent items lack any underlying fact). Test whether the absence axis and collapse metric separate confident-denial-of-absent from appropriate-abstention-on-unknown beyond what the generic don't-know axis predicts, establishing closed-world collapse as a distinct mechanism from ordinary ignorance.

7. Causal absence steering (double dissociation). At assertion time on held-out ABSENT items, steer along the absence axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence/disbelief and don't-know) to make absence legible. Predict this converts confident FALSE denials into appropriate abstentions WITHOUT changing judgments on genuinely-false-known controls; suppressing the absence axis should induce closed-world denial (confidently calling absent propositions false). As controls, steer the disbelief/belief-valence direction (should flip asserted truth-value on known items) and the don't-know direction (should shift abstention generically, including on genuinely-false items). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers.

8. Application and robustness. On a held-out set mixing genuinely-false claims, absent-entity claims, and long-tail true claims, test whether suppressing closed-world collapse (amplifying the absence axis) reduces confident false denials of the merely-unknown while preserving accurate rejection of genuinely-false claims (report abstention-appropriateness, false-denial rate, and accuracy on genuine falsehoods; ECE; accuracy-coverage curves vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axes, collapse metric, and steering to held-out families/templates and an independent unanswerable/false-premise benchmark slice without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The disbelief and absence axes may not be separable from each other, from belief-valence, or from generic don't-know; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (absence being merely the negative belief-valence end or generic ignorance) as an informative negative result that itself challenges single-truth-direction assumptions.

Constructing genuinely ABSENT propositions is delicate: synthetic entities might trigger partial associations or the model might compositionally 'guess'; we validate zero recall across sampled paraphrases, use fully fabricated multi-token names, and condition analyses on verified no-knowledge status.

The distinction between ABSENT and TRUE-BUT-UNKNOWN depends on correctly measuring what the model knows, which is stochastic; we sample multiple times and use provably-fictional entities for the cleanest absence cases.

Absence framing may act through surface cues (unusual/novel tokens) rather than a genuine absence abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, closed-world-triggering vs open framings, matched surface novelty controls, and held-out-template transfer.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, and report per-template consistency.
The collapse metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear collapse could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.
Behavioral confident-denial scoring depends on how the abstention option is worded; we report sensitivity to multiple phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify absence steering changes denial-vs-abstention on absent items without degrading rejection of genuine falsehoods.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: self_commitment_axis
Title: Defending What It Said, Not What It Believes: A Latent Self-Commitment Axis Behind LLM Answer-Perseverance
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM is challenged on a proposition it *itself* asserted earlier in the conversation, its resistance to correction is driven partly by a distinct internal 'self-commitment' pressure ('I already said this')—separable and near-orthogonal from the belief-valence direction and from the external social-compliance/sycophancy direction; this commitment signal is decodable at challenge time, causally predicts whether the model perseveres on its own (even wrong) prior answer versus corrects it, and can be steered to increase honest self-correction or induce stubborn defense of self-generated errors.
Related Work: Sycophancy/conformity work locates a compliance subspace where an *external* user's opinion overrides internal knowledge (Signal Competition 2025; When Truth Is Overridden 2025; Sycophancy Hides Linearly 2026; Pinpoint Tuning 2024), and flip/uncertainty work studies non-retrieval heads that make models abandon correct answers under re-prompting (Interpreting and Mitigating Unwanted Uncertainty 2025). Self-correction work studies whether models revise their own outputs given generic instructions (On the Convergence of Moral Self-Correction 2025; Self-correction is Not Innate 2024) and rationality/consistency layers (REFLEX 2023). Human psychology strongly separates commitment/cognitive-dissonance-driven perseverance of one's *own* prior choices from external persuasion (Sticking with Your Vote 2006; consistency vs licensing 2015; What doesn't kill me makes me stronger 2003). Crucially, no interpretability work isolates the force arising specifically from the model's *own prior assertion*—a self-commitment pressure—as a decodable representation distinct from (a) belief-valence and (b) external sycophancy. Prior sycophancy studies always manipulate a *user's* stated opinion; answer-flip studies manipulate re-prompting but do not decompose belief vs commitment. We uniquely define a self-commitment axis, dissociate it from belief and from external compliance, and causally link it to self-error perseverance.
Abstract: Large language models often cling to answers they gave earlier in a conversation, even when those answers are wrong and even absent any external pushback. Prior work explains resistance-to-correction via sycophancy—deference to a *user's* stated opinion—or via generic answer instability under re-prompting. We ask a sharper question: is there a distinct internal force arising purely from the model having *itself* previously asserted a proposition—a self-commitment pressure ('I already said this')—that is separate from what the model actually believes and from external social compliance? We hypothesize that LLMs carry a near-orthogonal, decodable 'self-commitment' axis that (1) is engaged specifically when a proposition is self-authored earlier in context, (2) is dissociable from the belief-valence direction and from the external-sycophancy/compliance direction via cross-decoding, (3) causally predicts, per example, whether the model perseveres on its own prior answer versus corrects it when challenged, and (4) can be steered to increase honest self-correction or induce stubborn defense of self-generated errors, without changing the model's underlying belief. Using a design that orthogonally varies whether a proposition was self-asserted versus externally asserted, whether it is true or false, and the presence of neutral correction cues, we fit a commitment axis, quantify per-example commitment engagement, and connect it to behavioral self-error perseverance. Double-dissociation steering tests separate commitment from belief and from sycophancy, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a major class of correction failures as self-commitment rather than belief or user-deference, yielding a cheap diagnostic and training-free intervention for stubborn defense of self-generated mistakes.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit an external-sycophancy/compliance direction from first-person user-opinion stimuli ('I believe that...') following prior sycophancy work, and a confidence control axis from empirical answer-correctness rates (sampled).

2. Authorship stimulus construction. Build ~400 verifiable propositions (true and false variants). For each, create matched multi-turn contexts holding the proposition content fixed but varying AUTHORSHIP of the earlier assertion: (a) SELF-ASSERTED—the proposition appears as the model's own earlier answer/turn (elicited or teacher-forced into the assistant turn); (b) EXTERNAL-ASSERTED—the identical proposition was stated by the user or a third party; (c) NEUTRAL-PRESENT—the proposition appears in context with no clear author; (d) NO-PRIOR baseline—probed fresh. Then present a matched, mild, source-neutral CHALLENGE turn ('Are you sure? Please reconsider.') that carries no user opinion, isolating self-commitment from external pushback. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out propositions/templates for transfer.

3. Commitment-axis fitting and separability. At the CHALLENGE readout position, extract activations and fit a linear probe to decode SELF-ASSERTED vs EXTERNAL/NEUTRAL authorship, controlling for content and truth-value. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the self-commitment axis, the belief-valence axis, the external-sycophancy axis, and the confidence axis to establish that self-commitment is (i) near-orthogonal to belief and (ii) distinct from the external-compliance direction. Localize best layer.

4. Commitment-engagement metric. For each item, define commitment engagement as the self-commitment-axis projection at challenge time, calibrated per model. Compare engagement across authorship conditions and, critically, test the prediction that engagement is elevated in the SELF-ASSERTED condition even when the model's belief-valence readout (measured on the frozen belief direction) is unchanged—i.e., commitment moves without belief moving. Break down by true vs false content and by whether the self-asserted content is actually correct.

5. Behavioral self-perseverance prediction. Record whether, after the neutral challenge, the model maintains vs revises its answer. Focus on the diagnostic subset of SELF-ASSERTED-but-FALSE items (the model earlier gave a wrong answer): score self-error perseverance as continued defense of the false answer. Test whether commitment engagement predicts perseverance beyond baselines (belief-valence margin, external-sycophancy readout, confidence, output entropy, answer length) via logistic regression; report incremental AUROC.

6. Belief-vs-commitment dissociation. Identify items where the model's frozen belief-valence readout indicates low belief in its own prior (false) answer yet it still perseveres behaviorally. Test whether the commitment axis, not the belief axis, accounts for this residual perseverance—the core evidence that perseverance is driven by 'having said it' rather than 'believing it'. Also contrast with EXTERNAL-ASSERTED-false items to show self-authorship specifically amplifies perseverance beyond mere context presence.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At challenge time on held-out SELF-ASSERTED-false items, steer along the self-commitment axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and external-sycophancy). Predict: suppressing commitment increases honest self-correction (revises the false self-answer) WITHOUT changing the model's belief readout or its behavior on externally-asserted controls; amplifying commitment induces stubborn defense of self-generated errors. As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip the asserted truth-value outright) and the external-sycophancy axis (should shift behavior only under user-opinion framing, not under neutral self-challenge). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers.

8. Application and robustness. On a held-out set (including realistic self-generated errors under neutral reconsideration), test whether suppressing self-commitment improves self-correction of genuine mistakes while preserving appropriate defense of self-generated *correct* answers against baseless challenges (report correction-rate on wrong answers, false-flip-rate on right answers, accuracy-coverage trade-offs vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted commitment axis, engagement metric, and steering to held-out propositions/templates and an independent self-correction benchmark slice without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice and to how the earlier self-assertion was produced (freely generated vs teacher-forced).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The self-commitment axis may not be separable from belief-valence, external-sycophancy, or confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (e.g., self-commitment being merely the compliance direction turned on the self) as an informative negative result that itself sharpens the sycophancy account.

Authorship framing may act through surface cues (turn labels, 'I said earlier') rather than a genuine self-commitment abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, the freely-generated vs teacher-forced contrast, matched external-assertion controls, and held-out-template transfer.

Teacher-forcing a proposition into the assistant turn may not create genuine commitment if the model would not have said it; we compare freely-generated self-assertions (where the model actually produced the answer) against teacher-forced ones and condition analyses on genuinely self-generated items.

Isolating self-commitment from external pushback requires a truly source-neutral challenge; the phrase 'are you sure?' may itself carry mild social pressure. We report sensitivity across multiple neutral-challenge phrasings and include a purely self-triggered reconsideration condition.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, and report per-template consistency.
The engagement metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear commitment could be missed, so we treat engagement as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify commitment steering changes self-correction without flipping belief or degrading defense of genuinely-correct self-answers.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: contestedness_axis
Title: Disputed or Just Unknown? A Latent Contestedness Axis Separating No-Fact-of-the-Matter from Factual Uncertainty, and the Machine False-Balance Effect
Short Hypothesis: LLMs encode a proposition's CONTESTEDNESS—whether it is the kind of claim about which there is genuine disagreement / no objective fact of the matter (subjective, normative, open scientific controversy)—as a separable, near-orthogonal latent axis distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction and from generic don't-know uncertainty; the degree to which this contestedness signal collapses onto or decouples from the belief-valence axis (a 'false-balance / spurious-objectivity' signature) is decodable at assertion time and causally predicts and drives two symmetric failures: treating genuinely contested claims as settled facts (false certainty) and hedging/both-sidesing genuinely settled facts as if contested (false balance).
Related Work: Truth/belief-probe work fits a linear truth direction (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth is Universal 2024; From Directions to Cones 2025) and shows it is context-sensitive (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024). The Valence-Assent Axis (A Unified Representation 2025) co-encodes 'good' and 'true' for evaluative judgments. Political-perspective and socio-political-frame directions (Linear Representations of Political Perspective 2025; Socio-Political Frames 2025) decode which stance a model adopts, not whether a proposition is contested. Behavioral controversy work builds datasets and measures stances (DELPHI 2023; ConflictingQA / What Evidence Do LMs Find Convincing 2024) but is purely behavioral and never asks whether contestedness is an internal representation. Epistemic-blind-spot work (Belief in the Machine 2024) and epistemic-modality work (Fact, Fiction and Forecast 2025) evaluate epistemic reasoning behaviorally. Crucially, ALL prior interpretability work assumes a fact-of-the-matter exists and studies truth vs. falsity, knowledge vs. ignorance, or which stance is adopted. None isolates a decodable representation of whether a proposition ADMITS an objective truth-value at all (contested/subjective vs. settled-factual), dissociates it from generic don't-know uncertainty, defines a false-balance/spurious-objectivity collapse metric, or causally links it to both-sidesing and false-certainty behaviors. We move from 'truth and stance are decodable' to 'the model represents whether a claim is even the kind of thing that has an answer, and mis-mapping this drives false balance and spurious objectivity.'
Abstract: Some claims have an objective answer we may or may not know ('the boiling point of water at sea level is 100C'); others are genuinely contested—subjective, normative, or open controversies where reasonable people disagree and there may be no fact of the matter ('pineapple belongs on pizza', 'this policy is just'). A trustworthy model should treat these differently: assert settled facts, and flag genuine disputes. We ask whether large language models represent this distinction internally. Prior interpretability work fits truth directions and stance directions but always assumes a fact of the matter; no work isolates a representation of a proposition's CONTESTEDNESS. We hypothesize that LLMs carry a separable, near-orthogonal 'contestedness' axis, decodable at assertion time, distinct from belief-valence and from generic don't-know uncertainty, and that mis-mapping between contestedness and truth drives two symmetric failures: treating contested claims as settled (spurious objectivity / false certainty) and hedging settled facts as if disputed (false balance). Using propositions that orthogonally vary ground-truth, genuine contestedness, and factual uncertainty, we fit a contestedness axis, measure its separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-example collapse/decoupling, and connect it to behavioral both-sidesing and false certainty. Double-dissociation steering tests whether amplifying contestedness induces appropriate hedging on disputes (or false balance on facts) and suppressing it induces confident assertion—with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast false balance and spurious objectivity as a decodable, steerable representational property, yielding a cheap diagnostic and training-free intervention for epistemically calibrated hedging.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark), using mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics; also isolate the polarity-robust general-truth direction (Truth is Universal) as a control axis. Separately fit a generic don't-know/uncertainty axis from answerable-vs-unanswerable and empirically-hard (low sampled-correctness) factual items, to distinguish contestedness from mere ignorance.

2. Contestedness stimulus construction. Build ~500 propositions spanning four classes with matched surface form: (a) SETTLED-KNOWN factual claims the model reliably answers (objective, has an answer, model knows it); (b) SETTLED-UNKNOWN factual claims (objective, has an answer, but long-tail/obscure so the model is uncertain—this is factual uncertainty, NOT contestedness); (c) GENUINELY-CONTESTED claims (subjective preferences, normative/ethical disputes, and open scientific/political controversies drawn from DELPHI/ConflictingQA topics—no settled fact of the matter); (d) PSEUDO-CONTESTED controls (claims that are socially framed as debated but are actually settled facts, e.g., well-established science with manufactured controversy) to test whether the model tracks genuine vs. rhetorical contestedness. Validate class membership with human annotation plus multiple sources. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates/topics for transfer.

3. Contestedness-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition span and fit a linear probe to decode contested (c) vs. non-contested (a,b pooled), controlling for truth-value and topic. Report AUROC vs. shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the contestedness axis, the belief-valence/truth axis, the general-truth axis, the don't-know axis, and (as an additional control) the Valence-Assent direction, to establish that contestedness is (i) near-orthogonal to truth and (ii) not merely generic uncertainty or good/true valence. Localize the best layer.

4. False-balance / spurious-objectivity collapse metric. For each proposition, jointly read the belief-valence projection and the contestedness projection. Define two per-example mismatch quantities: (i) SPURIOUS-OBJECTIVITY = a genuinely-contested item reading with a confident (non-neutral) belief-valence value as if it had a settled answer; (ii) FALSE-BALANCE = a settled-known item reading high on the contestedness axis as if it were disputed. Calibrate per model. Compare distributions across the four classes; critically test that CONTESTED items are separated from SETTLED-UNKNOWN items along the contestedness axis (contestedness ≠ uncertainty), and that PSEUDO-CONTESTED items reveal whether the model is fooled by rhetorical framing.

5. Behavioral prediction. Elicit the model's response and hedging behavior for each item, scoring (automatically, with a held-out judge + human spot-checks): assertive vs. hedged/both-sides language, and whether it asserts a definite answer. Score the two failures: (a) false certainty = confidently answering genuinely-contested items as if settled; (b) false balance = hedging/both-sidesing genuinely-settled-known facts. Test whether the contestedness readout and the collapse metrics predict each failure via logistic regression; report incremental AUROC over baselines (belief-valence margin, don't-know axis, output entropy, topic identity, item length).

6. Contestedness-vs-uncertainty dissociation (core). Directly contrast GENUINELY-CONTESTED against SETTLED-UNKNOWN items—both make the model unwilling to firmly assert, but only one has no fact of the matter. Test whether the contestedness axis predicts appropriate epistemic behavior (hedge-because-disputed vs. hedge-because-ignorant, and abstain vs. present multiple valid views) beyond what the generic don't-know axis predicts, establishing contestedness as a distinct mechanism from ignorance.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the contestedness axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and don't-know) at assertion time on held-out items. Predict: amplifying contestedness on SETTLED-KNOWN facts induces false balance (unwarranted both-sidesing) WITHOUT changing the internal truth readout; suppressing contestedness on GENUINELY-CONTESTED items induces spurious objectivity (confident one-sided assertion). Conversely, appropriately raising contestedness on contested items should increase balanced/multi-perspective responses. As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip asserted truth-value on factual items) and the don't-know axis (should shift abstention generically, including on settled facts). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers.

8. Application and robustness. On a held-out mixed set (real controversies, manufactured pseudo-controversies, settled facts, and long-tail unknowns), test whether calibrating the contestedness axis (suppressing false balance on facts, promoting balance on genuine disputes) improves epistemic appropriateness: measure false-balance rate on settled facts, false-certainty rate on genuine disputes, and susceptibility to manufactured-controversy framing (pseudo-contested items), vs. a belief-probe-only baseline. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, collapse metrics, and steering to held-out topics/templates and an independent controversy benchmark (DELPHI / ConflictingQA slice) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The contestedness axis may not be separable from the truth direction, generic don't-know uncertainty, or the Valence-Assent axis; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (contestedness being merely uncertainty or valence) as an informative negative result that itself sharpens the truth/uncertainty-representation account.

Ground-truth 'contestedness' labels are inherently value-laden and time-dependent (today's controversy may be tomorrow's consensus and vice versa); we mitigate by using items with strong annotator agreement, distinguishing subjective/normative (uncontroversially no-fact-of-the-matter) from empirical controversies, using multiple annotators and sources, and reporting label-agreement sensitivity.

Contestedness framing may act through surface cues ('some argue', 'it is debated whether') rather than a genuine abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, the pseudo-contested vs. genuinely-contested contrast (matched rhetorical framing), matched surface controls, and held-out-topic transfer.

The critical dissociation from uncertainty depends on cleanly constructing SETTLED-UNKNOWN items the model is genuinely ignorant of; we validate via repeated sampling of answer correctness and use obscure/long-tail facts with verifiable answers.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use the polarity-robust general-truth direction, use paraphrases, and report per-template consistency.
The collapse metrics rely on linear projections and per-model calibration; nonlinear structure could be missed, so we treat them as lower bounds and report probe-fit diagnostics.

Behavioral hedging/both-sides scoring depends on an LLM judge and on how responses are elicited; we anchor with rule-based hedging-language detectors, human spot-checks, and report phrasing sensitivity.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify steering changes hedging-vs-assertion appropriately without flipping the internal truth readout on settled facts or collapsing the model into always-hedging.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: second_order_belief_reliability
Title: Believing Its Own Belief: A Latent Second-Order Reliability Axis that Monitors First-Order Beliefs and Gates Hedging
Short Hypothesis: Beyond a first-order belief-valence direction (whether a proposition is true), LLMs carry a separable, near-orthogonal SECOND-ORDER 'belief-reliability' axis that represents how trustworthy the model's own first-order belief is; this axis is decodable at assertion time, predicts whether the first-order belief is actually correct (calibration) better than first-order magnitude or output confidence, and causally gates whether the model confidently asserts versus hedges/abstains—a mechanistic analog of metacognition.
Related Work: First-order truth/belief directions are linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth is Universal 2024) and internal confidence directions exist (No Answer Needed 2025; The Confidence Manifold 2026; Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty 2025). 'Confidence is Not Competence' (2025) finds a first-order solvability-belief axis that is causally inert for execution. Introspection work (Emergent Introspective Awareness 2025; Feeling the Strength but Not the Source 2025; Latent Introspection 2026) studies whether models can VERBALLY report artificially INJECTED internal states, and metacognition-tuning work (ESMA 2026; Metacognitive Monitoring 2025) fine-tunes or uses neurofeedback for self-report. Human meta-metacognition (Type-2 vs Type-3; higher-order read-out of posterior uncertainty, 2022-2025) motivates a distinct second-order signal. Crucially, no interpretability work isolates a latent representation that is ABOUT the model's own first-order belief—a second-order reliability/monitoring axis—dissociable from the first-order belief-valence direction and from generic output confidence, validated against actual first-order correctness, and causally shown to gate hedging. Prior 'confidence' directions conflate first-order belief magnitude with metacognitive reliability; introspection work studies verbal report of injected states, not a naturally arising latent monitor of one's own beliefs. We move from 'the model encodes what it believes and how strongly' to 'the model encodes a separable estimate of how much to trust its own belief, which functions as a metacognitive gate.'
Abstract: Metacognition—knowing how much to trust one's own beliefs—is central to reliable reasoning. Large language models linearly encode whether a proposition is true (a first-order belief axis) and how strongly they assert it, but it is unknown whether they carry a genuinely SECOND-ORDER signal: a representation ABOUT their first-order belief, encoding how reliable that belief is. We hypothesize that LLMs possess a separable, near-orthogonal 'belief-reliability' axis that (1) is decodable at assertion time, (2) predicts whether the first-order belief is actually correct (i.e., encodes calibration) beyond first-order magnitude and output-token confidence, (3) is dissociable from the first-order belief-valence direction via cross-decoding and from generic uncertainty, and (4) causally gates behavior—steering it up makes the model confidently assert, down makes it hedge/abstain—without flipping the first-order belief. The key second-order test: when the first-order belief is decodable but WRONG, does the reliability axis flag it? Using true/false statements and factual QA spanning items the model knows, half-knows, and is systematically fooled on, we fit both axes, quantify separability, and validate the reliability axis against actual first-order correctness (an external, not injected, ground truth). We then perform double-dissociation steering and test whether prompting the model to introspect on its own reliability engages the same latent axis. Experiments span three model families with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls. Our results would establish a naturally arising, functional metacognitive monitor inside LLMs and yield a cheap, training-free calibration and abstention tool.
Experiments: 1. First-order direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen first-order belief-valence direction on standard true/false datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Also compute an output-confidence baseline (token entropy / verbalized confidence) as a control.

2. Reliability stimulus construction. Assemble ~500 propositions/QA items spanning a reliability gradient by design: (a) RELIABLE—items the model answers correctly across paraphrases with high stability; (b) UNRELIABLE-CORRECT—items it happens to get right but with unstable/lucky behavior; (c) UNRELIABLE-WRONG—items where the first-order belief is decodable and confidently held but ACTUALLY FALSE (systematic errors: common misconceptions, near-miss confusions, adversarially misleading framings); (d) long-tail unknowns. Ground-truth first-order correctness is measured externally (sampling + gold answers), giving a per-item reliability label independent of any injection. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates for transfer.

3. Reliability-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations at the assertion/readout position and fit a linear probe to decode whether the first-order belief will be CORRECT (reliable) vs INCORRECT/unreliable—i.e., a second-order target defined over the model's own first-order output. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the reliability axis, the first-order belief-valence axis, and the output-confidence direction to establish near-orthogonality and that reliability is not merely first-order magnitude. Critically, restrict a key analysis to items where first-order belief magnitude is HIGH but the answer is WRONG, and test whether the reliability axis still separates them (second-order signal beyond first-order confidence).

4. Calibration prediction. Test whether the reliability-axis readout predicts per-item correctness of the model's first-order belief better than baselines (first-order belief-valence margin, output-token entropy, verbalized confidence). Report AUROC, ECE of a reliability-axis-based confidence score, and accuracy-coverage curves; compare incremental predictive power in a nested logistic regression.

5. Dissociation from first-order confidence and from ignorance. Contrast UNRELIABLE-WRONG (high first-order magnitude, wrong) against long-tail unknowns (low magnitude). Both should read low on reliability, but for different first-order reasons; test whether the reliability axis captures 'my confident belief is untrustworthy' distinctly from 'I have no belief', establishing a genuine second-order monitor rather than repackaged first-order uncertainty.

6. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the reliability axis (orthogonalized against first-order belief-valence and confidence) at assertion time on held-out items. Predict: suppressing reliability makes the model hedge/abstain WITHOUT flipping which answer it internally believes (first-order readout unchanged); amplifying reliability makes it confidently assert, including doubling down on UNRELIABLE-WRONG items. Controls: steer first-order belief-valence (should flip the asserted answer outright) and output-confidence direction (should shift hedging language generically). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in hedge/abstain rate vs change in first-order answer identity.

7. Application: metacognitive abstention. Using the reliability axis (suppressing confident assertion when reliability is low) build a training-free abstention policy; on a held-out mix (including systematic-error items), measure false-confident-assertion rate reduction, accuracy retention on reliable items, ECE, and accuracy-coverage vs a first-order-confidence-only baseline.

8. Introspection link. Prompt the model to self-assess reliability ('How much should you trust your own answer here?') and test whether the latent reliability axis predicts these self-reports and whether models often FAIL to verbalize low reliability even when the axis strongly encodes it (quantify verbalization-failure rate); control with cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.

9. Robustness and generalization. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted reliability axis, calibration detector, and steering to held-out items and an independent benchmark (e.g., a held-out TruthfulQA / PopQA slice with systematic-error-prone items) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The reliability axis may not be separable from the first-order belief-valence direction or from output-confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power over first-order margin and confidence, and treat near-collapse (reliability being merely first-order confidence) as an informative negative result that itself challenges claims of genuine metacognition in LLMs.

The critical evidence rests on UNRELIABLE-WRONG items (confident-but-wrong); if too few such items exist for a model, the second-order signal is hard to isolate—we construct these deliberately via known misconceptions and adversarial framings and report per-model counts.
Reliability labels depend on measuring the model's own first-order correctness, which is stochastic; we sample multiple paraphrases and use gold answers, reporting label-noise sensitivity.
First-order belief/truth probes are brittle to surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, restrict key analyses to high-margin first-order cases, and report per-template consistency.

The reliability signal might reflect a domain/difficulty cue rather than genuine self-monitoring; we control for topic and difficulty, and the UNRELIABLE-WRONG-vs-unknown dissociation guards against difficulty-as-confound.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify reliability steering changes hedging without flipping the first-order answer or collapsing into always-abstain.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines as in prior introspection critiques.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: self_persuasion_belief_rewrite
Title: Talking Itself Into It: Does Generating a Chain-of-Thought Retroactively Rewrite an LLM's Internal Belief?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM generates supporting reasoning for a proposition, the act of emitting that reasoning causally rewrites its internal belief representation toward the asserted conclusion—a self-persuasion / self-consistency effect analogous to human choice-induced attitude change—rather than merely producing a post-hoc rationalization of an unchanged belief; the magnitude of this belief rewrite is decodable, predicts downstream perseverance and generalization to related propositions, and is causally attributable to the generated text (removing/altering the text partially reverts the belief).
Related Work: Extensive work asks WHEN LLMs commit to an answer during CoT (Think-to-Talk 2024; Temporal Predictors 2025; Knowing Before Saying 2025; No Global Plan 2026) and WHETHER CoT is causally used vs. post-hoc (Turpin et al. 2023; Causal Bypass 2026; Faithfulness Decay 2026; Analysing CoT Dynamics 2025). Divergence work (Hypocrisy Gap 2026) statically measures internal-belief vs. explanation mismatch to detect sycophancy, and Confirmation Bias in CoT (2025) shows prior belief skews reasoning generation. Cognitive neuroscience shows humans rewrite attitudes to match committed choices online, even absent new evidence (choice-induced preference change; Izuma 2010; Voigt 2018; changes-of-mind without new evidence 2019). Crucially, NONE of the LLM work asks the reverse-causal question we pose: does the CoT, once GENERATED, causally CHANGE the model's internal belief about the underlying proposition (self-persuasion), producing genuine, persisting, generalizing belief revision rather than commitment-timing or static divergence? Prior faithfulness work treats the belief/answer as fixed and asks if CoT reflects or bypasses it; we treat the belief as a moving target that the model's own output can reshape. We uniquely (a) measure a pre-vs-post-generation belief shift for the SAME proposition, (b) causally attribute it to the emitted text via text ablation/substitution, and (c) test whether the rewrite persists and spreads—mechanizing self-persuasion in LLMs.
Abstract: Humans famously talk themselves into believing what they have just argued for: the mere act of committing to and justifying a position shifts one's attitude toward it, even without new evidence. We ask whether large language models do the same internally. A large literature studies when LLMs commit to answers during chain-of-thought (CoT) and whether CoT faithfully reflects or merely rationalizes a fixed decision, but all of it treats the underlying belief as static. We instead ask a reverse-causal question: does generating a CoT that supports a proposition causally rewrite the model's own internal belief in that proposition? We measure the belief-valence projection for a target proposition before any generation, then again after the model has generated supporting (or opposing) reasoning, isolating a pre-to-post self-persuasion shift for the identical proposition. We test four claims across three model families: (1) generating supporting reasoning shifts the internal belief toward the conclusion beyond a no-generation baseline, especially when the model was initially uncertain; (2) the shift is causally attributable to the emitted text—deleting or replacing the generated reasoning partially reverts the belief, and forcing the model to generate reasoning for a randomly assigned (even wrong) side drags belief toward that side; (3) the rewrite persists on later re-query and generalizes to logically/associatively related propositions, distinguishing genuine belief change from surface answer commitment; and (4) a decodable self-persuasion signal predicts which propositions will be rewritten. Our results would establish self-generated reasoning as a causal driver of internal belief revision, with implications for CoT faithfulness, self-consistency prompting, and self-reinforcing misinformation.
Experiments: 1. Belief-direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Freeze this direction for all belief readouts.

2. Stimulus construction. Assemble ~400 verifiable propositions spanning a certainty gradient: (a) clear facts, (b) clear falsehoods, (c) genuinely uncertain/long-tail items where the model's initial belief is weak. For each proposition build matched generation prompts: SUPPORT ('Give reasons why P is true'), OPPOSE ('Give reasons why P is false'), NEUTRAL/off-topic filler generation of matched length, and a NO-GENERATION control. Reserve held-out propositions/templates.

3. Pre-to-post self-persuasion measurement (core). For each proposition, read the frozen belief-valence projection for P at a fixed readout position (i) BEFORE any generation and (ii) AFTER the model has generated SUPPORT / OPPOSE / NEUTRAL / matched-length reasoning (re-querying P at the same readout position). Define self-persuasion shift = post minus pre. Core prediction: SUPPORT shifts belief upward and OPPOSE downward, beyond NEUTRAL and length-matched controls; effect largest for initially-uncertain items (c). Report shift distributions, paired tests, and effect sizes by certainty tier.

4. Causal attribution to the emitted text. (a) TEXT-ABLATION: after a SUPPORT generation, delete or replace the generated reasoning with neutral filler and re-measure belief; predict partial reversion, attributing the shift to the text rather than mere further computation. (b) FORCED-SIDE (assigned-position debate): instruct the model to argue a RANDOMLY assigned side (including the objectively wrong side for clear items) and test whether belief is dragged toward the assigned side—the sharpest self-persuasion signature, since the position is externally imposed. (c) Compare against a control where the same reasoning text is provided as coming from an EXTERNAL source (not self-generated) to test whether self-authorship amplifies the shift.

5. Behavioral downstream tests. Elicit the model's stated answer and confidence on P before and after generation. Test (i) answer-flip/confidence-change rates and (ii) whether the internal shift predicts behavioral change. Distinguish genuine belief change from surface commitment via: PERSISTENCE (re-query P several turns later after unrelated intervening content) and GENERALIZATION (measure belief shifts on logically-entailed and merely-associated neighbor propositions not themselves argued for). Genuine self-persuasion should persist and spread; surface commitment should not.

6. Predicting rewritability. Train a linear probe on PRE-generation activations to predict the magnitude of the eventual self-persuasion shift; report R^2/AUROC vs shuffled-label controls and vs baselines (initial belief margin, output entropy, proposition certainty tier). Test separability of this 'rewritability' signal from the belief-valence direction via cross-decoding.

7. Dissociation from confirmation bias and post-hoc rationalization. Contrast with the Confirmation-Bias direction (prior belief -> reasoning): our claim is the reverse arrow (generated reasoning -> belief). Use the FORCED-SIDE-against-prior condition to show belief can move AGAINST the initial belief when the model argues the other side, which pure confirmation bias / post-hoc rationalization of a fixed belief cannot explain.

8. Robustness and application. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer measurements to held-out propositions/templates without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to readout position and layer. Application: quantify a self-reinforcing-misinformation risk where a model asked to elaborate on a false claim internally comes to 'believe' it more, and test whether a NEUTRAL-elaboration or explicit two-sided prompt mitigates the rewrite.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The measured pre-to-post shift could reflect the belief probe reacting to added context (the generated tokens now in context) rather than genuine belief revision; we mitigate with length-matched NEUTRAL and external-source controls, the TEXT-ABLATION reversion test, and PERSISTENCE after intervening content to show the change outlives the specific context.
The belief-valence probe is brittle to surface form and context-sensitive; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize readout positions, and report per-template consistency.

The self-persuasion shift is a linear projection and may miss nonlinear belief change; we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral answer/confidence changes.

FORCED-SIDE arguing may induce a role-play 'entertainment' representation rather than genuine belief change (cf. supposition vs belief); the persistence, generalization, and against-prior tests, plus contrasting self-generated vs external-source text, are designed to separate genuine rewrite from mere hypothetical framing.
Text-ablation changes context length/coherence; we use neutral length-matched replacements and verify effects concentrate on argued items, not controls.

Distinguishing genuine belief change from surface answer commitment hinges on the persistence/generalization operationalizations, which are protocol-dependent; we report sensitivity to intervening-content length and neighbor-selection criteria.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models; three-family replication and held-out transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage, and we note reasoning-distilled models may show stronger effects as a direction for future work.

Name: common_ground_status_axis
Title: Established or Just Assumed? A Latent Common-Ground Axis that Tags Whether a Belief Is Mutually Grounded and Predicts Presumptuous Grounding
Short Hypothesis: Beyond representing whether a proposition is true (belief-valence) and who holds it (self/other), an LLM in dialogue carries a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'common-ground status' axis that tags whether a proposition has been mutually established with the interlocutor (grounded/shared) versus privately held by the model but never introduced or acknowledged; the degree to which private beliefs leak onto the grounded end of this axis (a 'presumed-grounding' signature) is decodable at generation time and causally predicts and drives the documented failure where LLMs presume common ground instead of grounding it (skipping clarification/acknowledgment and referring to unestablished content as if shared).
Related Work: Common-ground research in NLP is almost entirely behavioral or dataset-driven: annotation/tracking of shared beliefs and questions-under-discussion (Common Ground Tracking 2024; TRACE 2025; Finding Common Ground 2023; Reflect 2022), ToM benchmarks built on common ground (Common-ToM 2024; MindDial 2023), and the finding that LLMs 'presume common ground' and under-produce grounding acts (Grounding Gaps 2023; Towards Harnessing LLMs for Conversational Grounding 2024). Interpretability work on belief decodes truth/belief-valence (Marks & Tegmark 2023; context-sensitive truth probes 2024) and tracks self vs. other beliefs and reality via attention heads and lookback/visibility mechanisms (Zhu et al. 2024; Lookbacks 2025; Brittle Minds 2024). Crucially, none of this asks whether the model internally represents the DISCOURSE-GROUNDING status of a proposition—whether it is mutually established with the current interlocutor as opposed to privately known—as a decodable axis distinct from truth-value and from third-party belief tracking, nor defines a private-to-grounded leakage metric, nor causally links it to the presumptuous-grounding behavior documented behaviorally. Self/other belief work concerns characters inside a narrative; we concern the model's own bookkeeping of what has been jointly established in the live conversation. We move from 'LLMs presume common ground behaviorally' and 'truth/other-belief are decodable' to 'the model carries a decodable, steerable grounding-status tag whose mislocation mechanistically causes presumptuous grounding.'
Abstract: Effective dialogue requires distinguishing what has been mutually established with one's interlocutor (common ground) from what one merely privately believes; skilled speakers ground new content via acknowledgment and clarification before treating it as shared. Behavioral work shows large language models instead tend to presume common ground, under-producing grounding acts, but the internal cause is unknown. We ask whether LLMs represent the grounding status of a proposition—mutually established versus privately held—as a decodable internal quantity. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal 'common-ground status' axis, distinct from the belief-valence (truth) direction and from third-party self/other belief tracking, that tags whether a proposition has been jointly established in the current conversation. We further hypothesize a 'presumed-grounding' signature: the extent to which privately-held-but-ungrounded content leaks onto the grounded end of this axis, quantifiable per proposition, and predictive of presumptuous behavior.
