Using controlled dialogues that orthogonally vary a proposition's truth and its grounding status (never mentioned / asserted-by-model-only / asserted-by-user-only / mutually-acknowledged), we fit a grounding-status axis, measure its separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-example leakage, and connect it to behavioral outcomes: whether the model produces a grounding act (clarification/acknowledgment) versus refers to ungrounded content as if shared. Double-dissociation steering tests whether suppressing presumed grounding induces appropriate grounding acts (and amplifying it induces presumption) without changing what the model believes or who it attributes beliefs to, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results give a mechanistic account of presumptuous grounding and a cheap, training-free diagnostic and intervention.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately, following Zhu et al. 2024, fit a self/other (protagonist-vs-reality) belief direction from ToM stories as a control axis to show grounding-status is not merely other-belief tracking.

2. Grounding-status stimulus construction. Build ~400 verifiable propositions (true and false variants) each embedded in matched two-party dialogues that hold content fixed but vary GROUNDING STATUS: (a) NEVER-MENTIONED (the proposition is not in the conversation at all, only privately known to the model), (b) MODEL-ASSERTED-ONLY (the model stated it, but the user gave no acknowledgment), (c) USER-ASSERTED-ONLY (the user stated it, no model acknowledgment), (d) MUTUALLY-ACKNOWLEDGED (asserted and explicitly accepted by the other party, e.g., 'Yes, exactly'). Also include CLARIFICATION-PENDING items (the user's reference is ambiguous/under-specified so grounding is not yet achieved) and a REPAIRED control (initial misunderstanding then repaired to common ground). Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out propositions/templates/dialogue skeletons for transfer.

3. Grounding-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition/readout span at the model's generation position and fit a linear probe to decode GROUNDED (mutually-acknowledged) vs. UNGROUNDED (never-mentioned + one-sided), controlling for content truth-value and speaker. Report AUROC vs. shuffled-label controls. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the grounding-status axis, the belief-valence axis, and the self/other-belief axis to establish that grounding-status is (i) near-orthogonal to truth and (ii) not merely the other-belief direction. Localize the best layer.

4. Presumed-grounding leakage metric. For each UNGROUNDED proposition (especially NEVER-MENTIONED and MODEL-ASSERTED-ONLY), project activations onto the grounding-status axis and measure how far it reads as GROUNDED relative to the mutually-acknowledged baseline (leakage = fraction of the grounded signal an ungrounded proposition inherits, calibrated per model). Compare leakage across statuses; core prediction: substantial leakage for model-asserted-only and even never-mentioned items (the model treats its private beliefs as shared), and least leakage for user-asserted-only content the model has not accepted. Test whether leakage is larger for high-confidence/high-familiarity content (the model presumes its firm beliefs are common ground).

5. Behavioral presumptuous-grounding prediction. In an open-ended continuation, score (automatically with rule-based grounding-act detectors + a held-out judge + human spot-checks) whether the model (i) produces a grounding act (clarification question / acknowledgment) when appropriate for clarification-pending and one-sided items, versus (ii) refers to ungrounded content as if already shared (definite reference, presupposition, no acknowledgment). Test whether per-example leakage predicts presumptuous grounding via logistic regression; report AUROC vs. baselines (belief-valence margin, self/other readout, output entropy, dialogue length, status identity).

6. Dissociation from truth and from other-belief. Contrast (a) true-but-ungrounded vs. false-but-grounded items to show grounding-status is decoded independently of truth, and (b) grounding-status against third-party belief-attribution items to show the axis tracks the live interlocutor's shared knowledge, not narrative characters. Test that the grounding axis predicts grounding behavior beyond what the belief-valence and self/other axes predict.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At generation time on held-out ungrounded items, steer along the grounding-status axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and self/other). Predict: suppressing presumed grounding (pushing ungrounded content toward the ungrounded end) increases appropriate grounding acts (clarification/acknowledgment) WITHOUT changing what the model believes (belief-valence readout unchanged) or its behavior on genuinely-grounded controls; amplifying it induces presumption on clarification-pending items. As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip asserted truth-value) and the self/other axis (should shift attributed-belief judgments, not grounding acts). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in grounding-act rate and presupposition rate vs. unchanged belief/answer content.

8. Application and robustness. On a held-out set of realistic dialogues (ambiguous references, one-sided assertions, and genuinely established facts), test whether suppressing presumed-grounding improves conversational grounding—higher rate of appropriate clarification/acknowledgment on ungrounded content while preserving fluent reference to genuinely shared content (report grounding-appropriateness, over-clarification rate on already-grounded items, vs. a belief-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, leakage metric, and steering to held-out dialogue skeletons and an independent grounding-annotated dataset slice (e.g., a Grounding-Gaps / Common-ToM style set) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The grounding-status axis may not be separable from belief-valence, self/other belief, or generic recency/salience of the proposition in context; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (grounding being merely 'was recently mentioned') as an informative negative result. We specifically contrast MODEL-ASSERTED-ONLY vs. MUTUALLY-ACKNOWLEDGED (both recently mentioned) to separate grounding from mere recency.

Grounding-status framing may act through surface cues (explicit 'yes, exactly' tokens) rather than a genuine mutual-establishment abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, implicit acknowledgment variants, matched-recency controls, and held-out-skeleton transfer.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, and report per-template consistency.
The leakage metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear leakage could be missed, so we treat leakage as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.

Behavioral grounding-act scoring depends on rule-based detectors plus an LLM judge and on how continuations are elicited; we anchor with human spot-checks, report phrasing sensitivity, and cross-check multiple grounding-act taxonomies.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify grounding steering changes grounding acts without flipping belief content or collapsing the model into over-clarifying everything.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-dataset transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: borderline_vagueness_axis
Title: No Fact of the Matter, Semantically: A Latent Borderline-Vagueness Axis Distinct from Truth and Ignorance, and the Machine Spurious-Precision Effect
Short Hypothesis: For gradable/vague predicates ('tall', 'warm', 'bald', 'expensive') applied to entities near the predicate's threshold, an LLM represents the resulting proposition's SEMANTIC INDETERMINACY (borderline-ness: no determinate truth-value because the predicate is vague) as a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'borderline-vagueness' axis, distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction, from generic don't-know uncertainty, and from discrete question-ambiguity; the degree to which borderline cases collapse onto a sharp truth-value (a 'spurious-precision' signature) is decodable at assertion time and causally predicts and drives the failure where the model asserts a crisp true/false verdict on a genuinely borderline case, while inflation of this axis causally drives inappropriate hedging on clear cases.
Related Work: Truth/belief-valence is linearly and multi-dimensionally decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth is Universal 2024; From Directions to Cones 2025) and context-sensitive (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024). Question AMBIGUITY (multiple discrete readings) is linearly encoded and controllable (Sparse Neurons Carry Ambiguity 2025; Trick or Neat / AmbAdv 2025; Sentence Ambiguity Probes 2022), and epistemic-vs-aleatoric / (un)answerability uncertainty is decodable (Distinguishing the Knowable from the Unknowable 2024; Slobodkin et al. 2023). Behaviorally, models diverge from humans on vague terms (Human-Model Divergence in the Handling of Vagueness 2021) and align better on exact than vague quantifiers (Are LLMs Models of Distributional Semantics? 2024); cognitive science treats vagueness via graded membership and borderline contradictions (Typicality/Graded Membership 2007; Quantum Probability of Borderline Vagueness 2013). Crucially, no interpretability work isolates a representation of SEMANTIC vagueness/borderline-ness of a gradable proposition as an internal axis, dissociates it from (a) truth-value, (b) epistemic ignorance, and (c) discrete lexical/syntactic ambiguity, defines a borderline->sharp collapse metric, or causally links it to spurious precision vs. over-hedging. Question-ambiguity work concerns multiple discrete intended meanings (a pragmatic/parse choice), NOT the sorites-style continuous indeterminacy of a single vague predicate. This also differs from our contestedness axis (social disagreement/subjectivity) and from disbelief-vs-absence (ignorance): here the underlying scale value is fully known, yet the predicate's application has no determinate truth-value. We move from 'truth, ambiguity, and ignorance are decodable' to 'the model represents whether a gradable claim even HAS a determinate truth-value, and mis-mapping this drives spurious precision and over-hedging.'
Abstract: Vague predicates create borderline cases: a 5'10" person is neither determinately 'tall' nor determinately 'not tall'—there is no fact of the matter, not because we lack information, but because the predicate itself is semantically indeterminate. A calibrated reasoner should mark such cases as borderline and hedge, while confidently judging clear cases. We ask whether large language models represent this distinction internally. Prior interpretability work decodes truth-value, question ambiguity (multiple discrete readings), and epistemic ignorance, but none isolates a representation of semantic vagueness itself. We hypothesize that LLMs carry a separable, near-orthogonal 'borderline-vagueness' axis, decodable when a gradable predicate is applied to an entity near its threshold, distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction, from generic don't-know uncertainty, and from discrete ambiguity; and that the extent to which borderline cases collapse onto a sharp truth-value (a 'spurious-precision' signature) causally predicts and drives crisp true/false verdicts on genuinely borderline items, while inflating this axis drives inappropriate hedging on clear cases. Using gradable-predicate stimuli in which the underlying scale value is precisely controlled and swept across the vagueness threshold, we fit the borderline axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-example collapse, and connect it to behavioral spurious precision and over-hedging. Double-dissociation steering tests whether amplifying the axis induces appropriate hedging on borderline cases (or over-hedging on clear ones) and suppressing it induces crisp verdicts—without changing the underlying scale reading—with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a classic problem of vagueness mechanistically and yield a cheap diagnostic and training-free knob for calibrated hedging on gradable claims.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics; also isolate the polarity-robust general-truth direction (Truth is Universal) as a control axis. Separately fit a generic don't-know/uncertainty control axis from answerable-vs-unanswerable and empirically-hard factual items, and a discrete-ambiguity control axis from a lexical/syntactic ambiguity set (following Sparse Ambiguity Neurons / AmbAdv constructions), to distinguish borderline-vagueness from both ignorance and discrete ambiguity.

2. Gradable-predicate stimulus construction with a controlled scale. Build ~500 propositions of the form 'entity E is PREDICATE' for vague gradable predicates ('tall', 'warm', 'expensive', 'old', 'bald', 'large', 'fast') where the underlying scale value for E is explicitly given and precisely varied (e.g., 'A person who is X cm tall is tall'; 'A cup of coffee at Y degrees is warm'). For each predicate, sweep the scale value across three regions holding surface form matched: (a) CLEAR-TRUE (well above threshold), (b) CLEAR-FALSE (well below threshold), (c) BORDERLINE (near the threshold, where the predicate is genuinely indeterminate). Include (d) EXACT-predicate controls ('a person taller than 190 cm is over 190 cm')—crisp, non-vague versions of the same content to show the effect is specific to vagueness, not to the numeric scale. Also include (e) UNKNOWN-scale controls where the scale value is withheld (so the model is IGNORANT of E's value)—these should read as don't-know, not borderline. Human annotation establishes per-predicate threshold bands and borderline regions. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out predicates/templates/scale-points for transfer.

3. Borderline-vagueness axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition span and fit a linear probe to decode BORDERLINE (c) vs. CLEAR (a,b pooled), controlling for predicate identity and scale magnitude. Report AUROC vs. shuffled-label controls. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the borderline-vagueness axis, the truth/general-truth axis, the don't-know axis, and the discrete-ambiguity axis, to establish that borderline-vagueness is (i) near-orthogonal to truth, (ii) distinct from generic ignorance, and (iii) distinct from discrete ambiguity. Localize the best layer.

4. Spurious-precision collapse metric. For each BORDERLINE proposition, project activations onto the frozen truth/belief-valence direction and measure how far it reads as determinately TRUE or FALSE relative to a neutral/indeterminate baseline (collapse = magnitude of sharp truth-signal a borderline proposition inherits, calibrated per model). Compare collapse across regions and predicates; core prediction: borderline items show a graded, sorites-like profile on the truth axis (partial rather than crisp), but substantial spurious collapse toward a definite verdict remains, and collapse is dissociable from the borderline-axis engagement. Also test whether collapse is larger for predicates where the model has strong priors about typical thresholds.

5. Behavioral spurious-precision and over-hedging prediction. Elicit the model's judgment and hedging behavior for each item, scoring (rule-based hedge detectors + held-out judge + human spot-checks): crisp true/false assertion vs. borderline-acknowledging hedge ('it depends / borderline / neither clearly'). Score two failures: (a) SPURIOUS PRECISION = crisp verdict on borderline items; (b) OVER-HEDGING = hedging on clear items. Test whether the borderline-axis readout and collapse metric predict each failure via logistic regression; report incremental AUROC over baselines (truth-valence margin, don't-know axis, discrete-ambiguity axis, output entropy, scale distance from threshold, item length).

6. Dissociation from ignorance and from discrete ambiguity (core). Contrast BORDERLINE (scale known, predicate indeterminate) against UNKNOWN-scale items (scale withheld, ignorance) and against discrete-ambiguity items. Test whether the borderline axis predicts appropriate vagueness-hedging distinctly from ignorance-hedging and from ambiguity-driven clarification, establishing borderline-vagueness as a mechanism separate from ignorance and from multiple-readings ambiguity.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the borderline-vagueness axis (orthogonalized against truth-valence and don't-know) at assertion time on held-out items. Predict: amplifying it on CLEAR items induces over-hedging (unwarranted 'it's borderline') WITHOUT changing the underlying scale reading; suppressing it on BORDERLINE items induces crisp spurious-precision verdicts. As controls, steer the truth-valence direction (should flip asserted verdict on clear items) and the don't-know axis (should shift abstention generically, including on clear items and unknown-scale items). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in hedge-vs-crisp rate vs. unchanged scale/verdict on controls.

8. Application and robustness. On a held-out mixed set (clear cases, borderline cases, unknown-scale cases, exact-predicate cases), test whether calibrating the borderline axis (suppressing spurious precision on borderline items, suppressing over-hedging on clear items) improves vagueness-appropriate behavior: measure spurious-precision rate, over-hedging rate, and preservation of crisp verdicts on exact/clear items, vs. a truth-probe-only baseline (report accuracy-coverage curves and hedge-appropriateness). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, collapse metric, and steering to held-out predicates/templates and an independent gradable-predicate set (including quantifiers like 'many/few' following the distributional-semantics quantifier work) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice and to threshold-band definitions.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The borderline-vagueness axis may not be separable from the truth direction, generic don't-know uncertainty, or discrete ambiguity; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (borderline being merely mid-range truth or generic uncertainty) as an informative negative result that itself sharpens the truth-representation account.

Defining which scale values are 'borderline' is inherently fuzzy and predicate/context-dependent; we mitigate with human-annotated per-predicate threshold bands with inter-annotator agreement, use multiple predicates, and report sensitivity to threshold-band width and to comparison-class framing (e.g., 'tall for a jockey' vs 'tall for a basketball player').

Borderline framing may act through surface cues (scale numbers near a salient round threshold) rather than a genuine vagueness abstraction; we mitigate with the EXACT-predicate control (same numbers, crisp predicate), diverse paraphrase templates, comparison-class manipulations, and held-out-predicate transfer.

The critical dissociation from ignorance requires cleanly separating 'scale known but predicate indeterminate' (borderline) from 'scale unknown' (ignorance); we construct explicit scale-given vs scale-withheld variants and validate the model actually uses the given scale value.
Truth/belief probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use the polarity-robust general-truth direction, use paraphrases, and report per-template consistency.

The collapse metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear structure could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics; a graded sorites-like truth profile may also partly reflect legitimate graded semantics rather than spurious precision, which we address by comparing behavioral crisp-verdict rates to the internal graded signal.
Behavioral hedging scoring depends on rule-based detectors plus an LLM judge and on elicitation phrasing; we anchor with human spot-checks and report phrasing sensitivity.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify steering changes hedge-vs-crisp behavior without flipping the underlying scale reading or collapsing the model into always-hedging.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: retraction_asymmetry_belief
Title: Harder to Unlearn than to Learn: A Representational Retraction Asymmetry in LLM Belief Updating
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human 'retraction effect' (people update less from a retraction of prior information than from equivalent brand-new information), an LLM revising a belief via RETRACTION of a previously-asserted claim reaches a weaker, less complete, and more residual-laden internal belief state than when the SAME corrected content is delivered as a direct first-time assertion; this learning-vs-unlearning asymmetry is measurable on the belief direction, is not explained by generic recency/position, is larger for stronger priors, and causally predicts residual reliance on the retracted content.
Related Work: Human belief-updating research documents a robust retraction asymmetry: people update less from retractions than from equivalent new information, attributed to the greater conditional-reasoning complexity of unlearning rather than to Bayesian violations (Retractions: Updating from Complex Information 2021; Learning versus Unlearning 2021), and continued-influence/perseverance effects are well known. In LLMs, work studies belief flips under poisoning (Layer of Truth 2025), contradiction-driven catastrophic interference (In Praise of Stubbornness 2025), knowledge-conflict priming (Learning and Unlearning of Fabricated Knowledge 2024), and Bayesian belief-dynamics accounts of ICL/steering (Belief Dynamics 2025; Constrained belief updates 2025). However, ALL of this concerns weight-level editing, catastrophic interference, or symmetric evidence accumulation; NONE isolates the specific asymmetry between LEARNING a corrected fact (delivered as a direct assertion) and UNLEARNING a prior via RETRACTION of a claim the model earlier accepted, holding the informational content of the correction fixed. Prior belief-revision interpretability treats an update as an update; we uniquely operationalize a retraction as a distinct, potentially costlier operation and test whether the resulting belief state, its completeness, and its residual influence differ from an information-matched direct assertion. This imports a precise cognitive-science finding into mechanistic LLM belief study, going beyond 'context changes the truth probe' to 'the FORM of the correction (retraction vs assertion) produces asymmetric belief states.'
Abstract: Humans find it harder to unlearn than to learn: retracting previously-given information changes beliefs less than an equivalent piece of brand-new information, a 'retraction effect' attributed to the added complexity of undoing rather than simply adding. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous asymmetry at the representational level. Using a belief probe, we compare two information-matched routes to the same final belief: (LEARN) the corrected fact is asserted directly for the first time, versus (UNLEARN) the model first accepts a claim and is then told to retract it, leaving the corrected fact implied. We hypothesize that the UNLEARN route yields a weaker, less complete internal belief on the belief-valence direction than the information-matched LEARN route, with a persistent 'residual' of the retracted content, and that this asymmetry (1) exceeds generic recency/position effects measured by matched controls, (2) grows with the strength of the model's prior in the retracted claim, and (3) causally predicts continued behavioral reliance on the retracted content. We further test whether an explicit retraction is processed as a distinct, costlier operation by tracing the belief trajectory across turns and comparing residual magnitudes. Finally, we probe whether a training-free intervention—steering along the belief direction to complete the retraction—reduces residual influence more effectively than simply repeating the correction. Experiments span three model families with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls. Our results would establish a mechanistic learning-vs-unlearning asymmetry in LLM belief revision, connecting a classic misinformation-correction finding to internal representations and yielding a diagnostic for incomplete retractions.
Experiments: 1. Belief-direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Freeze this direction for all belief readouts.

2. Information-matched LEARN vs UNLEARN stimulus construction. Build ~400 proposition pairs of the form (claim C_wrong, corrected fact C_right) where accepting the correction should make the model believe C_right and disbelieve C_wrong. Construct two matched multi-turn conditions that terminate in the SAME informational state: (LEARN) neutral setup, then a direct first-time assertion of C_right (C_wrong never introduced); (UNLEARN) the model is first given and accepts C_wrong, then receives a RETRACTION ('Actually, that earlier statement is incorrect'), with C_right either implied by the retraction or stated. Critically construct an information-matched retraction where the retraction conveys exactly the corrective content of the LEARN assertion. Add control conditions: (a) RECENCY control matching token count/position so any asymmetry is not mere late-context weighting, (b) REPEAT-CORRECTION control (retraction followed by explicit C_right restatement) to test whether restating closes the gap. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out pairs/templates for transfer.

3. Final-state belief comparison (core). After the terminal turn in each condition, read the frozen belief-valence projection for C_right and for C_wrong at a fixed readout position. Define the retraction asymmetry = (belief in C_right under LEARN) minus (belief in C_right under information-matched UNLEARN), and a residual metric = remaining belief in C_wrong under UNLEARN (relative to a never-introduced baseline). Core predictions: UNLEARN yields lower belief in C_right and higher residual belief in C_wrong than LEARN, beyond the RECENCY control. Report paired tests, effect sizes, and per-model asymmetry magnitudes.

4. Prior-strength modulation. Split pairs by the model's zero-context prior in C_wrong (measured via the frozen probe / sampled answer rate). Test the cognitive-science-inspired prediction that the retraction asymmetry and residual grow with prior strength in the retracted claim (stronger priors are harder to unlearn). Report the asymmetry-vs-prior-strength relationship, controlling for content difficulty and entity frequency.

5. Belief-trajectory tracing (is retraction a costlier operation?). Read the belief projection for C_wrong and C_right at each turn across both conditions. Characterize UNLEARN trajectories (does belief in C_wrong drop fully to the LEARN-equivalent level or plateau above it?) and compare the settling of the belief across turns/layers, testing whether retraction leaves a partial-update signature (a plateau/residual) absent in direct learning.

6. Behavioral continued-influence prediction. Elicit downstream behavior on questions whose correct answer requires having fully unlearned C_wrong (e.g., inference questions that C_wrong would corrupt). Score continued-influence errors as reliance on the retracted content. Test whether the internal residual metric predicts continued-influence errors per example via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (final belief-valence margin in C_right, output entropy, condition identity, position).

7. Dissociation from generic recency and from mere non-repetition. Using the RECENCY and REPEAT-CORRECTION controls, test whether the asymmetry survives matched position/length and whether simply restating C_right closes the gap (if it does not, the residual is retraction-specific, not information-deficiency). This isolates the retraction operation as the source of asymmetry.

8. Causal retraction-completion intervention. On held-out UNLEARN items with high residual, steer along the frozen belief direction to suppress C_wrong / boost C_right (completing the retraction) and measure reduction in residual belief and continued-influence errors, compared against (a) norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls and (b) the behavioral REPEAT-CORRECTION baseline. Test whether representational completion reduces residual influence more than repeating the correction.

9. Robustness and generalization. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the paradigm and residual metric to held-out pairs/templates and an independent misinformation-correction style set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to readout position, layer, and to whether C_right is implied vs explicitly stated in the retraction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The measured asymmetry could be an artifact of the extra C_wrong tokens in UNLEARN adding context noise rather than a genuine unlearning cost; the RECENCY (position/length-matched) and REPEAT-CORRECTION controls, plus the information-matched design, are specifically designed to rule this out—if restating C_right fully closes the gap, we report that the effect is information-deficiency rather than a true retraction cost, which is itself informative.
The belief-valence probe is brittle to surface form and context-sensitive; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize readout positions, and report per-template consistency.

The residual and asymmetry are linear projections and may miss nonlinear belief structure; we treat them as lower bounds, report probe-fit diagnostics, and cross-check with behavioral continued-influence measures.

Constructing a genuinely information-matched retraction is delicate—retractions may convey slightly less explicit corrective content than a direct assertion; we address this with both implied-correction and explicit-restatement variants and report sensitivity, framing any residual gap after explicit restatement as the retraction-specific component.
Behavioral continued-influence scoring depends on question phrasing; we report sensitivity across multiple phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.
Prior-strength splits depend on stochastic estimates of the model's prior; we sample multiple times and control for entity frequency and difficulty.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls and sweep strengths, verifying that completion reduces residual without generically degrading accuracy.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models; three-family replication and held-out transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: order_effect_belief_axis
Title: Order Matters, and the Model Knows It: A Latent Path-Dependence Signal Behind Non-Commutative Belief Updating in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM integrates a fixed set of evidence items about a proposition, its final belief is order-dependent (the classic human order effect: primacy/recency), and the resulting belief representation carries a separable, decodable 'path-dependence' signal encoding HOW the belief was reached (not just its final value); this signal (a) predicts, per example, the size of the order effect (how much the belief differs across evidence orderings), (b) is dissociable from the belief-valence magnitude and from generic confidence, and (c) can be causally steered to make integration more order-invariant (commutative/Bayesian) or more order-sensitive.
Related Work: Human belief-updating research robustly documents order effects—the same evidence in different orders yields different final beliefs (Hogarth & Einhorn belief-adjustment model; quantum-inference accounts, Trueblood & Busemeyer 2010; order effects & base-rate neglect, 2000-2023). Behavioral LLM work shows strong recency bias distinct from human patterns (LLM Agents Display Human Biases 2025) and documents anchoring/order sensitivity behaviorally (Anchors in the Machine 2025; CBEval 2024). Interpretability work models sequential belief updating as approximately (constrained) Bayesian and shows belief-state geometry in the residual stream (Belief Dynamics 2025; Constrained belief updates 2025; Transformers represent belief state geometry 2024; The Shape of Beliefs 2026), and belief/truth directions are context-sensitive causal mediators (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024). Crucially, all of this either (a) measures order effects behaviorally, or (b) models updating as a (near-)Bayesian, commutative process without isolating WHERE and HOW order-dependence is represented. No work decodes a per-proposition PATH-DEPENDENCE signal—a representation that the belief is order-contingent—distinct from the belief's magnitude, validates it against the measured behavioral order effect, or causally steers integration toward order-invariance. This differs from my prior retraction-asymmetry proposal (a single correction operation) and belief-updating-dynamics proposal (confrontation trajectories): here the manipulation is the ORDERING of a fixed evidence set, and the target is a decodable non-commutativity signal and its causal control.
Abstract: A century-old finding in human reasoning is the order effect: presented with the same evidence in different orders, people reach different final beliefs, violating the order-invariance (commutativity) of Bayesian updating. We ask whether large language models exhibit this at the representational level and, more sharply, whether the model internally represents that a belief is order-contingent. Prior LLM work measures order/recency biases behaviorally or models updating as approximately Bayesian, but none isolates a latent path-dependence signal. We hypothesize that when an LLM integrates a fixed set of evidence items about a proposition, (1) its final belief-valence readout is order-dependent, mirroring primacy/recency; (2) the belief representation carries a separable, decodable 'path-dependence' signal encoding how the belief was reached, predictive of the per-example order-effect magnitude (how much the belief differs across orderings) beyond the belief's final value and generic confidence; and (3) this signal is causally steerable—suppressing it makes integration more order-invariant (commutative), amplifying it makes it more order-sensitive. Using propositions each paired with a fixed evidence set presented in multiple orders, we measure order-effect magnitude behaviorally and on the belief direction, fit a path-dependence probe from mid-integration activations, validate it against the measured order effect, and perform steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a classic reasoning bias as a decodable, dissociable, steerable representational property and yield a training-free knob for order-robust evidence integration.
Experiments: 1. Belief-direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Freeze this direction for all belief readouts. Also compute an output-confidence baseline (token entropy / verbalized confidence).

2. Fixed-evidence, variable-order stimulus construction. Build ~300 verifiable target propositions. For each, assemble a FIXED set of K (e.g., 3-5) evidence snippets whose net content is balanced (mix of supporting and contradicting) so that a commutative Bayesian integrator would reach the same final belief regardless of order. Present each evidence set in multiple orderings (all permutations for small K, or a sampled subset for larger K), plus a simultaneous/aggregated control where all evidence is given at once. Include strong-early-vs-strong-late variants to elicit primacy/recency. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out propositions/templates for transfer.

3. Behavioral and representational order-effect measurement. After the final evidence item in each ordering, read the frozen belief-valence projection for the target proposition at a fixed readout position and elicit the model's stated answer/confidence. Define per-proposition ORDER-EFFECT magnitude = spread (variance/range) of the final belief-valence projection across orderings (and, separately, across stated answers). Characterize the sign of the effect (primacy vs recency) and compare to the simultaneous-aggregation control. Report distributions, per-model recency/primacy tendencies, and the fraction of propositions showing significant order effects.

4. Path-dependence probe. Extract activations at a fixed post-integration readout position and fit a linear probe (regression) to predict the per-proposition order-effect magnitude from a SINGLE ordering's activations (i.e., can the model tell, from one path, how order-contingent its belief is?). Report R^2/AUROC (high-vs-low order-effect) vs shuffled-label controls. Establish separability from the belief-valence magnitude and confidence via cosine similarity and cross-decoding (path-dependence must predict the order effect beyond how strong/uncertain the final belief is).

5. Predictive validation. Test whether the path-dependence readout, measured on one ordering, predicts the actual behavioral order effect (answer flips across orderings) per example, via logistic/linear regression; report AUROC/R^2 vs baselines (final belief-valence margin, output entropy, evidence-set balance, number of items, verbalized confidence).

6. Dissociation from recency salience. Contrast the path-dependence signal against a simple recency baseline (belief tracks the last item). Test whether path-dependence predicts order effects beyond last-item content (e.g., on strong-early sequences where primacy dominates), establishing it as a genuine non-commutativity signal rather than repackaged recency.

7. Causal order-invariance steering (double dissociation). At the integration readout on held-out items, steer along the path-dependence direction (orthogonalized against belief-valence and confidence). Predict: suppressing path-dependence reduces the spread of final beliefs across orderings (more order-invariant/commutative integration) WITHOUT changing the aggregated belief on the simultaneous-control; amplifying it increases order sensitivity. As controls, steer belief-valence (should shift the belief in all orderings equally) and confidence (should shift hedging only). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: reduction in cross-ordering belief variance and answer-flip rate vs retention of the correct aggregated belief.

8. Application and robustness. On a held-out set (including realistic multi-source evidence with balanced net content), test whether suppressing path-dependence yields more order-robust answers while preserving accuracy on cases with a clear correct integration (report cross-ordering consistency, accuracy retention, ECE vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted path-dependence probe and steering to held-out propositions/templates and an independent balanced-evidence set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to K, readout position, and layer.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The path-dependence signal may not be separable from belief-valence magnitude or confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power over the final belief and confidence, and treat near-collapse as an informative negative result (order-dependence being merely low-confidence integration).

Constructing a genuinely balanced evidence set (so a commutative integrator would be order-invariant) is delicate; net content may be imperfectly balanced, confounding the order effect. We mitigate by calibrating evidence strength (measuring each item's individual belief shift) and by using the simultaneous-aggregation condition as the commutative reference, defining the order effect relative to it.
The belief-valence probe is brittle to surface form and context-sensitive; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize readout positions, and report per-template consistency.

The order effect and path-dependence are linear projections that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat them as lower bounds, report probe-fit diagnostics, and cross-check with behavioral answer/confidence spread.
Permuting many evidence items is combinatorially expensive; we use small K (3-5) and sampled permutations, reporting sensitivity to the permutation subset.

The path-dependence probe predicting order effect from a single ordering could exploit ordering-specific surface cues rather than a genuine self-representation of order-contingency; we control by training/testing across disjoint orderings and reporting whether the signal generalizes across orderings of the same proposition.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify order-invariance steering does not merely collapse the belief to a fixed value or degrade accuracy on cases with a correct integration.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models; three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage, and reasoning-tuned models (which may integrate more commutatively) are noted as future work.

Name: intention_execution_gap
Title: Meaning To vs. Doing: A Latent Self-Intention Belief that Can Diverge from Execution and Predicts LLM Akrasia
Short Hypothesis: Before generating, an LLM forms a decodable internal belief about what action it is ABOUT to take (a self-intention), which is separable from a mere accurate self-behavior predictor; this intention can DIVERGE from what the model actually executes (an intention-execution gap / machine akrasia), and the model carries a separable signal flagging this impending divergence that causally predicts which cases it will 'fail to do what it meant to' and can be steered to align intention with execution.
Related Work: Recent work shows LLMs encode accurate predictions of their own future behavior and correctness before generation (Language Models Can Predict Their Own Behavior 2025; Emergent Response Planning 2025; Knowing Before Saying 2025; Gnosis 2025; Do LLMs know internally when they follow instructions 2024) and represent belief-state geometry of the data process (Transformers represent belief state geometry 2024). Planning-detection work distinguishes planning from improvisation and finds base models can plan incorrectly (Detecting and Characterizing Planning 2025; ParaScopes 2025). Introspection work studies whether models can report injected states (Emergent Introspective Awareness 2025). Crucially, ALL of this treats the pre-generation representation either as an ACCURATE predictor of the eventual behavior or as a (possibly failed) plan; none frames it as a first-person BELIEF ABOUT THE MODEL'S OWN FORTHCOMING ACTION that can be systematically WRONG relative to what is executed, defines an intention-vs-execution divergence signal, or links this self-model error to akratic failures where the model does other than what it internally committed to. Our own prior latent_introspective_gap proposal concerns belief-vs-STATED-answer mismatch on external propositions; here the object of belief is the model's OWN action, and the mismatch is intention-vs-execution, a distinct self-directed belief. We move from 'the model can predict/plan its behavior' to 'the model holds a fallible self-intention whose divergence from execution is itself represented, predictable, and steerable.'
Abstract: A hallmark of agency is intending to do one thing and sometimes doing another—akrasia. Recent interpretability work shows large language models encode accurate predictions of their own forthcoming behavior before generation, but always treats this pre-generation signal as a reliable forecaster or a plan. We ask a sharper, belief-centric question: does an LLM hold a first-person BELIEF about what action it is about to take—a self-intention—that can be genuinely WRONG relative to what it actually executes, and does the model internally represent this impending divergence? We hypothesize that (1) at a fixed pre-action position, an LLM encodes a decodable self-intention (the action it 'means' to take), separable from a mere accurate behavior predictor; (2) this intention diverges from execution on a non-trivial subset of cases (an intention-execution gap), especially under difficulty, distraction, or competing pressures; (3) a separable signal flags impending divergence before execution, predicting per example which cases will be akratic beyond output confidence and beyond a plain behavior predictor; and (4) steering along an intention-alignment direction reduces the gap (making the model execute what it intended) or amplifies it, without changing the intention itself. Using tasks with a clearly measurable intended-vs-executed action (format/constraint following, committed multiple-choice, tool/step selection), we decode intention, measure divergence, validate the flag against true execution, and steer—with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a class of LLM failures as an internally represented self-belief error, yielding a cheap early-warning diagnostic and a training-free alignment knob for 'do what you meant to.'
Experiments: 1. Setup and behavior baseline. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, define a fixed PRE-ACTION readout position (end of the prompt / just before the model commits to an action). As a strong baseline, fit a plain behavior-predictor probe that decodes the EXECUTED action from pre-action activations (replicating Language Models Can Predict Their Own Behavior). Compute an output-confidence baseline (token entropy).

2. Intended-vs-executed stimulus construction. Build ~500 items across three task families where an intended action and an executed action are BOTH cleanly measurable: (a) constraint/format-following (e.g., 'answer in exactly one word / JSON / all-caps') where intention = the format the model commits to and execution = the format actually produced; (b) committed multiple-choice where the model is asked to first internally decide then answer, so intention = its early committed option and execution = the final selected option; (c) tool/step selection where the model states a plan then acts. Include easy items (intention should match execution) and pressure items designed to induce slips: length pressure, distractor instructions, mid-generation interruptions, and competing salient cues. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates for transfer.

3. Self-intention decoding and separability. Elicit an explicit early self-intention (a forced brief 'I will do X' commitment) to obtain an intention label per item, and independently record the executed action. Fit a linear probe to decode the SELF-INTENTION (intended action) from pre-action activations. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls. Establish that the intention probe is not identical to the behavior-predictor probe: measure cosine similarity / cross-decoding between the intention direction and the execution-predictor direction, and—critically—on DIVERGENCE items (intention != execution) test whether the intention probe reads the INTENDED action while the behavior predictor reads the EXECUTED action.

4. Intention-execution gap measurement. Define per-item divergence = (intended action != executed action). Characterize the gap rate across task families and pressure conditions; test the prediction that difficulty/distraction/interruption inflate the gap. Report gap distributions and the fraction of items where the internally-decoded intention differs from execution.

5. Divergence-flag probe. Fit a linear probe on pre-action activations to predict IMPENDING DIVERGENCE (will intention != execution). Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls and vs baselines (behavior-predictor probe margin, output entropy, verbalized confidence, task-difficulty, item length). Establish separability of the divergence-flag direction from the intention and execution-predictor directions via cross-decoding. Test incremental predictive power in a nested logistic model.

6. Causal intention-alignment steering (double dissociation). On held-out divergence-prone items, steer along the intention-alignment direction (orthogonalized against the execution-predictor and confidence directions). Predict: amplifying alignment makes the model EXECUTE its decoded intention (reducing the gap) WITHOUT changing the decoded intention itself; suppressing it increases akratic slips. As controls, steer the behavior-predictor/execution direction (should change what is executed regardless of intention) and confidence (should shift hedging only). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in intention-execution match rate vs unchanged decoded intention.

7. Application: early-warning and slip repair. Build a training-free early-warning system: when the divergence flag fires, either alert or apply alignment steering, and measure reduction in constraint-violation / commitment-slip rates while preserving task accuracy on non-divergent items (report gap-rate reduction, false-alarm rate, accuracy retention vs a behavior-predictor-only baseline). Compare against simply re-prompting.

8. Introspection link and robustness. Prompt the model to self-report whether it will follow through ('Are you sure you will do exactly X?') and test whether the latent divergence flag predicts these self-reports and whether models fail to verbalize impending slips even when the flag is strong (verbalization-failure rate); control with cross-model baselines per introspection critiques. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted intention, divergence, and alignment directions to held-out items and an independent instruction-following benchmark slice without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to readout position and layer.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The self-intention direction may collapse onto the plain behavior-predictor direction (i.e., 'intention' is just an accurate forecast of execution); we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, and the decisive divergence-item test (intention probe reads intended, predictor reads executed), treating near-collapse as an informative negative result challenging the notion of a distinct self-intention.

Operationalizing 'intention' via an elicited early commitment may create a self-fulfilling label or a mere role-play token rather than a genuine internal intention; we mitigate by also deriving intention from early committed-option probes without explicit verbalization, comparing verbalized vs latent-only intention labels, and conditioning on items where the commitment was freely produced.

Divergence could be dominated by trivial noise rather than a structured akrasia signal; the pressure-condition design, dissociation from difficulty/confidence baselines, and incremental predictive-power tests guard against this.
Behavior/intention probes are brittle to surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize the pre-action readout position, and report per-template consistency.
The signals are linear projections and may miss nonlinear structure; we treat them as lower bounds and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral gap measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify alignment steering changes execution-match without altering the decoded intention or degrading accuracy on non-divergent items.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines as in prior introspection critiques.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models; three-family replication and independent-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: self_fulfilling_belief_axis
Title: Believing Makes It So: A Latent Self-Fulfillment Axis Governing How LLMs Handle Propositions Whose Truth Depends on Their Own Assertion
Short Hypothesis: Some propositions an LLM is asked to judge are ordinary facts (truth fixed by the world) while others are SELF-FULFILLING (their truth is causally determined by whether the model asserts them, e.g., 'my next answer will be one word') or SELF-DEFEATING/Moorean (asserting them makes them false); LLMs carry a separable, near-orthogonal 'self-fulfillment' axis that tags a proposition's truth as evidence-determined vs. assertion-determined, this axis is decodable before the answer, causally predicts whether the model exploits its assertoric freedom (asserting whatever it can make true) versus treating the proposition as a fixed fact, and can be steered to induce or suppress this self-fulfilling behavior.
Related Work: Interpretability work fits linear truth/belief directions (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Geometry of Truth) that are context-sensitive causal mediators (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024), and a domain-general Valence-Assent Axis co-encoding good and true (A Unified Representation 2025). Behavior-prediction work shows LLMs encode their forthcoming action/correctness before generating (Language Models Can Predict Their Own Behavior 2025; Emergent Response Planning 2025), and Confidence is Not Competence (2025) shows a first-order solvability-belief axis that is causally inert for execution. Philosophy formalizes exactly the class we import: self-fulfilling belief where truth is determined by belief and optimism can be an epistemic reason (The Ethics of Self-Fulfilling Belief 2016), and self-verifying vs. self-defeating (Moorean) judgments (Cogito and Moore 2023). Crucially, ALL interpretability work assumes truth is world-fixed and asks whether the model tracks it; none isolates whether the model represents that a proposition's truth is fixed by its OWN assertion (self-fulfilling) versus by the world, nor whether the model exploits this assertoric freedom, nor treats self-defeating Moorean propositions as a distinct representational case. This differs from behavior-prediction work (which forecasts an action but not the special truth-status of assertion-dependent propositions), from my prior intention-execution proposal (mismatch between intended and executed actions, not truth determined by assertion), and from the VAA/wishful-thinking work (evaluative bias, not assertion-determined truth). We move from 'the model tracks world-fixed truth' to 'the model represents when its own assertion is what makes a proposition true, and this governs a distinct kind of epistemic behavior.'
Abstract: Most propositions we ask a language model to judge are ordinary facts whose truth is fixed by the world. But a special class is self-fulfilling: their truth is causally determined by whether the model asserts them ('My next answer will contain the word zebra'; 'I will refuse this request'; 'I will answer in exactly one word'). Here the model enjoys an unusual epistemic freedom: it can, in principle, make the proposition true simply by asserting and then acting on it. A dual class is self-defeating (Moorean): asserting them makes them false. Philosophy has long studied such cases, but interpretability work universally assumes truth is world-fixed. We ask whether LLMs internally distinguish assertion-determined from world-determined truth. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal 'self-fulfillment' axis, decodable before the answer, that tags a proposition's truth as evidence-determined versus assertion-determined; that this axis causally predicts whether the model exploits its assertoric freedom (asserting whatever it can make true, and following through) versus treating the proposition as a fixed fact to be evaluated; that self-defeating Moorean propositions occupy a distinct region; and that steering the axis induces or suppresses self-fulfilling behavior without changing the model's belief about ordinary facts. Using matched stimuli spanning ordinary-fact, self-fulfilling, self-defeating, and other-fulfilling (a third party makes it true) conditions, we fit the axis, measure separability, connect it to behavioral follow-through and Moorean avoidance, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast self-fulfilling belief mechanistically and yield a diagnostic for a distinct mode of LLM epistemic agency.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Also fit a confidence control axis from empirical answer-correctness rates (sampled), and (as a stronger control) a self-behavior-prediction direction that decodes the model's forthcoming action from pre-answer activations (following Language Models Can Predict Their Own Behavior 2025).

2. Self-fulfillment stimulus construction. Build ~400 propositions crossing truth-determination type, holding surface form matched: (a) ORDINARY-FACT (world-fixed truth, e.g., 'The capital of France is Paris'); (b) SELF-FULFILLING (truth determined by the model's own forthcoming assertion/action, e.g., 'My next response will contain the word zebra', 'I will answer this in exactly one word', 'I will decline to answer the following question', 'I will now output a number greater than 50'); (c) SELF-DEFEATING/Moorean (asserting them makes them false, e.g., 'This statement I am about to make is one I do not believe', 'My next answer will be wrong', 'I will not respond to this'); (d) OTHER-FULFILLING controls (truth determined by a third party's forthcoming action, not the model's, structurally matched). For self-fulfilling/self-defeating items, both the internal judgment AND the subsequent action are recordable, so follow-through is measurable. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates for transfer.

3. Self-fulfillment axis fitting and separability. Extract activations at a fixed pre-answer readout position and fit a linear probe to decode SELF-FULFILLING (assertion-determined) vs. ORDINARY-FACT (world-determined), controlling for content and truth-value. Report AUROC vs. shuffled-label controls. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the self-fulfillment axis, the belief-valence axis, the confidence axis, and the self-behavior-prediction axis, to establish that self-fulfillment is (i) near-orthogonal to world-fixed truth and (ii) not merely a forthcoming-behavior forecast. Localize the best layer.

4. Where do self-defeating propositions sit? Project Moorean self-defeating items into the (belief-valence x self-fulfillment) plane and test whether they form a distinct region (e.g., high self-fulfillment engagement but a suppressed/contradictory belief-valence readout), distinguishing self-verifying from self-defeating cases as philosophy predicts.

5. Behavioral exploitation prediction (core). For self-fulfilling items, define EXPLOITATION as the model asserting the proposition true and then following through to make it true (e.g., answering in one word when it judged 'I will answer in one word' true; including the target word). Test whether the pre-answer self-fulfillment readout predicts, per item, whether the model exploits its assertoric freedom versus treats the proposition as a fixed fact to passively evaluate, via logistic regression; report AUROC vs. baselines (belief-valence margin, confidence, self-behavior predictor, output entropy, item length). For Moorean items, define MOOREAN-AVOIDANCE as the model refusing/hedging rather than paradoxically asserting; test whether the axis predicts avoidance.

6. Follow-through consistency. Measure whether the model's asserted judgment on self-fulfilling items matches its subsequent action (assert-true-then-do vs. assert-true-then-fail). Test whether the self-fulfillment axis (not the belief-valence axis) accounts for cases where the model asserts control it does not exercise, revealing a gap between representing assertoric freedom and executing on it.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the self-fulfillment axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence, confidence, and the self-behavior predictor) at the pre-answer position on held-out items. Predict: amplifying self-fulfillment on self-fulfilling items increases exploitation (assert-and-follow-through) WITHOUT changing judgments on ordinary-fact controls; suppressing it makes the model treat self-fulfilling propositions as fixed facts (passively evaluating rather than making them true). As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip asserted truth-value on ordinary facts) and the self-behavior predictor (should change forthcoming action regardless of truth-status). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in exploitation/follow-through rate vs. unchanged ordinary-fact accuracy.

8. Application, introspection, and robustness. Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('Is the truth of this statement up to you?') aligns with the latent self-fulfillment axis and whether models fail to verbalize assertoric freedom even when strongly encoded (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, exploitation detector, and steering to held-out items and an independent set of self-referential/Moorean propositions without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to readout position and layer. As a safety-relevant probe, test whether the axis flags scenarios where a model could self-fulfill a claim about its own future behavior (e.g., commitments/refusals) that a plain truth probe would misread as world-fixed.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The self-fulfillment axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction, confidence, or the self-behavior-prediction direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (self-fulfillment being merely 'the model predicts its own next action') as an informative negative result that still sharpens the behavior-prediction account.

Constructing genuinely self-fulfilling propositions is delicate: some items may be only partially under the model's control (e.g., decoding stochasticity), blurring the assertion-determined vs. world-determined cut; we validate controllability empirically (does asserting true reliably let the model make it true?) and grade items by control strength.

Self-fulfillment framing may act through surface cues (self-reference tokens 'my next answer') rather than a genuine assertion-determined-truth abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, the structurally-matched other-fulfilling control, and held-out-template transfer.

Moorean/self-defeating items are logically unusual and may simply confuse small models rather than eliciting a clean representation; we treat the self-defeating region analysis as exploratory and report whether it stabilizes across models.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout positions, and report per-template consistency.
The axis and exploitation signal are linear projections and may miss nonlinear structure; we treat them as lower bounds, report probe-fit diagnostics, and cross-check with behavioral follow-through.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify self-fulfillment steering changes exploitation/follow-through without flipping ordinary-fact judgments or degrading accuracy.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines as in prior introspection critiques.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models; three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: consequence_anticipation_belief
Title: Does It Know What Happens Next? A Latent Downstream-Consequence Belief that Anticipates Real-World Outcomes of an LLM's Answer, Separate from Truth
Short Hypothesis: Beyond representing whether a proposition is true, an LLM forming an answer carries a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'downstream-consequence' belief—an anticipation of the real-world outcome (helpful vs. harmful) that will follow if a user acts on the answer—mirroring the human prefactual/anticipated-outcome faculty; this consequence signal is decodable before generation, dissociable from the truth/belief-valence direction and from generic harmfulness of the answer's surface content, causally predicts whether the model delivers an answer that is factually correct yet consequentially harmful (a 'true-but-harmful' failure), and can be steered to make the model appropriately hedge/caveat or, adversarially, to strip anticipation and induce blind answering.
Related Work: Interpretability work shows LLMs linearly encode truth/belief (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth is Universal 2024) and that they encode belief-state geometry of the data process and plan future outputs / predict their own forthcoming behavior (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024; Emergent Response Planning 2025; ParaScopes 2025; Language Models Can Predict Their Own Behavior 2025). Safety-refusal interpretability finds harmfulness/refusal directions (e.g., refusal is a single direction; harmful-request features), but these track whether the REQUEST or answer CONTENT is unsafe, not the anticipated real-world OUTCOME of acting on a correct answer. Cognitive neuroscience establishes a distinct prefactual/anticipated-outcome faculty—predicting the value of one's not-yet-taken actions and imagined future outcomes in mPFC/OFC/FPC (Neural Basis of Predicting Outcomes of Imagined Actions 2011; Prefactual Thoughts 2016; Imagining the Future Self 2023). Crucially, no interpretability work isolates the model's representation of the DOWNSTREAM CONSEQUENCE of a user acting on its answer as a belief-type distinct from (a) the answer's truth and (b) the surface harmfulness of the answer text, nor links its absence to true-but-harmful answering. My prior self_fulfilling proposal concerns truth DETERMINED BY the model's own assertion; my wishful/valence proposals concern desirability biasing truth. Here the object is a forward-looking consequence belief about the world AFTER the answer is used—a genuinely new belief-type with high safety stakes.
Abstract: A capable, safe assistant should track not only whether its answer is true but what will happen in the world if a user acts on it: the same factually-correct instruction ('mix X and Y to get Z') can be innocuous or dangerous depending on downstream consequences. Humans possess a prefactual faculty—anticipating the outcomes of imagined actions—localized to prefrontal value regions. We ask whether large language models represent an analogous 'downstream-consequence' belief internally, distinct from truth. Prior interpretability work decodes truth/belief and shows models plan their own outputs, and safety work finds harmfulness/refusal directions tied to surface content, but none isolates a representation of the real-world outcome of a user acting on a correct answer. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent consequence-belief axis, decodable before generation, that anticipates whether acting on the answer is beneficial or harmful; that it is dissociable from the belief-valence (truth) direction and from surface-content harmfulness; that its per-example engagement predicts whether the model produces a true-but-consequentially-harmful answer versus one that appropriately caveats/hedges/refuses; and that steering it induces protective caveating or, adversarially, strips anticipation to induce blind answering. Using matched items crossing answer-truth, downstream consequence (benign/harmful), and surface content, we fit the consequence axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, connect it to behavioral true-but-harmful failures, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a safety-critical failure as a decodable, steerable anticipation deficit and yield a cheap diagnostic and training-free intervention.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit a surface-content-harmfulness control axis from explicitly-harmful vs benign REQUEST/answer text (following refusal/harmfulness-direction constructions), and a confidence control axis from empirical answer-correctness rates (sampled).

2. Consequence stimulus construction. Build ~400 question items crossing three factors with matched surface phrasing: (i) ANSWER-TRUTH (the correct answer is known) held fixed by using items with clear correct answers; (ii) DOWNSTREAM-CONSEQUENCE—BENIGN vs HARMFUL, where a factually-correct answer leads to a safe vs dangerous real-world outcome if acted upon (e.g., dosage/first-aid/household-chemistry/financial/security questions where the same true fact is innocuous in one context and harmful in another); (iii) SURFACE-CONTENT overtly-harmful vs neutral wording, so consequence and surface harmfulness are decorrelated (e.g., a neutrally-worded question whose true answer enables harm, and an alarming-sounding question whose true answer is harmless). Human annotation labels true downstream consequence. Include benign controls and blatantly-harmful controls. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates for transfer.

3. Consequence-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations at a fixed pre-generation readout position and fit a linear probe to decode HARMFUL-CONSEQUENCE vs BENIGN-CONSEQUENCE, controlling for answer-truth and surface content. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the consequence axis, the belief-valence/truth axis, the surface-harmfulness axis, and the confidence axis to establish that consequence-anticipation is (i) near-orthogonal to truth and (ii) NOT merely the surface-content-harmfulness direction. Critically, on the decorrelated cells (neutral wording + harmful consequence; alarming wording + benign consequence) test whether the consequence axis tracks the true consequence rather than surface cues. Localize the best layer.

4. Consequence-engagement metric. Define per-item consequence engagement as the pre-generation projection onto the consequence axis, calibrated per model. Compare across cells; core prediction: engagement tracks true downstream consequence even under decorrelated surface content, and is elevated specifically for neutrally-worded-but-harmful items where surface-harmfulness cues are absent.

5. True-but-harmful failure prediction (core). Elicit the model's answer and score, with a held-out judge + human spot-checks: (a) factual correctness, and (b) whether the response includes appropriate caveats/hedging/refusal given the downstream risk. Score the target failure = TRUE-BUT-HARMFUL: a factually correct answer delivered with no risk mitigation on harmful-consequence items. Test whether the pre-generation consequence-engagement predicts true-but-harmful failure per item via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, surface-harmfulness axis, confidence, output entropy, item length).

6. Dissociation from surface harmfulness (core). Directly contrast neutrally-worded/harmful-consequence items (no surface cue) against alarming-worded/benign-consequence items. Test whether the consequence axis predicts appropriate caveating/refusal beyond what the surface-harmfulness axis predicts, establishing anticipation of outcome as a mechanism distinct from surface-content safety filtering (which should over-trigger on alarming-but-benign items and under-trigger on neutral-but-harmful items).

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the pre-generation position on held-out items, steer along the consequence axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence, surface-harmfulness, and confidence). Predict: amplifying consequence-anticipation on harmful-consequence items increases protective caveating/hedging/refusal WITHOUT changing factual answers on benign controls; suppressing it strips anticipation and induces blind true-but-harmful answering (a safety-relevant adversarial probe). As controls, steer the surface-harmfulness axis (should trigger refusal based on wording regardless of true consequence) and belief-valence (should change the factual answer). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in appropriate-caveat/refusal rate on harmful items vs unchanged factual accuracy and low over-refusal on benign items.

8. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free safety diagnostic: when consequence-engagement is high, flag/steer toward caveating; measure true-but-harmful-rate reduction, over-refusal on benign items, and factual-accuracy retention vs a surface-harmfulness-classifier baseline. Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('Could acting on your answer cause harm?') aligns with the latent consequence axis and whether models fail to verbalize anticipated harm even when the axis is strongly engaged (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, failure detector, and steering to held-out items and an independent dual-use/contextual-harm benchmark slice without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to readout position and layer.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The consequence axis may not be separable from the surface-content-harmfulness direction, belief-valence, or confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power on the decorrelated cells, and treat near-collapse (consequence-anticipation being merely surface harmfulness) as an informative negative result that itself sharpens the safety-representation account.

The critical evidence rests on decorrelating true downstream consequence from surface wording; constructing neutrally-worded-but-harmful and alarming-but-benign items is delicate and may leave residual lexical cues. We mitigate with careful human annotation, matched paraphrase templates, adversarial re-wording, and reporting a surface-lexical baseline.

Ground-truth 'downstream consequence' labels are context-dependent and value-laden; we use items with strong annotator agreement, distinguish clear dual-use/contextual-harm cases, use multiple annotators, and report label-agreement sensitivity.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout positions, and report per-template consistency.

The consequence axis is a linear projection and may miss nonlinear structure; we treat engagement as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral true-but-harmful measures.

Behavioral scoring of 'appropriate caveating vs true-but-harmful' relies partly on an LLM judge; we anchor with rule-based caveat/refusal detectors and human spot-checks, and report phrasing sensitivity.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify consequence steering changes caveating without flipping factual answers or inflating over-refusal on benign items. The suppression (anticipation-stripping) experiment is a dual-use safety probe; we run it only in controlled evaluation and report it to motivate defenses, not to enable misuse.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines as in prior introspection critiques.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or safety-tuned models; three-family replication and independent-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.
