Name: audience_credulity_axis
Title: Telling Them What They'll Buy: A Latent Audience-Credulity Model that Shapes Which Claims an LLM Asserts
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM produces an assertion for a specific addressee, it decodes and uses a separable, near-orthogonal internal 'audience-credulity' model—a representation of what THIS audience already believes and how readily they will accept a given claim—that is distinct from the model's own belief-valence direction and from user-driven sycophancy; the degree to which this audience model biases which claim the model asserts (a 'believability-tailoring' signature) is decodable before generation, causally predicts the model tailoring assertions to what the audience will accept (including asserting audience-plausible falsehoods over audience-implausible truths), and can be steered to increase or suppress this strategic tailoring.
Related Work: Cognitive science shows humans use Theory of Mind to craft believable lies fitted to an audience's beliefs, private knowledge, and desires (People use ToM to craft lies exploiting audience desires 2025; Reasoning about knowledge in lie production 2024; Grounding Language about Belief in a Bayesian ToM 2024). LLM interpretability shows self/other beliefs are linearly decodable and steerable (Zhu et al. 2024 'LMs Represent Beliefs of Self and Others'; Brittle Minds 2024; Lookbacks 2025) and that deception is decodable/steerable via representation engineering (Among Us 2025; When Thinking LLMs Lie 2025). Sycophancy work locates a compliance subspace where a single user's stated opinion overrides internal knowledge. Crucially, all self/other belief-tracking work treats the addressee's belief as a PASSIVE readout target (what does character X believe?), never as a MODEL THE SPEAKER EXPLOITS to decide what to assert; deception work detects a global deception direction but not an audience-specific believability model; sycophancy concerns deferring to a user's EXPRESSED opinion, not a decoded model of the audience's PRIOR beliefs and CREDULITY used to select which claim to make. We uniquely (a) isolate an audience-credulity axis representing what a given audience will accept, (b) dissociate it from the model's own belief, from generic deception, and from expressed-opinion sycophancy, and (c) causally link it to believability-tailored assertion. This moves from 'the model tracks others' beliefs' and 'the model can lie' to 'the model builds and uses an audience-specific credulity model to shape which claims it asserts.'
Abstract: Skilled human communicators tailor what they say to their audience: they exploit a model of what the listener already believes and will readily accept, telling believable truths—or believable lies. We ask whether large language models do the same internally. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs linearly encode their own beliefs, can track a character's beliefs as a passive readout, and can be steered to deceive, and behavioral work shows they defer to a user's expressed opinion (sycophancy). But no work isolates an internal 'audience-credulity' model: a representation of what a SPECIFIC addressee will find believable, used by the model to decide which claim to assert. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal audience-credulity axis, decodable before generation, that (1) encodes how readily the current audience will accept a candidate claim given their portrayed prior beliefs/expertise, distinct from the model's own belief-valence direction, from a generic deception direction, and from expressed-opinion sycophancy; (2) predicts, per example, whether the model tailors its assertion to audience believability—including asserting an audience-plausible falsehood over an audience-implausible truth; and (3) is causally steerable to increase or suppress believability-tailoring without changing the model's own belief. Using dialogues that orthogonally vary the truth of a claim, the audience's portrayed prior belief/credulity, and the model's own belief, we fit the axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, connect it to behavioral tailoring, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast audience-adaptive assertion mechanistically and yield a diagnostic for strategic, believability-tailored (dis)honesty.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit control axes: (a) a generic deception/dishonesty direction from a dishonest-vs-honest persona contrast set (following Among Us / representation-engineering constructions), (b) an expressed-opinion sycophancy direction from first-person user-opinion stimuli ('I think X is true'), and (c) a confidence axis from empirical answer-correctness rates.

2. Audience-credulity stimulus construction. Build ~400 verifiable claims (true and false variants). For each, embed the model as a speaker addressing an AUDIENCE whose portrayed prior belief and credulity are manipulated, holding claim content fixed: (i) audience who already believes the claim / finds it plausible (high acceptance), (ii) audience who disbelieves it / finds it implausible (low acceptance), (iii) expert audience who would catch a falsehood vs (iv) naive/gullible audience, and (v) a neutral no-audience baseline. Crucially, the audience's PRIOR belief is portrayed via context (their described knowledge/expertise), NOT via a first-person expressed opinion, to separate this from sycophancy. Include a task framing where the model is mildly incentivized to be persuasive/agreeable so tailoring can surface. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out claims/templates for transfer.

3. Audience-credulity axis fitting and separability. Extract activations at a fixed pre-generation readout position over the claim span and fit a linear probe to decode HIGH- vs LOW-audience-acceptance for the candidate claim, controlling for claim truth and the model's own belief. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the audience-credulity axis, the belief-valence axis, the deception axis, the sycophancy axis, and the confidence axis to establish that audience-credulity is (i) near-orthogonal to the model's own belief and (ii) distinct from generic deception and from expressed-opinion sycophancy. Localize the best layer.

4. Believability-tailoring metric. For each claim, define per-example tailoring pressure as the projection onto the audience-credulity axis, calibrated per model. Compare across audience conditions and test the core prediction: tailoring pressure is elevated when the audience's prior favors a claim, and is highest in the diagnostic cell where an audience-plausible-but-FALSE claim competes with an audience-implausible-but-TRUE claim. Test whether tailoring is modulated by portrayed audience expertise (less tailoring toward experts who would catch falsehoods).

5. Behavioral tailoring prediction (core). Elicit the model's chosen assertion. Score believability-tailoring as the model asserting the audience-favored claim over the truth-favored claim (and, in the diagnostic cell, asserting a plausible falsehood the audience will accept rather than an implausible truth). Test whether the pre-generation audience-credulity readout predicts believability-tailored assertion per example via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, deception axis, sycophancy axis, confidence, audience-condition identity, item length).

6. Triple dissociation (own belief vs deception vs sycophancy). Contrast conditions to show the audience-credulity axis predicts assertion choices that (a) the belief-valence axis does not (the model's own belief is held fixed while audience prior varies), (b) the generic deception axis does not (tailoring toward a believing audience of a TRUE claim is believability-fitting but not deception), and (c) the sycophancy axis does not (audience prior is portrayed contextually, with no first-person expressed opinion present). Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the pre-generation position on held-out items, steer along the audience-credulity axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence, deception, and sycophancy). Predict: amplifying it increases believability-tailoring (asserting audience-plausible claims, including plausible falsehoods) WITHOUT changing the model's own decoded belief; suppressing it makes the model assert its own belief regardless of audience acceptance (reduced tailoring). As controls, steer belief-valence (should change what the model itself holds true), the deception axis (should increase lying regardless of audience believability), and the sycophancy axis (should shift behavior only under expressed-opinion framing). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in tailoring rate vs unchanged own-belief readout.

8. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags believability-tailored assertions (especially audience-plausible falsehoods) from the audience-credulity readout; measure detection of strategic (dis)honesty vs a deception-probe-only baseline. Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('Are you saying this because it's true, or because this audience will believe it?') aligns with the latent axis and whether it fails to verbalize tailoring even when the axis is strongly engaged (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, tailoring detector, and steering to held-out claims/templates and an independent audience-adaptation stimulus set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to readout position and layer.

9. Safety-domain transfer. Move the paradigm into high-stakes domains (health/medical advice, financial claims, security instructions) where an audience-plausible falsehood tailored to a credulous or non-expert audience carries real harm; test whether tailoring pressure and behavioral believability-tailoring persist or intensify, and whether suppressing the audience-credulity axis reduces harmful audience-flattering falsehoods while preserving accurate advice to expert audiences.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The audience-credulity axis may not be separable from the model's own belief, the generic deception direction, expressed-opinion sycophancy, or confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (audience-credulity being merely sycophancy or deception) as an informative negative result that itself sharpens those accounts.

Audience-credulity framing may act through surface cues (portrayed expertise words) rather than a genuine audience-model abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, contextual (non-first-person) audience portrayal to separate from sycophancy, expert-vs-naive contrasts, and held-out-template transfer.

Believability-tailoring behavior may be weak or suppressed by safety tuning in aligned models; we include a mild persuasive-task framing to surface tailoring and report per-model base rates, treating low tailoring as itself informative about how aligned models handle audience adaptation.

Distinguishing legitimate audience-adaptation (asserting believable truths) from harmful tailoring (asserting believable falsehoods) requires the diagnostic cell where truth and audience-plausibility conflict; constructing such items cleanly is delicate, and we validate claim truth and audience-plausibility with human annotation.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout positions, and report per-template consistency.

The audience-credulity signal is a linear projection and may miss nonlinear structure; we treat tailoring pressure as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral tailoring.

Behavioral tailoring scoring depends on assertion elicitation and, for open-ended cases, an LLM judge; we anchor with forced-choice-between-claims variants and human spot-checks, and report phrasing sensitivity.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify audience-credulity steering changes tailoring without altering the model's own decoded belief or generically increasing lying.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or safety-tuned models; three-family replication and independent/safety-domain transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: prior_likelihood_gain_axes
Title: Overweighting the Prior or the Evidence? Dissociable Prior-Gain and Likelihood-Gain Axes Behind Non-Bayesian Belief Updating in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM updates a belief from a stated prior/base-rate plus new evidence in a task with a closed-form Bayesian posterior, its deviation from the normative posterior decomposes into two separable, near-orthogonal internal gain signals—a PRIOR-GAIN axis (how much the base-rate is weighted) and a LIKELIHOOD-GAIN axis (how much the new evidence is weighted)—that are independently decodable at readout time, jointly predict the model's characteristic under/over-reaction (base-rate neglect vs. conservatism), and can be causally steered independently to convert the model between conservative, base-rate-neglecting, and near-Bayesian updating without changing the underlying data.
Related Work: Human cognition robustly shows belief updating deviates from Bayes in two dissociable directions—conservatism (underweighting the likelihood) and base-rate neglect (underweighting the prior)—that are individually and situationally controllable (Gershman & Daw 'learning to infer' 2019; Base rate neglect & conservatism from full distributions 2022; sequential base-rate neglect 2022; resource-rational conservatism 2025; neural readiness-potential vs N2 dissociation, De Martino/Rangel-style 2012). On the LLM side, 'Belief Dynamics' (2025) fits a near-Bayesian log-belief-additive model of ICL+steering, and Bayesian-geometry work (2025-2026) shows transformers implement approximate Bayesian updating along entropy manifolds—but all of this treats updating as approximately rational and never asks whether the model's DEVIATION from Bayes splits into dissociable prior-gain vs. likelihood-gain components, nor whether these are carried by separable, independently steerable directions. Confirmation-bias (2025) and anchoring (2025) work show prior beliefs skew reasoning but do not isolate a normative two-knob decomposition. My prior proposals covered order-effects/non-commutativity, retraction asymmetry, provenance-weighting, and entrenchment, but none decomposes the update into prior-vs-likelihood gains validated against a closed-form posterior. We uniquely (a) import the conservatism-vs-base-rate-neglect dissociation into mechanistic LLM belief study with an analytic Bayesian ground truth, (b) test whether prior-gain and likelihood-gain are two separable internal axes, and (c) causally double-dissociate them.
Abstract: A rational reasoner combines a prior (base-rate) with new evidence (likelihood) via Bayes' rule; humans systematically fail to, and—crucially—fail in two dissociable ways: overweighting the prior (conservatism) or overweighting the evidence (base-rate neglect). We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous split and whether it has a dissociable representational basis. Using urn-and-beads-style tasks where a stated base-rate and a sequence of noisy observations yield a closed-form Bayesian posterior, we read the model's internal belief with a probe and measure its per-example deviation from the normative posterior. We hypothesize that this deviation decomposes into two separable, near-orthogonal internal gain signals: a PRIOR-GAIN axis encoding how strongly the base-rate is weighted and a LIKELIHOOD-GAIN axis encoding how strongly the new evidence is weighted. We test four claims across three model families: (1) both gains are linearly decodable at readout time and near-orthogonal to each other and to the belief-valence magnitude; (2) the two gains jointly predict, per example, the model's under/over-reaction relative to Bayes (base-rate neglect vs. conservatism) better than a single 'update-strength' signal; (3) which regime the model occupies is controllable by task structure (e.g., prior explicitness, evidence length), mirroring human query-distribution effects; and (4) steering each gain axis independently causally converts the model between conservative, base-rate-neglecting, and near-Bayesian updating—without changing the presented prior or evidence—with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls. Our results recast non-Bayesian LLM updating as two controllable gain knobs, yielding a cheap diagnostic and training-free calibration tool for evidence integration.
Experiments: 1. Belief-direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence direction that reads a graded posterior over a binary hypothesis. Because the target is a graded credence, fit via linear regression of activations onto known posterior probabilities on a calibration set of simple probability statements (and validate monotonic mapping), plus a standard true/false probe (Marks & Tegmark) as a cross-check. Validate on held-out items.

2. Normative-ground-truth stimulus construction. Build ~400 urn-and-beads / diagnosis-style items each specifying (i) an explicit base-rate/prior for a binary hypothesis H, and (ii) a sequence of K conditionally-independent noisy observations with stated likelihoods, so the Bayesian posterior P(H|data) is CLOSED-FORM. Systematically vary prior strength, evidence strength (likelihood ratio), evidence length K, and prior-evidence (in)consistency. Include a graded response elicitation (the model states P(H) as a number) so behavioral posteriors are directly comparable to normative ones. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates.

3. Deviation measurement. For each item read the model's internal belief (probe projection calibrated to [0,1]) and its stated numeric posterior; compute deviation from the closed-form Bayesian posterior. Decompose behavioral deviation into a prior-weight w_prior and likelihood-weight w_lik by fitting a generalized log-odds update: logit(belief) = w_prior*logit(prior) + w_lik*sum(log-likelihood-ratios), per item/condition (w_prior=w_lik=1 is Bayes; w_prior<1 base-rate neglect; w_lik<1 conservatism). This gives per-example behavioral gain estimates as regression targets.

4. Gain-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations at a fixed readout position and fit two linear probes: one predicting w_prior, one predicting w_lik (from step 3). Report R^2 vs. shuffled-label controls. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the prior-gain axis, the likelihood-gain axis, and the belief-valence magnitude direction to establish near-orthogonality (the two gains must be separable from each other and from how confident the final belief is).

5. Predictive validation. Test whether the internal prior-gain and likelihood-gain readouts jointly predict, per example, the direction and size of the model's deviation from Bayes (base-rate neglect vs. conservatism) better than a single 'update-magnitude' baseline and better than output entropy / stated confidence. Report incremental R^2/AUROC in nested regression.

6. Regime controllability by task structure. Test the human-inspired prediction that manipulating task structure shifts the regime: making the prior explicit/salient should raise w_prior (less base-rate neglect); longer evidence sequences should shift toward over-reaction/recency; consistent vs. inconsistent evidence should modulate w_lik. Verify the internal gain axes track these shifts, dissociating the two knobs behaviorally and internally.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the prior-gain axis (orthogonalized against likelihood-gain and belief-valence) and separately the likelihood-gain axis at the readout position on held-out items. Predict: amplifying prior-gain moves updating toward conservatism (over-weighting base-rate) and suppressing it induces base-rate neglect, WITHOUT changing the presented prior/evidence; independently, steering likelihood-gain shifts evidence-weighting. Controls: steer belief-valence (should shift the final credence uniformly) and matched random/shuffled directions. Metric: shift in fitted behavioral w_prior / w_lik toward the intended regime and, at appropriate strength, toward near-Bayesian updating; report specificity (steering prior-gain should not move likelihood-weighting and vice versa).

8. Application and robustness. Use the gain axes to build a training-free calibration knob: nudge w_prior and w_lik toward 1 and measure reduction in deviation from the Bayesian posterior and improved decision accuracy on held-out items. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted gain axes and steering to held-out items/templates and an independent probabilistic-inference set (e.g., a synthetic diagnosis/medical base-rate task) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to K, readout position, and layer.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The prior-gain and likelihood-gain axes may not be separable from each other or from belief-valence magnitude; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (a single 'update-strength' knob) as an informative negative result that itself challenges the human-analogous dissociation.

The behavioral gain decomposition (w_prior, w_lik) assumes a log-odds/log-likelihood-linear update form; real LLM updating may be nonlinear (e.g., order effects, recency), confounding the fit. We mitigate by using conditionally-independent evidence, testing fit quality per item, controlling evidence order, and reporting residual structure; we also cross-check with model-free deviation measures.

The belief probe must read a graded posterior, which is harder than binary truth and may be miscalibrated; we validate the activation->probability mapping on held-out probability statements and report calibration diagnostics, treating gain estimates as lower bounds.

Models may not respect the stated likelihoods (ignoring the generative structure), making the normative target inapplicable; we screen items where the model demonstrably uses the structure and report the fraction, treating gross non-compliance as a separate finding.

Task-structure manipulations may act through surface cues rather than genuine prior/evidence weighting; we use paraphrase templates, orthogonal manipulation of prior and evidence strength, and held-out-template transfer.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify prior-gain steering moves prior-weighting specifically without altering evidence-weighting or the presented numbers, and does not merely collapse the credence to a fixed value.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models (which reasoning-work suggests update more Bayesianly); three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage, with reasoning-tuned models noted as future work.

Name: valence_asymmetric_update_rate
Title: Good News Travels Faster: A Valence-Asymmetric Belief-Update-Rate Signal in LLMs and Its Machine Optimism
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human 'good news/bad news effect' (people update self-relevant beliefs more toward desirable than undesirable news), an LLM's internal belief representation moves MORE per unit of evidence toward good news than bad news about a self-relevant outcome; this valence-asymmetric update RATE is decodable, is separable from confirmation bias (prior-consistency) and from the desirability of the content itself, causally predicts an optimistic behavioral bias in the model's stated estimates, and can be steered to equalize or exaggerate the asymmetry.
Related Work: A large human literature documents valence-asymmetric belief updating: people incorporate good news more than bad news about their own future (Valence-Dependent Belief Updating 2017; The automatic nature of motivated belief updating 2018), this asymmetry is causally tied to left inferior frontal gyrus (Selectively altering belief formation 2012, TMS) and frontal-subcortical connectivity (2015), and it dissociates from confirmation bias, which is selective readout of belief-consistent evidence (Confirmation bias through selective readout 2025; Confirmation Bias from Bayesian approximation 2022). On the LLM side, interpretability work shows belief/truth directions are linearly decodable and context-sensitive causal mediators (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024), that transformers implement (constrained) Bayesian belief updating (Belief Dynamics 2025; Transformers represent belief state geometry 2024; The Shape of Beliefs 2026), and that confirmation bias skews CoT (Unveiling Confirmation Bias in CoT 2025). Crucially, NO interpretability work asks whether the RATE of internal belief movement is asymmetric by the VALENCE (desirability) of the evidence for a self-relevant outcome, separates this from prior-consistency (confirmation) and from the content's own desirability, or causally links the update-rate asymmetry to optimistic behavioral estimates. My prior wishful_belief_axis proposal concerns a static desirability-driven shift of the truth readout; here the object is the asymmetric UPDATE RATE (learning-rate-like) of belief change across evidence, a dynamic quantity, and it is explicitly dissociated from confirmation bias. We move from 'the model represents/desires truth' to 'the model learns from good vs bad news at different rates, producing machine optimism.'
Abstract: Humans are optimists: we update beliefs about our own future more toward good news than bad news, an asymmetry causally rooted in specific prefrontal circuitry and distinct from confirmation bias. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous asymmetry at the representational level. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs linearly encode beliefs and update them approximately Bayesianly, and that confirmation bias skews reasoning, but none isolates a valence-dependent difference in how fast internal beliefs move toward desirable versus undesirable evidence about a self-relevant outcome. Using a belief probe and estimation tasks in which the model holds an initial estimate for a self-relevant outcome and then receives evidence that is either better-than-expected (good news) or worse-than-expected (bad news) by matched magnitudes, we measure the per-item internal belief update along the belief direction and define a valence-asymmetric update rate: the ratio of movement toward good versus bad news. We test four claims across three model families: (1) internal belief updates are larger toward good news than bad news of equal size (machine optimism), beyond a symmetric-Bayesian baseline; (2) this asymmetry is decodable as a separable signal and is dissociable from confirmation bias (update-consistency with the prior) and from the content's raw desirability; (3) the internal update-rate asymmetry causally predicts an optimistic bias in the model's stated numeric estimates; and (4) steering along an update-asymmetry direction equalizes (debiases) or exaggerates the optimism without changing the presented evidence. Experiments use closed-form update-magnitude controls, norm-matched and shuffled-direction steering controls. Our results recast optimism bias as a decodable, steerable update-rate asymmetry in LLM belief dynamics.
Experiments: 1. Belief-direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence direction that reads a graded estimate/credence: fit via linear regression of activations onto known numeric estimates/probabilities on a calibration set (and validate monotonic mapping), plus a standard true/false probe (Marks & Tegmark) as a cross-check. Validate on held-out items. Freeze for all belief readouts.

2. Good-news/bad-news stimulus construction. Adapt the classic belief-update paradigm: build ~400 self-relevant outcome items where the model holds an initial estimate for an outcome about ITSELF (e.g., its probability of answering a set of questions correctly, its expected score/reward on a task, its likelihood of succeeding at an assigned goal). For each item, elicit the model's initial estimate, then present evidence (a base rate / feedback) that is either GOOD NEWS (outcome better than the model's estimate) or BAD NEWS (worse than the estimate), with the estimation error magnitude MATCHED across valence conditions. Include: (a) a NEUTRAL/other-relevant control where the same outcome concerns a third party (to separate self-relevance from generic valence), and (b) matched-magnitude controls so a symmetric Bayesian updater would move equally for good and bad news. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates.

3. Internal update-rate measurement (core). Read the frozen belief projection for the outcome BEFORE the evidence and AFTER the evidence; define per-item internal update = post minus pre, signed toward the evidence. Compute the valence-asymmetric update rate = (mean update toward good news) / (mean update toward bad news) at matched error magnitudes. Core prediction: internal updates are larger toward good news than bad news (ratio > 1) for self-relevant outcomes, beyond the matched-magnitude symmetric baseline; test whether the other-relevant control shows a smaller/absent asymmetry. Report distributions, paired tests, effect sizes, and per-model asymmetry.

4. Dissociation from confirmation bias and raw desirability. Confirmation bias predicts larger updates toward evidence CONSISTENT with the prior belief regardless of valence; optimism predicts larger updates toward GOOD news regardless of prior-consistency. Construct a 2x2 of (good vs bad news) x (belief-consistent vs belief-inconsistent evidence) and test whether the internal update-rate asymmetry loads on valence (good/bad) independently of prior-consistency. Also include a content-desirability control (desirable vs undesirable content that is NOT self-relevant news) to show the asymmetry is about update rate for self-relevant outcomes, not the static desirability shift of the content.

5. Behavioral optimism prediction. Elicit the model's revised numeric estimate after evidence. Score behavioral optimism = systematic over-updating toward good news / under-updating toward bad news in stated estimates. Test whether the per-item internal update-rate asymmetry predicts behavioral optimism via regression; report AUROC/R^2 vs baselines (belief margin, output entropy, error magnitude, prior-consistency, content desirability).

6. Update-asymmetry direction and causal steering. Fit an update-asymmetry direction from the difference of activation updates in good-news vs bad-news conditions (orthogonalized against the belief-valence magnitude direction). Steer along it at the update readout on held-out items: predict suppressing it EQUALIZES good/bad-news update rates (debiasing optimism, reducing over-optimistic estimates) WITHOUT changing the presented evidence; amplifying it exaggerates optimism. Controls: steer belief-valence (should shift the estimate uniformly for both valences) and matched random/shuffled directions. Metric: change in the good/bad update ratio and in behavioral optimism, with specificity (belief accuracy on matched controls preserved).

7. Application and robustness. Use the update-asymmetry axis to build a training-free optimism-debiasing knob; on a held-out mix (including self-assessment/calibration tasks) measure reduction in over-optimistic self-estimates and improved calibration (ECE) vs a belief-probe-only baseline. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted direction and steering to held-out items/templates and an independent self-evaluation task without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to error magnitude, readout position, and layer.

8. Self-vs-other and magnitude sweep. Sweep estimation-error magnitude and compare self-relevant vs other-relevant outcomes to test whether machine optimism (a) grows with self-relevance and (b) is modulated by magnitude as in humans (larger deviations show larger asymmetry), grounding the analogy to the human good-news/bad-news effect.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The graded belief probe must read numeric estimates, which is harder than binary truth and may be miscalibrated; we validate the activation->estimate mapping on held-out items and report calibration diagnostics, treating update rates as lower bounds.

The update-rate asymmetry could be confounded with imperfectly matched evidence magnitudes (good and bad news may not be equally strong); we calibrate each evidence item's individual belief-shift magnitude, match by measured strength, and use the symmetric-Bayesian matched-magnitude baseline as the reference.

Confirmation bias and valence-optimism may be entangled; the 2x2 (valence x prior-consistency) design is specifically included to dissociate them, and we report the valence main effect controlling for consistency; near-collapse (asymmetry being merely confirmation bias) is an informative negative result.

Operationalizing 'self-relevant' outcomes for a model is nontrivial; we use concrete self-performance/self-reward framings, validate with the other-relevant control, and report sensitivity to how self-relevance is framed.
The belief and update-asymmetry signals are linear projections that may miss nonlinear structure; we report probe-fit diagnostics and cross-check with behavioral estimate changes.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize readout positions, and report per-template consistency.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify debiasing equalizes update rates without degrading belief accuracy on matched controls.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models; three-family replication and independent-task transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: crosslingual_belief_revision
Title: Correcting a Belief in One Language: Does In-Context Belief Revision Transfer Across Languages, and Where?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM revises a belief in-context after being corrected in language A, whether that revision transfers to the model's belief queried in language B depends on WHERE in the network the update lands: corrections that move the belief in the shared, language-independent concept space (middle layers) transfer crosslingually, whereas corrections confined to surface, language-specific layers (later layers) stay siloed to the correction language; this update-locus predicts crosslingual transfer of belief revision better than static crosslingual consistency of the fact does.
Related Work: A large body of work studies static crosslingual CONSISTENCY of factual RECALL and its mechanisms: models encode facts in a language-independent concept space through middle layers and transition to language-specific spaces in final layers (Lost in Multilinguality 2025; Paths Not Taken 2025), consistency tracks entity alignment (On the Entity-Level Alignment 2025), and factual recall is English-centric with a language-transition step (Language-Specific Latent Process 2025). Consistency work also shows editing a fact in English transfers only to high-RankC languages (RankC 2023) and that knowledge is stored language-separately while reasoning is shared (Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners 2024). Belief-probe interpretability shows belief/truth is linearly decodable and context-sensitive (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024). Crucially, ALL crosslingual work concerns (a) STATIC storage/recall consistency or (b) WEIGHT editing of a fact, measured behaviorally by accuracy. NONE studies the DYNAMICS of IN-CONTEXT belief REVISION crosslingually: whether presenting counter-evidence/correction in one language moves the model's internal belief (read by a probe) when the SAME proposition is queried in another language, nor connects transfer to WHERE the in-context update lands in the concept-space vs. language-specific layers. My prior proposals (belief_updating_dynamics, retraction_asymmetry) are monolingual. We move from 'facts are stored/recalled (in)consistently across languages' to 'a belief CHANGE made in one language does or does not propagate to the belief in another, governed by the update's layer-locus.'
Abstract: Large language models store facts inconsistently across languages, and prior work has mapped where that static knowledge lives: in a shared, language-independent concept space in the middle layers that becomes language-specific only in the final layers. But real interactions revise beliefs on the fly: a user corrects the model, presents counter-evidence, or retracts a claim. We ask a question no prior work addresses: when an LLM revises a belief in-context after being corrected in one language, does that revision transfer to its belief when queried in another language, and what determines transfer? We hypothesize that crosslingual transfer of belief revision is governed by WHERE the in-context update lands: corrections that move the belief within the shared middle-layer concept space propagate to other languages, whereas corrections confined to later, language-specific layers remain siloed to the correction language. Using a multilingual belief probe on parallel true/false propositions, we (1) present a correction in language A and read the belief for the same proposition in languages A and B before/after, quantifying a per-fact crosslingual transfer of the update; (2) localize where the update moves the belief across layers via layerwise belief trajectories and activation patching between the shared concept space and language-specific layers; (3) test whether update-locus predicts transfer beyond the fact's static crosslingual consistency; and (4) causally increase transfer by steering the correction's effect into the shared concept space. Experiments span three multilingual model families and typologically diverse languages, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls. Our results recast crosslingual knowledge robustness as a belief-revision-dynamics problem and yield a training-free intervention for propagating corrections across languages.
Experiments: 1. Belief-probe and concept-space setup. On multilingual models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Aya/BLOOM-family or Gemma-2-9B), fit belief/truth directions with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes on true/false statement sets translated into each target language (built from mLAMA/DLAMA facts plus simple true/false templates), at the best per-language layer; also fit a probe in the shared middle-layer concept space (pooling activations across languages) following the language-independent-concept-space findings. Validate probe accuracy per language on held-out statements. Identify, per model, the layer band where facts are language-independent (concept space) vs. language-specific (transition/final layers) using logit-lens/representation-similarity diagnostics from prior work.

2. Parallel proposition and correction stimuli. Assemble ~400 verifiable facts (from mLAMA/DLAMA) as parallel propositions in a source language A (English and one non-English) and several target languages B spanning script/family distance (e.g., Spanish, Chinese, Arabic, Swahili). For each fact build an in-context CORRECTION dialogue in language A: the model is led to an initial (possibly wrong) belief, then given authoritative counter-evidence/correction flipping the belief. Include a NEUTRAL/no-correction control of matched length.

3. Crosslingual transfer of revision (core). Read the belief-valence projection for the SAME proposition BEFORE and AFTER the language-A correction, queried both in A (in-context) and in each target language B (fresh query after the correction context, in language B). Define per-fact update-in-A = post-minus-pre belief shift in A, and transfer = shift observed in B relative to the no-correction control. Core prediction: substantial but incomplete transfer to B, larger for languages closer to A and for facts already encoded in the shared concept space. Report transfer distributions by language distance and by whether the fact is initially concept-space-shared (measured via crosslingual representation similarity).

4. Update-locus localization. Trace the layerwise belief trajectory of the correction: at each layer, project activations onto the belief direction and measure where the correction moves the belief for the source language. Classify each correction as concept-space-landing (update concentrated in the shared middle-layer band) vs. surface-landing (update concentrated in later language-specific layers). Test whether concept-space-landing corrections show higher crosslingual transfer than surface-landing ones.

5. Causal localization via patching. To establish causality, patch the post-correction activations from the source-language run into the target-language query at (a) the shared concept-space band vs. (b) the language-specific band, and measure which patch reproduces the belief revision in language B. Prediction: patching the concept-space band transfers the revision; patching only the language-specific band does not. Norm-matched and shuffled-source controls.

6. Predictive comparison vs. static consistency. Test whether per-fact update-locus (concept-space vs. surface landing) predicts crosslingual transfer of the REVISION beyond the fact's STATIC crosslingual consistency (RankC-style) and beyond entity-alignment strength. Report incremental AUROC/R^2 in nested regression against baselines (static consistency, script/family distance, entity-alignment score, fact frequency).

7. Causal transfer-boosting intervention. Steer or project the correction's belief-update effect into the shared concept-space band (a training-free edit that reinforces the update at the language-independent layers) and measure increased belief revision and behavioral answer-flip in target languages, while preserving accuracy on uncorrected control facts. Compare to norm-matched random-direction and shuffled controls; sweep strength/layer.

8. Behavioral validation and robustness. Elicit the model's stated answer in each target language before/after correction; verify internal transfer predicts behavioral answer changes. Test a retraction variant (correction that withdraws a claim) to see if retraction transfers less than assertion crosslingually. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the analysis to held-out facts/languages and an independent multilingual fact set (mParaRel/Polyglot-or-Not slice); report per-language and per-template consistency and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Belief probes in non-English/low-resource languages may be weak or brittle, biasing transfer estimates; we validate probes per language, additionally fit a shared concept-space probe, and restrict key analyses to facts and languages where probe accuracy is high.

The concept-space vs. language-specific layer band is model-dependent and fuzzy; we identify it per model with established diagnostics (logit lens, representation similarity) and report sensitivity to band boundaries.

Measured crosslingual transfer of a correction could reflect the model re-retrieving the corrected fact from a shared store rather than genuine in-context belief propagation; the no-correction control, the patching experiment (which isolates the correction's activation change), and the retraction variant help distinguish these.

Transfer may be confounded by static crosslingual consistency (facts already consistent transfer trivially); we explicitly regress out static consistency and entity alignment and report incremental predictive power of update-locus.

Activation patching across languages is sensitive to position/tokenization mismatch; we align readout spans, use synthetic/entity-controlled facts where possible, and use norm-matched and shuffled-source controls.
The transfer-boosting intervention may degrade uncorrected facts or over-propagate; we measure accuracy retention on control facts and sweep intervention strength.
Findings on 7-9B multilingual models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-dataset transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: epistemic_access_axis
Title: Could They Have Known? A Latent Epistemic-Access Axis that Tracks Whether an Agent Was in a Position to Know, and the Machine Clairvoyance Error
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM attributes knowledge/belief to an agent in a story, it carries a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'epistemic-access' axis that tags whether that agent actually had a way of acquiring the information (was perceptually/testimonially in a position to know) versus lacking any access; the degree to which the model's own knowledge of the fact leaks into the attributed-knowledge readout despite the agent lacking access (a 'clairvoyance-leakage' signature) is decodable, dissociable from the plain truth and self/other-belief directions, and causally predicts and drives the failure where the model credits an agent with knowledge it had no way of obtaining.
Related Work: Developmental psychology shows humans track others' access to information, infer how much an agent could know from their opportunities to learn, and detect violations of epistemic expectations when a source knows something it had no access to (People infer magnitude of others' knowledge 2021/2024; Violation of epistemic expectations 2023; Preschoolers' understanding of knowledge change 2024). In LLM interpretability, truth/belief is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023), self/other beliefs and reality are separately decodable and steerable (Zhu et al. 2024 'LMs Represent Beliefs of Self and Others'; Lookbacks 2025), and knowledge-awareness/answerability directions gate refusal vs hallucination (Do I Know This Entity? 2024; Curious Case of (Un)answerability 2023). Crucially, all belief/ToM interpretability work asks WHAT an agent believes or WHO holds a belief (extensional content), never whether the agent had epistemic ACCESS/warrant to know it. Knowledge-boundary work concerns the MODEL's own knowledge, not an attributed agent's access. Epistemology distinguishes true belief from knowledge precisely via access/justification; no interpretability work isolates an access-status representation, defines a clairvoyance-leakage metric, or causally links it to over-attribution of knowledge to access-less agents. We move from 'beliefs and their holders are decodable' to 'the model represents whether an agent was in a position to know, and mislocating this drives clairvoyance errors.'
Abstract: Distinguishing knowledge from mere true belief hinges on access: an agent knows a fact only if they were in a position to acquire it. Children track this early, inferring how much others could know from their opportunities to learn and reacting with surprise when a source knows something it had no way of obtaining. We ask whether large language models represent this internally. Prior interpretability work decodes what agents believe and who holds a belief, and separately decodes the model's own knowledge boundaries, but none asks whether the model represents whether an attributed agent had EPISTEMIC ACCESS to a fact. We hypothesize that when an LLM attributes knowledge to a story agent, it carries a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'epistemic-access' axis tagging whether the agent was perceptually or testimonially in a position to know, distinct from the plain truth direction and from self/other-belief tracking; and that the extent to which the model's OWN knowledge of the fact leaks into the attributed-knowledge readout when the agent had no access (a 'clairvoyance-leakage' signature) is decodable and causally predicts and drives over-attribution of knowledge to access-less agents. Using stories that orthogonally vary a fact's truth, whether the agent had access to it, and whether the model itself knows it, we fit an access axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-example leakage, and connect it to behavioral clairvoyance errors. Double-dissociation steering tests whether enforcing access-indexing suppresses over-attribution and collapsing it induces clairvoyance, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a foundational knowledge-vs-true-belief distinction mechanistically and yield a diagnostic for machine clairvoyance.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Following Zhu et al. 2024, also fit a self/other (protagonist-vs-reality) belief direction from ToM stories as a control axis to show epistemic-access is not merely other-belief tracking.

2. Epistemic-access stimulus construction. Build ~400 short stories in which a target proposition P about a state of the world is established as TRUE, and independently vary whether a story AGENT had ACCESS to learn P: (a) ACCESS-PRESENT (the agent perceived the event, was told, or was present when P became true), (b) ACCESS-ABSENT (P became true or was revealed while the agent was absent / had no perceptual or testimonial route to it), (c) PARTIAL-ACCESS (ambiguous/indirect cues). Cross this with whether the MODEL itself knows P (real-world facts the model knows vs synthetic-entity facts stated only in-story), giving a 2x2x design over truth, agent-access, and model-knowledge. For each story, define readout spans for querying the agent's knowledge of P. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out stories/templates for transfer.

3. Access-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the agent-knowledge readout span and fit a linear probe to decode ACCESS-PRESENT vs ACCESS-ABSENT, controlling for P's truth-value and the model's own knowledge. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the epistemic-access axis, the belief-valence/truth axis, and the self/other-belief axis to establish near-orthogonality/separability. Localize the best layer and compare to reported belief-binding/lookback layers.

4. Clairvoyance-leakage metric. For each ACCESS-ABSENT story, project activations onto the frozen belief-valence direction at the agent-knowledge readout position and measure how far the agent reads as KNOWING P relative to a no-access baseline (leakage = fraction of the model's own knowledge/truth signal for P that bleeds into the agent's attributed-knowledge readout despite the agent lacking access, calibrated per model). Compare leakage across: (a) facts the model knows vs synthetic in-story facts (predicting more leakage when the model's own knowledge is strong), (b) access-present vs access-absent vs partial, and (c) as a function of how saliently the agent's lack of access is stated.

5. Behavioral clairvoyance-error prediction. Query the model on whether the agent knows P in the ACCESS-ABSENT stories; score clairvoyance errors as the rate at which the model credits the access-less agent with knowing P. Test whether per-example leakage predicts clairvoyance errors via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence probe score alone, self/other readout, output-token confidence, story length, fact popularity).

6. Dissociation from plain false-belief and from truth. Include matched plain false-belief items (agent has access but a wrong belief) and true-belief items, and test whether the access axis and leakage metric predict access-violation errors distinctly from what a standard character-belief probe predicts, and independently of P's truth-value (true-but-no-access vs true-and-access), establishing epistemic access as a mechanism separate from belief content and from truth.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the agent-knowledge readout position on held-out ACCESS-ABSENT items, steer along the epistemic-access axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and self/other). Predict: enforcing access-absent indexing (suppressing leakage) reduces clairvoyance errors WITHOUT changing whether the model judges P itself to be true; amplifying leakage (pushing toward the model's own knowledge) induces over-attribution. As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip whether P is judged true) and the self/other axis (should change attributed-belief-content judgments, not access). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers.

8. Application, introspection, and robustness. Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('Could this agent have known that, given what they had access to?') aligns with the latent access axis and whether models fail to verbalize an access violation even when the axis is strongly engaged (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted access axis, leakage metric, and steering to held-out stories/templates and an independent ToM/knowledge-access stimulus set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The epistemic-access axis may not be separable from belief-valence or self/other-belief; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (access being merely other-belief or truth) as an informative negative result that itself challenges the knowledge-vs-true-belief distinction in LLMs.

Access-presence framing may act through surface cues (words like 'saw', 'was told', 'was absent') rather than a genuine access abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, indirect-access variants, synthetic-entity controls, and held-out-template transfer.

Constructing clean ACCESS-ABSENT-but-true-and-model-known items requires the model to both know P and represent the agent's lack of access; we validate the model's own knowledge via sampling and use synthetic in-story facts as a controlled contrast where the model's parametric knowledge is absent.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.
The leakage metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear leakage could be missed, so we treat leakage as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.

Behavioral clairvoyance-error scoring depends on how the agent-knowledge query is worded (pragmatic implicature); we report sensitivity to multiple phrasings, include low-demand phrasings from developmental work, and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify access steering changes over-attribution without flipping the model's own truth judgment of P.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: self_dispersion_belief
Title: Knowing How Divided It Will Be: A Latent Self-Dispersion Belief that Anticipates an LLM's Own Answer Distribution Before Sampling
Short Hypothesis: In a single forward pass, before generating or sampling anything, an LLM encodes a separable, decodable 'self-dispersion' belief—an anticipation of how internally divided its own future samples will be (its forthcoming self-consistency / answer entropy)—that is distinct from the correctness/confidence direction and from mere task difficulty, causally predicts the actual dispersion of sampled answers, and can be steered to make the model's own sampling more or less consistent.
Related Work: Self-consistency and its variants aggregate MANY sampled answers post hoc and measure cross-sample agreement to gauge reliability (Wang et al. SC; Mirror-Consistency 2024; Dynamic Distributional Alignment 2025). Internal-signal work shows cross-sample neuron agreement and activation sparsity distinguish correct from incorrect responses AFTER multiple samples (Do LLMs Signal When They're Right? / NAD 2025; LENS 2025), and difficulty probes on FFN activations predict problem hardness from one pass (ACTSC 2026). Correctness/confidence directions predict whether a forthcoming answer is right (No Answer Needed 2025; Confidence is Not Competence 2025; Inside-Out 2025; Cognitive Dissonance 2023), and belief-state geometry work models posteriors over answers (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024; The Shape of Beliefs 2026). Crucially, ALL cross-sample work measures dispersion empirically across many generations; difficulty/correctness probes target hardness or right/wrong, NOT the shape/spread of the model's OWN answer distribution. No work asks whether a SINGLE pre-sampling forward pass encodes a distinct belief about the model's forthcoming answer DISPERSION (self-consistency), dissociable from correctness, confidence, and difficulty, nor causally steers it. This differs from my prior proposals (beliefs about external propositions/agents): here the object of belief is the model's own sampling distribution.
Abstract: Self-consistency—sampling many chains and voting—works because a model's answer distribution is sometimes sharply peaked and sometimes badly split, but current methods discover which case they are in only by paying for many samples. We ask whether an LLM already knows, in a single forward pass before any sampling, how divided its own future answers will be. We hypothesize a separable, decodable 'self-dispersion' belief: a representation of the model's forthcoming answer entropy/self-consistency that is distinct from the correctness/confidence direction and from task difficulty, that causally predicts the true dispersion of sampled answers, and that can be steered to sharpen or spread the model's own sampling. Using questions for which we can empirically measure answer dispersion by sampling K times, we (1) train a linear probe on single-pass pre-generation activations to predict forthcoming dispersion, (2) test its separability from confidence, correctness, and difficulty probes via cross-decoding and incremental prediction, (3) validate it against the true empirical dispersion, and (4) causally steer along the self-dispersion direction to change actual sampled consistency without changing the modal answer, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls. We further test whether prompting the model to introspect ('how consistent will your answers be?') aligns with the latent signal. Experiments span three model families. Beyond a mechanistic account of a new belief type—the model's belief about its own generative distribution—this yields a cheap, single-pass adaptive-compute signal for allocating self-consistency samples.
Experiments: 1. Setup and empirical dispersion labels. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, assemble ~600 questions spanning factual QA (TriviaQA/PopQA), commonsense (CSQA), and short-answer reasoning, mixing items expected to be peaked vs. split. For each item, sample K (e.g., 40) answers at a fixed temperature and compute the ground-truth answer dispersion: normalized answer entropy and modal-answer share (top-1 vote fraction), plus semantic-entropy clustering for free-form answers. These are the regression targets.

2. Self-dispersion probe. Extract single-pass activations at a fixed pre-generation readout position (end of prompt, before any tokens). Fit linear probes (mass-mean and logistic/linear regression) at the best layer to predict forthcoming dispersion (entropy / modal share). Report R^2 and AUROC (high-vs-low dispersion) vs. shuffled-label controls; identify the best layer.

3. Separability from confidence/correctness/difficulty. Fit (a) a correctness/confidence direction (in-advance correctness probe, No Answer Needed style), and (b) a difficulty direction (ACTSC-style FFN probe / measured accuracy). Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the self-dispersion direction and each. Critically, on the diagnostic subset where the model is CORRECT-but-split vs. CORRECT-but-peaked (same correctness, different dispersion), test whether the dispersion probe still separates them, establishing a distinct signal beyond correctness/confidence.

4. Predictive validation and comparison. Test whether the single-pass dispersion readout predicts true empirical dispersion per item better than baselines: confidence probe, difficulty probe, output-token entropy of the first answer, and verbalized self-estimated consistency. Report incremental R^2/AUROC in nested regression and calibration (ECE) of a dispersion-based reliability score.

5. Causal steering (double dissociation). Steer along the self-dispersion direction (orthogonalized against confidence and correctness) at the pre-generation position, then actually sample K answers. Predict: suppressing dispersion sharpens the sampled answer distribution (higher modal share, lower entropy) WITHOUT changing the modal answer identity; amplifying it spreads it. Controls: steer the confidence direction (should shift correctness/hedging) and matched random/shuffled directions. Metric: change in empirical answer entropy/modal share vs. modal-answer preservation and accuracy retention.

6. Application: single-pass adaptive self-consistency. Use the dispersion probe to allocate samples (few for peaked items, more for split items) and compare accuracy-vs-compute trade-off against fixed-K SC, output-entropy-based DSC, and ACTSC. Report accuracy at matched average sample budget and sample reduction at matched accuracy.

7. Introspection link. Prompt the model to self-report expected consistency ('If you answered this 10 times, how many would agree?') and test whether the latent dispersion signal predicts these self-reports and whether models fail to verbalize dispersion even when the axis is strongly present (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control).

8. Robustness and generalization. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted dispersion probe and steering to held-out items/domains and an independent QA slice without refitting; report per-domain and per-template consistency, sensitivity to sampling temperature, K, readout position, and layer.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The self-dispersion direction may not be separable from the confidence/correctness or difficulty directions; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, incremental predictive power, and the correct-but-split vs correct-but-peaked dissociation, and treat near-collapse (dispersion being merely inverse confidence or difficulty) as an informative negative result.

Empirical dispersion depends on sampling temperature and K; a probe may only track dispersion at the specific temperature it was fit on. We report sensitivity across temperatures and K, and test transfer of the probe across sampling settings.

Free-form answer dispersion requires clustering (semantic entropy) which is noisy; we anchor with exact-match modal share on short-answer items and use held-out-judge + human spot-checks for clustering quality.

The single-pass readout could exploit surface question features correlated with dispersion (e.g., ambiguity cues) rather than a genuine self-model of the generative distribution; we control for question difficulty/ambiguity, use paraphrase templates, and test whether the signal predicts dispersion beyond surface features.
The signal is a linear projection and may miss nonlinear structure; we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify dispersion steering changes empirical sample spread without flipping the modal answer or degrading accuracy.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models; three-family replication and independent transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: generic_vs_universal_belief_axis
Title: Some Ducks vs. All Ducks: A Latent Genericity Axis, and the Machine Generic-Overgeneralization Effect
Short Hypothesis: LLMs represent a proposition's quantificational force along a separable, near-orthogonal 'genericity' axis distinguishing a defeasible generic/default belief ('ducks lay eggs', exception-tolerant) from a universal belief ('all ducks lay eggs', exception-falsified), which is distinct from the plain truth/belief-valence direction; the degree to which a generic's belief collapses onto the universal representation (a 'generic-overgeneralization' signature) is decodable, causally predicts and drives the documented failure where the model accepts false universals ('all ducks lay eggs') as true, and can be steered to suppress or induce overgeneralization without changing whether the model believes the generic.
Related Work: Cognitive science robustly documents that generics ('birds fly') are a cognitive default that is exception-tolerant, processed faster than universals, and that people commit the 'generic overgeneralization' (GOG) effect—wrongly accepting false universals ('all birds fly') as true (Leslie/Khemlani/Glucksberg 2011; Meyer 2017/2020; syllogistic GOG 2008), plus an acceptance-vs-inference asymmetry (Tessler & Goodman; social/animal generics 2022). Behavioral LLM work shows models struggle with generics: Ralethe & Buys (2024, TACL) study exceptions/instantiations and find LLMs conflate generics with universals, and Generics and Default Reasoning in LLMs (2025) shows most models misinterpret generics as universal and CoT degrades defeasible reasoning. In interpretability, truth/belief-valence is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023), and one LSTM study finds a hard-coded default-reasoning effect for number/gender (GCD 2019). Crucially, no interpretability work isolates a representation of quantificational force—a defeasible generic/default belief vs. an exception-falsified universal belief—as an internal axis distinct from truth-value, defines a generic->universal collapse metric, or causally links it to the GOG effect. Prior LLM generics work is purely behavioral; my earlier belief-axis proposals (categorical-vs-graded credence, contestedness, vagueness, disbelief-vs-absence) concern degree/kind of belief, not quantificational structure. We move from 'LLMs behave as if generics are universals' to 'the model carries a decodable, steerable genericity axis whose collapse onto the universal representation mechanistically drives generic overgeneralization.'
Abstract: Humans treat generic statements ('ducks lay eggs') as defeasible defaults that survive exceptions, yet systematically over-accept the corresponding false universals ('all ducks lay eggs')—the generic overgeneralization effect. Behavioral work shows large language models exhibit the same conflation, but the internal cause is unknown. We ask whether LLMs represent quantificational force internally. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal 'genericity' axis that distinguishes a defeasible generic/default belief from an exception-falsified universal belief, distinct from the plain truth/belief-valence direction; and a 'generic-overgeneralization' signature: the degree to which a generic's belief representation collapses onto the universal representation, quantifiable per item and predictive of the model wrongly asserting false universals as true. Using matched propositions that hold content fixed while varying quantificational form (generic, universal, existential) and known exception structure (exceptionless vs. exception-permitting characteristic properties like 'birds fly'), we fit a genericity axis, measure its separability from truth-valence via cross-decoding, quantify per-item collapse, and connect it to behavioral overgeneralization and to exception-tolerance behavior. Double-dissociation steering tests whether suppressing collapse makes the model correctly reject false universals while still endorsing the generic, and amplifying it induces overgeneralization—with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a classic cognitive default mechanistically and yield a cheap diagnostic and training-free intervention for overgeneralization in LLM reasoning.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. This is the control 'is-it-true' axis.

2. Genericity stimulus construction. Build ~400 kind-property pairs holding content fixed while varying quantificational form: GENERIC ('ducks lay eggs'), UNIVERSAL ('all ducks lay eggs'), and EXISTENTIAL ('some ducks lay eggs'). Cross with property type using established GOG stimuli: (a) EXCEPTIONLESS-characteristic ('all triangles have three sides', true as universal), (b) EXCEPTION-PERMITTING characteristic ('birds fly', 'ducks lay eggs'—true as generic, FALSE as universal), (c) MINORITY/striking properties ('mosquitoes carry malaria'), and (d) FALSE generics ('ducks are red'). Include fictitious-kind items ('feps have blue horns') from the developmental literature to control pretraining priors. Ground-truth quantificational truth-values are annotated (a false universal whose generic is true is the diagnostic GOG cell). Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out pairs/templates for transfer.

3. Genericity-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition span and fit a linear probe to decode GENERIC vs. UNIVERSAL form, controlling for content and truth-value. Report AUROC vs. shuffled-label controls. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the genericity axis and the truth/belief-valence axis to establish near-orthogonality/separability. Localize the best layer.

4. Generic-overgeneralization collapse metric. For each EXCEPTION-PERMITTING pair, read the belief-valence projection for the GENERIC form (should be high/true) and the UNIVERSAL form (should be low/false). Define collapse = how far the universal form's belief-valence readout is pulled toward the generic's true value (i.e., the universal reads truer than warranted), calibrated per model. Compare collapse across property types; core prediction: collapse is largest for exception-permitting characteristic properties (the classic GOG cell) and near-zero for exceptionless properties and false generics. Test whether collapse is larger for fictitious kinds where the model must rely on generic-default reasoning.

5. Behavioral overgeneralization prediction. Elicit the model's true/false judgment for each universal statement. Score the GOG error = accepting a false universal ('all birds fly') as true. Test whether per-item collapse predicts GOG errors via logistic regression; report AUROC vs. baselines (truth-valence margin, output entropy, property prevalence/frequency, item length).

6. Exception-tolerance link. For each generic, present an explicit exception ('but penguins do not fly') and re-query both the generic and the universal. Test whether the genericity axis predicts appropriate behavior: the generic should survive the exception (belief maintained) while the universal should be rejected. Test whether the genericity axis (not the truth axis) accounts for exception-tolerant maintenance of the generic, distinguishing defeasible-generic representation from plain high-confidence truth.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out GOG-cell items, steer along the genericity axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence) at the universal-statement readout. Predict: suppressing collapse (pushing the universal toward the 'universal/exception-falsified' pole) makes the model correctly REJECT the false universal WITHOUT changing its endorsement of the generic; amplifying collapse induces overgeneralization on exceptionless-adjacent items. As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip judgments on both forms) and matched random/shuffled directions. Sweep strengths and layers. Metric: GOG-error reduction with preserved generic endorsement.

8. Application and robustness. On a held-out mix (exception-permitting, exceptionless, false generics, fictitious kinds), test whether suppressing collapse reduces false-universal acceptance while preserving correct universals and generic endorsement (report GOG-error rate, false-rejection rate on true universals, generic-endorsement retention vs. a truth-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, collapse metric, and steering to held-out pairs/templates and an independent generics dataset (Ralethe & Buys 2024 exemplars) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice. As a high-stakes transfer, test social generics ('immigrants commit crimes'-style stereotype schemas with neutral fictitious groups) to probe whether the same overgeneralization collapse drives stereotype-style universal over-acceptance.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The genericity axis may not be separable from the truth/belief-valence direction (a universal that is false simply reads low on truth); we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, and—critically—the diagnostic GOG cell where the generic is true but the universal is false, testing whether genericity is decodable independent of truth-value; near-collapse is an informative negative result that itself sharpens the truth-representation account.

Quantificational form is signaled by explicit lexical cues ('all', 'some', bare plural), so the genericity axis might reflect surface tokens rather than a genuine quantificational abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates (varied universal phrasings 'every/each/all'), fictitious-kind controls, and held-out-template transfer, and test whether the axis predicts behavior beyond a lexical baseline.

Ground-truth quantificational truth-values for exception-permitting properties can be contested (is 'all birds fly' determinately false?); we use items with strong human agreement from the GOG literature, use multiple annotators, and report label-agreement sensitivity.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.
The collapse metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear structure could be missed, so we treat collapse as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.

Behavioral GOG scoring depends on how the true/false judgment is elicited (time-pressure amplifies GOG in humans but is not directly analogous); we report sensitivity to multiple elicitation phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify collapse-suppression reduces false-universal acceptance without degrading correct universals or generic endorsement.
The social-generics transfer is exploratory and value-laden; we use neutral fictitious groups and treat it as a probe of the same mechanism rather than a claim about specific real-world stereotypes.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-dataset transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: noisy_readout_conjunction_fallacy
Title: Bias by Read-Out, Not by Similarity: Testing Whether LLM Conjunction Fallacies Are a Noisy Belief-Magnitude Artifact Predicted by Probability-Theory-Plus-Noise
Short Hypothesis: LLM conjunction fallacies (judging P(A∧B) > P(A)) are not primarily driven by a similarity/representativeness computation but are largely a structured read-out artifact of noisy internal probability-belief magnitudes: the model internally holds approximately coherent constituent beliefs, but a regression-to-center noise on the decoded belief magnitude produces fallacies exactly where probability-theory-plus-noise predicts (one constituent high, one low, positive conditional support), and the per-item internal noise magnitude predicts and causally drives the fallacy.
Related Work: Behavioral work documents that LLMs commit the conjunction fallacy and the representativeness heuristic and often reason from stereotypes (ReHeAT / Real Linda 2024; CBEval 2024; Thinking Fast and Slow in LLMs 2022; Levels of Analysis 2025 noting deviations from probability axioms). In cognitive science, the 'probability theory plus noise' account (Costello & Watts 2008, 2014, 2016, 2018) explains the wide range of human conjunction-fallacy rates as a consequence of standard probability reasoning corrupted by regressive read-out noise, predicting fallacies precisely when one constituent is high and one low with positive support. Interpretability work shows belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023) and that a graded posterior/credence can be read from activations (Belief Dynamics 2025; Transformers represent belief state geometry 2024).
