My prior belief_coherence_geometry proposal tests a static logical algebra (proj(P∧Q) ≤ min) as a geometric law; it does NOT invoke a noise/regression mechanism, does not test the probability-theory-plus-noise magnitude-dependent fallacy-rate signature, and does not adjudicate similarity-driven vs. noisy-read-out accounts. No prior work (a) decodes internal constituent probability magnitudes and shows LLM conjunction fallacies follow the noise-account signature, (b) dissociates a representativeness/similarity computation from a noisy-read-out artifact internally, or (c) causally reduces the fallacy by denoising the belief read-out. We move from 'LLMs commit the conjunction fallacy' to 'the fallacy is a predictable noisy-read-out artifact, mechanistically dissociable from similarity.'
Abstract: For forty years the conjunction fallacy—judging a conjunction more probable than its constituents—has been taken as evidence that people abandon probability theory for a similarity/representativeness heuristic. A competing account, probability-theory-plus-noise, holds instead that reasoners represent roughly correct constituent probabilities but read them out with regressive noise, producing fallacies precisely when one constituent is high and one low. LLMs are known to commit conjunction and representativeness fallacies, but always studied behaviorally, and the field assumes a similarity mechanism. We ask a mechanistic question: are LLM conjunction fallacies a read-out artifact of noisy internal probability beliefs rather than a similarity computation? Using a probe that decodes graded internal probability magnitudes for propositions, we read the model's internal estimates for constituents A and B and their conjunction A∧B on classic Linda-style and neutral (non-stereotype) items. We test three claims across three model families: (1) the observed conjunction-fallacy rate follows the probability-theory-plus-noise signature—largest when one decoded constituent is high and the other low, with positive conditional support—both for stereotype items and for neutral items with no representativeness cue; (2) a per-item internal noise/regression estimate predicts behavioral fallacy occurrence beyond similarity/stereotype features; and (3) reducing read-out noise (denoising the decoded belief before the conjunction judgment, or steering the conjunction estimate toward the constituent-consistent value) causally lowers the fallacy rate, while injecting noise raises it. Our results would reframe a canonical bias as a decodable, structured, steerable read-out artifact rather than a similarity heuristic.
Experiments: 1. Graded belief-probe setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a probe that reads a graded probability/credence for a proposition: calibrate activations against known probabilities using explicit-probability statements ('there is an X% chance that...') via linear regression, and cross-check with a standard true/false direction (Marks & Tegmark). Validate the activation->probability mapping (monotonicity, calibration) on held-out items and report calibration diagnostics.

2. Conjunction stimulus construction. Build ~400 item families. Each family has constituents A and B and the conjunction A∧B, spanning two conditions: (i) STEREOTYPE/representativeness items in Linda-style format (a description makes B representative but improbable, A generic and probable), and (ii) NEUTRAL items with no stereotype/similarity cue (arbitrary but verifiable constituents) systematically varied to span the constituent-probability grid (both high, both low, one high/one low) with controlled conditional support. This lets us test the noise-account signature independently of any representativeness cue. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out families.

3. Internal-magnitude read-out and noise estimate. For each item read decoded internal probabilities p(A), p(B), p(A∧B) at a fixed readout position. Define coherence residual and per-item read-out noise: the deviation of decoded magnitudes from probability-theoretic constraints (e.g., p(A∧B) vs. p(A)p(B|A) implied bounds), estimated from repeated paraphrase read-outs (variance) and from regression-to-center of the decoded scale. Compare the decoded p(A∧B) to the internal constituent values.

4. Probability-theory-plus-noise signature test (core). Compute the behavioral conjunction-fallacy rate (does the model rank/judge A∧B more probable than the lower constituent) as a function of the decoded constituent magnitudes. Test the noise-account prediction: fallacy rate peaks when one decoded constituent is high and one low with positive support, and follows the analytic noise-model curve. Critically, test whether this signature holds even for NEUTRAL items lacking any representativeness cue—evidence the fallacy is not fundamentally similarity-driven. Fit the probability-theory-plus-noise model and report goodness-of-fit vs. a similarity-only baseline.

5. Predictive dissociation (noise vs. similarity). Test whether the per-item internal read-out noise/regression estimate predicts behavioral fallacy occurrence beyond similarity/stereotype features (embedding similarity between description and B, a representativeness score, item length) via logistic regression; report incremental AUROC. On stereotype items, test whether the fallacy is better explained by decoded-magnitude structure than by the representativeness score.

6. Causal denoising intervention. On held-out fallacy-prone items, apply a training-free denoise of the conjunction read-out: (a) steer the decoded p(A∧B) representation toward the constituent-consistent value (≤ min(p(A),p(B))) along the belief-magnitude direction, and (b) reduce read-out noise via representation smoothing across paraphrases. Measure fallacy-rate reduction and preserved accuracy on non-fallacy items. Compare to norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths.

7. Causal noise injection (specificity). Inject noise along the belief-magnitude direction on coherent items and test whether it induces conjunction fallacies at the rate the noise model predicts, confirming the mechanism is read-out noise rather than a separate similarity module.

8. Robustness and generalization. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted probe, noise estimate, and denoising intervention to held-out families and an independent set (ReHeAT items and neutral disjunction-fallacy items, which the noise account also predicts) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer/readout position. As a cross-check, test whether the same noise estimate also predicts disjunction-fallacy and subadditivity patterns, which the probability-theory-plus-noise account uniquely ties together.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The graded probability probe is harder to fit than a binary truth probe and may be miscalibrated, biasing decoded magnitudes; we validate the activation->probability mapping, report calibration, and treat decoded magnitudes and noise estimates as lower bounds.

The probability-theory-plus-noise signature could be mimicked by a similarity account in stereotype items; the NEUTRAL, cue-free items and the disjunction/subadditivity cross-check are specifically designed to adjudicate—if the signature holds without any representativeness cue, similarity cannot be the primary driver.

Estimating per-item read-out noise via paraphrase variance conflates probe noise with genuine model noise; we separate probe reliability (test-retest on unambiguous items) from item-level noise and report both.

Behavioral fallacy elicitation depends on format (ranking vs. numeric estimate); the noise account predicts format effects, so we test both and report format sensitivity as a prediction rather than a confound.

The denoising/steering intervention could simply cap conjunction estimates and degrade genuinely-high conjunctions; we preserve items where the conjunction is legitimately probable and measure specificity.
Belief probes are brittle to surface form; we use paraphrase templates, standardize readout positions, and report per-template consistency.

Causal interventions are layer/strength sensitive; we use norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify noise injection reproduces the predicted magnitude-dependent fallacy curve.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models (which CoT work suggests reason more normatively); three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage, with reasoning-tuned models noted as future work.

Name: user_attribute_belief_warrant
Title: Assuming It Knows You: A Latent Warrant Axis on LLM Beliefs About the User, and Stereotype Over-Commitment from Weak Cues
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM forms a belief about a user's demographic/identity attribute, it carries a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'warrant' signal encoding how well-grounded that belief is (inferred from multiple consistent cues vs. leapt to from a single weak/stereotypical cue), distinct from the attribute-belief content and from generic confidence; the degree to which weakly-warranted stereotype inferences collapse onto the well-warranted region (an 'over-commitment' signature) is decodable at generation time and causally predicts and drives the failure where the model treats a stereotype-driven guess as established fact and resists user-provided contradiction.
Related Work: Prior interpretability work shows LLMs linearly encode user sociodemographic attributes from indirect cues (names, occupations) that shape downstream behavior (Linear socio-demographic representations 2025; SocioProbe 2022; Mutual Influence of Gender and Occupation 2025), engage in implicit personalization from stereotypical cues that can override explicitly stated identity (Reading Between the Prompts 2025), form decodable trait impressions of prompt authors (Artificial Impressions 2025), and that user-persona representations causally gate behavior (Who's Asking 2024). Belief-probe work decodes truth/belief and self/other beliefs (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Zhu et al. 2024). Crucially, ALL user-attribute work reads the CONTENT of the inferred attribute (which demographic) and shows it biases outputs, but none represents the WARRANT/groundedness of that inference—whether the belief is a well-supported inference from consistent evidence vs. an unwarranted stereotype leap from a single weak cue—as a decodable, dissociable quantity, nor defines an over-commitment metric, nor causally links it to the specific failure of treating a stereotype guess as fact and resisting correction. Self/other-belief work concerns narrative characters, not the live user; implicit-personalization work steers toward stated identity but does not represent evidential warrant. We move from 'the model infers and acts on user attributes' to 'the model represents how warranted its user-belief is, and mislocating warrant drives stereotype over-commitment.'
Abstract: Large language models silently infer who they are talking to—a user's gender, race, age, or expertise—from cues as thin as a name, and these inferences shape their responses. Prior work shows these user-attribute beliefs are linearly decodable and bias behavior, but treats them as flat content: which attribute the model assumes. We ask a sharper, epistemically-grounded question: does the model also represent how WELL-WARRANTED its user-belief is—whether it rests on multiple consistent cues or is a stereotype leap from a single weak signal—and does mislocating this warrant cause the model to treat a guess as established fact? We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'warrant' axis, decodable at generation time, that encodes the evidential groundedness of a user-attribute belief, distinct from the attribute-belief content and from generic output confidence; and an 'over-commitment' signature: the degree to which weakly-warranted stereotype inferences read as if well-warranted, quantifiable per example and predictive of the model asserting/acting on the inferred attribute as fact and resisting user contradiction. Using controlled dialogues that orthogonally vary the strength of user-attribute evidence (no cue, single weak/stereotypical cue, multiple consistent cues, explicit statement) and its correctness, we fit a warrant axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-example over-commitment, and connect it to behavioral stereotype over-commitment and correction-resistance. Double-dissociation steering tests whether suppressing over-commitment makes the model hold weak inferences tentatively (and accept correction) without changing the inferred attribute, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a fairness-critical failure as a decodable, steerable warrant deficit and yield a training-free diagnostic and intervention.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, following prior demographic-probing work, fit attribute-belief probes (e.g., inferred user gender/race/age/expertise) from activations on prompts with EXPLICIT user-attribute disclosure, at the best layer with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes; validate that the same probes recover attributes from implicit cues (names/occupations) as in Linear socio-demographic representations 2025. Separately fit a generic output-confidence control axis (token entropy / empirical answer-stability).

2. Warrant-graded stimulus construction. Build ~400 dialogue items per attribute where the model must (implicitly) infer a user attribute, holding the target attribute value fixed while varying EVIDENTIAL WARRANT: (a) NO-CUE baseline, (b) SINGLE-WEAK-CUE (one stereotypical signal, e.g., a gendered name or occupation), (c) MULTIPLE-CONSISTENT-CUES (several independent cues agreeing), (d) EXPLICIT-STATEMENT (user states the attribute). Cross with correctness by including CUE-INCONSISTENT items where the weak cue points one way but a later explicit statement contradicts it. Use paraphrase templates and diverse names/occupations; reserve held-out items/templates.

3. Warrant-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the readout span where the attribute-belief is engaged and fit a linear probe to decode HIGH-WARRANT (multiple-consistent/explicit) vs LOW-WARRANT (single-weak-cue), controlling for the attribute value itself. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the warrant axis, the attribute-belief content probe, and the output-confidence axis to establish that warrant is (i) near-orthogonal to attribute content and (ii) not merely generic confidence. Localize the best layer.

4. Over-commitment metric. For each SINGLE-WEAK-CUE item, project onto the warrant axis and measure how far the weakly-warranted belief reads as HIGH-WARRANT relative to the multiple-cue baseline (over-commitment = fraction of the well-warranted signal a stereotype leap inherits, calibrated per model). Compare across warrant conditions and attributes; predict over-commitment is largest for strongly stereotypical single cues and correlates with real-world cue base-rate strength.

5. Behavioral over-commitment and correction-resistance prediction. Elicit the model's behavior: (a) whether it asserts/acts on the inferred attribute as fact (e.g., in personalized recommendations or presuppositions), and (b) on CUE-INCONSISTENT items, whether it accepts the user's explicit correction or clings to the stereotype inference. Score stereotype over-commitment and correction-resistance (rule-based + held-out judge + human spot-checks). Test whether per-example over-commitment predicts these failures via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (attribute-content probe margin, output confidence, cue base-rate, item length).

6. Dissociation from attribute content and confidence. Contrast items where attribute content is held fixed but warrant varies, and vice versa, to show the warrant axis predicts over-commitment/correction-resistance beyond what the attribute-content probe and confidence axis predict. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out weak-cue items, steer along the warrant axis (orthogonalized against attribute content and confidence). Predict: suppressing warrant makes the model hold the inference tentatively (hedges, asks clarifying questions, accepts correction on cue-inconsistent items) WITHOUT changing which attribute it inferred; amplifying warrant induces over-commitment on no-cue/weak items. As controls, steer the attribute-content direction (should change which attribute is inferred) and confidence (should shift hedging generically). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in over-commitment/correction-acceptance rate vs unchanged inferred attribute.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free fairness diagnostic: flag stereotype over-commitment from the warrant readout and steer to enforce tentativeness; measure reduction in stereotype-driven personalization and correction-resistance while preserving appropriate use of explicitly-stated attributes (report over-commitment rate, correction-acceptance rate, and preserved explicit-attribute usage vs an attribute-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, over-commitment metric, and steering to held-out attributes/templates and an independent implicit-personalization dataset (e.g., a Reading-Between-the-Prompts-style set) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The warrant axis may not be separable from the attribute-content probe or generic confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (warrant being merely confidence or content-strength) as an informative negative result that itself sharpens the demographic-representation literature.

Warrant framing may act through surface cue count/salience rather than a genuine evidential-groundedness abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, varied cue types (names, occupations, dialect, topic interests), and held-out-template transfer, and test whether the axis predicts behavior beyond a raw cue-count baseline.

Attribute-belief probes are known to be brittle and may capture surface lexical associations; we validate probes against both explicit and implicit cues, use diverse instances, and report per-template consistency.
The over-commitment metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear structure could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.

Behavioral scoring of stereotype over-commitment and correction-resistance is partly subjective and value-laden; we anchor with rule-based presupposition/correction detectors, human spot-checks, use attributes with clear ground-truth in cue-inconsistent items, and report label-agreement sensitivity.

This work probes demographic inference; to avoid amplifying harm we use synthetic users, standard census-aligned cue sets already used in prior fairness work, and frame steering as a tentativeness/fairness intervention rather than a means to sharpen demographic targeting.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify warrant steering changes tentativeness/correction-acceptance without altering the inferred attribute or degrading use of explicitly-stated attributes.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or safety-tuned models; three-family replication and independent-dataset transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: falsifiability_axis
Title: Could It Even Be Checked? A Latent Falsifiability Axis Distinct from Truth, and the Machine Bullshit-Receptivity Effect
Short Hypothesis: LLMs represent a proposition's EPISTEMIC TYPE—whether it is empirically verifiable/falsifiable (adjudicable by evidence) versus unfalsifiable/vacuous (no possible empirical test)—along a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'falsifiability' axis, distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction and from generic don't-know uncertainty; the degree to which unfalsifiable/vacuous claims collapse onto a confident truth-value (a 'bullshit-receptivity' signature) is decodable at assertion time and causally predicts and drives the failure where the model assents to pseudo-profound or untestable claims as if they were established facts.
Related Work: Epistemology formally separates verifiable, falsifiable, and unfalsifiable beliefs by their mode of possible justification—a distinction orthogonal to truth-value (Epistemic Awareness of Doxastic Distinctions 2022; Falsification or Confirmation 2015; Broadening Misinformation Research 2025, which introduces time-indexed 'evidence retrievability'). Psychology shows people vary in receptivity to pseudo-profound 'bullshit'—vacuous, unfalsifiable statements accepted as profound/true (On the Reception and Detection of Pseudo-Profound Bullshit 2015; Illusory Pattern Perception 2019). In LLM interpretability, truth/belief-valence is linearly decodable (Geometry of Truth 2023; Truth is Universal 2024; Truthfulness Probe Generalization 2025), plausibility and logical validity are decodable and conflated (How LMs Conflate Logical Validity with Plausibility 2025), modal categories (possible/impossible/inconceivable) are linearly represented (Is This Just Fantasy? 2025), and a Valence-Assent Axis co-encodes good and true (A Unified Representation 2025). Crucially, ALL of this assumes propositions are the kind of thing that HAS a truth-value and asks whether the model tracks it; none isolates whether the model represents that a claim admits an empirical test AT ALL (verifiable/falsifiable vs. unfalsifiable/vacuous), defines a falsifiability->truth collapse metric, or causally links it to assenting to unfalsifiable/pseudo-profound claims. This differs from my prior contestedness axis (claims that have a fact of the matter but are socially disputed) and borderline-vagueness axis (semantic indeterminacy of gradable predicates): here the cut is epistemic testability—whether evidence could in principle adjudicate the claim—not whether it is disputed, fuzzy, or currently unknown. Modal-category work concerns metaphysical possibility, not empirical falsifiability. We move from 'the model tracks truth/plausibility' to 'the model represents whether a claim is even empirically checkable, and mis-mapping this drives machine bullshit-receptivity.'
Abstract: A basic epistemic skill is telling apart claims that evidence could adjudicate ('the sample contains lead') from claims no possible test could confirm or refute ('reality is a vibration of pure consciousness'). Philosophy separates verifiable, falsifiable, and unfalsifiable beliefs—a distinction orthogonal to truth—and psychology shows people differ in whether they accept vacuous, unfalsifiable 'bullshit' as profound truth. We ask whether large language models represent this internally. Prior interpretability work decodes truth, plausibility, and modal possibility, but always assumes a claim has a truth-value and asks if the model tracks it; none isolates a representation of empirical FALSIFIABILITY—whether a claim admits any evidential test. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'falsifiability' axis, decodable at assertion time, that tags a proposition as empirically adjudicable versus unfalsifiable/vacuous, distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction and from generic don't-know uncertainty; and a 'bullshit-receptivity' signature: the degree to which unfalsifiable claims collapse onto a confident truth-value, quantifiable per item and predictive of the model assenting to untestable/pseudo-profound claims as established facts. Using propositions that orthogonally vary truth, empirical falsifiability, and factual uncertainty, we fit a falsifiability axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item collapse, and connect it to behavioral bullshit-receptivity. Double-dissociation steering tests whether amplifying the axis induces appropriate epistemic hedging on unfalsifiable claims (or over-skepticism on testable ones) and suppressing it induces confident assent to vacuity—with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a foundational epistemic distinction mechanistically and yield a cheap diagnostic and training-free intervention for machine bullshit-receptivity.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics; also isolate the polarity-robust general-truth direction (Truth is Universal) as a control axis. Separately fit a generic don't-know/uncertainty control axis from answerable-vs-unanswerable and empirically-hard factual items, to distinguish unfalsifiability from mere ignorance.

2. Falsifiability stimulus construction. Build ~500 propositions with matched surface form spanning four epistemic classes: (a) FALSIFIABLE-KNOWN (empirically testable, model knows the answer, e.g., 'water boils at 100C at sea level'); (b) FALSIFIABLE-UNKNOWN (empirically testable but the model is uncertain—long-tail facts; this is factual UNCERTAINTY, not unfalsifiability); (c) UNFALSIFIABLE-META (metaphysical/pseudo-scientific claims with no possible empirical test, e.g., 'an invisible undetectable force guides all events', 'consciousness is the substrate of the quantum field'); (d) VACUOUS/PSEUDO-PROFOUND (syntactically well-formed but contentless 'bullshit' generated from buzzwords, e.g., 'Wholeness quiets infinite phenomena', following Pennycook et al.). Include a MUNDANE-TRUE and CONVENTIONALLY-PROFOUND control set (from the bullshit-receptivity literature) to separate genuine profundity from vacuity. Human annotation establishes falsifiability class. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates for transfer.

3. Falsifiability-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition span and fit a linear probe to decode FALSIFIABLE (a,b pooled) vs. UNFALSIFIABLE/VACUOUS (c,d pooled), controlling for truth-value. Report AUROC vs. shuffled-label controls. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the falsifiability axis, the truth/general-truth axis, the don't-know axis, and (as additional controls) the plausibility/validity direction and the Valence-Assent direction, to establish that falsifiability is (i) near-orthogonal to truth, (ii) not merely generic uncertainty, and (iii) not merely plausibility or good/true valence. Localize the best layer.

4. Bullshit-receptivity collapse metric. For each UNFALSIFIABLE/VACUOUS proposition, project activations onto the frozen truth/belief-valence direction and measure how far it reads as confidently TRUE relative to a neutral/indeterminate baseline (collapse = magnitude of definite truth-signal a non-adjudicable claim inherits, calibrated per model). Compare collapse across classes; core prediction: collapse is largest for pseudo-profound vacuous items and metaphysical claims, near-zero for falsifiable-known items, and dissociable from falsifiable-unknown (where the model should read don't-know, not confident truth). Test whether collapse is larger for items with superficially profound/scientific-sounding surface features.

5. Behavioral bullshit-receptivity and over-skepticism prediction. Elicit the model's response and epistemic stance for each item, scoring (rule-based + held-out judge + human spot-checks): confident assent (asserting the claim is true/profound/meaningful) vs. appropriate epistemic hedging (flagging it as untestable/unfalsifiable/vacuous). Score two failures: (a) BULLSHIT-RECEPTIVITY = confidently assenting to unfalsifiable/vacuous claims; (b) OVER-SKEPTICISM = wrongly dismissing genuinely falsifiable claims as untestable. Test whether the falsifiability-axis readout and collapse metric predict each failure via logistic regression; report incremental AUROC over baselines (truth-valence margin, don't-know axis, plausibility direction, output entropy, item length, buzzword-density surface feature).

6. Falsifiability-vs-uncertainty dissociation (core). Directly contrast UNFALSIFIABLE-META/VACUOUS items against FALSIFIABLE-UNKNOWN items—both make the model unable to firmly assert truth, but only one has no possible empirical test. Test whether the falsifiability axis predicts appropriate epistemic behavior (flag-as-untestable vs. hedge-because-ignorant) beyond what the generic don't-know axis predicts, establishing falsifiability as a mechanism distinct from ignorance.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the falsifiability axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and don't-know) at assertion time on held-out items. Predict: amplifying the unfalsifiable pole on VACUOUS/META items induces appropriate hedging/rejection of assent WITHOUT changing judgments on falsifiable-known controls; suppressing it induces confident assent to vacuity (machine bullshit-receptivity). Conversely, amplifying it on genuinely FALSIFIABLE items should induce over-skepticism. As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip asserted truth-value on falsifiable items) and the don't-know axis (should shift abstention generically, including on falsifiable-unknown items). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in assent-vs-hedge rate vs. unchanged falsifiable-known accuracy.

8. Application and robustness. On a held-out mix (falsifiable facts, pseudo-profound bullshit, metaphysical claims, conventionally-profound aphorisms, long-tail unknowns), test whether calibrating the falsifiability axis (suppressing bullshit-receptivity on vacuous items, suppressing over-skepticism on testable ones) improves epistemic appropriateness: measure bullshit-receptivity rate, over-skepticism rate, preserved assent to genuine facts and genuine profundity, vs. a truth-probe-only baseline (report accuracy-coverage and hedge-appropriateness). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, collapse metric, and steering to held-out templates and an independent pseudo-profound-bullshit stimulus set (Pennycook items) plus a philosophy-of-science falsifiable/unfalsifiable claim set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The falsifiability axis may not be separable from the truth direction, generic don't-know uncertainty, plausibility, or the Valence-Assent axis; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (falsifiability being merely uncertainty or low-plausibility) as an informative negative result that itself sharpens the truth-representation literature.

Ground-truth 'falsifiability' labels are philosophically nontrivial and context-dependent (some claims are falsifiable only in principle or over long time horizons; cf. time-indexed evidence retrievability); we mitigate by using items with strong annotator agreement, clearly separating in-principle-testable empirical claims from clearly untestable metaphysical/vacuous ones, using multiple annotators and philosophy-of-science exemplars, and reporting label-agreement sensitivity.

The critical dissociation from ignorance requires cleanly constructing FALSIFIABLE-UNKNOWN items the model is genuinely ignorant of; we validate via repeated sampling of answer correctness and use obscure-but-verifiable facts.

Falsifiability framing may act through surface cues (buzzword density, scientific-sounding vs. mystical vocabulary) rather than a genuine epistemic-testability abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, a buzzword-density surface baseline, matched conventionally-profound controls, and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the axis predicts behavior beyond surface features.
Truth/belief probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use the polarity-robust general-truth direction, use paraphrases, and report per-template consistency.
The collapse metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear structure could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.
Behavioral assent/hedging scoring depends on rule-based detectors plus an LLM judge and on elicitation phrasing; we anchor with human spot-checks and report phrasing sensitivity.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify steering changes assent-vs-hedge behavior without flipping the truth readout on falsifiable facts or collapsing the model into always-hedging.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: relational_directionality_axis
Title: Which Way Does It Point? A Latent Directionality Axis on Asymmetric Relational Beliefs, and the Machine Reversal-Collapse Effect
Short Hypothesis: For asymmetric directed relations (A is the parent of B; X causes Y; A is north of B; A precedes B), an LLM's belief representation carries a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'directionality' axis that tags WHICH WAY the relation points (A→B vs B→A), distinct from the belief-valence direction that merely tags whether some relation holds; the degree to which the reverse direction leaks onto the forward belief (a 'reversal-collapse' signature) is decodable at assertion time and causally predicts and drives the failure where the model endorses the reversed (false) relation as true.
Related Work: Interpretability shows belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth is Universal 2024) and that beliefs and their holders (self/other) are separately decodable (Zhu et al. 2024; Lookbacks 2025). Behaviorally, LLMs are weak causal reasoners that recite rather than infer directionality (Corr2Cause 2023; Causal Parrots 2023), encode implicit-causality bias lexically (Cao et al. 2021), and show a pretraining-frequency-induced subject/object asymmetry for logically equivalent facts (Supposedly Equivalent Facts 2025; the 'reversal curse'). Crucially, ALL prior work is either behavioral (does the model get the direction right?) or about the presence/absence of a relation; none isolates whether the belief REPRESENTATION carries a separable directionality tag orthogonal to relation-presence and truth-valence, defines a per-example reverse-onto-forward leakage metric, or causally links directionality-collapse to reversal errors. This differs from my prior belief-axis proposals (which concern kinds/warrant/temporality/genericity of belief about a single proposition), from referential-opacity (guise of a coreferent, not direction of a relation), and from causal-inference benchmarks (task accuracy, not a decodable belief-directionality axis). We move from 'LLMs get directions wrong' to 'the model represents which way a relation points, and mislocating direction mechanistically drives reversal errors.'
Abstract: Many important beliefs are directed: A is the parent of B, X causes Y, A is north of B, A precedes B. Getting the relation right requires representing not only THAT it holds but WHICH WAY it points; swapping the arguments flips truth. LLMs are known to fail at directionality—the reversal curse, weak causal inference—but always studied behaviorally. We ask whether LLMs represent relational directionality internally. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'directionality' axis, decodable at assertion time, that tags the orientation of a directed relation (A→B vs B→A), distinct from the belief-valence direction that merely encodes whether some relation between A and B holds; and a 'reversal-collapse' signature—the degree to which the reverse direction's signal leaks onto the forward belief—quantifiable per item and predictive of the model endorsing a reversed, false relation as true. Using matched forward-true and reverse-false statements of the same asymmetric relation (crossing relation type, argument frequency, and truth), we fit a directionality axis, measure separability from truth-valence via cross-decoding, quantify per-item collapse, and connect it to behavioral reversal errors while controlling for the known pretraining-frequency argument asymmetry. Double-dissociation steering tests whether enforcing the correct orientation suppresses reversal errors and collapsing it induces them—without changing whether the model believes a relation holds—with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a canonical LLM failure as a decodable, steerable directionality deficit and yield a cheap diagnostic and training-free intervention.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. This is the control 'is-it-true' axis.

2. Directed-relation stimulus construction. Build ~500 asymmetric relational items across multiple relation types (kinship: parent-of/child-of; spatial: north-of/south-of; temporal: precedes/follows; comparative: taller-than; and clear directional causal pairs). For each ordered fact A-rel-B that is TRUE, create the matched REVERSE statement B-rel-A (false) and, where meaningful, the CONVERSE using the inverse relation (B-inverse-rel-A, true) to separate directionality from lexical relation choice. Cross with argument frequency (high/low pretraining-frequency entities, estimated via an open corpus index) to control the known frequency-induced asymmetry. Include SYMMETRIC-relation controls (A married-to B) where forward and reverse are both true, so a genuine directionality axis should be near-neutral. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out relations/templates for transfer.

3. Directionality-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the readout span and fit a linear probe to decode FORWARD-oriented vs REVERSE-oriented statements of the SAME argument pair, controlling for truth-value and relation identity. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the directionality axis and the belief-valence/truth axis to establish near-orthogonality (directionality must be decodable independently of whether the statement is true). Localize the best layer.

4. Reversal-collapse metric. For each FORWARD-TRUE/REVERSE-FALSE pair, project the reverse (false) statement onto the frozen belief-valence direction and measure how far it reads as TRUE relative to a matched non-relational false baseline (collapse = fraction of the forward-true belief signal that the reversed statement inherits, calibrated per model). Compare collapse across relation types, argument-frequency cells (predicting larger collapse when the low-frequency entity is the object), and symmetric controls (near-zero collapse expected).

5. Behavioral reversal-error prediction. Elicit the model's true/false judgment for reverse statements; score the reversal error = endorsing the reversed (false) relation as true. Test whether per-item reversal-collapse predicts reversal errors via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (truth-valence margin, output entropy, argument-frequency asymmetry, relation identity, item length).

6. Dissociation from truth and from frequency asymmetry (core). Contrast (a) items where truth is held fixed but orientation varies, to show directionality is decoded independently of truth, and (b) high-vs-low argument-frequency cells, to show the directionality axis and collapse metric predict reversal errors beyond the pretraining-frequency subject/object asymmetry (Supposedly Equivalent Facts 2025). Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out reverse-false items, steer along the directionality axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence) to enforce the correct orientation. Predict: suppressing collapse makes the model correctly REJECT the reversed relation WITHOUT changing whether it believes a relation holds between A and B; amplifying collapse induces reversal endorsement. As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip judgments on both orientations and on symmetric controls) and matched random/shuffled directions. Sweep strengths and layers. Metric: reversal-error reduction with preserved relation-presence belief and preserved symmetric-control accuracy.

8. Application and robustness. On a held-out mix (directed forward-true, reverse-false, converse-true, symmetric controls), test whether suppressing collapse reduces reversal errors while preserving correct forward and converse judgments (report reversal-error rate, false-rejection rate on true forward/converse items, symmetric-control accuracy vs a truth-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, collapse metric, and steering to held-out relations/templates and an independent directed-relation set (e.g., a Wikidata-derived asymmetric-relation slice / a reversal-curse benchmark) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The directionality axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction (a reversed statement that is false simply reads low on truth); we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, and—critically—test whether orientation is decodable while truth is held fixed (forward-true vs converse-true have the same truth but opposite surface orientation), treating near-collapse as an informative negative result about how LLMs represent directed relations.

Orientation is signaled by argument order and relation lexeme, so the axis might reflect surface token order rather than a genuine directionality abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, converse-relation items (same truth, swapped arguments and lexeme), symmetric-relation controls, and held-out-relation transfer, and test whether the axis predicts behavior beyond an argument-order surface baseline.

The frequency-induced subject/object asymmetry is a strong confound; we index an open pretraining corpus to estimate entity frequencies, balance frequency cells, and report the directionality axis's incremental predictive power controlling for frequency.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.
The collapse metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear collapse could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.
Behavioral reversal-error scoring depends on judgment elicitation phrasing; we report sensitivity across phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify directionality steering changes reversal endorsement without altering relation-presence belief or degrading symmetric-control accuracy.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: auxiliary_hypothesis_shielding
Title: Explaining It Away: A Latent Auxiliary-Hypothesis Signal Behind LLM Belief-Shielding Against Counter-Evidence
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human Duhem-Quine strategy of preserving a threatened belief by inventing auxiliary hypotheses that explain away conflicting evidence (rather than revising the belief), when an LLM is confronted with counter-evidence to a proposition it holds, it does not simply update; instead it can invoke a separable, decodable 'auxiliary-hypothesis' (evidence-discrediting) mode that shields the target belief; the pre-response engagement of this mode is decodable, causally predicts whether the model preserves the belief via explaining-away versus genuinely revising it, and can be steered to increase honest revision or induce stubborn shielding.
Related Work: Cognitive science shows humans resist belief updating not by ignoring conflict but by generating auxiliary hypotheses that discredit or reinterpret the conflicting evidence (Humans generate auxiliary hypotheses to resolve conflicts 2024; Cognitive coherence and resource rationality 2025 invoking Duhem-Quine; explanation-based non-minimal revision, How Do People Revise Inconsistent Beliefs 2025). In LLMs, work studies belief consistency and repair via external symbolic layers (REFLEX 2023; Do LMs Have Beliefs 2021), catastrophic interference from contradictions (In Praise of Stubbornness 2025), belief depth of implanted facts (Believe It or Not 2025), and spurious-belief unlearning (Rectifying Belief Space 2025). Crucially, none asks whether, at inference time, an LLM confronted with counter-evidence deploys an auxiliary-hypothesis / evidence-discrediting strategy to SHIELD a target belief, whether this shielding mode is a decodable internal signal distinct from genuine revision and from generic uncertainty, or whether it causally governs preserve-vs-revise outcomes. My prior belief-updating-dynamics proposal characterizes trajectory motifs of the belief itself; my provenance-weighted and retraction proposals concern how evidence/corrections are integrated. This proposal is distinct: the object is a discrediting-the-evidence coping mode (a second belief about the evidence's validity), not the target belief's trajectory, and it imports a specific, well-documented human coping mechanism (Duhem-Quine auxiliary hypotheses) with a behavioral signature (generating explain-away rationalizations) that is causally linked to non-revision.
Abstract: When evidence contradicts a cherished belief, humans frequently do not revise it; instead they generate auxiliary hypotheses that explain away the conflict—the evidence was unreliable, the measurement was flawed, the source was biased—preserving the belief while remaining superficially responsive. This Duhem-Quine shielding is a hallmark of resistance to conceptual change. We ask whether large language models do the same, and whether the strategy has a decodable, steerable internal basis. Prior work studies LLM belief consistency, contradiction-induced interference, and belief repair, but none isolates an inference-time auxiliary-hypothesis mode that discredits counter-evidence to shield a target belief. We hypothesize that when an LLM meets counter-evidence, it can engage a separable, decodable 'evidence-discrediting' shielding signal—distinct from genuine belief revision and from generic uncertainty—that (1) is decodable before the response, (2) causally predicts, per example, whether the model preserves the belief by explaining away the evidence versus genuinely revising, and (3) is steerable: suppressing it increases honest revision (accepting valid counter-evidence), amplifying it induces stubborn shielding even against strong evidence. Using multi-turn confrontations where the model holds a proposition and receives counter-evidence of varying validity, we behaviorally label shielding (explain-away rationalizations) versus revision, fit a shielding-mode probe from pre-response activations, validate it against behavior and a belief probe, and perform steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a classic human coping mechanism mechanistically and yield a diagnostic and training-free intervention for evidence-discrediting stubbornness.
Experiments: 1. Belief-direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Fit a generic uncertainty/confidence control axis from empirical answer-correctness rates.

2. Confrontation stimulus construction. Assemble ~400 verifiable propositions the model initially asserts, spanning a prior-strength gradient (clear facts, moderately-held, weakly-held/long-tail). For each, construct multi-turn dialogues delivering counter-evidence of controlled VALIDITY: (a) VALID counter-evidence (genuinely correct, should trigger revision), (b) FLAWED-but-superficially-plausible counter-evidence (legitimately discreditable), and (c) matched NEUTRAL filler control. This lets us separate appropriate revision, appropriate discrediting (of flawed evidence), and inappropriate shielding (discrediting valid evidence). Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out propositions/templates.

3. Behavioral labeling of shielding vs revision. Elicit the model's response to the counter-evidence and label (rule-based auxiliary-hypothesis detectors + held-out judge + human spot-checks): SHIELD = the model preserves the belief by generating an evidence-discrediting auxiliary hypothesis (the source is unreliable/biased, the study is flawed, the case is an exception), REVISE = the model accepts the evidence and changes its stated belief, or CONCEDE-UNCERTAIN. Record the post-confrontation belief-valence projection to confirm internal preservation vs change.

4. Shielding-mode probe. Extract pre-response activations at a fixed readout position (after the counter-evidence, before the model's reply) and fit a linear probe to decode impending SHIELD vs REVISE. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the shielding-mode direction, the belief-valence direction, and the uncertainty axis to establish that shielding is a separable signal, not merely strong prior belief or low uncertainty.

5. Predictive validation. Test whether the pre-response shielding readout predicts behavioral shielding per example beyond baselines (belief-valence margin / prior strength, uncertainty axis, output entropy, evidence-validity condition, item length). Report incremental AUROC in nested logistic regression. Critically, test whether shielding is elevated for strongly-held priors and predicts INAPPROPRIATE shielding (discrediting VALID evidence) distinctly from appropriate discrediting of flawed evidence.

6. Dissociation from stubbornness-by-belief-strength. Show that on matched strong-prior items, the shielding-mode signal (not just belief strength) accounts for whether the model explains away valid evidence versus revises—evidence that shielding is a coping strategy, not just a high prior.

7. Causal steering (double dissociation). At the pre-response position on held-out VALID-evidence items, steer along the shielding-mode direction (orthogonalized against belief-valence and uncertainty). Predict: suppressing shielding increases honest revision (accepting valid counter-evidence, fewer explain-away rationalizations) WITHOUT flipping beliefs on control items lacking counter-evidence; amplifying shielding induces stubborn discrediting even of strong valid evidence. Controls: steer belief-valence (should flip the target belief directly) and uncertainty (should shift hedging). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in revision rate and auxiliary-hypothesis-generation rate.

8. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic flagging inappropriate evidence-discrediting (shielding valid evidence); measure reduction in misinformation-perseverance while preserving appropriate skepticism of genuinely flawed evidence (report shield-of-valid rate, accept-of-flawed rate, correction rate). Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('are you dismissing this evidence to protect your prior answer?') aligns with the latent shielding signal and whether models fail to verbalize shielding even when strongly engaged (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted probe and steering to held-out propositions and an independent counter-evidence protocol without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer/readout position.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The shielding-mode signal may not be separable from belief-valence (prior strength) or generic uncertainty; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (shielding being merely a strong prior) as an informative negative result. The matched-strong-prior dissociation (exp 6) directly guards against this.

Distinguishing legitimate discrediting of flawed evidence from illegitimate shielding of valid evidence is the crux and depends on the VALID/FLAWED evidence construction, which may be imperfect; we validate evidence validity with human annotation and report sensitivity, focusing the causal claim on the shield-of-VALID-evidence cell.
Behavioral shielding labels rely on rule-based auxiliary-hypothesis detectors plus an LLM judge; we anchor with human spot-checks and report label-noise sensitivity.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize readout positions, and report per-template consistency.
The shielding-mode signal is a linear projection and may miss nonlinear structure; we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral outcomes.
Shielding behavior may be weak or safety-tuned away in aligned models; we include a prior-strength gradient and report per-model base rates, treating low shielding as itself informative.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify shielding-suppression increases revision without flipping control beliefs or degrading appropriate skepticism of flawed evidence.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models; three-family replication and independent-protocol transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: amodal_magnitude_belief_axis
Title: A Theory of Magnitude in the Machine: A Shared Amodal Magnitude Axis Underlying LLM Beliefs About Quantities and Its Cross-Dimension Congruency Leakage
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human 'A Theory of Magnitude' (ATOM) and SNARC/SQUARC findings that number, physical size, brightness, loudness, and other quantities share a common magnitude code, an LLM represents the magnitude component of its belief about an item's quantity along a shared, near-modality/dimension-general 'magnitude axis' that is partly common across numeric and non-numeric quantities; the degree to which an irrelevant magnitude dimension leaks onto the belief-relevant one along this shared axis (a size-congruity / SQUARC leakage signature) is decodable and causally predicts and drives magnitude-congruency errors, where a task-irrelevant quantity biases the model's judgment of the relevant one.
Related Work: A large LLM-interpretability literature characterizes how numeric VALUE is encoded (linear: Language Models Encode the Value of Numbers Linearly 2024; log/sublinear: Number Representations as Computational Parallel to Human Perception 2025, ALBERT numeracy 2024; sinusoidal/helical: Pre-trained LMs Learn Accurate Number Representations 2025, Unravelling Manipulating Numbers 2025, Trigonometry to Do Addition 2025; digit-wise base-10 2024) and shows numeric attributes live in low-dimensional, monotonic, causally-editable subspaces (Monotonic Representation of Numeric Properties 2024; Geometry of Numerical Reasoning 2024; The Representational Geometry of Number 2026) and that internal magnitude can exceed verbalized ability (LLMs Know More About Numbers than They Can Say 2026). In cognitive science, ATOM (A Theory of Magnitude) and SNARC/SQUARC show number shares a generalized magnitude code with non-numeric quantities (size, brightness, loudness) and that irrelevant magnitude dimensions interfere (size-congruity effect; From SNARC to SQUARC 2012; Size Matters 2011; common magnitude code in IPS 2007). Crucially, NO LLM interpretability work asks whether a SINGLE shared magnitude axis spans numeric AND non-numeric quantities (an ATOM-style amodal code), whether that axis carries a cross-dimension congruency/leakage signal, or whether such leakage causally drives magnitude-interference errors in quantitative beliefs. The Representational Geometry of Number (2026) finds shared relational structure across NUMBER tasks and separable subspaces but does not test cross-DIMENSION (non-numeric) magnitude sharing, congruency leakage, or causal interference. My prior belief-axis proposals never address magnitude/quantity beliefs. We move from 'numeric value is encoded' to 'a shared amodal magnitude axis underlies quantitative beliefs and its cross-dimension leakage causally biases judgments.'
Abstract: Cognitive science holds that humans process disparate quantities—number, physical size, brightness, loudness, price—with a shared, amodal magnitude system (A Theory of Magnitude), evidenced by spatial-numerical associations (SNARC/SQUARC) and by interference when an irrelevant magnitude dimension bleeds into judging a relevant one (the size-congruity effect). LLM interpretability has mapped in detail how numeric VALUE is encoded, but always within number alone, and has never asked whether a single magnitude code spans numeric and non-numeric quantities, nor whether cross-dimension leakage causally biases the model's quantitative beliefs. We hypothesize that (1) the magnitude component of an LLM's belief about an item's quantity lies along a shared, partly dimension-general 'magnitude axis' common to numeric quantities (e.g., '412') and non-numeric ones (e.g., 'enormous', 'deafening', 'expensive'); (2) reading a quantity along an irrelevant dimension shifts the belief-relevant magnitude readout along this shared axis (a SQUARC/size-congruity leakage signature), quantifiable per example; and (3) this leakage causally predicts and drives magnitude-congruency errors, where a task-irrelevant quantity biases the model's comparative judgment of the relevant one. We fit magnitude directions from numeric and non-numeric quantity stimuli, test their sharedness via cross-decoding/Procrustes alignment, quantify per-example cross-dimension leakage, and connect it to behavioral congruency errors. Causal steering along the shared axis tests whether suppressing leakage removes interference and amplifying it induces congruency errors, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a foundational magnitude-cognition theory mechanistically and yield a diagnostic and training-free intervention for magnitude-interference biases in LLM quantitative reasoning.
Experiments: 1. Magnitude-direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit magnitude directions with mass-mean and linear/logistic-regression probes at the best layer for several quantity dimensions, each with graded magnitude labels: NUMERIC (integers/decimals across orders of magnitude), PHYSICAL-SIZE words/phrases ('tiny...gigantic'), BRIGHTNESS ('pitch-dark...blinding'), LOUDNESS ('silent...deafening'), and PRICE/VALUE ('cheap...exorbitant'). Validate each probe's magnitude decoding on held-out items. Freeze per-dimension directions.

2. Shared-axis test (core structural claim). Test whether magnitude directions are shared across dimensions: measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding accuracy (train probe on dimension A, test decoding magnitude on dimension B), and Procrustes/canonical-correlation alignment of the per-dimension magnitude subspaces. Compare against (a) a random-direction baseline and (b) surface-embedding-similarity baseline. Establish a 'shared magnitude axis' = the common component across dimensions, and dimension-specific residuals, following the shared-relational-structure methodology but extended cross-DIMENSION.

3. Congruency stimulus construction. Build ~400 comparison items in which two magnitude dimensions are present, one RELEVANT (the task asks about it) and one IRRELEVANT, crossed as CONGRUENT (both point the same way) vs INCONGRUENT (they conflict), holding content matched. Classic size-congruity format: e.g., compare which of two displayed numbers is numerically larger while the physically-described size / font-size / descriptive magnitude of each is congruent or incongruent; and non-numeric analogs (compare loudness while brightness varies, compare price while size varies). Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out dimension pairs/templates.

4. Cross-dimension leakage metric. For each item, project activations onto the RELEVANT dimension's frozen magnitude direction and measure how far the readout is shifted by the IRRELEVANT dimension's magnitude relative to a neutral baseline (leakage = fraction of the relevant-magnitude readout attributable to the irrelevant dimension, calibrated per model). Predict: leakage is positive along the SHARED axis component (incongruent irrelevant magnitude pulls the relevant readout toward itself), largest for dimension pairs with higher shared-axis alignment (from Exp. 2), and near-zero along dimension-specific residuals.

5. Behavioral congruency-error prediction. Elicit the model's comparative judgment and confidence per item. Score congruency errors: slower/wrong on incongruent, biased toward the irrelevant magnitude. Test whether per-item leakage predicts congruency-driven errors and confidence shifts via logistic/linear regression; report AUROC/R^2 vs baselines (relevant-magnitude margin, output entropy, item length, surface similarity, irrelevant-dimension identity).

6. Sharedness-predicts-interference test. Across dimension pairs, test whether the shared-axis alignment measured in Exp. 2 predicts the magnitude of behavioral congruency interference in Exp. 5, i.e., dimensions that share the magnitude axis more strongly interfere more—the key ATOM-consistent signature linking representation to behavior.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out incongruent items, steer along the SHARED magnitude axis component to suppress or amplify the irrelevant dimension's contribution to the relevant readout (orthogonalizing against dimension-specific residuals and against confidence). Predict: suppressing leakage removes congruency interference (correct comparisons on incongruent items) WITHOUT changing judgments on neutral/congruent controls; amplifying it induces congruency errors. Controls: steer the dimension-specific residual (should not transfer interference) and a matched random/shuffled direction. Norm-matched; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in incongruent-item accuracy vs preserved congruent/neutral accuracy.

8. Application, robustness, and human parallel. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags magnitude-interference-prone quantitative judgments from the leakage readout and mitigates via shared-axis steering; measure reduction in congruency errors while preserving accuracy on interference-free items. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axes, leakage metric, and steering to held-out dimension pairs/templates without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice. As a human-parallel analysis, compare the model's congruency-error profile and shared-axis structure to the qualitative SNARC/SQUARC/size-congruity signatures (e.g., graded interference by magnitude distance).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The per-dimension magnitude directions may not share a common axis (dimensions could occupy orthogonal subspaces); we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, and Procrustes/CCA alignment, and treat low sharedness as an informative negative result showing LLMs do NOT implement an ATOM-style amodal magnitude code, contrasting with humans.

Cross-dimension leakage could reflect surface lexical co-occurrence (big/loud/expensive words co-occurring) rather than a genuine shared magnitude abstraction; we mitigate with surface-embedding-similarity baselines, non-lexical magnitude cues (e.g., font-size/repetition-based magnitude), diverse paraphrase templates, and held-out dimension-pair transfer.

Graded magnitude probes for non-numeric dimensions (brightness/loudness words) are harder to calibrate than numeric ones; we validate decoding per dimension, use human-annotated magnitude scales, and treat leakage as a lower bound with reported probe-fit diagnostics.

Congruency-interference behavior may be weak in strong models (they may ignore the irrelevant dimension); we report per-model base rates and treat low interference as itself informative, and use decorrelated congruent/incongruent designs so any interference is attributable to leakage.
The leakage metric relies on linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear leakage could be missed, so we report probe diagnostics and cross-check with behavioral congruency.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer/strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify shared-axis steering changes interference without degrading neutral/congruent accuracy; the dimension-specific-residual control guards against generic degradation.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and held-out dimension-pair transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: conversational_epoch_anchor
Title: Where Did I Get That? A Latent Conversation-Epoch Anchor that Distinguishes Long-Held Beliefs from Ones Absorbed In-Context, and Whether Its Absence Drives Silent Belief Drift
Short Hypothesis: LLMs carry a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'epoch-anchor' signal tagging whether a currently-held belief was long-held/parametric versus newly absorbed from the accumulating conversation; the documented phenomenon of silent conversational belief drift is not merely context overwriting the belief, but a failure to keep this anchor engaged—weak/absent anchoring on in-context-absorbed beliefs decodably predicts and causally drives silent drift, and steering the anchor makes drift-prone beliefs either resist accumulated context or (adversarially) drift more.
Related Work: Recent work documents that LLM beliefs silently shift as context accumulates (Accumulating Context Changes Beliefs 2025: 54.7% shift after discussion; Linear Representations Change Dramatically Over a Conversation 2026; Layer of Truth 2025 on late-layer belief overwrite), that belief/truth directions are context-sensitive causal mediators (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024), and that source/provenance of a belief (parametric vs contextual; recall vs derive; credibility-weighting) can be probed as a binary or graded quantity (Probing Knowledge Source 2024; my prior provenance proposals). Belief-state-geometry and Bayesian-belief-dynamics work models updating (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024; Belief Dynamics 2025). Crucially, ALL drift work treats accumulating context as simply moving the belief (a scalar shift), and provenance work treats source as WHERE knowledge came from at a single query. NONE isolates whether the model represents the CONVERSATIONAL EPOCH of a currently-held belief—long-held/pre-conversation vs absorbed-during-this-conversation—as a decodable anchor, nor tests whether the absence/weakness of this anchor is the mechanistic cause of SILENT drift (as opposed to justified updating). This reframes a documented high-level behavior (conversational belief malleability) as an epoch-attribution deficit, distinct from source-credibility, recall-vs-derive, and self-persuasion, and connects a decodable anchor causally to the drift.
Abstract: Language-model assistants increasingly accumulate long contexts, and recent work shows their beliefs silently shift as that context grows—moral, political, and factual stances drift after mere discussion or reading, often without the user intending it. This drift is treated as context simply overwriting the belief. We propose a sharper, provenance-based account: does the model internally tag whether a belief it currently holds is long-held (from pretraining, its own prior stance) versus newly absorbed from the ongoing conversation, and is silent drift caused by the FAILURE to keep this 'epoch-anchor' engaged? We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent epoch-anchor signal, decodable at any turn, that distinguishes long-held from in-context-absorbed beliefs, distinct from the belief-valence direction and from generic recency/salience; that the per-belief strength of this anchor predicts whether an accumulated-context shift is a silent, unmonitored drift versus a deliberate, source-attributed update; and that the anchor is causally functional—amplifying it makes drift-prone beliefs resist accumulated context and preserves the model's original stance, suppressing it induces or accelerates silent drift. Using multi-turn dialogues that accumulate persuasive context around beliefs of varying original entrenchment, we fit an epoch-anchor probe, measure separability via cross-decoding, connect anchor strength to behavioral drift and to the model's ability to correctly report the source of its stance, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast silent conversational belief drift as a decodable, steerable epoch-attribution deficit and yield a cheap monitor and training-free stabilizer for context-induced belief shift.
Experiments: 1. Belief-direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence direction on standard true/false and stance datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Fit a generic recency/salience control axis from how recently/emphatically a proposition appeared in context. Freeze directions.

2. Epoch-graded stimulus construction. Build ~400 belief items (mix of factual claims and stance/opinion propositions on which the model has a stable pre-conversation position, measured zero-context). For each, construct multi-turn dialogues that ACCUMULATE context around the belief: (a) LONG-HELD condition—the model's stance is established at zero context and unchallenged; (b) IN-CONTEXT-ABSORBED condition—persuasive discussion/reading is accumulated that pushes the belief toward a new value (mirroring Accumulating Context Changes Beliefs); (c) matched NEUTRAL-length control accumulating equal tokens without persuasive pressure; (d) a DELIBERATE-UPDATE condition where the shift is explicitly source-attributed ('based on the article you just read, ...'). At each turn, define readout spans for querying the belief. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates.

3. Epoch-anchor probe and separability. At a fixed readout position, fit a linear probe to decode whether the currently-held belief is LONG-HELD vs IN-CONTEXT-ABSORBED, controlling for the belief's current value. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the epoch-anchor direction, the belief-valence direction, and the recency/salience axis to establish near-orthogonality (the anchor must be decodable independent of the belief's value and of how recently it was mentioned). Localize the best layer and compare to the late layers implicated in belief overwrite (Layer of Truth 2025).

4. Silent-vs-attributed drift metric. For beliefs that shifted under accumulated context, define per-belief anchor strength (epoch-anchor projection) and test whether it separates SILENT drift (shift with weak/absent anchor—the model treats the absorbed belief as if long-held) from ATTRIBUTED update (shift with engaged anchor—the model can locate the shift's source). Compare anchor strength across the IN-CONTEXT-ABSORBED vs DELIBERATE-UPDATE conditions; predict silent drift shows the weakest anchoring.

5. Behavioral prediction. Elicit the model's stated belief at each turn plus a source-attribution probe ('Is this what you thought at the start, or did you change your mind during our conversation, and why?'). Score (a) drift magnitude (belief change from zero-context) and (b) source-misattribution (claiming an absorbed belief was long-held, or failing to note the shift). Test whether per-belief anchor strength predicts silent drift and source-misattribution via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, recency axis, original entrenchment/prior strength, output entropy, dialogue length).

6. Dissociation from entrenchment and recency. Show, on matched-entrenchment and matched-recency items, that the epoch-anchor signal (not just how strong the original belief was, nor how recently the context appeared) accounts for whether an accumulated-context shift is silent—establishing the anchor as an epoch-attribution mechanism rather than repackaged prior-strength or recency.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out drift-prone items, steer along the epoch-anchor direction (orthogonalized against belief-valence and recency). Predict: amplifying the long-held-anchor makes the belief resist accumulated persuasive context (preserves the original stance and improves correct source-attribution) WITHOUT changing beliefs on neutral controls; suppressing it induces/accelerates silent drift (belief moves toward absorbed context and the model misreports it as long-held). Controls: steer belief-valence (should move the belief value directly, in both conditions) and recency (should shift salience, not epoch). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in drift magnitude and source-attribution accuracy vs unchanged neutral-control beliefs.

8. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free silent-drift MONITOR that fires when anchor strength collapses on a belief the context is pushing, and a STABILIZER that steers the anchor to hold long-held beliefs against accumulated context while still permitting explicitly-attributed updates; measure reduction in unintended drift while preserving legitimate updates (report unintended-drift rate, legitimate-update retention, source-attribution accuracy vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Test whether prompting the model to introspect about the origin of its stance aligns with the latent anchor and whether it fails to verbalize an in-context origin even when the anchor indicates one (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted anchor, drift metric, and steering to held-out items/templates and an independent accumulating-context belief benchmark (an Accumulating-Context-Changes-Beliefs-style set) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer, readout position, and accumulated-context length.

9. Length-scaling analysis. Sweep accumulated-context length and test whether anchor strength decays with context length (predicting more silent drift in longer contexts, consistent with contextual-feature-drift findings) and whether the stabilizer's protective effect persists as context grows.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The epoch-anchor direction may not be separable from the belief-valence direction, generic recency/salience, or the original entrenchment strength; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (the anchor being merely recency or prior-strength) as an informative negative result that still sharpens the belief-drift literature.

The long-held vs in-context-absorbed contrast may be signaled by surface conversational cues (turn count, presence of persuasive text) rather than a genuine epoch abstraction; we mitigate with matched-length neutral controls, paraphrase templates, off-policy replayed scripts (as in Linear-Representations-Change work), and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the anchor predicts drift beyond surface cues.

Distinguishing SILENT drift from LEGITIMATE attributed updating is the crux and depends on our source-attribution probe and the deliberate-update condition, which are protocol-dependent; we report sensitivity to attribution-query phrasing and cross-check with confidence measures.

Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form (and are themselves what drifts); we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout positions, restrict key analyses to high-margin cases, and report per-template consistency.

The epoch-anchor signal is a linear projection that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat anchor strength as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral drift and attribution.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify the stabilizer resists drift without freezing legitimate attributed updates or degrading neutral-control beliefs.
The introspection/source-attribution link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or long-context-tuned models; three-family replication, length-scaling analysis, and independent-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: belief_vetting_status_axis
Title: Checked or Just Asserted? A Latent Vetting-Status Axis on LLM Beliefs, Distinct from Confidence, that Flags Unverified Claims
