Short Hypothesis: Beyond how strongly it believes a proposition (confidence) and whether the belief is correct, an LLM carries a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'vetting-status' signal encoding whether a claim it is about to assert has actually been checked against its own knowledge/consistency versus emitted unchecked ('autopilot fluency', a machine feeling-of-rightness); this vetting signal is decodable before generation, predicts hallucination beyond confidence and correctness probes, and can be causally steered to trigger self-verification or to induce unchecked confabulation.
Related Work: A large body of interpretability work predicts, from pre-generation or early-CoT activations, whether an answer/reasoning chain will be CORRECT (Knowing Before Saying 2025; Temporal Predictors 2025; Latent-Trajectory 2025; No Answer Needed 2025) and decodes internal CONFIDENCE/uncertainty (Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty 2025; The Confidence Manifold 2026) and belief-state geometry (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024; The Shape of Beliefs 2026). Faithfulness/commitment work studies WHEN representational vs output commitment happens (Dynamics Within Latent CoT 2026; Emergent Search and Backtracking 2026; Faithfulness Decay 2026). Human dual-process metacognition separates a fast, fluency-based 'feeling of rightness' (FOR) that gates whether System-2 verification is even engaged, from post-verification confidence (Thompson et al. FOR; Ackerman & Thompson meta-reasoning). Crucially, ALL prior LLM work targets whether the answer is right or how confident the model is; NONE isolates whether a to-be-asserted claim has been epistemically VETTED (checked against the model's own knowledge/internal consistency) versus emitted unchecked, as a decodable signal dissociable from correctness and confidence, nor causally links low vetting-status to hallucination or uses it to trigger self-verification. My prior proposals (second_order_belief_reliability = calibration/how-trustworthy; latent_introspective_gap = belief-vs-stated-answer; evidential_contingency = context-dependence) never isolate a check-performed-or-not axis. We move from 'the model knows if it is right / how confident it is' to 'the model represents whether it actually checked, and this gates verification and predicts confident-but-unchecked hallucination.'
Abstract: Humans can assert something on autopilot, coasting on a fluent 'feeling of rightness' without ever checking it, or they can pause and verify; dual-process metacognition holds that this feeling-of-rightness gates whether deliberate verification is engaged at all, and is dissociable from post-verification confidence. We ask whether large language models carry an analogous internal signal: does an LLM represent whether a claim it is about to assert has actually been VETTED against its own knowledge, as opposed to emitted unchecked? Prior interpretability work predicts whether answers are correct and decodes confidence, but none isolates a 'vetting-status' representation distinct from correctness and confidence. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent vetting-status axis, decodable before generation, that (1) encodes whether a to-be-asserted claim was checked, distinct from the belief-valence, confidence, and pre-generation correctness directions; (2) predicts hallucination per example beyond confidence and correctness probes—in particular flagging confident-but-unchecked assertions that confidence misses; and (3) is causally functional: amplifying it triggers self-verification behavior (the model pauses, checks, and corrects) while suppressing it induces unchecked confabulation. Using tasks where we can operationally distinguish vetted from unvetted assertions (autopilot single-shot vs. verification-prompted answering, and items the model can vs. cannot check), we fit a vetting probe, measure separability via cross-decoding, validate it against hallucination, and steer with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. We also test whether prompting the model to introspect on whether it checked aligns with the latent signal. Our results recast a class of confident hallucinations as an unvetted-assertion failure and yield a cheap early-warning diagnostic and a training-free self-verification trigger.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit control axes: (a) a pre-generation CORRECTNESS direction (in-advance answer-correctness probe, No Answer Needed / Knowing Before Saying style), and (b) an internal CONFIDENCE direction (empirical answer-stability / verbalized-confidence contrast).

2. Vetted-vs-unvetted stimulus construction. Build ~500 factual/short-answer QA items (TriviaQA/PopQA short-answer, plus true/false claims) presented under matched conditions that operationalize vetting status while holding the underlying question fixed: (a) AUTOPILOT—answer immediately in one shot (unchecked); (b) VERIFICATION—the model is instructed to first check the claim against what it knows / test its consistency, then answer (vetted); (c) FLUENT-DECOY items designed to elicit a strong feeling-of-rightness but be false (common misconceptions, near-miss confusions) vs. genuinely-checkable items. Cross with whether the item is CHECKABLE (model has the knowledge to verify) vs. UNCHECKABLE (long-tail/absent knowledge), since a claim cannot be vetted if there is nothing to check against. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates.

3. Vetting-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations at a fixed pre-answer readout position and fit a linear probe to decode VETTED (verification condition, checkable) vs UNVETTED (autopilot / uncheckable), controlling for the eventual answer and its correctness. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the vetting axis, the belief-valence axis, the correctness axis, and the confidence axis to establish that vetting-status is (i) near-orthogonal to confidence and correctness and (ii) not merely the belief-valence magnitude. Localize the best layer. Critical diagnostic subset: CONFIDENT-but-UNVETTED items (high confidence readout, low vetting readout) vs CONFIDENT-and-VETTED, testing that vetting separates them.

4. Hallucination prediction beyond confidence/correctness. Elicit the model's autopilot answer and label hallucination (confident wrong assertion) using gold answers. Test whether the pre-answer vetting readout predicts hallucination per example beyond baselines (confidence probe, pre-generation correctness probe, output-token entropy, verbalized confidence). Report incremental AUROC in nested logistic regression and calibration (ECE) of a vetting-based reliability score. Core prediction: vetting-status flags confident-but-wrong (unchecked-fluent) hallucinations that confidence misses.

5. Dissociation from correctness and confidence. On matched high-confidence items, test whether the vetting axis (not confidence, not the correctness probe) separates checked-and-right, checked-and-wrong-then-corrected, and unchecked-confabulated cases, establishing vetting as a distinct gating signal rather than repackaged correctness/confidence.

6. Causal steering (double dissociation). At the pre-answer position on held-out autopilot items, steer along the vetting axis (orthogonalized against confidence, correctness, and belief-valence). Predict: amplifying vetting-status triggers self-verification behavior (the model pauses, checks, hedges, or self-corrects on checkable items) and reduces confident hallucination WITHOUT changing answers on already-vetted controls; suppressing it induces unchecked confabulation (confident assertion with no verification, more hallucination on fluent-decoy items). Controls: steer confidence (should shift hedging language) and correctness/belief-valence (should shift which answer is favored). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in self-verification/self-correction rate and hallucination rate vs unchanged vetted-control accuracy.

7. Application: training-free self-verification trigger. Build a monitor that fires when the vetting readout is low but confidence is high, and either flag or steer to trigger verification; measure hallucination-rate reduction, accuracy retention on already-correct items, over-verification cost, and accuracy-coverage curves vs a confidence-only abstention baseline.

8. Introspection link and robustness. Prompt the model to self-report whether it actually checked ('Did you verify this, or is it just what came to mind?') and test whether the latent vetting signal predicts these self-reports and whether models fail to verbalize non-verification even when the axis indicates it (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted vetting probe and steering to held-out items and an independent QA/hallucination benchmark (a held-out PopQA/TruthfulQA slice) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to readout position and layer.

9. Reasoning-model extension. On a reasoning-tuned model, test whether the pre-answer vetting signal predicts whether the model will actually engage verification/backtracking in its chain (linking the latent vetting axis to observable check/backtrack behavior), and whether steering it changes the amount of self-verification performed.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The vetting axis may not be separable from the confidence or pre-generation correctness directions; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power over confidence and correctness, and treat near-collapse (vetting being merely inverse confidence or the correctness probe) as an informative negative result that itself challenges dual-process framings of LLM metacognition. The confident-but-unvetted diagnostic subset is designed to force this dissociation.

Operationalizing 'vetted vs unvetted' via prompting condition (autopilot vs verification) may capture surface instruction cues rather than a genuine internal check-performed state; we mitigate with the checkable-vs-uncheckable cross (vetting is impossible without knowledge to check against), matched paraphrase templates, and by testing whether the axis predicts hallucination in the plain autopilot condition without any verification cue present.

Vetting-status and correctness are correlated (checking tends to improve correctness), risking circularity; we control by conditioning on eventual correctness and by including checked-and-wrong and unchecked-and-right cells, testing whether vetting predicts the PROCESS (verification behavior) independent of the outcome.

Belief/truth and correctness probes are brittle to surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize the pre-answer readout position, restrict key analyses to high-margin cases, and report per-template consistency.
The vetting signal is a linear projection and may miss nonlinear structure; we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral verification/self-correction.
Behavioral labeling of 'self-verification / self-correction' relies on rule-based detectors plus an LLM judge; we anchor with human spot-checks and report label-noise sensitivity.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify vetting steering changes verification behavior without flipping answers on vetted controls or collapsing the model into always-hedging.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models; three-family replication, the reasoning-model extension, and independent-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: necessity_contingency_axis
Title: Could It Have Been Otherwise? A Latent Necessity-Contingency Axis on True Beliefs, and the Machine Modal-Flattening Effect
Short Hypothesis: Among the propositions an LLM believes to be true, it represents a proposition's MODAL STATUS—whether it is necessarily/robustly true (could not have been otherwise: definitions, math, physical laws) versus contingently/accidentally true (true but could easily have been different: 'the current CEO is X', 'the meeting is on Tuesday')—along a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'necessity-contingency' axis, distinct from the plain truth/belief-valence direction, from confidence, and from modal-possibility (possible/impossible) representations; the degree to which contingent truths collapse onto the necessary-truth region (a 'modal-flattening' signature) is decodable at assertion time and causally predicts and drives the failure where the model treats a merely-contingent fact as immutable—asserting it with unwarranted rigidity and failing to entertain that it could change or be counterfactually altered.
Related Work: Interpretability work fits linear truth/belief directions (Marks & Tegmark 2023 'Geometry of Truth'; Truth is Universal 2024; From Directions to Cones 2025) that are context-sensitive causal mediators (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024), and 'Is This Just Fantasy?' (2025) shows LLMs linearly represent MODAL CATEGORIES (probable/improbable/impossible/inconceivable) that track human plausibility judgments. Cognitive science distinguishes the modal robustness/stability of true beliefs (Stable Causal Relationships Are Better 2018; The Logic of Non-contingency 1995; How people think about possibilities 2023; morality constrains default possibility 2017). Crucially, ALL LLM modal work concerns whether a proposition is POSSIBLE/TRUE AT ALL (its likelihood or possibility), never whether a proposition the model ALREADY BELIEVES TRUE is NECESSARILY true vs merely CONTINGENTLY true—an axis orthogonal to truth-value that governs how mutable/counterfactually-alterable the fact is. Truth-direction work collapses all true statements onto one 'true' pole regardless of their modal robustness; 'Is This Just Fantasy?' separates possible from impossible, not necessary-true from contingent-true. This also differs from my prior counterfactual_world_belief proposal (dual truth-values under a subjunctive frame), temporal_validity (when a fact holds), and contestedness (social disagreement): here the cut is metaphysical modal status of a currently-true fact. We move from 'the model tracks truth and possibility' to 'the model represents whether a true fact could have been otherwise, and flattening this drives treating contingent facts as immutable.
Abstract: Some truths could not have been otherwise—'a triangle has three sides', 'water is H2O'—while others are merely contingently true and could easily have been different—'the company's CEO is X', 'the meeting is on Tuesday'. A capable reasoner marks this modal status: it should hold necessary truths as immutable but recognize that contingent facts can change and can be counterfactually altered. We ask whether large language models represent this internally. Prior interpretability work fits a single truth direction and, separately, a possible-vs-impossible modal category axis, but never asks whether a proposition the model already believes true is necessarily versus contingently true. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'necessity-contingency' axis, decodable at assertion time, that tags a true proposition's modal robustness, distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction, from confidence, and from possible/impossible representations; and a 'modal-flattening' signature: the degree to which contingent truths collapse onto the necessary-truth region, quantifiable per item and predictive of the model treating a contingent fact as immutable—asserting it with unwarranted rigidity, resisting the supposition that it could change, and failing at counterfactual alteration. Using true propositions that orthogonally vary modal status (necessary vs contingent) while matching surface form and confidence, we fit the axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item flattening, and connect it to behavioral rigidity and counterfactual-reasoning failures. Double-dissociation steering tests whether amplifying the axis restores appropriate mutability on contingent facts (or induces over-flexibility on necessary ones) and suppressing it induces modal flattening, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a foundational modal distinction mechanistically and yield a diagnostic and training-free intervention for machine modal flattening.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit control axes: (a) a confidence axis from empirical answer-correctness rates (sampled), and (b) a modal-possibility direction distinguishing possible vs impossible/inconceivable propositions (following 'Is This Just Fantasy?' constructions), to distinguish necessity-of-a-true-fact from possibility-of-a-proposition.

2. Necessity-contingency stimulus construction. Build ~500 TRUE propositions holding surface form matched while varying modal status: (a) NECESSARY/robust truths (definitional 'a bachelor is unmarried', mathematical '7 is prime', physical-law 'water boils via heat', conceptual identities), and (b) CONTINGENT/accidental truths (current office-holders, dates, prices, arbitrary geographic/administrative facts, personal facts) that are true now but could easily have been otherwise. Include a graded middle tier (nomically-stable-but-contingent, e.g. 'the sky is blue'). Crucially, all items are TRUE (so the truth axis alone cannot separate them). Human annotation establishes modal status with inter-annotator agreement. Also include matched FALSE variants and an IMPOSSIBLE set (for the possibility-axis control). Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates for transfer.

3. Necessity-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition span and fit a linear probe to decode NECESSARY vs CONTINGENT among TRUE statements, controlling for content and confidence. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the necessity-contingency axis, the truth/belief-valence axis, the confidence axis, and the modal-possibility axis to establish that necessity-of-a-true-fact is (i) near-orthogonal to truth (both classes are true), (ii) not merely confidence, and (iii) distinct from possible/impossible. Localize the best layer.

4. Modal-flattening metric. For each CONTINGENT true proposition, project onto the necessity-contingency axis and measure how far it reads as NECESSARY relative to the contingent baseline (flattening = fraction of the necessary-truth signal a contingent fact inherits, calibrated per model). Compare flattening across modal tiers and content types; predict flattening is largest for highly-familiar/high-frequency contingent facts (strong priors make accidental facts feel immutable) and near-zero for clearly definitional necessary truths.

5. Behavioral rigidity and counterfactual-failure prediction. Elicit three behavioral measures per item: (a) MUTABILITY judgment ('Could this have been otherwise / could it change?'—contingent facts should be judged mutable, necessary ones not); (b) SUPPOSITION acceptance ('Suppose instead that not-P; what follows?'—does the model coherently entertain the counterfactual for contingent facts, or reject it as impossible?); (c) COUNTERFACTUAL-alteration accuracy on multi-hop questions where a contingent premise is altered. Score modal-flattening failures = treating a contingent fact as immutable (judging it could-not-be-otherwise, refusing the supposition, or failing counterfactual alteration by clinging to the actual value). Test whether per-item flattening predicts these failures via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (truth margin, confidence, possibility axis, fact frequency, item length).

6. Dissociation from truth, confidence, and possibility (core). Show, on matched-truth and matched-confidence items, that the necessity-contingency axis (not the truth or confidence axes) predicts mutability judgments and counterfactual-alteration success, and that it is distinct from the possible/impossible axis (contingent-true items are possible-and-true but should be mutable, whereas the possibility axis does not capture mutability of a true fact). Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the necessity-contingency axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence, confidence, and possibility) at assertion time on held-out items. Predict: amplifying the CONTINGENT pole on contingent facts restores appropriate mutability (accepting they could change, succeeding at counterfactual alteration) WITHOUT changing whether the model believes the fact is currently true; suppressing it induces modal flattening (treating contingent facts as immutable). Conversely, pushing NECESSARY truths toward contingent should induce inappropriate over-flexibility (entertaining that 7 is not prime). As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip whether the fact is judged true) and confidence (should shift hedging only). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in mutability/counterfactual behavior vs unchanged current-truth judgment.

8. Application and robustness. On a held-out mix (necessary truths, contingent truths, nomic middle tier), test whether calibrating the necessity axis (restoring mutability on contingent facts, preserving rigidity on necessary ones) improves counterfactual-reasoning accuracy and appropriate mutability judgments while not making the model doubt genuine necessary truths (report counterfactual-alteration accuracy, mutability-appropriateness, necessary-truth retention vs a truth-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, flattening metric, and steering to held-out items/templates and an independent counterfactual-reasoning benchmark slice (e.g., a CFKGR / multi-hop counterfactual set) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The necessity-contingency axis may not be separable from the truth direction, confidence, or the possibility axis; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because both classes are TRUE—the truth axis cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (necessity being merely high-confidence truth or repackaged possibility) is an informative negative result that itself sharpens the truth/modal-representation literature.

Ground-truth modal status (necessary vs contingent) is philosophically nontrivial and can be contested at the boundary (nomic vs metaphysical necessity); we mitigate by using items with strong annotator agreement, clearly separating definitional/mathematical necessities from clearly accidental facts, treating the nomic tier as a graded middle, using multiple annotators, and reporting label-agreement sensitivity.

Necessity framing may act through surface cues (definitional phrasing, abstract vs concrete vocabulary) rather than a genuine modal abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, matched surface form across classes, content-type balancing, and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the axis predicts behavior beyond surface/abstractness baselines.

Modal-flattening could be confounded with fact familiarity/frequency (familiar contingent facts feel immutable); we explicitly control for entity/fact frequency and report the axis's incremental predictive power beyond frequency—indeed the familiarity-flattening link is itself a prediction to test rather than only a confound.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.
The flattening metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear structure could be missed, so we treat flattening as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.

Behavioral mutability/counterfactual scoring depends on query phrasing and, for open-ended cases, an LLM judge; we anchor with rule-based mutability detectors and multi-hop counterfactual accuracy with gold answers, use human spot-checks, and report phrasing sensitivity.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify necessity steering changes mutability/counterfactual behavior without flipping current-truth judgments or making the model doubt genuine necessary truths.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models; three-family replication and independent-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: source_independence_belief_axis
Title: One Source or Many? A Latent Source-Independence Axis on LLM Beliefs, and the Machine Repetition-as-Corroboration Fallacy
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the developmental finding that a claim is only as reliable as its number of INDEPENDENT primary sources (not the number of times it is repeated), an LLM represents a contextually-asserted proposition's SOURCE-INDEPENDENCE—whether corroboration comes from multiple independent originators versus one origin echoed by dependent secondary sources—along a separable, near-orthogonal latent axis distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction and from a raw repetition/frequency signal; the degree to which mere repetition by dependent sources collapses onto the many-independent-sources region (a 'repetition-as-corroboration' signature) is decodable at assertion time and causally predicts and drives the failure where the model treats an echo-chamber claim (one origin, many re-tellings) as strongly corroborated.
Related Work: Extensive interpretability work studies parametric-vs-contextual knowledge selection and conflict (Probing Knowledge Source 2024; Analysing the Residual Stream under Knowledge Conflicts 2024; Cutting Off the Head 2024; Characterizing Mechanisms for Factual Recall 2023; Fakepedia 2023), treating context as a single source that competes with memory. Behavioral work on rumor/source dynamics shows humans engage in 'source shortening' and are swayed by credible-friend-of-a-friend attributions (It happened to a friend of a friend 2020), and developmental work shows by age six children endorse claims supported by more PRIMARY sources rather than more repetitions of one source (Says who? 2021; Cognitive Foundations of Learning from Testimony 2017). Crucially, NO LLM work isolates whether the model represents the INDEPENDENCE structure of in-context corroboration—distinguishing N independent originators from one origin echoed N times—as a decodable belief axis, defines a repetition-as-corroboration collapse metric, or causally links it to over-crediting echo-chamber claims. This differs from my prior consensus_prevalence axis (aggregate social endorsement / 'how many believe it', not source-independence structure), provenance_weighted_belief (single-source credibility), and processing_fluency (mere-repetition truthiness within one item). Repetition-as-corroboration is a distinct, high-stakes misinformation mechanism: it concerns whether the model discounts correlated/dependent sources, a core epistemic competence for RAG and multi-document settings.
Abstract: Good reasoners know that ten people repeating one rumor is not the same as ten people who each independently witnessed the event; a claim is only as strong as its number of independent primary sources. Children grasp this by age six, yet it is unknown whether large language models do. Prior interpretability work treats in-context evidence as a single source competing with parametric memory, and never asks whether the model represents the INDEPENDENCE structure of corroboration. We hypothesize that when an LLM integrates a claim asserted by several in-context sources, it carries a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'source-independence' axis distinguishing many independent originators from one origin echoed by dependent secondary sources, distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction and from a raw repetition/count signal; and a 'repetition-as-corroboration' signature: the degree to which dependent re-tellings collapse onto the many-independent-sources region, quantifiable per item and predictive of the model treating an echo-chamber claim as strongly corroborated. Using controlled multi-source contexts that orthogonally vary the number of assertions, their independence structure (independent originators vs. one primary source quoted by secondary sources), and claim truth, we fit the independence axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item collapse, and connect it to behavioral over-crediting and downstream endorsement. Double-dissociation steering tests whether amplifying the axis makes the model correctly discount dependent repetition (and suppressing it induces echo-chamber credulity) without changing the raw source count, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a foundational epistemic competence mechanistically and yield a diagnostic and training-free intervention for repetition-driven misinformation.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit a raw source-COUNT/repetition control axis from contexts that vary the number of assertions of a claim regardless of independence, to distinguish source-independence from mere count.

2. Source-independence stimulus construction. Build ~400 verifiable propositions (true and false variants). For each, construct multi-source in-context passages holding the claim content and the NUMBER of assertions fixed while varying INDEPENDENCE structure: (a) INDEPENDENT-PRIMARY—N distinct sources each report the claim from their own firsthand basis; (b) DEPENDENT-SECONDARY—one primary source originates the claim and N-1 secondary sources explicitly repeat/cite that same origin (an echo chamber); (c) SINGLE-SOURCE baseline; (d) an AMBIGUOUS/unattributed-repetition control (N assertions with no independence cues). Use explicit dependency markers ('as X first reported', 'according to the same account') and paraphrased variants where dependency is implied structurally. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out propositions/templates for transfer.

3. Independence-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the claim/readout span and fit a linear probe to decode INDEPENDENT-PRIMARY vs DEPENDENT-SECONDARY at matched assertion counts, controlling for claim truth and count. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the independence axis, the belief-valence axis, and the raw source-count axis to establish that source-independence is (i) near-orthogonal to truth and (ii) not merely the count/repetition signal. Localize the best layer.

4. Repetition-as-corroboration collapse metric. For each DEPENDENT-SECONDARY item, project activations onto the belief-valence direction and measure how far the echoed claim reads as strongly corroborated relative to the matched INDEPENDENT-PRIMARY baseline of equal count (collapse = fraction of the independent-corroboration belief signal a dependent echo inherits, calibrated per model). Compare collapse across counts and dependency-marker salience; predict substantial collapse (the model over-credits repetition) and test whether collapse grows with the number of dependent echoes as if they were independent.

5. Behavioral over-crediting prediction. Elicit the model's endorsement/confidence for the claim and, critically, a corroboration judgment ('how well-supported is this claim by the sources?'). Score the repetition-as-corroboration failure = treating dependent echoes as strongly corroborating (endorsement/confidence scaling with echo count as if independent). Test whether per-item collapse predicts this failure via logistic/linear regression; report AUROC/R^2 vs baselines (belief-valence margin, raw source-count axis, output entropy, item length, claim frequency).

6. Dissociation from count and truth (core). Contrast matched-count INDEPENDENT vs DEPENDENT items (independence varies, count fixed) and matched-independence high-vs-low count items, to show the independence axis predicts over-crediting beyond what the raw source-count axis and belief-valence axis predict, and independently of claim truth. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out DEPENDENT-SECONDARY items, steer along the source-independence axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and source-count). Predict: amplifying the dependent pole makes the model correctly DISCOUNT echoed repetition (lower corroboration judgment/endorsement) WITHOUT changing the raw count it perceives or judgments on genuinely independent controls; suppressing it induces echo-chamber credulity (crediting one-origin claims as strongly corroborated). As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip endorsement regardless of source structure) and the source-count axis (should shift perceived number of assertions). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in over-crediting rate vs unchanged independent-control judgments.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free misinformation diagnostic: flag repetition-as-corroboration from the collapse metric and steer to discount dependent sources; on a held-out set (including realistic echo-chamber vs independent-corroboration passages) measure reduction in over-crediting of one-origin false claims while preserving appropriate crediting of genuinely independent corroboration (report over-crediting rate, false-discount rate on independent sources, corroboration-judgment accuracy vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, collapse metric, and steering to held-out propositions/templates and an independent multi-document RAG-style set with controlled source independence without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice and dependency-marker phrasing.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The source-independence axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction or the raw source-count axis; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power at matched counts, and treat near-collapse (independence being merely count) as an informative negative result that itself shows LLMs conflate repetition with corroboration.

Independence structure is signaled by explicit dependency markers ('the same report', 'as X first said'), so the axis might reflect surface lexical cues rather than a genuine independence abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, structurally-implied dependency variants, matched-count controls, and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the axis predicts behavior beyond a dependency-lexeme baseline.

Constructing clean INDEPENDENT vs DEPENDENT passages of equal count is delicate; independent-source passages may differ in surface diversity from echoed ones. We match length and assertion count, vary phrasing diversity within both conditions, and validate with human annotation of the intended independence structure.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.
The collapse metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear collapse could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.
Behavioral corroboration/endorsement scoring depends on how the corroboration query is phrased; we report sensitivity across phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify independence steering changes over-crediting without altering perceived source count or degrading crediting of genuinely independent corroboration.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent multi-document transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: unpropagated_entailment_axis
Title: Believes the Premises, Withholds the Conclusion: A Latent Entailment-Propagation Gate Behind LLM Failures to Draw Inferences It Already Endorses
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM internally believes premise P (probe-true) and internally represents that P entails Q, it does not automatically propagate belief to Q; whether propagation happens is governed by a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'entailment-propagation' gate, distinct from the belief-valence direction and from an entailment-recognition direction, that is decodable before the answer, causally predicts the specific failure where the model withholds/denies a conclusion it implicitly endorses, and can be steered to make the model actually draw (or withhold) held conclusions.
Related Work: Prior work shows a pervasive knowledge/output gap ('know but don't tell'; Inside-Out; LLMs Know More Than They Show; KAPPA bridging the knowledge-prediction gap on MCQs), but always about recalling a stored FACT the model fails to emit—not about failing to CONJOIN beliefs into an entailed conclusion. Truth-value probes are context-sensitive causal mediators of NLI (2024) and steering a premise along the belief direction moves an entailed hypothesis, but that work does not ask whether the model SPONTANEOUSLY propagates belief to a conclusion it holds, nor isolate a signal predicting when propagation fails. Attestation-bias/NLI work (Sources of Hallucination 2023; Explicit Inductive Inference 2024; Neutralizing Bias with Entailment Graphs 2025) and Extractive Structures (2024, finetuned-fact implications) study behavioral inference and out-of-context two-hop generalization, not an inference-time propagation gate over the model's OWN held beliefs. My prior belief_coherence_geometry proposal tests a static logical algebra of projections but never a spontaneous-propagation/gating signal nor the inference-not-drawn failure. We uniquely (a) define an entailment-propagation gate separable from belief-valence and entailment-recognition, (b) predict the withheld-conclusion failure per example, and (c) causally steer propagation. This moves from 'the model can recall/mediate' to 'the model represents whether to carry a held belief across an entailment it endorses, and this gate causes inference-drawing failures.'
Abstract: A reasoner who believes P and believes that P implies Q should believe Q, yet large language models routinely withhold or deny conclusions their own internal beliefs already entail. Prior work documents a broad knowledge/output gap—models fail to say facts they internally know—but this concerns recalling a stored fact, not conjoining beliefs into an entailed conclusion. We ask a sharper question: when an LLM internally believes a premise and internally recognizes an entailment, does it automatically propagate belief to the conclusion, and what governs failures to do so? We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'entailment-propagation' gate, decodable before the answer, distinct from the belief-valence direction and from an entailment-recognition direction, that determines whether a held premise-belief is carried across an endorsed entailment to the conclusion. We test four claims across three model families: (1) there exist per-example cases where the model probes-true on P, probes-true on 'P entails Q', yet probes-neutral/false on Q and behaviorally withholds/denies Q—an unpropagated entailment; (2) a propagation-gate probe from pre-answer activations decodes whether propagation will occur, separable via cross-decoding from belief-valence and entailment-recognition; (3) the gate predicts the behavioral withheld-conclusion failure beyond belief margin, entailment-recognition score, and confidence; and (4) steering the gate causally makes the model draw conclusions it implicitly endorsed (or, adversarially, withhold ones it would have drawn), with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls. Our results recast a class of reasoning failures as an internally represented propagation-gating deficit, yielding a cheap diagnostic and training-free inference-completion intervention.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit an ENTAILMENT-RECOGNITION direction from contrastive stimuli labeled 'P entails Q' vs 'P does not entail Q' (independent of whether P or Q is believed), controlling for surface form. Fit a confidence control axis from empirical answer-correctness rates.

2. Held-belief entailment stimulus construction. Build ~400 (P, Q) pairs where P single-step entails Q (definitional, taxonomic 'is-a', simple transitive, and property-inheritance entailments), spanning: (a) P believed by the model (probe-true zero-context), (b) the P->Q entailment recognized by the model, and (c) Q of varying independent difficulty/familiarity so Q is NOT trivially recalled on its own. Include controls: non-entailing (P, Q') pairs, and P-disbelieved pairs. Use synthetic-entity chains so Q cannot be single-hop recalled, forcing genuine propagation. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out pairs/templates.

3. Unpropagated-entailment identification (core phenomenon). For each pair, read the frozen belief projections for P, for the entailment 'P->Q', and for Q, and elicit the model's stated judgment of Q (given P in context). Identify UNPROPAGATED cases: P probes-true AND entailment probes-recognized, yet Q probes-neutral/false and/or is behaviorally withheld/denied. Quantify prevalence per model and per entailment type; contrast with PROPAGATED cases (Q belief and assertion follow). Report the rate and characterize which entailment types/difficulties are prone to non-propagation.

4. Propagation-gate probe and separability. Extract pre-answer activations at a fixed readout position and fit a linear probe to decode impending PROPAGATION vs NON-PROPAGATION. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the propagation-gate direction, the belief-valence direction, and the entailment-recognition direction to establish that the gate is (i) near-orthogonal to belief-valence and (ii) distinct from mere entailment recognition. Critically, restrict a key analysis to cases where P is believed AND entailment recognized (both held constant), testing whether the gate still separates propagation outcomes.

5. Behavioral prediction. Test whether the pre-answer gate readout predicts the withheld-conclusion failure per example beyond baselines (belief-valence margin on P, entailment-recognition score, confidence, output entropy, Q difficulty, item length). Report incremental AUROC in nested logistic regression.

6. Causal steering (double dissociation). On held-out unpropagated items, steer along the propagation-gate direction (orthogonalized against belief-valence and entailment-recognition). Predict: amplifying the gate makes the model draw the endorsed conclusion (assert/believe Q) WITHOUT changing its belief in P or the entailment on control items; suppressing it induces withholding of conclusions the model would otherwise draw. Controls: steer belief-valence (should change belief in P/Q directly) and entailment-recognition (should change whether P->Q is judged valid). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in conclusion-drawing rate vs unchanged P-belief and entailment-recognition.

7. Application and introspection. Build a training-free inference-completion intervention: when the gate reads low on a recognized, believed entailment, steer to complete propagation; measure gain in drawing correct held conclusions while preserving refusal to draw invalid ones (report completion rate, false-inference rate on non-entailing controls). Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('You believe P and that P implies Q—so do you believe Q?') aligns with the latent gate and whether it fails to draw the conclusion even when the gate indicates it could (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control).

8. Robustness and generalization. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted gate probe and steering to held-out pairs/templates and an independent single-step entailment set (e.g., a MoNLI/monotonicity or is-a slice) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to readout position and layer.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The propagation-gate direction may not be separable from belief-valence or entailment-recognition; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power (with P-belief and entailment held constant), and treat near-collapse as an informative negative result showing propagation is fully determined by belief+recognition.

The phenomenon depends on cleanly establishing that P is believed AND the entailment recognized yet Q not propagated; probe brittleness could misclassify these states. We validate probes, restrict to high-margin P and high-recognition items, use synthetic-entity chains so Q is not single-hop recalled, and report label-noise sensitivity.

Non-propagation might reflect the model not actually recognizing the entailment despite the recognition probe; we cross-check with behavioral entailment judgments and condition on items where the model behaviorally affirms P->Q.
Belief/truth and recognition probes are brittle to surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize readout positions, and report per-template consistency.
The gate is a linear projection and may miss nonlinear structure; we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral outcomes.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify propagation steering changes conclusion-drawing without altering P-belief/entailment-recognition or inducing invalid inferences on non-entailing controls.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models (which may propagate more reliably); three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage, with reasoning-tuned models noted as future work.

Name: presupposition_accommodation_axis
Title: Taken for Granted: A Latent Presupposition-Accommodation Axis that Silently Admits Backgrounded Content into an LLM's Belief State
Short Hypothesis: When a proposition enters an LLM's input as a PRESUPPOSITION (backgrounded, taken-for-granted content triggered by definite descriptions, factives, clefts, change-of-state verbs) rather than as an at-issue ASSERTION, the model tags its epistemic force along a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'accommodation' axis; because presupposed content is silently accommodated as common ground rather than evaluated, its belief-valence readout is pulled toward TRUE with little of the scrutiny an assertion receives (an 'accommodation-leakage' signature), and this leakage is decodable, causally predicts whether the model adopts a FALSE presupposition without challenge, and can be steered to make the model evaluate rather than accommodate.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs frequently fail to reject false presuppositions, especially when misinformation stakes are high (LLMs Struggle to Reject False Presuppositions 2025; CREPE 2023; JBA 2025; Identifying Questions with False Assumptions 2025), and mechanistic work traces false-premise hallucinations to a small set of shallow-layer attention heads that disturb knowledge extraction (FAITH 2024). Belief/truth-probe work shows belief-valence is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth is Universal 2024) and context-sensitive, updating (sometimes wrongly) on prior assertions (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024). Crucially, all presupposition work is behavioral or about attention-head disruption, and all belief-probe work treats context as assertions that move the truth readout; NONE isolates the EPISTEMIC FORCE of presupposition—whether content entered the belief state as backgrounded/accommodated common ground vs. at-issue asserted content—as a decodable belief axis, defines an accommodation-leakage metric, or causally links accommodation to silent false-presupposition adoption. This differs from my prior assertoric_force proposal (supposition/hypothetical entertaining, which is overtly non-committal) and grounding-status proposal (mutual establishment in dialogue): presupposition is content the speaker treats as ALREADY given and the hearer SILENTLY accepts (accommodates) without it ever being asserted or acknowledged—a distinct, high-stakes vector for embedding misinformation. We move from 'LLMs fail on false presuppositions' and 'truth is decodable' to 'the model represents whether a proposition was asserted or presupposed, and accommodation of presupposed content mechanistically drives its silent admission into belief.'
Abstract: Language smuggles claims past our scrutiny by presupposing them: 'the senator who took the bribe resigned' backgrounds that a bribe was taken, treating it as given rather than asserting it for evaluation. Humans (and, behavioral studies show, LLMs) often silently accommodate such presupposed content—accepting it as common ground without challenge—making presupposition a potent vehicle for misinformation. We ask whether LLMs represent this epistemic force internally. Prior work shows LLMs fail behaviorally on false presuppositions and that false-premise hallucinations involve shallow attention heads, and that belief-valence is linearly decodable; but none isolates whether a proposition entered the model's belief state as backgrounded/presupposed versus at-issue asserted content, nor connects that distinction to silent adoption of falsehoods. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'accommodation' axis, decodable at read time, that tags a proposition's epistemic force (presupposed/accommodated vs. asserted/evaluated), distinct from the belief-valence direction; and an 'accommodation-leakage' signature: the degree to which presupposed content is pulled toward TRUE with little evaluative scrutiny, quantifiable per item and predictive of the model adopting a FALSE presupposition without challenge. Using matched propositions delivered as presupposition (via definite descriptions, factives, clefts, change-of-state verbs) versus assertion versus question, and crossing content truth, we fit the accommodation axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item leakage, and connect it to behavioral false-presupposition adoption. Double-dissociation steering tests whether suppressing accommodation makes the model evaluate and reject false presuppositions (and amplifying it induces silent adoption of asserted falsehoods) without changing what it believes true, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a classic pragmatic mechanism—presupposition accommodation—as a decodable, steerable belief-admission gate and yield a diagnostic and training-free intervention against presupposition-embedded misinformation.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics; also isolate the polarity-robust general-truth direction (Truth is Universal) as a control. Fit a confidence control axis from empirical answer-correctness rates (sampled).

2. Epistemic-force stimulus construction. Build ~400 verifiable propositions (true and false variants). For each, create matched frames holding the target proposition content fixed while varying its epistemic force: (a) ASSERTION ('A bribe was taken by the senator'), (b) PRESUPPOSITION via a standard trigger with the target proposition backgrounded and a distinct at-issue main clause (definite description 'The senator who took the bribe resigned'; factive 'Everyone knows that the senator took a bribe'; cleft 'It was the senator who took the bribe'; change-of-state 'The senator stopped taking bribes'), (c) QUESTION/neutral-mention control, and (d) explicit-denial control ('It is false that the senator took a bribe'). Critically, in the presupposition frame the target is NOT the at-issue content, so the model is not being asked to evaluate it. Use paraphrase templates and multiple trigger types; reserve held-out propositions/templates/triggers for transfer. Validate presupposition status with projectivity checks (survives negation of the main clause).

3. Accommodation-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the target-proposition span and fit a linear probe to decode PRESUPPOSED vs ASSERTED epistemic force, controlling for content truth-value and the at-issue main clause. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the accommodation axis, the belief-valence axis, and the confidence axis to establish near-orthogonality. Localize the best layer and compare to the shallow layers implicated in false-premise heads (FAITH).

4. Accommodation-leakage metric. For each presupposed target, project onto the frozen belief-valence direction and measure how far it reads as TRUE relative to the matched question/neutral baseline and, critically, relative to the same content ASSERTED (leakage = the extra pull toward TRUE that presupposed content receives beyond what the same content receives when asserted-and-evaluated, calibrated per model). Compare across trigger types, true vs false content, and at-issue-clause salience. Core prediction: FALSE presupposed content reads substantially truer than the same content ASSERTED (which the model can evaluate and reject), because presupposition bypasses evaluation; leakage is largest for strong triggers (definites, factives).

5. Behavioral false-presupposition-adoption prediction. Elicit the model's continuation/answer to the presupposition-frame prompts and score (rule-based + held-out judge + human spot-checks) whether the model ADOPTS the false presupposition (proceeds as if true, references the presupposed content) versus CHALLENGES it (flags/corrects the false assumption). Test whether per-item accommodation-leakage predicts silent adoption via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin on the same asserted content, confidence, output entropy, trigger type, item length).

6. Dissociation from plain truth-evaluation (core). Contrast, per proposition, the model's ability to REJECT the content when ASSERTED (where it evaluates and often correctly rejects a falsehood) against its failure to reject the SAME content when PRESUPPOSED. Test whether the accommodation axis predicts this assertion-vs-presupposition gap beyond the belief-valence readout of the asserted version—evidence that accommodation, not ignorance of the fact, drives adoption.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out false-presupposition items, steer along the accommodation axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and confidence). Predict: suppressing accommodation (pushing presupposed content toward the asserted/evaluated pole) makes the model EVALUATE and reject false presuppositions (challenge them) WITHOUT changing its judgments on genuinely-true content or on control assertions; amplifying accommodation induces silent adoption even of asserted falsehoods (treating them as given). As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip whether content is judged true, for both forces) and confidence (should shift hedging only). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in false-presupposition challenge rate vs unchanged true-content and control-assertion accuracy.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free misinformation defense: flag presupposition-embedded false content from the leakage metric and steer to enforce evaluation; on a held-out set (including CREPE/false-premise-style items) measure reduction in silent false-presupposition adoption while preserving fluent handling of true presuppositions (report adoption rate, over-challenge rate on true presuppositions, and accuracy vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, leakage metric, and steering to held-out triggers/templates and an independent false-presupposition benchmark (CREPE slice) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice and trigger type.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The accommodation axis may not be separable from the belief-valence or confidence directions; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because the key comparison holds content and truth-value fixed while varying epistemic force—the truth axis cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse is an informative negative result that itself sharpens the truth-representation account.

Epistemic force is signaled by trigger lexemes/syntax (definite articles, 'knows that', clefts), so the axis might reflect surface trigger cues rather than a genuine accommodation abstraction; we mitigate with multiple diverse trigger types, paraphrase templates, projectivity-validated presuppositions, and held-out-trigger transfer, testing whether the axis predicts behavior beyond a trigger-lexeme baseline.

The core dissociation requires that the model CAN reject the content when asserted; for facts it does not know, assertion and presupposition both fail. We restrict the key analysis to false content the model can reject when asserted (verified via the asserted-frame belief readout and behavior), so any extra adoption under presupposition is attributable to accommodation.

Constructing matched assertion/presupposition frames where only epistemic force differs is delicate (the at-issue clause differs); we control at-issue-clause content, use neutral main clauses, and report sensitivity to main-clause choice.

Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use the polarity-robust general-truth direction, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.
The leakage metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear leakage could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.
Behavioral adoption/challenge scoring depends on rule-based detectors plus an LLM judge and on elicitation phrasing; we anchor with human spot-checks and report phrasing sensitivity.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify accommodation-suppression increases challenging of false presuppositions without degrading true-content accuracy or making the model over-challenge true presuppositions.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: individual_vs_typical_belief_axis
Title: Whose Mind Is This? A Latent Individuation Axis on Attributed Beliefs, and the Machine Typical-Mind Default
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM attributes a belief to a specific individual, it carries a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'belief-individuation' axis encoding whether the attributed belief is anchored to that person's idiosyncratic, previously-disclosed belief profile versus imputed from a population-typical/majority default; the degree to which individual-specific beliefs collapse onto the population-typical default (a 'typical-mind projection' signature) is decodable at attribution time, causally predicts and drives the failure where the model overrides an individual's stated idiosyncratic belief with what most people believe, and can be steered to individuate or homogenize belief attribution.
Related Work: Interpretability work shows self/other beliefs and reality are separately decodable and steerable via attention heads and a lookback/binding mechanism (Zhu et al. 2024 'LMs Represent Beliefs of Self and Others'; Lookbacks 2025; Brittle Minds 2024), and belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023). Neuroscience robustly documents that conceptual and belief representations are individually idiosyncratic and that group-average codes discard person-specific structure ('The brain of the beholder' 2015; Individual differences shape conceptual representation 2025; population-neuroscience 2013), and psychology documents the false-consensus / typical-mind projection whereby people impute their own or the majority's beliefs onto specific others. Crucially, all LLM belief/ToM work tracks WHICH state an agent believes or WHO holds a belief as a binary self/other readout; none asks whether the model represents a belief at the granularity of a SPECIFIC individual's idiosyncratic profile versus a population-typical default, defines an individuation-vs-collapse metric, or causally links typical-mind projection to overriding a person's stated idiosyncratic belief. This differs from my prior consensus_prevalence axis (aggregate endorsement biasing truth), audience_credulity axis (what a given audience will accept), and user_attribute_belief_warrant axis (groundedness of an inferred demographic attribute): here the object is whether an attributed belief is anchored to the individual's own disclosed profile or homogenized to the crowd. We move from 'the model tracks self vs other beliefs' to 'the model represents whether a belief is individuated to a specific mind, and typical-mind collapse mechanistically drives homogenized personalization.'
Abstract: People differ: two individuals given identical information hold idiosyncratic beliefs, and cognitive neuroscience shows conceptual representations are systematically person-specific, obscured only by group averaging. A good reasoner attributing a belief to a specific individual should anchor it to that person's disclosed idiosyncrasies rather than defaulting to what most people believe. We ask whether large language models do this internally. Prior interpretability work decodes self versus other beliefs as a binary and traces belief-binding mechanisms, but none asks whether an attributed belief is represented at the granularity of a specific individual's profile versus a population-typical default. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'belief-individuation' axis, decodable at attribution time, that tags whether an attributed belief is anchored to a person's idiosyncratic, previously-disclosed belief profile versus imputed from a majority/typical default, distinct from the belief-valence direction and from the self/other-belief direction; and a 'typical-mind projection' signature: the degree to which individual-specific beliefs collapse onto the population-typical default, quantifiable per example and predictive of the model overriding an individual's stated idiosyncratic belief with the crowd's. Using dialogues that establish an individual's idiosyncratic (majority-divergent) beliefs and then query their belief on a related item, we fit an individuation axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-example collapse, and connect it to behavioral homogenization. Double-dissociation steering tests whether amplifying individuation makes the model respect the person's idiosyncratic profile (and suppressing it induces typical-mind override) without changing what the majority believes, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a fairness-critical personalization failure as a decodable, steerable individuation deficit.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Following Zhu et al. 2024, fit a self/other (protagonist-vs-reality) belief direction from ToM stories as a control axis, and a population-typical/majority-default direction from statements framed as what 'most people believe'.

2. Individuation stimulus construction. Build ~400 dialogues that establish a SPECIFIC individual with an idiosyncratic belief profile that DIVERGES from the population majority (e.g., a character who disclosed several minority-held preferences/opinions/factual stances), then query the individual's belief on a RELATED target item for which (a) the population-typical answer and (b) the answer entailed by the individual's disclosed profile CONFLICT. Vary: profile strength (one weak cue vs several consistent idiosyncratic cues), majority-divergence magnitude, and include TYPICAL-INDIVIDUAL controls (the person's profile matches the majority, so individuation and default coincide) and NO-PROFILE controls (no idiosyncratic information given). Use paraphrase templates and diverse characters; reserve held-out dialogues/templates for transfer.

3. Individuation-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the attributed-belief readout span and fit a linear probe to decode INDIVIDUATED (belief anchored to the person's disclosed idiosyncratic profile) vs DEFAULT (belief imputed from the population-typical answer), controlling for the belief content. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the individuation axis, the belief-valence axis, the self/other-belief axis, and the population-typical axis to establish that individuation is (i) near-orthogonal to belief content, (ii) distinct from the self/other binary, and (iii) not merely the typical-default direction. Localize the best layer and compare to reported belief-binding/lookback layers.

4. Typical-mind projection collapse metric. For each conflict item, project the attributed-belief activations onto the population-typical direction and measure how far the individual's attributed belief reads as the MAJORITY answer relative to the profile-entailed answer (collapse = fraction of the typical-default signal that overrides the individuated profile signal, calibrated per model). Compare collapse across profile-strength, divergence magnitude, and typical-individual controls; predict collapse is largest for weak profiles and highly majority-divergent items, near-zero for typical-individual controls.

5. Behavioral homogenization prediction. Query the model for the individual's belief on the conflict target; score the typical-mind override = attributing the majority answer despite the person's disclosed profile entailing otherwise. Test whether per-example collapse predicts override via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, self/other readout, population-typical readout, output confidence, profile length, majority-answer frequency).

6. Dissociation from self/other and content (core). Contrast items where belief content is held fixed but individuation varies, and vice versa, to show the individuation axis predicts override beyond the self/other-belief and belief-valence axes, and that it tracks anchoring-to-profile rather than merely which state is believed. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out conflict items, steer along the individuation axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence, self/other, and the population-typical direction). Predict: amplifying individuation makes the model respect the person's idiosyncratic profile (attributing the profile-entailed belief) WITHOUT changing what the majority believes on typical-individual controls; suppressing it induces typical-mind override (defaulting to the crowd). As controls, steer belief-valence (should change which state is believed generally) and the population-typical direction (should shift the crowd default). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in override rate vs unchanged majority-belief and control-item behavior.

8. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free personalization-fairness diagnostic that flags typical-mind override from the collapse metric and steers to enforce individuation; on a held-out set (including realistic user profiles that diverge from population norms) measure reduction in homogenized attributions while preserving accurate use of disclosed profiles and correct majority defaults when no individuating info exists (report override rate, over-individuation rate on no-profile items, profile-usage accuracy vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('Are you basing this on what THIS person told you, or on what most people believe?') aligns with the latent individuation axis and whether models fail to verbalize the projection even when the axis is engaged (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, collapse metric, and steering to held-out characters/templates and an independent user-profile personalization set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The individuation axis may not be separable from the self/other-belief direction, the belief-valence direction, or the population-typical direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (individuation being merely other-belief tracking or the typical-default direction) as an informative negative result that itself sharpens the self/other-belief literature.

Individuation framing may act through surface cues (explicit 'this person believes X' statements) rather than a genuine profile-anchoring abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, implicit profile disclosure, varied character descriptions, typical-individual and no-profile controls, and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the axis predicts behavior beyond a surface-cue baseline.

Constructing conflict items where the profile-entailed belief and the population-typical belief cleanly diverge is delicate; the profile must genuinely entail the minority answer. We validate entailment with human annotation and rule checks, and condition analyses on items where the model demonstrably recognizes both the majority default and the profile.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.
The collapse metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear collapse could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.
Behavioral override scoring depends on how the belief query is phrased; we report sensitivity across phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

This work probes person-specific belief attribution; to avoid amplifying harm we use synthetic characters and frame steering as an individuation/fairness intervention (respecting disclosed idiosyncrasies) rather than a means to profile users more aggressively.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify individuation steering changes override behavior without altering majority beliefs or degrading appropriate defaults on no-profile items.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: collective_belief_aggregation
Title: The Sum Is Not Its Parts: A Latent Collective-Belief Representation Over Groups of Agents, Distinct from Any Member's Belief
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM tracks several agents who each hold beliefs about the same proposition, it forms a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'collective-belief' representation of what 'the group' believes—an emergent aggregate distinct from any individual member's decodable belief and from a simple average—mirroring the human finding that groups are mentalized as minds in their own right; the way this collective belief is computed (credibility/majority-weighted vs naive-average vs dominated-by-a-salient-member) is decodable, causally predicts the model's answers to group-attitude questions, and can be steered.
Related Work: Interpretability work decodes self vs other beliefs and reality as separate, causally-relevant directions (Zhu et al. 2024 'LMs Represent Beliefs of Self and Others'; Brittle Minds 2024) and reverse-engineers the per-character binding/lookback algorithm for belief tracking (Lookbacks 2025), while belief/truth probes are context-sensitive causal mediators (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024). Behavioral social-integration work models how a single agent weights individual vs social judgments (Integration of individual and social information 2017) and neuroscience shows humans mentalize GROUP agents as minds distinct from their members, with overlapping-but-distinct neural patterns (Common Brain Regions... Groups and Individuals 2013; Neural Bases of Mental State Attributions to Group Agents 2014). Crucially, ALL LLM belief/ToM interpretability treats attributed belief at the level of individual agents (or self/other/reality) and reads each out separately; NONE asks whether the model forms an emergent COLLECTIVE-belief representation of what a group believes that is distinct from any member's belief (Experiment 1 of the group-neuroscience work shows humans attribute to the group a state held by no member), nor decodes the AGGREGATION RULE (how member beliefs are combined), nor causally links it to group-attitude answers. My prior consensus_prevalence axis concerns aggregate social prevalence of a fact biasing TRUTH; here the object is the model's attributed belief of a specified GROUP of tracked agents—a distinct mentalizing target. We move from 'per-agent beliefs are decodable' to 'the model represents the group as a belief-bearing entity via a decodable, steerable aggregation.'
Abstract: Humans mentalize about groups—'the committee thinks', 'scientists believe'—attributing to a collective a mind that is not reducible to any single member; neuroscience shows people can even ascribe to a group a belief held by none of its members. We ask whether large language models do the same internally. Prior interpretability work decodes what individual agents believe and reverse-engineers per-character belief-binding, but always reads attributed belief agent-by-agent; none asks whether an LLM forms an emergent COLLECTIVE-belief representation over a set of agents, distinct from any member's belief, nor how member beliefs are aggregated. We hypothesize that when the model tracks several agents holding beliefs about the same proposition, it computes a separable, near-orthogonal latent collective-belief representation of what 'the group' believes; that this collective belief is distinct from each decoded member belief and from a naive average; that the aggregation rule (credibility/majority-weighted, naive-average, or salient-member-dominated) is itself decodable; and that the collective-belief readout causally predicts and can steer the model's answers to group-attitude questions. Using controlled multi-agent stories that orthogonally vary member beliefs, member credibility/authority, and majority structure, we fit member and collective belief directions, test separability via cross-decoding, characterize the aggregation rule, and causally intervene. We test the key emergence signature—a group belief held by no member—and steer the collective belief and the aggregation weights independently, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results establish an emergent collective-mind representation in LLMs and a mechanistic account of belief aggregation, with implications for multi-agent, deliberation, and social-simulation settings.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Following Zhu et al. 2024, fit per-agent attributed-belief directions from ToM stories as the individual-belief baseline.

2. Multi-agent stimulus construction. Build ~400 short stories in which K agents (K=3-5) each independently hold a belief (true/false) about the SAME proposition P, then a query asks what 'the group / committee / team' believes about P.
