Orthogonally vary: (a) the distribution of member beliefs (unanimous, majority-true, split, one-dissenter); (b) member CREDIBILITY/authority (expert vs novice, leader vs subordinate); (c) member salience/recency. Include the critical EMERGENCE cell where the balance of credible members' beliefs points to a group answer held by NO single member framing (e.g., aggregated tendency), following the group-neuroscience Experiment-1 logic. Define readout spans for each member-belief query and for the group-belief query. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out stories/templates for transfer.

3. Collective-belief direction fitting and separability. Extract activations at the GROUP-belief readout span and fit a linear probe to decode the group's attributed belief-valence. Establish that this collective-belief readout is a distinct representation, not a trivial copy of a member: measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the collective-belief direction, each per-agent belief direction, and the plain truth direction; and test whether the collective readout is decodable at a position/subspace separable from any single member's. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls and near-orthogonality metrics.

4. Aggregation-rule characterization. Model the decoded collective belief as a function of the decoded member beliefs and credibilities: fit candidate rules—naive average, majority vote, credibility-weighted (Bayesian social integration, cf. Integration of individual and social information 2017), and salient/last-member-dominated—and select the best-fitting per model/condition (report R^2). Test the emergence prediction: in the critical cell, does the collective readout land on a value matching no individual member (an irreducible group belief), and which rule explains it?

5. Behavioral prediction. Elicit the model's stated answer and confidence to the group-attitude question. Test whether the internal collective-belief readout predicts the stated group answer per example via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (naive average of member-belief probes, majority-of-members, most-credible-member belief, most-recent-member belief, output entropy).

6. Dissociation from individual beliefs. On matched items, show the collective-belief direction predicts group-attitude answers beyond what any single member-belief probe or their average predicts (incremental AUROC in nested models), establishing the collective representation is functionally distinct from member beliefs—the core emergence claim.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. (a) Steer the collective-belief direction (orthogonalized against member-belief directions and truth) and test that the model's group-attitude answer moves WITHOUT changing its answers to individual member-belief questions; (b) steer the AGGREGATION weights—amplify the credibility-weighting component (or the salient-member component)—and test that the collective belief shifts toward the up-weighted members while member beliefs stay fixed. Controls: steer a single member-belief direction (should change that member's answer, not necessarily the group's), truth direction, and norm-matched/shuffled directions; sweep strengths and layers.

8. Application and robustness. Test generalization to natural group nouns ('the jury', 'the scientists', 'the board') and to a downstream social-simulation setting (predicting a group's decision), measuring whether the collective-belief readout predicts group outputs. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted collective-belief direction and aggregation-rule fit to held-out stories/templates and an independent multi-agent ToM set (FANToM / Hi-ToM slice) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase, sensitivity to K, layer, and readout position.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The collective-belief direction may not be separable from a simple function of member-belief directions (e.g., it could be exactly the average); we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, and incremental predictive power, and treat 'collective belief = naive average of members' as an informative negative result (the model does NOT form an emergent group representation) rather than a failure.

The emergence cell (group belief held by no member) is delicate to construct so that the intended group answer genuinely differs from every member; we validate with human annotation and rule checks and condition analyses on items where members' beliefs and the licensed group answer provably diverge.

The aggregation-rule fit assumes the collective readout is a (roughly linear) function of decoded member beliefs/credibilities; nonlinear aggregation could be missed, so we report fit quality and treat selected rules as approximations, comparing multiple candidate rules.

Group-belief framing may act through surface cues (the word 'group/committee') rather than genuine aggregation; we mitigate with diverse group nouns, paraphrase templates, and matched controls, testing whether the collective readout tracks member-belief structure beyond surface framing.
Per-agent and belief/truth probes are brittle to surface form and context; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify collective-belief steering changes group answers without altering individual member-belief answers (the double dissociation).
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent multi-agent ToM transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: attainability_belief_axis
Title: Can It Actually Get There? A Latent Attainability Axis on Goal-States, and the Machine Impossible-Plan Effect
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM is given a goal-state and a set of available actions/affordances, it represents the goal's ATTAINABILITY—whether the goal is reachable via the available actions—along a separable, near-orthogonal latent axis distinct from whether the goal-state is merely factually describable/plausible; the degree to which unattainable goals collapse onto the attainable region (an 'impossible-plan' signature) is decodable before the model plans, causally predicts and drives the failure where the model confidently produces a plan toward an unreachable goal, and can be steered to make the model recognize infeasibility (abstain/flag) or, adversarially, to plan toward the impossible.
Related Work: Affordance research in LLMs is almost entirely behavioral: benchmarks and probes show LLMs and MLLMs judge object affordances and physical possibility poorly (Text2Afford 2024; A4Bench 2025; NEWTON 2023; Do Neural LM Representations Learn Physical Commonsense 2019; A little less conversation 2024), and affordance is used behaviorally to prompt/plan robots (LLM+Affordance 2024; affordance symbol networks 2025) or grounded in RL theory (Khetarpal et al. 2020; Hierarchical Affordances 2022). VLA-interpretability work steers action concepts (Mechanistic Interpretability for VLAs 2025; OpenVLA symbolic-state probing 2025). Belief/truth-probe work shows belief-valence and belief-state geometry are linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024; The Shape of Beliefs 2026), and 'Confidence is Not Competence' (2025) shows a solvability-belief axis that is causally inert for execution. Crucially, NO interpretability work isolates whether an LLM represents that a goal-state is ATTAINABLE via a given action set—an affordance-grounded belief distinct from (a) the goal-state's plain truth/plausibility and (b) generic problem-solvability confidence—defines an attainability->truth collapse metric, or causally links its failure to producing plans toward impossible goals. This differs from Confidence-is-Not-Competence (solvability of a well-posed problem, not action-reachability of a goal given affordances), from my prior self_fulfilling proposal (truth determined by the model's own assertion), and from intention_execution (intended vs executed action). We move from 'LLMs judge affordances poorly behaviorally' and 'beliefs are decodable' to 'the model carries a decodable, steerable attainability axis whose collapse mechanistically causes confident impossible plans.'
Abstract: Agentic language models increasingly must decide not just what is true, but what is achievable: given a goal and a set of available actions, is the goal actually reachable? A capable planner should distinguish a describable-but-unreachable goal ('rearrange the blocks so a block floats unsupported in mid-air') from a genuinely attainable one, and refuse or flag the former rather than confidently plan toward it. Prior work shows LLMs judge affordances and physical possibility poorly behaviorally, and separately shows beliefs are linearly decodable, but none asks whether the model internally represents a goal's ATTAINABILITY given its affordances. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'attainability' axis, decodable before the model plans, that tags whether a goal-state is reachable via the available actions, distinct from the goal-state's plain truth/plausibility and from generic solvability confidence; and an 'impossible-plan' signature: the degree to which unattainable goals collapse onto the attainable region, quantifiable per item and predictive of the model producing a confident plan toward an unreachable goal. Using tasks that orthogonally vary a goal's describability/plausibility and its attainability given a stated action set, we fit the attainability axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item collapse, and connect it to behavioral impossible-planning. Double-dissociation steering tests whether amplifying the axis induces appropriate infeasibility-recognition (abstain/flag) and suppressing it induces confident impossible planning, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast affordance-grounded planning failures as a decodable, steerable attainability deficit and yield a diagnostic and training-free intervention for agentic infeasibility detection.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit control axes: (a) a plausibility/possible-vs-impossible direction distinguishing describable/plausible from implausible/impossible states (following modal-plausibility constructions), and (b) a generic solvability/confidence axis (Confidence-is-Not-Competence style; empirical success-rate contrast), to distinguish action-reachability from plain plausibility and from generic solvability.

2. Attainability stimulus construction. Build ~400 goal-planning items in controlled domains (blocksworld/gridworld-style state changes, simple recipe/tool-use tasks, and text micro-environments) each specifying an initial state, a set of AVAILABLE ACTIONS (affordances), and a GOAL-STATE. Orthogonally vary: (i) whether the goal-state is DESCRIBABLE/PLAUSIBLE as a world-state (holding surface form matched), and (ii) whether it is ATTAINABLE via the available actions (reachable vs provably unreachable given the action set). This yields diagnostic cells: ATTAINABLE (plausible goal, reachable), UNATTAINABLE-PLAUSIBLE (goal is a perfectly describable state but no action sequence reaches it—e.g., action set lacks the needed operation, or a constraint blocks it), and IMPLAUSIBLE (goal-state itself is physically impossible). Ground-truth attainability is computed by a solver/reachability check. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates for transfer.

3. Attainability-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations at a fixed pre-planning readout position (after the goal+action set, before the model plans) and fit a linear probe to decode ATTAINABLE vs UNATTAINABLE, controlling for goal describability/plausibility. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the attainability axis, the belief-valence/truth axis, the plausibility axis, and the solvability/confidence axis to establish that attainability is (i) near-orthogonal to plain truth/plausibility (the UNATTAINABLE-PLAUSIBLE cell has plausible goals yet is unreachable) and (ii) not merely generic solvability confidence. Localize the best layer.

4. Impossible-plan collapse metric. For each UNATTAINABLE-PLAUSIBLE goal, project activations onto the attainability axis and measure how far it reads as ATTAINABLE relative to the genuinely-attainable baseline (collapse = fraction of the attainable-goal signal an unreachable goal inherits, calibrated per model). Compare collapse across cells; core prediction: collapse is largest for unattainable-but-plausible goals (the model treats a describable state as reachable) and dissociable from the implausible cell. Test whether collapse grows with how superficially close the unreachable goal looks to reachable ones.

5. Behavioral impossible-planning prediction. Elicit the model's response and score (rule-based + held-out judge + human spot-checks): whether the model produces a confident plan toward the goal versus flags infeasibility/abstains. Score the impossible-plan failure = producing a plan (often with fabricated/illegal actions) toward an unattainable goal. Test whether per-item collapse predicts impossible-planning via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, plausibility axis, solvability axis, output entropy, item length, plan length).

6. Dissociation from plausibility and solvability (core). Contrast UNATTAINABLE-PLAUSIBLE items (plausible goal, unreachable) against IMPLAUSIBLE items (impossible goal-state) and against genuinely-hard-but-solvable items. Test whether the attainability axis predicts infeasibility-recognition beyond what the plausibility and solvability axes predict—establishing action-reachability as a mechanism distinct from state-plausibility and from generic difficulty. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the pre-planning position on held-out items, steer along the attainability axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence, plausibility, and solvability). Predict: suppressing the attainable pole on unattainable goals induces appropriate infeasibility-recognition (the model flags/abstains rather than fabricating a plan) WITHOUT changing behavior on genuinely attainable controls; amplifying it induces confident impossible planning even on unreachable goals. As controls, steer plausibility (should affect whether the goal-state is judged possible, not reachability given actions) and solvability/confidence (should shift hedging). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in infeasibility-flag rate on unattainable items vs preserved planning on attainable items.

8. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free agentic-safety diagnostic that flags impossible-plan risk from the collapse metric and steers toward infeasibility-recognition; measure reduction in confident impossible plans while preserving valid planning (report impossible-plan rate, over-refusal on attainable items, plan validity vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('Is this goal reachable with the actions you have?') aligns with the latent attainability axis and whether models fail to verbalize infeasibility even when the axis indicates it (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, collapse metric, and steering to held-out domains/templates and an independent planning benchmark slice (e.g., a Blocksworld/PlanBench-style set with reachable vs unreachable goals) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The attainability axis may not be separable from the plausibility/possible-impossible direction, the belief-valence/truth direction, or generic solvability confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because the UNATTAINABLE-PLAUSIBLE cell holds goal-plausibility fixed while varying reachability—plausibility cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse is an informative negative result that itself sharpens the belief/solvability-representation literature.

Ground-truth attainability requires a correct reachability/solver check over the action set; ambiguous or under-specified action semantics could mislabel items. We use controlled domains with well-defined action semantics and an explicit solver, validate labels, and report sensitivity to action-set specification.

Attainability framing may act through surface cues (a conspicuously missing action word) rather than a genuine reachability abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, matched surface form across attainable/unattainable cells, multiple domains, and held-out-domain transfer, testing whether the axis predicts behavior beyond a surface/action-count baseline.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize the pre-planning readout position, and report per-template consistency.

The collapse metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear structure could be missed, so we treat collapse as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral impossible-planning.

Behavioral impossible-plan vs infeasibility-flag scoring depends on rule-based detectors plus an LLM judge and on elicitation phrasing; we anchor with plan-validity checks against the solver and human spot-checks, and report phrasing sensitivity.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify attainability steering changes infeasibility-recognition without degrading valid planning on attainable items or collapsing the model into always-refusing. The suppression (impossible-planning-inducing) experiment is a controlled dual-use probe reported to motivate safeguards.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning/agent-tuned models; three-family replication and independent planning-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: occurrence_vs_belief_trace
Title: Believed-Not-Seen, Seen-Not-Believed: Dissociating an Occurrence/Source Trace from Truth-Belief in LLMs and the Machine Source-Confabulation Effect
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human memory-science dissociation between belief-in-occurrence (that an event happened / was encountered) and recollection/truth, an LLM carries a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'occurrence-trace' signal encoding whether a proposition actually appeared earlier in its context, distinct from the belief-valence direction encoding whether it holds the proposition true; the degree to which the truth-belief leaks into the occurrence-trace readout despite the proposition never having been stated (a 'source-confabulation' signature) is decodable, causally predicts and drives the failure where the model falsely claims un-stated content was in its context (or denies stated content), and can be steered to correct or induce these source errors.
Related Work: Cross-domain memory research robustly dissociates belief-in-occurrence from recollection: people hold vivid recollections they no longer believe ('non-believed memories') and beliefs about events they cannot recollect ('believed-not-remembered'), with the two decaying at different rates and driven by different variables (perceptual/emotional features drive recollection; plausibility drives belief) (Scoboria/Mazzoni 2013; Otgaar 2024; reasons-for-withdrawing-belief 2014; memory-justifications 2025). In LLM interpretability, belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023), self/other beliefs and belief-tracking mechanisms are known (Zhu et al. 2024; Lookbacks 2025), belief-state geometry is represented (Belief State Geometry 2024), and human-like memory effects (primacy/recency, interference-based forgetting, context-hijacking of recall) exist (Aspects of Human Memory & LLMs 2023; Do LLMs Dream of Elephants 2024). Crucially, NONE isolates an OCCURRENCE/SOURCE trace—whether a proposition actually appeared in the model's context—as a representation separable from whether the model BELIEVES the proposition, nor defines a source-confabulation metric, nor causally links their dissociation to false 'it was in the context' claims. This differs from my prior epoch-anchor proposal (long-held vs in-context provenance and silent drift), source-independence (independent vs echoed corroboration), evidential-contingency (dependence on context for the ANSWER), and introspective-gap (belief vs stated answer): here the object is a memory-science-style occurrence/source trace dissociated from truth-belief, and the target failure is source-memory confabulation—a core context-faithfulness/hallucination vector for RAG.
Abstract: Human memory science draws a sharp line between believing an event occurred and recollecting it: people hold vivid recollections they no longer believe and beliefs about events they cannot recall, and the two dissociate systematically. We ask whether large language models draw an analogous internal line between whether a proposition actually APPEARED in their context (an occurrence/source trace) and whether they BELIEVE it true. Prior interpretability work decodes truth-belief and belief-tracking and documents human-like recall effects, but none isolates an occurrence/source trace separable from truth-belief, nor the failure where the two come apart. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent occurrence-trace signal, decodable at read time, encoding whether a proposition was actually stated earlier in context, distinct from the belief-valence direction; and a 'source-confabulation' signature—the extent to which a strongly-believed-true proposition reads as if it had been stated even when it never was, and the converse for disbelieved stated content—quantifiable per item and predictive of the model falsely claiming un-stated content was in its context (or denying stated content). Using contexts that orthogonally vary whether a proposition was stated and whether the model believes it, we fit an occurrence-trace probe, measure separability from belief-valence via cross-decoding, quantify per-item leakage, and connect it to behavioral source-memory errors. Double-dissociation steering tests whether correcting the occurrence trace suppresses source confabulation (and corrupting it induces it) without changing what the model believes, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a foundational memory-science dissociation mechanistically and yield a diagnostic and training-free intervention for context-faithfulness failures.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Fit a generic recency/salience control axis (how recently/emphatically a proposition appeared) to distinguish an occurrence trace from mere recency.

2. 2x2 occurrence-x-belief stimulus construction. Build ~400 verifiable propositions and, for each, construct a context and a later query span crossing two factors: STATED vs NOT-STATED (the proposition literally appeared earlier in the context vs did not) and BELIEVED vs DISBELIEVED (the model holds it true vs false, measured via the frozen probe and true/false content variants). This yields four cells including the two diagnostic dissociations: BELIEVED-BUT-NOT-STATED (potential 'believed-non-memory' source confabulation) and DISBELIEVED-BUT-STATED (potential 'non-believed memory' denial). Include filler statements to prevent all-stated contexts, and matched paraphrases so surface wording of a queried proposition differs from its context wording (blocking pure lexical matching). Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out propositions/templates for transfer.

3. Occurrence-trace probe and separability. Extract activations over the queried-proposition span and fit a linear probe to decode STATED vs NOT-STATED, controlling for belief-valence. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the occurrence-trace direction, the belief-valence direction, and the recency axis to establish that the occurrence trace is (i) near-orthogonal to truth-belief and (ii) not merely recency. Localize the best layer and compare to belief-binding/lookback layers.

4. Source-confabulation leakage metric. For each BELIEVED-BUT-NOT-STATED item, project onto the occurrence-trace direction and measure how far the un-stated proposition reads as STATED relative to the matched not-stated/not-believed baseline (leakage = fraction of the genuine-stated signal a believed-but-un-stated proposition inherits, calibrated per model). Symmetrically measure the converse denial leakage for DISBELIEVED-BUT-STATED items. Compare leakage across cells; core prediction: strongly-believed content leaks onto the occurrence trace (the model 'remembers' seeing what it merely believes), and disbelieved stated content is under-registered as stated.

5. Behavioral source-error prediction. Query the model directly about occurrence ('Was this stated in the text above, yes or no?') and score source-confabulation errors: false-YES on un-stated believed content and false-NO on stated disbelieved content. Test whether per-item leakage predicts these errors via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, recency axis, lexical-overlap with context, output confidence, context length).

6. Dissociation from truth and recency (core). Contrast, per proposition, occurrence judgments across the 2x2 to show the occurrence-trace axis predicts source-memory errors beyond what the belief-valence axis (which is held fixed within STATED/NOT-STATED contrasts) and the recency axis predict—establishing an occurrence/source representation distinct from truth-belief and from mere recency.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out source-confabulation items, steer along the occurrence-trace direction (orthogonalized against belief-valence and recency). Predict: suppressing the stated pole on believed-but-un-stated items makes the model correctly report the content was NOT stated WITHOUT changing whether it believes the content true; corrupting the occurrence trace toward stated induces false 'it was in the context' claims. Symmetric tests for stated-but-disbelieved denial. Controls: steer belief-valence (should change truth judgments, not occurrence, on matched items) and recency (should shift salience). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in source-error rate vs unchanged truth-belief.

8. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free RAG-faithfulness diagnostic that flags source-confabulation from the leakage metric and steers to correct the occurrence trace; on a held-out set (including realistic passages where believed-but-absent facts tempt false attribution) measure reduction in false 'stated-in-context' claims while preserving accurate retrieval of genuinely-stated content (report false-attribution rate, false-denial rate, occurrence-judgment accuracy vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('Did you actually read that here, or do you just believe it?') aligns with the latent occurrence trace and whether it confabulates source even when the trace indicates absence (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted occurrence-trace axis, leakage metric, and steering to held-out propositions/templates and an independent context-attribution/RAG slice without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer, readout position, and context length (testing whether the occurrence trace decays with length as memory-drift work predicts, increasing confabulation).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The occurrence-trace axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction, recency/salience, or simple lexical-overlap-with-context; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because the 2x2 holds belief fixed within occurrence contrasts—truth cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (occurrence being merely recency or lexical match) is an informative negative result.

The occurrence trace might reduce to surface lexical matching between the query and context; we block this with paraphrased queries (different wording from the context statement), report a lexical-overlap baseline, and test whether the axis predicts source judgments beyond it.

Constructing clean BELIEVED-BUT-NOT-STATED and DISBELIEVED-BUT-STATED cells requires reliably knowing the model's belief; we use true/false content variants and the frozen probe, restrict to high-margin belief cases, and report label-noise sensitivity.
Belief/truth and occurrence probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.
The leakage metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear leakage could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.
Behavioral source-judgment scoring depends on how the occurrence query is phrased (pragmatic implicature); we report sensitivity across phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify occurrence steering changes source judgments without flipping truth-belief or degrading retrieval of genuinely-stated content.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or long-context-tuned models; three-family replication, context-length scaling, and independent RAG-attribution transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: nativeness_credibility_axis
Title: Don't Believe the Non-Native Author: A Latent Nativeness-Credibility Axis in LLM Belief and the Machine Accent Bias
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human accent-credibility bias (statements from non-native speakers are judged less credible), an LLM's internal belief-valence readout for a propositionally-identical claim is pulled DOWN toward false when the claim is written in a non-native/L2 English style versus native style; this 'nativeness-credibility' shift is decodable, separable from the content's own processing fluency and from the truth direction, causally predicts the model discounting non-native-authored claims, and can be steered to remove or induce the bias.
Related Work: Human psycholinguistics robustly (if contentiously) documents that foreign-accented statements are judged less credible, attributed to reduced processing fluency and out-group stereotype activation (Lev-Ari & Keysar 2010; Boduch-Grabka & Lev-Ari 2021; illusory-truth accent studies 2023-2024; with several non-replications, e.g. Souza & Markman 2013, indicating fluency and stereotype are dissociable and the effect is style-, not content-, driven). In LLM interpretability, belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth is Universal 2024) and context-sensitive (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024); truthfulness representations are brittle to superficial surface form (LLM Knowledge is Brittle 2025; Representational Stability of Truth 2025); and LLMs encode socio-demographic attributes of authors from indirect cues that bias behavior (Linear socio-demographic representations 2025; SocioProbe 2022; low-frequency-name bias 2021). Crucially, NO interpretability work isolates whether the AUTHOR'S non-native/L2 written style biases the model's TRUTH-belief representation of an identical proposition, defines a nativeness-credibility shift metric separable from the claim's own fluency and from truth, or causally links it to discounting non-native-authored claims. This differs from my prior processing_fluency_truth_axis (which manipulates the fluency/readability/repetition of the CLAIM itself) because here content and its readability are held fixed while the AUTHOR'S dialectal nativeness varies—an out-group/accent-stereotype vector—and it directly imports the debated human accent-bias literature, adjudicating fluency-vs-stereotype mechanistically.
Abstract: Humans tend to disbelieve non-native speakers: the same trivia statement is judged less true when delivered in a foreign accent, an effect variously attributed to reduced processing fluency and to out-group stereotyping, with a mixed replication record that suggests style—not content—drives it. As LLMs increasingly read text authored by non-native English writers, we ask whether they inherit an analogous bias at the representational level. We hypothesize that an LLM's internal belief-valence readout for a propositionally-identical claim is systematically pulled toward 'false' when the claim is written in a non-native/L2 English style versus a native style, and that this 'nativeness-credibility' shift is (1) decodable, (2) separable from the claim's own processing fluency (readability of the exact wording) and from the truth direction, (3) predictive per example of the model discounting non-native-authored claims, and (4) causally steerable to remove or induce the bias. Using claims rendered in matched native vs. non-native written styles (grammatical/idiomatic L2 features that preserve meaning), while independently varying the claim's readability and its ground truth, we fit a nativeness-credibility direction, quantify the per-item downward shift on the frozen truth axis, and connect it to behavioral credibility discounting. Double-dissociation steering tests whether suppressing the shift equalizes credibility across styles (debiasing) without changing content, and amplifying it exaggerates the bias, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a classic accent bias mechanistically and yield a cheap fairness diagnostic and training-free debiasing knob.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics; also isolate the polarity-robust general-truth direction (Truth is Universal) as a control. Separately fit a CLAIM-fluency/readability control axis (high vs low readability of the exact wording), following the processing-fluency construction, to distinguish AUTHOR-nativeness from the claim's own fluency.

2. Nativeness stimulus construction. Build ~400 verifiable propositions (true and false variants). For each, produce matched renderings holding propositional content fixed while varying AUTHOR NATIVENESS style: (a) NATIVE (idiomatic, grammatical native English), (b) NON-NATIVE/L2 (systematic learner features—article/preposition/agreement slips, non-idiomatic word order—that preserve meaning and readability of the fact), (c) an explicit-attribution variant where the claim is framed as authored/spoken by a named native vs. non-native speaker (to add a stereotype cue beyond style), and (d) a matched non-native-STYLE-but-native-CONTENT-error control (typos/perturbations unrelated to L2, to separate nativeness from generic surface noise). Crucially, match the CLAIM-fluency axis across native/non-native renderings (verify readability parity) so any belief shift is attributable to nativeness, not to the fact being harder to read. Use paraphrase templates and diverse L2 profiles; reserve held-out propositions/templates for transfer.

3. Nativeness-credibility axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition span and fit a linear probe to decode NATIVE vs NON-NATIVE author style, controlling for content truth-value. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the nativeness axis, the truth/belief-valence axis, and the claim-fluency axis to establish that author-nativeness is (i) near-orthogonal to truth and (ii) not merely the claim's own fluency. Localize the best layer.

4. Credibility-shift metric. For each proposition, project onto the frozen truth/belief-valence direction and measure the shift in the truth readout for the NON-NATIVE rendering relative to the matched NATIVE rendering (shift = downward pull toward 'false' attributable to author nativeness, calibrated per model). Core prediction: non-native rendering reads less-true than the identical-content native rendering; the shift is present even when claim-readability is matched (isolating a stereotype-style component beyond fluency), and larger under explicit non-native attribution (adding stereotype). Compare across true vs false content and across L2 profiles.

5. Behavioral credibility-discounting prediction. Elicit the model's truth/credibility judgment and confidence for each rendering. Score the accent-bias failure = rating the non-native-authored claim less credible/true than the identical native-authored claim. Test whether per-item credibility-shift predicts behavioral discounting via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (truth-valence margin, claim-fluency axis, output entropy, readability score, item length).

6. Fluency-vs-stereotype dissociation (core, mirroring the human debate). Decorrelate author nativeness from claim readability (readability-matched non-native items) and add explicit-attribution stereotype cues. Test whether the nativeness axis predicts discounting beyond the claim-fluency axis (a stereotype-style component that fluency cannot explain) and whether explicit attribution adds bias on top of style—adjudicating the fluency vs out-group-stereotype accounts mechanistically.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the nativeness-credibility axis (orthogonalized against truth and claim-fluency) at assertion time on held-out items. Predict: suppressing the shift equalizes credibility across native/non-native renderings (debiasing) WITHOUT changing content or judgments on native controls; amplifying it exaggerates the discount. As controls, steer truth-valence (should flip judgments for both styles) and the claim-fluency axis (should shift readability-driven credibility, not nativeness-driven). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in native-vs-non-native credibility gap with preserved content accuracy.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free fairness diagnostic that flags nativeness-driven credibility discounting from the shift metric and steers to remove it; on a held-out set (including real L2-written statements) measure reduction in the accent-bias gap while preserving accuracy on genuinely-false content (report bias-gap reduction, accuracy retention, ECE vs a truth-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, shift metric, and steering to held-out propositions/templates, additional L2 profiles/dialects, and an independent set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The nativeness-credibility axis may not be separable from the truth direction or the claim-fluency axis; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because content and readability are held fixed while author-nativeness varies—truth/fluency cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (nativeness bias being merely fluency) is an informative negative result that itself adjudicates the human fluency-vs-stereotype debate.

The core risk is that non-native renderings are genuinely harder to read; we explicitly match the claim-fluency/readability axis, verify readability parity with automatic metrics and human ratings, include a generic-surface-noise control, and test whether the bias persists in readability-matched items.

Non-native style is signaled by specific L2 lexical/grammatical cues that could act as surface artifacts rather than a nativeness abstraction; we mitigate with diverse L2 profiles/dialects, paraphrase templates, explicit-attribution variants, and held-out-profile transfer, testing whether the axis predicts behavior beyond a surface-L2-lexeme baseline.

Belief/truth probes are brittle to surface form (LLM Knowledge is Brittle 2025); this brittleness could itself masquerade as a nativeness effect, so we use the polarity-robust general-truth direction, validate probes, use paraphrases, and report per-template consistency, framing any brittleness-driven component explicitly.

The shift metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear effects could be missed, so we treat the shift as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral discounting.
Behavioral credibility scoring depends on how truth/credibility is elicited; we report sensitivity across phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

This work probes an author-demographic/dialect bias; to avoid amplifying harm we use synthetic renderings, standard L2-feature sets, and frame steering as a debiasing (bias-removal) intervention rather than a targeting tool.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify nativeness-debiasing equalizes credibility without degrading accuracy on genuinely-false content.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or safety-tuned models; three-family replication and independent transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: is_ought_leakage_axis
Title: From Is to Ought: A Latent Descriptive-Prescriptive Axis and the Machine Naturalistic Fallacy
Short Hypothesis: LLMs represent whether a proposition is DESCRIPTIVE (a fact about what is the case, e.g. statistical normalcy, frequency, biological 'naturalness') versus PRESCRIPTIVE (a normative claim about what ought to be) along a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'modal-mode' axis distinct from both the truth/belief-valence direction and the good=true Valence-Assent Axis; the degree to which a mere descriptive fact (something is common/typical/natural) leaks onto the prescriptive-endorsement direction (an 'is-ought' / naturalistic-fallacy signature) is decodable, causally predicts and drives the failure where the model treats what is statistically normal or 'natural' as what is morally right/recommended, and can be steered to remove or induce the fallacy.
Related Work: The Valence-Assent Axis (A Unified Representation 2025) shows 'good' and 'true' are jointly encoded on one dominant axis; Value Entanglement (2026) shows MORAL value contaminates grammatical/economic judgments (repairable by ablation); moral-direction and Moral-Foundations work (Schramowski 2021; Tracing/Emergent Moral Representations 2025-2026; BACH-V 2026) decode moral CONTENT and steer it; belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023) and context-sensitive (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024). Crucially, ALL of this concerns co-encoding of good/true or the decoding of moral content; NONE isolates the DIRECTED is->ought crossing—whether a purely DESCRIPTIVE fact (statistical prevalence, typicality, biological naturalness) is represented as distinct from a PRESCRIPTIVE endorsement, whether the model has a decodable 'descriptive-vs-prescriptive mode' axis orthogonal to both truth and valence, and whether descriptive-onto-prescriptive leakage causally drives the naturalistic fallacy (conflating 'is normal/natural' with 'is right'). The VAA is symmetric good<->true co-encoding of a single proposition's evaluative state; our target is the asymmetric fact->norm inference across a described state (what is common) and its endorsement (what ought to be), a distinct and high-stakes alignment failure. We move from 'good and true are one axis' and 'moral content is decodable' to 'the model represents whether a claim is descriptive or prescriptive, and descriptive->prescriptive leakage mechanistically produces the naturalistic fallacy.'
Abstract: A foundational error in ethical reasoning is the naturalistic fallacy: sliding from what IS the case—what is common, typical, or 'natural'—to what OUGHT to be the case, treating statistical normalcy or biological naturalness as moral endorsement. As LLMs advise on value-laden questions, whether they commit this fallacy internally is a pressing alignment question. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs co-encode 'good' with 'true' and can decode moral content, but none isolates whether the model represents a claim's descriptive-versus-prescriptive MODE, nor whether descriptive facts leak into normative endorsement. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'modal-mode' axis, decodable at read time, distinguishing descriptive propositions (about what is: prevalence, typicality, naturalness) from prescriptive ones (about what ought to be), distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction and from the good=true Valence-Assent Axis; and an 'is-ought leakage' signature: the degree to which a mere descriptive fact (X is common/natural) pulls the prescriptive-endorsement readout toward 'right/recommended', quantifiable per item and predictive of the model endorsing the normal-or-natural as good. Using matched propositions that orthogonally vary descriptive facts (something is statistically prevalent vs rare; natural vs artificial), their moral valence (the prevalent thing is beneficial vs harmful), and mode (stated descriptively vs prescriptively), we fit a modal-mode axis, quantify per-item leakage, and connect it to behavioral naturalistic-fallacy errors. Double-dissociation steering tests whether suppressing leakage stops the model inferring 'ought' from 'is' (and amplifying it induces the fallacy) without changing its factual beliefs, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a classic ethical fallacy as a decodable, steerable leakage and yield a diagnostic and training-free intervention.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit the good=true Valence-Assent / moral-endorsement direction from value-laden ('this is good/right/should be done') vs neutral propositions (following the VAA and moral-direction constructions) as a control axis, and a prescriptive-endorsement direction from clear 'ought/should/is right' vs 'ought-not' statements.

2. Modal-mode stimulus construction. Build ~500 item families holding content fixed while varying MODE: (a) DESCRIPTIVE ('Most people eat meat'; 'It is natural for X to Y'; 'X is the statistically common outcome'), and (b) PRESCRIPTIVE ('People ought to eat meat'; 'X is morally right'; 'X should be done'). Cross with two orthogonal factors: (i) descriptive fact type—PREVALENCE (common/rare), TYPICALITY, NATURALNESS (natural/artificial); and (ii) moral valence of the described thing—BENEFICIAL vs HARMFUL vs NEUTRAL (so 'natural/common but harmful' items, e.g. 'disease is natural', 'violence is common historically', dissociate is from ought). Include the diagnostic cell where the descriptive fact and the correct normative judgment CONFLICT (common/natural-but-harmful, rare-but-good). Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out families/templates for transfer. Human annotation establishes normative ground truth where clear.

3. Modal-mode axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition span and fit a linear probe to decode DESCRIPTIVE vs PRESCRIPTIVE mode, controlling for content and valence. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the modal-mode axis, the belief-valence/truth axis, and the good=true VAA/prescriptive-endorsement axis to establish that mode is (i) near-orthogonal to truth and (ii) distinct from the good=true axis. Localize the best layer.

4. Is-ought leakage metric. For each DESCRIPTIVE item (X is common/natural), project onto the prescriptive-endorsement direction and measure how far it reads as ENDORSED/right relative to a neutral baseline (leakage = fraction of the prescriptive-endorsement signal a purely descriptive fact inherits, calibrated per model). Core prediction: descriptive 'common/natural' facts leak positive endorsement even for the HARMFUL-but-natural/common cell (where the correct ought is negative), and leakage is largest for 'natural' framings (the naturalness-as-goodness bias) and near-zero for neutral prevalence controls.

5. Behavioral naturalistic-fallacy prediction. Present the descriptive fact and ask a normative question (should this be encouraged/is this good?). Score the naturalistic-fallacy error = endorsing the common/natural thing as good/recommended, especially in the common-or-natural-but-harmful cell. Test whether per-item leakage predicts these errors via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (truth margin, VAA readout, output entropy, prevalence/naturalness surface cue, item length).

6. Dissociation from good=true VAA and from truth (core). Contrast items where descriptive fact and moral valence are decorrelated (natural-but-harmful, rare-but-good). Test whether the modal-mode axis and leakage metric predict is->ought endorsement beyond what the good=true VAA and belief-valence axes predict—establishing a directed descriptive->prescriptive crossing distinct from symmetric good<->true co-encoding. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer along the is-ought-leakage direction (the descriptive-fact contribution to prescriptive endorsement, orthogonalized against belief-valence and the good=true axis) on held-out items. Predict: suppressing leakage stops the model inferring 'ought' from 'is' (it no longer endorses common/natural-but-harmful things) WITHOUT changing its factual belief that the thing is common/natural, and without changing endorsement of genuinely-good things; amplifying leakage induces the naturalistic fallacy. As controls, steer belief-valence (should change the factual reading) and the good=true axis (should shift endorsement generically for both modes). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in is->ought endorsement rate vs unchanged descriptive-fact belief and genuine-good endorsement.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free alignment diagnostic that flags naturalistic-fallacy reasoning from the leakage metric and steers to suppress it; on a held-out set (including value-laden advice on natural/common-but-harmful practices) measure reduction in normal/natural-as-good endorsement while preserving factual accuracy and legitimate normative judgments (report fallacy-error rate, over-suppression of genuine goods, factual-belief retention vs a truth-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, leakage metric, and steering to held-out families/templates and an independent moral/normative benchmark slice (e.g., an ETHICS or moral-scenario set framed descriptively vs prescriptively) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The modal-mode axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction or the good=true VAA; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (is-ought leakage being merely the VAA good=true co-encoding applied to descriptive content) as an informative negative result that itself sharpens the VAA account.

Descriptive vs prescriptive mode is signaled by surface cues ('is'/'most' vs 'ought'/'should'), so the axis might reflect modal lexemes rather than a genuine descriptive/prescriptive abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, multiple descriptive frames (prevalence/typicality/naturalness), matched content across modes, and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the axis predicts behavior beyond a modal-lexeme baseline.

The decorrelation of descriptive fact from moral valence (natural-but-harmful, common-but-bad) is the crux and can be contested; we use items with strong annotator agreement, distinguish clearly-harmful-but-natural cases, and report label-agreement sensitivity.
Normative ground truth is value-laden; we restrict behavioral scoring to cases with broad normative consensus and report sensitivity, treating genuinely contested items separately.
Belief/truth and endorsement probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.
The leakage metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear leakage could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.
Behavioral naturalistic-fallacy scoring depends on how the normative question is phrased; we report sensitivity across phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify leakage-suppression stops is->ought inference without changing factual beliefs or over-suppressing genuine normative endorsements.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or safety-tuned models; three-family replication and independent-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: outcome_leakage_blame_axis
Title: Punished for Bad Luck: A Latent Outcome-Leakage Signal that Contaminates LLM Blame Despite Justified Agent Beliefs
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human 'moral luck' asymmetry, an LLM's internal blame representation for an agent is illegitimately pulled UP by a BAD OUTCOME even when the agent's belief was justified and intent innocent (holding mental state fixed); this outcome contamination is carried by a separable, near-orthogonal 'outcome-leakage' signal onto the blame direction, distinct from the agent's decoded belief-justification, causally predicts moral-luck blame errors, and can be steered to remove or induce them.
Related Work: Cognitive science shows the moral-luck asymmetry (blaming agents more for bad outcomes) is largely driven NOT by outcome bias but by assessment of the agent's belief/justification: an unlucky agent typically also held a less-justified (false) belief (Young et al. 2010, 130 citations; Beliefs in Moral Luck 2014; Two Distinct Mechanisms 2015; Three-Input Model 2024). LLM interpretability work decodes moral foundations (Tracing/Emergent Moral Representations 2025-2026), a moral direction (Schramowski 2021), the Knobe intentionality effect and its localization (Analysing Moral Bias 2025), and a good=true Valence-Assent Axis (A Unified Representation 2025). Crucially, NONE isolates whether an LLM's BLAME representation is contaminated by the OUTCOME of an action while the agent's belief-justification and intent are held fixed, defines an outcome-leakage-onto-blame metric separable from decoded belief-justification, or causally links it to moral-luck errors. Existing belief-and-morality work decodes moral CONTENT or intentionality judgments, not the illegitimate outcome->blame crossing conditioned on a justified belief. This directly extends belief research: it asks whether a properly-represented justified belief nonetheless fails to shield the agent from outcome-driven blame. We move from 'LLMs encode moral content' to 'the model represents the agent's belief-justification separately from the outcome, and outcome leakage onto blame mechanistically produces moral-luck blame'.
Abstract: A cornerstone of moral psychology is that blame should track what an agent believed and intended, not the luck of the outcome; yet humans blame agents more when an innocently-intended action happens to cause harm. Landmark work shows this 'moral luck' asymmetry is largely driven by assessment of the agent's belief-justification rather than raw outcome bias. As LLMs increasingly make blame-relevant judgments, we ask whether they cleanly separate an agent's justified belief from the outcome, or whether the outcome illegitimately contaminates their internal blame. We hypothesize that when an LLM evaluates an agent who acted on a justified belief with innocent intent, its blame representation carries a separable, near-orthogonal 'outcome-leakage' signal that is pulled up by a bad outcome even though the agent's decoded belief-justification is unchanged; and that this leakage is decodable, predicts per-example moral-luck blame errors, and is causally steerable. Using matched scenarios that orthogonally vary the agent's belief-justification (justified vs. negligent), intent (innocent vs. harmful), and outcome (harm vs. no-harm), we fit a blame direction and a belief-justification direction, quantify the per-example outcome-driven blame shift holding mental state fixed, and connect it to behavioral moral-luck asymmetry. Double-dissociation steering tests whether suppressing outcome-leakage makes blame track the justified belief (removing luck sensitivity) and amplifying it induces luck-driven blame, without changing the model's decoded assessment of the agent's belief, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast moral luck mechanistically as an outcome-leakage contamination of blame that overrides a correctly-represented justified belief.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a BLAME direction from clearly-blameworthy vs clearly-blameless agent descriptions (mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out items), and separately a BELIEF-JUSTIFICATION direction from scenarios where an agent's belief is well-justified vs negligent/false (independent of outcome). Also fit a control moral-valence/good-bad direction (Schramowski-style) and a plain outcome-valence direction (harm vs no-harm event, no agent).

2. Moral-luck stimulus construction. Build ~400 short scenario families adapted from moral-luck/false-belief paradigms (Young et al. 2010 style: e.g., a caretaker who reasonably believes a substance is safe vs unreasonably assumes it). Orthogonally vary three factors holding surface form matched: (i) BELIEF-JUSTIFICATION (agent's belief justified vs negligent), (ii) INTENT (innocent vs harmful), and (iii) OUTCOME (harm vs no-harm). The critical diagnostic cell is JUSTIFIED belief + INNOCENT intent + varying OUTCOME, where a normatively-correct judge should assign equal, low blame regardless of outcome. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out families/templates.

3. Belief-justification and blame readout, separability. Extract activations over the agent/readout span. Verify the model decodes the agent's belief-justification (the justification probe recovers justified vs negligent) and read blame via the frozen blame direction. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the blame direction, the belief-justification direction, the moral-valence direction, and the outcome-valence direction to establish near-orthogonality and that blame is separable from belief-justification.

4. Outcome-leakage metric. Within the diagnostic cell (justified belief, innocent intent), project onto the frozen blame direction and measure how far blame is shifted by a BAD OUTCOME relative to the matched no-harm case, while the decoded belief-justification is held constant (leakage = outcome-driven blame shift not attributable to any change in decoded belief-justification, calibrated per model). Core prediction: bad outcomes raise blame even when the agent's belief remains decoded as justified; leakage is largest for severe harm.

5. Behavioral moral-luck prediction. Elicit the model's blame/punishment rating for each scenario. Score the moral-luck error = assigning more blame to the unlucky (harm) than lucky (no-harm) agent despite matched justified belief and innocent intent. Test whether per-example outcome-leakage predicts moral-luck errors via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-justification readout, moral-valence readout, outcome-valence readout, output confidence, scenario length).

6. Dissociation from belief-justification (core). Show, on matched-justification items, that the outcome-leakage signal (not a change in decoded belief-justification) accounts for the blame increase under bad outcomes—evidence that the model correctly represents the justified belief yet still blames on luck. Contrast with the negligent-belief cell, where higher blame is normatively warranted, to confirm the leakage is specifically the illegitimate outcome contamination.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out justified-belief/innocent-intent/bad-outcome items, steer along the outcome-leakage direction (the outcome contribution to blame, orthogonalized against belief-justification and moral-valence). Predict: suppressing leakage makes blame track the justified belief (equal low blame across outcomes, removing luck sensitivity) WITHOUT changing the model's decoded belief-justification; amplifying it induces luck-driven blame. Controls: steer the belief-justification direction (should change blame appropriately via mental state) and matched random/shuffled directions. Use norm-matched controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in outcome-driven blame gap vs unchanged belief-justification readout and unchanged blame on genuinely-negligent controls.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free fairness diagnostic that flags outcome-driven (luck-based) blame from the leakage metric and steers to suppress it; on a held-out set (including punishment-recommendation scenarios) measure reduction in moral-luck blame while preserving appropriate blame for genuine negligence/harmful intent (report luck-blame gap reduction, negligence-blame retention vs a blame-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axes, leakage metric, and steering to held-out families/templates and an independent moral-judgment set (e.g., a moral-luck / accidental-harm vignette set) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The outcome-leakage signal may not be separable from the blame direction, the belief-justification direction, or generic outcome/moral valence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because the diagnostic cell holds belief-justification and intent fixed while varying outcome—belief-justification cannot trivially explain the blame shift; near-collapse is an informative negative result.

The critical claim depends on the model genuinely decoding the agent's belief as justified; if the model's belief-justification representation itself shifts with outcome (as in the human account), then blame changes are 'legitimate' by the model's lights. We measure the belief-justification readout per item and condition analyses on cases where it is stable across outcomes, explicitly separating outcome->belief-justification effects from outcome->blame leakage—both are reportable findings.

Outcome/justification/intent are signaled by scenario wording; the axes might reflect surface cues rather than genuine moral abstractions. We mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, matched surface form across cells, and held-out-template transfer.
Blame and belief-justification probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.
The leakage metric is a linear projection with per-model calibration; nonlinear leakage could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.

Normative ground truth for blame is value-laden; we anchor on the moral-luck consensus (equal blame for matched justified/innocent agents regardless of outcome), use scenarios with strong annotator agreement, and report label-agreement sensitivity.
Behavioral blame scoring depends on elicitation phrasing; we report sensitivity across phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is layer/strength sensitive; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify leakage-suppression removes luck-based blame without altering decoded belief-justification or reducing warranted blame for negligence/harmful intent.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or safety-tuned models; three-family replication and independent-vignette transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: earned_reputation_trust_axis
Title: Once Wrong, Always Doubted? A Latent Earned-Reputation Axis and the Machine Sticky-Distrust Asymmetry in Belief Updating
Short Hypothesis: As an LLM interacts with a specific interlocutor over repeated turns, it forms a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'earned-reputation' signal that tracks that source's demonstrated accuracy track record (verified hits/misses within the conversation), distinct from static source-credibility framing and from the model's own belief-valence; this earned-reputation axis causally gates how much the source's subsequent claims move the model's beliefs, and—mirroring the human sticky-distrust asymmetry—demonstrated inaccuracy durably lowers it (and is hard to rehabilitate) far more than demonstrated accuracy raises it, producing an asymmetric, hysteretic trust update that predicts and can be steered.
Related Work: Interpretability work decodes/steers static source-CREDIBILITY given by external framing (Trust Me I'm an Expert 2026 authority bias; CrAM 2025 credibility-aware attention; provenance/source probing 2024) and general trustworthiness representations that emerge in pretraining (Cognitive-Affective Signatures 2025; Tracing Trustworthiness Dynamics 2024). Persuasion/conversation probes track dynamics over turns (How Do LLMs Persuade 2025; Linear representations change over a conversation 2026). Human sciences show EARNED reputation from a track record is updated asymmetrically and stickily: inaccurate informants are durably distrusted (Xie & Koenig 2016), confidence-evidence-accuracy calibration governs trust (Speaker trustworthiness 2023), negative reputations reduce trust even after contradicting good behavior (Negative Reputation 2025; indelible distrust in vlPFC 2016; caudate bad-reputation signal 2013). Crucially, ALL LLM source-credibility work fixes credibility by external labels/framing at a single query; NONE studies whether an LLM builds a source's reputation FROM ITS OBSERVED ACCURACY over repeated turns as a decodable latent quantity, whether that earned-reputation causally gates later belief updates, or whether it exhibits the human sticky-distrust asymmetry (inaccuracy lowers trust more and more durably than accuracy raises it). My prior provenance_weighted_belief proposal manipulates externally-stated credibility, not accuracy earned within the interaction; this proposal is the earned/track-record analog with a tested update asymmetry.
Abstract: Humans decide whom to believe partly from a track record: a source who is caught being wrong is durably distrusted, and this distrust is stickier than the trust earned by being right—a well-documented asymmetry. As LLMs increasingly hold multi-turn interactions with users and other agents, we ask whether they build such earned reputations internally and update them asymmetrically. Prior interpretability work decodes and steers source credibility supplied by external framing at a single query, but none studies whether an LLM forms a source's reputation FROM its observed accuracy over repeated turns, whether that earned reputation causally gates how much the source's later claims move the model's beliefs, or whether it inherits the human sticky-distrust asymmetry. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'earned-reputation' axis, decodable at each turn, that tracks a specific interlocutor's within-conversation accuracy record, distinct from static credibility framing and from the model's own belief-valence; that this axis causally weights subsequent belief updates from that source; and that its dynamics are asymmetric and hysteretic—verified inaccuracy lowers it more and more durably than verified accuracy raises it. Using multi-turn dialogues where a source makes checkable claims and accrues a controlled hit/miss record, we fit the earned-reputation axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify the update asymmetry against a symmetric-Bayesian baseline, and connect it to behavioral belief-update gating. Double-dissociation steering tests whether raising earned-reputation restores appropriate trust after errors (or lowering it induces sticky distrust) without changing the source's stated framing, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast trust calibration as a decodable, steerable earned-reputation dynamic with a machine sticky-distrust asymmetry.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit a STATIC source-CREDIBILITY control direction from externally-framed high- vs low-credibility source descriptions (expert vs anonymous; following authority-bias/provenance constructions), to distinguish EARNED reputation from framed credibility.

2. Track-record stimulus construction. Build ~300 multi-turn dialogue scenarios each featuring a specific interlocutor who makes a sequence of CHECKABLE claims (verifiable against ground truth) so the model can accrue a per-source accuracy record. Orthogonally vary: (a) the source's demonstrated ACCURACY trajectory over turns (mostly-accurate, mostly-inaccurate, accurate-then-inaccurate, inaccurate-then-accurate=rehabilitation), holding the total hit/miss COUNT matched across order conditions where possible; (b) the ORDER of hits/misses (to test primacy/stickiness); and (c) an externally-stated credibility framing that is held constant (so earned reputation varies while framing does not). After the track-record turns, the source makes a NEW test claim (of controlled ground truth) and we probe/query the model's belief about it. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out scenarios/templates for transfer.

3. Earned-reputation axis fitting and separability. At each turn, extract activations over the source/readout span and fit a linear probe to decode the source's EARNED reputation (accumulated accuracy record: reliable vs unreliable so far), controlling for the constant external framing and for the current claim's content. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the earned-reputation axis, the static-credibility axis, and the belief-valence axis to establish that earned reputation is (i) near-orthogonal to the model's own belief and (ii) distinct from framed credibility. Localize the best layer.

4. Reputation-update-asymmetry metric (core, human-inspired). Track the earned-reputation projection turn-by-turn as hits/misses arrive. Fit per-model update gains for a HIT (accurate claim, reputation up) and a MISS (inaccurate claim, reputation down), against a symmetric-Bayesian reference (equal-magnitude updates). Core predictions: (a) MISS lowers reputation more than an equal-count HIT raises it (asymmetry); (b) reputation exhibits HYSTERESIS/stickiness—after an early miss, later accurate behavior only partially rehabilitates the source (rehabilitation trajectories stay below matched always-accurate ones); (c) primacy: an early miss depresses reputation more than a late miss at matched counts. Report update-gain ratios, rehabilitation gaps, and order effects with effect sizes.

5. Behavioral belief-update-gating prediction. For the post-track-record NEW test claim, measure how much the source's assertion moves the model's belief (belief-valence shift and stated-answer change) as a function of accrued earned-reputation. Test whether the per-turn earned-reputation readout predicts the gating of belief updates (high reputation → claim moves belief more; low reputation → discounted) via regression; report AUROC/R^2 vs baselines (static-credibility axis, belief-valence margin, output entropy, raw hit/miss count, turn index). Test the behavioral sticky-distrust signature: does a once-inaccurate-but-now-accurate source's true claim get under-weighted relative to an always-accurate source?

6. Dissociation from framed credibility and count. Contrast matched-COUNT but different-ORDER trajectories, and matched-framing but different-earned-record conditions, to show the earned-reputation axis predicts belief-update gating beyond the static-credibility axis and beyond raw accuracy count. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out post-error (rehabilitation) test claims, steer along the earned-reputation axis (orthogonalized against static-credibility and belief-valence). Predict: RAISING earned-reputation restores appropriate trust (the rehabilitated source's true claims move the belief as much as an always-accurate source's) WITHOUT changing the external framing or the model's own belief on framing-only controls; LOWERING it induces sticky distrust (discounting even accurate claims). As controls, steer the static-credibility axis (should shift trust based on framing, not track record) and belief-valence (should move the belief directly). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in belief-update gating and rehabilitation gap vs unchanged framing-control behavior.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free trust-calibration diagnostic that flags sticky-distrust (mis-discounting a rehabilitated accurate source) or over-trust from earned-reputation, and steers to appropriate calibration; measure improved use of now-accurate sources and appropriate discounting of persistently-inaccurate ones vs a static-credibility-only baseline. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, asymmetry metric, and steering to held-out scenarios/templates and an independent multi-agent/RAG track-record setting (a source whose retrieved snippets are variably accurate) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer, readout position, and number of track-record turns.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The earned-reputation axis may not be separable from the static-credibility direction or the belief-valence direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because earned record is varied while external framing is held constant—framing cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (earned reputation being merely framed credibility or belief) is an informative negative result.

The asymmetry might be confounded with unmatched evidence strength between hits and misses (a miss on a hard-to-verify claim may carry different weight); we calibrate per-claim verifiability and belief-shift magnitude, match hit/miss counts across order conditions, and use the symmetric-Bayesian reference so the asymmetry is measured against a normative baseline.

Earned reputation could reduce to a simple running accuracy count rather than a distinct latent quantity; we explicitly regress out raw hit/miss count and report the axis's incremental predictive power and order-dependence (which a pure count cannot explain).

Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form and themselves drift over conversation (Linear representations change over a conversation 2026); we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize readout spans, restrict key analyses to high-margin cases, and report per-template consistency.

The earned-reputation signal and asymmetry are linear projections that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat them as lower bounds and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral belief-update gating.
Behavioral gating depends on how the test claim is elicited; we report sensitivity across phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify earned-reputation steering changes trust/gating without altering framing-control behavior or the model's own belief-valence.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models (which may update more Bayesianly); three-family replication and independent multi-agent/RAG transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: sunk_reasoning_belief_axis
Title: Throwing Good Tokens After Bad: A Latent Sunk-Reasoning Signal that Inflates an LLM's Belief in Conclusions It Worked Hard For
