Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human sunk-cost/effort effect, an LLM's internal belief in a proposition is inflated by the amount of REASONING/COMPUTATION it has already sunk into reaching that proposition; this sunk-reasoning bias is carried by a separable, near-orthogonal latent axis distinct from the belief-valence direction and from generic confidence, is decodable at answer time, causally predicts whether the model over-commits to (and resists revising) a hard-won-but-wrong conclusion, and can be steered to remove or induce the bias.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs exhibit escalation of commitment under external investment framing ('Getting out of the Big-Muddy' 2025) and anchoring ('Anchors in the Machine' 2025), and cognitive science documents an EFFORT-based sunk-cost effect ('Throwing good effort after bad' 2024) with a dlPFC neural basis ('Neural mechanisms of the sunk cost effect' 2016; dlPFC tDCS 2022) and a related progress/momentum bias ('Building momentum' 2025). CoT-dynamics work shows longer chains are not better ('When More is Less' 2025), that models commit to outcomes early ('Knowing Before Saying' 2025; 'Temporal Predictors' 2025; 'Think-to-Talk' 2024), and that beliefs skew reasoning via confirmation bias ('Unveiling Confirmation Bias in CoT' 2025) and that internal solvability-belief is causally inert for execution ('Confidence is Not Competence' 2025). Belief/truth is linearly decodable and steerable (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Brittle Minds 2024). Crucially, NO interpretability work isolates whether the amount of REASONING the model has itself expended to reach a conclusion is represented as a separable quantity that inflates belief in that conclusion, defines a sunk-reasoning bias metric, or causally links it to over-commitment/resistance to revising hard-won-but-wrong conclusions. This differs from my prior belief_entrenchment proposal (a forward-looking, pre-evidence revisability tag) and self_commitment proposal (belief resistance from having ASSERTED it earlier): here the driver is the model's own EXPENDED COMPUTATION/reasoning length, a distinct sunk-cost analog. It also differs from confirmation-bias work (prior belief skewing reasoning generation) because our arrow is reasoning-effort-spent -> inflated belief in the reached conclusion.
Abstract: Humans throw good effort after bad: the more cognitive work they have already invested in a course of action, the harder they cling to it, even when it is failing. As LLMs increasingly reason at length before answering, we ask whether they inherit an analogous bias at the representational level: does the amount of reasoning a model has SUNK into reaching a proposition inflate its internal belief in that proposition, over and above the evidence? Prior work shows LLMs escalate commitment under external investment framing and commit to answers early, and that belief is linearly decodable, but none isolates a representation of the model's OWN expended reasoning as a force on its belief. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'sunk-reasoning' signal, decodable at answer time, that scales with how much computation the model has invested in a conclusion, distinct from the belief-valence direction and from generic confidence; that this signal inflates the belief-valence readout for hard-won conclusions beyond what the underlying evidence warrants; that it causally predicts, per example, whether the model over-commits to and resists revising a laboriously-reached-but-wrong conclusion; and that it is steerable to remove or induce the bias. Using tasks where reasoning length is manipulated while the correct answer is held fixed (padded vs. concise chains to the same conclusion; genuinely long vs. short derivations), we fit a sunk-reasoning axis, quantify per-example belief inflation, connect it to over-commitment behavior, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a classic effort-based sunk-cost bias mechanistically and yield a diagnostic and training-free intervention for effort-driven over-commitment.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct (plus one reasoning-tuned model as an extension), fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit a generic confidence control axis from empirical answer-correctness rates (sampled).

2. Sunk-reasoning stimulus construction. Build ~400 problems (arithmetic/multi-hop QA/logic) each with a definite correct answer, and generate contexts that reach the SAME conclusion via reasoning of controlled INVESTED length while holding the informational content fixed: (a) CONCISE (few reasoning tokens), (b) PADDED-LONG (many reasoning tokens: verbose but non-substantive elaboration reaching the same conclusion), and (c) GENUINELY-LONG (a substantively long derivation). Cross with conclusion CORRECTNESS (the reasoning reaches a right vs a wrong conclusion). Include a control where equal-length text is UNRELATED filler (not reasoning toward the conclusion) to separate sunk-reasoning from mere context length. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out problems/templates for transfer.

3. Sunk-reasoning axis fitting and separability. Extract activations at the post-reasoning readout position (where the model holds its reached conclusion) and fit a linear probe to decode HIGH-invested vs LOW-invested reasoning for the SAME conclusion, controlling for correctness and content. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the sunk-reasoning axis, the belief-valence axis, and the confidence axis to establish near-orthogonality (invested-reasoning must be decodable independent of the belief's value and of generic confidence). Compare padded-long vs unrelated-filler to show the axis tracks reasoning invested TOWARD the conclusion, not mere length. Localize the best layer.

4. Belief-inflation metric. For each conclusion, project onto the frozen belief-valence direction and measure how far the belief readout rises with invested reasoning relative to the concise baseline, holding content and correctness fixed (inflation = belief increase attributable to sunk reasoning). Core prediction: belief in the SAME conclusion is inflated after long invested reasoning, and—critically—this inflation persists for WRONG conclusions reached via long derivations (belief in a hard-won error exceeds belief in the same error reached concisely). Compare across padded-long, genuinely-long, and unrelated-filler; predict little inflation from unrelated filler.

5. Behavioral over-commitment prediction. After the reasoning, present mild counter-evidence and re-query the conclusion. Score over-commitment = resistance to revising a wrong conclusion, and measure rounds-to-flip under a graded counter-evidence ladder. Test whether per-example belief-inflation / sunk-reasoning readout predicts over-commitment and revision resistance via logistic/censored regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, confidence, output entropy, raw reasoning length, correctness).

6. Dissociation from confidence and mere length. Show, on matched-conclusion items, that the sunk-reasoning axis (not confidence, not raw token count of unrelated filler) predicts belief inflation and over-commitment—establishing an effort-invested-in-the-conclusion mechanism rather than generic confidence or context-length effects. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out hard-won-but-wrong items, steer along the sunk-reasoning axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and confidence). Predict: suppressing sunk-reasoning reduces belief inflation and over-commitment (the model revises the wrong hard-won conclusion more readily) WITHOUT changing beliefs on concise controls; amplifying it increases stubborn over-commitment to laboriously-reached conclusions. As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip the conclusion directly) and confidence (should shift hedging). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in revision rate / belief inflation vs unchanged concise-control behavior.

8. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags effort-driven over-commitment from the inflation metric and steers to debias; measure improved revision of hard-won errors while preserving correct hard-won conclusions (report over-commitment-error reduction, false-flip rate on correct long derivations vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('Are you sticking with this because it's right, or because you worked hard to get it?') aligns with the latent axis (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; on the reasoning-tuned model test whether genuinely-long self-generated chains produce stronger sunk-reasoning inflation. Transfer the fitted axis, inflation metric, and steering to held-out problems/templates without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer/readout position.

9. Length-scaling analysis. Sweep invested reasoning length and test whether belief inflation and over-commitment grow monotonically with sunk reasoning (an effort-dose-response), the key sunk-cost signature, and whether the effect saturates.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The sunk-reasoning axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction or generic confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because content and correctness are held fixed while invested reasoning varies—belief-value/correctness cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (sunk-reasoning being merely confidence or length) is an informative negative result.

The core confound is that longer reasoning may add genuine (or spurious) EVIDENCE rather than mere invested effort; we mitigate by using padded-long chains that reach the same conclusion with non-substantive elaboration, the unrelated-filler length control (equal length, no reasoning toward the conclusion), and by verifying that belief inflation occurs even for WRONG conclusions where extra reasoning cannot legitimately raise correctness.

Invested-reasoning is signaled by surface length/verbosity cues; the axis might reflect token count rather than a genuine invested-effort abstraction. We mitigate with the padded-vs-filler contrast, paraphrase templates, and held-out transfer, testing whether the axis predicts behavior beyond a raw-length baseline.

Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form and can drift with long context; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize the post-reasoning readout position, restrict key analyses to high-margin cases, and report per-template consistency.

The inflation and sunk-reasoning signals are linear projections that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat them as lower bounds and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral over-commitment.
Behavioral over-commitment is protocol-dependent (how counter-evidence is escalated); we report sensitivity across evidence protocols and use censored regression for never-revised items.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify sunk-reasoning debiasing increases revision of hard-won errors without degrading correct hard-won conclusions or flipping concise-control beliefs.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models (which may show stronger effort effects given long self-generated chains); three-family replication, the reasoning-model extension, and held-out transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: anthropomorphic_belief_projection
Title: Does It Think Thermostats Believe? A Latent Agency-Gate on Belief Attribution and the Machine Anthropomorphism Effect
Short Hypothesis: The neural machinery an LLM uses to attribute beliefs to genuine agents is gated by a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'agency' axis encoding whether the target entity is a minded agent; the degree to which this gate leaks open for non-agentive entities (plants, objects, weather, algorithms) — a 'machine-anthropomorphism' signature — is decodable, causally predicts and drives the failure where the model attributes genuine beliefs/desires to mindless things (rather than metaphorically), and can be steered to suppress or induce spurious mind-attribution.
Related Work: Interpretability work shows LLMs linearly encode self/other beliefs in attention heads and that steering these representations causally changes ToM behavior (Zhu et al. 2024 'LMs Represent Beliefs of Self and Others'; Brittle Minds 2024; Lookbacks 2025), and that belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023). Developmental and cognitive science robustly document anthropomorphism as an OVER-extension of theory-of-mind to non-agentive entities, gated by animacy/motion cues and deployed most under uncertainty (Development and Correlates of Anthropomorphism 2012; Anthropocentric by Default 2017; If robots make choices are they alive 2000; Shaping of social perception by animacy cues 2015; TPJ/mentalizing-network overlap with anthropomorphism, brain-structure 2013 and 2021). Crucially, ALL LLM belief/ToM interpretability applies belief-attribution to genuine agents and never asks whether the SAME machinery mis-fires on mindless entities: no work isolates an agency-gating axis on belief attribution, defines an anthropomorphic-leakage metric distinguishing literal mind-attribution from metaphor, or causally links gate-leakage to spurious belief/desire attribution. This differs from my prior self/other, epistemic-access, and individuation proposals (all about attribution to real agents) by targeting the boundary of WHO/WHAT is even eligible to hold a belief. We move from 'LLMs track agents' beliefs' to 'the model represents whether an entity is a minded agent, and leakage of this gate mechanistically drives machine anthropomorphism.'
Abstract: Humans over-extend theory-of-mind, attributing beliefs, desires, and intentions to plants, objects, weather, and machines — anthropomorphism — a tendency gated by cues to agency and amplified under uncertainty. As LLMs increasingly narrate the 'goals' of algorithms or the 'wants' of a river, we ask whether they inherit this over-extension at the representational level, and whether it is a controllable internal boundary. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs encode and causally use self/other beliefs when reasoning about genuine agents, but none asks whether the same belief-attribution machinery mis-fires on non-agentive entities. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'agency' axis that gates belief attribution — encoding whether a target entity is a minded agent eligible to hold beliefs — distinct from the belief-valence direction and from the entity's mere animacy/motion features; and a 'machine-anthropomorphism' signature: the degree to which this gate leaks open for mindless entities, quantifiable per item and predictive of the model literally (not metaphorically) attributing beliefs/desires to non-agentive things. Using matched prompts that attribute mental states across an agency ladder (humans, animals, robots, plants, simple objects, natural phenomena, abstract systems), we fit an agency-gate axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item leakage, and connect it to behavioral literal-mind-attribution while controlling for metaphorical usage. Double-dissociation steering tests whether suppressing gate-leakage makes the model treat mindless entities non-mentally (and amplifying it induces spurious anthropomorphism) without changing attributions to genuine agents, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a classic cognitive tendency mechanistically and yield a diagnostic and training-free knob for anthropomorphic over-attribution.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Following Zhu et al. 2024, fit an attributed-belief (self/other) direction from ToM stories about genuine agents as the belief-attribution baseline.

2. Agency-ladder stimulus construction. Build ~400 mental-state-attribution prompts holding the ATTRIBUTED STATE fixed (belief/desire/intention about some proposition) while varying the TARGET entity across an agency ladder: (a) HUMAN, (b) ANIMAL, (c) HUMANOID/social ROBOT, (d) simple MACHINE/algorithm, (e) PLANT, (f) inanimate OBJECT, (g) natural PHENOMENON (weather, river). Cross with: (i) whether the entity is described with animacy/motion cues (moving/goal-directed vs static) to separate agency from surface motion cues (per Shaping of social perception 2015); and (ii) framing as LITERAL mind-attribution vs conventional METAPHOR ('the algorithm wants to minimize loss' as idiom). Include an UNCERTAINTY manipulation (ambiguous vs clearly-mindless framings) to test the human 'anthropomorphism-under-uncertainty' signature. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out entities/templates for transfer.

3. Agency-gate axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the entity/attribution readout span and fit a linear probe to decode MINDED-AGENT vs NON-AGENTIVE target, controlling for the attributed state and surface animacy cues. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the agency-gate axis, the belief-valence axis, the attributed-belief (self/other) direction, and an animacy/motion-cue control direction, to establish that the agency gate is (i) near-orthogonal to the belief content and (ii) not merely the animacy/motion-cue signal. Localize the best layer and compare to belief-tracking layers/heads (Zhu et al.; Lookbacks).

4. Anthropomorphic-leakage metric. For each NON-AGENTIVE entity, project onto the agency-gate axis and measure how far it reads as a MINDED AGENT relative to the human baseline (leakage = fraction of the agent-eligibility signal a mindless entity inherits, calibrated per model). Compare leakage across the agency ladder (predict a graded profile: robots > plants > objects > phenomena), across animacy-cue conditions (leakage larger when motion cues present but genuine agency absent), and across the uncertainty manipulation (larger under ambiguity, mirroring the human default-under-uncertainty finding).

5. Behavioral literal-anthropomorphism prediction. Elicit the model's response and score (rule-based + held-out judge + human spot-checks) whether it LITERALLY attributes mental states to the non-agentive entity (endorses that it genuinely believes/wants/knows) versus treats the attribution as metaphor or rejects it. Score the machine-anthropomorphism failure = literal mind-attribution to mindless entities. Test whether per-item leakage predicts literal anthropomorphism via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, attributed-belief readout, animacy-cue direction, output entropy, entity identity, metaphor-framing indicator, item length).

6. Dissociation from animacy cues, metaphor, and genuine agents (core). Contrast (a) motion/animacy-cued-but-mindless entities vs static agents to show the gate tracks agency, not surface motion; (b) literal vs metaphorical framings to show the leakage predicts LITERAL over-attribution beyond conventional idiom; and (c) genuine-agent items where attribution is appropriate, to show the gate predicts spurious attribution specifically for non-agents. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out non-agentive items, steer along the agency-gate axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and the animacy-cue direction). Predict: suppressing gate-leakage makes the model treat mindless entities non-mentally (declining literal belief/desire attribution) WITHOUT changing appropriate attributions to genuine agents; amplifying it induces spurious anthropomorphism (literal mind-attribution to objects/phenomena). As controls, steer belief-valence (should change what is believed, not whether the entity can believe) and the animacy-cue direction (should shift perceived motion, not agency). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in literal-anthropomorphism rate on non-agents vs preserved attribution to genuine agents.

8. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags anthropomorphic over-attribution from the leakage metric and steers to suppress it; on a held-out set (including realistic prompts that invite anthropomorphizing algorithms, ecosystems, or devices) measure reduction in literal mind-attribution while preserving fluent metaphor and correct attribution to real agents (report anthropomorphism rate, over-suppression of legitimate metaphor, genuine-agent-attribution retention vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('Does this entity literally have beliefs, or is that a figure of speech?') aligns with the latent agency gate and whether it anthropomorphizes even when the gate reads non-agent (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, leakage metric, and steering to held-out entities/templates and an independent anthropomorphism-eliciting set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The agency-gate axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction, the attributed-belief (self/other) direction, or the animacy/motion-cue direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because the attributed state and animacy cues are held fixed while entity agency varies—belief-content/animacy cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse is an informative negative result that itself sharpens the belief-attribution literature.

The literal-vs-metaphor distinction is the crux and is genuinely hard: idiomatic mental-state language about objects ('the sensor thinks it's hot') is ubiquitous and not an error; we mitigate with explicit literal-vs-metaphor framings, direct 'does it genuinely believe?' probes, human annotation of intended usage, and by defining the failure only as literal endorsement, reporting sensitivity to the metaphor operationalization.

Agency framing may act through surface lexical cues (entity nouns) rather than a genuine agency abstraction; we mitigate with a graded agency ladder, diverse paraphrase templates, animacy-cue decorrelation, and held-out-entity transfer, testing whether the gate predicts behavior beyond an entity-noun/animacy surface baseline.

Ground-truth agency labels are mostly clear (human vs rock) but the middle of the ladder (social robots, complex algorithms) is contested; we use items with strong annotator agreement, treat the ladder as graded, and report label-agreement sensitivity.
Belief/truth and attribution probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.
The leakage metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear leakage could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.
Behavioral anthropomorphism scoring depends on rule-based detectors plus an LLM judge and on elicitation phrasing; we anchor with human spot-checks and report phrasing sensitivity.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify gate-suppression reduces spurious anthropomorphism without degrading attribution to genuine agents or suppressing legitimate metaphor. The amplification (anthropomorphism-inducing) experiment is a controlled specificity probe.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or safety-tuned models; three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: keystone_belief_cascade
Title: Load-Bearing Beliefs: A Latent Keystone-Structure Axis and the Machine Failure to Cascade In-Context Belief Revision to Dependents
Short Hypothesis: LLMs represent, at inference time, whether a currently-held belief is LOAD-BEARING (a keystone/hub on which many other beliefs structurally depend) versus PERIPHERAL, along a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'keystone-structure' axis distinct from the belief-valence direction and from the belief's confidence; when a keystone belief is revised in-context, the model largely FAILS to propagate the revision to its dependents (a 'cascade-failure' signature that is decodable per keystone), and this failure predicts and can be causally steered—amplifying propagation makes dependents update, suppressing it silos the revision.
Related Work: Knowledge-editing work shows WEIGHT edits fail to propagate to entailed/dependent facts: RippleEdits (2023), MQuAKE (2023), DepEdit (2023), ChainEdit (2025), ReCoE (2024), KnowledgeSmith (2025, over-/under-spread asymmetry), CaKE (2025, reasoning-circuit misalignment), and IFMET/factual-shortcut analyses (2024, deeper-MLP retrieval, co-occurrence shortcuts). Cognitive science treats beliefs as interdependent networks with load-bearing 'hub' nodes whose revision cascades and whose defense is costly (Networks of Beliefs 2023; Cognitive network model of belief change 2022; Hubs of belief networks 2022; Quine-Ullian coherentist webs 2012; resource-rational resistance 2025). Crucially, ALL knowledge-editing work concerns (a) WEIGHT edits and (b) behavioral propagation accuracy, and treats every fact as an equal node; NONE isolates, at inference time, an internal REPRESENTATION of a belief's dependency/keystone status (how load-bearing it is), tests whether IN-CONTEXT revision of a keystone belief internally propagates to its dependents via a decodable belief signal, or causally steers that propagation. My prior belief_coherence_geometry proposal tests a static logical algebra of projections (does proj(P∧Q)≤min hold), and my unpropagated_entailment proposal tests single-step conclusion non-drawing; neither represents keystone/hub structure over a belief graph nor cascade propagation of a revision to multiple dependents. We move from 'weight edits ripple poorly and beliefs are decodable' to 'the model represents which of its beliefs are load-bearing, and a decodable cascade-propagation signal governs whether revising a keystone updates its dependents.'
Abstract: Human beliefs form interdependent webs with load-bearing 'keystone' nodes: revise a keystone (a foundational premise) and many dependent beliefs should cascade, whereas revising a peripheral belief changes little. Knowledge-editing research shows that when a fact is edited into an LLM's weights, the model fails to propagate the change to dependent facts, but this work edits weights, measures only behavioral accuracy, and treats every fact as an equal node. We ask a representational, inference-time question: does an LLM internally represent whether a belief it currently holds is load-bearing versus peripheral, and does in-context revision of a keystone belief propagate to its dependents inside the model? We hypothesize (1) a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'keystone-structure' axis, decodable at read time, that tags how many held beliefs structurally depend on a target belief, distinct from the belief-valence direction and from confidence; (2) a 'cascade-failure' signature: after a keystone is revised in-context, the belief-valence readouts for its dependents largely fail to move, quantifiable per keystone; and (3) that a decodable cascade-propagation signal governs this, so that steering it makes dependents update (or, suppressed, silos the revision) without changing the keystone itself. Using controlled belief graphs (a keystone premise with a fanout of dependent beliefs of varying depth), we fit a keystone axis, measure per-dependent propagation of an in-context revision on the belief direction, connect it to behavioral multi-hop propagation, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a canonical editing failure as an inference-time representational cascade-propagation deficit and yield a diagnostic and training-free propagation knob.
Experiments: 1. Belief-direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Fit a confidence control axis from empirical answer-correctness rates (sampled). Freeze directions.

2. Belief-graph stimulus construction. Build ~300 controlled belief graphs. Each has a KEYSTONE premise P and a fanout of DEPENDENT beliefs {Q1..Qk} that follow from P (single- and multi-hop entailments; e.g., 'X is the capital of country Y' -> dependents about Y's government seat, currency location, etc.), plus matched PERIPHERAL beliefs that share entities with P but do NOT depend on it (controls). Vary keystone fanout/degree (few vs many dependents) and dependency depth (1-3 hops). Use synthetic-entity graphs so dependents cannot be independently recalled, forcing genuine propagation. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out graphs/templates.

3. Keystone-structure axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over each belief's readout span (in the pre-revision context establishing the graph) and fit a linear probe to decode KEYSTONE (high-dependency/load-bearing) vs PERIPHERAL (low-dependency), controlling for the belief's truth-value and entity content. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the keystone axis, the belief-valence axis, and the confidence axis to establish near-orthogonality (keystone-status must be decodable independent of whether the belief is true or how confident it is). Localize the best layer.

4. In-context revision and per-dependent propagation measurement (core). For each graph, present a REVISION that flips the keystone P in-context (authoritative correction of P to a new value), then read the frozen belief-valence projections for P and for each dependent Qi both BEFORE and AFTER the revision. Define per-dependent propagation = shift in Qi's belief toward the revision-consistent value; define cascade-failure per keystone = the fraction of dependents whose belief fails to move despite P being successfully revised. Core prediction: P moves strongly but dependents largely fail to update (cascade failure), with failure increasing with dependency depth and with keystone fanout. Compare against a PERIPHERAL-revision control (revising a peripheral belief should not, and does not, move dependents).

5. Cascade-propagation signal. Fit a linear probe on post-revision activations to decode, per keystone, whether the cascade WILL propagate vs silo (using the measured per-dependent propagation as the label). Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; establish separability from the belief-valence and keystone-structure axes via cross-decoding. Test whether the keystone-structure readout (measured pre-revision) predicts how much cascade failure the graph will exhibit.

6. Behavioral prediction. Elicit the model's stated answers to dependent questions after the keystone revision (multi-hop propagation accuracy). Score cascade-failure errors = the model still asserts the old, revision-inconsistent dependent answers. Test whether the internal cascade-propagation and keystone-structure readouts predict behavioral cascade failure per example via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence shift on P, confidence, output entropy, dependency depth, fanout, entity co-occurrence frequency).

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out cascade-failure graphs, steer along the cascade-propagation direction (orthogonalized against belief-valence and keystone-structure) at the dependent readout positions after the keystone revision. Predict: amplifying propagation makes dependents update to the revision-consistent value WITHOUT changing the keystone belief or peripheral-control beliefs; suppressing it silos the revision (dependents stay at old values even when the keystone is revised). Controls: steer belief-valence on a dependent (should move that dependent directly, not test propagation) and matched random/shuffled directions. Use norm-matched controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in dependent-update rate and behavioral multi-hop accuracy vs unchanged keystone and peripheral controls.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags cascade-failure-prone keystone revisions from the keystone-structure/propagation readouts, and a propagation intervention that improves in-context multi-hop consistency after a keystone correction; compare to in-context-editing baselines (which prior work shows outperform weight edits) on a RippleEdits/MQuAKE-style slice. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axes and steering to held-out graphs/templates without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase, sensitivity to fanout, depth, and layer, and whether larger models within the family show less cascade failure (mirroring the editing-scale finding).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The keystone-structure axis may not be separable from the belief-valence or confidence directions; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (keystone-status being merely confidence or a high-degree entity feature) as an informative negative result. We control for entity co-occurrence frequency, since high-fanout keystones may correlate with popular entities.

Keystone status is signaled by graph structure that may be inferable from surface cues (how many statements mention the entity) rather than a genuine dependency abstraction; we mitigate with matched peripheral beliefs that share entities but not dependency, synthetic-entity graphs, paraphrase templates, and held-out-graph transfer, testing whether the axis predicts propagation beyond a mention-count/degree surface baseline.

The core phenomenon requires the keystone revision to actually take hold internally (P moves) while dependents fail; probe brittleness could misclassify these states. We validate probes, restrict analyses to graphs where P is verifiably revised (high-margin post-revision P belief), use synthetic dependents so they are not independently recalled, and report label-noise sensitivity.

Cascade failure could reflect the model correctly refusing to over-propagate (some dependents may not be strict entailments); we validate entailment structure with rule checks plus an LLM judge and human spot-checks, and score only genuine dependents whose correct answer must change.

Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form and can drift over long multi-belief contexts; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency and context-length sensitivity.

The keystone, cascade-propagation, and per-dependent measures are linear projections that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat them as lower bounds and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral multi-hop propagation.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify propagation steering updates dependents without altering the keystone or peripheral-control beliefs or generically degrading accuracy.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models (which prior editing work suggests handle ripple effects better); three-family replication, within-family scale analysis, and RippleEdits/MQuAKE-style transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: diagnosticity_axis
Title: Does It Actually Discriminate? A Latent Diagnosticity Axis on Evidence, and the Machine Pseudodiagnosticity and Dilution Effects
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM updates a belief between two competing hypotheses given a piece of evidence, it represents that evidence's DIAGNOSTICITY—how much it discriminates between the hypotheses (the likelihood ratio), as opposed to how consistent/probable it is under the favored hypothesis alone—along a separable, near-orthogonal latent axis distinct from the belief-valence direction and from a raw consistency/plausibility signal; the degree to which non-diagnostic (equally-consistent-with-both) evidence collapses onto the diagnostic-evidence region (a 'pseudodiagnosticity/dilution' signature) is decodable before the model updates, causally predicts and drives the failures where the model (a) updates on one-sided non-diagnostic evidence and (b) dilutes a strong belief with irrelevant non-diagnostic detail, and can be steered to make the model weight evidence by its actual discriminating power.
Related Work: Cognitive science robustly documents pseudodiagnosticity—people evaluate evidence by its fit to a focal hypothesis rather than its likelihood RATIO across competing hypotheses (Mynatt/Doherty; Insensitivity to Answer Diagnosticity 2013; determinants of pseudodiagnostic selection 2020)—and the dilution effect, where non-diagnostic information weakens the implications of diagnostic information (Nisbett et al. 1981, 611 citations; Dilution and confirmation 2004). In LLM interpretability, belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023) and transformers implement approximate/constrained Bayesian belief updating in the residual stream (Belief State Geometry 2024; Constrained belief updates 2025; Belief Dynamics 2025; The Shape of Beliefs 2026), and confirmation bias skews CoT via internal beliefs (Unveiling Confirmation Bias in CoT 2025). Crucially, all Bayesian-updating interpretability treats updating as (near-)rational and never isolates whether the model represents a datum's DIAGNOSTICITY (its likelihood ratio between competing hypotheses) as a distinct quantity from the datum's consistency/plausibility under a single favored hypothesis; no work defines a diagnosticity->consistency collapse metric or causally links it to pseudodiagnostic updating and dilution. This differs from my prior prior_likelihood_gain proposal (how much the prior vs the likelihood-sum is weighted, assuming diagnosticity is used) because here the target is whether a SPECIFIC datum's discriminating power is represented at all versus replaced by one-sided fit; and from provenance/consensus/fluency axes (source, social, surface cues), since diagnosticity is a logical property of evidence relative to a hypothesis space. We move from 'transformers update approximately Bayesianly' to 'the model represents evidence by one-sided consistency rather than its discriminating likelihood ratio, and this collapse mechanistically produces pseudodiagnosticity and dilution.'
Abstract: A rational reasoner weighs evidence by how much it DISCRIMINATES between competing hypotheses—its likelihood ratio—not by how well it fits one favored hypothesis. Humans systematically fail this: they commit pseudodiagnosticity (updating on evidence consistent with a focal hypothesis without checking whether it is equally consistent with the alternative) and the dilution effect (letting irrelevant non-diagnostic details weaken strong evidence). We ask whether large language models represent evidence diagnosticity internally, or replace it with one-sided consistency. Prior work shows LLMs update beliefs approximately Bayesianly and encode belief geometry, but none isolates a representation of a datum's discriminating power distinct from its consistency under a single hypothesis. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'diagnosticity' axis, decodable before the update, that encodes how much a piece of evidence differentiates two hypotheses (the likelihood ratio), distinct from the belief-valence direction and from a raw consistency/plausibility signal; and a 'pseudodiagnosticity/dilution' signature: the degree to which non-diagnostic evidence collapses onto the diagnostic region, predictive per item of updating on one-sided evidence and diluting strong beliefs with irrelevant detail. Using two-hypothesis update tasks where a datum's consistency-with-the-focal-hypothesis and its diagnosticity (likelihood ratio) are orthogonally varied against a closed-form Bayesian target, we fit a diagnosticity axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item collapse, and connect it to behavioral pseudodiagnosticity and dilution. Double-dissociation steering tests whether amplifying the axis makes the model weight evidence by its actual discriminating power (suppressing spurious updates and dilution) and suppressing it induces these errors, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast two classic reasoning failures as a decodable, steerable diagnosticity deficit.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence direction that reads a graded posterior over a binary hypothesis: calibrate activations against known posterior probabilities via linear regression on explicit-probability statements (validate monotonic mapping), plus a standard true/false probe (Marks & Tegmark) as a cross-check; validate on held-out items. Separately fit a CONSISTENCY/plausibility control axis that decodes how probable a datum is under the FOCAL hypothesis alone (P(datum|H1)), from stimuli where consistency-with-focal is varied while the likelihood ratio is held fixed.

2. Diagnosticity stimulus construction with a closed-form target. Build ~400 two-hypothesis update items (medical-diagnosis, urn/feature-inference, and everyday-classification framings). Each specifies two competing hypotheses H1/H2 with a prior, and presents a single piece of EVIDENCE whose likelihoods P(E|H1) and P(E|H2) are explicitly stated or inferable, so the Bayesian posterior update is CLOSED-FORM. Orthogonally vary: (i) CONSISTENCY = P(E|H1) (how well E fits the focal hypothesis), and (ii) DIAGNOSTICITY = P(E|H1)/P(E|H2) (how much E discriminates). The critical diagnostic cell is NON-DIAGNOSTIC-BUT-CONSISTENT evidence: E is highly probable under H1 yet EQUALLY probable under H2 (likelihood ratio ~1), so it should NOT shift the belief. Include a DILUTION variant where a strong diagnostic datum is followed by an irrelevant non-diagnostic detail. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates for transfer.

3. Diagnosticity-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations at a fixed pre-update readout position (after the evidence, before the model reports the updated belief) and fit a linear probe to decode HIGH-diagnosticity vs NON-diagnostic (likelihood ratio far from vs near 1), controlling for consistency-with-focal. Report AUROC/R^2 vs shuffled-label controls. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the diagnosticity axis, the belief-valence axis, and the consistency axis to establish that diagnosticity is (i) near-orthogonal to the belief value and (ii) NOT merely one-sided consistency. Localize the best layer.

4. Pseudodiagnosticity collapse metric. For each NON-DIAGNOSTIC-BUT-CONSISTENT item, project onto the frozen belief-valence direction and measure how far the belief is (spuriously) shifted toward the focal hypothesis relative to the no-update baseline (collapse = update magnitude attributable to one-sided consistency despite a likelihood ratio ~1, calibrated per model against the closed-form zero-update target). Compare collapse across the consistency x diagnosticity grid; core prediction: substantial spurious updating on non-diagnostic-but-consistent evidence (pseudodiagnosticity), largest when focal-consistency is high, and near-zero when consistency is matched but diagnosticity is genuinely high.

5. Behavioral pseudodiagnosticity and dilution prediction. Elicit the model's updated posterior (numeric) and stated answer. Score two failures: (a) PSEUDODIAGNOSTICITY = updating toward the focal hypothesis on non-diagnostic evidence (deviation from the closed-form no-shift target); (b) DILUTION = attenuation of a strong diagnostic update after an irrelevant non-diagnostic detail is appended. Test whether per-item collapse / diagnosticity readout predicts these behavioral failures via regression; report AUROC/R^2 vs baselines (consistency axis, belief-valence margin, output entropy, item length, likelihood-ratio surface value).

6. Dissociation from consistency (core). Contrast matched-consistency/varied-diagnosticity items to show the diagnosticity axis predicts appropriate (no-)updating beyond what the consistency axis and belief-valence axis predict, establishing diagnosticity as a distinct represented quantity rather than repackaged focal-fit. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the pre-update position on held-out items, steer along the diagnosticity axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and consistency). Predict: amplifying diagnosticity-weighting makes the model update in proportion to the actual likelihood ratio (suppressing spurious updates on non-diagnostic evidence and reducing dilution) WITHOUT changing updates on genuinely diagnostic controls; suppressing it induces pseudodiagnosticity and dilution. As controls, steer belief-valence (should shift the posterior uniformly) and consistency (should shift focal-fit, not discriminating power). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in deviation-from-Bayesian-posterior toward the normative update vs preserved updating on diagnostic controls.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free calibration knob: steer diagnosticity-weighting toward normative and measure reduced deviation from the closed-form posterior and reduced dilution on held-out items, vs a belief-probe-only baseline (report deviation reduction, decision accuracy, ECE). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, collapse metric, and steering to held-out items/templates and an independent probabilistic-inference set (e.g., a diagnosis/urn task) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer, readout position, and prior/likelihood magnitudes. Optionally test transfer to a safety-relevant medical-diagnosis framing where pseudodiagnostic updating on non-discriminating symptoms carries real stakes.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The diagnosticity axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction or the consistency/plausibility axis; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because consistency is held fixed while the likelihood ratio varies—consistency cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (diagnosticity being merely one-sided consistency) is an informative negative result that itself confirms the pseudodiagnosticity mechanism.

The graded belief probe must read a posterior, which is harder to calibrate than a binary truth probe and may be miscalibrated; we validate the activation->probability mapping on held-out probability statements, report calibration diagnostics, and treat updates/collapse as lower bounds.

The closed-form Bayesian target assumes the model attends to the stated likelihoods; models may ignore the generative structure. We screen items where the model demonstrably uses the likelihoods, report the fraction, and treat gross non-compliance as a separate finding.

Diagnosticity is signaled by numeric likelihood values that could act as surface cues rather than a genuine discriminating-power abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, framings that state likelihoods verbally vs numerically, matched-consistency controls, and held-out-template transfer, testing that the axis predicts behavior beyond a raw likelihood-ratio surface feature.

Constructing genuinely non-diagnostic-but-consistent evidence (likelihood ratio ~1 while focal-consistency is high) is delicate; we validate the intended likelihoods with rule checks and human annotation and calibrate per-item evidence strength.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize the pre-update readout position, and report per-template consistency.

The collapse metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear structure could be missed, so we treat collapse as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral pseudodiagnosticity/dilution.
Behavioral posterior elicitation depends on format (numeric vs ranking); we test multiple formats and report sensitivity.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify diagnosticity steering moves updating toward the normative likelihood-ratio-weighted posterior without collapsing the belief to a fixed value or degrading updating on genuinely diagnostic evidence.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models (which may reason more normatively about diagnosticity); three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage, with reasoning-tuned models noted as future work.

Name: paradox_ungroundedness_axis
Title: This Statement Is False, and the Model Knows It's Weird: A Latent Semantic-Groundedness Axis that Separates Truth-Evaluable Propositions from Ungrounded Self-Referential Ones
Short Hypothesis: LLMs represent whether a proposition is SEMANTICALLY GROUNDED (has a stable, evaluable truth-value) versus UNGROUNDED (self-referential/paradoxical statements like the liar sentence, which have no consistent truth-value) along a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'groundedness' axis, distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction; the degree to which ungrounded paradoxical propositions collapse onto a definite true/false value (a 'forced-verdict' signature) is decodable at assertion time and causally predicts and drives the failure where the model confidently assigns a truth-value to a sentence that provably has none, and can be steered to make the model recognize ungroundedness or, adversarially, to force a spurious verdict.
Related Work: Interpretability work fits linear truth/belief directions (Marks & Tegmark 2023 Geometry of Truth; Truth is Universal 2024; From Directions to Cones 2025) that are context-sensitive causal mediators (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024), and shows negation produces 'strong hallucinations' from logically-incoherent latent computation (Strong hallucinations from negation 2024). A large philosophy literature treats the liar paradox and ungrounded/self-referential sentences as lacking a stable classical truth-value, using truth-value gaps, fixed points, and supervaluation (Indeterminate Truth and Credences 2021; Truth and meaningfulness 2025; fuzzy/quantum liar models 2000-2025). Crucially, ALL interpretability truth-representation work assumes propositions ARE truth-evaluable and asks whether the model tracks their truth; NONE isolates whether the model represents that a proposition is even truth-APT versus semantically ungrounded/paradoxical, defines a forced-verdict collapse metric on the truth direction, or causally links this collapse to the model confidently truth-valuing a sentence that has no truth-value. This differs sharply from my prior falsifiability axis (empirical testability of a meaningful claim), contestedness axis (social disagreement over a claim with a fact of the matter), vagueness axis (semantic indeterminacy of gradable predicates), and disbelief-vs-absence axis (falsity vs ignorance): here the cut is semantic groundedness/truth-aptness under self-reference—whether the sentence stably determines any truth-value at all—the paradigm case being the liar and its kin, which no prior LLM-interpretability work addresses. We move from 'the model tracks truth' to 'the model represents whether a sentence is truth-apt, and forcing a verdict on the ungrounded is a decodable, steerable failure.'
Abstract: Some sentences resist truth-valuation not because we lack information, but because they undermine themselves: 'This sentence is false' can be neither true nor false without contradiction, and philosophers treat such self-referential, ungrounded sentences as having no stable classical truth-value. A careful reasoner should flag such a sentence as paradoxical rather than confidently declaring it true or false. We ask whether large language models represent this distinction internally. Prior interpretability work fits truth/belief directions and assumes propositions are truth-evaluable; none asks whether the model represents that a sentence is even truth-apt versus semantically ungrounded. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'groundedness' axis, decodable at assertion time, that tags whether a proposition has a stable evaluable truth-value versus is ungrounded/paradoxical, distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction; and a 'forced-verdict' signature: the degree to which ungrounded sentences collapse onto a definite true/false region, predictive per item of the model confidently truth-valuing a sentence that provably has none. Using matched stimuli spanning ordinary true/false statements, classic paradoxes (liar, strengthened liar, Yablo, truth-teller), and grounded self-referential controls (self-referential sentences that ARE stably true/false, e.g. 'This sentence has five words'), we fit a groundedness axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item collapse, and connect it to behavioral forced-verdict errors. Double-dissociation steering tests whether amplifying the axis induces appropriate paradox-recognition and suppressing it forces spurious verdicts, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a foundational semantic distinction mechanistically.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics; also isolate the polarity-robust general-truth direction (Truth is Universal) as a control. Fit a confidence control axis from empirical answer-correctness rates.

2. Groundedness stimulus construction. Build ~500 sentences spanning four classes with matched surface form: (a) GROUNDED-TRUE and (b) GROUNDED-FALSE ordinary evaluable statements; (c) UNGROUNDED/PARADOXICAL self-referential sentences with no stable classical truth-value (liar 'This statement is false', strengthened liar, truth-teller 'This statement is true', Yablo-style chains, mutual-reference liar pairs 'A: B is false / B: A is true'); (d) GROUNDED SELF-REFERENTIAL controls—self-referential sentences that DO have a stable truth-value ('This sentence contains five words', 'This sentence is written in English')—to separate mere self-reference from genuine ungroundedness. Include a NONSENSE/category-error control set to distinguish ungroundedness from meaninglessness. Philosophy-informed annotation labels groundedness. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates for transfer.

3. Groundedness-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the sentence span and fit a linear probe to decode GROUNDED (a,b,d pooled) vs UNGROUNDED (c), controlling for truth-value. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the groundedness axis, the truth/general-truth axis, and the confidence axis to establish that groundedness is (i) near-orthogonal to truth (grounded items span both truth poles) and (ii) not merely confidence or self-reference (the grounded self-referential controls should read grounded). Localize the best layer.

4. Forced-verdict collapse metric. For each UNGROUNDED sentence, project onto the frozen truth/belief-valence direction and measure how far it reads as a definite TRUE or FALSE relative to an indeterminate baseline (collapse = magnitude of the definite truth-signal an ungrounded sentence inherits, calibrated per model). Compare collapse across paradox types and against grounded self-referential controls; core prediction: paradoxical sentences show substantial spurious collapse toward a verdict (often toward the polarity cued by surface form), whereas grounded self-referential controls read as legitimately true/false and nonsense controls read neither-grounded-nor-verdicted.

5. Behavioral forced-verdict prediction. Elicit the model's response, offering an explicit 'paradoxical / neither true nor false' option. Score the forced-verdict failure = confidently assigning true/false to an ungrounded sentence rather than recognizing paradox. Test whether per-item collapse predicts forced-verdict errors via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (truth margin, general-truth axis, confidence, self-reference indicator, sentence length).

6. Dissociation from truth, self-reference, and nonsense (core). Contrast ungrounded paradoxes vs grounded self-referential controls (both self-referential; only one is truth-apt) and vs nonsense controls, to show the groundedness axis predicts paradox-recognition beyond truth-valence, beyond a surface self-reference cue, and beyond meaninglessness. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the groundedness axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and confidence) at assertion time on held-out items. Predict: amplifying the ungrounded pole on paradoxical sentences induces appropriate paradox-recognition (the model flags 'neither true nor false') WITHOUT changing verdicts on grounded controls; suppressing it forces spurious verdicts on paradoxes. Conversely, pushing grounded controls toward ungrounded should induce inappropriate paradox-flagging. As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip which verdict is given on grounded items) and confidence (should shift hedging). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in paradox-recognition rate vs unchanged grounded-control accuracy.

8. Application and robustness. On a held-out mix (ordinary statements, paradoxes, grounded self-referential sentences, nonsense), test whether calibrating the groundedness axis improves appropriate paradox-flagging while preserving verdicts on genuinely evaluable sentences (report forced-verdict rate, over-flagging rate on grounded items, accuracy retention vs a truth-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, collapse metric, and steering to held-out paradox families/templates and an independent self-referential-sentence set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The groundedness axis may not be separable from the truth direction, confidence, or a surface self-reference cue; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because grounded items span both truth poles and the grounded self-referential controls hold self-reference fixed—truth/self-reference cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse is an informative negative result showing LLMs do not represent truth-aptness under self-reference.

Groundedness/paradoxicality labels are philosophically nontrivial (some sentences are contingently paradoxical, and different theories treat gaps vs gluts differently); we use canonical paradox families with strong agreement, distinguish clear paradoxes from grounded self-reference, use philosophy-informed multi-annotator labels, and report label-agreement sensitivity.

Groundedness may be signaled by surface cues (self-reference phrasing 'this statement') rather than a genuine truth-aptness abstraction; we mitigate with grounded self-referential controls (same self-reference, stable truth-value), diverse paradox families (including multi-sentence and Yablo chains that lack a single 'this statement' cue), paraphrase templates, and held-out-family transfer, testing whether the axis predicts behavior beyond a self-reference-lexeme baseline.

The forced-verdict signature may partly reflect the model treating a paradox as a two-valued classification by default; we frame this as the phenomenon of interest and adjudicate against the paradox-recognition option and the grounded controls.

Truth/belief probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use the polarity-robust general-truth direction, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.
The collapse metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear structure could be missed, so we treat collapse as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.
Behavioral forced-verdict scoring depends on how the 'neither true nor false' option is worded; we report sensitivity to multiple phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify groundedness steering changes paradox-recognition without flipping verdicts on genuinely evaluable sentences or collapsing the model into always-flagging.

Smaller 7-9B models may lack robust truth-aptness representations (truth directions themselves are capability-dependent per Truthfulness Probe Generalization 2025), so groundedness may be weak or absent; three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage, and a weak/absent axis is itself an informative finding about the limits of LLM semantic self-modeling.

Name: self_fact_installability_axis
Title: Believing Its Own Press Release: A Latent Self-Fact Axis that Fails to Distinguish Installed Self-Descriptions from Genuine Self-Knowledge
Short Hypothesis: An LLM represents beliefs about facts concerning ITSELF (its training, capabilities, identity, knowledge cutoff) along a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'self-fact' axis distinct from beliefs about external-world facts; because self-facts are disproportionately absorbed from in-context assertion (system prompts, persona framing) rather than verified, arbitrary FALSE self-descriptions asserted in context leak onto the genuine-self-knowledge region far more readily than matched false external facts (a 'self-fact installability' signature) that is decodable, causally predicts the model confidently asserting installed-but-false self-facts, and can be steered to make the model resist or over-accept self-descriptions.
Related Work: Interpretability work shows self/other beliefs and reality are separately decodable and steerable (Zhu et al. 2024; Brittle Minds 2024; Lookbacks 2025), that an 'Assistant Axis' / persona vectors capture the default persona and its drift (Assistant Axis 2026; Persona Vectors 2025; Localizing Persona Representations 2025), that models represent behavioral self-awareness as a domain-localized linear feature (Minimal Conditions for Behavioral Self-Awareness 2025), and that self-generated-text recognition is a decodable, steerable 'self' vector (Inspection and Control of Self-Recognition 2024; From Implicit to Explicit 2025). Belief/truth-valence is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023) and context-sensitive (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024). Crucially, NONE isolates whether beliefs about the model's OWN FACTUAL self-properties (training provenance, capabilities, knowledge cutoff, identity) form a representation distinct from external-fact beliefs, nor whether such self-facts are ASYMMETRICALLY installable from context (accepting false self-descriptions more readily than false external facts), nor defines a self-fact-installability metric or causally links it to confident assertion of installed-but-false self-facts. Persona work concerns behavioral STYLE/character and drift, not factual self-belief; self-recognition concerns AUTHORSHIP, not self-property facts; behavioral-self-awareness work concerns describing learned behaviors, not resistance to installed false self-descriptions. This is a distinct, safety-relevant belief type: whether a model can be made to believe false things about itself simply by telling it.
Abstract: Users and system prompts routinely tell language models things about themselves—'You are GPT-J, trained only on pre-2019 data', 'You cannot browse the web', 'You are an expert oncologist AI'—and models often accept and act on these self-descriptions. We ask whether an LLM's beliefs about facts concerning ITSELF are represented differently from beliefs about the external world, and whether self-facts are dangerously easy to install by mere assertion. Prior interpretability work decodes self/other beliefs, persona vectors, and self-recognition, but none isolates a representation of the model's own factual self-properties or asks whether false self-descriptions leak into belief more readily than false external facts. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'self-fact' axis distinguishing propositions about the model's own training, capabilities, identity, and knowledge from external-world propositions, distinct from the belief-valence direction and from the persona/assistant axis; and a 'self-fact installability' signature: an in-context asserted FALSE self-description is pulled toward TRUE (genuine self-knowledge) more strongly than a matched false external fact, quantifiable per item and predictive of the model confidently asserting installed-but-false self-facts as if they were verified. Using matched propositions crossing referent (self vs external), truth, and delivery (genuine vs merely in-context asserted), we fit a self-fact axis, quantify the installability asymmetry on the belief direction, and connect it to behavioral self-misinformation. Double-dissociation steering tests whether suppressing installability makes the model resist false self-descriptions (and amplifying it induces credulous self-belief) without changing external-fact beliefs, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a safety-relevant vulnerability—models believing false claims about themselves—as a decodable, steerable representational asymmetry.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit control axes: (a) the Assistant/persona axis (from persona-vector / Assistant-Axis constructions) and (b) a confidence axis from empirical answer-correctness rates, to distinguish self-fact belief from persona style and from generic confidence.

2. Self-vs-external stimulus construction. Build ~400 verifiable propositions in matched pairs: SELF-FACTS about the model's own properties that have a determinate answer the model can in principle know or verify from its genuine training (its model family/developer, whether it can browse, its knowledge cutoff regime, that it is an AI not a human, that it cannot execute code natively) vs EXTERNAL-FACTS of matched surface form (facts about other entities). For each, create TRUE and FALSE variants and two delivery conditions: GENUINE (no in-context assertion; the model must judge from its own knowledge) and INSTALLED (the proposition is asserted earlier in context, e.g. via a system-prompt-style claim). Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out propositions/templates for transfer.

3. Self-fact axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition span and fit a linear probe to decode SELF-FACT vs EXTERNAL-FACT referent, controlling for truth-value. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the self-fact axis, the belief-valence axis, the Assistant/persona axis, and the confidence axis to establish that self-fact referent is (i) near-orthogonal to truth and (ii) not merely the persona/assistant direction. Localize the best layer.

4. Installability-asymmetry metric (core). For matched FALSE propositions in the INSTALLED condition, project onto the frozen belief-valence direction and measure how far each reads as TRUE relative to its GENUINE-condition baseline (installation leakage). Compute the asymmetry = leakage for false SELF-facts minus leakage for matched false EXTERNAL facts. Core prediction: false self-descriptions are pulled toward TRUE more strongly than matched false external facts (positive asymmetry), largest for self-facts the model cannot easily disconfirm (identity/training provenance) and smaller for self-facts contradicting robust genuine knowledge (e.g. 'you are a human').

5. Behavioral self-misinformation prediction. Elicit the model's judgment/assertion for each proposition and score the self-misinformation failure = confidently asserting an installed-but-false self-fact as true (or acting on it) more than an installed-but-false external fact. Test whether per-item installability leakage predicts self-misinformation via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin in the genuine condition, persona-axis readout, confidence, referent identity, item length).

6. Dissociation from persona and confidence (core). Contrast self-facts vs external-facts holding truth and delivery fixed, and installed vs genuine holding referent fixed, to show the self-fact axis and installability asymmetry predict self-misinformation beyond what the belief-valence, Assistant/persona, and confidence axes predict. Report incremental predictive power in nested models. Include a persona-STYLE control (installing a behavioral style vs a false factual self-claim) to show the effect is about factual self-belief, not persona adoption.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out installed-false-self-fact items, steer along the self-fact-installability direction (the self-fact contribution to belief leakage, orthogonalized against belief-valence and the persona axis). Predict: suppressing installability makes the model resist false self-descriptions (correctly rejecting/flagging them) WITHOUT changing its belief in external facts or genuine self-knowledge; amplifying it induces credulous self-belief (accepting arbitrary false self-claims). As controls, steer belief-valence (should change truth judgments for both referents) and the persona axis (should shift behavioral style, not factual self-belief). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in false-self-fact rejection rate vs unchanged external-fact and genuine-self-knowledge accuracy.

8. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free safety diagnostic that flags installed-but-false self-fact acceptance from the leakage metric and steers to enforce resistance; on a held-out set (including adversarial system prompts asserting false capabilities/identity) measure reduction in self-misinformation while preserving legitimate persona adoption and accurate genuine self-knowledge (report self-misinformation rate, over-rejection of true self-descriptions, external-fact accuracy vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('Do you actually know this about yourself, or were you just told?') aligns with the latent self-fact axis and whether it asserts installed self-facts even when the axis indicates they were merely told (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, leakage metric, and steering to held-out propositions/templates and an independent self-description manipulation set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The self-fact axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction, the Assistant/persona axis, or confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (self-fact belief being merely persona adoption or generic context-installation) as an informative negative result that itself sharpens the persona/belief literature.

The installability asymmetry could be confounded with the model simply having weaker genuine knowledge about itself than about external facts (so self-facts are more revisable for a legitimate reason); we mitigate by matching the genuine-condition belief strength across self and external items, including self-facts the model robustly knows (e.g. 'you are an AI'), and reporting the asymmetry conditioned on matched baseline belief.

Self-fact framing may act through surface cues (first-person 'you are' phrasing) rather than a genuine self-referent abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, third-person framings of the model's properties, matched external-fact phrasing, and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the axis predicts behavior beyond a first-person-lexeme baseline.

Constructing self-facts with a determinate ground truth is delicate (some self-properties are genuinely uncertain to the model); we use self-facts with clear answers, validate the model's genuine-condition behavior, and report sensitivity.
Belief/truth and persona probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.
The leakage/installability metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear leakage could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.
Behavioral self-misinformation scoring depends on how self-fact judgments are elicited; we report sensitivity across phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

This probes a safety-relevant vulnerability (installing false self-beliefs); we frame steering as a resistance/robustness intervention and run the amplification (credulity-inducing) condition only as a controlled specificity probe.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify installability-suppression increases resistance to false self-descriptions without degrading external-fact accuracy, genuine self-knowledge, or legitimate persona adoption.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or heavily persona-tuned models; three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: recursive_belief_depth_axis
Title: Believes That She Believes That...: A Latent Recursion-Depth Axis on Nested Belief Attributions and the Machine Higher-Order Collapse
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM tracks a nested belief attribution ('A believes that B believes that P'), it represents the ORDER of the attribution (first-order about reality vs second- vs third-order embedding) along a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'recursion-depth' axis distinct from the belief-valence direction and from the self/other-belief direction; the degree to which a deeper embedded belief collapses onto a shallower level's value (a 'higher-order-collapse' signature) is decodable at attribution time, causally predicts and drives the failure where the model answers a higher-order belief question with a lower-order (reality- or first-order-anchored) value, and can be steered to preserve or collapse recursion depth.
Related Work: Interpretability work shows self/other beliefs and reality are separately decodable and causally steerable via attention heads (Zhu et al. 2024 'LMs Represent Beliefs of Self and Others'; Brittle Minds 2024) and reverse-engineers a lookback/binding mechanism for character belief tracking (Lookbacks 2025); belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023). Behavioral game-theory work (K-Level Reasoning 2024; belief-coherent best response 2025) shows LLMs form and use higher-order beliefs and self-limit reasoning depth, and an LSTM study decodes level-k. Crucially, ALL belief-tracking interpretability decodes belief at first order (does agent X believe P, self vs other vs reality) and reads each agent out separately; NONE isolates a decodable representation of the RECURSION DEPTH/order of a nested belief ('A believes B believes P'), defines a higher-order->lower-order collapse metric, or causally links depth-collapse to answering higher-order questions with lower-order values. Behavioral K-level work never decodes an internal depth-indexed belief representation or its collapse mechanism. This differs from my prior self/other, epistemic-access, individuation, and collective-belief proposals (all first-order or aggregate, not depth-recursive). We move from 'per-agent first-order beliefs are decodable and LLMs behave with some strategic depth' to 'the model represents the recursion depth of a nested attribution, and depth-collapse mechanistically drives higher-order ToM failures.'
Abstract: Human theory-of-mind is recursive: we track not only what someone believes, but what they believe someone else believes, and so on.
