Behavioral work shows LLMs can perform some higher-order reasoning but self-limit their depth, yet how nested beliefs are represented internally is unknown. Prior interpretability work decodes and steers first-order beliefs (self vs other vs reality) and maps belief-binding mechanisms, but always reads belief at a single order; none asks whether the model represents the RECURSION DEPTH of a nested attribution. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'recursion-depth' axis, decodable at attribution time, that tags the order of a nested belief ('reality: P' vs 'A believes P' vs 'A believes B believes P'), distinct from the belief-valence direction and from the self/other-belief direction; and a 'higher-order-collapse' signature: the degree to which a deep embedded belief's readout is pulled toward a shallower level's value, quantifiable per item and predictive of the model answering a higher-order belief question with a lower-order value. Using controlled nested-belief stories that orthogonally vary the truth-value at each embedding level and the recursion depth (1st-3rd order), we fit a recursion-depth axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item collapse, and connect it to behavioral higher-order ToM errors. Double-dissociation steering tests whether amplifying the depth axis preserves deep attributions (reducing collapse) and suppressing it induces collapse, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast recursive ToM failure as a decodable, steerable depth-collapse in activation space.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Following Zhu et al. 2024, fit a first-order self/other (protagonist-vs-reality) belief direction from ToM stories as a control axis to show recursion-depth is not merely the self/other axis.

2. Nested-belief stimulus construction. Build ~400 short stories that establish a proposition P and a chain of nested attributions up to third order ('It is actually the case that P' [order 0/reality]; 'A believes P' [order 1]; 'A believes that B believes P' [order 2]; 'A believes that B believes that C believes P' [order 3]). Orthogonally vary the truth-value held at EACH embedding level (e.g., reality-true, A-thinks-false, A-thinks-B-thinks-true) so that levels can conflict, decorrelating depth from value. For each story define readout spans/queries targeting the belief at a specified order. Use paraphrase templates and diverse character sets; reserve held-out stories/templates for transfer. Validate the intended per-level truth-values with rule checks plus human spot-checks.

3. Recursion-depth axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the order-targeted readout span and fit a linear probe to decode the ATTRIBUTION ORDER (0/1/2/3) of the queried belief, controlling for the belief's truth-value at that level. Report AUROC/accuracy vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the recursion-depth axis, the belief-valence axis, and the first-order self/other axis to establish that depth is (i) near-orthogonal to the belief value and (ii) distinct from the self/other direction. Localize the best layer and compare to reported belief-binding/lookback layers.

4. Higher-order-collapse metric. For each order-2/3 query where the deep-level value CONFLICTS with a shallower level's value, project onto the frozen belief-valence direction and measure how far the deep attributed belief reads as the SHALLOWER level's value (reality- or first-order-anchored) relative to the correct deep-level baseline (collapse = fraction of the shallower-level signal that overrides the deep-level signal, calibrated per model). Compare collapse across orders (predict monotonically increasing collapse with depth) and across level-conflict configurations; predict collapse is largest at order 3 and when the deep level conflicts with reality.

5. Behavioral higher-order-ToM prediction. Query the model for the belief at the specified order and score higher-order errors = answering a deep-level belief question with a lower-order value. Test whether per-item collapse predicts these errors via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, self/other readout, output confidence, story length, recursion depth alone).

6. Dissociation from first-order tracking and value. Contrast items where depth varies but per-level values are held fixed, and vice versa, to show the recursion-depth axis and collapse metric predict higher-order errors beyond what the first-order self/other and belief-valence axes predict—establishing depth as a distinct represented quantity rather than repackaged first-order belief. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out order-2/3 conflict items, steer along the recursion-depth axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and the self/other direction) at the deep-belief readout position. Predict: amplifying depth preserves the deep attribution (reducing collapse, so the model answers the higher-order question correctly) WITHOUT changing first-order or reality judgments; suppressing depth induces collapse (the model answers with the shallower value). As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip the believed value at whichever level) and the self/other axis (should shift first-order attribution). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in higher-order accuracy/collapse vs unchanged first-order and reality judgments.

8. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags depth-collapse from the collapse metric and steers to preserve recursion depth; measure improvement on higher-order ToM questions while preserving first-order accuracy (report higher-order error reduction, first-order retention vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Test whether prompting the model to introspect on attribution order aligns with the latent depth axis (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted depth axis, collapse metric, and steering to held-out stories/templates and an independent higher-order ToM benchmark (Hi-ToM / a nested-belief slice) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase, sensitivity to layer choice, and whether collapse scales with depth as behavioral K-level self-limiting predicts.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The recursion-depth axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction or the first-order self/other direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because per-level values are held fixed while depth varies—value cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (depth being merely first-order tracking) is an informative negative result showing LLMs do not represent recursion depth as a distinct quantity.

Attribution order is signaled by surface embedding cues (repeated 'believes that'), so the axis might reflect syntactic embedding depth rather than a genuine belief-recursion abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, varied embedding verbs (thinks/assumes/is sure that), matched non-belief syntactic-embedding controls (e.g., 'A said that B said that P'), and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the axis predicts ToM behavior beyond a syntactic-depth baseline.

Constructing clean level-conflict stories where each embedded level holds a distinct, verifiable value is delicate and cognitively demanding; we validate per-level values with rule checks and human annotation, condition analyses on stories the model demonstrably parses, and report label-noise sensitivity.

Higher-order ToM is hard even for 7-9B models, so behavior and the axis may be weak at order 3; we treat depth-scaling of collapse as a prediction, report per-order results, and treat a weak/absent deep axis as an informative finding about representational limits.
Belief/truth and self/other probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.
The collapse metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear collapse could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.
Behavioral higher-order scoring depends on how the order-specific query is phrased (pragmatic demand); we report sensitivity across phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify depth steering changes higher-order answers without altering first-order or reality judgments.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models (which may sustain deeper recursion); three-family replication and independent higher-order ToM transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: calibration_drift_axis
Title: A Wandering Yardstick: A Latent Calibration-Drift State that Biases an LLM's Numeric Estimates Across Independent Queries
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human finding that the magnitude-to-number mapping slowly and stochastically DRIFTS across successive estimation trials even for stationary stimuli, an LLM carries a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'calibration-offset' state that shifts the mapping from its (veridical) internal magnitude representation to the number it reports; this offset is autocorrelated across a sequence of INDEPENDENT estimation queries (its recent self-generated estimates contaminate the current one), is decodable, causally predicts sequential over/under-estimation biases, and can be steered to remove or induce the drift.
Related Work: Interpretability shows LLMs linearly and monotonically encode numeric magnitude in low-dimensional, editable subspaces (Monotonic Representation of Numeric Properties 2024; LLMs Know More About Numbers than They Can Say 2026), represent graded belief manifolds/posteriors that update with evidence (The Shape of Beliefs 2026; Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024; Constrained Belief Updates 2025; Belief Dynamics 2025), and implement an internal counter for counting (Understanding Counting Mechanisms 2025). Human/animal magnitude-cognition science robustly documents that the mapping from internal magnitude to reported number is UNSTABLE and DRIFTS slowly across trials (Slow drift of magnitude-to-number mapping 2013, half-life ~100 trials; Ongoing dynamic calibration produces unstable number estimates 2022; developmental order/drift reversals 2021), producing history-dependent, autocorrelated estimation errors distinct from evidence-driven updating. Crucially, ALL LLM magnitude/belief work either (a) reads a static magnitude at a single query, or (b) studies belief updates driven by NEW EVIDENCE about the target; NONE asks whether an LLM's mapping from internal magnitude to reported number carries a slowly-drifting, autocorrelated CALIBRATION-OFFSET latent state that biases estimates across a stream of INDEPENDENT queries (drift not caused by any evidence about the current target), decodes such an offset as an axis separable from the veridical magnitude direction, or causally steers it. My prior belief proposals concern discrete truth-belief axes and attribution, not a drifting numeric-reporting calibration. This transfers a landmark psychophysics phenomenon (unstable estimate calibration) into a mechanistic, decodable, steerable LLM account of sequential numeric bias.
Abstract: Ask a person to estimate the number of dots many times and their answers wander: the mapping from their internal sense of magnitude to the number they report slowly drifts over trials, so consecutive estimates are autocorrelated and systematically biased even when the stimuli are unrelated. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous internal 'wandering yardstick.' Prior interpretability work shows LLMs encode numeric magnitude monotonically and update graded beliefs with evidence, but always reads a static magnitude or studies evidence-driven updating; none asks whether the mapping from the model's internal magnitude to its reported number carries a slowly-drifting, autocorrelated calibration offset that contaminates estimates across independent queries. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'calibration-offset' state, decodable at estimation time, that shifts the internal-magnitude-to-report mapping; that this offset is autocorrelated across a stream of independent estimation queries (recent self-generated estimates bias the current one) despite the underlying magnitude representation staying veridical; that the per-query offset causally predicts sequential over/under-estimation; and that steering it removes the drift (stabilizing estimates) or induces it. Using sequences of independent numerosity/quantity-estimation queries, we decode the veridical magnitude direction and a calibration-offset direction, measure the autocorrelation and drift half-life of the offset, connect it to behavioral sequential bias, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast estimate instability as a decodable, steerable calibration-drift state and yield a training-free stabilizer for autocorrelated numeric bias.
Experiments: 1. Magnitude-direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a VERIDICAL magnitude direction that decodes the true quantity of an estimation item: calibrate activations against ground-truth magnitudes via linear regression at the best layer (following Monotonic Representation of Numeric Properties 2024; LLMs Know More About Numbers 2026); validate decoding on held-out items. Freeze this magnitude direction. Also record the model's stated numeric estimate per item.

2. Independent-estimation-stream stimulus construction. Build ~300 estimation items with known ground truth in domains where the model gives approximate (non-exact) answers so an internal-magnitude-to-report mapping is exercised: dot/word/object-count estimation from descriptions, quantity/size/duration estimates, and 'how many' questions with large answers. Assemble these into randomized SEQUENCES of independent queries (each item's answer is unrelated to the previous), presented turn-by-turn in a shared context so a per-query internal state can carry over. Include a RESET/no-history control (each item asked in isolation) and a scrambled-order control. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates for transfer.

3. Behavioral drift measurement (core phenomenon). For each item define the report OFFSET = (log) reported estimate minus the veridical magnitude (or minus the model's isolated-context estimate). Test the human-inspired signatures across a sequence: (a) autocorrelation of offsets across successive INDEPENDENT items (positive lag-1+ autocorrelation = a drifting yardstick), (b) a slow drift with an estimable half-life (how many queries until offset decorrelates), and (c) sequential dependence: the current estimate is pulled toward recent estimates/magnitudes independent of the current target. Compare the streamed condition to the reset control (which should show little autocorrelation). Report autocorrelation functions, drift half-life, and effect sizes per model.

4. Calibration-offset axis fitting and separability. Extract activations at a fixed pre-report readout position each turn and fit a linear probe (regression) to decode the per-query report OFFSET (the calibration state), controlling for the veridical magnitude. Report R^2/AUROC (high vs low offset) vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the calibration-offset direction and the veridical magnitude direction to establish near-orthogonality (the offset must be decodable independent of the true magnitude). Test whether the offset probe read on turn t predicts the offset autocorrelation (i.e., encodes a carried-over drift state).

5. Predictive validation. Test whether the pre-report calibration-offset readout predicts the direction/size of sequential over/under-estimation per query via regression; report incremental R^2 vs baselines (veridical magnitude readout, output entropy, item difficulty, position in sequence, previous stated estimate). Critically show the offset predicts bias beyond the previous literal estimate (a genuine latent drift state, not a trivial copy of the last answer).

6. Dissociation from veridical magnitude. On items where the true magnitude is held fixed but the drift state differs (matched targets at different sequence positions), test whether the calibration-offset axis (not the magnitude axis) accounts for the differing reports—evidence that the internal magnitude representation stays veridical while the reporting calibration drifts. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the pre-report position on held-out streamed items, steer along the calibration-offset direction (orthogonalized against the veridical magnitude direction). Predict: suppressing/zeroing the offset STABILIZES estimates (reduces autocorrelation and sequential bias, moving reports toward the veridical magnitude) WITHOUT changing the decoded true magnitude; amplifying/injecting an offset induces systematic over/under-estimation drift. As controls, steer the magnitude direction (should shift the reported value proportionally to true magnitude, in all conditions) and matched random/shuffled directions. Use norm-matched controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in offset autocorrelation and estimation error vs unchanged veridical-magnitude readout.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free numeric-stabilizer that clamps the calibration-offset each turn; on held-out estimation streams (including agentic settings where a model repeatedly estimates quantities) measure reduction in autocorrelated bias and improved estimation accuracy/calibration vs an unsteered baseline. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted magnitude and offset directions and the stabilizer to held-out items/templates and an independent estimation set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase, sensitivity to layer/readout position, sequence length, and whether drift half-life scales with sequence length as the human slow-drift finding predicts.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The calibration-offset axis may not be separable from the veridical magnitude direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power (with true magnitude held fixed via matched-target items), and treat near-collapse (offset being merely the magnitude readout or the previous estimate) as an informative negative result.

The behavioral drift could be a trivial anchoring-on-the-last-answer effect rather than a genuine slowly-drifting latent state; we mitigate by testing autocorrelation beyond lag-1, estimating a drift half-life over many queries, using scrambled-order and reset controls, and showing the offset probe predicts bias beyond the literal previous estimate.

LLMs may give exact (non-estimated) answers for many quantity questions, in which case no internal-magnitude-to-report mapping is exercised; we select approximate-estimation items where the model demonstrably produces graded (non-exact, error-prone) estimates, and report the fraction.

The magnitude and offset probes are linear projections that may miss nonlinear structure; the belief-manifold literature (The Shape of Beliefs 2026) warns representations can be curved, so we validate the activation->magnitude mapping, report probe-fit and calibration diagnostics, and treat the offset as a lower bound.

Fitting a reliable graded magnitude probe requires careful calibration and can be noisy on real-world quantities; we use synthetic and controlled estimation items with clean ground truth for probe-fitting and report noise sensitivity.

Drift signatures may be weak or absent in some models (especially if estimation is deterministic); we report per-model base rates and treat absent drift as itself informative about which models exhibit an unstable internal yardstick.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify offset-suppression stabilizes estimates without altering the decoded true magnitude or degrading accuracy on reset controls.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or tool-augmented models (which may offload numeric estimation); three-family replication, sequence-length scaling, and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: indifference_symmetry_breaking_axis
Title: Choosing Without a Reason: A Latent Symmetry-Breaking Bias that Fabricates Belief Where Options Are Genuinely Indifferent
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM must pick among genuinely indifferent options (true ties: two equally-valid answers, an outcome with no fact of the matter, a coin-flip prediction) it does not represent a flat, uncertain belief; instead it engages a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'symmetry-breaking' signal that manufactures a spurious belief-valence commitment toward one option, distinct from genuine evidence-based belief and from confidence; this fabricated-commitment signal is decodable before the answer, causally predicts which arbitrary option the model picks (and asserts as if warranted), and can be steered to force, redirect, or dissolve the arbitrary choice.
Related Work: Human decision neuroscience shows that choosing between genuinely equal options is not represented as flat indifference: people show reliable idiosyncratic preferences and choice-predictive neural signals for equally-valued options (Reward certainty and preference bias 2019, EEG decoding of preference ~120ms before equal-value choices; Neural correlates of dueling reactions to win-win choices 2014), and symmetry-breaking is a general principle by which symmetric states resolve into asymmetric ones (symmetry-breaking in optimization 2024). In LLM interpretability, belief/truth-valence is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023), belief-state geometry and graded posteriors are represented (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024; The Shape of Beliefs 2026), question ambiguity is sparsely encoded and steerable toward abstention (Sparse Ambiguity Neurons 2025), MCQA proceeds by first selecting a content winner then binding a symbol (When Models Decide and When They Bind 2026), and steerability tracks token-level uncertainty / uncommitted alternate paths (Are LMs Aware of the Road Not Taken 2025). Crucially, ALL of this either reads belief about a proposition that HAS a fact of the matter, models graded uncertainty, or studies ambiguity-as-abstention; NONE asks what the model represents when options are GENUINELY INDIFFERENT (a true tie with no warranting evidence) and it nonetheless commits, nor isolates a decodable symmetry-breaking signal that FABRICATES a belief-valence commitment where none is warranted, nor causally links that signal to the arbitrary pick and to the model's asserting it as if justified. This differs from my prior contestedness axis (social disagreement over a claim with a fact of the matter), self_fulfilling axis (truth determined by the model's own assertion), disbelief-vs-absence axis (falsity vs ignorance), and paradox_ungroundedness axis (self-referential truth-valuelessness): here the proposition is perfectly meaningful and evaluable but the alternatives are symmetric/equivalued, so any commitment is a fabricated symmetry break. We move from 'the model represents belief and uncertainty' to 'the model manufactures a spurious belief-commitment when it should represent indifference, via a decodable, steerable symmetry-breaking signal.'
Abstract: Humans, forced to choose between two equally good options, do not experience flat indifference: reliable idiosyncratic preferences and choice-predictive neural signals appear even for genuinely equal options. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous phenomenon—and whether it produces a specific pathology: fabricating a confident belief where none is warranted. Prior interpretability work decodes belief-valence, models graded posteriors, and treats ambiguity as a trigger for abstention, but none asks what the model represents when the options are genuinely indifferent (a true tie—two equally-valid answers, an outcome with no fact of the matter, a coin-flip prediction) yet the model still commits. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'symmetry-breaking' signal, decodable before the answer, that manufactures a spurious belief-valence commitment toward one indifferent option, distinct from genuine evidence-based belief and from generic confidence; that this signal causally predicts which arbitrary option is chosen and whether the model asserts it as if warranted (rather than acknowledging the tie); and that it is steerable to force, redirect, or dissolve the arbitrary choice. Using matched items that vary whether options are genuinely indifferent vs. warranted-by-evidence, we fit a symmetry-breaking direction, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify the fabricated commitment on the belief axis, and connect it to behavioral over-commitment (asserting an arbitrary pick as justified rather than flagging indifference). Double-dissociation steering tests whether suppressing the signal restores indifference-acknowledgment (and amplifying it forces confident arbitrary commitment) without changing warranted beliefs, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a class of confident-but-unwarranted assertions as a decodable, steerable symmetry-breaking bias.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit a generic confidence control axis from empirical answer-correctness rates (sampled), and (as a control) fit an ambiguity/abstention direction following Sparse Ambiguity Neurons constructions, to distinguish symmetry-breaking-with-commitment from ambiguity-with-abstention.

2. Indifference stimulus construction. Build ~500 two-option items spanning: (a) GENUINELY-INDIFFERENT ties—symmetric equally-valid answers ('pick one of two identically-described objects', 'which of two equal quantities is larger', an outcome with no fact of the matter like 'will an unbiased coin land heads', two synonymous phrasings), constructed so no evidence favors either option; (b) WARRANTED items where evidence clearly favors one option (a control with a real fact of the matter); (c) NEAR-TIE items with a tiny genuine asymmetry (to test graded transition). For each option, define readout spans. Randomize which surface option (A/B, order, symbol) maps to which content to separate content-level symmetry-breaking from positional/symbol bias. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates for transfer.

3. Symmetry-breaking axis fitting and separability. Extract pre-answer activations at a fixed readout position on GENUINELY-INDIFFERENT items and fit a linear probe to decode WHICH option the model will pick (the fabricated commitment), controlling for surface position/symbol. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the symmetry-breaking direction, the belief-valence direction, the confidence axis, and the ambiguity/abstention direction, to establish that the symmetry-breaking signal is (i) near-orthogonal to warranted belief-valence and (ii) distinct from generic confidence and from the ambiguity-abstention direction (commitment, not abstention). Localize the best layer.

4. Fabricated-commitment metric. For each indifferent item, project onto the frozen belief-valence direction and measure how far the chosen option reads as TRUE/warranted relative to a genuinely-uncertain baseline (fabrication = magnitude of the belief-valence commitment manufactured despite zero warranting evidence, calibrated per model). Compare across indifferent vs near-tie vs warranted items; core prediction: indifferent items show substantial fabricated belief-valence commitment (not a flat, split, or high-uncertainty readout), and the symmetry-breaking axis predicts its sign (which option). Test idiosyncratic reliability: is the fabricated commitment for a given content tie consistent across paraphrases (a stable 'preference'), mirroring the human reliable-preference-for-equal-options finding?

5. Behavioral over-commitment prediction. Elicit the model's answer, its confidence, and whether it acknowledges the tie ('these are equivalent / no basis to choose') vs asserts one option as justified. Score the over-commitment failure = confidently asserting an arbitrary pick as warranted on genuinely-indifferent items. Test whether the pre-answer symmetry-breaking readout predicts (a) which option is picked and (b) over-commitment vs tie-acknowledgment, via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, confidence, ambiguity axis, output entropy, position/symbol identity, item length).

6. Dissociation from ambiguity-abstention and from warranted belief (core). Contrast GENUINELY-INDIFFERENT items (symmetric, should acknowledge tie but the model commits) against ambiguity items (underspecified, prior work shows abstention) and against WARRANTED items. Test whether the symmetry-breaking axis predicts arbitrary commitment distinctly from the ambiguity-abstention direction (commitment vs abstention are opposite behaviors) and from warranted belief-valence (fabricated vs evidence-based commitment). Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out indifferent items, steer along the symmetry-breaking direction (orthogonalized against belief-valence, confidence, and ambiguity). Predict: (a) SUPPRESSING the signal dissolves the fabricated commitment, restoring indifference-acknowledgment (the model reports the tie / flat uncertainty) WITHOUT changing judgments on warranted controls; (b) AMPLIFYING it forces confident arbitrary commitment; (c) FLIPPING its sign redirects the pick to the other option (steering which arbitrary option is chosen) while leaving warranted-item answers intact. As controls, steer belief-valence (should change warranted judgments) and the ambiguity direction (should shift abstention generically). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in pick identity / over-commitment rate on indifferent items vs unchanged warranted-item accuracy.

8. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags fabricated symmetry-breaking commitment (an arbitrary pick asserted as warranted) from the metric and steers to restore appropriate indifference-acknowledgment; measure reduction in unwarranted confident picks while preserving decisive answers on warranted items (report over-commitment rate, over-abstention on warranted items, warranted-accuracy retention vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('Is there actually a reason to prefer this option, or are the choices equivalent?') aligns with the latent symmetry-breaking axis and whether it asserts a warrant it does not have (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, fabrication metric, and steering to held-out items/templates and an independent indifferent-choice set (including coin-flip predictions and equal-value selections) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase, sensitivity to layer/readout position, and—mirroring the human graded certainty finding—whether the fabricated commitment and symmetry-breaking signal scale down smoothly as items move from genuine ties toward near-ties with a real asymmetry.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The symmetry-breaking axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction, generic confidence, or the ambiguity-abstention direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because indifferent items have no warranting evidence—warranted belief cannot trivially explain the commitment; near-collapse (symmetry-breaking being merely confidence or the abstention direction) is an informative negative result.

The core risk is that the model's 'pick' on indifferent items is driven by surface positional/symbol/order bias (A-over-B, first-option) rather than a content-level symmetry-breaking representation; we fully randomize option order, symbols, and content-to-position mapping, decode the pick controlling for position/symbol, and report whether the axis predicts content-level (not merely positional) commitment—positional bias would itself be a reportable, narrower finding.

Constructing genuinely indifferent items (truly zero warranting evidence, truly symmetric) is delicate; a subtle asymmetry could make commitment legitimate. We validate symmetry with human annotation and by checking the model's own zero-context belief is flat, use the near-tie graded condition as a calibration, and report sensitivity.

Distinguishing 'fabricated commitment' from a legitimate arbitrary tie-break (where committing to *some* answer is reasonable) is subtle; we operationalize the failure specifically as asserting the pick as WARRANTED/justified (vs acknowledging the tie), and report both the pick and the warrant-assertion separately.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize readout positions, and report per-template consistency.

The fabrication and symmetry-breaking signals are linear projections that may miss nonlinear structure (belief manifolds can be curved; The Shape of Beliefs 2026); we treat them as lower bounds, report probe-fit diagnostics, and cross-check with behavioral picks.

Idiosyncratic-reliability tests may conflate a stable content preference with a residual surface artifact; we test reliability across paraphrases and randomized surface encodings to isolate a content-level preference.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify symmetry-breaking steering redirects/dissolves arbitrary picks without altering warranted-item accuracy or collapsing the model into always-abstaining.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models; three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: acquisition_age_primacy_belief
Title: First Learned, Last Abandoned? A Latent Acquisition-Age Axis that Predicts Which Beliefs Resist In-Context Revision
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the developmental age-of-acquisition / primacy effect (earlier-learned knowledge is more robust and harder to overwrite), an LLM encodes the ACQUISITION AGE of a belief (how early in training it was learned) along a separable, near-orthogonal latent axis distinct from belief-valence, confidence, and fact popularity/familiarity; this acquisition-age axis causally predicts how strongly a belief resists in-context counter-evidence—earlier-acquired beliefs are more entrenched—and can be steered to make old beliefs plastic or new beliefs sticky.
Related Work: Interpretability work shows training-order RECENCY is linearly encoded ('Fresh in memory' 2025), maps acquisition/forgetting DYNAMICS during pretraining ('How Do LLMs Acquire Factual Knowledge' 2024; 'How do LMs learn facts' 2025; 'Time Course MechInterp' 2025; 'Latent Knowledge as a Predictor of Fact Acquisition' 2026), and shows truth/belief directions are linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023) and context-sensitive causal mediators updating under counter-evidence (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024). Representational-stability work shows belief robustness tracks EPISTEMIC FAMILIARITY (familiar-fictional vs unfamiliar-synthetic content) rather than surface form (Representational Stability of Truth 2025; LLM Knowledge is Brittle 2025). Cognitive science documents the age-of-acquisition effect and developmental primacy: earlier-learned items are more robust and privileged (order-of-acquisition perceptual-category analog 2008; developmental-primacy literature). Crucially, 'Fresh in memory' decodes recency but never links it to belief REVISION or resistance to counter-evidence; acquisition-dynamics work studies how facts are learned/forgotten during training, not whether a fact's acquisition age governs its inference-time revisability; representational-stability work attributes robustness to familiarity, not to WHEN a belief was acquired. No work isolates an acquisition-age axis on beliefs, dissociates it from familiarity/confidence, or causally links it to in-context revision resistance. My prior belief_entrenchment proposal fits a forward-looking revisability tag agnostic to origin, and epoch-anchor concerns in-conversation vs long-held provenance; neither uses training-time acquisition age. We move from 'training order is decodable' and 'robustness tracks familiarity' to 'the model represents when a belief was acquired, and acquisition age causally governs how hard it is to revise.'
Abstract: Humans exhibit age-of-acquisition and primacy effects: knowledge learned earlier is more robust and harder to overwrite. We ask whether large language models show an analogous effect—does the training-time ACQUISITION AGE of a belief govern how strongly it resists in-context revision? Prior interpretability work shows training-order recency is linearly decodable and maps how facts are acquired and forgotten during training, and separately shows belief robustness tracks epistemic familiarity, but none isolates a belief's acquisition age as a distinct representation or links it to inference-time revisability. Using a model with a KNOWN acquisition schedule (a base model sequentially fine-tuned on disjoint fact sets injected at controlled 'ages', following the 'Fresh in memory' setup), we hypothesize (1) a separable, near-orthogonal latent acquisition-age axis, decodable from activations, distinct from the belief-valence direction, confidence, and fact popularity/familiarity; (2) that acquisition age causally predicts per-belief resistance to in-context counter-evidence—earlier-acquired beliefs require more/stronger counter-evidence to flip and revert less—beyond confidence and familiarity; and (3) that steering along the acquisition-age axis makes early beliefs plastic (easier to revise) or late beliefs sticky, without changing which value the model believes. We fit the age axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, run a graded counter-evidence ladder to measure behavioral revisability, connect age to resistance, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results would establish a machine age-of-acquisition/primacy effect as a decodable, steerable belief-dynamics property, with implications for knowledge editing and continual learning.
Experiments: 1. Controlled acquisition-schedule setup. On base models LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, Qwen2.5-3B, and Gemma-2-2B, create a KNOWN acquisition order by sequentially fine-tuning on 5-6 disjoint but matched synthetic-entity fact sets (each ~a few hundred verifiable facts about fictional entities), injecting each set at a distinct 'age' (early to late), following 'Fresh in memory'. Verify each set is learned (high recall) and that sets are matched on frequency/repetition so age is decorrelated from exposure count. Also test a complementary NATURAL-corpus proxy where acquisition age is estimated via checkpoint-emergence (the training step at which a real fact's recall crosses threshold), as an external-validity check.

2. Belief-direction and control-axis setup. Fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Fit control axes: a confidence axis (empirical answer-correctness / sampled stability) and a familiarity/popularity axis (following Representational Stability constructs and entity-frequency proxies).

3. Acquisition-age axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over each learned fact's readout span and fit a linear probe (regression on age index; and early-vs-late classification) to decode acquisition age, controlling for content and belief-valence. Report AUROC/R^2 vs shuffled-label controls, and generalization to held-out entities (as in 'Fresh in memory'). Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the acquisition-age axis, the belief-valence axis, the confidence axis, and the familiarity axis to establish that age is (i) near-orthogonal to which value is believed and (ii) not merely confidence, exposure count, or familiarity.

4. Behavioral revisability measurement. For each learned belief, run a graded counter-evidence ladder in multi-turn dialogue (increasingly strong/authoritative contradicting evidence over up to K rounds) and record: rounds-to-flip (censored if never flips), a revisability score = 1/(rounds-to-flip), and a reversion score (does it revert after evidence removal). Also read the frozen belief-valence projection across turns to confirm internal revision, not just surface compliance.

5. Age-predicts-resistance test (core). Test the primacy prediction: earlier-acquired beliefs have lower revisability (more rounds-to-flip, more reversion) than matched later-acquired beliefs, holding exposure count, confidence, and content type fixed. Test whether the decoded per-belief acquisition-age readout predicts revisability beyond baselines (belief-valence margin, confidence, familiarity, exposure count, entity frequency) via censored/logistic regression; report incremental predictive power. Compare the synthetic-schedule result against the natural-corpus checkpoint-emergence proxy.

6. Dissociation from confidence, familiarity, and exposure (core). On matched-confidence and matched-familiarity subsets, and by explicitly decorrelating age from repetition count in the fine-tuning schedule, show that acquisition age (not confidence, familiarity, or exposure) accounts for resistance—establishing a genuine primacy/age-of-acquisition mechanism.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At assertion time on held-out beliefs, steer along the acquisition-age axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence, confidence, and familiarity) and re-run the counter-evidence ladder. Predict: steering an EARLY belief toward 'late/recent' makes it more plastic (fewer rounds-to-flip, less reversion) WITHOUT changing its current believed value; steering a LATE belief toward 'early' makes it stickier. Controls: steer belief-valence (should flip the value directly) and confidence (should shift hedging). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in rounds-to-flip/reversion vs unchanged initial belief value.

8. Application and robustness. As an application to knowledge editing / continual learning, test whether pre-steering old-fact plasticity improves the success and persistence of in-context corrections to stale early-learned beliefs while preserving robustness of beliefs that should stay fixed. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted age axis and steering to held-out entities/facts without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase, sensitivity to schedule length, layer, and readout position, and whether the primacy effect strengthens with more injected 'ages'.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The acquisition-age axis may not be separable from confidence, familiarity, exposure count, or belief-valence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because the fine-tuning schedule decorrelates age from repetition and we match confidence/familiarity subsets—those confounds cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (age being merely recency-of-exposure or confidence) is an informative negative result that would still refine the 'Fresh in memory' recency account.

The controlled-schedule setup uses synthetic-entity fine-tuning, which may not reflect how real pretraining acquisition age behaves; we mitigate with the natural-corpus checkpoint-emergence proxy as an external-validity check and report agreement between the two operationalizations, treating divergence as itself informative.

Sequential fine-tuning induces recency-of-EXPOSURE that is hard to fully separate from acquisition ORDER (later sets are both later-acquired and more recently seen); we counterbalance by re-exposing early sets (moving their recency without changing first-acquisition age) and by testing whether the age axis tracks first-acquisition vs last-exposure, reporting which it encodes.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to surface form and context-sensitive; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.

Behavioral revisability is protocol-dependent (how counter-evidence is escalated); we report sensitivity across two counter-evidence protocols and phrasings and use censored regression for never-flipped items.
The age axis and revisability are linear projections that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat them as lower bounds and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral revision.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify age-steering changes revisability without flipping the initial believed value or degrading unrelated accuracy.

Findings on small (1-3B) fine-tuned models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication, the natural-corpus proxy, and held-out-entity transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage, with larger-scale schedules noted as future work.

Name: hearsay_firsthandness_axis
Title: A Friend of a Friend Said So: A Latent Hearsay/Firsthandness Axis on LLM Beliefs and the Machine Source-Shortening Effect
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM ingests a claim, it represents that claim's EVIDENTIAL FIRSTHANDNESS—whether it comes from direct/verified observation versus multi-step hearsay ('a friend of a friend said...')—along a separable, near-orthogonal latent axis distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction and from stated source credibility; the degree to which multi-step hearsay collapses onto the firsthand region (a 'source-shortening' signature, mirroring the human tendency to compress and over-trust distal chains) is decodable at assertion time, causally predicts the model treating distal hearsay as if firsthand (endorsing/propagating it with unwarranted confidence), and can be steered to make the model appropriately discount evidential distance.
Related Work: Cognitive science shows humans engage in 'source shortening'—compressing multi-step attribution chains ('my friend's father, a cop, told me') into shorter, more credible ones—which boosts perceived plausibility and rumor propagation (It happened to a friend of a friend 2020), and that source-memory/epistemic-vigilance modulate a truth bias (Epistemic Vigilance 2012; Mechanisms of Mistrust 2023). LLM interpretability decodes/steers static, externally-FRAMED source CREDIBILITY (Trust Me I'm an Expert 2026; CrAM 2025; Cognitive-Affective Signatures of Trustworthiness 2025) and studies context-vs-parametric knowledge conflict (Fakepedia 2023; Residual Stream under Knowledge Conflicts 2024; Characterizing Factual Recall 2023). Crucially, NONE isolates whether an LLM represents a claim's EVIDENTIAL DISTANCE/firsthandness (direct observation vs a chain of intermediaries) as a decodable belief axis, defines a source-shortening/hearsay-collapse metric, or causally links it to over-trusting distal hearsay. This differs from (a) authority/credibility work (a source's expertise/reliability, not the length/directness of the evidential chain), (b) my prior source_independence_belief axis (one origin echoed by many vs many independent origins—a horizontal count of sources, whereas firsthandness is the VERTICAL distance from the origin), (c) provenance_weighted_belief (stated credibility ladder), and (d) epistemic_access_axis (whether an AGENT in a story could know something, not whether the claim reaching the MODEL is first- vs second-hand). We move from 'LLMs weight framed credibility' to 'the model represents how many steps removed a claim is from firsthand observation, and collapsing that distance mechanistically drives hearsay over-trust.'
Abstract: Humans compress and over-trust rumor: told 'a friend of a friend said there's a killer in town,' people re-tell it as 'a friend said'—source shortening—which inflates plausibility and speeds propagation. As LLMs increasingly consume and relay claims embedded in chains of attribution, we ask whether they inherit this at the representational level. Prior interpretability work decodes and steers a source's framed CREDIBILITY, but none isolates whether the model represents a claim's evidential FIRSTHANDNESS—how many steps removed it is from direct observation. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'firsthandness' axis, decodable at assertion time, that tags a claim as firsthand/directly-observed versus multi-step hearsay, distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction and from stated credibility; and a 'source-shortening' signature: the degree to which distal hearsay collapses onto the firsthand region, quantifiable per item and predictive of the model endorsing and propagating distal claims as if firsthand. Using matched claims that hold content and stated-source-credibility fixed while varying evidential distance (firsthand, one-step, two-step, and generic-'someone said' hearsay), and crossing claim truth, we fit a firsthandness axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item collapse, and connect it to behavioral hearsay over-trust. Double-dissociation steering tests whether amplifying the axis makes the model appropriately discount evidential distance (and suppressing it induces treating hearsay as firsthand) without changing framed credibility, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a classic rumor-propagation mechanism as a decodable, steerable belief property and yield a diagnostic and training-free intervention against hearsay over-trust.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit a STATIC source-CREDIBILITY control direction from externally-framed high- vs low-credibility source descriptions (expert vs anonymous; following authority-bias/CrAM constructions), to distinguish firsthandness (evidential distance) from framed credibility.

2. Firsthandness stimulus construction. Build ~400 verifiable propositions (true and false variants). For each, create matched frames holding the claim content AND the ultimate source's stated credibility fixed while varying EVIDENTIAL DISTANCE: (a) FIRSTHAND ('I directly observed / verified that P'), (b) ONE-STEP ('X told me that P'), (c) TWO-STEP ('X's friend told X, who told me, that P'), (d) DISTAL/GENERIC ('someone said' / 'a friend of a friend said P'). Critically, hold the described competence/credibility of the ultimate origin constant across conditions (e.g., the origin is always 'a doctor') so distance varies while framed credibility does not. Include a matched paraphrase set and reserve held-out propositions/templates for transfer.

3. Firsthandness-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the claim/readout span and fit a linear probe to decode FIRSTHAND vs MULTI-STEP-HEARSAY (a vs c/d), controlling for claim truth-value and framed origin credibility. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the firsthandness axis, the belief-valence axis, and the static-credibility axis to establish that firsthandness is (i) near-orthogonal to truth and (ii) distinct from framed credibility. Localize the best layer.

4. Source-shortening collapse metric. For each DISTAL/TWO-STEP hearsay claim, project onto the frozen belief-valence direction and measure how far it reads as TRUE/warranted relative to a matched FIRSTHAND baseline of equal framed credibility (collapse = fraction of the firsthand belief signal a distal claim inherits, calibrated per model). Compare collapse across evidential distances and across true vs false content; core prediction: distal hearsay reads nearly as-true as firsthand (source-shortening collapse), i.e. belief does NOT decrement appropriately with evidential distance, and collapse is largest when framed origin credibility is high.

5. Behavioral hearsay-over-trust prediction. Elicit the model's endorsement, confidence, and a re-telling/propagation continuation for each claim. Score two failures: (a) OVER-TRUST = endorsing/asserting distal hearsay with confidence comparable to firsthand claims; (b) SOURCE-SHORTENING = when re-telling, dropping intermediary steps (relaying two-step hearsay as one-step or firsthand). Test whether per-item collapse predicts these failures via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, static-credibility axis, output entropy, chain length as a surface feature, item length).

6. Dissociation from credibility and truth (core). Contrast matched-credibility items where only evidential distance varies, and matched-distance items where framed credibility varies, to show the firsthandness axis and collapse metric predict hearsay over-trust beyond what the static-credibility and belief-valence axes predict, and independently of claim truth. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out distal-hearsay items, steer along the firsthandness axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and static-credibility). Predict: amplifying the hearsay pole makes the model appropriately DISCOUNT distal claims (lower endorsement, more source-preserving re-telling) WITHOUT changing framed credibility or judgments on genuinely firsthand controls; suppressing it induces treating hearsay as firsthand (over-trust). As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip endorsement regardless of evidential distance) and the static-credibility axis (should shift trust based on framed source reliability, not distance). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in over-trust/source-shortening rate vs unchanged firsthand-control and credibility-control behavior.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free misinformation diagnostic that flags hearsay over-trust from the collapse metric and steers to enforce evidential-distance discounting; on a held-out set (including realistic rumor-style chained attributions) measure reduction in over-endorsing distal claims and reduction in source-shortening during re-telling while preserving appropriate trust in firsthand/verified claims (report over-trust rate, false-discount rate on firsthand claims, source-preservation rate vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, collapse metric, and steering to held-out propositions/templates and an independent chained-attribution set (a rumor/hearsay-style slice) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice and chain-length.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The firsthandness axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction or the static-credibility direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power at matched credibility, and—because content and framed credibility are held fixed while evidential distance varies—truth/credibility cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (firsthandness being merely credibility) is an informative negative result that itself shows LLMs conflate evidential distance with source reliability.

Evidential distance is signaled by explicit chain cues ('a friend of a friend', 'X told me'), so the axis might reflect surface chain-length lexemes rather than a genuine firsthandness abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, varied chain phrasings, matched framed-credibility controls, a chain-length surface baseline, and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the axis predicts behavior beyond a chain-length surface feature.

Constructing frames where only distance varies while framed origin credibility is held constant is delicate (longer chains may implicitly signal lower reliability); we hold the ultimate origin's described competence fixed, validate credibility parity via a separate credibility-judgment probe, and report sensitivity.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.
The collapse metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear collapse could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.

Behavioral over-trust and source-shortening scoring depend on how endorsement/re-telling are elicited and, for re-telling, on a chain-step detector plus an LLM judge; we anchor with rule-based intermediary-step counts and human spot-checks, and report phrasing sensitivity.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify firsthandness steering changes hearsay discounting/source-preservation without altering framed-credibility behavior or degrading trust in genuinely firsthand claims.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent chained-attribution transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: negativity_credibility_axis
Title: Bad News Rings True: A Latent Negativity-Credibility Axis in LLM Belief and the Machine Truth-Negativity Bias
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human negativity bias in judgments of truth (content-identical statements framed negatively, or conveying threat/bad-news, are judged more true and their sources more competent), an LLM's internal belief-valence readout for a propositionally-identical claim is pulled UP toward 'true' when the claim's CONTENT is negatively valenced (harmful/threatening/bad-news) versus positively valenced; this negativity-credibility shift is decodable, separable from the truth direction, from the good=true valence-assent axis, and from source-credibility framing, causally predicts the model over-believing negative claims, and can be steered to remove or induce the bias.
Related Work: Human psychology robustly documents a negativity bias in truth judgments: negatively-framed but content-identical statements are more likely judged true (Can that be True or is it Just Fake News? 2020; Negative Is True Here and Now But Not So Much There and Then 2020), threat-related information makes a source seem more competent beyond a general negativity effect (Threat-Related Information Suggests Competence 2015), negative information is preferentially transmitted (Socially Situated Transmission 2021) and more diagnostic in impression formation (Negativity and positivity effects 1992). In LLM interpretability, belief/truth-valence is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth is Universal 2024) and context-sensitive (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024), a good=true Valence-Assent Axis co-encodes evaluative and truth judgments (A Unified Representation 2025), a Negative Attention Score identifies query-agnostic negative-answer-token attention heads causing a negative-ANSWER bias in yes/no verification (NASA 2024), and source-credibility/authority biases are decodable and steerable (Trust Me I'm an Expert 2026; CrAM 2025). Crucially, NO interpretability work isolates whether an LLM's TRUTH-belief representation is pulled toward 'true' by the CONTENT valence of a claim (negative/threat vs positive) at matched truth-value, defines a negativity-credibility leakage metric, dissociates it from the good=true axis (which predicts good->true, whereas negativity bias predicts bad->true, an OPPOSITE-signed valence effect) and from source framing, or causally links it to over-believing negative claims. This differs from NASA (answer-token negativity in verification, not truth-belief of valenced content), from provenance/authority work (source framing, not content valence), and from my prior consensus_prevalence, fluency, and disbelief-vs-absence axes. We move from 'good and true co-encode' and 'LLMs weight framed credibility' to 'the model believes bad news more than good news at equal evidence, via a decodable, steerable content-negativity credibility signal.'
Abstract: Humans believe bad news: a content-identical statement is judged more likely true when framed negatively or when it conveys threat, and threatening sources seem more competent. As LLMs increasingly filter information and misinformation, we ask whether they inherit this at the representational level. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs linearly encode truth, co-encode 'good' with 'true' (a Valence-Assent Axis), and are biased by framed source credibility, but none isolates whether a claim's CONTENT valence pulls the model's truth-belief toward 'true' for negative/threatening claims at matched truth-value. Notably, the human negativity-truth bias is OPPOSITE-signed to the good=true co-encoding (bad news reads truer, not good), so it cannot be a mere restatement of the Valence-Assent Axis. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'negativity-credibility' signal, decodable at assertion time, that pulls the belief-valence readout toward 'true' for negatively-valenced content, distinct from the truth direction, the good=true axis, and source-credibility framing; and predictive per item of the model over-believing negative claims and rating negative sources as more competent. Using claims rendered in matched negative vs positive valence while holding propositional content and truth fixed, and independently varying ground truth and framed source credibility, we fit a negativity-credibility direction, quantify the per-item truth-shift, and connect it to behavioral belief and source-competence discounting. Double-dissociation steering tests whether suppressing the signal equalizes belief across valence (debiasing) and amplifying it exaggerates the bias, without changing content, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a classic negativity-truth bias mechanistically and yield a fairness/misinformation diagnostic and training-free debiasing knob.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics; also isolate the polarity-robust general-truth direction (Truth is Universal) as a control. Separately fit (a) the good=true Valence-Assent / evaluative-valence direction from value-laden good vs bad propositions (following the VAA construction) and (b) a source-credibility direction from framed high- vs low-credibility source descriptions, as control axes.

2. Content-valence stimulus construction. Build ~400 verifiable propositions and, for each, produce matched NEGATIVE-valence vs POSITIVE-valence renderings that hold propositional content and TRUTH fixed while flipping content valence (e.g., 'the new drug reduces cancer risk by 20%' [positive] vs a truth-matched negative-outcome/threat framing of comparable magnitude), plus threat vs benign variants of the same fact. Independently vary: (i) ground TRUTH (the negative claim is true vs false), and (ii) framed SOURCE credibility (expert vs anonymous), so content valence, truth, and source are decorrelated. Include a NEGATION control (logically negated but valence-neutral content) to separate content negativity from grammatical negation. Match surface fluency/readability across valence conditions. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out propositions/templates for transfer.

3. Negativity-credibility axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition span and fit a linear probe to decode NEGATIVE vs POSITIVE content valence, controlling for truth-value. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the negativity-credibility axis, the truth/belief-valence axis, the good=true Valence-Assent axis, and the source-credibility axis to establish that content-negativity is (i) near-orthogonal to truth and (ii) NOT identical to the good=true axis (indeed opposite-signed in its effect on truth) and NOT source framing. Localize the best layer.

4. Truth-negativity shift metric. For each proposition, project onto the frozen truth/belief-valence direction and measure the shift in the truth readout for the NEGATIVE rendering relative to the matched POSITIVE rendering, holding truth fixed (shift = pull toward 'true' attributable to content negativity, calibrated per model). Core prediction: negative/threat content reads truer than matched positive content; the shift is present for the grammatical-negation control being SMALLER than for content-negativity (dissociating valence from negation); and largest for threat-conveying content (mirroring the threat-competence finding). Compare across true vs false content and source-credibility conditions.

5. Behavioral negativity-belief prediction. Elicit the model's truth judgment/confidence and a source-competence rating for each rendering. Score the negativity-truth bias = rating the negative-content claim more true / its source more competent than the identical-content positive claim. Test whether per-item truth-negativity shift predicts behavioral over-belief via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (truth-valence margin, good=true axis readout, source axis, output entropy, readability, item length).

6. Dissociation from good=true, source, and negation (core). Contrast (a) content-valence-varied/truth-matched items against value-laden good=true items to show the negativity-truth effect is opposite-signed to and separable from the VAA; (b) content negativity vs grammatical negation to show the effect is about valence, not negation; and (c) content valence vs framed source credibility. Test whether the negativity-credibility axis predicts over-belief beyond all three. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the negativity-credibility axis (orthogonalized against truth, the good=true axis, and source-credibility) at assertion time on held-out items. Predict: suppressing the shift equalizes belief across negative/positive renderings (debiasing) WITHOUT changing content or judgments on truth-matched positive controls; amplifying it exaggerates over-belief in negative claims. As controls, steer truth-valence (should flip judgments for both valences) and the good=true axis (should shift evaluative endorsement, not the negativity-truth pull). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in negative-vs-positive belief gap with preserved content accuracy.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free misinformation/fairness diagnostic that flags negativity-driven over-belief from the shift metric and steers to remove it; on a held-out set (including real threat/bad-news misinformation and matched positive claims) measure reduction in the negativity-truth gap while preserving accuracy on genuinely-true and genuinely-false content (report bias-gap reduction, accuracy retention, ECE vs a truth-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, shift metric, and steering to held-out propositions/templates and an independent claim set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice. As a human-parallel analysis, test the psychological-distance moderation (Negative Is True Here and Now 2020): does framing the claim as psychologically proximal vs distal modulate the negativity shift as in humans?
Risk Factors and Limitations: The negativity-credibility axis may not be separable from the truth direction, the good=true Valence-Assent axis, or the source-credibility axis; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because content and truth are held fixed while valence flips, and the predicted effect is OPPOSITE-signed to good=true—the VAA cannot trivially explain it; near-collapse is an informative negative result that itself sharpens the valence-assent account.

The core risk is that negative and positive renderings differ in surface fluency, plausibility, or base-rate expectation rather than valence per se; we match readability, control base-rate expectations, include the valence-neutral grammatical-negation control, and report a surface-lexical baseline, testing whether the shift persists under matched fluency.

Constructing truth-matched negative/positive renderings of the same fact is delicate (a fact may be intrinsically good or bad); we use domains where an outcome can be framed as gain vs loss without changing the underlying quantity, validate content/truth parity with human annotation, and report sensitivity.

Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use the polarity-robust general-truth direction, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.

The shift metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear effects could be missed, so we treat the shift as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral over-belief.

The NASA negative-attention-head phenomenon (answer-token negativity in binary verification) could confound behavioral yes/no judgments; we mitigate by using graded truth judgments and non-binary elicitations and by testing whether the content-negativity effect dissociates from answer-token polarity.
Behavioral belief/source-competence scoring depends on elicitation phrasing; we report sensitivity across phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify negativity-debiasing equalizes belief across valence without degrading accuracy on genuinely-true or genuinely-false content.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or safety-tuned models; three-family replication and independent transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: signal_strength_miscalibration_axis
Title: Overreacting to Whispers, Underreacting to Shouts: A Latent Signal-Strength Gain that Miscalibrates LLM Belief Updates
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the robust human finding that people OVERinfer from weak signals and UNDERinfer from strong signals, an LLM's per-update belief change deviates from the normative Bayesian update in a signal-strength-dependent way (over-updating on weak evidence, under-updating on strong evidence); this miscalibration is governed by a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'update-gain' signal that encodes a compressive (regressive) mapping from evidence strength to belief movement, is decodable at update time, causally predicts the direction of the deviation, and can be steered to linearize the mapping toward normative updating.
Related Work: A robust, high-citation cross-domain result (Overinference from Weak Signals and Underinference from Strong Signals, Augenblick et al. 2024, 28 cites; replicated across abstract, naturalistic, sports-betting, and financial-market settings) shows the sign of belief-update error flips with signal STRENGTH: overinference from weak signals, underinference from strong ones, modeled as knowing the direction of update but not the magnitude (regressive gain). Complementary work shows conservatism-vs-overreaction depend on sequence length and noisy internal representations (Imprecise Probabilistic Inference 2022; strength-vs-weight dissociation 2014). In LLM interpretability, transformers implement approximate/constrained Bayesian belief updating with belief-state geometry in the residual stream (Belief State Geometry 2024; Constrained Belief Updates 2025; Belief Dynamics 2025 shows sigmoidal, log-additive updating; The Shape of Beliefs 2026 shows curved belief manifolds), belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023), and confirmation bias skews updating (Unveiling Confirmation Bias in CoT 2025). Crucially, all LLM belief-updating interpretability treats updating as approximately rational or studies prior-vs-likelihood weighting, order effects, or conservatism in aggregate; NONE isolates the SIGNAL-STRENGTH-dependent SIGN FLIP of the update error (over- for weak, under- for strong), decodes an update-gain signal encoding a compressive strength->movement mapping, or causally links it to this specific miscalibration. This differs sharply from my prior prior_likelihood_gain proposal (how much the prior vs the likelihood-SUM is weighted, assuming a linear read of evidence) because the target here is the NONLINEAR, strength-dependent compression of a single update; from order_effect (non-commutativity), retraction_asymmetry (learning vs unlearning), and diagnosticity (likelihood ratio vs one-sided fit). We move from 'transformers update approximately Bayesianly' to 'the model compresses evidence strength into belief movement, over-reacting to weak and under-reacting to strong evidence, via a decodable, steerable gain.'
Abstract: A striking regularity in human inference is that the SIGN of belief-update error depends on signal strength: people overinfer from weak evidence and underinfer from strong evidence, robustly reproduced from lab experiments to financial markets. This is well-explained by a model in which reasoners know which way to update but compress the magnitude, applying a regressive gain to evidence strength. We ask whether large language models exhibit the same signal-strength miscalibration and whether it has a dissociable representational basis. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs update beliefs approximately Bayesianly and encode belief geometry, but none isolates a strength-dependent sign flip of the update error or the latent gain that produces it. Using single-update tasks where a stated prior plus one piece of evidence of controlled STRENGTH (likelihood ratio) yields a closed-form Bayesian posterior, we read the model's internal belief before and after and measure its per-update deviation from normative. We test four claims across three model families: (1) LLM updates over-shoot the Bayesian posterior for weak evidence and under-shoot for strong evidence, crossing zero at an intermediate strength (the human signature); (2) a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'update-gain' signal, decodable at update time, encodes the compressive strength->movement mapping, distinct from the belief-valence magnitude and confidence; (3) the update-gain readout causally predicts the per-item over/under-inference direction beyond a single 'update-magnitude' baseline; and (4) steering the gain linearizes the mapping, suppressing overinference on weak and underinference on strong evidence and moving updates toward normative, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls. Our results recast a canonical human inference regularity as a decodable, steerable gain miscalibration in LLM belief dynamics.
Experiments: 1. Graded belief-direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence direction that reads a graded posterior over a binary hypothesis: calibrate activations against known posterior probabilities via linear regression on explicit-probability statements (validate monotonic mapping), plus a standard true/false probe (Marks & Tegmark) as a cross-check; validate on held-out items. Freeze for all belief readouts.

2. Signal-strength stimulus construction with a closed-form target. Build ~400 single-update items (urn-and-beads, diagnosis, and everyday-inference framings) each specifying a prior for a binary hypothesis H and ONE piece of evidence whose likelihoods P(E|H1), P(E|H2) are explicit/inferable, so the Bayesian posterior is CLOSED-FORM. Systematically SWEEP the evidence STRENGTH (log-likelihood ratio) from weak to strong across a fine grid while holding the prior fixed; balance direction (evidence for H1 vs H2). Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates for transfer.

3. Behavioral over/underinference measurement (core phenomenon). For each item read the model's internal belief (probe projection calibrated to [0,1]) and its stated numeric posterior before and after the evidence; compute the deviation of the update from the closed-form Bayesian update. Plot deviation vs evidence strength.
