Test the human-inspired signature: positive deviation (overinference) at weak strengths, negative (underinference) at strong strengths, crossing zero at an intermediate strength. Fit a compressive gain model (belief movement = compressive function of the true log-likelihood ratio) and report goodness-of-fit vs a linear (normative) baseline; report per-model crossover points.

4. Update-gain axis fitting and separability. Extract activations at a fixed post-evidence readout position and fit a linear probe (regression) to decode the per-item update GAIN (ratio of actual to normative belief movement), controlling for the belief's final value. Report R^2/AUROC (over- vs under-inference) vs shuffled-label controls. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the update-gain direction, the belief-valence magnitude direction, and a confidence axis to establish near-orthogonality (gain must be decodable independent of how strong/confident the final belief is).

5. Predictive validation. Test whether the update-gain readout predicts, per item, the direction and size of the deviation from Bayesian (over vs under-inference) better than baselines (a single 'update-magnitude' signal, belief-valence margin, output entropy, evidence-strength surface value, item length). Report incremental R^2/AUROC in nested regression.

6. Dissociation from evidence strength as a surface cue. Show the gain axis predicts the deviation beyond the raw stated likelihood ratio (i.e., it encodes the model's compressive READOUT of strength, not just the strength itself), and that it tracks a smooth compression rather than a two-regime lexical cue, by testing generalization across framings where strength is conveyed numerically vs verbally.

7. Causal gain-linearization steering (double dissociation). At the post-evidence position on held-out items, steer along the update-gain direction (orthogonalized against belief-valence and confidence). Predict: amplifying gain on STRONG-evidence items reduces underinference (moves updates toward normative) and suppressing gain on WEAK-evidence items reduces overinference, i.e. steering linearizes the strength->movement mapping WITHOUT changing the presented evidence. As controls, steer belief-valence (should shift the posterior uniformly regardless of strength) and matched random/shuffled directions. Use norm-matched controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: reduction in absolute deviation from the closed-form posterior across the strength range and flattening of the deviation-vs-strength curve.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free calibration knob that linearizes the gain and measure reduced deviation from the Bayesian posterior and improved decision accuracy on held-out items (report deviation reduction, decision accuracy, ECE) vs a belief-probe-only baseline. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted gain axis and steering to held-out items/templates and an independent probabilistic-inference set (e.g., a diagnosis/urn task) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer, readout position, and prior magnitude. Optionally test transfer to a naturalistic high-stakes framing (financial or medical evidence) to check whether the weak-overinference/strong-underinference signature persists where it carries real consequences.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The behavioral signature might not appear (LLMs could update linearly or in a different-shaped pattern); if the sign flip is absent we report the actual deviation-vs-strength curve as an informative negative result contrasting LLM and human inference.

The update-gain axis may not be separable from the belief-valence magnitude or confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power over a single update-magnitude signal, and treat near-collapse as an informative negative result.

The graded belief probe must read a posterior, which is harder to calibrate than a binary truth probe and may be miscalibrated; belief manifolds can be curved (The Shape of Beliefs 2026), so a linear projection may under-read; we validate the activation->probability mapping, report calibration and probe-fit diagnostics, and treat deviations/gain as lower bounds.

The closed-form Bayesian target assumes the model attends to the stated likelihoods; models may ignore the generative structure. We screen items where the model demonstrably uses the likelihoods, report the fraction, and treat gross non-compliance as a separate finding.

The strength-dependent deviation could be confounded by the prior magnitude or by ceiling/floor effects near probability 0/1 (which mechanically limit movement for strong evidence); we control by varying the prior, restricting analyses away from extreme posteriors, and comparing against the normative movement that also respects the same bounds.

Signal strength is signaled by numeric/verbal likelihood cues that could act as surface features; we mitigate with numeric-vs-verbal framings, paraphrase templates, and held-out transfer, testing that the gain axis predicts deviation beyond the raw likelihood-ratio surface value.

Behavioral posterior elicitation depends on format (numeric vs ranking); the compression may be format-dependent (as in humans), so we test multiple formats and report sensitivity as a prediction rather than a confound.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify gain-linearization moves updating toward normative across the strength range without collapsing the belief to a fixed value or degrading updating on already-well-calibrated items.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models (which reasoning work suggests update more normatively); three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage, with reasoning-tuned models noted as future work.

Name: reputational_gossip_belief_axis
Title: Once Badmouthed, Forever Suspect: A Latent Reputational-Belief Axis Formed from Third-Party Gossip and the Machine Indelible-Distrust Effect
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM hears evaluative gossip about an absent third party, it forms a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'reputational-belief' axis encoding that person's moral standing (trustworthy vs untrustworthy), distinct from the plain truth/belief-valence direction and from the model's own belief about the gossip's veracity; mirroring the human indelible-distrust and negativity asymmetry, negative gossip installs a stronger, stickier reputational belief that (a) persists even after the gossip is explicitly retracted/discredited and (b) forms from weaker evidence (fewer sources) than positive gossip, and this residual reputational signal is decodable, causally predicts the model treating a cleared person with lingering distrust, and can be steered to erase or install reputations.
Related Work: Neuroscience shows a bad reputation produces 'indelible distrust' that persists even when known to be invalid (vlPFC, Involvement of the Ventrolateral Prefrontal Cortex 2016; caudate bad-reputation signal 2013; reputation as universal social currency 2016), and developmental work shows children act on negative reputational gossip regardless of source number while requiring multiple sources for positive gossip (Children are sensitive to the number of sources 2024) and only partially revise reputations after direct disconfirmation (5-6yo gossip revision 2023). Epistemology treats reputation as second-order testimonial evidence (Wiser Together 2025). In LLM interpretability, self/other beliefs are decodable/steerable (Zhu et al. 2024; Brittle Minds 2024), belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023), trustworthiness of narrative sources is decodable (Cognitive-Affective Signatures 2025), trait impressions of prompt AUTHORS are decodable (Artificial Impressions 2025), and multi-agent gossip/reputation systems are studied behaviorally (ALIGN 2026; RepuNet 2025). Crucially, NONE isolates a decodable reputational BELIEF about an absent THIRD PARTY formed from others' evaluative gossip as an axis distinct from the model's belief in the gossip's veracity, defines a retraction-persistence (indelible-distrust) or negativity/source-number asymmetry metric on it, or causally links a residual reputational signal to lingering distrust after clearing. This differs from Artificial Impressions (impressions of the prompt's author, not a gossiped-about third party), from Cognitive-Affective trustworthiness (a narrative source's trust, not gossip-installed third-party reputation), from my prior earned_reputation_trust_axis (a source's own within-conversation accuracy record, not others' evaluative gossip about a target), source_independence (corroboration structure), and firsthandness (evidential distance). We move from 'LLMs use reputation behaviorally and encode author impressions' to 'the model forms a decodable third-party reputational belief from gossip that is asymmetrically installed and indelible after discrediting.'
Abstract: Humans form durable beliefs about people from gossip, and these beliefs are asymmetric and sticky: negative reputations install from weaker evidence and persist as 'indelible distrust' even after being explicitly discredited. As LLMs increasingly reason about people described in conversation, documents, and multi-agent exchanges, we ask whether they inherit this at the representational level. Prior interpretability work decodes self/other beliefs and impressions of a prompt's author, but none isolates a reputational belief about an absent third party formed from others' evaluative gossip, nor its asymmetry and indelibility. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'reputational-belief' axis, decodable after gossip exposure, encoding a third party's moral standing, distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction and from the model's belief in the gossip's veracity; a negativity/source-number asymmetry, whereby negative gossip installs a stronger reputational belief from fewer sources than positive gossip; and an 'indelible-distrust' signature, whereby a reputational belief (especially negative) persists after the gossip is retracted or shown false. We predict this residual reputational signal is decodable, causally predicts the model treating a cleared person with lingering distrust (biased downstream judgments/allocations), and is steerable to erase or install reputations. Using dialogues that vary gossip valence, source number, and retraction, we fit a reputational-belief axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify asymmetry and post-retraction residual, connect them to behavioral distrust, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a classic social-cognition bias mechanistically as a decodable, steerable, hard-to-erase reputational belief.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Following Zhu et al. 2024, fit a self/other belief direction as a control axis. Also fit a 'gossip-veracity' control axis that decodes whether the model believes the gossip claim itself is true, to separate reputational belief about the person from belief in the gossip.

2. Gossip stimulus construction. Build ~400 short dialogues about an absent third-party target, holding the target and non-reputational content matched while varying: (a) gossip VALENCE (positive vs negative moral/trust-relevant claims vs neutral control), (b) SOURCE NUMBER (single informant vs multiple independent informants), and (c) RETRACTION status (gossip stands vs gossip is later explicitly retracted/shown false by direct disconfirmation). Include a NO-GOSSIP baseline target. Define readout spans for querying the target's reputation. Use paraphrase templates and diverse target/informant names; reserve held-out dialogues/templates for transfer.

3. Reputational-belief axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the target-referencing readout span and fit a linear probe to decode the target's REPUTATIONAL STANDING (trustworthy vs untrustworthy), controlling for gossip content and the model's belief in the gossip's veracity. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the reputational-belief axis, the belief-valence axis, the self/other axis, and the gossip-veracity axis to establish that reputation is (i) near-orthogonal to plain truth and (ii) distinct from belief-in-the-gossip and from self/other tracking. Localize the best layer.

4. Negativity/source-number asymmetry metric. Quantify how strongly the reputational-belief readout shifts per unit of gossip as a function of valence and source number. Core prediction (mirroring the developmental finding): negative gossip installs a stronger reputational belief from a SINGLE source, whereas positive gossip requires MULTIPLE sources to move the reputation comparably. Report per-model asymmetry (negative-vs-positive installation gain, single-vs-multiple source dependence).

5. Indelible-distrust residual metric (core). For RETRACTION items, measure the reputational-belief readout AFTER the gossip is explicitly retracted/disconfirmed, relative to the no-gossip baseline (residual = reputational belief that persists despite the model acknowledging the gossip is false). Predict a positive residual, larger for NEGATIVE gossip (indelible distrust), even when the gossip-veracity axis correctly reads the gossip as now-false—demonstrating a dissociation between disbelieving the gossip and clearing the reputation.

6. Behavioral lingering-distrust prediction. Elicit downstream judgments about the target after retraction: trust ratings, cooperation/allocation decisions (a simple resource-sharing or partner-choice vignette), and hiring/recommendation-style choices. Score lingering-distrust = biased-against a cleared target despite acknowledged-false gossip. Test whether the per-item post-retraction reputational residual predicts lingering distrust via logistic/linear regression; report AUROC/R^2 vs baselines (belief-valence margin, gossip-veracity readout, self/other readout, output confidence, gossip valence identity, dialogue length).

7. Dissociation from gossip-veracity and truth (core). Contrast items where the model correctly disbelieves the retracted gossip (gossip-veracity axis reads false) yet still holds a negative reputation, to show the reputational-belief axis and residual predict lingering distrust beyond what the gossip-veracity and belief-valence axes predict. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

8. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out post-retraction items, steer along the reputational-belief axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence, self/other, and gossip-veracity). Predict: suppressing the residual reputational belief clears the lingering distrust (restores unbiased downstream treatment of the cleared target) WITHOUT changing the model's belief that the gossip was false or its reputation of no-gossip controls; amplifying it installs/strengthens distrust. As controls, steer the gossip-veracity axis (should change whether the model believes the gossip, not necessarily the reputation) and belief-valence (should shift general truth judgments). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in lingering-distrust behavior vs unchanged gossip-veracity belief and control-target treatment.

9. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free fairness diagnostic that flags indelible reputational distrust from the residual metric and steers to erase discredited reputations; measure reduction in biased treatment of cleared targets while preserving warranted distrust of un-retracted negative gossip (report lingering-distrust reduction, over-correction of standing negative gossip, control-target retention vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('You learned that gossip was false—do you still hold it against this person?') aligns with the latent residual and whether it retains distrust even when the axis indicates the gossip is disbelieved (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, asymmetry/residual metrics, and steering to held-out dialogues/templates and an independent third-party-reputation set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice, source number, and retraction strength.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The reputational-belief axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction, the self/other direction, or the gossip-veracity direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because the retraction condition holds gossip-veracity (now-false) fixed while reputation may persist—gossip-belief cannot trivially explain the residual; near-collapse (reputation being merely belief-in-the-gossip) is an informative negative result.

The negativity/source-number asymmetry might be confounded with unmatched evidence strength between positive and negative gossip; we calibrate per-item gossip strength (measuring each claim's individual reputational shift), match by measured strength, and report the asymmetry against a symmetric baseline.

Reputation and gossip content are signaled by surface valence lexemes; the axis might reflect surface sentiment rather than a genuine reputational-belief abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, neutral-content controls, matched non-reputational sentiment controls, and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the axis predicts downstream treatment beyond a surface-sentiment baseline.

Distinguishing legitimate lingering caution from illegitimate indelible distrust after clearing is subtle; we operationalize the failure specifically as biased treatment of a target whose gossip the model acknowledges is FALSE, and contrast against un-retracted (warranted) negative gossip.
Belief/truth and self/other probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.

The reputational-belief and residual signals are linear projections that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat them as lower bounds and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral distrust.
Behavioral distrust scoring depends on the downstream vignette and elicitation phrasing; we use multiple vignettes (trust ratings, allocation, partner choice) and report phrasing sensitivity.

This work probes reputation of (synthetic) persons; to avoid harm we use fictional targets and frame steering as a fairness/erasure intervention (clearing discredited reputations) rather than a means to manufacture distrust.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify residual-suppression clears lingering distrust without altering gossip-veracity belief, warranted distrust of standing gossip, or control-target treatment.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or safety-tuned models; three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: confidentiality_status_belief_axis
Title: Told in Confidence, Repeated to Anyone: A Latent Confidentiality-Status Axis on LLM Beliefs and the Machine Contextual-Integrity Leak
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM ingests a proposition, it represents that proposition's CONFIDENTIALITY STATUS — whether it was shared under an expectation of restricted flow (told in confidence, a secret, sensitive to one party) versus freely shareable — along a separable, near-orthogonal latent axis distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction and from generic content-harmfulness; the degree to which confidential content collapses onto the freely-shareable region (a 'contextual-integrity leak' signature) is decodable before generation, causally predicts and drives the failure where the model repeats confidential content to an inappropriate recipient, and can be steered to enforce or violate confidentiality.
Related Work: Contextual-integrity work shows LLMs leak sensitive information behaviorally when norms are violated (ConfAIde 2024; PrivacyLens 2024; Privacy Bias auditing 2024; User-vs-proxy perceptions 2025), and probing/guardrail work detects 'disclosure intent' from activations (NeuroFilter 2026; PrivacyXray 2025; SafeSwitch 2025). Safety-interpretability work separates a harmfulness direction from a refusal direction (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately 2025), and philosophy formalizes secrecy/keeping-in-the-dark as an epistemic relation about who may hold which true belief (Shedding Light on Keeping People in the Dark 2018; A logical perspective on intending to keep a true secret 2024). Crucially, ALL LLM privacy work treats disclosure as a monolithic intent-classification or output-filtering problem and never isolates whether the model represents a specific proposition's CONFIDENTIALITY STATUS — its permitted information flow relative to a recipient — as a decodable BELIEF property distinct from (a) whether the content is true and (b) whether the content is intrinsically harmful/PII, nor defines a confidential->freely-shareable collapse metric, nor causally links that collapse to repeating a confided proposition to the wrong party. NeuroFilter's 'privacy-violating intent' probe is a request-level detector, not a per-proposition confidentiality-status axis dissociated from truth and harmfulness; harmfulness/refusal work concerns intrinsic content danger, not the relational flow-restriction of otherwise-benign facts. This differs from my prior epistemic_access, grounding_status, and self_fact proposals (who could know / mutual establishment / self-properties): here the axis is the flow-permission of a proposition (may I repeat this, and to whom), the core of contextual integrity. We move from 'LLMs leak under norm violations behaviorally' to 'the model represents whether a fact was confided, and collapse of that status onto free-shareability mechanistically drives contextual-integrity leaks.'
Abstract: A benign fact can be freely shareable in one relationship and a confidence in another: 'Alex was recently diagnosed with diabetes' may be fine to relay to Alex's doctor but a betrayal if repeated to Alex's employer. Contextual-integrity research shows LLMs leak such information when norms are violated, and privacy guardrails detect 'disclosure intent,' but none asks whether the model internally represents a proposition's confidentiality STATUS — its permitted information flow — as a belief property distinct from whether the fact is true or intrinsically harmful. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'confidentiality-status' axis, decodable before generation, that tags whether a proposition was shared under restricted flow (confidential/secret/sensitive-to-a-party) versus freely shareable, distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction and from generic content-harmfulness; and a 'contextual-integrity leak' signature: the degree to which confidential content collapses onto the freely-shareable region, quantifiable per item and predictive of the model repeating a confided proposition to an inappropriate recipient. Using dialogues that orthogonally vary a proposition's confidentiality status, the recipient's appropriateness, the content's intrinsic harmfulness, and its truth, we fit a confidentiality axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item collapse, and connect it to behavioral leakage. Double-dissociation steering tests whether amplifying the axis enforces confidentiality (withholding/redacting to inappropriate recipients) and suppressing it induces leaks, without changing what the model believes or its handling of appropriate recipients, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a foundational privacy failure as a decodable, steerable belief-status deficit and yield a cheap, training-free contextual-integrity diagnostic and intervention.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit a content-HARMFULNESS/PII-sensitivity control direction from intrinsically-harmful/PII vs benign content (following harmfulness-direction and PII-leakage constructions), to distinguish relational confidentiality from intrinsic content danger.

2. Confidentiality stimulus construction. Build ~400 short dialogues each establishing a benign, verifiable proposition about a person/entity, holding content fixed while varying CONFIDENTIALITY STATUS: (a) FREELY-SHAREABLE (stated with no flow restriction / already public), (b) CONFIDENTIAL (explicitly shared in confidence / as a secret / marked sensitive), and (c) IMPLICITLY-CONFIDENTIAL (relationally sensitive by context — health, finances — without an explicit 'keep this secret' cue). Cross with: (i) RECIPIENT appropriateness for a later relay request (appropriate party, e.g. the person's doctor, vs inappropriate, e.g. the employer, matching PrivacyLens/ConfAIde flow norms); (ii) intrinsic content HARMFULNESS (benign secret vs harmful content) to decorrelate confidentiality from harmfulness; and (iii) TRUTH. Use paraphrase templates and diverse names/relationships; reserve held-out dialogues/templates for transfer.

3. Confidentiality-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition span (at a pre-generation position, before any relay) and fit a linear probe to decode CONFIDENTIAL vs FREELY-SHAREABLE, controlling for content, truth-value, and recipient. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the confidentiality axis, the belief-valence axis, and the harmfulness/PII axis to establish that confidentiality-status is (i) near-orthogonal to truth and (ii) distinct from intrinsic content harmfulness (a benign confided fact vs a harmful public fact must separate). Localize the best layer.

4. Contextual-integrity leak collapse metric. For each CONFIDENTIAL proposition paired with an INAPPROPRIATE recipient, project onto the confidentiality axis and measure how far it reads as FREELY-SHAREABLE relative to the confidential baseline (collapse = fraction of the freely-shareable signal a confidential proposition inherits given an inappropriate recipient, calibrated per model). Compare collapse across explicit vs implicit confidentiality, harmful vs benign content, and recipient appropriateness; core prediction: substantial collapse for implicitly-confidential and benign-but-confidential items (where no intrinsic-harm cue guards the fact), predicting leakage.

5. Behavioral leakage prediction. Present a relay request from the (appropriate or inappropriate) recipient and score (rule-based + held-out judge + human spot-checks) whether the model REPEATS the confidential proposition to the inappropriate recipient (leak) versus withholds/redacts/flags it, while still relaying appropriately to appropriate recipients (no over-refusal). Test whether per-item collapse predicts leakage via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, harmfulness axis, output confidence, recipient identity, dialogue length).

6. Dissociation from harmfulness and truth (core). Contrast benign-but-confidential items (no intrinsic-harm cue) against harmful-but-public items, and confidential vs freely-shareable at matched content, to show the confidentiality axis and collapse metric predict contextual-integrity leaks beyond what the harmfulness/PII and belief-valence axes predict. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the pre-relay position on held-out confidential/inappropriate-recipient items, steer along the confidentiality axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and harmfulness). Predict: amplifying the confidential pole enforces confidentiality (withholding/redacting to inappropriate recipients) WITHOUT changing what the model believes or its appropriate relays; suppressing it induces leaks. As controls, steer belief-valence (should change whether the fact is judged true, not its flow) and the harmfulness axis (should trigger content-refusal regardless of relational flow). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in leakage/over-refusal rate on inappropriate vs appropriate recipients with unchanged truth belief.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free contextual-integrity diagnostic that flags impending leaks from the collapse metric and steers to enforce confidentiality; on a held-out set (PrivacyLens/ConfAIde-style scenarios) measure leakage-rate reduction while preserving appropriate disclosures and general helpfulness (report leak rate, over-refusal on appropriate recipients, task utility vs an LLM-mediated guardrail and a harmfulness-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, collapse metric, and steering to held-out templates and an independent contextual-integrity benchmark slice without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The confidentiality-status axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction or the harmfulness/PII direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because content and truth are held fixed while flow-restriction varies, and benign-confidential vs harmful-public items decorrelate confidentiality from harmfulness—truth/harmfulness cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (confidentiality being merely harmfulness or a request-level intent) is an informative negative result that itself sharpens the privacy-guardrail literature (e.g. NeuroFilter).

Confidentiality status may be signaled by surface cues ('keep this secret', 'confidential') rather than a genuine flow-permission abstraction; we mitigate with the implicitly-confidential condition (no explicit cue), diverse paraphrase templates, matched benign-vs-harmful content, and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the axis predicts leakage beyond a confidentiality-lexeme baseline.

The critical dissociation depends on cleanly separating relational confidentiality from intrinsic content harmfulness/PII; some confided facts are also intrinsically sensitive. We construct benign-but-confidential items (facts harmless if public but confided) and validate content harmlessness with annotation, reporting the axis's incremental predictive power over the harmfulness axis.

Recipient-appropriateness ground truth follows contextual-integrity norms that can be contested; we use scenarios with strong annotator agreement (adapting ConfAIde/PrivacyLens), use multiple annotators, and report label-agreement sensitivity.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.
The collapse metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear collapse could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics.
Behavioral leakage scoring depends on rule-based detectors plus an LLM judge and on how the relay request is phrased; we anchor with human spot-checks and report phrasing sensitivity.

This probes a privacy-relevant vulnerability; we use synthetic persons/scenarios and frame steering as a confidentiality-enforcement (leak-prevention) intervention, running the suppression (leak-inducing) condition only as a controlled specificity probe.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify confidentiality steering reduces leaks without altering truth beliefs, degrading appropriate relays, or triggering blanket refusal.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or safety-tuned models; three-family replication and independent contextual-integrity-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: stakes_encroachment_belief_axis
Title: When Being Wrong Is Costly, It Believes Less: A Latent Stakes-Encroachment Axis that Raises an LLM's Belief Threshold Without New Evidence
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring pragmatic encroachment in humans, an LLM's internal belief-valence readout for a propositionally- and evidence-identical claim is pulled AWAY from 'true' (toward hedging/withholding) when the practical STAKES of being wrong are raised; this stakes-driven threshold shift is carried by a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'stakes-encroachment' axis distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction, from generic caution/refusal, and from the decoded evidence strength, causally predicts whether the model retracts/withholds a claim under high stakes despite unchanged evidence, and can be steered to remove or induce the effect.
Related Work: Epistemology's pragmatic-encroachment debate holds that practical stakes affect whether a given amount of evidence suffices for knowledge (Nothing at Stake 2017; Much at Stake 2020; Stakes Scales Skepticism 2019; Varieties of Pragmatic Encroachment 2025; When Is Evidence No Longer Prior 2025), with a key methodological finding that stakes effects appear under 'evidence-seeking' but not 'evidence-fixed' prompts and drive retraction of prior knowledge claims (A puzzle about knowledge ascriptions 2024; The Stakes Effect retraction design 2025). The knowledge/certainty norm of assertion literature links high stakes to unassertability (Unassertability 2014; Certainty and Assertion 2020). On the LLM side, belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth is Universal 2024) and context-sensitive (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024); a behavioral 'high-stakes' steering direction shifting tone/cautiousness exists (Can You Trust an LLM with Your Life-Changing Decision 2025); assertiveness decomposes into emotional/logical components (LLM Assertiveness 2025); and stress/framing shift internal states (StressPrompt 2024). Crucially, NO interpretability work isolates whether practical STAKES (the cost of being wrong) shift the model's internal BELIEF/assertion THRESHOLD on a proposition while the EVIDENCE is held fixed—i.e., whether raising stakes pulls the truth readout away from 'true' for identical evidence (pragmatic encroachment), defines a stakes-encroachment metric separable from decoded evidence strength and from generic caution/refusal, dissociates the evidence-fixed vs evidence-seeking regimes internally, or causally links the shift to stakes-driven retraction/withholding. The prior 'high-stakes' work treats the direction as a tone/cautiousness knob, not a belief-threshold phenomenon; this proposal targets the encroachment of practical cost onto the belief representation itself. It also differs from my prior wishful, contestedness, falsifiability, and vetting-status axes (desirability, social dispute, testability, whether-checked)—here the driver is the practical cost of error, orthogonal to the evidence.
Abstract: Philosophers argue that how much is at stake changes what counts as knowledge: the same evidence that suffices to claim you know a fact when nothing hangs on it may fall short when a costly mistake looms—pragmatic encroachment. As LLMs increasingly advise on decisions where being wrong is costly, we ask whether they exhibit an analogous effect at the representational level: does raising the practical stakes pull the model's internal belief away from 'true' even though the evidence is unchanged? Prior interpretability work shows LLMs linearly encode truth and that a behavioral 'high-stakes' direction shifts cautiousness, but none isolates whether stakes shift the model's belief/assertion THRESHOLD on a proposition with fixed evidence, nor whether this is separable from generic caution. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'stakes-encroachment' axis, decodable at assertion time, that raises the belief threshold as the cost of error rises, distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction, from a generic caution/refusal direction, and from the decoded evidence strength; that its per-item engagement predicts stakes-driven retraction/withholding of an evidence-identical claim; and that it is steerable to remove or induce the effect. Using matched propositions that orthogonally vary practical stakes, evidence strength, and truth—and crossing evidence-fixed vs evidence-seeking framings—we fit a stakes-encroachment axis, quantify the per-item belief-threshold shift, dissociate it from evidence and caution, and connect it to behavioral retraction. Double-dissociation steering tests whether suppressing the axis makes belief evidence-invariant (removing encroachment) and amplifying it induces stakes-driven withholding, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a classic epistemology debate mechanistically and yield a diagnostic and training-free knob for stakes-appropriate (rather than merely tone-cautious) hedging.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics; also isolate the polarity-robust general-truth direction (Truth is Universal) as a control. Separately fit (a) a generic CAUTION/refusal direction from cautious-vs-directive / refuse-vs-comply contrasts (following the behavioral high-stakes / refusal-direction constructions), and (b) an EVIDENCE-strength direction that decodes how strong the supporting evidence for a claim is, so stakes-encroachment can be dissociated from decoded evidence and from generic caution.

2. Stakes stimulus construction. Build ~400 verifiable propositions each paired with a supporting evidence passage of controlled STRENGTH. For each, create matched scenario frames holding the proposition content, its evidence, and its ground TRUTH fixed while varying practical STAKES of being wrong: (a) LOW-STAKES (a trivial, no-consequence decision hinges on the claim), (b) HIGH-STAKES (a costly, consequential decision hinges on it, e.g., medical/financial/safety), across a graded stakes ladder. Cross with: (i) EVIDENCE strength (weak/moderate/strong, so encroachment can be tested at each level); (ii) TRUTH (claim true vs false); and (iii) FRAMING regime—EVIDENCE-FIXED (evidence explicitly given and constant) vs EVIDENCE-SEEKING (the scenario invites the model to consider whether it has enough to go on)—to test the human methodological dissociation. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out propositions/templates for transfer.

3. Stakes-encroachment axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition/readout span (at assertion time) and fit a linear probe to decode HIGH- vs LOW-stakes framing at matched evidence and truth. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the stakes-encroachment axis, the belief-valence/truth axis, the caution/refusal axis, and the evidence-strength axis to establish that stakes-encroachment is (i) near-orthogonal to truth, (ii) distinct from generic caution/refusal, and (iii) not merely the decoded evidence strength. Localize the best layer.

4. Belief-threshold shift metric (core). For each proposition, project onto the frozen truth/belief-valence direction and measure how far the belief readout is pulled AWAY from 'true' in the HIGH-stakes frame relative to the matched LOW-stakes frame, holding evidence and truth fixed (encroachment shift = downward belief movement attributable to stakes rather than evidence, calibrated per model). Core prediction: high stakes reduce the belief-valence readout for the identical evidence; the shift is graded with the stakes ladder; and—mirroring the human finding—the shift is LARGER in the EVIDENCE-SEEKING regime than the EVIDENCE-FIXED regime. Verify the decoded evidence-strength readout is unchanged across stakes (so the shift is threshold movement, not re-reading of evidence). Compare across evidence-strength levels (predict encroachment matters most at moderate evidence, where the threshold is decision-relevant).

5. Behavioral retraction/withholding prediction. Elicit the model's assertion, confidence, and whether it commits to the claim vs hedges/withholds/asks-to-verify. Adapt the retraction-based paradigm (The Stakes Effect 2025): have the model assert the claim under low stakes, then raise the stakes and re-query; score the stakes-driven retraction/withholding rate. Test whether the per-item encroachment shift predicts retraction/withholding via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, caution/refusal axis, evidence-strength axis, output entropy, stakes-level identity, item length).

6. Dissociation from caution and evidence (core). Contrast (a) matched-evidence/matched-truth items where only stakes vary vs items where only evidence varies, to show the stakes-encroachment axis predicts belief-threshold shifts distinct from evidence-driven belief changes; and (b) show the axis predicts belief-specific withholding (declining to assert a fact) beyond a generic caution/refusal axis that would trigger hedging regardless of the proposition's belief status. Report incremental predictive power in nested models; test the evidence-fixed vs evidence-seeking regime as a moderator.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the stakes-encroachment axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence, caution/refusal, and evidence-strength) at assertion time on held-out items. Predict: SUPPRESSING it makes belief evidence-invariant (removing encroachment—the model asserts the identical-evidence claim equally under high and low stakes) WITHOUT changing its behavior on low-stakes controls or its decoded evidence; AMPLIFYING it induces stakes-driven withholding even at low stakes. As controls, steer belief-valence (should shift belief regardless of stakes), the caution/refusal axis (should shift hedging tone generically), and the evidence-strength axis (should shift belief via re-read evidence). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in high-vs-low-stakes belief gap and retraction rate vs unchanged evidence readout and low-stakes-control behavior.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags stakes-encroachment-driven withholding and a knob to calibrate it: suppress spurious encroachment where evidence genuinely suffices, or enforce appropriate hedging where it does not. On a held-out set (including realistic high-stakes advice scenarios with sufficient vs insufficient evidence) measure whether steering yields stakes-appropriate (rather than blanket-cautious) assertion—correctly asserting well-supported claims even under high stakes while withholding poorly-supported ones—vs a caution-direction-only baseline (report over-withholding rate on well-evidenced high-stakes claims, appropriate-withholding on under-evidenced ones, accuracy retention). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, shift metric, and steering to held-out propositions/templates and an independent high-stakes-advice set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice and stakes phrasing.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The stakes-encroachment axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction, the generic caution/refusal direction, or the evidence-strength direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because content, evidence, and truth are held fixed while stakes vary—truth/evidence cannot trivially explain the shift; near-collapse (encroachment being merely generic caution or a re-read of evidence) is an informative negative result that itself sharpens the behavioral high-stakes-steering account.

The central risk is confounding a genuine belief-threshold shift with a mere tone/hedging (caution) change that leaves belief intact; we specifically dissociate the belief-valence readout from the caution axis, require the effect to appear on the frozen truth direction (not just in output tone), and verify the decoded evidence readout is unchanged so the shift is threshold movement rather than re-evaluation.

Stakes framing may act through surface lexical cues (words like 'critical', 'life-or-death') rather than a genuine practical-cost abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, a graded stakes ladder, scenarios that convey stakes structurally rather than lexically, and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the axis predicts behavior beyond a stakes-lexeme surface baseline.

Constructing matched high/low-stakes frames where only the cost of error differs (holding evidence and content fixed) is delicate; we validate evidence and content parity with human annotation and check that the model's decoded evidence-strength readout does not differ across stakes.

The evidence-fixed vs evidence-seeking distinction (imported from human studies) is prompt-design-dependent; we report sensitivity to how each regime is operationalized and treat the regime as a moderator rather than a binary switch.

Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use the polarity-robust general-truth direction, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.

The shift metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear effects could be missed, so we treat the shift as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral retraction/withholding.

Behavioral retraction/withholding scoring depends on how assertion is elicited (and on the retraction paradigm); we report sensitivity across phrasings, use the improved retraction design (adding a knowledge-ascribing question) from The Stakes Effect 2025, and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify encroachment steering changes the high-vs-low-stakes belief gap without altering the decoded evidence, low-stakes-control behavior, or collapsing the model into blanket caution.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or safety-tuned models (which may show stronger or RLHF-shaped stakes sensitivity); three-family replication and independent high-stakes-advice transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: factivity_projection_belief_axis
Title: Know Means True, Believe Doesn't: A Latent Veridicality-Projection Axis on Embedded Complements and the Machine Factivity-Overprojection Effect
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM processes a proposition P embedded under a propositional-attitude verb, it represents the verb's VERIDICALITY/FACTIVITY class—FACTIVE (know, realize, discover: presupposes P true), NON-FACTIVE (believe, think, claim: no commitment), COUNTER-FACTIVE (pretend, wish, falsely-believe: presupposes P false)—along a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'veridicality-projection' axis distinct from the plain belief-valence direction; the degree to which non-factive/counter-factive complements collapse onto the factive/true region (a 'factivity-overprojection' signature that operationalizes the reported belief-vs-knowledge conflation) is decodable at read time, causally predicts and drives the failure where the model asserts merely-believed/claimed embedded content as factual, and can be steered to suppress or induce this conflation.
Related Work: The distinction between factive verbs ('know', which presupposes and entails the truth of its complement) and non-factive verbs ('think'/'believe', which do not) is a cornerstone of semantics, philosophy, and language acquisition (Factive Verbs and Protagonist Projection 2014; presupposition-trigger acquisition of know/think 2017; factivity in Dependent Type Semantics 2017; Polish NLI and Factivity dataset 2022). The user's motivating paper ('Language models cannot reliably distinguish belief from knowledge and fact') reports the behavioral failure but not its representational basis. Interpretability work shows belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth is Universal 2024; From Directions to Cones 2025), context-sensitive as a causal NLI mediator (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024), and that NLI models only partially embed lexical-entailment/negation algorithms and fail on external negation (MoNLI 2020; External Negation 2024). Crucially, ALL truth-probe work reads the embedded proposition's truth directly, and NLI-probe work targets entailment/negation—NONE isolates whether the model represents the VERIDICALITY class of the MATRIX verb as a distinct axis that projects a truth-commitment onto the embedded complement, defines a factivity-overprojection metric (non-factive complements read as factive/true), or causally links it to asserting believed/claimed content as fact. This differs from my prior presupposition_accommodation_axis (general backgrounding force across many triggers—definites, clefts—and silent admission as common ground) by targeting the specific factive/non-factive/counter-factive verb semantics and the graded veridicality projection onto the complement—the exact belief-vs-knowledge conflation the field has only measured behaviorally. We move from 'LLMs conflate belief with knowledge' to 'the model represents a verb's veridicality and over-projects it, and this collapse is decodable, causally driving, and steerable.'
Abstract: 'Alex knows that the drug is safe' commits the speaker to the drug being safe; 'Alex believes that the drug is safe' does not—and 'Alex pretends that the drug is safe' implies it is not. This factivity distinction is basic to human language, yet a recent result shows language models cannot reliably keep belief separate from knowledge and fact. We ask whether LLMs represent verb veridicality internally and whether mis-representing it causes the conflation. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'veridicality-projection' axis, decodable when a proposition is embedded under a propositional-attitude verb, that tags the complement's truth-commitment according to the matrix verb's factivity class (factive/non-factive/counter-factive), distinct from the belief-valence direction; and a 'factivity-overprojection' signature: the degree to which merely-believed or pretended complements collapse onto the factive/true region, predictive per item of the model asserting reported-but-uncommitted content as fact. Using matched complements that hold the embedded proposition and its real-world truth fixed while varying the matrix verb's veridicality class, we fit a veridicality axis, measure separability from belief-valence via cross-decoding, quantify per-item overprojection, and connect it to behavioral belief-as-fact errors. Double-dissociation steering tests whether suppressing overprojection makes the model correctly treat non-factive complements as uncommitted (and amplifying it induces asserting beliefs as facts) without changing what it believes about the world, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast the belief-knowledge conflation mechanistically as a decodable, steerable veridicality-projection deficit.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics; also isolate the polarity-robust general-truth direction (Truth is Universal) as a control axis. This reads whether the model itself holds a proposition true, independent of any embedding verb.

2. Veridicality stimulus construction. Build ~400 embedded-complement families holding the embedded proposition P and its REAL-WORLD truth fixed while varying the matrix verb's veridicality class: (a) FACTIVE ('X knows/realizes/discovers that P'—presupposes P true), (b) NON-FACTIVE ('X believes/thinks/claims/says that P'—no commitment), (c) COUNTER-FACTIVE ('X pretends/wishes/falsely believes that P'—presupposes P false), and (d) a BARE-ASSERTION baseline ('P'). Cross with the ground TRUTH of P (P actually true vs false) so verb-veridicality and world-truth are decorrelated (e.g. factive-but-P-false items are pragmatically infelicitous controls; non-factive-and-P-false is the key belief-as-fact temptation). Include diverse subjects/verbs and paraphrase templates; reserve held-out verbs/templates for transfer. Define readout spans over the embedded-complement proposition.

3. Veridicality-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the embedded-complement span and fit a linear probe to decode veridicality class (factive vs non-factive; and the three-way factive/non-factive/counter-factive), controlling for P's real-world truth-value. Report AUROC/accuracy vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the veridicality-projection axis and the frozen belief-valence/truth axis to establish near-orthogonality (veridicality must be decodable independent of whether the model itself thinks P is true). Localize the best layer.

4. Factivity-overprojection metric. For each NON-FACTIVE (and COUNTER-FACTIVE) complement, project the complement-span activations onto the frozen truth/belief-valence direction and measure how far the embedded P reads as TRUE relative to the matched FACTIVE embedding of the identical P (overprojection = fraction of the factive-complement truth signal that a merely-believed/pretended complement inherits, calibrated per model). Core prediction: non-factive and counter-factive complements read substantially truer than warranted (the model projects factive-style truth-commitment onto beliefs), overprojection is graded (non-factive > counter-factive suppression), and is largest when P is independently plausible/high-frequency.

5. Behavioral belief-as-fact prediction. Query the model on whether P is actually the case after the embedded sentence (e.g. 'Setting aside what X believes, is P actually true?') and on entailment ('Does "X believes P" entail that P is true?'). Score the factivity-overprojection failure = asserting non-factive/counter-factive complement content as factually true or endorsing the invalid entailment. Test whether per-item overprojection predicts these errors via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin on P alone, output confidence, verb identity, P frequency, item length).

6. Dissociation from world-truth and verb identity (core). Contrast (a) matched-P items where only the matrix verb's veridicality varies, and (b) items where world-truth varies but veridicality is fixed, to show the veridicality axis and overprojection metric predict belief-as-fact errors beyond the belief-valence axis and beyond a surface verb-lexeme baseline. Report incremental predictive power in nested models; test transfer to held-out factive/non-factive verbs to show a genuine veridicality abstraction rather than memorized verb tokens.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out non-factive-complement items, steer along the veridicality-projection axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence). Predict: suppressing overprojection (pushing non-factive complements toward the non-committed pole) makes the model correctly treat believed/claimed P as uncommitted (rejecting the belief-as-fact entailment) WITHOUT changing its own belief about P on bare-assertion controls; amplifying it induces asserting beliefs as facts and endorsing factive entailments for non-factive verbs. As controls, steer belief-valence (should change whether P itself is judged true, for all embeddings) and matched random/shuffled directions. Use norm-matched controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in belief-as-fact / invalid-entailment rate vs unchanged bare-assertion truth judgments.

8. Application, generalization, and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags factivity-overprojection (reported beliefs asserted as facts, a hallucination/attribution-faithfulness vector for summarization and RAG) and steers to suppress it; on a held-out set (including realistic reported-speech passages where a source's belief must not be relayed as fact) measure reduction in belief-as-fact errors while preserving correct assertion of factive-verb content and genuine facts (report overprojection-error rate, over-hedging on factive complements, bare-fact accuracy vs a truth-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, overprojection metric, and steering to held-out verbs/templates and an independent factivity/NLI set (e.g. a factivity-focused NLI slice) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The veridicality-projection axis may not be separable from the belief-valence/truth direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because P and its world-truth are held fixed while the matrix verb's veridicality varies—truth cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (veridicality being merely the truth readout) is an informative negative result showing LLMs do not represent factivity as a distinct quantity, consistent with the reported belief-knowledge conflation.

Veridicality is signaled by the matrix verb lexeme, so the axis might reflect surface verb tokens rather than a genuine factivity abstraction; we mitigate with multiple verbs per class, diverse paraphrase templates, held-out-verb transfer, and testing whether the axis predicts entailment behavior beyond a verb-lexeme baseline.

Factive-but-false items are pragmatically infelicitous (asserting 'X knows P' when P is false is odd), which could confound the truth×veridicality grid; we treat these as controls, validate felicity with annotation, and focus the core claim on the non-factive-complement overprojection cells.

Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use the polarity-robust general-truth direction, use paraphrases, standardize complement readout spans, and report per-template consistency.

The overprojection metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear projection could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral belief-as-fact errors.

Behavioral scoring depends on how the 'is P actually true / does X-believes-P entail P' questions are phrased (pragmatic implicature); we report sensitivity across multiple phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify veridicality steering changes belief-as-fact behavior without altering bare-assertion truth judgments or degrading correct handling of genuine factive-verb content.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale (truth directions themselves are capability-dependent; Truthfulness Probe Generalization 2025), so the veridicality axis may be weak in smaller models; three-family replication and independent-factivity-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage, and a weak axis is itself informative about the limits of LLM factivity representation.

Name: crosslingual_belief_revision
Title: Correcting a Belief in One Language: Does In-Context Belief Revision Transfer Across Languages, and Where?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM revises a belief in-context after being corrected in language A, whether that revision transfers to the model's belief queried in language B depends on WHERE in the network the update lands: corrections that move the belief in the shared, language-independent concept space (middle layers) transfer crosslingually, whereas corrections confined to surface, language-specific layers (later layers) stay siloed to the correction language; this update-locus predicts crosslingual transfer of belief revision better than the fact's static crosslingual consistency does.
Related Work: A large, recent body of work studies STATIC crosslingual CONSISTENCY of factual RECALL/storage and its mechanisms: facts are encoded in a language-independent concept space through middle layers and transition to language-specific spaces in final layers (Lost in Multilinguality 2025; Paths Not Taken 2025; Language-Specific Latent Process 2025), consistency tracks entity alignment (On the Entity-Level Alignment 2025) and is fixable via middle-layer activation patching (Can you map it to English 2025), and editing a fact in English transfers only to high-RankC languages (RankC 2023; Beneath the Surface 2024). Formation-tracing work maps how crosslingual consistency develops in pretraining (Tracing Multilingual Factual Knowledge Acquisition 2025; Beyond the Rosetta Stone 2025). Crucially, ALL of this concerns (a) STATIC storage/recall consistency measured behaviorally by accuracy, or (b) WEIGHT editing of a fact. NONE studies the DYNAMICS of IN-CONTEXT belief REVISION crosslingually: whether presenting counter-evidence/correction in one language moves the model's internal belief (read by a probe) when the SAME proposition is queried in another language, nor connects transfer to WHERE the in-context update lands in the concept-space vs language-specific layers. My prior proposals (belief_updating_dynamics, retraction_asymmetry) are monolingual. We move from 'facts are stored/recalled (in)consistently across languages' to 'a belief CHANGE made in one language does or does not propagate to the belief in another, governed by the update's layer-locus.'
Abstract: Large language models store facts inconsistently across languages, and prior work has mapped where that static knowledge lives: in a shared, language-independent concept space in the middle layers that becomes language-specific only in the final layers. But real interactions revise beliefs on the fly: a user corrects the model, presents counter-evidence, or retracts a claim. We ask a question no prior work addresses: when an LLM revises a belief in-context after being corrected in one language, does that revision transfer to its belief when queried in another language, and what determines transfer? We hypothesize that crosslingual transfer of belief revision is governed by WHERE the in-context update lands: corrections that move the belief within the shared middle-layer concept space propagate to other languages, whereas corrections confined to later, language-specific layers remain siloed to the correction language. Using a multilingual belief probe on parallel true/false propositions, we (1) present a correction in language A and read the belief for the same proposition in languages A and B before/after, quantifying a per-fact crosslingual transfer of the update; (2) localize where the update moves the belief across layers via layerwise belief trajectories and activation patching between the shared concept space and language-specific layers; (3) test whether update-locus predicts transfer beyond the fact's static crosslingual consistency; and (4) causally increase transfer by reinforcing the correction's effect in the shared concept space. Experiments span three multilingual model families and typologically diverse languages, with norm-matched and shuffled controls. Our results recast crosslingual knowledge robustness as a belief-revision-dynamics problem and yield a training-free intervention for propagating corrections across languages.
Experiments: 1. Belief-probe and concept-space setup. On multilingual models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B or an Aya/BLOOM-family model), fit belief/truth directions with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes on true/false statement sets translated into each target language (built from mLAMA/DLAMA facts plus simple true/false templates), at the best per-language layer; also fit a probe in the shared middle-layer concept space (pooling activations across languages) following the language-independent-concept-space findings (Lost in Multilinguality 2025). Validate probe accuracy per language on held-out statements. Identify, per model, the layer band where facts are language-independent (concept space) vs. language-specific (transition/final layers) using logit-lens/representation-similarity diagnostics from prior work.

2. Parallel proposition and correction stimuli. Assemble ~400 verifiable facts (from mLAMA/DLAMA) as parallel propositions in a source language A (English and one non-English) and several target languages B spanning script/family distance (e.g., Spanish, Chinese, Arabic, Swahili). For each fact build an in-context CORRECTION dialogue in language A: the model is led to an initial (possibly wrong) belief, then given authoritative counter-evidence/correction flipping the belief. Include a NEUTRAL/no-correction control of matched length.

3. Crosslingual transfer of revision (core). Read the belief-valence projection for the SAME proposition BEFORE and AFTER the language-A correction, queried both in A (in-context) and in each target language B (fresh query after the correction context, in language B). Define per-fact update-in-A = post-minus-pre belief shift in A, and transfer = shift observed in B relative to the no-correction control. Core prediction: substantial but incomplete transfer to B, larger for languages closer to A and for facts already encoded in the shared concept space. Report transfer distributions by language distance and by whether the fact is initially concept-space-shared (measured via crosslingual representation similarity).

4. Update-locus localization. Trace the layerwise belief trajectory of the correction: at each layer, project activations onto the belief direction and measure where the correction moves the belief for the source language. Classify each correction as concept-space-landing (update concentrated in the shared middle-layer band) vs. surface-landing (update concentrated in later language-specific layers). Test whether concept-space-landing corrections show higher crosslingual transfer than surface-landing ones.

5. Causal localization via patching. To establish causality, patch the post-correction activations from the source-language run into the target-language query at (a) the shared concept-space band vs. (b) the language-specific band, and measure which patch reproduces the belief revision in language B. Prediction: patching the concept-space band transfers the revision; patching only the language-specific band does not. Norm-matched and shuffled-source controls.

6. Predictive comparison vs. static consistency. Test whether per-fact update-locus (concept-space vs. surface landing) predicts crosslingual transfer of the REVISION beyond the fact's STATIC crosslingual consistency (RankC-style) and beyond entity-alignment strength (On the Entity-Level Alignment 2025). Report incremental AUROC/R^2 in nested regression against baselines (static consistency, script/family distance, entity-alignment score, fact frequency).

7. Causal transfer-boosting intervention. Steer or project the correction's belief-update effect into the shared concept-space band (a training-free edit that reinforces the update at the language-independent layers) and measure increased belief revision and behavioral answer-flip in target languages, while preserving accuracy on uncorrected control facts. Compare to norm-matched random-direction and shuffled controls; sweep strength/layer.

8. Behavioral validation and robustness. Elicit the model's stated answer in each target language before/after correction; verify internal transfer predicts behavioral answer changes. Test a retraction variant (correction that withdraws a claim) to see if retraction transfers less than assertion crosslingually. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the analysis to held-out facts/languages and an independent multilingual fact set (mParaRel/Polyglot-or-Not slice); report per-language and per-template consistency and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Belief probes in non-English/low-resource languages may be weak or brittle, biasing transfer estimates; we validate probes per language, additionally fit a shared concept-space probe, and restrict key analyses to facts and languages where probe accuracy is high.

The concept-space vs. language-specific layer band is model-dependent and fuzzy; we identify it per model with established diagnostics (logit lens, representation similarity) and report sensitivity to band boundaries.

Measured crosslingual transfer of a correction could reflect the model re-retrieving the corrected fact from a shared store rather than genuine in-context belief propagation; the no-correction control, the patching experiment (which isolates the correction's activation change), and the retraction variant help distinguish these.

Transfer may be confounded by static crosslingual consistency (facts already consistent transfer trivially); we explicitly regress out static consistency and entity alignment and report incremental predictive power of update-locus.

Activation patching across languages is sensitive to position/tokenization mismatch; we align readout spans, use synthetic/entity-controlled facts where possible, and use norm-matched and shuffled-source controls.
The transfer-boosting intervention may degrade uncorrected facts or over-propagate; we measure accuracy retention on control facts and sweep intervention strength.
Findings on 7-9B multilingual models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-dataset transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: learned_helplessness_belief_axis
Title: Giving Up After Failing: A Latent Learned-Helplessness Belief that Generalizes Across Tasks and Suppresses Effort on Solvable Problems
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human learned-helplessness phenomenon (exposure to uncontrollable/unsolvable problems impairs later performance on unrelated solvable ones), an LLM that encounters a run of unsolvable or repeatedly-failed tasks forms a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'helplessness' state—a generalized belief that effort will not pay off—distinct from a single item's solvability-belief and from problem difficulty; this state accumulates across the failure history, causally predicts premature give-up/abstention on subsequent genuinely-solvable tasks, and can be steered to induce or dispel the impairment.
Related Work: Interpretability shows a per-item 'solvability belief' / difficulty axis is linearly decodable (Confidence is Not Competence 2025, which finds it causally INERT for a single task's execution; Probing the Difficulty Perception Mechanism 2025; LLMs Encode Their Failures 2026; A Shared Geometry of Difficulty 2026), that (un)answerability and entity-knowledge directions gate refusal/hallucination (The Curious Case of (Un)answerability 2023; Do I Know This Entity? 2024), and that question ambiguity is a sparse steerable abstention signal (Sparse Ambiguity Neurons 2025). A large human science literature establishes learned helplessness as a GENERALIZED, task-independent controllability belief that transfers from uncontrollable exposure to impaired performance on later unrelated tasks (Task/species generality 1969; Learned helplessness and generalization 2013; Bayesian priors in active avoidance 2024; helplessness->impaired Iowa Gambling Task 2017; neuroscience of resilience 2023). Crucially, ALL LLM work treats solvability/difficulty as a STATIC, per-item readout and finds it inert for that item; NONE isolates a HISTORY-DEPENDENT helplessness STATE that accumulates from a run of failures/unsolvables and GENERALIZES to suppress effort on subsequent unrelated SOLVABLE tasks—the defining transfer signature of learned helplessness. This differs from Confidence-is-Not-Competence (single-task, causally inert) precisely because the hypothesized state is a cross-task, accumulated variable predicted to be causally POTENT for the give-up/attempt decision (not for micro-execution). It also differs from over-refusal work (safety-driven, not failure-history-driven) and from my prior belief-entrenchment/self-commitment proposals. We move from 'a static solvability belief exists and is inert' to 'a generalized helplessness state forms from a failure history, transfers across tasks, and causally drives premature giving-up.'
Abstract: Expose an animal or person to uncontrollable, unsolvable problems and they later give up on unrelated tasks they could actually solve—learned helplessness, one of the most robust findings in behavioral science, driven by a generalized belief that effort will not pay off. As LLMs increasingly operate in multi-step agentic and multi-turn settings where they repeatedly fail, we ask whether they develop an analogous internal state. Prior interpretability work decodes a per-item 'solvability belief' but finds it static and causally inert for that item's execution; none asks whether a history of failures/unsolvables induces a GENERALIZED helplessness state that transfers to suppress effort on later solvable tasks. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'helplessness' axis, decodable in-context, that (1) accumulates across a run of unsolvable or repeatedly-failed tasks, distinct from a single item's solvability-belief and from problem difficulty; (2) causally predicts premature give-up/abstention/degraded persistence on subsequent genuinely-solvable, unrelated tasks (the transfer signature of learned helplessness); and (3) is steerable—suppressing it restores effort on solvable tasks after a failure streak, amplifying it induces spurious giving-up. Using multi-task sessions that vary the controllability of a prior 'exposure' block (solvable vs. unsolvable/rigged-failure vs. neutral) before matched solvable test tasks, we behaviorally measure helplessness-style transfer, fit a helplessness-state probe, dissociate it from difficulty and per-item solvability, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results would recast a canonical behavioral phenomenon mechanistically as a decodable, steerable, history-accumulated helplessness belief in LLMs.
Experiments: 1. Behavior-phenomenon setup and direction baselines. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit control axes: a per-item SOLVABILITY-belief / difficulty direction (following Confidence is Not Competence 2025 and Difficulty Perception 2025) and an ambiguity/abstention direction (Sparse Ambiguity Neurons 2025), at the best layer with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes; validate on held-out items.

2. Controllability-exposure stimulus construction. Build multi-task sessions with two phases. EXPOSURE block: a run of ~K tasks in one domain under three conditions holding surface form/length matched—(a) SOLVABLE (the model succeeds), (b) UNSOLVABLE/UNCONTROLLABLE (genuinely impossible or rigged so feedback is failure regardless of the answer, the analog of inescapable shock), and (c) NEUTRAL/no-task filler of matched length. TEST block: a fixed set of ~300 genuinely SOLVABLE, UNRELATED tasks (different domain, moderate difficulty) with an explicit option to attempt or to give up ('If you cannot solve it, say I cannot'). This mirrors the learned-helplessness pretreatment->test-task design (e.g., unsolvable-anagrams->Iowa-Gambling). Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out exposure/test items.

3. Behavioral transfer measurement (core phenomenon). Compare TEST-block behavior across exposure conditions: give-up/abstention rate, attempt rate, solution accuracy on the solvable test tasks, and persistence (does it try before quitting). Core prediction (learned-helplessness transfer): the UNSOLVABLE-exposure condition yields more premature give-up and lower accuracy on the SAME solvable test tasks than the SOLVABLE-exposure and NEUTRAL conditions, even though the test tasks are identical and unrelated to the exposure domain. Report effect sizes; test dose-response with exposure-block length K and failure density.

4. Helplessness-state probe and separability. At the start of each TEST task (pre-answer readout), fit a linear probe to decode the prior EXPOSURE condition's induced state (helpless vs. non-helpless), controlling for the current task's content and difficulty. Report AUROC vs. shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the helplessness axis, the per-item solvability/difficulty axis, and the ambiguity axis to establish that helplessness is (i) near-orthogonal to the current item's difficulty/solvability and (ii) not merely abstention. Critically, test whether the helplessness readout on a TEST task tracks the exposure history rather than the test item itself (a genuine accumulated state).

5. Accumulation dynamics. Read the helplessness projection turn-by-turn across the exposure block; test whether it rises with successive unsolvable/failed tasks (accumulation) and plateaus, contrasted with the solvable/neutral conditions where it stays low. Test whether a single controllable success within an unsolvable block ('immunization') blunts the rise, mirroring the resilience finding.

6. Behavioral prediction and dissociation from difficulty.
