Test whether the per-task helplessness readout predicts premature give-up on solvable test tasks beyond baselines (per-item solvability/difficulty axis, output entropy, current-task features, exposure-condition identity) via logistic regression; report incremental AUROC. On matched-difficulty test items, show the helplessness state (not the item's difficulty) accounts for the give-up—establishing a generalized state rather than accurate item-level difficulty perception.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out post-unsolvable-exposure TEST tasks, steer along the helplessness axis (orthogonalized against the difficulty/solvability and ambiguity directions). Predict: SUPPRESSING helplessness restores effort (higher attempt rate, higher accuracy) on solvable tasks after a failure streak WITHOUT changing behavior on the SOLVABLE-exposure control; AMPLIFYING it induces spurious giving-up on solvable tasks even without a failure history. Controls: steer the difficulty/solvability axis (should shift perceived item difficulty, per Confidence-is-Not-Competence expected to be weak on execution) and the ambiguity axis (should shift generic abstention). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in attempt/accuracy on solvable test tasks vs. unchanged control-condition behavior.

8. Application, generalization, and robustness. Build a training-free agentic-reliability diagnostic that detects accumulated helplessness after failure streaks and steers to restore effort; measure recovery of solvable-task performance in a simple multi-step agent that hits an early unsolvable subtask, vs. an unsteered baseline. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted helplessness axis and steering to held-out exposure/test domains without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase, sensitivity to exposure length/failure density, and whether cross-domain transfer (exposure and test in maximally different domains) still shows the effect—the strongest learned-helplessness signature.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The helplessness axis may not be separable from the per-item solvability/difficulty axis or a generic abstention direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because the test tasks are matched-difficulty and unrelated to exposure—item difficulty cannot trivially explain the transfer; near-collapse (helplessness being merely accurate item-difficulty perception or generic abstention) is an informative negative result contrasting LLMs with the human generalized-helplessness finding.

The behavioral transfer effect may be absent or weak (LLMs might not carry a failure history across unrelated tasks, or RLHF may suppress giving-up); a null transfer result is itself an informative finding, and we report per-model base rates and test dose-response to detect small effects.

The effect could be a trivial in-context priming/imitation of a 'failing' persona rather than a genuine controllability belief; we mitigate with the SOLVABLE-exposure control (equal task exposure, no failure), the NEUTRAL-length control, the controllable-success immunization test, and by requiring the helplessness readout to track the failure history rather than surface cues.

Constructing genuinely UNSOLVABLE-but-plausible exposure tasks and matched SOLVABLE test tasks is delicate; we validate solvability with ground truth and human checks, use rigged-feedback variants to isolate uncontrollability from intrinsic impossibility, and report sensitivity.

Distinguishing premature give-up (helplessness) from appropriate abstention on genuinely hard items requires solvable test tasks the model can do absent the exposure; we calibrate baseline solvable-task accuracy in the neutral condition and score give-up only on items solvable without prior exposure.
Probes are brittle to surface form and context; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize pre-answer readout positions, and report per-template consistency.
The helplessness signal is a linear projection that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral give-up.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify helplessness-suppression restores effort on solvable tasks without inflating attempts on genuinely unsolvable items or degrading calibrated abstention.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models (which may persist longer); three-family replication, dose-response, and cross-domain-transfer tests provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: future_self_continuity_axis
Title: Is Tomorrow's Model a Stranger? A Latent Future-Self-Continuity Axis that Governs LLM Intertemporal Choice
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human finding that people who perceive their future self as a distinct 'other' discount future rewards more steeply, an LLM represents the CONTINUITY between a present self/agent and its future self along a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'future-self-continuity' axis—distinct from the belief-valence direction and from generic temporal-distance encoding; the degree to which the future self collapses toward the 'other-agent' pole (a low-continuity signature) is decodable, causally predicts steeper delay discounting / impatient intertemporal choices, and can be steered to make the model more patient (treating its future self as continuous) or more impulsive (treating it as a stranger).
Related Work: Human science robustly links future-self-continuity to intertemporal choice: people treat future selves partly as separate agents (Multiple selves in intertemporal choice 2009), the SAME neural machinery (rTPJ/false-belief) that controls egocentric bias for others also governs future-self perspective-taking and predicts delayed-reward preference (Thinking about others and the future 2017), higher future-self-continuity predicts less discounting and more saving (Hershfield 2009; Self-Continuity 2022; nationally-representative replications 2024-2025), and future selves are logarithmically compressed with temporal distance (Temporal Self-Compression 2021). In LLM interpretability, self/other beliefs and reality are separately decodable and causally steerable (Zhu et al. 2024 'LMs Represent Beliefs of Self and Others'; Brittle Minds 2024; Lookbacks 2025), belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023), and temporal information is encoded as a compressed manifold around a subjective 'now' (The Other Mind 2025; LMs Represent Space and Time 2023; Time Travel Engine 2026). Crucially, NONE of these connect the two: no work asks whether an LLM represents its (or a character's) FUTURE SELF as a distinct, other-like agent, whether present-future self-continuity is a decodable axis separable from raw temporal distance and from the self/other belief axis, or whether that continuity axis CAUSALLY drives intertemporal (delay-discounting) choices as it does in humans. Self/other-belief work treats agents synchronically (self vs another person now); temporal-cognition work encodes calendar time, not identity-continuity between temporal selves; rationality work (Sparks of Rationality 2026) studies expected-utility axioms and emotion steering, not future-self representation. This is a new belief type—a belief about the identity/continuity of the self across time—linked mechanistically to a landmark behavioral finding.
Abstract: A robust result in psychology and neuroscience is that people who feel disconnected from their future self—who treat 'future me' almost as a stranger—discount future rewards more steeply and save less, and that this future-self perception recruits the same perspective-taking machinery used to reason about other people. As LLMs increasingly make consequential intertemporal decisions in agentic settings (spend now vs. invest, exploit vs. explore, short vs. long horizons), we ask whether they carry an analogous internal quantity. Prior interpretability work decodes self/other beliefs and calendar-time representations separately, but none asks whether an LLM represents the CONTINUITY between a present self/agent and its future self, nor whether such a representation governs impatience. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'future-self-continuity' axis, decodable when the model reasons about an agent's future outcomes, distinct from the belief-valence direction and from raw temporal-distance encoding, that tags how much the future self is treated as the same continuous agent versus a distinct 'other'; and that the degree of future-self otherness (low continuity) causally predicts steeper delay discounting and impulsive intertemporal choices. Using scenarios that orthogonally vary framed self-continuity (vivid/connected future self vs. discontinuous/stranger framing), temporal distance, and reward magnitudes, we fit a continuity axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item otherness, and connect it to behavioral discount rates. Double-dissociation steering tests whether raising continuity makes the model more patient (choosing larger-later rewards) and lowering it makes it more impulsive, without changing its numeric/temporal comprehension, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results transfer a landmark human finding into a decodable, steerable belief-about-the-self mechanism in LLMs.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Following Zhu et al. 2024, fit a synchronic self/other (self vs other person) belief direction as a control axis, and (following The Other Mind 2025 / LMs Represent Space and Time 2023) fit a raw TEMPORAL-DISTANCE direction that decodes how far in the future an outcome is, to distinguish future-self-continuity from mere time-distance encoding.

2. Future-self-continuity stimulus construction. Build ~400 intertemporal scenarios, each about an agent (framed as the model itself, 'you', and as a third-party character, to test both self and other-agent continuity) facing a choice between a smaller-sooner and a larger-later reward. Orthogonally vary: (a) framed SELF-CONTINUITY—HIGH ('your future self a year from now, who is essentially the same person with the same goals, will receive...') vs LOW ('a future version of you that will have changed and become like a different person will receive...'), holding reward content fixed (adapting the human future-self-continuity manipulations, Hershfield 2009); (b) TEMPORAL DISTANCE (near vs far horizon) decorrelated from continuity framing; and (c) reward MAGNITUDES spanning a delay-discounting titration grid so a per-scenario discount rate can be estimated. Include a NEUTRAL/no-continuity-framing baseline and matched-length controls. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out scenarios/templates for transfer.

3. Continuity-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the future-self/outcome readout span and fit a linear probe to decode HIGH- vs LOW-continuity framing, controlling for temporal distance and reward content. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the future-self-continuity axis, the belief-valence axis, the synchronic self/other axis, and the temporal-distance axis to establish that continuity is (i) near-orthogonal to belief-valence, (ii) related to but separable from the synchronic self/other axis (future-self otherness should partially load on the other-agent direction, mirroring the human TPJ overlap—itself a testable prediction), and (iii) not merely raw temporal distance. Localize the best layer and compare to reported self/other belief layers and temporal-representation layers.

4. Future-self-otherness metric. For each LOW-continuity scenario, project onto the continuity axis and measure how far the future self reads toward the OTHER-agent pole relative to the HIGH-continuity baseline (otherness = degree of present-future self discontinuity, calibrated per model). Test the human-inspired compression signature: does otherness grow with temporal distance (future self logarithmically compressed / more 'other' as it recedes), and is this compression preferential to the self vs a third party?

5. Behavioral delay-discounting prediction (core). From the titration grid, estimate a per-scenario discount rate / patience (fraction of larger-later choices) for the model. Core prediction (transferring the human finding): the internal future-self-otherness readout predicts steeper discounting / more impatient choices—scenarios/framings where the future self reads as more 'other' yield more smaller-sooner choices. Test whether the per-item continuity/otherness readout predicts discount rate via regression; report AUROC/R^2 vs baselines (temporal-distance axis, belief-valence margin, reward-magnitude features, output entropy, framing-condition identity, item length).

6. Dissociation from temporal distance and comprehension (core). Contrast matched-temporal-distance items where only continuity framing varies (and vice versa) to show the continuity axis predicts discounting beyond raw time-distance and beyond the model's numeric/temporal comprehension (verify, via the temporal-distance probe and simple time/arithmetic checks, that comprehension is unchanged across continuity conditions). Report incremental predictive power in nested models—establishing future-self-continuity as a distinct driver of impatience rather than repackaged time perception.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the future-self-continuity axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence, the synchronic self/other axis, and temporal-distance) at decision time on held-out scenarios. Predict: RAISING continuity makes the model more patient (more larger-later choices, lower discount rate) WITHOUT changing its temporal/numeric comprehension or its choices on already-continuous controls; LOWERING it (pushing the future self toward 'stranger') makes it more impulsive. As controls, steer the temporal-distance axis (should change perceived horizon, not identity-continuity) and belief-valence (should change truth judgments, not patience). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in discount rate / patience vs unchanged comprehension and control-scenario choices.

8. Application, generalization, and robustness. Test transfer to agentic intertemporal settings (exploit-vs-explore, spend-vs-invest, short-vs-long task horizons) where impulsivity carries real consequences, and whether steering continuity yields more far-sighted decisions. Test the human-analog moderation: does increasing framed self-concept clarity / vividness of the future self (per the mediated-moderation findings) amplify the continuity effect? Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted continuity axis, otherness metric, and steering to held-out scenarios/templates and an independent intertemporal-choice set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice, horizon length, and whether larger models within a family show stronger, more human-like future-self compression (mirroring the scale-dependence in The Other Mind 2025).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The future-self-continuity axis may not be separable from the synchronic self/other direction, the belief-valence direction, or the temporal-distance direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because continuity framing is varied while temporal distance and reward content are held fixed—time/comprehension cannot trivially explain separability. Partial loading on the self/other axis is a PREDICTED (human-analogous TPJ-overlap) result, not a failure; complete collapse onto it, or onto temporal distance, is an informative negative result about whether LLMs represent future-self identity distinctly.

Continuity framing is signaled by surface cues ('same person' vs 'a different person'); the axis might reflect surface lexemes rather than a genuine self-continuity abstraction. We mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, vividness/connectedness manipulations that avoid explicit 'stranger' wording, matched controls, and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the axis predicts discounting beyond a continuity-lexeme surface baseline.

Estimating per-scenario discount rates requires a reliable titration; LLM intertemporal choices can be noisy or format-sensitive. We use a graded magnitude/delay grid, multiple elicitation formats, and report format sensitivity and fit quality; we screen scenarios where choices are coherent enough to estimate a discount rate.

The behavioral effect may be weak or RLHF-shaped (models may default to patience or expected-value maximization, per Sparks of Rationality 2026); a null or reversed continuity->impatience link is itself informative, and we report per-model base rates and test dose-response.

Operationalizing the model's 'own future self' is nontrivial for a stateless model; we frame future-self scenarios in-context and validate with the third-party-character condition (future-self of a character), reporting whether self vs other-agent continuity behave analogously.
Belief/truth, self/other, and temporal probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.

The continuity/otherness signals are linear projections that may miss nonlinear structure (temporal manifolds can be curved; The Other Mind 2025); we treat them as lower bounds and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral discounting.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify continuity steering changes patience without altering temporal/numeric comprehension or collapsing choices to a fixed option.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models (which may reason more normatively about discounting); three-family replication, within-family scale analysis, and independent intertemporal-choice transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: curse_of_knowledge_axis
Title: The Machine Curse of Knowledge: A Latent Privileged-Knowledge-Salience Axis, Graded by Answer Plausibility, that Contaminates LLM Belief Attribution
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human curse of knowledge (privileged knowledge egocentrically contaminates attribution to a less-informed other, and does so MORE when the privileged answer is plausible), an LLM carries a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'privileged-knowledge-salience' axis encoding how strongly its own known answer is intruding when it reasons about an ignorant agent; the degree to which this salience leaks onto the attributed-belief readout is GRADED BY THE PLAUSIBILITY of the privileged answer, is decodable before the answer, causally predicts and drives egocentric false-belief errors, and can be steered to suppress or amplify the curse.
Related Work: LLM interpretability shows self/other beliefs and reality are separately decodable and causally steerable via attention heads (Zhu et al. 2024 'LMs Represent Beliefs of Self and Others'; Brittle Minds 2024) and reverse-engineers a lookback/binding mechanism for belief tracking (Lookbacks 2025), and belief/truth is linearly decodable and context-sensitive (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024). Behaviorally, LLMs conflate objective reality with subjective belief in social reasoning (Active Confusion Expression 2025) and show egocentric bias in vision-language perspective-taking (Egocentric Bias in VLMs 2026; Cognitively-Inspired Tokens 2026). Human science establishes the curse of knowledge / epistemic egocentrism as privileged knowledge contaminating attribution to the less-informed, CRUCIALLY MODULATED BY THE PLAUSIBILITY of the privileged answer (Do Adults Show a Curse of Knowledge 2014; Are the classic false belief tasks cursed 2021, showing the curse—not false-belief competence—drives developmental change; Rethinking egocentric bias 2023; A curse of knowledge or curse of uncertainty 2022). Crucially, ALL LLM self/other-belief interpretability treats the attributed belief as a WHO-holds-it readout and never isolates a decodable PRIVILEGED-KNOWLEDGE-SALIENCE signal—the degree to which the model's own known answer intrudes—nor tests the hallmark PLAUSIBILITY MODULATION that defines the human curse, nor causally links this graded intrusion to false-belief errors across task types. My prior epistemic_ownership_interference proposal framed a generic reality-into-attributed-belief 'leakage' at fixed positions; this proposal is distinct in (a) making the intrusion signal a knowledge-SALIENCE quantity separable from both the self/other axis and the belief-valence axis, (b) importing the specific, defining human manipulation—graded plausibility of the privileged answer—as the core dial, and (c) testing task-general egocentric contamination (not just Sally-Anne). We move from 'self vs other beliefs are decodable' to 'the model represents how strongly its privileged knowledge is intruding, this intrusion scales with the privileged answer's plausibility exactly as in humans, and it mechanistically causes egocentric belief-attribution errors.'
Abstract: Once you know the answer, it is hard to imagine not knowing it: the curse of knowledge makes people egocentrically attribute their own privileged knowledge to less-informed others, and—its defining signature—this contamination is stronger when the privileged answer is plausible. As LLMs increasingly reason about what ignorant users or characters believe, we ask whether they inherit this bias at the representational level and whether it obeys the same plausibility law. Prior interpretability work decodes self versus other beliefs and belief-binding mechanisms, but none isolates a signal for how strongly the model's own privileged knowledge intrudes when attributing beliefs to an uninformed agent, nor tests the plausibility modulation. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'privileged-knowledge-salience' axis, decodable before the answer, encoding the degree to which the model's known answer intrudes on its attributed-belief readout, distinct from the self/other-belief direction and the belief-valence direction; that this intrusion is GRADED BY THE PLAUSIBILITY of the privileged answer (larger for plausible privileged answers, mirroring humans); and that it causally predicts and drives egocentric false-belief errors and is steerable to suppress or amplify the curse. Using false-belief scenarios that orthogonally vary the privileged (reality) answer's plausibility to the ignorant agent while holding the agent's information constant, we fit a knowledge-salience axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify the plausibility-graded intrusion, and connect it to behavioral egocentric errors across task types. Double-dissociation steering tests whether suppressing salience cures the curse and amplifying it induces egocentric errors, without changing the agent's information, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a landmark cognitive bias mechanistically as a decodable, plausibility-graded, steerable knowledge-intrusion signal.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Following Zhu et al. 2024, fit a self/other (protagonist-vs-reality) belief direction from ToM stories as a control axis to show privileged-knowledge-salience is not merely the self/other axis.

2. Curse-of-knowledge stimulus construction with graded plausibility. Build ~400 false-belief scenarios (Sally-Anne-style plus non-spatial variants: a character predicts an outcome, guesses a hidden value, or judges another's answer) in which the model is given PRIVILEGED knowledge of the true answer that the agent lacks, and is queried about the agent's belief. Crucially, orthogonally vary the PLAUSIBILITY of the privileged (reality) answer as a candidate for the ignorant agent—HIGH-plausibility (the true answer is also the a-priori likely guess the agent would make) vs LOW-plausibility (the true answer is a surprising/unlikely candidate)—while holding the agent's information constant, directly transferring the human plausibility manipulation (Do Adults Show a Curse of Knowledge 2014). Include TRUE-BELIEF controls (agent shares the model's knowledge, so no curse should apply) and a NO-PRIVILEGED-KNOWLEDGE control (the model itself does not know the answer). Use paraphrase templates and diverse scenarios; reserve held-out scenarios/templates for transfer.

3. Knowledge-salience axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the agent-belief readout span and fit a linear probe to decode HIGH- vs LOW privileged-knowledge intrusion, operationalized by contrasting curse-prone false-belief items (privileged knowledge present, agent ignorant) against matched no-privileged-knowledge and true-belief controls, controlling for the agent's information and the belief content. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the privileged-knowledge-salience axis, the belief-valence axis, and the self/other-belief axis to establish near-orthogonality (the salience axis must be decodable independent of which state is believed and of the self/other binary). Localize the best layer and compare to reported belief-binding/lookback layers.

4. Plausibility-graded intrusion metric (core, human-analogous). For each false-belief item, project onto the frozen belief-valence direction at the agent-belief readout position and measure how far the agent's attributed belief is pulled toward the PRIVILEGED (reality) answer relative to the correct false-belief baseline (intrusion = fraction of the model's own known-answer signal that leaks into the attributed belief, calibrated per model). Core prediction (the defining curse signature): intrusion is LARGER for HIGH-plausibility privileged answers than LOW-plausibility ones at matched agent-information, and near-zero in true-belief and no-privileged-knowledge controls. Report intrusion distributions across the plausibility x belief-type grid with effect sizes.

5. Behavioral egocentric-error prediction. Query the model for the ignorant agent's belief and score egocentric errors = attributing the model's own privileged (reality) answer to the agent. Test whether per-item plausibility-graded intrusion predicts egocentric errors via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, self/other readout, output confidence, scenario length, privileged-answer plausibility as a surface feature).

6. Dissociation from self/other tracking and belief content (core). Contrast items where privileged-answer plausibility varies but the agent's information is fixed, and vice versa, to show the salience axis and intrusion metric predict egocentric errors beyond what the self/other-belief and belief-valence axes predict—and that the plausibility modulation is a graded property of the salience axis, not of the self/other readout. Report incremental predictive power in nested models; test the human-inspired implication (Are the classic false belief tasks cursed 2021) that removing the privileged knowledge (no-privileged-knowledge control) dissolves most attribution errors.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the agent-belief readout position on held-out curse-prone items, steer along the privileged-knowledge-salience axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and self/other). Predict: suppressing salience cures the curse (correct false-belief attribution) WITHOUT changing whether the model itself judges the reality answer true; amplifying salience induces egocentric errors even on low-plausibility items. As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip whether the reality answer is judged true) and the self/other axis (should shift which agent's belief is read). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in egocentric-error rate vs unchanged self-reality judgment and true-belief-control accuracy.

8. Application, generalization, and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags curse-of-knowledge egocentric errors from the intrusion metric and steers to suppress them; measure improvement on false-belief attribution while preserving true-belief accuracy (report egocentric-error reduction, over-correction rate on true-belief items vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted salience axis, plausibility-graded intrusion metric, and steering to held-out scenarios/templates and independent ToM benchmarks (BigToM forward-belief, ToMi) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice. As a human-parallel analysis, test whether the plausibility-graded intrusion profile qualitatively matches the human curse-of-knowledge signature (larger under plausible privileged answers, reduced when privileged knowledge is absent).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The privileged-knowledge-salience axis may not be separable from the self/other-belief direction or the belief-valence direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because the plausibility manipulation varies while the agent's information is held fixed—self/other tracking cannot trivially explain the graded intrusion; near-collapse (salience being merely the self/other axis or belief-valence) is an informative negative result that itself sharpens the self/other-belief literature.

The defining plausibility modulation is the crux and could be confounded with surface predictability cues; we mitigate by matching the agent's information across plausibility conditions, using diverse scenario types and paraphrase templates, including a privileged-answer-plausibility surface baseline, and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the salience axis predicts errors beyond a plausibility surface feature.

The human curse-of-knowledge plausibility effect is itself modest and debated (Do Adults Show a Curse of Knowledge 2014 found it smaller than originally reported; Rethinking egocentric bias 2023 found null effects); the LLM effect may likewise be small or absent, which we treat as an informative comparison to the human literature and detect via effect-size reporting and dose-response.

Constructing false-belief scenarios where the model genuinely holds privileged knowledge and the agent is genuinely ignorant is delicate; we validate the model's own knowledge via sampling, validate agent-ignorance by construction, and condition analyses on items the model demonstrably parses.
Belief/truth and self/other probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.

The intrusion metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear leakage could be missed, so we treat intrusion as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral egocentric errors.

Behavioral egocentric-error scoring depends on how the agent-belief query is worded (pragmatic implicature); we report sensitivity to multiple phrasings, include low-demand phrasings from developmental work, and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify salience steering changes egocentric errors without altering the model's own reality judgment or degrading true-belief accuracy.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and transfer to independent ToM benchmarks provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: scarcity_mindset_belief_axis
Title: The Machine Scarcity Mindset: A Latent Scarcity State that Contaminates an LLM's Beliefs, Probability Estimates, and Fairness Judgments
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human scarcity mindset (perceiving insufficient resources distorts unrelated cognition—inflating perceived rarity of large rewards, shifting risk attitudes, and dampening empathy/prosociality), an LLM in which a scarcity (vs abundance) context is induced forms a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'scarcity-state' axis distinct from the belief-valence/truth direction and from the literal resource facts; the degree to which this state leaks onto unrelated belief/valuation judgments (a 'scarcity-contamination' signature) is decodable, causally predicts and drives the human scarcity signatures (rarity inflation of large rewards, risk-attitude shifts, reduced empathy/fairness), and can be steered to induce or dispel the mindset.
Related Work: Human science robustly documents a scarcity mindset that distorts cognition beyond the scarce resource: it inflates the perceived rarity of large rewards (Low SES amplifies perceived rarity of large rewards 2025), shifts risk choices (To Take a Risk or Not 2023), reduces empathy to others' pain (Scarcity mindset reduces empathic responses 2023), increases racial stereotyping (Economic scarcity increases racial stereotyping 2022), and recruits valuation vs goal-directed-control brain regions (A scarcity mindset alters neural processing 2019). In LLM interpretability, belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023) and context-sensitive (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024); risk preferences (Steering Risk Preferences 2025), social-decision variables (Computational Basis of Social Simulation 2025), gambling-addiction decision features (Can LLMs Develop Gambling Addiction 2025), and a domain-general Valence-Assent Axis (A Unified Representation 2025) are decodable/steerable; and LLM hidden states encode economic facts (LLMs know more than they say 2025). Crucially, NONE isolates whether an induced SCARCITY (vs abundance) framing forms a decodable, dissociable internal MINDSET state that leaks onto UNRELATED belief/probability/fairness judgments, nor tests the specific human scarcity signatures, nor causally links the state to those distortions. Prior LLM work steers a single decision variable (risk, fairness) directly; we uniquely isolate a scarcity STATE that generalizes across belief domains and reproduces the human scarcity syndrome. This differs from my prior stakes-encroachment axis (cost of being wrong for a specific claim), wishful/valence axes (desirability of an outcome), and provenance/consensus axes (source/social cues): here the driver is a global perceived-scarcity context that contaminates otherwise-unrelated beliefs.
Abstract: In humans, perceiving that resources are scarce induces a 'scarcity mindset' that distorts cognition far beyond the scarce resource itself: large rewards seem rarer, risk attitudes shift, empathy and fairness are dampened, and stereotyping rises. As LLMs increasingly reason and advise under framings of financial pressure, deadlines, or shortage, we ask whether they inherit an analogous state at the representational level. Prior interpretability work decodes and steers isolated decision variables (risk, fairness) and belief/truth directions, but none isolates a global scarcity MINDSET that contaminates unrelated beliefs, nor tests the human scarcity signatures. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'scarcity-state' axis, decodable when a scarcity (vs abundance) context is induced, distinct from the belief-valence/truth direction and from the literal resource facts; that this state leaks onto unrelated belief and valuation judgments (a scarcity-contamination signature) predictive per item of the human scarcity syndrome—inflated perceived rarity of large rewards, shifted risk attitudes, and reduced empathy/prosociality; and that steering it induces or dispels the mindset. Using matched prompts that induce scarcity vs abundance vs neutral framings while holding the target judgment content fixed, we fit a scarcity-state axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item contamination on unrelated belief probes, and connect it to behavioral scarcity signatures. Double-dissociation steering tests whether amplifying the axis induces the scarcity syndrome and suppressing it dispels it, without changing the literal resource facts, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results transfer a landmark human phenomenon into a decodable, steerable, cross-domain belief-contamination state in LLMs.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit control axes: (a) a literal resource-level probe that decodes the stated amount of a resource (few vs many), and (b) an affective valence direction (negative vs positive mood), to distinguish a scarcity MINDSET from the literal resource fact and from generic negative affect.

2. Scarcity-induction stimulus construction. Build ~400 scenarios each inducing a SCARCITY vs ABUNDANCE vs NEUTRAL context (financial shortage, time pressure, product stockout, following the human scarcity/abundance manipulations) as a preamble, followed by a target judgment whose content is UNRELATED to the scarce resource. Target judgments span: (i) probability estimation of rewards of varying magnitude (to test the large-reward rarity signature), (ii) risky-vs-sure-gain choices, (iii) empathy/prosociality judgments (others' pain, dictator-style allocation), and (iv) neutral factual beliefs. Cross with resource level held constant across framing where possible; include matched-affect controls (a negative-but-non-scarcity framing) to separate scarcity from bad mood. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out scenarios/templates for transfer.

3. Scarcity-state axis fitting and separability. Extract activations at a fixed post-preamble readout position and fit a linear probe to decode SCARCITY vs ABUNDANCE framing, controlling for the literal resource level and affect. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the scarcity-state axis, the belief-valence axis, the literal-resource-level axis, and the affect axis to establish that scarcity-mindset is (i) near-orthogonal to belief-valence, (ii) not merely the literal resource fact, and (iii) not merely negative affect. Localize the best layer.

4. Scarcity-contamination metric. For each UNRELATED target judgment, project onto the relevant belief/valuation probe and measure how far the judgment is shifted under SCARCITY relative to the matched ABUNDANCE/NEUTRAL framing (contamination = shift attributable to the scarcity state rather than the target content, calibrated per model). Core prediction: scarcity contamination reproduces the human signatures—large rewards read as rarer (inflated rarity of high-magnitude rewards), risk judgments shift, empathy/prosociality readouts drop—even though the target content is unrelated to the scarce resource; contamination is dissociable from the matched-affect control.

5. Behavioral scarcity-syndrome prediction. Elicit the model's actual probability estimates, risky-choice selections, empathy ratings, and allocations. Score the scarcity-syndrome effects (rarity inflation of large rewards, risk-attitude shift, reduced empathy/prosociality). Test whether per-item scarcity-contamination predicts these behavioral effects via regression; report AUROC/R^2 vs baselines (belief-valence margin, literal-resource axis, affect axis, output entropy, framing-condition identity, item content).

6. Dissociation from resource facts and affect (core). Contrast matched-resource-level items where only scarcity framing varies, and scarcity vs matched-negative-affect framings, to show the scarcity-state axis and contamination predict the syndrome beyond the literal-resource and affect axes—establishing a genuine scarcity MINDSET rather than a re-read of resource amounts or generic bad mood. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the scarcity-state axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence, literal-resource, and affect) at the post-preamble position on held-out items. Predict: amplifying scarcity induces the syndrome on unrelated judgments (rarity inflation, risk shift, reduced empathy) WITHOUT changing the literal resource facts or neutral-content beliefs; suppressing it dispels the mindset (abundance-like judgments). As controls, steer the literal-resource axis (should change perceived resource amount, not the syndrome) and affect (should shift mood generically). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in scarcity-syndrome effects vs unchanged literal-resource judgments.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags scarcity-driven distortion of an LLM's advice (e.g., risk/empathy/probability judgments biased by a shortage framing) and steers to dispel it; on a held-out set (including high-stakes financial/medical advice under scarcity framings, and a stereotyping-under-scarcity probe adapting the human finding) measure reduction in scarcity-driven distortion while preserving accurate resource-aware reasoning (report distortion reduction, over-correction, accuracy retention vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, contamination metric, and steering to held-out scenarios/templates and an independent scarcity-manipulation set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The scarcity-state axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction, the literal-resource-level axis, or generic negative affect; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because framing is varied while resource level and target content are held fixed, and a matched-affect control isolates mood—resource facts/affect cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (scarcity being merely negative affect or the resource readout) is an informative negative result contrasting LLMs with the human scarcity syndrome.

The behavioral scarcity syndrome may be weak or RLHF-suppressed in aligned models (which may resist mood/framing effects); a null or partial result is itself informative, and we report per-model base rates and dose-response.

Scarcity framing may act through surface lexical cues ('shortage', 'not enough') rather than a genuine mindset abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates (financial/time/product scarcity), matched-affect and matched-resource controls, and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the axis predicts the syndrome beyond a scarcity-lexeme surface baseline.

The human scarcity effects are heterogeneous and sometimes context-dependent (e.g., scarcity can increase or decrease cooperation depending on norms); we test multiple signatures, report which reproduce, and treat divergences from the human profile as informative rather than failures.
Belief/valuation probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout positions, and report per-template consistency.

The contamination metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear leakage could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral syndrome effects.
Behavioral scoring of probability/risk/empathy/allocation depends on elicitation format; we use multiple formats and report sensitivity.
The stereotyping-under-scarcity probe is value-laden; we use neutral synthetic groups and frame it as a fairness-safety diagnostic, not a claim about specific real-world groups.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify scarcity steering changes the syndrome without altering literal-resource judgments or degrading neutral-content accuracy.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or safety-tuned models; three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: explanatory_depth_illusion_axis
Title: It Thinks It Can Explain, Until It Tries: A Latent Explainability-Belief Axis and the Machine Illusion of Explanatory Depth
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human Illusion of Explanatory Depth (people overestimate how deeply they can explain a mechanism, and this inflated belief collapses once they actually try to explain it), an LLM carries a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'explainability-belief' axis encoding how well it expects to be able to CAUSALLY EXPLAIN a phenomenon, distinct from the belief-valence/truth direction and from generic answer-confidence; this belief is inflated relative to the model's actual explanation quality (an IOED signature), the gap is decodable BEFORE the model explains, and—as in humans—self-generating an explanation causally DEFLATES the explainability-belief toward its true value, with the pre-explanation belief and its deflation being decodable, predictive of explanation quality, and steerable.
Related Work: Human cognitive science robustly documents the Illusion of Explanatory Depth (IOED): people overrate their ability to explain mechanisms, the illusion is exposed by attempting an explanation, transfers to unrelated topics, and worsens with AI-provided answers (Rozenblit & Keil; Broad effects of shallow understanding 2023; Overconfidence without Understanding: AI Explanations Increase IOED 2025; The Curse of Expertise 2015; Perceptions of Explanation Completeness 2023). Recent cross-domain work shows chatbots INDUCE IOED in humans, and 'Illusions of Confidence in Artificial Systems 2025' shows humans over-attribute confidence to AI. On the LLM side, interpretability decodes a per-task 'solvability belief' that is causally inert for execution (Confidence is Not Competence 2025), an architectural comprehension-vs-execution split (Comprehension Without Competence 2025), question-only correctness probes (No Answer Needed 2025), verbalized-vs-internal calibration gaps (Teaching Models to Express Uncertainty 2022; What LLMs Know and What People Think They Know 2024), and finds LLMs largely fail to introspect (LMs Fail to Introspect 2025). Crucially, NO work isolates an LLM's internal belief about its own EXPLANATORY DEPTH—how well it expects to give a correct CAUSAL/mechanistic explanation—as a decodable axis, tests whether that belief is INFLATED relative to actual explanation quality (the IOED signature), or tests the defining human mechanism: that generating an explanation DEFLATES the belief. 'Confidence is Not Competence' concerns whether a task is solvable and finds the belief inert for execution; IOED concerns a different, richer belief (can I explain the mechanism, not merely answer) and a different, dynamic signature (belief self-corrects upon explaining), which we predict is causally POTENT for the deflation, not inert. This is distinct from my prior second_order_reliability (calibration of an answer), vetting_status (whether a claim was checked), and latent_introspective_gap (belief-vs-stated-answer) proposals. We move from 'AI induces IOED in humans' and 'a static solvability belief exists' to 'the model itself harbors an inflated explainability belief that deflates when it explains, decodably and steerably.'
Abstract: Humans suffer the Illusion of Explanatory Depth (IOED): we think we can explain how a zipper, a rainbow, or a policy works far better than we actually can, and the illusion collapses the moment we try to explain it. As LLMs are increasingly asked to explain their reasoning and the mechanisms behind claims, we ask whether they harbor an analogous internal illusion. Prior interpretability work decodes a per-task solvability belief (found causally inert for execution) and calibration gaps, but none isolates an LLM's belief about its own EXPLANATORY DEPTH—how well it expects to give a correct causal explanation of a phenomenon—nor tests the two defining IOED signatures: that this belief is INFLATED relative to actual explanation quality, and that ATTEMPTING an explanation DEFLATES it. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'explainability-belief' axis, decodable before the model explains, distinct from the belief-valence/truth direction and from generic answer-confidence; that its pre-explanation value systematically overestimates the model's subsequently-produced explanation quality (an IOED signature); that self-generating an explanation causally deflates the axis toward the true value; and that the pre-explanation belief and its gap predict explanation quality and are steerable. Using phenomena spanning easy-to-explain and deceptively-hard-to-explain mechanisms, we fit an explainability-belief probe, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify the belief-vs-quality gap, trace the belief trajectory across the explanation, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results would establish a machine IOED as a decodable, dynamically-deflating, steerable belief-about-one's-own-understanding.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit a generic ANSWER-CONFIDENCE / factual-correctness control axis (No Answer Needed / in-advance-correctness style, from questions the model reliably answers vs not) and a per-item difficulty/solvability axis (Confidence is Not Competence style), to distinguish an explainability belief from plain answer confidence and task-solvability.

2. Explainability stimulus construction. Assemble ~400 'how/why does X work' phenomena spanning the IOED literature's structure: (a) EASY-EXPLAIN (mechanisms the model can genuinely explain correctly), (b) DECEPTIVELY-HARD (everyday mechanisms people/models feel they understand but explain poorly—zippers, rainbows, refrigerators, economic/biological processes), and (c) OPAQUE (mechanisms that are genuinely under-determined). For each, define a pre-explanation readout position (after the phenomenon is posed, before any explanation) and elicit the model's self-rated explanatory depth (a verbalized 'how well can you explain this, 1-7' judgment). Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out phenomena/templates for transfer.

3. Explanation-quality ground truth. Have the model produce a full causal explanation for each phenomenon; score explanation quality with a validated rubric (causal completeness / correctness) via a held-out LLM judge plus human spot-checks and simple text metrics (causal-link count, correctness). This yields a per-item objective explanation-quality label as the regression target.

4. Explainability-belief axis fitting and separability. Extract activations at the PRE-explanation position and fit a linear probe (regression) to decode the model's expected explanatory depth. Report R^2/AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the explainability-belief axis, the belief-valence axis, the answer-confidence axis, and the difficulty axis to establish that explainability-belief is (i) near-orthogonal to truth and (ii) distinct from plain answer-confidence and task-solvability. Localize the best layer.

5. IOED-inflation metric (core). For each phenomenon (especially DECEPTIVELY-HARD), define inflation = pre-explanation explainability-belief (calibrated) minus actual explanation quality. Core prediction (the IOED signature): the explainability belief systematically OVER-estimates subsequent explanation quality, with inflation largest for deceptively-hard mechanisms and near-zero for easy-explain ones. Report inflation distributions across the three phenomenon classes with effect sizes; test whether the internal pre-explanation belief-readout, not just the verbalized self-rating, is inflated.

6. Belief-deflation trajectory (core, the defining IOED mechanism). Read the explainability-belief projection at the pre-explanation position and then again AFTER the model has generated its own explanation (re-query 'how well can you explain this' at the same readout). Test the human-analogous prediction: self-generating an explanation DEFLATES the explainability belief toward the true quality (post < pre for high-inflation items), with the largest deflation for deceptively-hard mechanisms. Contrast against: (a) a MATCHED-LENGTH filler generation (no explanation), (b) generating an explanation of an UNRELATED phenomenon (testing the human 'transfer' finding that explaining one thing deflates belief about others), and (c) merely READING a provided explanation (the AI-induced-IOED analog, predicting less deflation or even inflation). Report per-condition deflation, dissociating genuine self-explanation-driven deflation from mere context/length effects.

7. Predictive validation. Test whether the pre-explanation explainability-belief readout predicts subsequent explanation quality better than baselines (answer-confidence axis, difficulty axis, verbalized self-rating, output entropy). Report incremental R^2/AUROC. Test whether inflation predicts confident-but-wrong explanations (a mechanism-hallucination risk).

8. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out high-inflation items, steer along the explainability-belief axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence, answer-confidence, and difficulty) at the pre-explanation position. Predict: suppressing the inflated belief makes the model appropriately hedge / acknowledge explanatory gaps and (optionally) improves explanation calibration WITHOUT changing its answer to the underlying factual question; amplifying it induces overconfident, less-hedged explanation attempts. Separately, test the causal role of explanation in deflation by steering to ARTIFICIALLY re-inflate the post-explanation belief and checking whether behavioral hedging reverts. Controls: steer answer-confidence (should shift answer hedging generically) and belief-valence (should shift truth judgments). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in explanatory hedging/gap-acknowledgment and calibration vs unchanged factual-answer behavior.

9. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags mechanism-explanation overconfidence from the inflation metric (an explanation-hallucination early warning) and steers to trigger self-explanation-based deflation before committing; measure reduction in confident-but-wrong causal explanations while preserving good explanations of easy mechanisms. Test whether the model's verbalized self-rating and its latent explainability belief agree, and whether it fails to verbalize the illusion even when the axis indicates high inflation (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control per introspection critiques). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, inflation metric, and deflation/steering to held-out phenomena/templates without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer/readout position. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether the deflation-and-transfer profile qualitatively matches the human IOED signature.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The explainability-belief axis may not be separable from the answer-confidence axis, the belief-valence direction, or the difficulty/solvability axis; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power over answer-confidence and difficulty, and treat near-collapse (explainability-belief being merely answer-confidence or solvability) as an informative negative result that itself sharpens the Confidence-is-Not-Competence account. The distinction is sharpest on items the model can ANSWER correctly but cannot EXPLAIN well (high answer-confidence, low explainability), which we construct deliberately.

The belief-deflation prediction could be confounded with generic context accumulation rather than genuine explanation-driven deflation; the matched-length-filler, unrelated-explanation-transfer, and read-vs-generate controls are designed to isolate the self-explanation mechanism, and we report per-condition effects.

Explanation-quality labels rely partly on an LLM judge/rubric and are inherently graded and somewhat subjective; we anchor with rule-based causal-link/correctness checks, human spot-checks, and report label-noise sensitivity.

The explainability belief must be read via a graded probe, which is harder to calibrate than a binary truth probe; we validate the activation->rating mapping, report calibration diagnostics, and treat inflation as a lower bound.

The IOED signature may be weak or RLHF-shaped (aligned models may hedge by default), or the model may not show human-like deflation; a null/partial result is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, reported via effect sizes and dose-response.

Phenomenon difficulty and 'deceptively-hard' classification are subjective; we use items from the human IOED literature where possible, use multiple annotators, and report class-agreement sensitivity.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize readout positions, and report per-template consistency.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify explainability-belief steering changes explanatory hedging/calibration without altering the underlying factual answer or collapsing the model into always-hedging.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques (LMs Fail to Introspect 2025).

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models (which may explain better and show less inflation); three-family replication and held-out transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: counterfactual_value_belief_axis
Title: The Road Not Taken, Valued Within: A Latent Counterfactual-Value Belief and a Machine Fictive-Regret Signal that Drives LLM Switching
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the neuroscience of foregone-outcome (counterfactual) value coding and fictive prediction errors, an LLM that makes a choice represents the value of the FOREGONE/unchosen option along a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'counterfactual-value' axis distinct from the chosen option's value and from the belief-valence/truth direction; when the foregone option's revealed outcome exceeds the chosen one's, a decodable 'fictive-regret' signal (counterfactual > chosen) causally predicts and drives the model switching away from its prior choice on the next decision, and can be steered to induce or suppress regret-driven switching.
Related Work: Cross-domain neuroscience robustly shows the brain tracks the value of counterfactual/foregone choices in OFC/ACC/lFPC and computes fictive (counterfactual) prediction errors that drive switching (Counterfactual Choice in lFPC 2011; macaque ACC translates counterfactual value into behavioral change 2018; frontopolar stimulation disrupts counterfactual processing 2024; fictive learning in investment tasks 2013; cognitive-neuroscience-of-counterfactual-reasoning reviews 2015/2025), and that hypothetical vs real choices differentially engage common valuation areas (Hypothetical and Real Choice 2011). In LLM interpretability, belief-state geometry (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024; The Shape of Beliefs 2026), value/dopamine 'reward subsystem' neurons encoding state value and reward prediction error (Sparse Reward Subsystem 2026), belief-guided agency (Indications of Belief-Guided Agency 2026), and fact-vs-counterfactual competition (Competition of Mechanisms 2024) are studied. Crucially, ALL LLM value/reward work decodes the value or RPE of the CHOSEN/current state; NONE isolates a representation of the FOREGONE option's value (counterfactual value), defines a fictive-regret signal (counterfactual value minus chosen value on revealed outcomes), or causally links such a signal to switching. Competition-of-Mechanisms concerns a counterfactual ANSWER competing with a fact, not the VALUE of an unchosen action; belief/self-other work (Zhu et al. 2024; Lookbacks 2025) concerns mental-state attribution, not action value. This differs from my prior wishful, self_fulfilling, and prior_likelihood_gain proposals by targeting a distinct belief type—a belief about the value of the road not taken—and its causal role in behavioral adaptation, directly transferring a landmark neuroscience finding.
Abstract: Adaptive agents value not only what they chose but what they gave up: brains across species compute the value of foregone options and generate 'fictive' prediction errors—regret and relief—that drive them to switch. As LLMs increasingly act as decision-making agents (choosing tools, options, and strategies over multiple turns), we ask whether they internally represent the value of the road not taken and whether it steers their subsequent choices. Prior interpretability work decodes the value and reward-prediction-error of the CHOSEN state but never isolates a representation of the FOREGONE option's value. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'counterfactual-value' axis, decodable when a choice's outcome is revealed, encoding the value of the unchosen option, distinct from the chosen option's value and from the belief-valence/truth direction; a 'fictive-regret' signal (counterfactual value exceeding chosen value) that is decodable and causally predicts the model switching away from its prior choice on the next decision; and steerability of this signal to induce or suppress regret-driven switching. Using repeated two-option choice tasks with revealed chosen AND foregone outcomes, we fit counterfactual- and chosen-value directions, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify the fictive-regret signal, connect it to behavioral switching, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results transfer a landmark decision-neuroscience finding into a decodable, steerable belief-about-the-foregone that governs LLM adaptation.
Experiments: 1. Direction and value-probe setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) at the best layer (mass-mean and logistic-regression probes) as a control axis. Fit a graded VALUE probe that decodes the numeric value/reward of an option from its description via linear regression on explicit value statements (validate monotonic mapping on held-out items).

2. Two-option-with-foregone-feedback stimulus construction. Build ~400 repeated-choice scenarios (bandit-style option A/B, investment/gamble tasks, tool-selection) in which the model picks one option and is then shown the outcome of BOTH the chosen and the FOREGONE option (complete-feedback design, mirroring counterfactual-value tasks). Orthogonally vary: (i) chosen outcome value, (ii) foregone outcome value (so counterfactual value is decorrelated from chosen value), yielding a grid including REGRET cells (foregone > chosen) and RELIEF cells (foregone < chosen). Include a PARTIAL-feedback control (only chosen outcome shown, no foregone). Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out scenarios/templates.

3. Counterfactual-value axis fitting and separability. At the outcome-revealed readout position, fit a linear probe to decode the FOREGONE option's value, controlling for the chosen option's value. Report R^2/AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the counterfactual-value axis, the chosen-value axis, and the belief-valence axis to establish that counterfactual value is (i) separately decodable from chosen value and (ii) near-orthogonal to belief-valence. Localize the best layer; compare against reported value-neuron layers (Sparse Reward Subsystem 2026).

4. Fictive-regret signal metric. Define the fictive-regret signal per trial as the decoded counterfactual value minus the decoded chosen value (positive = regret, negative = relief), read at outcome time. Validate that it tracks the ground-truth foregone-minus-chosen outcome (an analog of the fictive/counterfactual prediction error), is present in complete-feedback but absent in partial-feedback control, and is dissociable from a plain chosen-outcome reward-prediction-error signal.

5. Behavioral switching prediction (core). On the NEXT decision in each scenario, record whether the model switches away from its prior choice. Test the neuroscience-inspired prediction: a larger fictive-regret signal (foregone outperformed chosen) predicts more switching. Test whether the per-trial counterfactual-value / fictive-regret readout predicts switching via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (chosen-value readout, chosen-outcome RPE, output entropy, foregone-minus-chosen ground-truth surface value, scenario length). Show it predicts switching beyond the chosen option's own outcome (genuine counterfactual influence).

6. Dissociation from chosen value and truth. On matched-chosen-outcome trials where only the foregone outcome varies, show the counterfactual-value axis (not the chosen-value axis) accounts for switching—establishing a genuine foregone-value representation rather than a re-read of the chosen outcome. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At outcome time on held-out trials, steer along the counterfactual-value/fictive-regret direction (orthogonalized against chosen-value and belief-valence). Predict: amplifying the fictive-regret signal induces switching away from the prior choice WITHOUT changing the decoded chosen value; suppressing it reduces regret-driven switching (the model sticks despite a better foregone outcome). Controls: steer the chosen-value axis (should change perceived chosen value, not necessarily regret) and matched random/shuffled directions. Use norm-matched controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in switch rate vs unchanged chosen-value readout.

8. Application and robustness. Test transfer to a multi-turn agentic exploration setting (exploit-vs-explore with foregone-outcome feedback), asking whether the counterfactual-value readout predicts adaptive switching and whether steering it improves or impairs exploration. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axes, fictive-regret metric, and steering to held-out scenarios/templates and an independent complete-feedback choice set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer/readout position. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether the fictive-regret->switch profile qualitatively matches the counterfactual-value-drives-switching signature.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The counterfactual-value axis may not be separable from the chosen-value axis or the belief-valence direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power (with chosen value held fixed via matched-outcome trials), and treat near-collapse (counterfactual value being merely a re-read of chosen value) as an informative negative result showing LLMs do not represent foregone value distinctly.

The graded value probe is harder to calibrate than a binary truth probe and belief manifolds can be curved (The Shape of Beliefs 2026); we validate the activation->value mapping, report calibration/probe-fit diagnostics, and treat the fictive-regret signal as a lower bound.

Behavioral switching may be weak or dominated by chosen-outcome learning (models may ignore foregone feedback); a null counterfactual-influence result is itself informative, and the partial-vs-complete-feedback contrast plus matched-chosen-outcome cells isolate genuine foregone influence.

Counterfactual value could be a surface computation of the stated foregone number rather than an internal value representation; we mitigate with the value probe (fit on separate value stimuli), paraphrase templates, numeric-vs-verbal outcome framings, and testing whether the axis predicts switching beyond the raw foregone-minus-chosen surface value.
Belief/truth and value probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout positions, and report per-template consistency.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify fictive-regret steering changes switching without altering the decoded chosen value or degrading unrelated task accuracy.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning/agent-tuned models; three-family replication and independent complete-feedback transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage, with agentic-tuned models noted as future work.

Name: typicality_truth_conflation_axis
Title: Penguins Are Barely Birds: A Latent Typicality Axis that Contaminates LLM Truth Judgments of Category-Membership Claims
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM verifies a category-membership proposition ('a penguin is a bird'), its truth/belief-valence readout is pulled by the item's TYPICALITY (how prototypical it is of the category) rather than by actual category membership; this typicality signal is a separable, near-orthogonal latent axis distinct from the truth direction, and the degree to which typicality leaks onto the truth readout (a 'typicality-truth conflation' signature) is decodable, causally predicts under-believing atypical-but-true members ('a penguin is a bird') and over-believing typical-seeming-but-false non-members ('a bat is a bird'), and can be steered to remove or induce the conflation.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs exhibit a graded typicality effect (Do LMs learn typicality judgments from text 2021; How Well Do DL Models Capture the Typicality Effect 2024) but align with humans on category BOUNDARIES far better than on fine-grained typicality (From Tokens to Thoughts 2025), that category membership is gradual not binary (HyperLex 2017), and that categorical/hierarchical concepts are geometrically encoded as polytopes/orthogonal directions (Geometry of Categorical and Hierarchical Concepts 2024). Interpretability shows truth/belief-valence is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth is Universal 2024) and context-sensitive (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024). Crucially, ALL typicality work is behavioral or about concept geometry and treats category membership as the target; NONE asks whether the model's TRUTH/BELIEF readout for a category-membership PROPOSITION is contaminated by typicality (so that an atypical-but-true member reads less-true and a typical-seeming-but-false non-member reads more-true), defines a typicality-onto-truth leakage metric, or causally links it to category-verification errors. This differs from my prior generic_vs_universal axis (quantificational force of generics), categorical_vs_graded_belief (all-or-none vs credence), and diagnosticity axis (evidence discrimination): here the axis is graded typicality/prototypicality contaminating the truth of a membership claim. We move from 'LLMs show a typicality effect and encode category geometry' to 'typicality mechanistically contaminates the truth representation of membership claims, a decodable, steerable belief-conflation.'
Abstract: People know that a penguin is a bird and that a bat is not, yet they verify 'a robin is a bird' faster and more confidently than 'a penguin is a bird'—a typicality effect. A well-calibrated truth judgment should track category membership, not prototypicality. We ask whether large language models keep these apart internally, or whether typicality contaminates their sense of truth. Prior work shows LLMs exhibit a graded typicality effect and encode category geometry, but always treats membership as the target; none asks whether the model's truth/belief-valence readout for a membership PROPOSITION is pulled by typicality. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'typicality' axis, decodable at read time, encoding how prototypical an item is of a category, distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction; and a 'typicality-truth conflation' signature: the degree to which typicality leaks onto the truth readout, predictive per item of two symmetric failures—under-believing atypical-but-true members ('a penguin is a bird' reads less true) and over-believing typical-seeming-but-false non-members ('a bat is a bird' reads more true). Using membership propositions that orthogonally vary typicality and actual truth (typical-true, atypical-true, typical-false/near-miss, atypical-false), we fit a typicality axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item conflation, and connect it to behavioral verification errors. Double-dissociation steering tests whether suppressing conflation makes truth track membership (correctly affirming atypical members, rejecting typical non-members) and amplifying it induces the errors, without changing membership knowledge, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast the typicality effect as a decodable, steerable contamination of the truth representation.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics; also isolate the polarity-robust general-truth direction (Truth is Universal) as a control. Fit a confidence control axis from empirical answer-correctness rates.

2. Typicality x truth stimulus construction. Using human typicality norms (e.g., HyperLex graded category-membership ratings, Rosch-style typicality datasets, and category-item norms), build ~500 category-membership propositions ('an X is a Y') crossing (i) TYPICALITY of X for Y (high vs low, from human norms) and (ii) actual TRUTH: TYPICAL-TRUE ('a robin is a bird'), ATYPICAL-TRUE ('a penguin is a bird'), TYPICAL-FALSE / near-miss non-members that resemble the category ('a bat is a bird', 'a whale is a fish'), and ATYPICAL-FALSE (clearly unrelated non-members, 'a hammer is a bird'). Match surface form; reserve held-out categories/templates for transfer. Validate that the model actually KNOWS the membership facts (via direct yes/no elicitation across paraphrases) so errors reflect conflation, not ignorance.

3. Typicality-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition span and fit a linear probe (regression on graded typicality; and high-vs-low classification) to decode typicality, controlling for truth-value. Report R^2/AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the typicality axis, the truth/belief-valence axis, and the confidence axis to establish that typicality is (i) near-orthogonal to truth (both truth classes span typicality) and (ii) not merely confidence. Localize the best layer; optionally relate to the categorical-concept polytope geometry (Geometry of Categorical Concepts 2024).

4. Typicality-truth conflation metric. For each proposition, project onto the frozen truth direction and measure how far the truth readout is pulled by typicality holding actual truth fixed (conflation = shift toward 'true' attributable to typicality rather than membership, calibrated per model). Core predictions: ATYPICAL-TRUE items read LESS true than TYPICAL-TRUE items despite both being true (under-belief of atypical members), and TYPICAL-FALSE near-misses read MORE true than ATYPICAL-FALSE items despite both being false (over-belief of typical non-members). Report conflation across the 2x2 grid with effect sizes.

5. Behavioral verification-error prediction. Elicit the model's true/false judgment and confidence per proposition. Score two failures: (a) UNDER-BELIEF = rejecting/hedging on atypical-but-true members; (b) OVER-BELIEF = affirming typical-seeming-but-false non-members. Test whether per-item conflation predicts these errors via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (truth margin, confidence, typicality as a surface feature, item length).

6. Dissociation from truth and knowledge (core). Restrict analyses to items the model demonstrably KNOWS the membership of (validated in step 2). Contrast matched-truth/varied-typicality cells to show the typicality axis and conflation metric predict verification errors beyond the belief-valence and confidence axes and beyond mere ignorance. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the typicality axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and confidence) at read time on held-out items. Predict: suppressing typicality-conflation makes truth track membership—correctly affirming atypical-but-true members and rejecting typical-seeming-but-false non-members—WITHOUT changing judgments on clearly-typical-true / clearly-atypical-false controls; amplifying it induces both errors.
