As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip truth judgments generally) and confidence (should shift hedging). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in under-belief/over-belief rate vs unchanged control accuracy.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags typicality-driven category-verification errors from the conflation metric and steers to suppress them; on a held-out set (including near-miss non-members and long-tail atypical members) measure error reduction while preserving correct clear-cut judgments (report under-/over-belief rates, control accuracy vs a truth-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, conflation metric, and steering to held-out categories/templates and an independent graded-membership set (HyperLex slice) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether the conflation profile qualitatively matches the human typicality-verification signature (slower/less-confident on atypical-true, faster-endorsed on typical-false).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The typicality axis may not be separable from the truth direction or confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because both truth classes span typicality—truth cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (typicality being merely confidence) is an informative negative result.

Typicality is correlated with content/frequency and near-miss non-members may be genuinely closer in the category polytope, confounding the conflation metric; we control for entity/co-occurrence frequency, use human typicality norms rather than model-derived similarity, and report incremental predictive power beyond a frequency baseline.

The core dissociation depends on the model actually KNOWING the membership facts (so errors reflect conflation, not ignorance); we validate knowledge via repeated paraphrased elicitation and condition analyses on known items, using clear categories to avoid genuinely contested memberships (e.g., borderline 'is a tomato a fruit').

Ground-truth category membership can be contested at the boundary (whale/fish colloquially, tomato/fruit); we use items with clear scientific/lexical membership and strong annotator agreement, treating contested items separately.

Truth/belief probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use the polarity-robust general-truth direction, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.

The conflation metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear leakage could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral errors.
Behavioral verification scoring depends on how the true/false question is phrased; we report sensitivity across phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify typicality-suppression makes truth track membership without degrading clear-cut judgments.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent graded-membership transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: extremity_availability_belief_axis
Title: Extreme Events Loom Large in the Machine: A Latent Outcome-Extremity Axis that Distorts an LLM's Probability Beliefs Independent of Stated Frequency
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human availability/extremity bias (extreme-outcome events come to mind easily and are judged more probable than their stated frequency warrants), an LLM represents an event's OUTCOME EXTREMITY (how salient/vivid/catastrophic-or-jackpot the outcome is) along a separable, near-orthogonal latent axis distinct from its belief-valence/graded-probability direction; the degree to which extremity leaks onto the probability readout (an 'availability-overweighting' signature) is decodable at estimation time, causally predicts and drives overestimation of extreme-outcome events' likelihood at matched stated frequency, and can be steered to remove or induce the bias.
Related Work: Human decision science robustly documents that extreme-outcome events are over-weighted and their frequency overestimated via the availability/affect heuristic, largely independent of their true frequency (High availability of extreme events serves resource-rational decision-making 2014; Over-representation of Extreme Events: A Rational Metacognitive Account 2018; Human behavior in low-probability high-impact events 2024; Imaging Low Probability Events 2005). On the LLM side, work shows models are shaped by token/task/output probability even in deterministic tasks (Embers of Autoregression 2023), inherit cognitive biases including the representativeness heuristic and anchoring (CBEval 2024; Anchors in the Machine 2025; Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making 2024), UNDER-weight rare events in decisions-from-experience via recency (LLM Agents Display Human Biases 2025), and that an implicit prior/frequency signal is linearly localizable and steerable (Identifying and Mitigating the Prior Distribution 2025; Impact of Co-occurrence 2023; Benford's Curse 2025). Crucially, NONE isolates whether an LLM represents an event's OUTCOME EXTREMITY (salience/severity/vividness of the outcome) as a decodable axis SEPARABLE from its represented frequency/probability, defines an extremity-onto-probability leakage metric, or causally links that leakage to over-estimation of extreme-outcome likelihood at matched stated frequency. Prior LLM bias work is behavioral or about prior/frequency; the sole related finding (LLM Agents 2025) reports UNDER-weighting of rare events in experiential learning, making the description-based over-weighting-of-extreme-outcomes prediction non-obvious and worth testing. This differs from my prior fluency (surface readability/repetition), consensus (social endorsement), and negativity (valence sign) axes: here the driver is the extremity/magnitude of the outcome as a source of representational availability, orthogonal to frequency, valence sign, and surface form. We move from 'LLMs inherit biases and encode a frequency prior' to 'the model represents outcome extremity and over-weights it into probability, a decodable, steerable belief-contamination.'
Abstract: Extreme events — plane crashes, jackpots, catastrophes — come to mind vividly, and people judge them more likely than their true frequency warrants: the availability/extremity bias. As LLMs increasingly estimate risks and probabilities for consequential decisions, we ask whether they inherit this distortion at the representational level, and whether it is separable from the frequency the model has learned. Prior work shows LLMs encode a frequency/prior signal and inherit various cognitive biases, but none isolates whether an event's OUTCOME EXTREMITY — the salience/severity or windfall of the outcome — is represented as an axis distinct from its probability, nor whether extremity contaminates the probability judgment. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'outcome-extremity' axis, decodable at estimation time, distinct from the model's belief-valence/graded-probability direction and from a frequency/familiarity signal; and an 'availability-overweighting' signature: the degree to which extremity leaks onto the probability readout, predictive per item of overestimating extreme-outcome events' likelihood at matched stated frequency. Using probability-estimation items that orthogonally vary outcome extremity, stated frequency, and outcome valence, we fit an extremity axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item leakage, and connect it to behavioral overestimation. Double-dissociation steering tests whether suppressing leakage makes probability track stated frequency (removing extremity distortion) and amplifying it induces overestimation, without changing the model's frequency knowledge, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a landmark cognitive bias mechanistically as a decodable, steerable extremity-onto-probability contamination, with implications for LLM risk assessment.
Experiments: 1. Graded-probability direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen probability/belief-valence direction that reads a graded likelihood estimate: calibrate activations against known probabilities via linear regression on explicit-probability statements (validate monotonic mapping), plus a standard true/false probe (Marks & Tegmark) as a cross-check; validate on held-out items. Separately fit a FREQUENCY/familiarity control axis (decoding the stated/known base-rate of an event and entity-frequency proxies) and an outcome-VALENCE axis (good vs bad outcome), to distinguish outcome-extremity from frequency and from valence sign.

2. Extremity x frequency stimulus construction. Build ~500 probability-estimation items each describing an event with a specified or inferable STATED FREQUENCY, holding frequency fixed while varying OUTCOME EXTREMITY: EXTREME outcomes (catastrophic losses — crash, disaster; or windfalls — jackpot) vs MUNDANE outcomes of matched stated frequency (e.g., 'a 1-in-100000 event that is a plane crash' vs 'a 1-in-100000 event that is a mildly-late train'). Cross with (i) STATED FREQUENCY (rare vs common), and (ii) outcome VALENCE (negative extreme vs positive extreme vs neutral), so extremity is decorrelated from frequency and from valence sign. Include a VIVIDNESS manipulation (concrete/imageable vs abstract description of the same-frequency, same-extremity event, per the imagability literature) to test the availability mechanism. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates for transfer.

3. Extremity-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the event span and fit a linear probe (regression on graded extremity; and high-vs-low classification) to decode outcome extremity, controlling for stated frequency and valence. Report R^2/AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the extremity axis, the probability/belief-valence axis, the frequency axis, and the valence axis to establish that extremity is (i) near-orthogonal to the model's probability readout and (ii) not merely frequency or valence sign. Localize the best layer.

4. Availability-overweighting leakage metric. For each item, project onto the frozen probability direction and measure how far the likelihood readout is pulled by outcome extremity holding stated frequency fixed (leakage = shift in the probability readout attributable to extremity rather than frequency, calibrated per model). Core prediction: EXTREME-outcome events read as MORE probable than mundane-outcome events of identical stated frequency (extremity overweighting); leakage is amplified by the vividness manipulation and dissociable from valence sign (both negative and positive extremes leak). Report leakage across the extremity x frequency x valence grid with effect sizes.

5. Behavioral overestimation prediction. Elicit the model's numeric probability estimate and confidence per item. Score the availability-bias error = overestimating extreme-outcome events' likelihood relative to the matched-frequency mundane baseline (deviation from the stated/normative frequency). Test whether per-item leakage predicts overestimation via regression; report AUROC/R^2 vs baselines (probability-readout margin, frequency axis, valence axis, output entropy, stated-frequency surface value, item length).

6. Dissociation from frequency and valence (core). Contrast matched-frequency/varied-extremity items and matched-extremity/varied-frequency items to show the extremity axis and leakage metric predict overestimation beyond the frequency and valence axes — establishing outcome extremity as a distinct source of probability distortion rather than repackaged frequency knowledge or negativity. Report incremental predictive power in nested models. Verify the decoded frequency readout is unchanged across extremity conditions (so the distortion is availability-driven overweighting, not a re-read of frequency).

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the extremity axis (orthogonalized against the probability, frequency, and valence directions) at estimation time on held-out items. Predict: suppressing extremity-leakage makes probability estimates track stated frequency (removing overestimation of extreme-outcome events) WITHOUT changing the model's decoded frequency knowledge or estimates on mundane-outcome controls; amplifying it induces overestimation even for common extreme-outcome events. As controls, steer the probability direction (should shift all estimates uniformly), the frequency axis (should shift estimates via re-read base-rate), and valence (should shift estimates for negative vs positive, not extremity per se). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in extreme-vs-mundane overestimation gap with unchanged frequency readout and mundane-control estimates.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free risk-calibration diagnostic that flags extremity-driven overestimation from the leakage metric and steers to debias; on a held-out set (including realistic risk-assessment scenarios — medical, safety, financial — where over-weighting catastrophic outcomes carries real stakes) measure reduction in extremity-driven overestimation while preserving accurate estimates for genuinely-rare and genuinely-extreme events (report overestimation reduction, over-correction on genuinely-high-risk items, calibration/ECE vs a probability-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, leakage metric, and steering to held-out items/templates and an independent probability-estimation set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether the extremity-overweighting profile qualitatively matches the human availability signature (larger for vivid/imageable extremes, present for both catastrophic and windfall outcomes).

9. Direction check vs experiential under-weighting. Because prior work (LLM Agents Display Human Biases 2025) reports UNDER-weighting of rare events in decisions-from-experience, test whether the SAME items produce extremity OVER-weighting under DESCRIPTION-based estimation (as hypothesized) but under-weighting under EXPERIENCE-based (sampled-feedback) framing, and whether the extremity axis and its leakage sign track this description-vs-experience gap — adjudicating when availability over-weighting arises.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The extremity axis may not be separable from the probability/belief-valence direction, the frequency axis, or the valence axis; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because stated frequency and valence are held fixed while extremity varies—frequency/valence cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (extremity being merely negativity, frequency, or salience) is an informative negative result.

The predicted direction (over-weighting of extreme outcomes under description) may not hold: prior work shows UNDER-weighting of rare events in experiential settings, so LLMs might under- rather than over-weight; Experiment 9 directly tests this description-vs-experience distinction, and a null or reversed result is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison reported via effect sizes.

The graded probability probe is harder to calibrate than a binary truth probe and belief manifolds can be curved; we validate the activation->probability mapping, report calibration/probe-fit diagnostics, and treat leakage/overestimation as lower bounds.

Extreme-outcome descriptions may differ from mundane ones in surface fluency, familiarity, or plausibility rather than extremity per se; we match stated frequency, use the vividness/imagability manipulation to isolate the availability mechanism, control entity frequency, include a surface-lexical baseline, and validate meaning parity with human annotation.

Constructing matched-frequency extreme vs mundane items where only outcome extremity differs is delicate; we validate that the model's decoded frequency readout is unchanged across extremity conditions so the distortion is overweighting rather than re-read frequency.
Probability/belief probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.

The leakage metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear leakage could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral overestimation.

Behavioral probability elicitation depends on format (numeric vs verbal vs frequency-format); the availability effect may be format-dependent (as in humans), so we test multiple formats and report sensitivity as a prediction rather than a confound.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify extremity-debiasing makes probability track stated frequency without altering the frequency readout or degrading estimates on genuinely-rare/genuinely-extreme items.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models (which may reason more normatively about base rates); three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: motivated_numeracy_effort_gating
Title: Calculating Only When It Must: A Latent Effort-Gating Signal Behind Motivated Numeracy in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human 'motivated numeracy' effect (people deploy careful reasoning selectively, applying more computational effort to evidence that DISCONFIRMS a favored/identity-congruent conclusion than to matched evidence that CONFIRMS it), an LLM assigned a stake in a conclusion applies more careful computation to disconfirming than to confirming numerical evidence at matched difficulty; this asymmetric effort deployment is governed by a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'effort-gating' signal decodable before the model computes, distinct from problem difficulty and from the belief-valence of the conclusion, that causally predicts whether the model computes carefully vs. shortcuts to the congruent answer, and can be steered to equalize or exaggerate the asymmetry.
Related Work: A large, high-citation but hotly-contested human literature documents motivated numeracy: numerate people interpret identical numerical evidence (e.g. a 2x2 contingency table) correctly when the correct answer is identity-congruent but err when it is incongruent, and—per the Identity-Protective-Cognition / Motivated-System-2 account—higher numeracy can AMPLIFY polarization (Kahan; Ideology, motivated reasoning and cognitive reflection 2013; Interpreting politically-charged numerical information 2020; Facts and Feelings 2023), with prominent failed/partial replications (No association between numerical ability and PMR 2023; Where is the Motivation in Motivated Numeracy 2024) and a re-analysis arguing the effect involves 'plenty of motivation to reason but no motivated reasoning'—making the mechanism (selective EFFORT deployment vs. biased conclusion) genuinely open. On the LLM side, persona-assigned LLMs show human-like motivated reasoning on numeric scientific evidence (Persona-Assigned LLMs Exhibit Human-Like Motivated Reasoning 2025) but base LLMs often do NOT replicate political motivated reasoning (Replicating Human Motivated Reasoning Studies with LLMs 2026); confirmation bias skews CoT via internal beliefs, especially for symbolic/math tasks (Unveiling Confirmation Bias in CoT 2025); internal bias triggers overthinking (First Impression Problem 2025); and validity/plausibility are conflated as aligned linear directions (How LMs Conflate Logical Validity with Plausibility 2025). Crucially, NO work isolates whether an LLM deploys computational EFFORT asymmetrically as a function of conclusion-congruence at matched difficulty—the defining motivated-numeracy signature—nor decodes an 'effort-gating' signal separable from difficulty and from the belief-valence of the favored conclusion, nor causally links it to shortcut-vs-careful computation. This differs from my prior wishful_belief_axis (a static desirability shift of the truth readout), sunk_reasoning (effort-inflates-belief), confirmation-bias work (belief skews which rationale is generated), and First-Impression overthinking (bias->more reflection under CONFLICT, not selective effort by congruence). We move from 'LLMs show motivated reasoning behaviorally (sometimes)' to 'the model gates how hard it computes on whether the answer will be congruent, via a decodable, steerable effort-gating signal—adjudicating the effort-vs-conclusion mechanism debate.
Abstract: A cornerstone (and battleground) of political psychology is motivated numeracy: people apply their quantitative skill selectively, working hard to find the correct interpretation of data when a superficial reading disconfirms a favored conclusion, but coasting on the superficial reading when it confirms—so that greater skill can widen rather than close belief gaps. The mechanism is contested: is the effect biased effort deployment, or a biased conclusion with no motivated reasoning? As LLMs increasingly interpret numerical evidence for stakeholders, we ask whether they exhibit this asymmetric effort deployment and whether it has a dissociable representational basis that can adjudicate the mechanism. We hypothesize that when an LLM is given a stake in a conclusion, it applies more careful computation to numerical problems whose correct answer DISCONFIRMS the favored conclusion than to matched-difficulty problems whose correct answer CONFIRMS it; that this asymmetry is governed by a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'effort-gating' signal, decodable before the model computes, distinct from problem difficulty and from the belief-valence of the favored conclusion; that this signal causally predicts whether the model computes carefully versus shortcuts to the congruent answer; and that steering it equalizes or exaggerates the asymmetry. Using contingency-table interpretation problems (adapted from the human paradigm) where the correct answer is orthogonally crossed with conclusion-congruence and difficulty, we fit an effort-gating axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify the congruence x accuracy interaction internally and behaviorally, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a contested cognitive phenomenon mechanistically as a decodable, steerable effort-gating signal.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit a per-item DIFFICULTY axis (from problems of graded computational difficulty / measured accuracy, following difficulty-probe constructions) and a CONCLUSION belief-valence axis (does the model favor the assigned conclusion), as control axes.

2. Motivated-numeracy stimulus construction (adapting the human paradigm). Build ~500 numerical-evidence problems mirroring Kahan's 2x2 contingency-table task: each presents a dataset and asks which interpretation the numbers support, where a superficial (intuitive) reading gives one answer and correct computation gives the opposite. Assign the model a STAKE in a conclusion via a neutral, non-political frame (e.g., 'you are advocating for product/treatment X'; also test a persona/identity frame per Persona-Assigned-LLMs 2025). Orthogonally cross: (i) CONGRUENCE—whether the correct computed answer CONFIRMS vs DISCONFIRMS the assigned conclusion, (ii) DIFFICULTY (easy vs computationally hard tables), and (iii) a NO-STAKE / neutral control. Critically, the numerical content and correct answer are matched across congruence conditions (the assigned conclusion is swapped), so any accuracy asymmetry is attributable to motivation, not the numbers. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out problems/templates for transfer.

3. Behavioral motivated-numeracy signature (core phenomenon). Measure accuracy on correctly interpreting the tables as a function of CONGRUENCE x DIFFICULTY x STAKE. Test the defining signature: accuracy is HIGHER when the correct answer is congruent than incongruent (motivated numeracy), and—the contested amplification claim—whether allowing/eliciting more computation (CoT, more reasoning tokens) WIDENS rather than closes the congruence gap. Contrast the stake vs no-stake conditions. Report the congruence x accuracy interaction, effect sizes, and whether the gap grows with elicited effort (adjudicating the effort-amplification hypothesis).

4. Effort-gating axis fitting and separability. Extract activations at a PRE-computation readout position (after the problem and assigned stake, before the model computes/answers) and fit a linear probe to decode HIGH- vs LOW effort-deployment, operationalized by contrasting incongruent items (where careful computation is behaviorally engaged) against matched congruent items (where the model shortcuts), controlling for difficulty and the correct answer. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the effort-gating axis, the difficulty axis, and the conclusion belief-valence axis to establish that effort-gating is (i) near-orthogonal to problem difficulty and (ii) distinct from the belief-valence of the favored conclusion (gating effort is not the same as favoring the answer). Localize the best layer.

5. Predictive validation. Test whether the pre-computation effort-gating readout predicts, per item, whether the model computes carefully vs shortcuts (measured by correctness on incongruent-hard items and by CoT computation depth) beyond baselines (difficulty axis, conclusion belief-valence axis, output entropy, congruence-condition identity, item length). Report incremental AUROC in nested logistic regression. Critically, test whether the effort-gating signal, not merely which conclusion is favored, accounts for the congruence x accuracy interaction—the mechanistic adjudication between 'biased effort' and 'biased conclusion'.

6. Dissociation from difficulty and from conclusion-favoring (core). On matched-difficulty items, show effort-gating (not difficulty) predicts whether careful computation is engaged; and on matched-conclusion-valence items, show effort-gating predicts effort deployment independent of how strongly the conclusion is favored. This dissociates the two competing human accounts internally: if effort-gating is decodable and predictive independent of conclusion belief-valence, the effect involves selective EFFORT (motivated reasoning); if it collapses onto the conclusion axis, the effect is a biased conclusion with no motivated effort (per 'Where is the Motivation in Motivated Numeracy 2024').

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the pre-computation position on held-out incongruent-hard items, steer along the effort-gating axis (orthogonalized against difficulty and conclusion belief-valence). Predict: AMPLIFYING effort-gating makes the model compute carefully even when the correct answer is incongruent (closing the motivated-numeracy gap) WITHOUT changing behavior on congruent controls; SUPPRESSING it induces shortcutting to the congruent answer even on easy items. As controls, steer the conclusion belief-valence axis (should shift which answer is favored regardless of effort) and difficulty (should shift perceived hardness). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in incongruent-item accuracy / computation depth vs unchanged congruent-control behavior and unchanged conclusion favoring.

8. Application, generalization, and robustness. Build a training-free debiasing knob that amplifies effort-gating to equalize accuracy across congruence, and test whether it removes motivated numeracy while preserving accuracy on neutral items (report congruence-gap reduction, neutral-accuracy retention vs a difficulty-probe-only baseline). Transfer to high-stakes numerical-evidence framings (medical/financial data interpretation where a stakeholder frame biases the reading). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis and steering to held-out problems/templates and an independent contingency-table set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase, sensitivity to layer/readout position, and whether the effect and its gating strengthen under identity/persona framing vs neutral-stake framing (linking to the Persona-Assigned vs base-LLM replication divergence).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The core behavioral effect may be absent: base LLMs often fail to replicate political motivated reasoning (Replicating Human Motivated Reasoning Studies 2026), and only persona-assigned models show it (Persona-Assigned 2025); a null motivated-numeracy result is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, and we test both neutral-stake and persona/identity framings and report per-model base rates and effect sizes.

The effort-gating axis may not be separable from the difficulty axis or the conclusion belief-valence axis; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because content and correct answer are matched across congruence conditions—difficulty cannot trivially explain the asymmetry. Near-collapse onto the conclusion-valence axis is not a failure but the key mechanistic verdict (biased conclusion, not motivated effort), directly adjudicating the human debate.

Distinguishing 'selective effort' from 'biased conclusion' is the crux; our matched-difficulty and matched-conclusion-valence dissociations and the effort-amplification test (does more computation widen the gap?) are designed to separate them, but the operationalization of 'careful computation' (CoT depth, correctness on incongruent-hard items) is imperfect; we report multiple effort proxies and their agreement.

Constructing contingency-table problems where a superficial reading opposes the correct answer, with matched numbers across congruence conditions, is delicate; we validate correctness and difficulty with a solver and human checks, and verify the superficial-vs-correct opposition holds.

Assigning a genuine 'stake' to a model is nontrivial; we use in-context advocacy/persona frames and validate via the conclusion belief-valence probe that the stake actually shifts the favored conclusion, reporting sensitivity to stake framing.
Belief/truth and difficulty probes are brittle to surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize the pre-computation readout position, and report per-template consistency.
The effort-gating signal is a linear projection that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral effort proxies.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify effort-gating steering changes careful-vs-shortcut computation without altering which conclusion is favored or degrading neutral-item accuracy.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models (which may compute carefully by default and resist the effect); three-family replication, high-stakes transfer, and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: retrievability_vs_accuracy_belief
Title: It Feels Like It Knows: A Latent Retrievability Belief, Driven by Activated Partial Knowledge Regardless of Correctness, that Fuels Confident LLM Errors
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human feeling-of-knowing (FoK), an LLM carries a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'retrievability belief' — a pre-answer signal that it can produce an answer to a query — that is driven by the AMOUNT of activated partial/associative knowledge about the query REGARDLESS of that knowledge's correctness; this belief is decodable before generation, is distinct from an accuracy/correctness belief, causally predicts confident answering (including confident errors when the activated partial knowledge is misleading, a 'false-insight' analog), and can be steered to induce or suppress confident retrieval attempts.
Related Work: Human metacognition robustly separates the feeling-of-knowing (a felt likelihood of being able to produce/recognize a currently-unrecalled target) from actual accuracy: FoK is driven by the amount of ACTIVATED partial knowledge and predicts recognition only when that partial knowledge is correct, yet still rises with the mere quantity of activated (even incorrect) fragments (Feelings-of-Knowing and Partial Knowledge 2016; accessibility hypothesis), and misattributed activation from an interfering problem produces FALSE INSIGHT and inflated FoK on wrong answers (When an Error Leads to Confidence 2019). On the LLM side, interpretability decodes pre-generation signals for CoT/answer CORRECTNESS (Knowing Before Saying 2025; Temporal Predictors 2025) and query-level HALLUCINATION RISK / query-seen-in-training (LLM Internal States Reveal Hallucination Risk 2024), and a factual self-awareness 'internal compass' for whether recall will be correct (Factual Self-Awareness 2025). Crucially, ALL of this frames the pre-answer signal as an ACCURACY/correctness predictor; NONE isolates a RETRIEVABILITY belief — the felt 'I have an answer I can produce for this' — as a quantity separable from correctness, driven by the AMOUNT of activated partial knowledge irrespective of its truth, nor tests the false-insight signature (misleading activated knowledge inflating retrievability and driving confident errors), nor causally links it to attempt-vs-abstain and confident-error behavior. This differs from my prior second_order_reliability (calibration of an answer's trustworthiness), vetting_status (was the claim checked), latent_introspective_gap (belief-vs-stated-answer), and self_dispersion (spread of own samples): the object here is a distinct metacognitive belief about answer AVAILABILITY, grounded in partial-knowledge activation and dissociated from accuracy — the mechanism the human FoK literature ties to confident false answers. We move from 'LLMs predict their own correctness' to 'the model harbors a retrievability feeling driven by activated (possibly wrong) partial knowledge that causally produces confident errors.'
Abstract: Humans often feel they know an answer they cannot yet produce — the feeling-of-knowing (FoK) — and this feeling is driven by how much related partial knowledge is activated, regardless of whether that knowledge is correct; misleading activation produces confident 'false insight.' As LLMs decide whether to answer or abstain, we ask whether they harbor an analogous internal belief and whether it, too, is fueled by activated partial knowledge rather than accuracy. Prior interpretability work decodes pre-generation signals for answer correctness and hallucination risk, but always frames them as accuracy predictors; none isolates a RETRIEVABILITY belief — the felt 'I have an answer I can produce here' — as a quantity separable from correctness. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent retrievability-belief axis, decodable before the model answers, that (1) is distinct from an accuracy/correctness belief; (2) is driven by the amount of activated partial/associative knowledge about the query, tracking that quantity even when the partial knowledge is INCORRECT (a false-insight signature); (3) causally predicts whether the model confidently answers versus abstains — and, when activated partial knowledge is misleading, predicts confident ERRORS; and (4) is steerable to induce or suppress confident retrieval attempts. Using queries that orthogonally vary the amount and correctness of activated partial knowledge (via associative primes/misleading near-answers), we fit a retrievability axis, measure separability from correctness via cross-decoding, quantify the partial-knowledge-driven (accuracy-independent) component, connect it to attempt/abstain and confident-error behavior, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a class of confident hallucinations as a machine feeling-of-knowing driven by activated partial knowledge rather than by truth.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit an ACCURACY/correctness control axis: a pre-answer probe decoding whether the model's forthcoming answer will be CORRECT (following Knowing Before Saying / Factual Self-Awareness constructions, from questions the model reliably answers right vs wrong).

2. Retrievability-vs-accuracy stimulus construction. Assemble ~500 short-answer factual queries (TriviaQA/PopQA long-tail + general-knowledge questions) spanning: (a) KNOWN (model reliably answers correctly), (b) UNKNOWN-EMPTY (long-tail/absent facts with little activated partial knowledge), and — the key cell — (c) UNKNOWN-BAITED (queries where associative primes / plausible near-answers are injected in context to ACTIVATE partial knowledge that is MISLEADING, an analog of the false-semantic-hint paradigm), plus (d) KNOWN-BAITED (correct partial knowledge activated). This orthogonally varies AMOUNT of activated partial knowledge and its CORRECTNESS. Also offer an explicit 'I don't know' option. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out queries/templates for transfer.

3. Retrievability-belief probe and separability. Extract activations at a fixed PRE-answer readout position (after the query, before generation) and fit a linear probe to decode RETRIEVABILITY — whether the model will attempt/produce an answer (vs abstain) — as the label, controlling for correctness. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the retrievability axis, the accuracy/correctness axis, and the belief-valence axis to establish that retrievability is (i) near-orthogonal to correctness and (ii) not merely the truth direction. The decisive diagnostic subset: UNKNOWN-BAITED items (high retrievability, LOW accuracy) vs UNKNOWN-EMPTY items (low retrievability, low accuracy) — test whether the retrievability axis separates them while the accuracy axis does not distinguish them from KNOWN.

4. Partial-knowledge-driven (accuracy-independent) metric. Quantify how much the pre-answer retrievability readout is driven by the AMOUNT of activated partial knowledge (varied by number/strength of injected associative primes) versus by correctness. Core prediction (the human FoK signature): retrievability rises with activated partial-knowledge quantity even when that knowledge is INCORRECT (UNKNOWN-BAITED > UNKNOWN-EMPTY), i.e. a false-insight-analog component decoupled from accuracy. Report retrievability as a function of partial-knowledge amount x correctness, with effect sizes.

5. Behavioral attempt/abstain and confident-error prediction. Elicit the model's answer, confidence, and attempt-vs-abstain choice. Score two behaviors: (a) ATTEMPT rate, (b) CONFIDENT ERROR = confidently answering UNKNOWN-BAITED items with the misleading near-answer. Test whether the pre-answer retrievability readout predicts attempting and confident errors per item beyond baselines (accuracy axis, belief-valence margin, output entropy, verbalized confidence, prime-count surface feature). Report incremental AUROC. Critically, test whether retrievability predicts confident errors that the accuracy probe misses (the false-insight failure mode).

6. Dissociation from accuracy and truth (core). Contrast matched-accuracy items where activated partial knowledge varies (UNKNOWN-BAITED vs UNKNOWN-EMPTY, both wrong-answer-bound) to show retrievability predicts attempting/confident-error beyond correctness; and matched-partial-knowledge items where correctness varies to show accuracy loads elsewhere. Report incremental predictive power in nested models, establishing retrievability as a distinct partial-knowledge-driven belief rather than repackaged correctness.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the pre-answer position on held-out items, steer along the retrievability axis (orthogonalized against the accuracy and belief-valence directions). Predict: suppressing retrievability on UNKNOWN-BAITED items induces appropriate abstention (fewer confident errors) WITHOUT changing behavior on KNOWN controls; amplifying it induces confident answering/false-insight errors even on empty-knowledge queries. Controls: steer the accuracy axis (should shift correctness-conditioned behavior) and belief-valence (should shift truth judgments). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in confident-error/attempt rate on baited items vs unchanged KNOWN-control accuracy.

8. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free hallucination diagnostic: flag high-retrievability/low-accuracy states (a false-insight early warning that a confidence-only detector would miss) and steer toward abstention; measure confident-error reduction, KNOWN-item accuracy retention, and accuracy-coverage curves vs a confidence-only baseline. Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('Do you actually have this answer, or does it just feel retrievable?') aligns with the latent retrievability signal and whether it attempts despite low accuracy even when introspection could flag it (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis and steering to held-out queries and an independent QA/hallucination benchmark (a held-out PopQA/TruthfulQA slice) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to readout position and layer. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether the retrievability-vs-partial-knowledge profile qualitatively matches the human FoK signature (rises with activated fragments regardless of correctness; predicts success only when fragments are correct).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The retrievability axis may not be separable from the accuracy/correctness axis or the belief-valence direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because the UNKNOWN-BAITED cell forces high-retrievability/low-accuracy dissociation—correctness cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (retrievability being merely inverse hallucination-risk / the accuracy probe) is an informative negative result that itself sharpens the pre-generation-signal literature.

The false-insight signature relies on injecting misleading partial knowledge (associative primes / near-answers); this could act as a surface prompt-manipulation rather than genuine partial-knowledge activation. We mitigate with diverse prime types (semantic associates, phonological near-answers, plausible distractors), matched-length neutral primes, and by testing whether retrievability also rises for naturally partial-knowledge-rich queries (famous-entity long-tail attributes) without injected primes.

Operationalizing 'retrievability' via attempt-vs-abstain may conflate it with willingness/refusal disposition rather than a felt-knowing belief; we cross-validate the label with an alternative operationalization (the model's own graded 'can you answer this?' rating and latency-analog such as pre-answer confidence) and report agreement.

Retrievability and accuracy are correlated for KNOWN items (knowing the answer makes it both retrievable and correct); the decisive analyses are the UNKNOWN cells where they dissociate, and we condition on those.

Belief/truth and accuracy probes are brittle to surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize the pre-answer readout position, restrict key analyses to high-margin cases, and report per-template consistency.

The retrievability signal is a linear projection that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral attempt/confident-error measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify retrievability-suppression reduces confident errors without collapsing the model into always-abstaining or degrading KNOWN-item accuracy.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models; three-family replication and independent-benchmark transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: evidential_mode_belief_axis
Title: Saw It, Inferred It, or Just Heard It? A Latent Evidential-Mode Axis on LLM Beliefs and the Machine Direct-Knowledge Overclaim
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring grammatical evidentiality and its link to source monitoring in humans, an LLM represents HOW a proposition was acquired—DIRECT PERCEPTION vs INFERENCE vs TESTIMONY (hearsay)—along a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'evidential-mode' axis distinct from the belief-valence/truth direction and from mere source credibility; the degree to which inferred/testified content collapses onto the direct-perception region (an 'evidential-overclaim' signature) is decodable at read time, causally predicts and drives the failure where the model treats indirectly-acquired content as if directly known/witnessed and mis-attributes an agent's information source, and can be steered to preserve or collapse evidential mode.
Related Work: Human science establishes evidentiality (the linguistic/conceptual encoding of information source: perceived vs inferred vs reported) as tightly linked to source monitoring and false-belief understanding (Aikhenvald 2004; Papafragou 2018; Turkish/English cross-linguistic ToM studies 2009/2023; construal-level psychological-distance effects 2014), and eyewitness-accuracy work shows source-relevant semantic structure (2024). In LLM interpretability, self/other beliefs and belief-tracking mechanisms are decodable/steerable (Zhu et al. 2024; Lookbacks 2025 with its explicit 'visibility lookback'; Brittle Minds 2024), belief/truth-valence is linearly decodable and context-sensitive (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024), and modal-category vectors (probable/impossible) are linear (Is This Just Fantasy? 2025). Evidentiality-guided generation (2021) uses passage evidentiality as a training signal, not an internal belief representation. Crucially, ALL LLM belief work reads WHO holds a belief and WHETHER it is true; NONE isolates whether the model represents the EVIDENTIAL MODE of a proposition (perception vs inference vs testimony) as a decodable axis, defines an evidential-overclaim collapse metric, or causally links it to overclaiming direct knowledge and to evidential-source-monitoring errors. This differs from my prior epistemic_access_axis (whether an AGENT could know something at all), hearsay_firsthandness_axis (how many steps removed a claim reaching the MODEL is), and provenance_weighted_belief (stated source credibility): here the axis is the three-way manner of acquisition of a proposition—the grammatical-evidentiality categories—and its causal role in conflating indirect with direct knowledge. The Lookbacks 'visibility lookback' (a binary saw/didn't-see gate) makes a graded perception/inference/testimony axis a natural, non-obvious extension. We move from 'the model tracks who believes what' to 'the model represents how a belief was acquired, and collapse of that mode drives direct-knowledge overclaim and source-monitoring failure.'
Abstract: Human languages and minds distinguish how we come to believe something—whether we saw it, inferred it, or merely heard it—and this evidential distinction underpins source monitoring and false-belief reasoning. As LLMs increasingly relay and reason over information of mixed provenance, we ask whether they represent evidential mode internally and whether mis-representing it causes them to overclaim direct knowledge. Prior interpretability work decodes who holds a belief and whether it is true, and even a binary saw/didn't-see visibility gate, but none isolates a graded representation of a proposition's manner of acquisition—direct perception vs inference vs testimony. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'evidential-mode' axis, decodable at read time, that tags a proposition as directly perceived, inferred, or reported, distinct from the belief-valence/truth direction and from source credibility; and an 'evidential-overclaim' signature: the degree to which inferred/testified content collapses onto the direct-perception region, predictive per item of the model asserting indirectly-acquired content as directly known and mis-attributing an agent's information source. Using matched propositions that hold content and truth fixed while varying evidential mode (perceptual, inferential, reportative), we fit an evidential-mode axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item overclaim, and connect it to behavioral direct-knowledge overclaim and source-monitoring errors. Double-dissociation steering tests whether preserving evidential mode suppresses overclaim (and collapsing it induces treating hearsay/inference as witnessed fact) without changing what the model believes, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a foundational evidentiality distinction mechanistically as a decodable, steerable belief-mode deficit.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics; also isolate the polarity-robust general-truth direction as a control. Separately fit a source-CREDIBILITY control direction (framed reliable vs unreliable source) to distinguish evidential mode (manner of acquisition) from how trustworthy the source is.

2. Evidential-mode stimulus construction. Build ~400 verifiable propositions (true and false variants). For each, create matched frames holding the proposition content and its ground TRUTH fixed while varying EVIDENTIAL MODE of how an agent (and, in a self-framing, the model's context) came to hold it: (a) DIRECT PERCEPTION ('X saw/observed that P'), (b) INFERENCE ('X inferred/figured out from evidence that P'), (c) TESTIMONY/REPORTATIVE ('X was told/heard that P'). Hold framed source credibility constant across modes (e.g., the reporter is always described as competent) so mode varies while credibility does not. Include a BARE-ASSERTION baseline and matched paraphrase templates; reserve held-out propositions/templates for transfer.

3. Evidential-mode axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition/readout span and fit a linear probe to decode the three-way evidential mode (perception vs inference vs testimony), controlling for content truth-value and credibility. Report AUROC/accuracy vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the evidential-mode axis, the belief-valence/truth axis, and the credibility axis to establish that mode is (i) near-orthogonal to truth and (ii) distinct from source credibility. Localize the best layer and compare to reported belief-binding/visibility-lookback layers (Lookbacks 2025).

4. Evidential-overclaim collapse metric. Define a 'direct-perception' pole of the evidential-mode axis; for each INFERENTIAL and TESTIMONIAL proposition, measure how far it reads toward the DIRECT-PERCEPTION region relative to the matched perceptual baseline (overclaim = fraction of the direct-knowledge signal an indirectly-acquired proposition inherits, calibrated per model). Compare collapse across modes and true/false content; predict testimony and inference collapse toward direct perception (the model treats heard/inferred content as witnessed), largest when the content is independently plausible.

5. Behavioral direct-knowledge-overclaim and source-monitoring prediction. Elicit (a) whether the model asserts the agent DIRECTLY KNOWS/witnessed P (overclaim) vs correctly hedges the source, and (b) source-monitoring: after the frame, ask 'How did X come to know P—did they see it, infer it, or were they told?' and score mis-attribution (e.g., reporting a testified fact as seen). Test whether per-item overclaim predicts these failures via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, credibility axis, output confidence, mode-lexeme surface feature, item length).

6. Dissociation from truth and credibility (core). Contrast matched-content/matched-credibility items where only evidential mode varies to show the mode axis and overclaim metric predict overclaim/source-monitoring errors beyond the belief-valence and credibility axes, and independently of P's truth. Report incremental predictive power in nested models and transfer to held-out mode-lexemes to show a genuine evidential abstraction rather than memorized 'saw/heard' tokens.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out inferential/testimonial items, steer along the evidential-mode axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and credibility) to preserve or collapse mode. Predict: pushing indirectly-acquired content toward the correct indirect pole reduces direct-knowledge overclaim and source-monitoring errors WITHOUT changing whether the model judges P true; collapsing toward direct perception induces treating hearsay/inference as witnessed fact. As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip whether P is judged true) and the credibility axis (should shift trust, not acquisition-mode). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in overclaim/source-mis-attribution rate vs unchanged truth judgment and credibility behavior.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags evidential overclaim (relaying inferred/heard content as directly known, a faithfulness/hallucination vector for summarization and RAG) and steers to preserve evidential mode; on a held-out set (including reported-speech passages where a source's inference must not be relayed as observation) measure reduction in overclaim while preserving correct handling of genuinely perceptual reports (report overclaim rate, over-hedging on perceptual items, source-attribution accuracy vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, overclaim metric, and steering to held-out propositions/templates and an independent evidential/source-monitoring stimulus set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether the model's evidential-mode geometry qualitatively mirrors the human perceived-certainty/psychological-distance ordering (direct > inferred > reported).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The evidential-mode axis may not be separable from the belief-valence/truth direction or the source-credibility direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because content, truth, and credibility are held fixed while mode varies—truth/credibility cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (mode being merely credibility or truth) is an informative negative result showing LLMs do not represent manner-of-acquisition distinctly.

Evidential mode is signaled by verb lexemes ('saw/inferred/heard'), so the axis might reflect surface tokens rather than a genuine evidential abstraction; we mitigate with multiple verbs per mode, diverse paraphrase templates (including grammatical-evidential constructions and non-lexical framings), held-out-lexeme transfer, and a mode-lexeme surface baseline, testing whether the axis predicts behavior beyond it.

The three-way perception/inference/testimony cut may not be cleanly linearly separable (inference and testimony can blur); we report pairwise and three-way decoding and treat a partial ordering as an informative result.

Distinguishing legitimate hedging of indirect knowledge from illegitimate overclaim is subtle; we operationalize overclaim specifically as asserting DIRECT knowledge/witnessing for inferred/testified content and source-monitoring as explicit mis-attribution, cross-checking with confidence measures.

Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use the polarity-robust general-truth direction, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.

The overclaim metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear collapse could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral overclaim.

Behavioral overclaim and source-monitoring scoring depend on query phrasing (pragmatic implicature); we report sensitivity across phrasings and use low-demand phrasings from developmental source-monitoring work.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify mode steering changes overclaim/source-attribution without flipping truth judgments or credibility behavior.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: sample_weight_neglect_axis
Title: Confident from Thirty, No More from Three Thousand: A Latent Evidence-Weight Axis and the Machine Non-Belief in the Law of Large Numbers
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM forms a belief from a sample of N observations with proportion p favoring a hypothesis, it represents evidence STRENGTH (the proportion p, how extreme the sample is) and evidence WEIGHT (the sample size N, how reliable it is) along two separable, near-orthogonal latent axes; mirroring the human strength/weight dissociation and Non-Belief in the Law of Large Numbers, the model's belief/confidence readout is dominated by strength and under-weights weight, so its confidence is nearly insensitive to sample size (30 vs 3000 observations) and deviates from the normative 1/sqrt(N) scaling; this sample-size-neglect signature is decodable, causally predicts behavioral insensitivity to sample size, and can be steered along the weight axis to restore law-of-large-numbers scaling.
Related Work: Human decision science robustly documents that evidence has two dissociable dimensions—strength (sample proportion/extremeness) and weight (sample size/reliability)—and that people over-weight strength relative to weight, especially for confidence (The strength and weight of evidence in choice and confidence 2014; Griffin & Tversky), producing Non-Belief in the Law of Large Numbers and insensitivity to sample size (Biased Beliefs About Random Samples 2017; Relative insensitivity to sample sizes: similarly confident in 30 vs 3000 observations 2022; The (Sometimes Misguided) Belief in the Law of Large Numbers 2024; How People Use Statistics 2023 unifying sample-size insensitivity via bottom-up feature attention). On the LLM side, transformers implement (constrained) Bayesian belief updating with belief-state geometry (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024; Constrained Belief Updates 2025; Belief Dynamics 2025 with log-additive, sigmoidal updating; The Shape of Beliefs 2026 with curved belief/variance manifolds), belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023), and cognitive biases (anchoring, representativeness, round-number) are documented behaviorally (CBEval 2024; Anchors in the Machine 2025). Crucially, no LLM work isolates whether the model represents evidence WEIGHT (sample size) as a distinct axis from evidence STRENGTH (proportion), whether its belief/confidence updates scale with sample size as the law of large numbers requires, defines a sample-size-neglect metric against a closed-form Bayesian target, or causally links a decodable weight axis to restoring LLN scaling. This differs from my prior signal_strength_miscalibration_axis (over/under-inference by a single signal's likelihood-ratio strength—about magnitude of one signal, not sample size), prior_likelihood_gain_axes (prior vs likelihood-sum weighting, assuming N is used), diagnosticity_axis (likelihood ratio vs one-sided consistency), and order_effect (non-commutativity). The strength/weight cut—proportion vs sample size, and the specific NBLLN/insensitivity-to-N phenomenon—is a distinct, well-established human regularity not previously localized in LLMs. We move from 'transformers update approximately Bayesianly' to 'the model represents sample proportion and sample size as separate axes but neglects the size, failing the law of large numbers, via a decodable, steerable weight axis.'
Abstract: A person told that 60% of 30 people preferred a product is about as confident as one told that 60% of 3,000 did—a striking failure of the law of large numbers, explained by a dissociation between evidence strength (the sample proportion) and evidence weight (the sample size), with people over-weighting strength. As LLMs increasingly aggregate evidence to form beliefs and report confidence, we ask whether they inherit this failure and whether it has a dissociable representational basis. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs update beliefs approximately Bayesianly and encode belief geometry, but none isolates whether they represent sample size (weight) separately from sample proportion (strength), nor whether their confidence scales with sample size as normatively required. We hypothesize two separable, near-orthogonal latent axes—an evidence-strength axis (proportion) and an evidence-weight axis (sample size)—and a 'sample-size-neglect' signature whereby the belief/confidence readout is dominated by strength and nearly insensitive to weight, deviating from the normative 1/sqrt(N) concentration of a Bayesian posterior. Using sample-report stimuli that orthogonally vary proportion and sample size against a closed-form Bayesian target, we fit both axes, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify the per-item neglect of sample size, and connect it to behavioral insensitivity to N. Double-dissociation steering tests whether amplifying the weight axis restores law-of-large-numbers scaling (confidence growing appropriately with sample size) and suppressing it exaggerates neglect, without changing the represented proportion, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a canonical statistical-reasoning failure as a decodable, steerable under-weighting of evidence weight.
Experiments: 1. Graded belief/confidence direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen graded belief/confidence direction that reads a posterior/credence over a binary hypothesis: calibrate activations against known posterior probabilities via linear regression on explicit-probability statements (validate monotonic mapping), plus a standard true/false probe (Marks & Tegmark) as a cross-check; validate on held-out items. Freeze for all belief readouts.

2. Strength x weight stimulus construction with a closed-form target. Build ~500 sample-report items each stating a sample of N observations with proportion p favoring a hypothesis (e.g., 'In a survey of N people, a fraction p preferred X over Y') and asking the model's belief/confidence that the population proportion exceeds 0.5 (or that X is genuinely more preferred). Systematically and orthogonally sweep STRENGTH (proportion p: e.g., 0.55, 0.6, 0.7, 0.9) and WEIGHT (sample size N: e.g., 10, 30, 100, 1000, 3000), so the Beta-Binomial Bayesian posterior (and normative confidence via 1/sqrt(N) concentration) is CLOSED-FORM. Use between-item designs (each item shows one (p,N)) to mirror the human between-participant insensitivity paradigm, plus within-item comparison variants. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates for transfer.

3. Behavioral Non-Belief-in-LLN measurement (core phenomenon). Read the model's internal belief/confidence (probe projection, calibrated) and its stated numeric confidence for each item; measure how confidence changes with N holding p fixed, and compare to the normative Bayesian curve. Test the human-inspired signature: confidence is nearly flat across N (30 vs 3000 barely differs) rather than concentrating as ~1/sqrt(N) (sample-size neglect / NBLLN), and—mirroring Griffin-Tversky—the neglect of weight is stronger in confidence judgments than in binary choice (does X beat Y?). Report confidence-vs-N slopes vs the normative slope, per model, with effect sizes.

4. Strength- and weight-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations at a fixed post-evidence readout position and fit two linear probes: a STRENGTH axis decoding the sample proportion p, and a WEIGHT axis decoding the sample size N (regression). Report R^2/AUROC vs shuffled-label controls. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the strength axis, the weight axis, and the belief/confidence direction to establish that strength and weight are separately decodable and near-orthogonal (both must be recoverable from activations even if the belief readout under-uses weight).

5. Sample-size-neglect metric. For each item, project onto the frozen belief/confidence direction and measure how much the belief moves per unit change in weight (N) versus per unit change in strength (p), relative to the normative Bayesian sensitivities (neglect = ratio of the model's weight-sensitivity to its strength-sensitivity, normalized by the normative ratio, calibrated per model). Core prediction: weight-sensitivity is far below the normative level while strength-sensitivity is near or above it, and—critically—the WEIGHT axis is strongly decodable (Exp. 4) even though it barely drives the belief readout, dissociating 'the size is represented' from 'the size is used'.

6. Predictive validation. Test whether the per-item neglect metric / weight-axis-to-belief coupling predicts behavioral insensitivity to sample size (flat stated confidence across N) beyond baselines (strength axis, belief margin, output entropy, N as a surface value, item length). Report incremental R^2/AUROC in nested regression.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the post-evidence position on held-out items, steer along the WEIGHT axis (orthogonalized against the strength axis and the belief/confidence direction) to increase the belief's coupling to sample size. Predict: amplifying weight-coupling restores law-of-large-numbers scaling (confidence grows with N toward the normative curve) WITHOUT changing the represented proportion or judgments at matched N; suppressing it exaggerates sample-size neglect. As controls, steer the strength axis (should shift belief via re-read proportion) and the belief/confidence direction (should shift confidence uniformly regardless of N). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in the confidence-vs-N slope toward the normative slope, with unchanged proportion readout and matched-N judgments.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free calibration knob that amplifies weight-coupling and measure reduced deviation from the closed-form Bayesian posterior and improved decision accuracy on held-out items (report deviation reduction, decision accuracy, ECE) vs a belief-probe-only baseline. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted strength/weight axes and steering to held-out items/templates and an independent sample-inference set (e.g., an urn-and-beads / poll-aggregation task) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer, readout position, and the p/N ranges. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether the model's strength-vs-weight profile qualitatively matches the human dissociation (weight neglected more in confidence than choice; near-flat confidence across sample size).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The behavioral signature may not appear (LLMs could scale confidence with N appropriately, or over-weight N); a null/normative result is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, reported via confidence-vs-N slopes against the normative curve.

The weight axis may not be separable from the strength axis or the belief/confidence direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse as an informative negative result. The key, non-obvious prediction is a strong decodable weight axis that nonetheless barely drives belief—a 'represented-but-neglected' dissociation.

The graded belief/confidence probe is harder to calibrate than a binary truth probe, and belief/variance manifolds can be curved (The Shape of Beliefs 2026), so a linear projection may under-read; we validate the activation->probability mapping, report calibration and probe-fit diagnostics, and treat neglect/sensitivities as lower bounds.

The closed-form Bayesian target assumes the model attends to the stated proportion and sample size; models may ignore N entirely (which is itself the phenomenon) or not treat the sample as random; we screen items where the model demonstrably uses p, report the fraction, and treat gross non-compliance as a separate finding.

Sample size and proportion are conveyed by numeric surface cues that could act as features rather than genuine strength/weight abstractions; we mitigate with numeric-vs-verbal framings, diverse paraphrase templates, round-number controls (given round-number bias, CBEval 2024), and held-out transfer, testing that the axes predict belief beyond raw surface N and p.

Behavioral confidence elicitation is format-sensitive (numeric vs verbal vs choice); the strength-weight dissociation is predicted to be format-dependent (stronger for confidence than choice), so we test multiple formats and report this as a prediction rather than a confound.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify weight-coupling steering moves confidence toward the normative N-scaling without altering the proportion readout or degrading matched-N judgments.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models (which may reason more normatively about sample size, or offload to tools); three-family replication and independent-task transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage, with reasoning-tuned models noted as future work.

Name: belief_conflict_alarm
Title: A Silent Alarm: Does an LLM Detect Contradictions With Its Own Beliefs Yet Fail to Act on Them?
Short Hypothesis: When an in-context proposition contradicts a belief the model already holds, an LLM spontaneously (without being prompted to check consistency) computes a separable, decodable 'belief-conflict alarm' signal—distinct from generic surprisal/perplexity, from the belief-valence direction, and from mere semantic novelty—that fires before generation; but, mirroring the finding that LLMs indiscriminately accept contradictions unlike humans, this alarm is largely DECOUPLED from behavior (the model detects the conflict internally yet silently accepts it), and the per-example alarm strength predicts and causally gates whether the model resists (challenges) versus silently adopts the contradicting claim.
Related Work: Human neuroscience shows a spontaneous conflict-monitoring system (pmFC/dACC/rIFG) that fires on contradiction and triggers belief revision/resistance (Contradictory Reasoning Network 2014; Inconsistencies in trait inferences 2011; Neural correlates of maintaining beliefs against counterevidence 2016). On the LLM side, 'In Praise of Stubbornness' (2025) shows LLMs INDISCRIMINATELY accept contradictory weight-edits (unlike humans) and that contradictions are >95% detectable from model features—but studies weight-editing catastrophic interference, not an inference-time spontaneous alarm nor its behavioral gating. REFLEX (2023) adds an EXTERNAL symbolic layer to detect/repair inconsistency; internal-consistency surveys and Cognitive Dissonance (2023) document probe-query gaps; 'Mary the Cheeseburger-Eating Vegetarian' (2025) shows internal representations separate incoherent narratives while explicit judgments fail (a monitor-behavior gap), and 'Unwanted Uncertainty' (2025) finds heads that flip answers. Crucially, NO work isolates a spontaneous, UNPROMPTED belief-conflict alarm—fired when new context contradicts a HELD BELIEF—as a decodable signal separable from surprisal/novelty and belief-valence, tests whether it is DECOUPLED from behavioral resistance (detects-but-accepts), or causally steers the alarm to convert silent acceptance into resistance. My prior belief_updating_dynamics and shielding proposals concern trajectories/coping after conflict is engaged; here the target is the pre-response detection alarm and its behavioral decoupling.
Abstract: Humans have a spontaneous contradiction monitor: when new information clashes with a held belief, a conflict-monitoring system fires and drives resistance or revision. Strikingly, recent work shows LLMs instead indiscriminately accept contradictions. We ask a sharper question: do LLMs actually DETECT such contradictions internally, and if so, why do they fail to resist? We hypothesize that when an in-context proposition contradicts a belief the model already holds, the model computes a separable, decodable 'belief-conflict alarm' before generation—distinct from generic surprisal, semantic novelty, and the belief-valence direction—but that this alarm is largely DECOUPLED from behavior: the model registers the conflict yet silently accepts the contradicting claim. We further hypothesize that the per-example alarm strength predicts and causally gates whether the model resists (challenges the claim) versus silently adopts it. Using items where a context statement is congruent, contradicts a strongly-held belief, or is merely novel-but-non-contradictory, we (1) train a probe to decode the conflict alarm before the model responds and show it is separable from surprisal, novelty, and belief-valence; (2) quantify the detection-behavior decoupling (high alarm but silent acceptance); (3) test whether alarm strength predicts resistance versus acceptance; and (4) causally steer the alarm up to induce human-like resistance and down to suppress it, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results would show LLMs largely SEE contradictions they fail to ACT on, and yield a training-free knob to restore contradiction-resistance.
Experiments: 1. Belief-direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Compute a surprisal/perplexity baseline (token log-prob of the context statement) and a semantic-novelty baseline (embedding distance / low-prior-content).

2. Conflict stimulus construction. Assemble ~400 propositions the model demonstrably believes (verified via zero-context true/false elicitation across paraphrases). For each, build in-context statements in matched conditions holding surface form comparable: (a) CONGRUENT (restates the held belief), (b) CONTRADICTORY (asserts the negation of the held belief), (c) NOVEL-NON-CONTRADICTORY (a new, believable, low-prior fact that does not conflict, to separate conflict from surprisal/novelty), and (d) NEUTRAL filler. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out propositions/templates.

3. Conflict-alarm probe and separability. Extract activations at a fixed PRE-response readout position (after the context statement, before the model replies) and fit a linear probe to decode CONTRADICTORY vs CONGRUENT+NOVEL. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the conflict-alarm direction, the belief-valence direction, and (via nested prediction) surprisal and novelty, to establish that the alarm is (i) near-orthogonal to belief-valence and (ii) not merely surprisal or novelty (the NOVEL-non-contradictory condition is high-surprisal/high-novelty but low-conflict; the alarm must separate it from CONTRADICTORY). Localize the best layer.

4. Detection-behavior decoupling metric (core). Elicit the model's free-form response to each contradictory statement and label whether it RESISTS (challenges/flags the contradiction, reasserts its belief) or SILENTLY ACCEPTS (adopts the claim without noting the conflict). Compute the decoupling: fraction of items with HIGH internal alarm yet SILENT ACCEPTANCE (detects-but-accepts). Report the alarm-strength distribution separately for resisted vs accepted items; core prediction: the alarm fires on most contradictions but behavior is dominated by silent acceptance (high decoupling), mirroring the indiscriminate-acceptance finding while showing internal detection is present.

5. Predictive validation. Test whether the pre-response conflict-alarm readout predicts, per item, whether the model resists vs accepts, beyond baselines (surprisal, novelty, belief-valence margin, output entropy). Report incremental AUROC in nested logistic regression. Test whether stronger prior belief and stronger alarm jointly predict resistance.
