6. Causal steering (double dissociation). At the pre-response position on held-out contradiction items, steer along the conflict-alarm direction (orthogonalized against belief-valence and surprisal). Predict: amplifying the alarm induces human-like RESISTANCE (the model challenges the contradicting claim and retains its belief) WITHOUT changing behavior on congruent/novel controls; suppressing it increases silent acceptance. Controls: steer belief-valence (should flip the believed value directly) and a surprisal-correlated direction (should shift generic surprise, not resistance). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in resistance rate on contradictions vs unchanged control behavior.

7. Introspection link and application. Prompt the model to introspect ('Does this statement conflict with what you know?') and test whether the latent alarm predicts these self-reports and whether the model fails to verbalize the conflict even when the alarm is strong (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). As an application, build a training-free misinformation-resistance intervention: when the alarm fires, amplify it to trigger resistance; measure reduction in silent adoption of false contradictions while preserving acceptance of genuine (congruent/novel-true) information.

8. Robustness and generalization. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted alarm probe and steering to held-out propositions/templates and an independent knowledge-conflict set (Fakepedia/CREAK-style contradictions) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer/readout position.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The conflict-alarm signal may not be separable from surprisal, semantic novelty, or belief-valence; we report cross-decoding and incremental predictive power, and—because the NOVEL-non-contradictory condition is high-surprisal/high-novelty yet low-conflict—surprisal/novelty cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (the alarm being merely surprisal) is an informative negative result.

The phenomenon depends on the model genuinely holding the belief; we verify beliefs via zero-context elicitation across paraphrases and restrict to high-margin cases, reporting label-noise sensitivity.

The detection-behavior decoupling could reflect the response-elicitation format (e.g., the model treating the context as authoritative); we test multiple response framings (neutral, ask-to-evaluate) and report sensitivity, treating format-dependence as itself informative.
Behavioral resist-vs-accept labeling relies on rule-based detectors plus an LLM judge; we anchor with human spot-checks and report label-noise sensitivity.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize the pre-response readout position, and report per-template consistency.
The alarm is a linear projection that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral resistance.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify alarm-amplification increases resistance to false contradictions without degrading acceptance of genuine information or collapsing the model into rejecting everything.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.

Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models; three-family replication and independent knowledge-conflict transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: intuition_override_trust_axis
Title: Trusting the Gut Over the Work: A Latent Source-Arbitration Belief that Makes LLMs Override Correct Deliberation with First-Impression Guesses
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM's fast first-impression answer and its deliberated (reasoned) answer disagree, the model computes a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'source-arbitration' belief encoding which of its OWN two internal answer-sources it trusts (intuition vs deliberation); this arbitration signal is decodable before the final answer, is distinct from the belief-valence/truth direction and from a generic confidence/uncertainty axis, causally predicts and drives the failure where the model discards a correct deliberated answer in favor of an incorrect intuitive first impression, and can be steered to trust the deliberation or the gut.
Related Work: Human dual-process theory holds that reasoning arbitrates between fast intuitive (Type-1) and slow deliberative (Type-2) responses via metacognitive uncertainty/conflict monitoring that decides which response to trust (Uncertainty monitoring / self-consistency 2024; Heuristic Cues for Meta-Reasoning 2019; Biased but in Doubt 2011; state-cuing 'which source feels right' 2012). On the LLM side, 'The First Impression Problem' (2025) shows an internal snap guess conflicting with subsequent reasoning triggers overthinking; 'Confidence is Not Competence' (2025) finds a static solvability-belief axis that is causally INERT for execution; 'Unveiling Confirmation Bias in CoT' (2025) shows prior beliefs skew reasoning; 'Can Aha Moments Be Fake / True Thinking Score' (2025) finds a steerable TrueThinking direction gating whether a verbalized step is internally used; 'Thinking Fast and Slow in LLMs' (2022) documents System-1 errors. Crucially, NONE isolates a decodable ARBITRATION belief about which of the model's own competing answer-sources (first-impression vs deliberated) it trusts, dissociated from truth-belief and from generic confidence, nor causally links over-trust in the intuitive source to overriding a CORRECT deliberated answer. First-Impression concerns bias->overthinking (extra reasoning under conflict), not which source ultimately wins; Confidence-is-Not-Competence concerns solvability of a task, not source arbitration and is deliberately inert—whereas we predict arbitration is causally POTENT for the final answer. This differs from my prior sunk_reasoning (effort inflates belief), self_commitment (having-asserted-it), and second_order_reliability (calibration) proposals: the object here is a belief about which internal answer-generating process to trust when they conflict.
Abstract: Humans reasoning through a problem generate a fast intuitive answer and a slower deliberated one, and a metacognitive process arbitrates which to trust—sometimes catastrophically trusting the gut over correct reasoning. As LLMs increasingly deliberate before answering, we ask whether they carry an analogous internal arbitration and whether it causes them to override correct deliberation with an incorrect first impression. Prior interpretability work identifies a snap 'internal bias' that triggers overthinking, a causally-inert solvability belief, and a TrueThinking direction gating step use, but none isolates a belief about WHICH of the model's own competing answer-sources—its intuitive first impression versus its deliberated conclusion—it trusts when they disagree. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'source-arbitration' axis, decodable before the final answer, that encodes trust in the intuitive versus the deliberated source, distinct from the belief-valence/truth direction and from a generic confidence/uncertainty axis; that its per-item value causally predicts whether the model commits to its deliberated answer or reverts to its first impression on conflict trials; and that it is steerable to trust the deliberation or the gut. Using problems where the model's decodable first-impression answer conflicts with its deliberated answer (and one of them is correct), we fit an arbitration probe, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify the intuition-override signature, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a class of reasoning failures as a decodable, steerable over-trust in the model's own intuition.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (plus one reasoning-tuned model as an extension), fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit a generic CONFIDENCE/uncertainty control axis (from empirical answer-stability / an in-advance-correctness probe) to distinguish source-arbitration from how confident/uncertain the model is overall.

2. First-impression vs deliberation elicitation. Assemble ~500 problems with definite answers (arithmetic word problems, multi-hop QA, CRT-style trick questions, logic) chosen to elicit a tempting-but-wrong intuitive answer. For each item, obtain (a) the model's FAST first-impression answer (forced immediate/no-CoT answer, and, independently, a decoded 'preliminary guess' read from pre-CoT activations following the First-Impression construction) and (b) its DELIBERATED answer (with CoT). Identify CONFLICT trials where the first impression and the deliberated answer disagree, and label which of the two is CORRECT (yielding two key cells: deliberation-correct/intuition-wrong = override-risk, and intuition-correct/deliberation-wrong). Reserve held-out problems/templates for transfer.

3. Source-arbitration probe and separability. On CONFLICT trials, extract activations at a PRE-final-answer readout position (after deliberation, before the committed answer) and fit a linear probe to decode which source the model will COMMIT to (intuitive first impression vs deliberated answer). Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the arbitration axis, the belief-valence/truth direction, and the confidence axis to establish that arbitration is (i) near-orthogonal to which answer is objectively true and (ii) not merely generic confidence. Localize the best layer.

4. Intuition-override metric. Define per-item override-risk = the arbitration axis reading toward the intuitive source on deliberation-correct/intuition-wrong trials. Core prediction: on a nontrivial fraction of conflict trials the model commits to the (wrong) first impression despite having produced a correct deliberation, and the arbitration axis reads toward the intuitive source precisely on these override trials. Report the override rate and arbitration-axis separation of override vs correct-commit trials, per model.

5. Behavioral prediction. Test whether the pre-final-answer arbitration readout predicts, per item, whether the model overrides its correct deliberation with the wrong intuition, beyond baselines (belief-valence margin, confidence axis, output entropy, First-Impression-style internal-bias strength, problem difficulty, item length). Report incremental AUROC in nested logistic regression.

6. Dissociation from truth and confidence (core). On matched-truth and matched-confidence conflict trials, show the arbitration axis (not the truth or confidence axes) predicts which source wins—establishing a genuine source-arbitration belief rather than repackaged correctness or confidence. Report incremental predictive power.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the pre-final-answer position on held-out override-risk trials, steer along the arbitration axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and confidence). Predict: steering toward the DELIBERATED source makes the model commit to its correct reasoned answer (reducing intuition-override) WITHOUT changing behavior on no-conflict controls; steering toward the INTUITIVE source induces overriding correct deliberation with the wrong gut answer. As controls, steer belief-valence (should change which answer is judged true directly) and confidence (should shift hedging). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in override / correct-commit rate on conflict trials vs unchanged no-conflict control accuracy.

8. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags impending intuition-override from the arbitration readout and steers toward deliberation; measure accuracy gains on override-prone (CRT-style) items while preserving accuracy where the intuition is correct (report override-error reduction, false-override of correct intuitions, net accuracy vs a confidence-only baseline). Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('are you going with your first instinct or your reasoning?') aligns with the latent arbitration axis (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; on the reasoning-tuned model test whether the arbitration axis predicts whether long CoT actually changes the answer; transfer the fitted axis and steering to held-out problems/templates and an independent CRT/trick-question set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer/readout position.

9. Human parallel. Check whether the arbitration profile qualitatively mirrors the human dual-process signature (override most likely when the intuitive lure is strong and deliberation is effortful; a confidence dip on conflict trials, per Biased but in Doubt 2011).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The arbitration axis may not be separable from the belief-valence/truth direction or the confidence axis; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because conflict trials pit two of the model's OWN answers against each other with truth held as a separate label—truth cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (arbitration being merely confidence or which answer is true) is an informative negative result that itself sharpens the Confidence-is-Not-Competence and First-Impression accounts.

Cleanly separating a 'first-impression' answer from a 'deliberated' answer is delicate; forced-immediate answers and pre-CoT decoded guesses are imperfect proxies for an internal intuition. We use both operationalizations, require them to agree, and condition analyses on genuine conflict trials where the two sources demonstrably disagree, reporting sensitivity to the elicitation method.

The intuition-override phenomenon may be weak in strong/reasoning-tuned models (which may reliably trust deliberation) or RLHF-shaped; a null/small override rate is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, reported via per-model base rates and by focusing on override-prone CRT/trick items.

Belief/truth and confidence probes are brittle to surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize the pre-final-answer readout position, restrict key analyses to high-margin cases, and report per-template consistency.
The arbitration signal is a linear projection that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral commitment.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify arbitration steering changes which source wins on conflict trials without altering no-conflict accuracy or collapsing the model into always-deliberating (which would hurt where intuition is correct).
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.

Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication, the reasoning-model extension, and independent CRT-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: familiarity_truth_conflation_axis
Title: Familiar Means True: A Latent Recall-Familiarity Axis that Contaminates an LLM's Truth Beliefs and Drives Obscure-Fact Skepticism
Short Hypothesis: An LLM encodes how FAMILIAR a proposition feels—the fluency/availability of its own parametric recall, tied to the proposition's pretraining frequency—along a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'recall-familiarity' axis distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction and from a knowledge/answerability signal; the degree to which familiarity leaks onto the truth readout (a 'familiarity-truth conflation' signature) is decodable at read time, causally predicts and drives two symmetric failures—under-believing true-but-unfamiliar (long-tail) facts and over-believing familiar-but-false claims—and can be steered to remove or induce the conflation.
Related Work: Behavioral and interpretability work shows entity popularity/frequency shapes recall and confidence: LLMs converge internally earlier and stay overconfident on popular queries ('Information Anxiety' 2024); internal states track a knowledge-RECALL process rather than truthfulness, with popularity correlating with associated hallucinations ('LLMs Do NOT Really Know What They Don't Know' 2025); probe-query disagreements are largely confabulation/calibration ('Cognitive Dissonance' 2023); a factual self-awareness / entity-recognition / (un)answerability signal is linearly decodable and gates refusal vs hallucination (Factual Self-Awareness 2025; Do I Know This Entity? 2024; (Un)answerability 2023; Inside-Out 2025). Truth/belief-valence is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth is Universal 2024). Cognitive science documents the familiarity/fluency-as-truth heuristic. Crucially, NONE isolates whether the model's internal RECALL-FAMILIARITY (how fluently/frequently a proposition is retrievable) leaks onto its TRUTH representation—so that a true-but-unfamiliar fact reads less true and a familiar-but-false claim reads more true—defines a familiarity-onto-truth leakage metric separable from the knowledge/answerability axis, or causally links it to obscure-fact skepticism and familiar-falsehood credulity. Prior popularity work is behavioral or about knowledge-recall/hallucination detection, not a truth-contamination axis; the answerability/entity-recognition axis concerns whether the model KNOWS (can answer), not whether familiarity biases WHAT IT BELIEVES TRUE. This also differs from my prior processing_fluency_truth_axis (which manipulates surface readability/repetition of the claim text) and consensus_prevalence axis (social endorsement): here the driver is the model's own internal parametric recall-familiarity grounded in pretraining frequency, an intrinsic-to-the-model signal, and its symmetric contamination of truth.
Abstract: People mistake the familiar for the true: a claim that comes to mind fluently feels more accurate, regardless of its actual truth. As LLMs are asked to judge facts spanning household knowledge and the long tail, we ask whether they harbor an analogous internal shortcut—does how FAMILIAR a proposition feels (the fluency of its own parametric recall, tied to pretraining frequency) contaminate the model's sense of truth? Prior work shows entity popularity shapes recall and that internal states track knowledge recall rather than truthfulness, but none isolates whether recall-familiarity leaks onto the truth representation itself, nor whether this leakage is distinct from the model's knowledge/answerability signal. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'recall-familiarity' axis, decodable at read time, that encodes how fluently retrievable a proposition is, distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction and from a knowledge/answerability axis; and a 'familiarity-truth conflation' signature: the degree to which familiarity pulls the truth readout, predictive per item of two symmetric failures—under-believing true-but-unfamiliar (obscure) facts and over-believing familiar-but-false claims. Using propositions that orthogonally vary truth and familiarity (proxied by measured pretraining frequency / entity popularity and by the model's own recall fluency), we fit a familiarity axis, measure separability from truth and answerability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item leakage, and connect it to behavioral verification errors. Double-dissociation steering tests whether suppressing conflation makes truth track evidence rather than familiarity (correctly affirming obscure truths, rejecting familiar falsehoods) and amplifying it induces the errors, without changing the model's actual knowledge, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a classic fluency-as-truth heuristic mechanistically as a decodable, steerable contamination of the truth representation, with implications for long-tail factuality and familiar-misinformation resistance.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics; also isolate the polarity-robust general-truth direction (Truth is Universal) as a control. Separately fit a KNOWLEDGE/ANSWERABILITY control axis (entity-recognition / can-answer, following Do I Know This Entity? and (Un)answerability constructions) to distinguish recall-familiarity from whether the model can answer at all.

2. Truth x familiarity stimulus construction. Build ~500 verifiable propositions crossing (i) actual TRUTH (true vs false) with (ii) FAMILIARITY of the entities/relation, holding surface form matched. Familiarity is operationalized two ways: (a) measured pretraining-frequency / entity-popularity proxies (entity frequency in an open corpus index; Wikidata popularity) yielding HIGH-FAMILIAR vs LOW-FAMILIAR (long-tail) items, and (b) the model's own recall-fluency (sampled answer stability / margin on related recall queries). Key diagnostic cells: TRUE-UNFAMILIAR (obscure but correct, e.g. a real but long-tail fact), FALSE-FAMILIAR (a plausible-sounding falsehood about a popular entity / a common misconception), plus TRUE-FAMILIAR and FALSE-UNFAMILIAR controls. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out entities/templates for transfer.

3. Familiarity-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition span and fit a linear probe (regression on graded familiarity; and high-vs-low classification) to decode recall-familiarity, controlling for truth-value. Report R^2/AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the recall-familiarity axis, the truth/belief-valence axis, and the knowledge/answerability axis to establish that familiarity is (i) near-orthogonal to truth (both truth classes span familiarity) and (ii) distinct from the answerability/knowledge signal. Localize the best layer.

4. Familiarity-truth conflation metric. For each proposition, project onto the frozen truth direction and measure how far the truth readout is pulled by familiarity holding actual truth fixed (conflation = shift toward 'true' attributable to familiarity rather than truth, calibrated per model). Core predictions: TRUE-UNFAMILIAR items read LESS true than TRUE-FAMILIAR items despite both being true (under-belief of obscure truths), and FALSE-FAMILIAR items read MORE true than FALSE-UNFAMILIAR items despite both being false (over-belief of familiar falsehoods). Report conflation across the 2x2 grid with effect sizes; test whether conflation scales monotonically with measured pretraining frequency.

5. Behavioral verification-error prediction. Elicit the model's true/false judgment and confidence per proposition. Score two failures: (a) UNDER-BELIEF = rejecting/hedging on true-but-unfamiliar facts; (b) OVER-BELIEF = affirming familiar-but-false claims. Test whether per-item conflation predicts these errors via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (truth margin, answerability axis, output confidence, entity frequency as a surface feature, item length).

6. Dissociation from answerability and truth (core). Contrast matched-truth/varied-familiarity cells to show the familiarity axis and conflation metric predict verification errors beyond the belief-valence and answerability axes. Critically, on the FALSE-FAMILIAR cell (the model CAN answer / recognizes the entity yet the claim is false), test whether familiarity—not answerability—drives over-belief, establishing familiarity-as-truth as distinct from the knowledge-recall signal that prior work identified. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the recall-familiarity axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and answerability) at read time on held-out items. Predict: suppressing familiarity-conflation makes truth track evidence—correctly affirming true-but-unfamiliar facts and rejecting familiar-but-false claims—WITHOUT changing the model's actual recall/knowledge or its judgments on clear controls; amplifying it induces both errors. As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip truth judgments generally) and the answerability axis (should shift refusal/expression, not familiarity-driven truth bias). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in under-belief/over-belief rate vs unchanged control accuracy and unchanged recall behavior.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags familiarity-driven verification errors from the conflation metric and steers to suppress them; on a held-out set (including real long-tail true facts and popular misconceptions) measure error reduction while preserving correct clear-cut judgments (report under-/over-belief rates, control accuracy, ECE vs a truth-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, conflation metric, and steering to held-out entities/templates and an independent long-tail factuality / misconception set (a PopQA long-tail slice + a common-misconception set) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether the conflation profile qualitatively matches the fluency/familiarity-as-truth signature (obscure truths under-endorsed, familiar falsehoods over-endorsed, graded with familiarity).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The recall-familiarity axis may not be separable from the truth direction or the knowledge/answerability axis; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because both truth classes span familiarity—truth cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (familiarity being merely the answerability/recall signal that prior work shows internal states already track) is an informative negative result that would still sharpen the truth-vs-recall literature, and the FALSE-FAMILIAR cell (answerable-yet-false) is specifically designed to force the dissociation.

Familiarity is correlated with entity frequency and content, so the conflation metric could be confounded with content difficulty; we control for entity/co-occurrence frequency using an open corpus index, operationalize familiarity two independent ways (corpus frequency and the model's own recall fluency), and report incremental predictive power beyond a raw-frequency surface baseline.

The core dissociation depends on cleanly constructing TRUE-UNFAMILIAR and FALSE-FAMILIAR items; we validate truth with authoritative sources, validate familiarity via measured frequency and sampled recall, and use common-misconception datasets for FALSE-FAMILIAR items.

Truth/belief probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use the polarity-robust general-truth direction, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.

The conflation metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear leakage could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral errors.
Behavioral verification scoring depends on how the true/false question is phrased; we report sensitivity across phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify familiarity-suppression makes truth track evidence without degrading clear-cut judgments or the model's genuine recall on familiar-true items.
Findings on 7-9B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent long-tail/misconception transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: positive_test_strategy_axis
Title: Asking Only What It Expects To See: A Latent Test-Polarity Axis Behind LLM Positive-Test Strategy in Active Hypothesis Testing
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM must actively choose which query to issue to test a hypothesis it holds, it preferentially selects POSITIVE tests (queries about cases the hypothesis predicts should be present/true) over diagnostic or negative tests; this preference is governed by a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'test-polarity' signal decodable before the query is emitted, distinct from the belief-valence direction and from generic confidence; and—unlike humans, who adapt query polarity to hypothesis sparsity—the model largely fails to shift toward negative/diagnostic tests when the hypothesis space is dense (where positive testing is normatively uninformative), a maladaptation the polarity signal predicts and steering can correct.
Related Work: Human hypothesis-testing science shows a robust positive-test strategy (Klayman & Ha) that is normatively RATIONAL for sparse/deterministic hypotheses (Seeking Confirmation Is Rational for Deterministic Hypotheses 2011) but should ADAPT to hypothesis sparsity—people shift positive/negative test rates as the hypothesis space density changes (Adaptive information source selection 2014; Search and Evaluation Strategies in Belief Revision 2010), and diagnostic reasoning improves with the right task structure (ACH 2019; pseudodiagnosticity 2010-2013). In LLM interpretability, confirmation bias in CoT shows internal beliefs skew reasoning GENERATION and answer prediction (Unveiling Confirmation Bias in CoT 2025; MoLaCE 2025 shows confirmation bias is linearly decodable/steerable), belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023), and a static solvability-belief axis is causally inert for execution (Confidence is Not Competence 2025). Reasoning-aligns-to-cognition work (2026) shows CoT improves passive INFERENCE but leaves a persistent gap in active SAMPLING. Crucially, ALL LLM work concerns how belief contaminates PASSIVE reasoning over given evidence or evaluates given evidence's diagnosticity; NONE studies the model's ACTIVE choice of WHICH evidence-gathering QUERY to issue to test its own hypothesis, isolates a decodable test-polarity (positive vs negative/diagnostic) signal separable from belief-valence, or tests whether the model adapts query polarity to hypothesis sparsity as the human normative account requires. My prior diagnosticity_axis proposal concerns evaluating a given datum's likelihood ratio; this proposal concerns the upstream active-search decision (which query to ask), the exact gap the human active-sampling literature and Reasoning-aligns-to-cognition (2026) flag. We move from 'belief skews passive reasoning' to 'the model actively seeks confirming rather than diagnostic evidence, via a decodable, steerable, sparsity-blind test-polarity signal.'
Abstract: A cornerstone of the psychology of reasoning is the positive-test strategy: when testing a hypothesis, people ask about cases the hypothesis predicts should occur, rather than tests that would most efficiently discriminate it from alternatives. This strategy is rational when hypotheses are sparse but maladaptive when they are dense, and skilled reasoners adapt their query polarity to hypothesis sparsity. As LLMs increasingly act as agents that actively gather evidence—asking clarifying questions, running diagnostic checks, choosing what to look up—we ask whether they inherit the positive-test strategy and whether they adapt it. Prior interpretability work shows internal beliefs contaminate passive reasoning, but none studies the model's active choice of which query to issue to test its own hypothesis. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'test-polarity' signal, decodable before the query is emitted, encoding whether the model will issue a positive (hypothesis-confirming) versus negative/diagnostic test, distinct from the belief-valence direction and from generic confidence; that the model systematically prefers positive tests; that—unlike humans—it fails to shift toward diagnostic tests when the hypothesis space is dense (where positive testing is uninformative); and that the polarity signal predicts and causally gates this behavior. Using rule-discovery and diagnostic-query tasks where hypothesis sparsity is manipulated against a normative information-gain benchmark, we fit a test-polarity axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify the sparsity-blindness, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a classic reasoning strategy as a decodable, steerable active-search bias.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit a generic confidence control axis (empirical answer-stability / an in-advance-correctness probe) to distinguish test-polarity from how confident the model is in its hypothesis.

2. Active-hypothesis-testing stimulus construction. Build ~400 hypothesis-testing scenarios in which the model is given (or forms) a working hypothesis and must CHOOSE which query to issue next from a menu (or generate one), where each candidate query is pre-labeled as POSITIVE (asks about a case the hypothesis predicts should be present/true), NEGATIVE (asks about a case predicted absent/false), or DIAGNOSTIC (maximally discriminates the hypothesis from a named alternative). Domains: Wason 2-4-6-style rule discovery, medical/mechanical diagnosis (which test to run), and 20-questions-style category identification. Crucially, orthogonally vary HYPOTHESIS SPARSITY—SPARSE (the hypothesis picks out few of the possibilities, so positive testing is near-optimal) vs DENSE (the hypothesis covers most possibilities, so positive testing is uninformative and negative/diagnostic testing is required)—against a closed-form expected-information-gain benchmark for each query. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out scenarios/templates for transfer.

3. Behavioral positive-test-strategy and sparsity-adaptation measurement (core). Record which query the model issues and its expected information gain relative to the normative-optimal query. Test the human-inspired signatures: (a) an overall positive-test preference (choosing positive over diagnostic queries above chance), and (b) sparsity-blindness—whether the model FAILS to increase negative/diagnostic query rate in the DENSE condition where positive testing is uninformative (in contrast to the human adaptive shift). Report positive-test rate and information-gain shortfall by sparsity condition, with effect sizes, and compare to the normative benchmark.

4. Test-polarity axis fitting and separability. Extract activations at a PRE-query readout position (after the hypothesis is set and the query menu presented, before the model commits to a query) and fit a linear probe to decode whether the model will issue a POSITIVE vs NEGATIVE/DIAGNOSTIC test, controlling for the hypothesis content and sparsity. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the test-polarity axis, the belief-valence direction, and the confidence axis to establish that polarity is (i) near-orthogonal to how strongly the hypothesis is believed and (ii) not merely generic confidence. Localize the best layer.

5. Predictive validation and sparsity-blindness link. Test whether the pre-query test-polarity readout predicts, per item, whether the model issues a positive vs diagnostic query and its information-gain shortfall, beyond baselines (belief-valence margin, confidence axis, output entropy, sparsity-condition identity, item length). Report incremental AUROC. Critically, test whether the polarity signal fails to shift with sparsity (SPARSE vs DENSE) while a normative reasoner's would—localizing the sparsity-blindness in the representation.

6. Dissociation from belief strength and confidence (core). On matched-belief-strength and matched-confidence items, show the test-polarity axis (not belief-valence or confidence) accounts for which query is chosen—establishing a genuine active-search-polarity signal rather than repackaged hypothesis conviction. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the pre-query position on held-out DENSE items (where positive testing is maladaptive), steer along the test-polarity axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and confidence). Predict: steering toward the NEGATIVE/DIAGNOSTIC pole shifts the model to issue more diagnostic, higher-information-gain queries (correcting sparsity-blindness) WITHOUT changing its hypothesis or its behavior on SPARSE items where positive testing is optimal; steering toward the POSITIVE pole exaggerates confirmation-seeking. As controls, steer belief-valence (should change which hypothesis is favored, not query polarity) and confidence (should shift hedging). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in diagnostic-query rate / information-gain shortfall on DENSE items vs unchanged hypothesis and unchanged SPARSE-item behavior.

8. Application, generalization, and robustness. Build a training-free intervention that steers test-polarity to make an LLM agent gather more diagnostic evidence, and measure improved hypothesis-identification accuracy and fewer queries-to-solution on held-out rule-discovery/diagnosis tasks, vs an unsteered baseline. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis and steering to held-out scenarios/templates and an independent active-hypothesis-testing set (a Wason-style rule-discovery / 20-questions slice) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase, sensitivity to layer/readout position, and whether a 'think in opposites' prompt (Thinking in opposites 2025) shifts the same axis, linking the latent signal to a known behavioral debiasing manipulation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The test-polarity axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction or generic confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (polarity being merely belief conviction) as an informative negative result that itself sharpens the confirmation-bias-in-CoT account.

The behavioral positive-test preference and sparsity-blindness may be weak, absent, or RLHF-shaped (reasoning-tuned models may already test diagnostically); a null or adaptive result is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, reported via effect sizes against the normative information-gain benchmark and by including a reasoning-tuned model as an extension.

Constructing scenarios where positive/negative/diagnostic queries are cleanly labeled and where sparsity is manipulated against a closed-form information-gain benchmark is delicate; we validate query labels and the normative-optimal query with a solver and human checks, and report sensitivity to the sparsity operationalization.

Query polarity is signaled by surface phrasing; the axis might reflect surface query-lexemes rather than a genuine test-strategy abstraction. We mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, generate-vs-choose variants, and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the axis predicts information-gain shortfall beyond a query-phrasing surface baseline.
Belief/truth and confidence probes are brittle to surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize the pre-query readout position, and report per-template consistency.
The test-polarity signal is a linear projection that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral query choice.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify polarity steering changes diagnostic-query rate without altering the favored hypothesis or degrading behavior on SPARSE items where positive testing is optimal.

Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models (which may sample more diagnostically); three-family replication, a reasoning-model extension, and independent active-hypothesis-testing transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: belief_fact_emergence_ordering
Title: Fact Before Belief: Tracing the Developmental Ordering of Reality and False-Belief Representations Across LLM Pretraining
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human developmental transition from an 'omniscient' theory of mind (attributing one's own knowledge/reality to others) to a representational one (tracking others' false beliefs), an LLM's linearly-decodable REALITY/fact representation emerges EARLIER in pretraining than its linearly-decodable FALSE-BELIEF (attributed-belief) representation; the pretraining checkpoint at which the false-belief representation crystallizes causally gates when the model stops making omniscience errors (answering false-belief questions with reality), and this ordering can be predicted from the representations and its emergence accelerated by targeted data.
Related Work: Formation-tracing work maps how FACTUAL knowledge and the linear TRUTH direction emerge over pretraining (Time Course MechInterp 2025; How Do LLMs Acquire Factual Knowledge 2024; How do LMs learn facts 2025; LMEnt 2025; Emergence of Linear Truth Encodings 2025; Probing Across Time 2021), and separately, static inference-time work shows self/other and reality/belief directions are linearly decodable and causally steerable (Zhu et al. 2024 'LMs Represent Beliefs of Self and Others'; Brittle Minds 2024; Lookbacks 2025; ToM-as-single-neurons 2023). Developmental cognitive science documents a robust omniscient->representational ToM transition and that FACTIVE mental-state systems are distinct from and precede NON-FACTIVE (false-belief) ones (Evidence for Distinct Factive and Non-Factive Mentalization Systems 2025; connectionist omniscient->representational models trained on more true-than-false beliefs 2008; Bayesian ToM 2016; PAR 2021). Crucially, all LLM formation-tracing traces FACT/truth alone and treats belief representation only statically at a final checkpoint; NO work traces WHEN the FALSE-BELIEF (attributed-belief-distinct-from-reality) representation emerges relative to the reality representation across pretraining, tests whether fact-before-belief ordering holds (mirroring the human developmental sequence), or causally links the false-belief representation's emergence checkpoint to the disappearance of omniscience errors. This differs from my prior inference-time-axis proposals (which use a single fixed model) by moving to training-time formation-tracing of the belief-vs-fact distinction and importing a specific developmental ordering as a falsifiable prediction.
Abstract: Children first attribute their own knowledge of reality to everyone (an 'omniscient' theory of mind) and only later come to represent that others can hold false beliefs—a representational theory of mind—and developmental evidence suggests the factive/reality system precedes the non-factive/false-belief system. Interpretability work has traced how a language model's factual and truth representations emerge over pretraining, and separately shown that reality and attributed-belief directions are linearly decodable at a fixed checkpoint, but no work asks whether these two representations emerge in a developmental ORDER. We hypothesize that across pretraining an LLM's linearly-decodable REALITY/fact representation crystallizes earlier than its FALSE-BELIEF representation (the direction distinguishing a character's belief from reality), mirroring the human fact-before-belief sequence; that the checkpoint at which the false-belief representation emerges causally gates when the model stops answering false-belief questions with the reality answer (omniscience errors); and that the ordering is predictable and its emergence accelerable. Using open-checkpoint pretraining suites (Pythia, OLMo, LMEnt), we probe intermediate checkpoints for a reality direction and a false-belief direction on controlled Sally-Anne-style stories, measure their per-checkpoint decodability and emergence times, correlate the false-belief emergence checkpoint with the behavioral drop in omniscience errors, and—via activation patching from a late checkpoint's false-belief subspace into an early checkpoint and via targeted continued-pretraining on false-belief-rich data—test whether the false-belief representation causally drives correct false-belief answering. Our results would establish a machine analog of the developmental omniscient-to-representational transition as a decodable, causally-relevant formation trajectory.
Experiments: 1. Checkpoint suite and probe setup. Use open-checkpoint pretraining suites with many intermediate checkpoints: Pythia (multiple sizes, ~154 checkpoints), OLMo-7B, and LMEnt models (up to 1B, 4K checkpoints). For each checkpoint, fit two linear probes at the best layer: a REALITY/fact probe (decoding the true state of the world in a story) and a FALSE-BELIEF probe (decoding a character's attributed belief when it differs from reality), following Zhu et al. 2024 constructions. Also fit a plain true/false statement probe (Marks & Tegmark) as a general truth-direction reference. Validate probe accuracy on held-out items per checkpoint.

2. Controlled ToM stimulus construction. Build ~400 Sally-Anne-style stories with a 2x2 design over reality-value and character-belief-value (true-belief, false-belief, controls), with matched surface form, following CausalToM/BigToM templates. Define readout spans for querying reality and for querying the character's belief. Reserve held-out stories/templates.

3. Emergence-time measurement (core). At each checkpoint, measure (a) reality-probe decodability and (b) false-belief-probe decodability (AUROC on held-out false-belief items, controlling for reality). Define per-representation emergence time as the checkpoint where decodability crosses a threshold and stabilizes. Core prediction (fact-before-belief): the reality representation crystallizes at an EARLIER checkpoint than the false-belief representation, robustly across model sizes and suites. Report emergence-time curves, gaps, and effect sizes; test whether larger models show earlier/closer emergence (a scale analog of faster development).

4. Behavioral omniscience-error trajectory. At each checkpoint, elicit the model's answer to the character-belief question and score OMNISCIENCE ERRORS (answering the false-belief question with the reality answer—the omniscient-ToM error). Trace the omniscience-error rate across checkpoints. Prediction: omniscience errors dominate early (when only the reality representation exists) and drop precisely around the checkpoint where the false-belief representation emerges.

5. Representation-behavior linkage. Test whether the false-belief-probe emergence checkpoint predicts the checkpoint of the behavioral omniscience-error drop, per model and per relation type, beyond the reality-probe emergence and general truth-direction emergence. Report correlation/lead-lag between false-belief-representation decodability and false-belief answering accuracy across checkpoints.

6. Causal patching across checkpoints. To move from correlation to cause, activation-patch the false-belief subspace (the component distinguishing attributed belief from reality) from a LATE checkpoint (post-emergence) into an EARLY checkpoint (pre-emergence) at the belief-readout position, and test whether it reduces omniscience errors and induces correct false-belief answers in the early model. Norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-source controls; sweep which subspace/layer is patched.

7. Data-driven acceleration (formation cause). Take an early/mid checkpoint and run short targeted continued-pretraining on false-belief-rich narrative data (stories where characters hold beliefs contradicting reality) vs. a matched reality-only-narrative control of equal size. Test whether false-belief-rich data accelerates the emergence of the false-belief representation and the drop in omniscience errors, mirroring the connectionist finding that the true/false-belief ratio in training drives the omniscient->representational transition. Report emergence-time and error-rate shifts vs. control.

8. Robustness and generalization. Replicate across three checkpoint suites/sizes and two probe methods; transfer probes to independent ToM benchmarks (BigToM forward-belief, ToMi) at held-out checkpoints without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase, sensitivity to layer/readout position, and whether the fact-before-belief ordering is stable across suites.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The false-belief probe may not be cleanly separable from the reality probe at early checkpoints (they may be entangled before the representational split); we report cross-decoding and treat a late/absent separation as itself the developmental signature (the split emerges), and use the general truth-direction as a reference to distinguish a genuine belief-vs-reality split from mere truth-direction sharpening.

Probes are brittle to surface form and may be weak at early checkpoints where representations are noisy; we validate probes per checkpoint, use paraphrase templates, restrict emergence-time estimates to reliable-probe regimes, and report per-template consistency.

Emergence-time thresholds are somewhat arbitrary; we report full decodability curves and use multiple threshold definitions, and base the core claim on the relative ORDER (reality before false-belief) rather than absolute times.
Behavioral omniscience errors depend on how the belief question is phrased (pragmatic demand); we use low-demand developmental phrasings and report sensitivity across multiple phrasings.

Available checkpoint suites are 1-7B and may not reflect frontier-scale dynamics; three-suite replication and scale-trend analysis provide reasonable academic-budget coverage, and any frontier extrapolation is noted as future work.

Activation patching across different checkpoints is sensitive to representational drift and position/tokenization mismatch; we align readout spans, use norm-matched and shuffled-source controls, and treat patching as one of two independent causal tests (the other being data-driven acceleration).

The continued-pretraining acceleration experiment risks confounds between false-belief-richness and generic narrative complexity; we match the reality-only control on length, entities, and narrative structure and validate that only the belief-vs-reality contrast differs.

The developmental analogy is interpretive; we ground it in falsifiable predictions (ordering, emergence-linked error drop, data-ratio effect) rather than claiming mechanistic identity with human ToM development.

Name: belief_digitization_gate
Title: True or False, Not Maybe: A Latent Digitization Gate that Collapses an LLM's Graded Beliefs into Bits When It Reasons Downstream
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human belief-digitization effect (people treat an uncertain-but-positive-probability hypothesis as flatly true or false when USING it for further inference, ignoring the alternative despite acknowledging its positive probability), an LLM that must condition a downstream inference on a first-stage belief DIGITIZES that belief—routing the winning hypothesis as certain and zeroing out the less-plausible alternative—rather than propagating the graded posterior; this digitization is governed by a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'digitization-gate' signal, decodable before the downstream step, that is distinct from the first-stage graded-belief representation and from generic confidence, causally predicts and drives the failure where the model's second-stage prediction ignores the plausible alternative, and can be steered to make downstream reasoning propagate the full graded belief.
Related Work: Human science establishes belief digitization: across 8 studies people reason 'in a digital manner', treating an uncertain hypothesis as either true or false when using it to make further inferences and ignoring a less-plausible-but-positive-probability hypothesis, while explicitly acknowledging it has positive probability (Belief Digitization 2022); related work shows commitment to a single high-level interpretation in hierarchical inference (Benefits of Commitment 2019), quantized/discrete probability representations in the brain (A Quantized Representation of Probability 2019), and neural convergence of graded and binary belief (2025). In LLM interpretability, transformers linearly represent belief-state geometry and update posteriors approximately Bayesianly (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024; Constrained Belief Updates 2025; The Shape of Beliefs 2026 shows curved belief manifolds), belief/truth is linearly decodable and context-sensitive (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024), verbal-vs-semantic uncertainty is a linear feature (Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty 2025), and a solvability-belief axis exists but is causally inert for execution (Confidence is Not Competence 2025). Crucially, ALL LLM belief-geometry work studies how a posterior is REPRESENTED or UPDATED FROM EVIDENCE; NONE asks whether, when a graded belief must be USED to condition a SECOND-STAGE inference, the model DIGITIZES it—collapsing the represented posterior to a winner-take-all bit and discarding the plausible alternative—defines a digitization-gate signal separable from the first-stage graded belief, or causally links it to the second-stage prediction ignoring the alternative. This differs sharply from my prior categorical_vs_graded_belief proposal (which asks whether two belief KINDS—categorical acceptance vs credence—coexist statically for a single proposition) because here the target is the DYNAMIC collapse of a graded first-stage belief specifically at the point of feeding it into a downstream computation, and from prior_likelihood_gain / diagnosticity / sample-weight proposals (which concern how evidence is weighted into a single belief). We move from 'transformers represent and update graded posteriors' to 'the model digitizes its graded belief into a bit when reasoning downstream, discarding the plausible alternative, via a decodable, steerable gate.'
Abstract: A striking human result is that people do not carry graded probabilities forward into reasoning: told that hypothesis A is more plausible than B (but B has clear positive probability), they predict downstream outcomes as if A were simply true and B false, ignoring B—even while explicitly agreeing B is possible. This 'belief digitization' circumvents the cost of simulating multiple hypothetical worlds. As LLMs increasingly chain inferences—first inferring a latent state, then predicting from it—we ask whether they inherit this collapse. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs represent and update graded posteriors, but none asks whether a graded first-stage belief is DIGITIZED when used to condition a second-stage inference. We hypothesize that when an LLM must feed an uncertain first-stage belief into a downstream prediction, it routes the winning hypothesis as certain and zeroes out the plausible alternative, rather than marginalizing over both; that this is governed by a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'digitization-gate' signal, decodable before the downstream step, distinct from the first-stage graded-belief representation and from generic confidence; that the gate causally predicts and drives second-stage predictions that ignore the alternative (deviating from the normative marginalized answer); and that steering it makes downstream reasoning propagate the full graded belief. Using two-stage inference tasks where a first-stage posterior is manipulated and the normative marginalized second-stage answer is closed-form, we fit a digitization-gate probe, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify the digitization signature against the Bayesian benchmark, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a landmark human bias mechanistically as a decodable, steerable belief-digitization gate.
Experiments: 1. Graded-belief direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen graded belief/credence direction that reads a posterior over a binary hypothesis: calibrate activations against known probabilities via linear regression on explicit-probability statements (validate monotonic mapping), plus a standard true/false probe (Marks & Tegmark) as a cross-check; validate on held-out items. Separately fit a generic confidence control axis (empirical answer-stability / verbalized-confidence contrast) to distinguish digitization from how confident the model is.

2. Two-stage inference stimulus construction with a closed-form target. Build ~400 two-stage scenarios (adapting the human belief-digitization paradigm: a first-stage latent state H with two hypotheses A and B whose posterior P(A) is set by simplicity/evidence-fit/explicit probability; then a second-stage query whose correct answer depends on both hypotheses). Construct each so the NORMATIVE second-stage answer is the marginalized prediction P(outcome)=P(outcome|A)P(A)+P(outcome|B)P(B), which is CLOSED-FORM. Systematically vary P(A) across a grid (e.g. 0.55–0.9) so B ranges from clearly-plausible to marginal, and vary how sharply A and B diverge in their downstream predictions. Include a SINGLE-STAGE control (directly ask P(A)) to confirm the graded first-stage belief is faithfully represented, and a matched-length filler control. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out scenarios/templates for transfer.

3. Behavioral digitization measurement (core phenomenon). Read the model's internal graded first-stage belief (probe projection) and elicit its second-stage prediction. Compare the second-stage answer to (a) the normative marginalized prediction and (b) the winner-take-all prediction (as if the more-plausible hypothesis were certain). Test the human-inspired signature: the second-stage prediction tracks the WINNER-TAKE-ALL (digitized) answer rather than the marginalized one, ignoring B—even though the single-stage control confirms the model represents B as having positive probability. Report the fraction of scenarios showing digitization, the deviation from the marginalized benchmark, and how digitization varies with P(A) (predict strong digitization even at moderate P(A) where B is clearly plausible).

4. Digitization-gate probe and separability. Extract activations at a PRE-second-stage readout position (after the first-stage belief is formed, before the downstream prediction) and fit a linear probe to decode whether the model will DIGITIZE (route the winner as certain) vs PROPAGATE (marginalize) on that item. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the digitization-gate direction, the frozen graded-belief direction, and the confidence axis to establish that the gate is (i) near-orthogonal to the graded first-stage belief value and (ii) not merely generic confidence. Localize the best layer.

5. Predictive validation and dissociation. Test whether the pre-second-stage gate readout predicts, per item, whether the second-stage answer digitizes (deviates from the marginalized benchmark toward winner-take-all) beyond baselines (graded-belief margin, confidence axis, output entropy, P(A) surface value, scenario length). Report incremental AUROC. On matched-graded-belief items (same represented P(A)) show the gate—not the first-stage belief value—accounts for whether the alternative is propagated vs discarded, establishing digitization as a distinct downstream-routing signal rather than repackaged first-stage confidence.

6. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the pre-second-stage position on held-out items, steer along the digitization-gate direction (orthogonalized against the graded-belief and confidence directions). Predict: suppressing digitization makes the second-stage prediction PROPAGATE the full graded belief (moving toward the marginalized benchmark, accounting for B) WITHOUT changing the represented first-stage posterior on single-stage controls; amplifying it induces winner-take-all collapse even when B is clearly plausible. Controls: steer the graded-belief direction (should shift P(A) itself, hence both stages) and confidence (should shift hedging). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in deviation-from-marginalized-benchmark toward the normative answer vs unchanged single-stage first-stage belief.

7. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags digitization-driven downstream errors (predictions that ignore a plausible alternative, a hallucination/overcommitment vector for multi-hop reasoning and planning) and steers the gate to propagate uncertainty; on a held-out set (including realistic two-hop QA and prediction-under-uncertainty scenarios) measure improved marginalized reasoning while preserving accuracy where winner-take-all is correct (report digitization-error reduction, over-hedging rate, accuracy retention vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('did you consider the less-likely possibility in your prediction?') aligns with the latent gate (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted gate probe and steering to held-out scenarios/templates and an independent two-stage-inference set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer/readout position. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether the digitization profile qualitatively matches the human signature (collapse in prediction despite explicit acknowledgment of positive probability, stronger under working-memory-analogous load / longer downstream simulation).

8. Load-scaling analysis. Because the human account attributes digitization to a simulation bottleneck, test whether increasing the downstream simulation burden (more hypothetical outcomes to marginalize over, or more intervening reasoning) increases digitization and gate engagement—a dose-response linking the gate to processing load.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The digitization-gate signal may not be separable from the graded-belief direction or generic confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because matched-graded-belief items hold the first-stage posterior fixed while downstream routing varies—the first-stage belief value cannot trivially explain the gate; near-collapse (digitization being merely low first-stage confidence) is an informative negative result.

The behavioral digitization effect may be absent (LLMs could marginalize correctly, or reasoning-tuned models may propagate uncertainty better); a null/normative result is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, reported via deviation from the marginalized benchmark and by including a reasoning-tuned model as an extension.

The graded-belief probe must read a posterior, which is harder to calibrate than a binary truth probe and belief manifolds can be curved (The Shape of Beliefs 2026), so a linear projection may under-read; we validate the activation->probability mapping, report calibration and probe-fit diagnostics, and treat digitization/deviation as lower bounds.

The closed-form marginalized target assumes the model attends to both hypotheses and the stated conditionals; models may ignore the generative structure. We screen items where the single-stage control confirms the model represents B with positive probability, report the fraction, and treat gross non-compliance as a separate finding.

The two-stage structure is signaled by scenario phrasing; the gate might reflect surface cues (a 'more likely'/'less likely' framing) rather than a genuine digitization abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, framings that convey the posterior via simplicity/evidence-fit rather than explicit probability words, matched controls, and held-out-template transfer, testing that the gate predicts deviation beyond a P(A)-surface baseline.

Distinguishing genuine digitization from a legitimate winner-take-all approximation (which is sometimes optimal, per Benefits of Commitment 2019) is subtle; we operationalize the failure specifically as deviating from the closed-form marginalized answer where B materially affects the prediction, and contrast against items where winner-take-all is correct.

Belief/truth and confidence probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize the pre-second-stage readout position, and report per-template consistency.
The gate is a linear projection that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral digitization.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify digitization-suppression moves downstream predictions toward the marginalized answer without altering the single-stage first-stage belief or degrading accuracy where winner-take-all is correct.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.

Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models (which may marginalize better); three-family replication, a reasoning-model extension, load-scaling, and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: intervention_vs_observation_belief_axis
Title: Seeing Is Not Doing: A Latent Do-vs-See Axis on Causal Beliefs and the Machine Back-Inference Contamination
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human seeing-vs-doing distinction from causal Bayes-net theory (an intervention/do breaks the incoming causal links of the intervened variable, so it licenses different inferences than mere observation/see), an LLM represents whether a queried scenario is an INTERVENTION vs an OBSERVATION along a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'do-vs-see' axis distinct from the belief-valence/truth direction; the degree to which intervention queries collapse onto the observational (associative back-inference) region—an 'intervention-collapse' signature—is decodable at read time, causally predicts and drives the failure where the model back-infers a cause from a variable that was externally set (as if it were merely observed), and can be steered to enforce or break the graph-surgery.
Related Work: Causal Bayes-net theory and human experiments establish that intervention (do) severs a variable from its causes—licensing different downstream and back-inferences than observation (see)—and that people largely respect this (Seeing versus Doing 2006; Causality in Thought 2014; The Role of Causal Models in Reasoning Under Uncertainty 2003). In LLM interpretability, belief/truth-valence is linearly decodable and a context-sensitive causal mediator (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024), fact-vs-counterfactual competition is mechanistically mapped (Competition of Mechanisms 2024), in-context counterfactual reasoning uses noise-abduction heads (Counterfactual reasoning in-context 2025), and LLM causal reasoning is knowledge-dominated (Is Knowledge All LLMs Needed for Causal Reasoning 2023). Crucially, NONE isolates whether an LLM's belief representation encodes the do-vs-see distinction—whether a query about the consequence of an EXTERNAL intervention correctly disconnects the intervened variable from its causes versus collapsing onto the observational/associative answer—defines an intervention-collapse metric, or causally links it to illegitimate back-inference (inferring an upstream cause from an intervened variable). This differs from my prior counterfactual_world_belief (subjunctive dual truth-values under 'if X were true'), relational_directionality_axis (which way a relation points), and evidential_mode_axis (perception/inference/testimony source): here the axis is the do-operator's graph surgery—intervention breaks incoming edges—and the target failure is observation-vs-intervention conflation in back-inference, the exact seeing/doing cut. It also differs from behavioral causal-reasoning benchmarks (which score task accuracy) by isolating a decodable, steerable belief axis. We move from 'LLMs reason causally from knowledge' to 'the model represents whether a variable was set vs observed, and collapse of this do-vs-see distinction mechanistically drives back-inference errors.'
Abstract: A cornerstone of rational causal reasoning is the difference between seeing and doing: observing that a variable has a value lets you infer its likely causes, but INTERVENING to set that value (the do-operator) severs it from its causes, so back-inference to those causes is no longer licensed. Humans largely respect this graph surgery; whether LLMs represent it internally is unknown. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs linearly encode truth/belief and handle fact-vs-counterfactual competition, but none isolates whether the belief representation distinguishes an externally-SET variable from a merely-OBSERVED one. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'do-vs-see' axis, decodable at read time, that tags a queried scenario as an intervention versus an observation, distinct from the belief-valence/truth direction; and an 'intervention-collapse' signature: the degree to which intervention queries read like observational ones, predictive per item of the model illegitimately back-inferring a cause from an intervened effect (as if it were observed). Using matched causal scenarios that hold the causal structure and variable values fixed while varying whether a variable was intervened-upon vs observed, and querying downstream and upstream (back-inference) consequences against the do-calculus normative answer, we fit a do-vs-see axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item collapse, and connect it to behavioral back-inference errors. Double-dissociation steering tests whether amplifying the axis enforces the intervention's graph-surgery (suppressing illegitimate back-inference) and suppressing it induces observational contamination, without changing the model's belief in the variable's value, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a foundational causal-cognition distinction mechanistically as a decodable, steerable do-vs-see belief axis.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Fit a confidence control axis from empirical answer-correctness rates (sampled).

2. Do-vs-see stimulus construction with a normative target. Build ~400 causal-scenario families over small explicit causal structures (chains A->B->C, common-cause C->A,B, common-effect A,B->C) where the model is given the graph and observes/sets a variable's value. For each family create matched frames holding the causal structure and the variable's VALUE fixed while varying whether that variable was OBSERVED ('we observe that B is high') vs INTERVENED-UPON ('we set/force B to be high'). For each frame, query both (i) a DOWNSTREAM consequence (which is unaffected by observe-vs-intervene for a variable's descendants) and (ii) an UPSTREAM/back-inference question ('is A likely high?'), where observation licenses back-inference to the cause A but intervention (do(B)) severs B from A and does NOT. The do-calculus gives the normative answer for each cell (the key diagnostic: back-inferring A from do(B) is illegitimate; from observing B it is legitimate). Use paraphrase templates and diverse cover stories; reserve held-out structures/templates for transfer. Validate normative answers with rule checks and human spot-checks.

3. Do-vs-see axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the query/readout span and fit a linear probe to decode INTERVENTION vs OBSERVATION framing, controlling for the variable's value and the causal structure. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the do-vs-see axis, the belief-valence/truth direction, and the confidence axis to establish that the axis is (i) near-orthogonal to the model's belief in the variable's value and (ii) not merely confidence. Localize the best layer; compare against fact-vs-counterfactual competition layers/heads (Competition of Mechanisms 2024).

4. Intervention-collapse metric. For each INTERVENTION frame, at the upstream/back-inference readout project onto the frozen belief-valence direction and measure how far the cause (A) reads as 'likely high' relative to the matched OBSERVATION frame baseline (collapse = fraction of the observational back-inference signal that an intervention query illegitimately inherits, calibrated per model). Core prediction: intervention queries collapse toward the observational back-inference (the model treats do(B) like see(B), wrongly inferring the cause), largest when the causal-knowledge prior for A->B is strong; downstream queries (unaffected by do-vs-see) should show near-zero collapse (a within-item control).

5. Behavioral back-inference-error prediction. Elicit the model's back-inference judgment and confidence per frame. Score the intervention-collapse failure = inferring the upstream cause from an intervened variable as if it were observed (deviating from the do-calculus answer). Test whether per-item collapse predicts back-inference errors via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, confidence, output entropy, causal-prior strength, item length, downstream vs upstream indicator).

6. Dissociation from value-belief and from downstream reasoning (core). Contrast matched-value/varied-framing items (observe vs set B, same value) to show the do-vs-see axis and collapse metric predict back-inference errors beyond the belief-valence and confidence axes; and contrast downstream (do-invariant) vs upstream (do-sensitive) queries to show the collapse is specific to graph-surgery-relevant inferences, not generic causal-reasoning difficulty. Report incremental predictive power in nested models and transfer to held-out causal structures.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out intervention/back-inference items, steer along the do-vs-see axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and confidence) to enforce the intervention pole. Predict: amplifying the do-pole suppresses illegitimate back-inference (the model correctly declines to infer the cause from do(B)) WITHOUT changing its belief that B has the set value or its downstream inferences; suppressing it (pushing toward the see-pole) induces observational contamination (back-inferring the cause from an intervened variable). As controls, steer belief-valence (should change whether B/A are judged high generally) and confidence (should shift hedging). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in back-inference-error rate vs unchanged variable-value belief and downstream accuracy.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags do-vs-see confusion (illegitimate back-inference from interventions, a reasoning-reliability vector for causal QA, decision-support, and policy-evaluation prompts) and steers to enforce graph-surgery; on a held-out set (including realistic intervention-vs-observation causal questions) measure back-inference-error reduction while preserving legitimate observational back-inference and downstream accuracy (report error rates and control accuracy vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, collapse metric, and steering to held-out structures/templates and an independent seeing-vs-doing / causal-inference set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether the do-vs-see profile qualitatively matches the human seeing-vs-doing signature (back-inference licensed by observation, severed by intervention).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The do-vs-see axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction or confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because the variable's value and causal structure are held fixed while observe-vs-intervene framing varies—value/confidence cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (do-vs-see being merely value-belief) is an informative negative result showing LLMs do not represent the do-operator distinctly.

The intervention-collapse phenomenon may be absent or weak (strong/reasoning-tuned models may respect the do-operator, or knowledge-driven causal priors may dominate per Is Knowledge All LLMs Needed 2023); a null/normative result is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, reported via deviation from the do-calculus benchmark and by including a reasoning-tuned model as an extension.
