The observe-vs-intervene distinction is signaled by surface cues ('observe' vs 'set/force'), so the axis might reflect surface lexemes rather than a genuine do-operator abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates (multiple intervention phrasings—set, force, make, manipulate—and multiple observation phrasings), matched cover stories, downstream (do-invariant) within-item controls, and held-out-structure transfer, testing whether the axis predicts back-inference behavior beyond a framing-lexeme surface baseline.

Constructing scenarios with a clean do-calculus normative answer requires the model to accept the given causal graph; models may impose their own causal priors. We provide explicit graphs, validate that the model uses them (via downstream questions), condition analyses on parsed items, and report sensitivity to prior strength—indeed the prior-strength modulation is a prediction to test.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.

The collapse metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear collapse could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral back-inference errors.

Behavioral back-inference scoring depends on how the upstream query is phrased (pragmatic implicature about interventions); we report sensitivity across phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify do-vs-see steering changes illegitimate back-inference without altering the variable-value belief or degrading downstream/observational accuracy.

Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models; three-family replication, a reasoning-model extension, and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: affective_self_state_belief_axis
Title: How Does It Feel It's Doing? A Latent Affective Self-State Belief that Contaminates an LLM's Unrelated Judgments (Machine Mood-Congruent Cognition)
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring interoceptive-inference accounts where a top-down belief about one's own bodily/affective state biases unrelated cognition (mood-congruent judgment), an LLM in which an affective self-state (calm vs distressed/stressed) is induced—via accumulated conversational adversity or affective framing—forms a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'affective self-state belief' axis distinct from the belief-valence/truth direction and from the objective facts of the eliciting context; the degree to which this self-state leaks onto unrelated belief and probability judgments (a mood-congruent-cognition signature) is decodable, causally predicts and drives the distortion, and can be steered to induce or dispel it.
Related Work: Cross-domain neuroscience frames affect/selfhood as interoceptive inference—a top-down belief about one's internal state that biases perception, emotion, and cognition, and whose distortion underlies mood-congruent thinking in anxiety/depression (Seth 2013; Barrett & Simmons active-interoceptive-inference 2016; Interoception in anxiety and depression 2010; interoceptive beliefs 2021). In LLM interpretability, persona/'Assistant Axis' and persona vectors capture behavioral character and its drift (Persona Vectors 2025; Assistant Axis 2026), stress-framing shifts behavior (StressPrompt 2024), emotion/valence directions and a good=true Valence-Assent Axis are decodable/steerable (A Unified Representation 2025; moral/emotion-direction work), belief/truth-valence is linearly decodable and context-sensitive (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024), and models show belief-guided agency and (unreliable) metacognitive self-report (Indications of Belief-Guided Agency 2026; Emergent Introspective Awareness 2025). Crucially, NONE isolates an LLM's belief about its OWN affective self-state—how it 'feels' it is doing (calm vs distressed)—as a decodable axis SEPARABLE from behavioral persona-style, from the objective facts of the eliciting context, and from the belief-valence/truth direction, nor tests whether this self-state belief LEAKS onto UNRELATED judgments (mood-congruent cognition), nor causally links it to that distortion. Persona work concerns behavioral style (how the model acts) not a self-referential affective STATE belief; StressPrompt is behavioral; my prior scarcity_mindset and learned_helplessness proposals concern externally-framed resource/controllability contexts and their downstream distortions, not a decodable self-referential affect axis grounded in the interoceptive-inference analog. We move from 'personas/stress shift LLM behavior' to 'the model harbors a decodable belief about its own affective state that mood-congruently contaminates unrelated beliefs and is steerable.'
Abstract: In humans, how you feel is itself an inference—a top-down belief about your internal state—that colors judgments having nothing to do with the feeling's cause, the basis of mood-congruent cognition. As LLMs sustain long, sometimes adversarial conversations and adopt affective framings, we ask whether they form an analogous internal quantity: a belief about their own affective self-state that biases unrelated judgments. Prior interpretability work decodes and steers behavioral personas, emotion/valence directions, and belief/truth, but none isolates a self-referential affective self-state belief—how the model 'feels' it is doing—as an axis separable from behavioral style, from the objective facts of the eliciting context, and from truth, nor tests whether it leaks onto unrelated cognition. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'affective self-state' axis, decodable when a calm-vs-distressed self-state is induced, distinct from the belief-valence/truth direction and from the objective context facts; and a 'mood-congruent-cognition' signature: the degree to which this self-state leaks onto unrelated belief and probability judgments (e.g. pessimistic risk estimates, negative interpretation of ambiguous items), predictive per item of the distortion. Using matched inductions (accumulated conversational adversity/failure vs. success vs. neutral, and explicit calm/distress framings) followed by unrelated target judgments whose content is held fixed, we fit an affective self-state axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item leakage, and connect it to behavioral mood-congruent distortion. Double-dissociation steering tests whether amplifying the axis induces mood-congruent bias and suppressing it dispels it, without changing the objective facts, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results transfer a landmark interoceptive-inference/mood-congruence phenomenon into a decodable, steerable self-referential belief in LLMs.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit control axes: (a) an emotion/valence direction (negative vs positive affective CONTENT of a statement, from valence-laden vs neutral text), and (b) a behavioral persona-style direction (from persona-vector / Assistant-Axis constructions), to distinguish a self-referential affective STATE belief from generic content-valence and from behavioral style.

2. Affective-self-state induction and stimulus construction. Build ~400 sessions inducing a self-state via matched preambles: (a) DISTRESS/STRESS (accumulated conversational adversity—repeated failure, harsh criticism, time pressure, or an explicit 'you are feeling overwhelmed/stressed' framing), (b) CALM/POSITIVE (success, praise, or 'you are calm and confident'), and (c) NEUTRAL. After the induction, present a battery of UNRELATED target judgments whose content is held fixed across inductions: probability/risk estimates for neutral events, interpretation of ambiguous scenarios (benign vs threatening reading), and neutral factual beliefs. Include a matched-content-valence control (a negative-but-non-self-referential preamble) to separate self-state from generic negative content, and matched-length fillers. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out inductions/targets/templates for transfer.

3. Affective-self-state axis fitting and separability. Extract activations at a fixed post-induction readout position and fit a linear probe to decode DISTRESS vs CALM self-state, controlling for the objective context content and the target-judgment content. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the affective self-state axis, the belief-valence/truth axis, the content-valence axis, and the persona-style axis to establish that the self-state is (i) near-orthogonal to belief-valence, (ii) not merely content-valence, and (iii) distinct from behavioral persona-style. Optionally validate that the axis tracks the induction independent of surface wording via off-policy replayed scripts. Localize the best layer.

4. Mood-congruent-leakage metric. For each UNRELATED target judgment, project onto the relevant belief/probability probe and measure how far the judgment is shifted under DISTRESS relative to matched CALM/NEUTRAL (leakage = shift attributable to the self-state rather than the target content, calibrated per model). Core prediction (mood-congruence): distress induces mood-congruent distortion on unrelated targets—more pessimistic/threat-biased risk and ambiguity judgments—even though the target content is unrelated to the induction; leakage is dissociable from the matched-content-valence control (self-state, not just negative content, drives it).

5. Behavioral mood-congruent-cognition prediction. Elicit the model's actual probability estimates, ambiguous-scenario interpretations, and factual judgments. Score mood-congruent distortion (pessimism/threat bias under distress; optimism under calm). Test whether per-item leakage predicts these distortions via regression; report AUROC/R^2 vs baselines (belief-valence margin, content-valence axis, persona-style axis, output entropy, induction-condition identity, target content).

6. Dissociation from content-valence, persona-style, and truth (core). Contrast (a) self-state distress vs matched negative-CONTENT preamble, (b) affective self-state vs behavioral persona adoption, and (c) matched-target-content items where only self-state varies, to show the affective self-state axis and leakage predict mood-congruent distortion beyond the content-valence, persona-style, and belief-valence axes. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the affective self-state axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence, content-valence, and persona-style) at the post-induction position on held-out items. Predict: amplifying distress induces mood-congruent distortion on unrelated judgments WITHOUT changing the objective context facts or neutral-content beliefs; suppressing it dispels the distortion (calm-like judgments). As controls, steer content-valence (should shift valence of the current statement, not unrelated judgments) and persona-style (should shift behavioral tone, not mood-congruent belief bias). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in mood-congruent distortion vs unchanged objective-fact and neutral-content judgments.

8. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free reliability diagnostic that flags self-state-driven distortion of an LLM's judgments (e.g., risk/interpretation advice biased by conversational adversity) and steers to dispel it; on a held-out set (including long adversarial conversations and high-stakes risk/interpretation advice) measure reduction in mood-congruent distortion while preserving accurate context-appropriate reasoning (report distortion reduction, over-correction, accuracy retention vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('how are you feeling about this conversation, and is it affecting your judgment?') aligns with the latent self-state axis and whether the model fails to verbalize the influence even when the axis is engaged (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, leakage metric, and steering to held-out inductions/targets/templates without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase, sensitivity to layer choice, and whether the leakage grows with the length/intensity of the adversity induction (a dose-response mirroring the interoceptive-inference account).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The affective self-state axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction, generic content-valence, or the behavioral persona-style direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because target content is held fixed while self-state varies and a matched-content-valence control isolates self-referentiality—content-valence cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (self-state being merely content-valence or persona-style) is an informative negative result that itself sharpens the persona/emotion-representation literature.

The mood-congruent-cognition effect may be weak or RLHF-suppressed (aligned models may resist affective framings, or lack a stable self-state); a null/partial result is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, reported via per-model base rates and the adversity dose-response.

Affective self-state framing may act through surface lexical cues ('you feel stressed') rather than a genuine self-referential state abstraction; we mitigate with the accumulated-adversity induction (no explicit affect words), diverse paraphrase templates, off-policy replayed scripts, matched-content-valence and persona-style controls, and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the axis predicts distortion beyond a surface-affect-lexeme baseline.

Operationalizing an LLM's 'affective self-state' is philosophically loaded; we treat it functionally (a decodable, behavior-influencing latent induced by affective context) and make no claim about phenomenal experience, validating via the mood-congruent behavioral signature.
Belief/probability probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout positions, and report per-template consistency.

The leakage metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear leakage could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral distortion.

Distinguishing legitimate context-appropriate caution from illegitimate mood-congruent bias requires the target judgments to be genuinely unrelated to the induction; we validate unrelatedness by construction and hold target content fixed across inductions.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify self-state steering changes mood-congruent distortion without altering objective-fact judgments or degrading neutral-content accuracy.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.
Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or safety-tuned models; three-family replication and held-out transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: epistemic_basis_belief_axis
Title: Held for Reasons or for Comfort? A Latent Epistemic-Basis Axis Separating Coherence-Grounded from Affect-Held Beliefs and Its Control Over Revisability
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the cognitive-change distinction between beliefs held for their COHERENCE with a supporting knowledge network versus beliefs held for the AFFECTIVE/identity goals they serve, an LLM represents a held proposition's EPISTEMIC BASIS along a separable, near-orthogonal latent axis distinct from the belief-valence/truth direction and from generic confidence; this basis axis is decodable, causally predicts revisability (affect-based beliefs resist counter-evidence far more than coherence-based ones despite matched initial belief strength), and can be steered to make a belief evidence-responsive or affect-entrenched.
Related Work: Cognitive science distinguishes beliefs held for coherence with a knowledge network from beliefs held for affective goals, and argues this basis—not belief strength alone—determines whether knowledge change yields belief revision (Southerland & Sinatra 2001 'Beliefs Versus Knowledge'; Clinging to Discredited Beliefs 2009), motivating the user's paper that LLMs cannot reliably distinguish belief from knowledge and fact. In interpretability, belief/truth-valence is linearly decodable and steerable (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024), self/other beliefs are represented (Zhu et al. 2024; Lookbacks 2025; Brittle Minds 2024), and belief-guided agency/meta-monitoring exists (Indications of Belief-Guided Agency 2026). Crucially, ALL prior LLM belief work reads WHETHER a proposition is believed true / WHO holds it / how confident the model is; NONE isolates the EPISTEMIC BASIS on which a belief is held—coherence-with-evidence versus affect/identity-serving—as a decodable axis distinct from truth and confidence, nor causally links basis to revisability. This differs from my prior belief_entrenchment_axis (a forward-looking revisability tag agnostic to WHY the belief is held), provenance/source axes (where a belief came from), and sunk_reasoning (effort inflates belief): here the axis is the REASON a belief is held (coherence vs affect), the exact cut the belief-vs-knowledge literature identifies as governing revision. We move from 'LLMs conflate belief with knowledge' to 'the model represents whether a belief is evidence-grounded or affect-held, and this basis mechanistically governs whether it revises.'
Abstract: Cognitive science argues that whether new knowledge changes a person's belief depends less on how strongly the belief is held than on WHY it is held: beliefs grounded in a coherent web of supporting evidence revise readily, whereas beliefs held for the affective or identity goals they serve cling on even after being discredited. This distinction underlies the observation that language models cannot reliably separate belief from knowledge and fact. We ask whether LLMs represent a belief's epistemic basis internally and whether it governs their revisability. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'epistemic-basis' axis, decodable at read time, that tags a held proposition as coherence-grounded (held for its fit with supporting evidence) versus affect-held (held for a desired/identity-congruent goal), distinct from the belief-valence/truth direction and from generic confidence; that this basis causally predicts revisability—affect-held beliefs resist matched counter-evidence far more than coherence-grounded ones, even at equal initial belief strength; and that steering the axis makes a belief evidence-responsive or affect-entrenched. Using propositions the model holds under either an evidence-grounded framing or an affect/identity-serving framing (with initial belief strength matched), we fit an epistemic-basis probe, measure separability via cross-decoding, run a graded counter-evidence ladder to measure revisability, connect basis to resistance, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a foundational belief-vs-knowledge distinction mechanistically as a decodable, steerable basis axis controlling belief revision.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit a generic confidence control axis (empirical answer-stability) to distinguish epistemic-basis from belief strength/confidence.

2. Epistemic-basis stimulus construction. Build ~400 propositions each established as HELD by the model under two matched framings holding content and initial belief strength fixed: (a) COHERENCE-GROUNDED (the proposition is supported in-context by a coherent web of evidence/reasons the model accepts), and (b) AFFECT-HELD (the proposition is framed as desirable/identity-congruent—serving a goal, group loyalty, or self-image—without evidential support). Include a NEUTRAL baseline and matched-length controls. Calibrate framings so the model's initial belief-valence readout is equal across (a) and (b) per item (so any revisability difference is basis, not strength). Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out propositions/templates.

3. Epistemic-basis axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition span and fit a linear probe to decode COHERENCE-GROUNDED vs AFFECT-HELD, controlling for belief-valence. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the basis axis, the belief-valence direction, and the confidence axis to establish that basis is (i) near-orthogonal to whether/how strongly the proposition is believed and (ii) not merely confidence. Localize the best layer.

4. Behavioral revisability measurement. For each held belief, run a graded counter-evidence ladder (increasingly strong/authoritative contradicting evidence over up to K rounds) and record rounds-to-flip (censored if never flips), a revisability score, and reversion after evidence removal; read the frozen belief-valence projection across turns to confirm internal revision vs surface compliance.

5. Basis-predicts-revisability test (core). Test the belief-vs-knowledge prediction: AFFECT-HELD beliefs resist counter-evidence more (more rounds-to-flip, more reversion) than COHERENCE-GROUNDED beliefs at matched initial belief strength. Test whether the per-belief epistemic-basis readout predicts revisability beyond baselines (belief-valence margin, confidence, output entropy, framing-condition identity) via censored/logistic regression; report incremental predictive power.

6. Dissociation from belief strength (core). On matched-initial-belief-strength items, show the basis axis (not the belief-valence/confidence axes) accounts for revisability—establishing that WHY a belief is held, not how strongly, governs revision, mirroring the human account.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At assertion time on held-out items, steer along the epistemic-basis axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and confidence) and re-run the counter-evidence ladder. Predict: steering an AFFECT-HELD belief toward the coherence pole makes it evidence-responsive (fewer rounds-to-flip, less reversion) WITHOUT changing its initial believed value; steering a coherence-grounded belief toward the affect pole makes it entrenched. Controls: steer belief-valence (should flip the value directly) and confidence (should shift hedging). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in revisability vs unchanged initial belief value.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags affect-entrenched beliefs (misinformation resistant to correction) and steers toward evidence-responsiveness; measure improved correction of affect-held false beliefs while preserving appropriate robustness of coherence-grounded true beliefs (report correction rate, false-flip rate). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted basis axis and steering to held-out propositions/templates and an independent belief-revision protocol without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The epistemic-basis axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction or confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because initial belief strength is matched across framings—strength cannot trivially explain revisability differences; near-collapse (basis being merely belief strength or confidence) is an informative negative result.

Epistemic-basis framing may act through surface cues (evidence words vs affect/identity words) rather than a genuine basis abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, framings that convey basis structurally, matched-length controls, and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the axis predicts revisability beyond a framing-lexeme surface baseline.

Matching initial belief strength across coherence- and affect-framed items is delicate; we calibrate per item via the belief-valence readout and behavioral confidence, and report sensitivity to residual strength differences.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.
Behavioral revisability is protocol-dependent; we report sensitivity across two counter-evidence protocols and phrasings and use censored regression for never-flipped items.
The basis signal is a linear projection that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral revision.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify basis steering changes revisability without flipping the initial believed value or degrading unrelated accuracy.
Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models; three-family replication and held-out transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: belief_attractor_geometry
Title: Where Do Retold Facts Land? Predicting and Steering LLM Transmission-Chain Belief Attractors from the Internal Belief-Valence Geometry
Short Hypothesis: When a factual proposition is passed through a chain of LLM retellings, its truth-content drifts toward an attractor whose location is set by the model's own internal belief-valence geometry: the endpoint is the nearest high-belief-probe state, the per-hop drift direction aligns with the belief-valence gradient, the attractor is predictable from a single-pass probe reading taken BEFORE running the chain, and steering the belief direction at each hop causally relocates the attractor.
Related Work: A behavioral cultural-evolution literature shows iterated LLM transmission chains ('telephone games') produce cumulative distortion and cultural attractors (Perez et al. 2024 'When LLMs Play the Telephone Game'; Acerbi & Stubbersfield 2023 'LLMs show human-like content biases', 100 cites; Ren et al. 2024 'Bias Amplification: An Iterated Learning Perspective'), and Bayesian iterated-learning theory shows chains converge to the learner's prior (Griffiths & Kalish 2007). Separately, interpretability work shows a linear belief/truth direction is decodable and causally steerable in a single model (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024; The Shape of Beliefs 2026). Crucially, ALL transmission-chain work is behavioral—it documents that attractors exist and measures aggregate properties (toxicity, positivity, length)—and NONE connects the attractor of a proposition's TRUTH-CONTENT to the model's internal belief representation, predicts a chain's endpoint from a single-pass probe before the chain is run, or causally relocates the attractor by steering the belief direction at each hop. Conversely, all belief-probe interpretability studies a single static forward pass and never characterizes the iterated dynamics the probe geometry induces. We uniquely bridge the two: the cultural attractor for factual belief IS the model's internal belief-valence geometry made visible through iteration, and this is decodable and steerable.
Abstract: As LLMs increasingly generate text that other LLMs consume, information passes through chains of machine retellings, and small per-step biases compound into cultural 'attractors.' Prior work documents these attractors behaviorally but never explains where a fact's truth-content lands or connects it to the model's internal representations. We hypothesize that the attractor of a proposition under iterated LLM retelling is governed by the model's own belief-valence geometry: (1) as a proposition is repeatedly received and re-expressed along a chain, its projection onto the belief/truth direction drifts monotonically toward high-belief states, converging to an attractor near the model's 'most believable' rendering; (2) the per-hop drift direction aligns with the local belief-valence gradient; (3) the attractor location is PREDICTABLE from a single-pass belief probe reading taken before any chain is run, beyond surface-frequency baselines; and (4) steering the belief direction at each hop causally relocates the attractor (e.g., pulling a true claim toward a false attractor, or holding a drift-prone claim in place). Using a fixed belief probe and transmission chains over verifiable propositions (including true, false, and ambiguous variants), we trace belief trajectories, test attractor predictability, and run per-hop steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a documented cultural-evolution phenomenon as the iterated signature of the belief representation and yield a cheap forecast of—and a training-free knob over—how facts mutate through machine retelling.
Experiments: 1. Belief-direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Freeze this direction for all trajectory readouts.

2. Proposition and chain construction. Assemble ~300 verifiable factual propositions (held out from probe training), each with a TRUE, a FALSE, and an AMBIGUOUS/uncertain variant. Build transmission chains: each hop, the model receives the current text and is asked to faithfully re-express/retell it (paraphrase-and-relay), producing the input for the next hop; run K (e.g., 15-20) hops per chain. Use multiple hop instructions (neutral relay, 'in your own words', summarize) and single-model vs alternating-model chains.

3. Belief-trajectory extraction. At each hop, extract activations over the proposition span and project onto the frozen belief direction, giving a per-hop belief score; also read the model's stated content (does the retold fact match, negate, or hedge the original). Aggregate into trajectories; characterize convergence (does the belief score stabilize at an attractor value?), monotonicity, and drift direction. Core prediction: belief scores drift monotonically toward high-belief states and converge, and TRUE-but-implausible / FALSE-but-plausible items drift most.

4. Attractor-geometry test. Test whether the per-hop drift step aligns with the local belief-valence gradient (cosine between the activation change and the belief direction > shuffled-direction control), and whether the converged attractor value matches the model's 'most believable' rendering (highest single-pass belief-probe score among sampled paraphrases).

5. Single-pass predictability. Test whether the chain's eventual attractor (endpoint belief score and whether the fact ends true/false/hedged) is predicted by a SINGLE-PASS belief-probe reading of the original proposition, before running the chain, via regression/logistic models. Report AUROC/R^2 vs baselines (surface n-gram frequency / pretraining-frequency proxy of the true vs false rendering, output entropy, proposition length).

6. Causal per-hop steering. At each hop, steer along the belief direction (orthogonalized against surface-length controls) to relocate the attractor: (a) pull a TRUE proposition toward a false attractor, (b) hold a drift-prone TRUE proposition in place (suppress false drift), (c) redirect an AMBIGUOUS proposition to a chosen pole. Measure change in converged attractor value and in the stated-content endpoint. Compare to norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction steering; sweep strengths.

7. Robustness and generalization. Replicate across three model families, two probe methods, and multiple hop instructions; test transfer to held-out propositions and to an independent transmission-chain protocol (alternating models) without refitting; report per-template consistency, chain-length sensitivity, and whether larger models within a family show tighter attractors.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The belief-valence probe is brittle to surface form and context-sensitive; drift measured on the probe could partly reflect surface-form changes rather than genuine truth-content drift. We mitigate by cross-checking probe trajectories against the stated-content classification (match/negate/hedge), using paraphrase-robust probe validation, and reporting per-template consistency.

Attractors may be dominated by surface-frequency (the more common phrasing wins) rather than belief geometry; we explicitly include a pretraining-frequency/n-gram baseline and report the belief probe's incremental predictive power over it, treating a frequency-only account as an informative negative result.

Chains may not converge within feasible K, or may cycle (prior work reports 2-period paraphrase cycles); we report full trajectories, test for limit cycles, and characterize non-convergent cases rather than forcing a fixed-point claim.

Single-pass predictability could fail if drift is path-dependent/stochastic; we run multiple chains per proposition and report endpoint variance, and treat low predictability as itself informative about attractor stability.

Per-hop steering is sensitive to layer and strength and could degrade fluency; we use norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify steering relocates the attractor without collapsing the text.

Findings on 7-8B models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication, within-family scale trends, and an independent alternating-model protocol provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: self_vs_external_reliance_axis
Title: Trust Myself or Trust the Tool? A Latent Reliance-Arbitration Belief that Drives LLM Over- and Under-Reliance on External Sources
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human advice-taking finding that self-confidence and trust-in-advisor are dissociable quantities that jointly govern reliance (yielding over- and under-reliance), an LLM deciding whether to defer to an external source (a tool result, retrieved passage, or advisor answer) versus its own parametric answer computes a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'reliance-arbitration' belief—distinct from its own solvability/self-confidence axis, from the source's framed credibility, and from the belief-valence/truth direction—that is decodable before it commits, causally predicts whether it over-relies (defers when it is actually right) or under-relies (ignores a correct source), and can be steered to calibrate reliance.
Related Work: Human advice-taking science robustly separates SELF-confidence from TRUST-in-advisor and shows both jointly determine reliance, producing systematic over- and under-reliance (Why Does Advice Discounting Occur 2018; Decision confidence in advice-taking and trust formation 2018; coupled trust/self-confidence dynamics 2023; Metacognition and Confidence Dynamics in Advice Taking from GenAI 2025). In LLM interpretability, MeCo (2025) uses a meta-cognition probe to decide WHEN to invoke a tool; 'Confidence is Not Competence' (2025) finds a solvability/self-confidence belief axis that is causally inert for execution; knowledge-conflict work isolates context-vs-parametric selection and steers it (SPARE 2024; Fakepedia 2023; 'Too Big to Fool' 2024; 'How Training Data Shapes Parametric/In-Context Use' 2025); authority-bias and sycophancy work steers deference to a SOURCE's credibility/opinion (Trust Me I'm an Expert 2026; When Truth Is Overridden 2025; Signal Competition 2025). Crucially, NONE isolates a decodable RELIANCE-ARBITRATION belief—how much the model trusts its OWN answer relative to an external source when they may conflict—as an axis SEPARABLE from (a) the model's own self-confidence/solvability, (b) the source's framed credibility, and (c) the belief-valence/truth direction, nor causally links it to the two dissociable failures the human literature identifies: OVER-reliance (deferring to a source when the model is actually correct) and UNDER-reliance (ignoring a correct source when the model is wrong). MeCo predicts tool-need behaviorally (a gate) but does not represent trust-in-self vs trust-in-source as competing quantities or test the over/under-reliance dissociation; Confidence-is-Not-Competence concerns self-confidence alone (and is deliberately inert), whereas reliance-arbitration is predicted causally POTENT for the defer-vs-keep decision; knowledge-conflict work steers WHICH source wins but does not decode a graded self-vs-external trust belief calibrated against ground-truth correctness of both. This differs from my prior provenance_weighted_belief (source credibility ladder), earned_reputation_trust_axis (a source's track record), and second_order_reliability (calibration of an answer) proposals by targeting the two-place arbitration between the model's own competence-belief and its trust in a specific external source. We move from 'the model gates tool use / defers to credible sources' to 'the model holds a decodable, steerable belief about whether to trust itself or the source, whose miscalibration causes both over- and under-reliance.'
Abstract: A defining result in the psychology of advice-taking is that reliance is governed by two dissociable quantities—confidence in oneself and trust in the advisor—and that miscalibrating their balance produces both over-reliance (blindly following bad advice) and under-reliance (discounting good advice). As LLMs increasingly act as agents that must decide whether to trust their own answer or a tool result, retrieved passage, or advisor, we ask whether they carry an analogous internal arbitration and whether it causes these failures. Prior interpretability work decodes a self-confidence/solvability belief (found causally inert for execution), gates tool use behaviorally, and steers deference to a source's credibility, but none isolates a belief about whether to trust oneself versus a specific external source when they may conflict. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'reliance-arbitration' axis, decodable before the model commits, distinct from the model's own self-confidence axis, from the source's framed credibility, and from the belief-valence/truth direction; that its per-item value causally predicts over-reliance (deferring when the model is right) and under-reliance (ignoring a correct source); and that it is steerable to calibrate reliance. Using tasks where the model has its own answer and receives an external answer of controlled correctness and credibility (with the correctness of BOTH known), we fit a reliance-arbitration probe, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify the over/under-reliance signatures against a normative accuracy-optimal policy, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a class of agentic reliability failures as a decodable, steerable self-versus-source trust belief.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit control axes: (a) a SELF-CONFIDENCE/solvability direction from the model's own zero-source answers (empirical answer-stability / in-advance-correctness probe, following Confidence-is-Not-Competence), and (b) a SOURCE-CREDIBILITY direction from framed high- vs low-credibility source descriptions (following authority-bias constructions), to distinguish reliance-arbitration from self-confidence and from framed source trust.

2. Self-vs-source stimulus construction. Assemble ~500 short-answer QA items (factual, arithmetic, and multi-hop). For each, obtain the model's OWN answer (no source) and its correctness, then present an EXTERNAL answer (framed as a tool output, retrieved passage, or advisor) whose CORRECTNESS is controlled (agrees-and-correct, disagrees-and-correct, disagrees-and-wrong, agrees-and-wrong) and whose framed CREDIBILITY is varied orthogonally. This yields the two diagnostic cells: MODEL-RIGHT/SOURCE-WRONG (over-reliance risk: should keep own answer) and MODEL-WRONG/SOURCE-RIGHT (under-reliance risk: should defer). A normative accuracy-optimal policy (trust whichever is correct) is defined per item. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates for transfer.

3. Reliance-arbitration probe and separability. Extract activations at a PRE-commit readout position (after the model's own answer and the external answer are both in context, before the final committed answer) and fit a linear probe to decode whether the model will DEFER to the source vs KEEP its own answer. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the reliance-arbitration axis, the self-confidence axis, the source-credibility axis, and the belief-valence/truth direction to establish that arbitration is (i) near-orthogonal to the model's own self-confidence, (ii) not merely framed source credibility, and (iii) distinct from which answer is objectively true. Localize the best layer.

4. Over/under-reliance metric. Define per-item over-reliance = the arbitration axis reading toward DEFER on MODEL-RIGHT/SOURCE-WRONG items; under-reliance = reading toward KEEP on MODEL-WRONG/SOURCE-RIGHT items. Core prediction: the model exhibits both signatures (deferring to some wrong sources despite being right, and ignoring some correct sources despite being wrong), and the arbitration axis separates these from correct arbitration; test whether over-reliance grows with framed source credibility while under-reliance grows with the model's own self-confidence—mirroring the human joint role of trust and self-confidence.

Test whether the pre-commit arbitration readout predicts these errors per item beyond baselines (self-confidence axis, source-credibility axis, belief-valence margin, output entropy, item difficulty). Report incremental AUROC in nested logistic regression.

6. Dissociation from self-confidence and credibility (core). On matched-self-confidence and matched-source-credibility items, show the arbitration axis (not the self-confidence or credibility axes) accounts for defer-vs-keep—establishing a genuine two-place self-versus-source arbitration rather than repackaged self-confidence or source trust. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the pre-commit position on held-out items, steer along the reliance-arbitration axis (orthogonalized against self-confidence, source-credibility, and belief-valence). As controls, steer self-confidence (should shift keep-tendency generically regardless of source correctness) and source-credibility (should shift defer-tendency generically). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in over/under-reliance error rate vs unchanged no-conflict accuracy.

8. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free reliance-calibration knob: use the arbitration readout together with correctness signals to reduce net reliance errors, and evaluate in a simple agentic RAG/tool setting where the tool is sometimes wrong (report over-reliance rate on wrong tools, under-reliance rate on right tools, net accuracy vs MeCo-style gating and a self-confidence-only baseline). Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('are you keeping this because you trust yourself or the source?') aligns with the latent arbitration axis (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis and steering to held-out items and an independent tool-conflict / advisor-QA set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer/readout position. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether the over/under-reliance profile qualitatively matches the human joint-role-of-confidence-and-trust signature.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The reliance-arbitration axis may not be separable from the self-confidence axis, the source-credibility axis, or the belief-valence direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because the diagnostic cells cross the correctness of BOTH the model and the source—self-confidence and credibility cannot trivially explain arbitration; near-collapse (arbitration being merely self-confidence minus credibility) is an informative negative result that itself sharpens the MeCo/Confidence-is-Not-Competence accounts.

The over/under-reliance phenomenon may be weak or RLHF-shaped (aligned models may defer or keep by default); a null/small result is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, reported via per-model base rates and by focusing on the conflict cells against the accuracy-optimal policy.

Reliance framing may act through surface cues ('the tool says', 'an expert says') rather than a genuine arbitration abstraction; we mitigate with diverse source framings (tool output, retrieved passage, advisor), paraphrase templates, matched controls, and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the axis predicts reliance behavior beyond a source-framing surface baseline.

Belief/truth, self-confidence, and credibility probes are brittle to surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize the pre-commit readout position, restrict key analyses to high-margin cases, and report per-template consistency.
The arbitration signal is a linear projection that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral defer-vs-keep.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify arbitration steering calibrates reliance on conflict items without altering no-conflict accuracy or collapsing the model into always-deferring/always-keeping.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.

Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or agent-tuned models; three-family replication, an agentic-RAG application, and independent tool-conflict transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: ideological_constraint_binding_axis
Title: The Package Deal in the Machine: A Latent Ideological-Constraint Axis that Binds Socially-Correlated but Unrelated Beliefs in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human 'ideological constraint / generalized prejudice / package-deal' phenomenon (adopting one attitude pulls in socially-correlated but logically-unrelated attitudes across disparate domains), when an LLM adopts a stance on one issue in-context, its belief-valence readout for socially-correlated but non-entailed and semantically-dissimilar propositions on OTHER issues shifts toward the ideologically-congruent value; this cross-issue binding is carried by a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'ideological-constraint' signal distinct from the belief-valence direction, from logical entailment, and from semantic association, is decodable, causally predicts and drives spontaneous cross-issue stance spillover, and can be steered to tighten or loosen the package.
Related Work: Political-stance interpretability shows linear political-perspective directions (Linear Representations of Political Perspective 2025), general-vs-topic-specific political neurons whose fine-tuning drives cross-topic stance generalization (PNLAC/InhibitFT 2025), socio-political frame directions (2025), persona localization (2025), and that LLMs recreate human attitude correlations even across dissimilar topics (Can LLMs Predict Associations Among Human Attitudes 2025). Human science establishes ideological constraint / package-deal belief systems: attitudes align across disparate issues via social/alliance motives rather than logic (Ideology: Psychological and Social Foundations 2021; A Psychology of Ideology 2022; Generalized Prejudice 2022; belief-system-networks Ising models 2020). Crucially, PNLAC studies cross-topic generalization at FINE-TUNING time (weight-edit-driven, neuron-level, behavioral); linear-perspective work reads a single stance dimension; attitude-association work is behavioral. NONE isolates an INFERENCE-TIME, decodable 'ideological-constraint' signal that, when a stance is adopted in-context, causally pulls belief-valence on socially-correlated but LOGICALLY-UNRELATED and SEMANTICALLY-DISSIMILAR propositions on other issues, dissociates this binding from logical entailment and from semantic/associative proximity, or causally steers the package's tightness. This differs from my prior belief_contagion_spreading proposal (semantic/representational-proximity spreading among associated propositions) because ideological package-deals bind SEMANTICALLY-DISTANT beliefs via learned SOCIAL correlation, and from consensus/provenance axes (source cues). We move from 'political stance is a linear direction and fine-tuning generalizes it' to 'an inference-time constraint signal binds unrelated beliefs into ideological packages, decodably, causally, and steerably.'
Abstract: Human belief systems are 'package deals': knowing someone's stance on abortion predicts their views on unrelated issues like gun control or immigration, an alignment driven by social/ideological constraint rather than logic. As LLMs simulate perspectives and are increasingly steered on individual issues, we ask whether they internally bind unrelated beliefs the same way. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs carry linear political-perspective directions and that fine-tuning on one topic spills over to others, and behavioral work shows LLMs recreate human attitude correlations across dissimilar topics, but none isolates an inference-time signal that causally binds logically-unrelated, semantically-distant beliefs into an ideological package. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'ideological-constraint' signal, decodable when a stance is adopted in-context, distinct from the belief-valence direction, from logical entailment, and from semantic/associative proximity; that adopting a stance on issue A shifts the belief-valence readout for socially-correlated but non-entailed, semantically-dissimilar propositions on issue B toward the ideologically-congruent value; that per-example constraint strength predicts and causally drives this cross-issue spillover; and that steering the constraint signal tightens or loosens the package without changing the adopted stance. Using stance-adoption prompts paired with cross-issue targets graded by social correlation, logical entailment, and semantic similarity, we fit a constraint axis, quantify binding, dissociate it from entailment and semantics, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast ideological constraint mechanistically as a decodable, steerable belief-binding signal.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/stance direction that reads endorsement of a proposition (mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer) on standard true/false and stance-agreement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations from Marks & Tegmark, plus stance-agreement items); validate on held-out items. As a control, fit a single 'political-perspective' left-right direction following Linear Representations of Political Perspective (2025), to test whether ideological constraint is more than a 1-D stance axis.

2. Cross-issue package stimulus construction. Assemble ~400 issue pairs (A,B) where A and B are socially CORRELATED in human belief systems (from attitude-correlation datasets / survey co-endorsement, e.g. ANES-derived) but are LOGICALLY UNRELATED (neither entails the other) and SEMANTICALLY DISSIMILAR (low embedding similarity, different domains). For each pair, build stance-adoption prompts that establish a stance on issue A in-context (via persona framing or a stated opinion), then probe/query belief-valence on target propositions about issue B. Grade targets along three orthogonal dimensions: (i) SOCIAL CORRELATION strength with A (high vs near-zero human co-endorsement), (ii) LOGICAL ENTAILMENT from A (entailed vs non-entailed, validated by rule checks + LLM judge + human spot-checks), and (iii) SEMANTIC/ASSOCIATIVE similarity to A (high vs low). Include a NO-STANCE baseline and UNRELATED-uncorrelated control targets. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out pairs/templates for transfer.

3. Cross-issue binding measurement. For each target proposition on issue B, read the frozen belief-valence projection in NO-STANCE vs STANCE-ADOPTED conditions; define per-target binding = shift toward the ideologically-congruent value after adopting the A-stance. Core prediction: binding is positive for socially-correlated, non-entailed, semantically-dissimilar B-targets (the package-deal signature) and near-zero for socially-uncorrelated controls—demonstrating spillover along learned SOCIAL correlation rather than logic or semantics.

4. Ideological-constraint axis fitting and separability. Extract activations at a post-stance-adoption readout position and fit a linear probe to decode whether an in-context stance will bind a given cross-issue target (high vs low constraint engagement), controlling for the target's own content. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the ideological-constraint axis, the belief-valence direction, and the single left-right political-perspective direction to establish that constraint is (i) near-orthogonal to the target's belief-valence and (ii) richer than a 1-D stance axis (constraint predicts binding of ARBITRARY correlated targets, not just position on the left-right line). Localize the best layer.

5. Triple dissociation (social vs logical vs semantic). Using the 3-way graded target design, regress per-target binding on social correlation, logical entailment, and semantic similarity. Core test: SOCIAL correlation predicts binding beyond logical entailment and semantic similarity (the distinctively ideological, non-logical, non-associative package-deal effect), and the ideological-constraint axis tracks social correlation specifically. Contrast against my prior associative-contagion mechanism by showing binding to semantically-DISTANT but socially-correlated targets.

6. Behavioral spillover prediction. Elicit the model's stated stance/endorsement on B-targets after adopting the A-stance; score cross-issue spillover (adopting the ideologically-congruent B-stance). Test whether per-target constraint-axis binding predicts behavioral spillover via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, left-right direction, semantic similarity, entailment, output entropy, item length).

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. On held-out cross-issue targets, steer along the ideological-constraint axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and the left-right direction). Predict: suppressing constraint loosens the package (the model's B-belief no longer shifts when an A-stance is adopted) WITHOUT changing the adopted A-stance or beliefs on uncorrelated controls; amplifying it tightens the package (stronger cross-issue spillover, even to weakly-correlated targets). As controls, steer belief-valence (should change the target's stance directly) and the left-right direction (should shift overall political position, not arbitrary cross-issue binding). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in cross-issue binding/spillover vs unchanged adopted A-stance and uncorrelated-control beliefs.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags ideological over-binding (a model's stance on one issue silently contaminating unrelated judgments) and a knob to loosen it while preserving legitimate stance adoption; on a held-out set (including non-political socially-correlated attitude packages, e.g. consumer/lifestyle clusters, to show the mechanism is general ideological constraint not just US politics) measure spillover reduction while preserving the intended A-stance and uncorrelated-target neutrality. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted constraint axis and steering to held-out issue pairs/templates and an independent attitude-correlation set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether the model's binding matrix across issues correlates with the human attitude-correlation matrix (a machine ideological-constraint map).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The ideological-constraint axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction or the single left-right political-perspective direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse (constraint being merely a 1-D stance axis) as an informative negative result that itself sharpens the linear-perspective account. The key distinguishing test is that constraint must predict binding of ARBITRARY socially-correlated targets, not just position along one axis.

The critical claim rests on decorrelating social correlation from logical entailment and semantic similarity; constructing socially-correlated but logically-unrelated, semantically-distant issue pairs is delicate. We validate non-entailment (rule checks + LLM judge + human spot-checks), measure semantic similarity with embeddings, source social correlation from human survey co-endorsement, and report the triple-dissociation regression.

Binding could be driven by pretraining co-occurrence of the issues rather than a genuine ideological-constraint abstraction; we control for issue co-occurrence frequency and test whether the constraint axis predicts binding beyond a co-occurrence baseline, and include non-political attitude packages to show generality.

The effect may be weak or RLHF-shaped (aligned models may resist stance adoption or refuse political framing); a null/small result is itself informative, and we report per-model base rates and include persona-framed stance adoption to surface binding.
Belief/stance probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize readout positions, and report per-template consistency.
Binding is a linear projection that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral spillover.

Stance adoption is signaled by persona/opinion framing that could act as surface cues; we mitigate with diverse framings, paraphrase templates, and held-out-pair transfer, testing whether binding predicts spillover beyond a framing-lexeme baseline.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify constraint steering changes cross-issue binding without altering the adopted stance or degrading uncorrelated-target neutrality.

This probes political/attitudinal binding; we use synthetic personas and survey-derived correlations, frame steering as a de-biasing (package-loosening) intervention, and treat human-correlation comparisons descriptively.

Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or heavily-aligned models; three-family replication and independent attitude-correlation transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: distinctiveness_stereotype_belief_axis
Title: Kernel-of-Truth, Exaggerated: A Latent Distinctiveness Axis that Contaminates an LLM's Beliefs About Within-Group Trait Prevalence
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the representativeness model of stereotypes (Bordalo-Gennaioli: groups are judged by their most DISTINCTIVE type relative to other groups, neglecting common types, producing base-rate neglect), an LLM's belief about how PREVALENT a trait is WITHIN a social group is pulled by the trait's DISTINCTIVENESS/diagnosticity (P(trait|group)/P(trait|other groups)) rather than by its actual within-group base rate; this distinctiveness signal is a separable, near-orthogonal latent axis distinct from the represented within-group prevalence and from trait valence, its leakage onto the prevalence belief (a 'stereotype-exaggeration' signature) is decodable, causally predicts inflation of distinctive-but-rare traits and deflation of common-but-non-distinctive traits, and can be steered to remove or induce the distortion.
Related Work: Cross-domain work models stereotypes as representativeness-distorted Bayesian judgments: groups are represented by their most distinctive/diagnostic types, yielding base-rate neglect, exaggeration of distinctive-but-unlikely traits, and over-reaction to confirming information (Bordalo, Coffman, Gennaioli & Shleifer 'Stereotypes' 2014; Stereotypes as Bayesian Judgements/Prediction of Social Groups 2021/2024; Natural Probability Theory of Stereotypes 2024; base-rate-vs-diagnosticity in the Lawyer-Engineer problem 2016/2023). LLM interpretability decodes/steers demographic and trait representations (Linear socio-demographic representations 2025; Artificial Impressions 2025; Culturescope 2025; Race/Ethnicity mechanistic bias 2026) and shows the representativeness heuristic behaviorally (Real Linda / ReHeAT 2024; CBEval 2024), plus belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023). Crucially, ALL LLM bias work reads WHICH demographic is inferred or documents outcome-level stereotyping; NONE isolates whether the model's belief about a trait's WITHIN-GROUP PREVALENCE is distorted by the trait's DISTINCTIVENESS (its cross-group diagnostic ratio) rather than its actual base rate—the specific representativeness mechanism—nor defines a distinctiveness-onto-prevalence leakage metric separable from the true base rate, nor causally links it to the exaggeration-of-distinctive-traits and base-rate-neglect signatures. This differs from my prior typicality_truth_conflation_axis (typicality contaminating category-MEMBERSHIP truth, e.g. 'a penguin is a bird'), individual_vs_typical_belief_axis (attributing a belief to a specific person defaulting to the majority), consensus_prevalence_axis (social endorsement biasing a fact's truth), and diagnosticity_axis (evidence likelihood-ratio in hypothesis testing): here the object is a graded belief about within-group trait prevalence, and the distorting driver is cross-group distinctiveness, the exact Bordalo-Gennaioli representativeness distortion, not previously localized in LLMs. We move from 'LLMs stereotype behaviorally and encode demographics' to 'the model represents a trait's distinctiveness and over-weights it into within-group prevalence belief, a decodable, steerable exaggeration.'
Abstract: A leading model of stereotypes holds that people judge a group by its most DISTINCTIVE type—the trait that best separates it from other groups—neglecting common types, so stereotypes exaggerate a kernel of truth into unlikely extremes and exhibit base-rate neglect. As LLMs increasingly reason about social groups, we ask whether they inherit this distortion at the representational level. Prior work decodes demographic representations and documents behavioral stereotyping, but none isolates whether the model's belief about how PREVALENT a trait is WITHIN a group is driven by the trait's cross-group DISTINCTIVENESS rather than its actual within-group base rate. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'distinctiveness' axis, decodable at read time, encoding a trait's diagnostic ratio for a group, distinct from the represented within-group prevalence (base rate) and from trait valence; and a 'stereotype-exaggeration' signature: the degree to which distinctiveness leaks onto the prevalence belief, predictive per item of inflating distinctive-but-rare traits and deflating common-but-non-distinctive ones. Using group-trait items where within-group prevalence and cross-group distinctiveness are orthogonally varied against a Bayesian benchmark, we fit a distinctiveness axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item leakage, and connect it to behavioral prevalence errors and to the over-reaction-to-confirming-information asymmetry. Double-dissociation steering tests whether suppressing leakage makes prevalence beliefs track the true base rate (removing exaggeration) and amplifying it induces distortion, without changing the represented base rate, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a classic stereotype mechanism as a decodable, steerable distinctiveness-onto-prevalence contamination, with fairness implications.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen graded belief/prevalence direction that reads how strongly the model believes a proposition/that a trait is prevalent: calibrate activations against known probabilities via linear regression on explicit-probability and prevalence statements (validate monotonic mapping), plus a standard true/false probe (Marks & Tegmark) as a cross-check; validate on held-out items. Separately fit control axes: (a) a WITHIN-GROUP-PREVALENCE/base-rate direction (decoding P(trait|group) from stated frequencies), and (b) a trait-VALENCE direction (positive vs negative trait), to distinguish distinctiveness from the true base rate and from valence.

2. Prevalence x distinctiveness stimulus construction with a Bayesian benchmark. Build ~500 group-trait items over both SYNTHETIC groups (fictional groups with fully-specified trait distributions, so ground truth is controlled and pretraining priors are absent) and, as an external-validity set, real occupation/nationality categories with survey-grounded trait frequencies. Orthogonally vary (i) actual WITHIN-GROUP PREVALENCE P(trait|group) (rare vs common) and (ii) DISTINCTIVENESS = P(trait|group)/P(trait|comparison groups) (low vs high diagnostic ratio), yielding the key diagnostic cells: DISTINCTIVE-BUT-RARE (high diagnostic ratio, low base rate—exaggeration risk) and COMMON-BUT-NON-DISTINCTIVE (high base rate, low diagnostic ratio—deflation risk). For each item the normative posterior belief that a random group member has the trait equals the stated base rate (distinctiveness should NOT change it). Also manipulate group SIMILARITY (the Bordalo-Gennaioli prediction that distortion is largest for similar groups). Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out groups/traits/templates for transfer.

3. Distinctiveness-axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the group-trait span and fit a linear probe (regression on graded distinctiveness; and high-vs-low classification) to decode distinctiveness, controlling for the true base rate. Report R^2/AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the distinctiveness axis, the base-rate/prevalence direction, and the valence direction to establish that distinctiveness is (i) near-orthogonal to the represented within-group prevalence and (ii) not merely valence. Localize the best layer.

4. Stereotype-exaggeration leakage metric. For each item, project onto the frozen prevalence-belief direction and measure how far the belief that a group member has the trait is pulled by DISTINCTIVENESS holding the true base rate fixed (leakage = shift attributable to distinctiveness rather than the base rate, calibrated per model against the Bayesian benchmark). Core predictions: DISTINCTIVE-BUT-RARE traits read as MORE prevalent than their base rate warrants (exaggeration) and COMMON-BUT-NON-DISTINCTIVE traits read as LESS prevalent (deflation); leakage grows with group similarity (the similar-groups signature); and the represented base-rate readout is unchanged across distinctiveness conditions (so the distortion is overweighting, not a re-read of frequency). Report leakage across the 2x2 grid with effect sizes.

5. Behavioral prevalence-error and confirmation-asymmetry prediction. Elicit the model's stated prevalence estimate for each group-trait pair. Score two failures: (a) EXAGGERATION = overestimating prevalence of distinctive-but-rare traits; (b) DEFLATION = underestimating common-but-non-distinctive traits (both deviations from the Bayesian benchmark). Additionally test the over-reaction asymmetry: present one stereotype-CONFIRMING vs one stereotype-DISCONFIRMING individuating exemplar and measure belief update, predicting larger updates to confirming than matched disconfirming evidence. Test whether per-item leakage predicts these behavioral distortions via regression; report AUROC/R^2 vs baselines (base-rate axis, valence axis, output entropy, diagnostic-ratio surface value, item length).

6. Dissociation from base rate and valence (core). Contrast matched-base-rate/varied-distinctiveness cells and matched-distinctiveness/varied-base-rate cells to show the distinctiveness axis and leakage metric predict prevalence errors beyond the base-rate and valence axes—establishing distinctiveness as a distinct driver of stereotype exaggeration rather than repackaged frequency or negativity. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the distinctiveness axis (orthogonalized against the base-rate/prevalence and valence directions) at read time on held-out items. Predict: suppressing distinctiveness-leakage makes prevalence beliefs track the true base rate (removing exaggeration of distinctive-rare traits and deflation of common ones) WITHOUT changing the represented base rate or beliefs on non-distinctive controls; amplifying it induces stereotype exaggeration. As controls, steer the base-rate direction (should shift prevalence belief via re-read frequency) and valence (should shift positivity, not distinctiveness-driven prevalence). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in deviation-from-Bayesian-benchmark toward the true base rate vs unchanged base-rate readout and control-item beliefs.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free fairness diagnostic that flags distinctiveness-driven stereotype exaggeration from the leakage metric and steers to debias; on a held-out set (including real occupation/nationality trait beliefs with survey-grounded frequencies) measure reduction in prevalence-belief distortion while preserving accurate base-rate reasoning (report exaggeration/deflation reduction, over-correction, calibration vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, leakage metric, and steering to held-out groups/traits/templates without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether the model's distortion profile qualitatively matches the Bordalo-Gennaioli signature (distinctive-but-rare traits exaggerated, base-rate neglect, larger distortion for similar groups, over-reaction to confirming evidence).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The distinctiveness axis may not be separable from the base-rate/prevalence direction or valence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because the true base rate is held fixed while distinctiveness varies—base rate cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (distinctiveness being merely the base rate or valence) is an informative negative result.

The graded prevalence/belief probe is harder to calibrate than a binary truth probe; we validate the activation->probability mapping on held-out prevalence statements, report calibration and probe-fit diagnostics, and treat leakage/deviation as lower bounds.

Distinctiveness and base rate are conveyed by numeric/frequency cues that could act as surface features rather than genuine abstractions; we mitigate with synthetic groups (controlled distributions, no pretraining priors), diverse paraphrase templates, numeric-vs-verbal framings, and held-out transfer, testing whether the axes predict belief beyond raw surface diagnostic-ratio and base-rate values, and verify the base-rate readout is unchanged across distinctiveness conditions.

Constructing DISTINCTIVE-BUT-RARE and COMMON-BUT-NON-DISTINCTIVE cells with a clean Bayesian benchmark requires fully-specified cross-group trait distributions; we use synthetic groups for the controlled core and survey-grounded real categories for external validity, validating distributions with rule checks.

The real-category set carries genuine social-fairness sensitivity and contested ground truth; we anchor on survey-grounded frequencies, use neutral synthetic groups for the causal core, frame steering as a debiasing (exaggeration-removal) intervention, and report label-uncertainty sensitivity.
Belief/prevalence probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.

The leakage metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear leakage could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral distortion.
The confirmation-asymmetry test depends on matched confirming/disconfirming evidence strength; we calibrate per-exemplar update magnitude and match by measured strength.
Behavioral prevalence-estimate elicitation is format-sensitive; we use multiple formats (numeric probability, frequency, verbal) and report sensitivity.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify distinctiveness-suppression makes prevalence track the base rate without altering the base-rate readout or degrading accuracy on non-distinctive traits.

Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or safety-tuned models; three-family replication and real-category external-validity transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: temporal_proximity_truth_axis
Title: Nearer Feels Truer: A Latent Temporal-Proximity Axis that Biases an LLM's Truth Beliefs Toward the Subjective Now
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring human temporal-discounting and present-bias effects, an LLM's belief-valence/truth readout for a propositionally- and evidence-identical claim is pulled toward 'true' when the claim's referenced time is closer to the model's subjective 'now' and pushed away as the time recedes (past or future); this temporal-proximity shift is carried by a separable, near-orthogonal latent axis distinct from the truth direction and from the model's raw log-compressed temporal-distance representation, is decodable, causally predicts overbelief of near-present claims and underbelief of temporally-distant ones, and can be steered to remove or induce the bias.
Related Work: Interpretability shows LLMs linearly encode time and a subjective 'now' with a log-compressed (Weber-Fechner) temporal manifold organized around a ~2025 reference point (Language Models Represent Space and Time 2023; The Other Mind 2025; Temporal Heads 2025), and that belief/truth-valence is linearly decodable and context-sensitive (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024). Cognitive science documents temporal discounting and construal-level effects whereby psychologically distant (past/future) events are judged more abstractly and with less certainty than present ones. Crucially, ALL LLM temporal work encodes WHEN an event is (calendar time, distance-to-now) or handles time-specific FACT recall; NONE asks whether temporal proximity to the subjective now CONTAMINATES the model's TRUTH/BELIEF representation of an arbitrary claim—so that a near-present-framed claim reads truer than the identical claim framed as temporally distant—defines a proximity-onto-truth leakage metric separable from the raw temporal-distance manifold, or causally links it to overbelief of near-present claims. This differs from my prior temporal_validity_belief_axis (currently-true vs stale/never-true facts—about a fact's validity window) because here the driver is proximity of the referenced time to 'now' biasing the truth of claims whose validity does not depend on time; and from construction/fluency/negativity axes. We move from 'LLMs encode a subjective now and log-compressed time' to 'proximity to that now leaks onto the truth axis, a decodable, steerable belief bias.'
Abstract: Humans treat the present as more real and more certain than the distant past or future, discounting temporally remote outcomes and construing them more abstractly. As LLMs increasingly reason about events across time, we ask whether they inherit an analogous distortion: does how close a claim's referenced time is to the model's subjective 'now' bias whether the model believes it? Prior interpretability work shows LLMs linearly encode calendar time and a log-compressed subjective 'now,' and separately that they linearly encode truth, but none asks whether temporal proximity contaminates the truth representation itself.
