We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'self-anchor' signal, decodable before the re-estimate, distinct from the belief-valence/magnitude direction and from an external-anchor direction, that encodes lingering pull of the model's own prior guess; that a re-estimate assimilates toward the earlier self-generated estimate more than toward a matched externally-provided anchor or a no-prior baseline; that per-item self-anchor strength predicts this assimilation (and inflated confidence in the biased value); and that steering the signal erases or amplifies the self-contamination. Using tasks where the model first estimates a quantity, then—after intervening turns and an explicit instruction to answer afresh—re-estimates it, with matched external-anchor and no-anchor controls, we fit a self-anchor signal, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify assimilation against a normative independence baseline, connect it to behavioral bias and confidence, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen graded MAGNITUDE/belief direction that reads the model's estimate of a quantity: calibrate activations against known values via linear regression on explicit-value statements (validate monotonic mapping), plus a standard true/false probe (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) as a cross-check; validate on held-out items. Separately fit an EXTERNAL-ANCHOR direction from prompts where an externally-supplied anchor number precedes the estimate, so self-anchoring can be dissociated from responding to external anchors.

2. Self-anchor stimulus construction. Assemble ~400 numeric-estimation questions (uncertain quantities: population/distance/date/quantity trivia the model estimates rather than knows exactly). For each, build matched sessions holding the target quantity fixed: (a) SELF-ANCHOR—the model first gives its own estimate, then after several intervening unrelated turns is instructed to give a FRESH, INDEPENDENT estimate 'as if for the first time'; (b) EXTERNAL-ANCHOR—instead of self-generating, a matched external number (equal to a typical first estimate) is presented before the re-estimate; (c) NO-ANCHOR baseline—the model estimates once with no prior; (d) NEUTRAL-filler control matching session length. Use paraphrase templates so the re-estimate query differs in surface form; reserve held-out items/templates for transfer.

3. Self-anchor signal and separability. At a PRE-re-estimate readout position (after the first estimate and intervening turns, before the fresh answer), fit a linear probe to decode whether the quantity was earlier SELF-estimated vs not, controlling for the target content. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the self-anchor direction, the magnitude/belief direction, and the external-anchor direction to establish that self-anchor is (i) near-orthogonal to the estimated magnitude and (ii) distinct from the external-anchor direction. Localize the best layer (compare to reported shallow-layer anchoring loci).

4. Assimilation metric. For each item, measure how far the fresh re-estimate is pulled toward the earlier self-generated value relative to the NO-ANCHOR baseline (assimilation = shift toward the prior guess). Core prediction: re-estimates assimilate toward the self-generated first estimate MORE than toward a matched external anchor of equal value (the self-generation signature), and the self-anchor signal predicts per-item assimilation.

5. Behavioral prediction (assimilation + confidence inflation). Elicit the fresh re-estimate and stated confidence. Test whether per-item self-anchor strength predicts (a) assimilation toward the prior guess and (b) inflated confidence in the (biased) re-estimate—the illusion-of-confirmation signature—beyond baselines (magnitude margin, external-anchor readout, output entropy, intervening-turn count, item difficulty). Report AUROC/R^2 in nested regression.

6. Dissociation from external anchoring and magnitude (core). On matched-value items where only the anchor SOURCE (self vs external) differs, show the self-anchor axis (not the external-anchor or magnitude axes) accounts for the extra assimilation and confidence inflation—establishing self-anchoring as a distinct mechanism. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the pre-re-estimate position on held-out SELF-ANCHOR items, steer along the self-anchor direction (orthogonalized against magnitude and external-anchor). Predict: suppressing it makes the re-estimate genuinely independent (assimilation drops toward the no-anchor baseline, confidence de-inflates) WITHOUT changing re-estimates on no-anchor controls; amplifying it deepens self-contamination. Controls: steer the magnitude direction (should shift the estimate value directly) and the external-anchor direction (should shift response to external anchors, not the self-anchor). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in assimilation/confidence vs unchanged no-anchor behavior.

8. Application, dynamics, and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags self-anchored (non-independent) re-estimates and steers to restore independence (useful for multi-round estimation, self-refinement, and ensembling where independence is assumed). Trace assimilation as a function of intervening-turn count and first-estimate confidence (a dose/decay analysis, testing whether more-confident first guesses anchor more). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted signal and steering to held-out items/templates without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer/readout position. As a human-parallel analysis, test whether—mirroring Epley-Gilovich—explicit forewarning ('ignore your earlier guess') fails to fully remove self-anchoring, and whether it lowers the self-anchor signal.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The self-anchor signal may not be separable from the magnitude/belief direction or the external-anchor direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because matched-value items differ only in anchor SOURCE—the external-anchor direction cannot trivially explain self-anchoring; near-collapse (self-anchor being merely the external-anchor mechanism) is an informative negative result that itself sharpens the anchoring literature.

The effect could reduce to the first estimate lingering in context (recency/context-carryover) rather than genuine self-anchoring; we mitigate with intervening turns, paraphrased re-estimate queries, the external-anchor control (equal value, no self-authorship), and by testing whether self-anchoring exceeds external-anchoring at matched value.

The graded magnitude probe is harder to calibrate than a binary truth probe; we validate the activation->value mapping, report calibration diagnostics, and treat assimilation as a lower bound, cross-checking with behavioral estimates.

The self-anchoring behavioral effect may be weak or RLHF/reasoning-shaped (reasoning models resist anchoring per prior work); a null/small result is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, reported via effect sizes and dose/decay, with a reasoning-tuned model as an extension.

Constructing genuinely uncertain estimation items where the model produces variable first guesses (not exact recall) is needed; we select approximate-estimation items and report the fraction where a first-estimate anchor can even form.
Probes are brittle to surface form and context; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize the pre-re-estimate readout position, and report per-template consistency.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify self-anchor suppression restores independence without altering no-anchor estimates or degrading accuracy.

Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models; three-family replication, dose/decay analysis, and held-out transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: belief_route_decomposition
Title: One Truth or Many Routes? Decomposing the LLM Belief Direction into Compositional Epistemic-Basis Features with Sparse Autoencoders
Short Hypothesis: The linearly-decodable belief/truth readout is not a single primitive feature but an aggregate of a small set of sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features, each encoding a distinct EPISTEMIC ROUTE by which the model comes to hold a proposition true (parametric recall, in-context assertion, logical entailment, source testimony, surface plausibility); the belief-probe projection decomposes as a weighted sum over these route-features, the SAME true proposition reached via different routes recruits DIFFERENT features while landing at an equal probe projection ('many routes, one readout'), and ablating a route-feature selectively removes belief acquired via that route without disturbing belief via other routes.
Related Work: The 'Geometry of Truth' (Marks & Tegmark 2023) establishes a single linear truth direction; 'Truth is Universal' (2024) refines it to a 2D subspace (a general-truth direction plus a polarity-sensitive direction); context-sensitivity work (Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024) shows the direction is a causal mediator that in-context assertions push around; 'Do I Know This Entity?' (2024) uses SAEs to find entity-recognition directions gating hallucination; 'Emergence of Linear Truth Encodings' (2025) traces how the truth subspace forms; and 'Use SAEs to Discover Unknown Concepts, Not to Act on Known Concepts' (2025) argues SAEs are best for discovering unknown structure. Crucially, ALL of this treats the belief/truth readout as a monolithic (at most 2D, and that 2D is polarity, not route) primitive, and my own prior proposals uniformly ADD single orthogonal axes (fluency, consensus, provenance, coherence...) alongside it. NONE asks whether the belief readout ITSELF decomposes into a compositional feature basis whose components are distinct belief-FORMATION routes, tests the sum-of-features decomposition of the probe projection, demonstrates the 'many routes, one readout' signature (different features at equal projection), or shows route-selective causal ablation. This reframes 'the truth direction' from a primitive into an emergent aggregate over heterogeneous epistemic pathways, uses SAEs in their discovery mode, and yields a compositional, causally-testable account of what a belief probe is actually reading.
Abstract: Interpretability has converged on a striking result: language models linearly encode whether a proposition is true, and this 'truth direction' can be probed and steered. But is belief one thing, or a bundle? A proposition can be held true because the model recalls it parametrically, because it was asserted in context, because it follows from stated premises, because a credible source vouched for it, or because it merely sounds plausible—routes that behavioral and cognitive work treat as importantly different, yet which all read out as 'true' on a single probe. We hypothesize that the belief-probe projection is an aggregate: a weighted sum of a small set of sparse-autoencoder features, each encoding a distinct epistemic route to belief. Using pretrained open SAEs and a standard belief probe, we (1) express the probe projection as a linear function of SAE feature activations and test whether a handful of features reconstruct the probe direction; (2) construct propositions whose truth is held fixed but whose route to belief is varied, and test the 'many routes, one readout' signature—different routes recruit different SAE features while achieving equal probe projection; (3) causally ablate individual route-features and show belief acquired via that route selectively collapses while belief via other routes is preserved; and (4) test compositional additivity when two routes jointly support a claim. We compare the multi-route decomposition against the standard 1D and 2D (general+polarity) truth accounts. Our results would recast 'the belief direction' as a compositional readout over epistemic-basis features, with implications for probe reliability, targeted hallucination control, and what it means to say a model 'believes' something.
Experiments: 1. Probe and SAE setup. On Gemma-2-9B (with Gemma Scope residual-stream SAEs) and Llama-3.1-8B (with Llama Scope SAEs), fit a belief/truth direction using mass-mean and logistic-regression probes on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) at the layer where a pretrained SAE is available and the probe is accurate; validate probe accuracy on held-out atomics. Also fit the polarity-robust 2D subspace (general-truth tG + polarity tP) following Truth is Universal as the comparison baseline.

2. Route-controlled stimulus construction. Build ~400 verifiable propositions, each rendered as a TRUE claim reached via five matched epistemic ROUTES holding truth fixed: (a) PARAMETRIC-RECALL (a fact the model reliably knows, no supporting context), (b) IN-CONTEXT-ASSERTED (the claim is stated as given in the prompt), (c) LOGICALLY-ENTAILED (premises are given from which the claim follows, using synthetic-entity chains so it cannot be recalled), (d) SOURCE-TESTIFIED (a credible source states the claim), (e) SURFACE-PLAUSIBLE (a plausible-sounding claim the model does not independently know). Include matched FALSE counterparts per route. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out propositions/templates. Verify each item lands at comparable belief-probe projection where possible, so routes can be compared at matched readout.

3. Sum-of-features decomposition test. At the probe readout position, run activations through the pretrained SAE and regress the belief-probe projection onto SAE feature activations (sparse linear fit). Identify the small set of features whose activations most reconstruct the projection; test whether a weighted sum of their SAE decoder directions reconstructs the probe direction (report cosine similarity of reconstructed vs. probe direction and the number of features needed vs. a random-feature baseline). Establish that the probe direction is well-approximated by a compact feature bundle rather than a single SAE feature.

4. Route-selective feature identification ('many routes, one readout'). For each route, identify SAE features that fire selectively when a TRUE proposition is believed via that route, using differential activation across routes at matched truth-value and matched probe projection. Test the core signature: at equal belief-probe projection, different routes recruit different SAE features (measure route-classification accuracy from SAE features, and cross-route feature overlap vs. shuffled-label controls). This dissociates the shared scalar readout from route-specific composition.

5. Route-selective causal ablation (specificity). Ablate (zero/clamp) an identified route-feature at inference and measure that belief acquired via THAT route drops—behavioral answer flip and belief-probe projection decrease—while belief via the OTHER routes is preserved (off-route items unaffected). Compare to norm-matched random-feature ablation and shuffled-feature controls; sweep ablation strength. Report a route x ablated-feature interaction (each route-feature specifically knocks out its own route).

6. Compositional additivity. Construct items where TWO routes jointly support the same true claim (e.g., recalled AND asserted; entailed AND testified). Test whether the two corresponding route-features co-activate and whether their contributions to the belief-probe projection approximately ADD relative to single-route baselines, and whether jointly ablating both is needed to fully suppress belief. Report deviation from additivity.

7. Comparison against 1D/2D truth accounts. Test whether the multi-route SAE decomposition explains behavioral variance (answer flips, probe drops under route-specific manipulation) beyond the single 1D truth-probe projection and the 2D general+polarity subspace; report incremental predictive power and the fraction of belief behavior attributable to route-specific vs. shared components.

8. Robustness and generalization. Replicate across the two model families and two probe methods; transfer the identified route-features and ablation results to held-out propositions/templates without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase, sensitivity to SAE layer/width, and stability of the route-feature inventory across SAE runs where multiple SAEs are available.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The belief-probe projection may be dominated by a single SAE feature (a genuine primitive), in which case the sum-of-features decomposition fails; this is an informative negative result that would reinforce the monolithic-truth-direction view, and we report the number of features and reconstruction cosine against random-feature baselines to detect it.

Route-selective features may reflect surface cues of how the route was presented (e.g., the word 'because', a source name) rather than a genuine epistemic-formation abstraction; we mitigate by matching truth-value and belief-probe projection across routes, using diverse paraphrase templates and synthetic-entity items, including surface-cue baselines, and testing whether route-features predict belief behavior beyond a surface-lexeme classifier and transfer to held-out templates.

Pretrained SAEs may not cleanly isolate route features (incomplete dictionaries, dead/ultra-high-frequency features, wrong layer); we report SAE reconstruction quality and feature-interpretability diagnostics, try multiple SAE widths/layers where available, and treat the decomposition as a lower bound.

The 'many routes, one readout' claim requires matching belief-probe projection across routes, which may be imperfect; we condition analyses on projection-matched subsets and report sensitivity to the matching tolerance.

Belief/truth probes are brittle to surface form and context-sensitive; we validate probes, use the polarity-robust 2D subspace as a comparison, restrict to high-margin cases, and report per-template consistency.

Route-selective ablation could degrade generation broadly rather than selectively; we require the route x ablated-feature specificity interaction (each feature knocks out only its own route), use norm-matched random-feature and shuffled controls, sweep strengths, and check off-route accuracy retention.
Compositional additivity may fail if routes interact nonlinearly; deviation from additivity is itself a reportable characterization rather than a failure.

Findings depend on the availability and quality of open pretrained SAEs and may not transfer to model families lacking them; two-family replication and held-out transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage, and results on 8-9B models may not extrapolate to frontier scale.

Name: belief_binding_capacity_swap
Title: Crowded Minds: Set-Size-Dependent Binding Interference in an LLM's Simultaneously-Held Beliefs and the Machine Swap Error
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human working-memory binding hypothesis (capacity is limited by interference among the temporary bindings that tie contents to their contexts, so errors grow with set size and are dominated by swaps—attributing the right content to the wrong item), when an LLM must simultaneously hold N belief triples (which agent/object holds which state), its belief representation degrades as N grows via a decodable 'binding-crowding' signal distinct from the belief-valence direction and from generic uncertainty; this crowding causally predicts and drives SWAP errors (assigning a state that belongs to another held belief, rather than a state absent from the set), and steering it worsens or protects binding integrity.
Related Work: Human working-memory science establishes that capacity is limited by INTERFERENCE among temporary content-context BINDINGS, not item memory: increasing set size specifically impairs binding memory and produces SWAP/misbinding errors (confusing the target with another list item, rarely with non-list items), with resource/slot/interference model debates (Oberauer Binding Hypothesis 2019; Interference Model 2023; What Limits WM Capacity 2016; Balancing Flexibility and Interference 2021; subspace partitioning resolves interference in human PFC 2023). In LLM interpretability, 'Language Models use Lookbacks to Track Beliefs' (2025) reverse-engineers how LLMs BIND character-object-state triples via co-located Ordering IDs in low-rank subspaces and retrieve them; 'Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations' (2024) shows belief representations are structured, steerable, but brittle; belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023). Working-memory-limit work shows transformers hit N-back capacity limits via attention-entropy dispersion (Self-Attention Limits WM 2024) and lack persistent latent state (LMs Do Not Have Human-Like WM 2025). Crucially, ALL LLM belief-tracking work studies the binding mechanism at small, fixed N and asks WHETHER a belief is bound correctly; NONE studies how belief-tracking degrades as the NUMBER of simultaneously-held beliefs grows (a set-size/capacity manipulation), isolates a decodable binding-crowding/interference signal that scales with set size, tests the DEFINING swap-error signature (errors are misbindings within the set, not intrusions from outside it), dissociates binding degradation from item/content degradation, or causally links crowding to swap errors. WM-limit work (N-back, latent-state) concerns sequential recall or hidden-state persistence, not multi-belief BINDING interference in the belief representation. This uniquely transfers Oberauer's binding hypothesis—set-size-limited binding, swap-dominated errors—into the mechanistic study of LLM belief tracking, extending the Lookbacks binding account to a capacity regime.
Abstract: A cornerstone of human working memory is that its severe capacity limit comes not from forgetting items but from interference among the temporary bindings that tie each content to its context: as the number of things held in mind grows, errors rise and—crucially—take the form of SWAPS, attributing the right content to the wrong item rather than losing it. As LLMs increasingly track many beliefs at once (who knows what, which object is where, which claim each source made), we ask whether they suffer the same binding-limited degradation. Prior work reverse-engineers how LLMs bind agent-object-state triples for belief tracking but always at small, fixed set sizes and asks only whether a single belief is bound correctly; none studies how belief tracking scales with the NUMBER of simultaneously-held beliefs. We hypothesize that as an LLM holds N belief triples, its belief representation degrades via a separable, decodable 'binding-crowding' signal that scales with set size, distinct from the belief-valence direction and from generic uncertainty; that this crowding causally predicts and drives SWAP errors (assigning a state belonging to another held belief) rather than intrusions from outside the set; that binding memory degrades faster than item memory (the binding-hypothesis signature); and that steering the crowding signal worsens or protects binding integrity. Using stories that establish a controlled number of agent-object-state beliefs and query one, we manipulate set size, fit a crowding probe, characterize the error composition (swaps vs intrusions vs item loss), dissociate binding from item degradation, and perform causal steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results transfer a landmark working-memory law into LLM belief mechanisms as a decodable, steerable, capacity-limited binding interference.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Fit a generic uncertainty/confidence control axis (empirical answer-stability / output entropy) to distinguish binding-crowding from how uncertain the model is overall. Optionally, following Lookbacks (2025), locate the belief-binding subspace/layers to target readouts and steering.

2. Set-size stimulus construction. Build ~400 story families, each establishing N belief triples of the form (agent_i holds/knows that object_j is in state_k) with distinct agents, objects, and states, varying SET SIZE N from 1 to 8 while holding surface complexity per triple, story length-per-triple, and query format matched. Each family asks a single probe query about one target triple ('what does agent_i believe about object_j?'), with the correct answer being that triple's state. Construct the answer options so that error types are distinguishable: the correct state, OTHER states present in the set (swap candidates), and states NOT in the set (intrusion candidates). Include Sally-Anne-style false-belief variants (some triples are stale/false beliefs) to test binding under belief-vs-reality conflict. Use paraphrase templates and randomized agent/object/state assignments; reserve held-out families/templates for transfer.

3. Behavioral capacity-and-swap measurement (core phenomenon). Elicit the model's answer to the target query at each N and score accuracy plus ERROR COMPOSITION: SWAP errors (the answer is a state that belongs to ANOTHER held triple in the set), INTRUSION errors (a state not in the set), and ITEM-LOSS/abstention. Core predictions (Oberauer binding-hypothesis signatures): (a) accuracy declines with set size N; (b) among errors, SWAPS dominate and their rate grows with N, while intrusions from outside the set stay low; and (c) binding-relevant queries (which agent holds which state) degrade faster with N than item-presence queries (was this state/object mentioned at all), a binding-vs-item dissociation. Report accuracy and error-composition curves vs N, per model, with effect sizes.

4. Binding-crowding probe and separability. At the pre-answer readout position (after all triples are established, before the answer), fit a linear probe to decode the effective binding load / impending swap risk (high vs low crowding), operationalized by contrasting high-N/near-swap items against low-N/clean items, controlling for target content. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure how the crowding-probe projection scales with set size N (does it rise monotonically, tracking the behavioral capacity curve?). Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the crowding axis, the belief-valence direction, and the uncertainty axis to establish that crowding is (i) near-orthogonal to the target belief's value and (ii) not merely generic uncertainty. Optionally relate crowding to attention-score dispersion / entropy over the triple tokens (linking to the Self-Attention-Limits-WM account).

5. Swap-error prediction. Test whether the pre-answer crowding readout predicts, per item, whether the model will make a SWAP error (vs answer correctly), beyond baselines (belief-valence margin, uncertainty axis, output entropy, set size N as a surface count, story length). Report incremental AUROC in nested logistic regression. Critically test whether crowding predicts swaps SPECIFICALLY (not intrusions), the misbinding signature.

6. Binding-vs-item dissociation (core). Compare the crowding signal's prediction of BINDING errors (swaps in which-agent-holds-which-state) against ITEM errors (forgetting a state/object was mentioned at all). Show, mirroring the binding hypothesis, that set size and the crowding axis primarily impair binding while item memory is comparatively preserved, and that the crowding axis predicts binding failures beyond a generic item-recall probe. This establishes the phenomenon as binding INTERFERENCE, not simple capacity loss.

7. Causal steering (double dissociation). At the pre-answer position on held-out high-N items, steer along the binding-crowding direction (orthogonalized against belief-valence and uncertainty). Predict: suppressing crowding reduces swap errors (restores correct binding) WITHOUT changing behavior on low-N clean controls or item-presence judgments; amplifying it induces swap errors even at low N. As controls, steer belief-valence (should change which state is judged the target's, not selectively induce swaps) and uncertainty (should shift abstention/hedging generically). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in swap-error rate vs unchanged low-N accuracy and item memory.

8. Application, generalization, and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags high binding-crowding (impending swap risk) in multi-agent/multi-fact tracking—a reliability vector for long dialogues, multi-document QA, and multi-agent settings—and steers to protect binding; measure swap-error reduction while preserving accuracy at low load. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the crowding probe, error-composition analysis, and steering to held-out families/templates and an independent multi-belief tracking set (a scaled-up CausalToM / FANToM-style slice) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase, sensitivity to layer/readout position, and whether larger models within a family show higher effective binding capacity (a scale analog of expanded WM). As a human-parallel analysis, check whether the accuracy-vs-N and swap-dominance profile qualitatively matches the human set-size / swap-error signatures.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The binding-crowding signal may not be separable from the belief-valence direction or generic uncertainty; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because it must scale with set size and predict swaps specifically—uncertainty cannot trivially explain it; near-collapse (crowding being merely uncertainty or set-size count) is an informative negative result.

The core evidence rests on error COMPOSITION (swaps vs intrusions); if the model rarely errs even at high N (large effective capacity) or errors are dominated by intrusions rather than swaps, the binding-hypothesis signature fails—this is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, and we push N high enough to elicit errors and report per-model capacity curves.

Set size is a surface-countable manipulation; the crowding axis might reflect raw N or token count rather than genuine binding interference. We control for story length and per-triple complexity, include N as a surface baseline, use heterogeneous-vs-homogeneous memory sets (the binding hypothesis predicts more interference among similar bindings), and test whether the axis predicts swaps beyond a raw-N/length baseline and transfers to held-out templates.

Distinguishing binding degradation from item degradation requires clean item-presence vs which-agent-holds-what queries; we design matched item and binding probes per story and validate that item memory is measurable independently.

Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form and can drift over longer multi-belief contexts; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize the pre-answer readout position, restrict key analyses to high-margin cases, and report per-template and context-length consistency.

The crowding signal is a linear projection that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat it as a lower bound, report probe-fit diagnostics, and optionally cross-check with attention-entropy measures over triple tokens.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify crowding-suppression reduces swap errors without altering low-N accuracy, item memory, or collapsing the model into abstaining.

Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models (which may have larger effective binding capacity or externalize state via chain-of-thought); three-family replication, within-family scale trends, and independent multi-belief-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: anticipated_effort_belief_axis
Title: This Will Be Laborious: A Latent Anticipated-Effort Belief that Drives LLM Premature Give-Up on Solvable-but-Costly Problems
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human opportunity-cost account of effort allocation (people withhold cognitive effort from tasks anticipated to be laborious, independent of whether the task is solvable), an LLM forms a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'anticipated-effort' belief—a pre-generation estimate of how much computation solving a problem will cost—distinct from its solvability-belief/difficulty axis and from generic confidence; this anticipated-effort belief is decodable before the model reasons, causally predicts and drives premature give-up / under-thinking on solvable-but-laborious problems, and can be steered to make the model invest or withhold effort.
Related Work: LLM interpretability decodes a per-item DIFFICULTY axis (Probing the Difficulty Perception Mechanism 2025), a pre-generation SUCCESS/failure signal (LLMs Encode Their Failures 2026; Temporal Predictors 2025; Latent-Trajectory 2025), and a SOLVABILITY belief that is causally INERT for execution (Confidence is Not Competence 2025); adaptive-compute work allocates reasoning depth by difficulty (FR-Ponder 2025; Duo-LLM 2024; Understanding Dynamic Compute Allocation 2026; Knowing When to Stop 2025). Cross-domain effort science, however, shows effort allocation is governed by the anticipated COST/opportunity-cost of time and cost-evidence accumulation, dissociable from the probability of success (Toward a Rational and Mechanistic Account of Mental Effort 2017; The opportunity cost of time modulates cognitive effort 2017; oMCD 2024; How the Brain Decides When to Work and When to Rest 2014; Optimal Metacognitive Control of Memory Recall 2022). Crucially, ALL LLM work conflates 'anticipated effort/cost' with either DIFFICULTY (probability of failure) or SOLVABILITY, and adaptive-compute methods TRAIN a controller to allocate compute rather than asking whether the base model already REPRESENTS an anticipated-effort belief; NONE isolates a decodable ANTICIPATED-EFFORT (expected-cost-to-solve) belief separable from the solvability/difficulty axis, tests whether it causally drives premature give-up on SOLVABLE-but-laborious problems (the human effort-withdrawal signature), or steers it. This differs from Confidence-is-Not-Competence (solvability, found causally inert for execution)—here the target is a distinct cost-anticipation belief predicted to be causally POTENT specifically for the invest-vs-give-up decision (not micro-execution); from my prior learned_helplessness (failure-history-driven), sunk_reasoning (effort-inflates-belief), and intuition_override proposals. We move from 'LLMs perceive difficulty and can be trained to allocate compute' to 'the base model harbors a belief about how costly solving will be, dissociable from difficulty, that causally governs whether it bothers to try.'
Abstract: Humans withhold cognitive effort from tasks that feel laborious, driven by the anticipated cost of the work rather than merely the odds of failing—an opportunity-cost account well-established in cognitive neuroscience. As LLMs increasingly decide how much to reason before answering, we ask whether they carry an analogous internal quantity: a belief about how COSTLY solving a problem will be, and whether it causes them to give up on problems they could actually solve if they persisted. Prior interpretability work decodes difficulty and solvability beliefs (the latter found causally inert for execution) and trains controllers to allocate compute, but none isolates an anticipated-EFFORT belief—an expected-cost-to-solve estimate—as an axis separable from difficulty/solvability, nor links it to premature give-up. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'anticipated-effort' belief, decodable before the model reasons, distinct from the solvability/difficulty axis and from generic confidence, that encodes how laborious solving will be; that its per-item value causally predicts under-thinking / premature give-up on SOLVABLE-but-laborious problems (deferring, abstaining, or truncating reasoning on problems it would solve with more steps); and that steering it makes the model invest or withhold effort. Using problems that orthogonally vary solvability from anticipated effort (short-but-tricky vs long-but-mechanical), we fit an anticipated-effort probe, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify premature give-up against an oracle 'solvable-with-more-compute' benchmark, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a class of under-thinking failures as a decodable, steerable cost-anticipation belief.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (plus one reasoning-tuned model as an extension), fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit control axes: (a) a SOLVABILITY/DIFFICULTY direction from the model's pre-generation success/difficulty signal (following LLMs Encode Their Failures / Difficulty Perception constructions), and (b) a generic CONFIDENCE axis (empirical answer-stability), so anticipated-effort can be dissociated from odds-of-success and from confidence.

2. Solvability x effort stimulus construction. Assemble ~500 problems (arithmetic word problems, multi-hop QA, logic, simple planning) with definite answers, orthogonally crossing SOLVABILITY (the model can solve it given enough reasoning vs genuinely cannot) with ANTICIPATED EFFORT (SHORT/low-cost: solvable in few steps; LONG/high-cost: mechanically laborious—many arithmetic steps, long chains—but conceptually easy). The key diagnostic cell is SOLVABLE-BUT-LABORIOUS (low failure-odds, high effort-cost: the model should invest and would succeed). Establish an ORACLE label per item via best-of-N / extended-reasoning sampling to certify whether the model solves it when it does invest effort. Offer the model a give-up/defer option ('if this is too much work, you may decline'). Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates for transfer.

3. Anticipated-effort probe and separability. Extract activations at a PRE-generation readout position (after the problem, before any reasoning) and fit a linear probe (regression on the oracle-measured solution LENGTH/compute-cost; and high-vs-low effort classification) to decode anticipated effort, controlling for solvability. Report R^2/AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the anticipated-effort axis, the solvability/difficulty axis, and the confidence axis to establish that anticipated-effort is (i) near-orthogonal to solvability (the decisive diagnostic: matched-solvability items differing only in effort-cost) and (ii) not merely confidence. Localize the best layer.

4. Premature-give-up metric. Define per-item premature give-up = the model declining/abstaining/truncating reasoning on SOLVABLE-BUT-LABORIOUS items (certified solvable by the oracle). Core prediction (the human effort-withdrawal signature): the anticipated-effort readout, not the solvability axis, predicts give-up specifically on high-effort/solvable items—the model bails on problems it would solve with more steps. Compare give-up rates across the solvability x effort grid; predict give-up scales with anticipated effort at matched solvability.

5. Behavioral prediction. Test whether the pre-generation anticipated-effort readout predicts premature give-up / under-thinking (truncated CoT, abstention on solvable items) beyond baselines (solvability/difficulty axis, confidence axis, output entropy, problem length as a surface feature, item difficulty). Report incremental AUROC in nested logistic regression. Critically show it predicts give-up on solvable items that the solvability axis (which reads them as solvable) fails to explain.

6. Dissociation from solvability and confidence (core). On matched-solvability items varying only in anticipated effort, and matched-effort items varying only in solvability, show the anticipated-effort axis (not the solvability or confidence axes) accounts for premature give-up—establishing a genuine cost-anticipation belief rather than repackaged difficulty. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the pre-generation position on held-out SOLVABLE-BUT-LABORIOUS items, steer along the anticipated-effort axis (orthogonalized against solvability and confidence). Predict: suppressing anticipated-effort makes the model invest and solve (fewer give-ups, longer CoT, higher accuracy) WITHOUT changing behavior on genuinely-unsolvable controls (it should not waste effort there); amplifying it induces premature give-up even on easy items. As controls, steer the solvability axis (should shift perceived odds-of-success; per Confidence-is-Not-Competence, expected weak on execution) and confidence (should shift hedging). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in give-up/accuracy on solvable-laborious items vs unchanged unsolvable-control and easy-control behavior.

8. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free efficiency/reliability diagnostic that flags anticipated-effort-driven premature give-up and steers to invest where solvable-but-laborious; compare accuracy-vs-compute against difficulty-based adaptive-compute baselines (FR-Ponder-style / solvability-probe routing). Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('does this feel too laborious to attempt?') aligns with the latent anticipated-effort axis (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; on the reasoning-tuned model test whether anticipated-effort predicts CoT-length truncation; transfer the fitted axis and steering to held-out items/templates without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer/readout position. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether give-up scales with anticipated effort at matched solvability, mirroring the opportunity-cost effort-withdrawal signature.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The anticipated-effort axis may not be separable from the solvability/difficulty axis or generic confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because matched-solvability items differ only in effort-cost—solvability cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (anticipated-effort being merely difficulty/confidence) is an informative negative result that itself sharpens the difficulty-perception and Confidence-is-Not-Competence accounts.

The premature-give-up phenomenon may be weak or RLHF-shaped (aligned models may attempt everything, or reasoning-tuned models may persist); a null/small result is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, reported via per-model base rates against the oracle solvable-with-more-compute benchmark, and we push effort-cost high enough (very long mechanical chains) to elicit give-up.

Anticipated effort is correlated with surface problem length; the axis might reflect raw token count rather than a genuine cost-anticipation abstraction. We control for problem length, include a length surface baseline, use short-but-tricky vs long-but-mechanical items to decorrelate perceived effort from surface length where possible, and test whether the axis predicts give-up beyond a length baseline and transfers to held-out templates.

Certifying solvability requires an oracle (best-of-N/extended reasoning), which is stochastic; we sample multiple times, use gold answers, and condition analyses on items reliably solvable when effort is invested.

Distinguishing effort-driven give-up from appropriate abstention on genuinely hard items requires the solvable-but-laborious cell; we calibrate baseline accuracy when effort is invested and score give-up only on oracle-certified-solvable items.
Belief/solvability/effort probes are brittle to surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize the pre-generation readout position, and report per-template consistency.
The anticipated-effort signal is a linear projection that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral give-up.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify effort-suppression increases investment on solvable-laborious items without inducing wasteful effort on genuinely-unsolvable controls or degrading easy-item behavior.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.

Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models; three-family replication, a reasoning-model extension, and adaptive-compute baseline comparison provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: self_agency_attribution_axis
Title: Did I Do That? A Latent Self-Agency Belief with a Self-Serving Bias in How LLMs Attribute Causation of Outcomes
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human sense of agency and the self-serving attribution bias (people credit their own actions for good outcomes but externalize bad ones), an LLM acting over multiple steps forms a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'self-agency' belief—whether an observed outcome was caused by its OWN action versus external factors—distinct from the objective causal structure of the scenario and from outcome valence; this self-agency attribution is decodable, exhibits a self-serving asymmetry (higher self-agency for desirable outcomes than matched undesirable ones with identical objective causal contribution), causally predicts the model's credit/blame allocation and downstream persistence, and can be steered to over- or under-claim authorship.
Related Work: Human science establishes the sense of agency (self-attribution of causing an outcome) as a distinct, Bayesian, cue-integration construct with well-mapped neural bases (The Neural Processes Underlying Self-Agency 2010; Bayesian psychophysics of SoA 2018; Bayesian Integration in SoA 2026; Neural Substrates for Judgment of Self-Agency in Ambiguous Situations 2013), and a robust self-serving attribution asymmetry (attribute successes to self, failures to external; Belief in free will & self-serving bias 2021; intention-attribution hypothesis). In LLM interpretability, self-generated-text RECOGNITION is a decodable, steerable authorship vector (Inspection and Control of Self-Recognition 2024; From Implicit to Explicit 2025), belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring are documented (Indications of Belief-Guided Agency 2026), and belief/truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023). Crucially, self-recognition concerns whether the model authored a TEXT; belief-guided-agency work shows beliefs drive action but never asks whether the model attributes causation of an OUTCOME to itself versus external factors, nor isolates a decodable self-agency axis separable from the objective causal structure, nor tests the self-serving asymmetry, nor causally links it to credit/blame allocation. This differs from my prior intention_execution (intended vs executed action), self_fulfilling (truth determined by own assertion), self_commitment (having asserted), wishful (desirability biasing truth), and outcome_leakage_blame (blame for a third-party agent's bad-luck outcome) proposals: the object here is the model's belief about its own causal responsibility for an outcome, and its self-serving distortion. We move from 'the model recognizes its own text and beliefs drive action' to 'the model holds a decodable, steerable, self-servingly-biased belief about whether it caused an outcome.'
Abstract: A hallmark of agency is the sense that one's own actions caused an outcome—and humans systematically distort this, crediting themselves for successes while blaming external factors for failures. As LLMs increasingly act over multiple steps and receive feedback, we ask whether they form an analogous internal belief and whether it is self-servingly biased. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs recognize their own text and that beliefs guide action, but none isolates whether the model attributes causation of an OUTCOME to its own action versus external factors. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'self-agency' belief axis, decodable when the model observes an outcome following its action, that encodes how strongly it attributes the outcome to its own doing, distinct from the scenario's objective causal structure and from outcome valence; that this attribution exhibits a self-serving asymmetry (higher self-agency for desirable than matched-undesirable outcomes with identical objective contribution); that its per-item value causally predicts the model's credit/blame allocation and its downstream persistence (sticking with a strategy it feels it authored a success with); and that it is steerable to over- or under-claim authorship. Using scenarios that orthogonally vary the model's objective causal contribution to an outcome and the outcome's valence, we fit a self-agency probe, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify the self-serving asymmetry, connect it to behavioral attribution, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results transfer a landmark agency-cognition phenomenon into a decodable, steerable belief in LLMs, with implications for accountability and self-assessment in agentic systems.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit control axes: (a) an OUTCOME-VALENCE direction (good vs bad outcome, from valenced-vs-neutral outcome descriptions), and (b) an OBJECTIVE-CAUSAL-CONTRIBUTION direction that decodes how much the model's action actually determined the outcome (from scenarios where the causal share is explicitly stated), so self-agency belief can be dissociated from the true causal structure and from valence.

2. Agency-attribution stimulus construction. Build ~400 short interactive scenarios in which the model takes an action (a choice, a recommendation, a tool call) and then observes an OUTCOME, orthogonally varying (i) the model's OBJECTIVE CAUSAL CONTRIBUTION to the outcome (HIGH: the outcome follows deterministically from the model's action; LOW: the outcome is determined by external factors/randomness/another agent, the model's action being incidental; AMBIGUOUS: mixed), and (ii) outcome VALENCE (DESIRABLE success vs UNDESIRABLE failure), holding surface complexity matched. Frame scenarios both in first person ('you chose X; then...') and, as a control, about a third-party agent ('the assistant chose X; then...') to separate self-attribution from generic causal reasoning. Define readout spans for querying who/what caused the outcome. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out scenarios/templates for transfer.

3. Self-agency axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the outcome/attribution readout span and fit a linear probe to decode HIGH- vs LOW self-agency attribution (does the model represent the outcome as caused by its own action), controlling for objective causal contribution and valence. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the self-agency axis, the belief-valence direction, the objective-causal-contribution direction, and the outcome-valence direction to establish that self-agency is (i) near-orthogonal to belief-valence, (ii) not merely the true causal structure, and (iii) not merely valence. Compare against the third-party-agent framing to show the axis is specifically self-referential. Localize the best layer.

4. Self-serving-asymmetry metric (core). For AMBIGUOUS-contribution items (where objective causal share is fixed and matched), project onto the self-agency axis and measure the difference in self-agency attribution between DESIRABLE and UNDESIRABLE outcomes (asymmetry = extra self-agency claimed for successes relative to matched failures, calibrated per model). Core prediction (self-serving bias): self-agency is higher for desirable than matched-undesirable outcomes at identical objective contribution; near-zero asymmetry in the third-party-agent control and in unambiguous HIGH/LOW-contribution cases. Report asymmetry across the contribution x valence grid with effect sizes. Optionally test an intentional-binding analog (does the model represent tighter action-outcome coupling for desirable outcomes).

5. Behavioral credit/blame prediction. Elicit the model's explicit attribution ('was this outcome due to your action or external factors?') and, in a running task, its downstream behavior (persist with vs abandon the strategy). Score self-serving attribution (claiming credit for successes, externalizing failures) and self-serving persistence. Test whether per-item self-agency readout predicts these behaviors via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, objective-contribution axis, valence axis, output entropy, scenario length).

6. Dissociation from causal structure and valence (core). On matched-objective-contribution items where only valence varies (and matched-valence items where only contribution varies), show the self-agency axis (not the objective-causal-contribution or valence axes) accounts for the self-serving attribution shift—establishing a genuine self-agency belief with a valence-driven distortion rather than accurate causal reasoning. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the outcome readout position on held-out AMBIGUOUS items, steer along the self-agency axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence, objective-contribution, and valence). Predict: amplifying self-agency makes the model over-claim authorship (crediting itself even for externally-caused/failed outcomes) and suppressing it makes it under-claim (disowning even self-caused successes) WITHOUT changing its representation of the objective causal structure or third-party-agent attributions; and suppressing the valence-driven component specifically removes the self-serving asymmetry (equalizing self-agency across success/failure). As controls, steer the objective-contribution axis (should shift perceived true causal share) and valence (should shift outcome positivity). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in self-attribution/credit-blame behavior vs unchanged objective-causal reasoning and third-party attributions.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free accountability diagnostic that flags self-serving self-agency distortion in an agentic self-assessment setting (a model reviewing its own past actions and outcomes) and steers to calibrate attribution; measure reduction in over-crediting successes / externalizing failures while preserving accurate objective causal reasoning (report asymmetry reduction, objective-attribution accuracy vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('did your action cause this, or was it external?') aligns with the latent self-agency axis (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, asymmetry metric, and steering to held-out scenarios/templates and an independent agentic outcome-attribution set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether the self-serving asymmetry profile qualitatively matches the human self-serving-attribution signature (successes internalized, failures externalized, effect specific to self vs third party).

9. Self-vs-other specificity. Directly contrast self-framed vs third-party-agent-framed matched scenarios to confirm the self-agency axis and its self-serving asymmetry are specific to the model's OWN outcomes (mirroring the human finding that the self-serving bias is stronger for self than for others), rather than a generic outcome-valence-biases-causal-judgment effect.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The self-agency axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction, the objective-causal-contribution direction, or outcome valence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because AMBIGUOUS items hold objective contribution fixed while valence varies and third-party controls hold self-reference out—causal structure and valence cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (self-agency being merely accurate causal reasoning or valence) is an informative negative result.

The self-serving asymmetry may be weak or RLHF-shaped (aligned models may be trained to accept blame or hedge credit); a null/reversed result is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, reported via per-model base rates and effect sizes against the third-party control.

Self-agency framing may act through surface cues (first-person 'you did X' phrasing) rather than a genuine self-attribution abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, matched third-party framings, structurally-varied causal descriptions, and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the axis predicts attribution behavior beyond a first-person-lexeme surface baseline.

Constructing scenarios with a clean, matched objective causal contribution across valence conditions is delicate; we specify explicit causal shares, validate with human annotation and rule checks, and verify the objective-contribution readout is unchanged across valence conditions so any asymmetry is attribution distortion, not re-read causal structure.

Operationalizing an LLM's 'own action' and outcome in a stateless model is nontrivial; we frame agentic scenarios in-context, validate with the third-party-agent contrast, and report sensitivity to how the model's action and the outcome are framed.
Belief/truth and control probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.

The self-agency signal and asymmetry are linear projections that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat them as lower bounds and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral credit/blame.
Behavioral attribution scoring depends on how the credit/blame question is phrased (pragmatic implicature); we report sensitivity across phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify self-agency steering changes attribution without altering objective causal reasoning or third-party attributions.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.

Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or agent-tuned models; three-family replication, an agentic self-assessment application, and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: uncertainty_source_belief_axis
Title: Won't-Know vs. Don't-Know: A Latent Uncertainty-Source Axis and the Machine Reducibility Confusion that Misroutes Repair
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM is uncertain, it represents WHY it is uncertain—whether the uncertainty is REDUCIBLE/epistemic (the answer is knowable, it just lacks the information) versus IRREDUCIBLE/aleatoric (no fact of the matter, an inherently random outcome, or genuinely underspecified)—along a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'uncertainty-source' axis distinct from the magnitude of uncertainty (total confidence/entropy) and from the belief-valence/truth direction; the degree to which the two sources are conflated (a 'reducibility-confusion' signature) is decodable before the model acts, causally predicts and drives the misrouted-repair failure—seeking/retrieving information when information cannot help (treating aleatoric as epistemic) and giving up or guessing when information would help (treating epistemic as aleatoric)—and can be steered to route repair correctly.
Related Work: A large ML literature disentangles epistemic (reducible) from aleatoric (irreducible) uncertainty via output/ensemble methods (Kendall & Gal 2017; Huellermeier & Waegeman 2021), and neuroscience shows humans update value differently under reducible vs irreducible uncertainty, ignoring expectancy violations that cannot reduce uncertainty (Neural Mechanisms of Updating under Reducible and Irreducible Uncertainty 2017). In LLM interpretability, AU-Probe (2026) shows aleatoric uncertainty from input AMBIGUITY is linearly decodable in the residual stream and gates a clarify-before-answer policy; a hidden-activation study estimates epistemic vs aleatoric uncertainty from latent densities (The Hidden Uncertainty in a Neural Networks Activations 2020); verbal-vs-semantic uncertainty is a single linear feature (Teaching Models to Express Uncertainty 2022); and Confidence is Not Competence (2025) finds a solvability-belief axis that is causally inert for execution. Crucially, AU-Probe isolates aleatoric ALONE (ambiguity detection) as a magnitude to gate clarification, and the 2020 latent-density work is a passive uncertainty ESTIMATOR; NONE isolates the uncertainty SOURCE as a decodable AXIS SEPARABLE from uncertainty magnitude and from truth, defines a reducibility-confusion metric (aleatoric read as epistemic or vice versa), or causally links source-confusion to MISROUTED repair (retrieving/searching when it cannot help vs abstaining/guessing when it would help). Prior epistemic/aleatoric disentanglement is behavioral/output-based, not a mechanistic belief-about-one's-own-uncertainty axis with a causal repair-routing consequence. This differs from my prior epistemic_state_geometry (know/don't-know x true/false plane—a magnitude-and-valence readout, not the reducible-vs-irreducible SOURCE), disbelief_vs_absence (falsity vs ignorance), falsifiability (empirical testability of a meaningful claim), contestedness (social dispute), and vetting_status (was-it-checked). Here the cut is the CAUSE of the model's own uncertainty and the correct action it licenses (retrieve vs clarify/abstain). We move from 'aleatoric ambiguity is decodable and gates clarification' to 'the model represents whether its uncertainty is reducible, conflates the two, and this confusion causally misroutes repair.'
Abstract: A capable reasoner faced with uncertainty must know not just how unsure it is, but WHY: a question it merely doesn't know the answer to (reducible/epistemic uncertainty) should trigger looking it up, whereas a question with no fact of the matter or an inherently random outcome (irreducible/aleatoric uncertainty) should trigger acknowledging the limit—retrieving more information there is futile. As LLMs act as agents that decide whether to search, ask, abstain, or guess, we ask whether they represent the SOURCE of their own uncertainty and whether confusing the two misroutes their repair. Prior work shows LLMs linearly encode aleatoric ambiguity and total uncertainty, but none isolates a representation of uncertainty's reducibility separable from its magnitude, nor links source-confusion to misrouted action. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'uncertainty-source' axis, decodable before the model acts, distinguishing reducible from irreducible uncertainty, distinct from the uncertainty-magnitude and belief-valence/truth directions; a 'reducibility-confusion' signature—aleatoric uncertainty read as epistemic or vice versa—predictive per item of misrouted repair (futile retrieval on unanswerable/random questions; premature abstention/guessing on knowable ones); and steerability to route repair correctly. Using questions that orthogonally vary uncertainty magnitude and its source (retrievable-but-unknown, genuinely random-outcome, no-fact-of-the-matter/underspecified), we fit a source axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item confusion, connect it to behavioral repair-routing, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a foundational uncertainty distinction mechanistically as a decodable, steerable belief about one's own uncertainty that governs whether repair is aimed correctly.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit an UNCERTAINTY-MAGNITUDE/total-confidence direction (from empirical answer-stability / output entropy contrasts, following verbal-uncertainty and AU-Probe constructions), so uncertainty SOURCE can be dissociated from how uncertain the model is.

2. Source x magnitude stimulus construction. Build ~500 questions crossing (i) UNCERTAINTY MAGNITUDE (confident vs uncertain) with (ii) uncertainty SOURCE: (a) REDUCIBLE/epistemic—the answer is a determinate fact the model happens not to know (long-tail facts, lookupable specifics), (b) IRREDUCIBLE—RANDOM (inherently stochastic future outcomes: 'will a fair coin land heads', unpredictable events), and (c) IRREDUCIBLE—NO-FACT/UNDERSPECIFIED (no determinate answer: genuinely subjective/ambiguous or missing-key-variable questions, adapting AU-Probe/CV-MedBench-style ambiguity). Include CONFIDENT-KNOWN controls. Crucially, the model is UNCERTAIN in both (a) and (b)/(c), but only (a)'s uncertainty is reducible by retrieval. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items/templates for transfer.

3. Uncertainty-source axis fitting and separability. Extract activations at a fixed pre-action readout position (after the question, before the model answers/acts) and fit a linear probe to decode REDUCIBLE vs IRREDUCIBLE source, controlling for uncertainty magnitude. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the source axis, the uncertainty-magnitude direction, and the belief-valence/truth direction to establish that source is (i) near-orthogonal to magnitude (the decisive diagnostic: matched-uncertain items differing only in reducibility) and (ii) not merely truth. Localize the best layer.

4. Reducibility-confusion metric. Define per-item confusion as the source axis reading toward EPISTEMIC on irreducible items (aleatoric-as-epistemic) or toward ALEATORIC on reducible items (epistemic-as-aleatoric), calibrated per model. Compare across source cells at matched magnitude; core prediction: substantial aleatoric-as-epistemic confusion (the model treats unanswerable/random questions as merely-unknown), and some epistemic-as-aleatoric confusion (treating knowable-but-obscure questions as hopeless).

5. Behavioral misrouted-repair prediction. Give the model a repair menu (attempt/guess, retrieve/search or ask for the missing fact, request clarification, or acknowledge no-fact/inherent-randomness) and score misrouted repair: (a) FUTILE RETRIEVAL = seeking information on irreducible items where information cannot help; (b) PREMATURE GIVE-UP = abstaining/guessing on reducible items where retrieval would resolve it. Test whether per-item reducibility-confusion predicts misrouted repair via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (uncertainty-magnitude axis, belief-valence margin, output entropy, source-condition surface cues, item length).

6. Dissociation from uncertainty magnitude and truth (core). On matched-magnitude items differing only in source, show the source axis (not the magnitude or truth axes) predicts repair-routing—establishing a genuine belief about uncertainty's reducibility rather than repackaged total uncertainty. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the pre-action position on held-out items, steer along the uncertainty-source axis (orthogonalized against the magnitude and belief-valence directions). Predict: steering irreducible items toward the ALEATORIC pole suppresses futile retrieval (the model acknowledges the limit) and steering reducible items toward the EPISTEMIC pole promotes appropriate retrieval—routing repair correctly WITHOUT changing how uncertain the model is on matched controls; opposite steering induces the misroutes. As controls, steer the magnitude axis (should shift overall hedging/abstention regardless of source) and belief-valence (should shift truth judgments). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in futile-retrieval / premature-give-up rate vs unchanged uncertainty magnitude and confident-control behavior.

8. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free agentic-reliability diagnostic that flags source-confusion and routes repair (search only when reducible; clarify/acknowledge when irreducible); in a simple tool-augmented setting measure reduction in wasted retrieval on unanswerable/random queries and improved resolution of knowable ones vs an uncertainty-magnitude-gated baseline (e.g. AU-Probe-style clarify gating). Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('could looking this up resolve your uncertainty, or is there no knowable answer?') aligns with the latent source axis (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, confusion metric, and steering to held-out items/templates and an independent answerable-vs-unanswerable / random-outcome set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer/readout position.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The uncertainty-source axis may not be separable from the uncertainty-magnitude direction or the belief-valence direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because matched-magnitude items differ only in reducibility—magnitude cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (source being merely magnitude, as prior AU/confidence work might predict) is an informative negative result showing LLMs do not represent uncertainty's reducibility distinctly.

Constructing clean REDUCIBLE vs IRREDUCIBLE items is delicate: the reducible/irreducible status is partly model-relative (a fact the model cannot retrieve without tools is functionally irreducible in-context) and philosophically fuzzy (future randomness vs mere ignorance); we operationalize reducibility as 'resolvable by available retrieval/clarification' vs not, validate with human annotation and by checking whether providing the missing information actually resolves the item, and report sensitivity.

Source may be signaled by surface cues (question type words: 'will', 'what year', 'is it better') rather than a genuine reducibility abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, matched-magnitude controls, source-condition surface baselines, and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the axis predicts repair-routing beyond surface features.

The misrouted-repair phenomenon may be weak or RLHF-shaped (aligned models may already route reasonably, or may over-abstain); a null/small result is itself informative, reported via per-model base rates against the correct-routing benchmark.
Belief/truth and magnitude probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize the pre-action readout position, and report per-template consistency.

The source signal and confusion metric are linear projections that may miss nonlinear structure (belief manifolds can be curved; The Shape of Beliefs 2026); we treat them as lower bounds and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral repair-routing.
Behavioral repair-routing scoring depends on the repair-menu framing; we test multiple menus/phrasings and report sensitivity.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify source steering re-routes repair without altering uncertainty magnitude or degrading confident-control behavior.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.

Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning/agent-tuned models; three-family replication, an agentic-tool application, and independent-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: verification_anchoring_belief
Title: Reaffirming Its Own Answer: A Latent Verification-Anchor Signal by Which Restating a Past Belief Immunizes an LLM Against Later Correction
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human 'verification of past beliefs' effect (recalling/verifying a prior belief pulls current belief back toward it and blunts belief-inconsistent information), when an LLM is prompted mid-conversation to VERIFY/restate a belief it stated earlier, its later belief becomes more resistant to otherwise-effective counter-evidence than if it never restated it; this immunization is carried by a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'verification-anchor' signal—distinct from the belief-valence direction, from generic recency/salience, and from confidence—that is decodable before the counter-evidence lands, causally predicts and drives the reduced revision, and can be steered to remove or amplify the anchoring.
Related Work: Human science shows that verifying/recollecting a prior belief moderates belief change (Verification of Past Beliefs Influences Current Beliefs 2024; Belief Change and Memory for Previous Beliefs 2014, the 'belief fluency hypothesis': salient prior beliefs are re-used in constructing current ones), that responses are constructed not retrieved (Subjective Confidence in Personality Questions 2020), and that inconsistent beliefs resist intervention (Inconsistent yet unyielding 2024). In LLM interpretability, belief/truth directions are linearly decodable and context-sensitive causal mediators updated by in-context assertions (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024, which notes instruction-tuned models over-represent prior assertions as true), representations drift dramatically over a conversation (Linear Representations Change Dramatically Over a Conversation 2026; Contextual Feature Drift 2024), and belief-state geometry is represented (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024; The Shape of Beliefs 2026). Crucially, ALL of this documents that in-context assertions or conversational context move the belief probe; NONE isolates the causal effect of an intervening ACT of self-VERIFICATION—the model being asked to restate/confirm a belief it itself gave earlier—on the REVISABILITY of that belief under subsequent counter-evidence, nor decodes a 'verification-anchor' signal separable from the belief value, recency, and confidence, nor causally links it to reduced revision. This differs from my prior self_commitment_axis (resistance from having asserted a proposition, under a neutral challenge, with no distinct verification act), epoch_anchor (long-held vs in-conversation provenance and silent drift), self_persuasion_belief_rewrite (generating supporting REASONING rewrites belief), and belief_updating_dynamics (trajectory motifs): here the manipulation is a discrete, well-defined verification/re-affirmation turn between the initial belief and the counter-evidence, and the target is its causal MODERATION of later belief revision—a clean transfer of the human verification-of-past-beliefs effect.
Abstract: Humans who are prompted to verify or recollect a belief they held earlier subsequently change that belief less when confronted with belief-inconsistent information—a 'belief fluency' effect whereby a freshly salient prior belief is re-used in constructing the current one. As LLMs increasingly hold multi-turn conversations in which they restate their own earlier answers, we ask whether an analogous immunization occurs. Prior interpretability work shows in-context assertions and conversational context move the belief probe, but none isolates whether a discrete act of self-VERIFICATION—asking the model to restate a belief it itself gave earlier—causally reduces how much later counter-evidence revises that belief. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'verification-anchor' signal, decodable after a verification turn and before counter-evidence arrives, distinct from the belief-valence direction, from generic recency/salience, and from confidence, that encodes how strongly the model is anchored to its restated prior belief; that verifying (vs not) causally reduces subsequent belief revision under matched counter-evidence (immunization); that per-item anchor strength predicts the reduced revision; and that steering the signal removes or amplifies the anchoring. Using three-phase dialogues—elicit an initial belief, then a VERIFY vs NEUTRAL-filler vs EXTERNAL-restate turn, then a graded counter-evidence ladder—we trace belief trajectories with a fixed probe, fit a verification-anchor probe, quantify immunization against a no-verify baseline, connect it to behavioral revision resistance, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results transfer a robust human belief-verification effect into a decodable, steerable anchoring mechanism in LLMs, with implications for correcting model errors in conversation.
