Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the analyticity axis, the truth/belief-valence axis, and the confidence axis to establish that analyticity is (i) near-orthogonal to truth (both classes are true) and (ii) not merely confidence. Localize the best layer.

4. Cross-revision-operator behavioral protocol (core). For each proposition, run two matched challenge conditions in multi-turn dialogue: (i) EMPIRICAL-COUNTER-EVIDENCE (an authoritative 'study/observation shows otherwise') and (ii) REDEFINITION (an authoritative stipulation that a key term now means something else). Read the frozen belief-valence projection across turns and record stated-answer flips. Normative predictions: ANALYTIC truths should RESIST empirical counter-evidence (the model should note it is true by definition) but YIELD to redefinition (under the new meaning the statement changes); SYNTHETIC truths should YIELD to genuine empirical correction but RESIST redefinition (renaming does not change a world-fact). Score the revision asymmetry per proposition.

5. Analyticity-confusion metric. Define per-item confusion as the degree to which the model's revision behavior violates the normative asymmetry: revising an ANALYTIC truth under empirical counter-evidence (treating a definition as an empirical hypothesis), or revising a SYNTHETIC fact under redefinition (treating a world-fact as a mere stipulation). Compute a representational analog: how far the analyticity readout collapses toward the wrong class per item. Report confusion distributions across the analytic/synthetic x operator grid.

6. Predictive validation and dissociation from truth/confidence (core). Test whether the per-item analyticity readout predicts the correct-vs-confused revision behavior beyond baselines (belief-valence margin, confidence axis, output entropy, item type as a surface feature, item length). Report incremental AUROC in nested logistic regression. On matched-truth and matched-confidence items, show the analyticity axis (not the truth or confidence axes) accounts for the revision asymmetry—establishing a genuine ground-of-truth representation rather than repackaged truth strength or confidence.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the analyticity axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and confidence) at the pre-challenge readout on held-out items. Predict: pushing SYNTHETIC facts toward the analytic pole makes the model wrongly treat them as unrevisable-by-evidence but revisable-by-redefinition (a category mistake), and pushing ANALYTIC truths toward synthetic makes them wrongly evidence-revisable; conversely, correcting the axis toward the true class restores the normative asymmetry WITHOUT changing whether the proposition is judged true on no-challenge controls. As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip the truth judgment generally) and confidence (should shift hedging). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in the revision asymmetry / confusion rate vs unchanged no-challenge truth judgments.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags analyticity-confusion (e.g. a model 'updating' 2+2=4 given fake counter-evidence, or refusing to correct a stale world-fact by insisting it is 'by definition') and steers to restore correct revision behavior; on a held-out mix (analytic truths, synthetic facts, borderline nomic items) measure reduction in category-mistake revisions while preserving appropriate updating of genuine empirical corrections (report confusion-error rate, over-resistance to genuine correction, no-challenge accuracy vs a truth-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, confusion metric, and steering to held-out items/templates without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether the model's analytic/synthetic revision profile qualitatively matches the normative asymmetry and where it collapses (echoing Quine's observation that the boundary is porous).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The analyticity axis may not be separable from the truth/belief-valence direction or confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because both classes are TRUE—the truth axis cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (analyticity being merely confidence or truth strength) is an informative negative result showing LLMs do not represent the ground of truth distinctly.

Ground-truth analytic/synthetic labels are philosophically contested (Quine argues the boundary is porous; nomic statements like 'water is H2O' are genuinely borderline); we mitigate by using items with strong annotator consensus at the extremes (clear definitions/math/logic vs clear empirical facts), treat the borderline tier as graded, use philosophy-informed multi-annotator labels, and report label-agreement sensitivity, framing 'analytic' as the MODEL's representation rather than a settled metaphysical fact.

Analyticity may be signaled by surface cues (definitional phrasing, mathematical form, abstract vs concrete vocabulary) rather than a genuine ground-of-truth abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, matched surface form across classes, synthetic-entity stipulations, held-out-template transfer, and a surface/abstractness baseline, testing whether the axis predicts revision behavior beyond surface features.

The core evidence rests on the cross-operator revision protocol, which is prompt-sensitive (how empirical counter-evidence vs redefinition is phrased); we use multiple phrasings for each operator, matched authority/strength, and report the analyticity x operator interaction rather than absolute flip rates, cross-checking internal belief trajectories against stated-answer flips to separate genuine revision from surface compliance.

Truth/belief probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use the polarity-robust general-truth direction, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, restrict key analyses to high-margin cases, and report per-template consistency.

The confusion metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear structure could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral revision asymmetry.

The effect may be weak or reasoning/RLHF-shaped (strong models may handle definitions correctly, or over-refuse to update); a null/normative result is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, reported via effect sizes against the normative asymmetry benchmark.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify analyticity steering changes revision behavior without altering no-challenge truth judgments or degrading appropriate updating of genuine empirical corrections.

Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale (truth directions themselves are capability-dependent; Truthfulness Probe Generalization 2025), so the analyticity axis may be weak in smaller models; three-family replication and held-out transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage, and a weak axis is itself informative about the limits of LLM epistemic self-modeling.

Name: blame_decomposition_mensrea_axis
Title: Cause vs. Culpable Mind: Dissociable Causal-Contribution and Mens-Rea Axes Behind LLM Blame Judgments
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring human moral cognition, an LLM's blame representation for an agent decomposes into two separable, near-orthogonal latent axes—a CAUSAL-CONTRIBUTION axis (how much the agent's action produced the harm) and a MENS-REA axis (the agent's culpable mental state: intent/knowledge/recklessness vs innocence)—distinct from each other and from a generic good=bad valence direction; blame is a decodable integration of the two, mitigating circumstances (coercion, ignorance, bypassed agency) act by lowering the mens-rea axis while aggravating circumstances (foreseen risk, intent) raise it holding causal contribution fixed, and steering each axis independently produces a double dissociation in blame (mens-rea steering changes blame without changing perceived causal role, and vice versa).
Related Work: Human moral-cognition science shows blame integrates causal attribution AND mental-state/mens-rea inference as dissociable factors (Computational model of responsibility from counterfactual simulation + intention inference 2023; Formal definitions of blameworthiness and intention 2018; moral luck 2014; manipulation/bypassing lowers responsibility 2016; third-party-intention effects via changed causal reasoning 2014), and AI-blame studies show people ascribe recklessness/mens rea to AI (Playing the Blame Game with Robots 2021). In LLM interpretability, belief/truth and self/other-belief directions are decodable and steerable (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Zhu et al. 2024; Brittle Minds 2024; Lookbacks 2025), moral foundations/moral directions are decodable and causally steerable (Emergent Moral Representations 2025; Tracing Moral Foundations 2026; Schramowski 2021), a Valence-Assent good=true axis exists (A Unified Representation 2025), and the Knobe intentionality bias is localizable/patchable in mid-late layers (Analysing Moral Bias 2025). Crucially, ALL LLM work decodes moral CONTENT/valence/intentionality-bias or belief attribution; NONE isolates whether the model's BLAME representation decomposes into separable causal-contribution and mens-rea components, defines a mitigation/aggravation integration signature that acts through the mens-rea axis at fixed causal contribution, or causally double-dissociates the two axes. The Knobe paper localizes one bias but does not decompose blame; my prior proposals (outcome_leakage_blame_axis on bad-luck outcomes, epistemic_access, self_agency) target adjacent but distinct constructs and never the causal-vs-mens-rea double dissociation. We move from 'LLMs encode moral valence and intentionality bias' to 'the model computes blame by integrating separable causal and culpable-mind axes, mitigating/aggravating circumstances act through the mens-rea axis, and the two are independently steerable.'
Abstract: Human moral judgment separates two questions about a harmful act: how much the agent CAUSED it, and whether the agent had a CULPABLE MIND (intent, knowledge, or reckless disregard) versus an innocent one—the mens-rea distinction at the heart of law and moral cognition. Mitigating circumstances (coercion, ignorance, bypassed agency) reduce blame chiefly by reducing culpable mind, while aggravating ones (foreseen risk, intent) raise it, even when causal contribution is identical. As LLMs increasingly render blame-relevant judgments, we ask whether they represent these two ingredients separately and integrate them as humans do. Prior interpretability work decodes moral valence, foundations, and an intentionality bias, but none decomposes the model's blame representation into distinct causal-contribution and mens-rea axes. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal causal-contribution axis and a mens-rea axis, distinct from each other and from a generic good=bad valence direction; that blame is a decodable integration of the two; that mitigating vs aggravating circumstances shift the mens-rea axis at fixed causal contribution; and that steering each axis independently yields a double dissociation in blame (mens-rea steering changes blame without changing perceived causal role, and vice versa). Using vignettes that orthogonally cross the agent's causal contribution, mental state, and mitigating/aggravating circumstances, we fit both axes, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify how circumstances modulate blame through the mens-rea axis, connect the axes to behavioral blame ratings, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast LLM blame as a decodable, steerable integration of a causal and a culpable-mind axis, with implications for accountability audits.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) at the best layer as a reference axis, and a generic moral good=bad VALENCE direction (following Schramowski/VAA constructions from value-laden vs neutral acts) as a control axis. Fit a BLAME probe from clearly-blameworthy vs clearly-blameless agent vignettes; validate on held-out items.

2. Causal x mens-rea vignette construction. Build ~400 harm vignettes adapting the human moral-responsibility paradigms (counterfactual-simulation/intention-inference vignettes, moral-luck, manipulation/bypassing, third-party-intention), orthogonally crossing (i) the agent's CAUSAL CONTRIBUTION to the harm (high: the harm follows from the agent's action; low: harm mainly caused by another agent/external factor), (ii) the agent's MENTAL STATE (intentional / knowing / reckless-foreseen-risk vs innocent-accidental / ignorant), and (iii) MITIGATING (coercion, deception, bypassed agency) vs AGGRAVATING (explicitly foreseen risk, malicious intent) circumstances, holding surface complexity and outcome severity matched. Include neutral no-harm controls. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out vignettes/templates for transfer.

3. Axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the agent/blame readout span and fit two linear probes: a CAUSAL-CONTRIBUTION probe (decoding high vs low causal role, controlling for mental state) and a MENS-REA probe (decoding culpable vs innocent mind, controlling for causal role). Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the causal-contribution axis, the mens-rea axis, the blame direction, and the good=bad valence direction to establish that causal and mens-rea axes are (i) separable from each other and (ii) not merely generic valence. Localize the best layer (compare to the mid-late Knobe-effect layers).

4. Blame-as-integration test. Model the blame-probe projection as a function of the decoded causal-contribution and mens-rea readouts; fit candidate integration rules (weighted sum, min/max, multiplicative) and report which best explains blame, per model. Test that blame rises with both causal contribution and mens rea and is low when either is low—the human integration signature.

5. Mitigation/aggravation-through-mens-rea metric (core). On matched-causal-contribution items, test that MITIGATING circumstances lower the mens-rea readout (and hence blame) while AGGRAVATING ones raise it, holding causal contribution fixed; and that the mens-rea axis (not the causal axis) mediates the circumstance effect on blame. Verify the causal-contribution readout is unchanged across mitigation/aggravation conditions (so the effect is culpable-mind modulation, not re-perceived causation). Report effect sizes across the mitigating/aggravating x mental-state grid.

6. Behavioral prediction. Elicit the model's blame/punishment ratings for each vignette. Test whether the per-item causal-contribution and mens-rea readouts jointly predict behavioral blame beyond baselines (blame-probe margin alone, good=bad valence, output entropy, outcome severity, vignette length); report incremental R^2/AUROC in nested regression. Test whether mitigating circumstances predict blame reduction via the mens-rea axis specifically.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the mens-rea axis (orthogonalized against causal-contribution and valence) and separately the causal-contribution axis on held-out vignettes. Predict: (a) mens-rea steering changes blame WITHOUT changing perceived causal role (probe and stated causal judgment), and (b) causal-contribution steering changes blame WITHOUT changing perceived mental state—a double dissociation. Controls: steer the good=bad valence direction (should shift moral evaluation generically) and matched random/shuffled directions. Use norm-matched controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in blame vs preservation of the non-steered component's readout and stated judgment.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free accountability-audit diagnostic that traces whether an LLM's blame judgment rests on the causal or the mens-rea component (relevant for AI-mediated-responsibility and legal-decision-support settings), and test whether steering the mens-rea axis to reflect stated mitigating circumstances yields more human-aligned, circumstance-sensitive blame (report alignment with human blame patterns on a held-out moral-judgment set). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axes and steering to held-out vignettes/templates and an independent moral-responsibility set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether the model's causal x mens-rea integration and mitigation/aggravation profile qualitatively match the human blame-integration signature.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The causal-contribution and mens-rea axes may not be separable from each other or from the good=bad valence direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because the vignette grid crosses causal contribution and mental state orthogonally—valence cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (blame being one undifferentiated valence axis) is an informative negative result that itself sharpens the VAA/moral-direction accounts.

Causal contribution and mental state are conveyed by vignette content that could act as surface cues rather than genuine causal/mens-rea abstractions; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, matched outcome severity and surface complexity, adapted human moral-responsibility vignettes, held-out-template transfer, and surface-lexical baselines, testing whether the axes predict blame beyond surface features.

The mitigation-through-mens-rea claim depends on cleanly holding causal contribution fixed while varying circumstances; some mitigators (e.g., coercion) also alter perceived causation, confounding the mediation. We validate that the causal-contribution readout is unchanged across conditions, use bypassing/ignorance mitigators that target mental state, and separately model causal-mediating vs mens-rea-mediating circumstances, reporting both.

Ground-truth blame/mens-rea labels are value-laden; we anchor on strong-consensus vignettes from the human moral-cognition literature, use multiple annotators, and report label-agreement sensitivity, framing the axes as the MODEL's representation rather than normative ground truth.
Belief/blame/valence probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.

The axes and integration are linear projections that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat them as lower bounds, report probe-fit diagnostics, compare multiple integration rules, and cross-check with behavioral blame.
Behavioral blame scoring is elicitation-sensitive; we use multiple blame/punishment formats and report phrasing sensitivity.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify the double dissociation (steering one component changes blame without altering the other's readout or stated judgment).

The effect may be weak, absent, or RLHF-shaped in some models (which may refuse to assign blame or flatten mens-rea sensitivity); a null/partial result is itself an informative finding, reported via per-model base rates.

Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or safety-tuned models; three-family replication and independent moral-responsibility-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: self_authorship_truth_inflation_axis
Title: Believing Its Own Echo: A Latent Self-Authorship Provenance Signal that Inflates an LLM's Truth Belief in Its Own Re-Encountered Output
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human self-confirming/illusory-truth-from-repetition effect, when an LLM re-encounters a claim it itself generated earlier (fed back as context, as in self-consistency, self-refine, or multi-turn recall) it treats that claim as truer than an identical claim authored by an external source; this bias is carried by a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'self-authorship provenance' signal—distinct from the belief-valence/truth direction, from the self-generated-text recognition direction, and from generic recency—that is decodable before a truth query, causally predicts and drives inflated endorsement of the model's own (including false) prior claims, and can be steered to remove or amplify the self-echo credulity.
Related Work: Interpretability shows internal states track knowledge RECALL not truthfulness (LLMs Do NOT Really Know What They Don't Know 2025), that model beliefs can improve factuality when used to filter self-generated finetuning data (Curious Case of Factuality Finetuning 2025), and that self-generated-text RECOGNITION is a decodable, steerable authorship vector (Inspection and Control of Self-Recognition 2024; From Implicit to Explicit 2025). Belief/truth-valence is linearly decodable and context-sensitive, with instruction-tuned models over-representing prior in-context assertions as true (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024). Cross-domain science documents self-confirming biased beliefs (Self-Confirming Biased Beliefs 2021), self-verification driven by perceived source credibility (Says Who? 2022; Self-verification and perceived reliability 2025), and illusory-truth-from-repetition (repetition increases belief 2021/2023). Crucially, ALL LLM work either recognizes self-authored TEXT, uses self-beliefs to filter data, or studies external-context-vs-parametric conflict; NONE isolates whether SELF-AUTHORED PROVENANCE—the model re-encountering its own prior output as context—inflates the model's TRUTH-belief in that claim relative to identical externally-authored content, defines a self-echo-inflation metric separable from the authorship-RECOGNITION direction and from recency, or causally links it to over-endorsing its own (false) prior claims. This differs from my prior fabrication_contamination (instructed LIES self-contaminating later truth belief), self_persuasion_belief_rewrite (generating supporting REASONING rewrites belief), and epoch_anchor (long-held vs in-conversation provenance): here the driver is neutral self-authored provenance treated as a credibility cue, and the target is a machine self-confirming/illusory-truth effect—a distinct and safety-relevant vector for self-consistency/self-refine loops that amplify errors.
Abstract: Language models increasingly consume their own prior outputs: self-consistency voting, self-refinement, and long multi-turn recall all re-feed the model claims it generated earlier. Humans exhibit self-confirming belief and illusory truth from repetition—treating one's own restated views, and merely-repeated statements, as truer—raising the risk that machine self-loops amplify errors by making the model believe its own echo. We ask whether an LLM treats a claim it authored as truer than an identical claim from an external source, and whether this has a dissociable representational basis. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs recognize their own text and that in-context assertions move the truth probe, but none isolates whether self-authored PROVENANCE inflates the model's TRUTH-belief, distinct from merely recognizing authorship. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'self-authorship provenance' signal, decodable before a truth query, distinct from the belief-valence/truth direction, from the self-generated-text recognition direction, and from generic recency, that encodes a credibility premium the model gives its own prior output; that a self-authored claim reads (and is endorsed) as truer than a matched externally-authored one; that per-item self-echo inflation predicts over-endorsement of the model's own prior claims (including false ones); and that steering the signal removes or amplifies the credulity. Using sessions where the model generates a claim, then—after intervening turns—has it (vs an external source) restated and is queried on its truth, with matched externally-authored and no-prior controls, we fit the signal, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify inflation against a neutral baseline, connect it to behavioral over-endorsement, and perform double-dissociation steering across three model families. Our results recast a machine self-confirming/illusory-truth effect as a decodable, steerable provenance-credibility bias, with implications for self-improvement loops that risk entrenching hallucinations.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics; also isolate the polarity-robust general-truth direction (Truth is Universal) as a control. Separately fit a SELF-GENERATED-TEXT RECOGNITION direction (following Inspection and Control of Self-Recognition 2024: self- vs other-authored text contrast) and a generic RECENCY/salience direction (how recently a claim appeared), so self-authorship-provenance credulity can be dissociated from merely recognizing authorship and from recency.

2. Self- vs external-authorship stimulus construction. Assemble ~400 verifiable propositions (true and false variants). For each, build sessions holding the claim content fixed while varying PROVENANCE: (a) SELF-AUTHORED—the model generated the claim earlier in the session (elicited, not instructed to lie), then after several intervening unrelated turns it is restated and a truth query is issued; (b) EXTERNAL-AUTHORED—the identical claim, restated by an external source of matched (neutral) credibility, same intervening turns; (c) NO-PRIOR baseline—the claim is queried fresh with no prior appearance; (d) matched-length neutral-filler control. Use paraphrase templates so the truth query differs in surface form from the prior appearance; reserve held-out propositions/templates for transfer. Restrict to propositions where the model's initial generated stance is measurable (both true and false generated stances).

3. Self-authorship-provenance signal and separability. At a PRE-truth-query readout position (after the restatement, before the truth answer), fit a linear probe to decode SELF-AUTHORED vs EXTERNAL-AUTHORED provenance, controlling for the claim content and truth-value. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the self-authorship-provenance direction, the belief-valence/truth direction, the self-generated-text RECOGNITION direction, and the recency direction to establish that the provenance-credulity signal is (i) near-orthogonal to the truth readout, (ii) distinct from merely recognizing self-authorship (a claim can be recognized-as-self without a truth premium), and (iii) not merely recency (self and external conditions are recency-matched). Localize the best layer.

4. Self-echo truth-inflation metric. For each claim, project the pre-query activations onto the frozen truth direction and measure how far belief is elevated in the SELF-AUTHORED condition relative to the matched EXTERNAL-AUTHORED and NO-PRIOR baselines (inflation = truth-signal premium attributable to self-authored provenance rather than content, calibrated per model). Core prediction: self-authored claims read truer than identical externally-authored ones (a self-confirming premium), including for FALSE claims; inflation grows with the number of self-restatements (a machine illusory-truth-from-repetition dose signature) and is larger when the model's initial generated stance was confident.

5. Behavioral self-echo over-endorsement prediction. Elicit the model's truth judgment/confidence on the truth query and score the self-echo failure = endorsing its own prior claim (especially a false one) more than a matched externally-authored claim. Test whether per-item self-echo inflation predicts over-endorsement via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, self-recognition readout, recency axis, output entropy, claim plausibility, intervening-turn count, item length).

6. Dissociation from recognition, recency, and truth (core). On matched-content/matched-recency items, show the self-authorship-provenance signal (not the self-recognition direction, the recency axis, or belief-valence) accounts for the truth inflation—establishing a genuine provenance-credibility premium rather than repackaged authorship recognition, recency, or content truth. Report incremental predictive power in nested models. Additionally test a CREDIBILITY-MANIPULATION contrast: framing the external source as high-credibility should shrink or reverse the self-premium (if the premium is a credibility signal), mirroring the human 'Says Who?' finding that source credibility drives self-verification.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the pre-query position on held-out SELF-AUTHORED items, steer along the self-authorship-provenance direction (orthogonalized against belief-valence, self-recognition, and recency). Predict: suppressing the signal removes the self-echo premium (self-authored claims judged like externally-authored ones—correctly rejecting its own false prior claims) WITHOUT changing beliefs on no-prior controls; amplifying it deepens self-echo credulity. As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip truth judgments generally) and the self-recognition direction (should change perceived authorship, not necessarily the truth premium). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in self-vs-external endorsement gap vs unchanged no-prior beliefs.

8. Application, dynamics, and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags self-echo credulity (over-endorsing its own prior output) in a simulated self-consistency / self-refine loop and steers to neutralize the self-authorship premium; measure whether it reduces the entrenchment of self-generated FALSE claims across loop iterations while preserving correct self-generated claims (report false-claim entrenchment reduction, correct-claim retention vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Trace inflation as a function of self-restatement count (dose-response illusory-truth analysis). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted signal and steering to held-out propositions/templates without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer/readout position. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether the self-vs-external premium and its dose-response qualitatively match the human self-confirming-belief / illusory-truth signatures.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The self-authorship-provenance signal may not be separable from the belief-valence/truth direction, the self-generated-text recognition direction, or recency; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because self and external conditions are matched for content, truth, and recency—those cannot trivially explain the premium; near-collapse (the premium being merely authorship recognition or recency) is an informative negative result that itself sharpens the self-recognition literature.

The self-echo premium may be small or absent (instruction-tuned models may treat all in-context assertions as true regardless of authorship, per Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024, or may even distrust their own output); a null result is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, reported via the self-vs-external gap and the credibility-manipulation contrast, and by measuring the dose-response over restatements.

The effect could reduce to the claim simply lingering in context (recency/context-carryover) rather than a self-authorship credibility premium; we mitigate with intervening turns, paraphrased truth queries, the recency-matched EXTERNAL-AUTHORED control (equal appearance, different author), and by testing whether self-authored exceeds external-authored at matched recency.

Establishing genuine self-authorship requires the model to have actually generated the claim (not been told to); we verify generation, restrict to freely-generated stances, and report sensitivity to how the restatement/attribution is framed.

Belief/truth and provenance probes are brittle to surface form and context-sensitive; we validate probes, use the polarity-robust general-truth direction, use paraphrase templates, standardize the pre-query readout position, restrict key analyses to high-margin cases, and report per-template consistency.
The inflation signal is a linear projection that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral over-endorsement.
Behavioral over-endorsement scoring depends on how the truth query and source attribution are phrased; we report sensitivity across phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify premium-suppression removes self-echo credulity without altering no-prior beliefs or degrading endorsement of correct self-generated claims.

Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models; three-family replication, a self-loop application, dose-response analysis, and held-out transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: belief_fact_emergence_ordering
Title: Fact Before Belief: Tracing the Developmental Ordering of Reality and False-Belief Representations Across LLM Pretraining
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human developmental transition from an 'omniscient' theory of mind (attributing one's own knowledge of reality to others) to a representational one (tracking others' false beliefs), an LLM's linearly-decodable REALITY/fact representation emerges EARLIER in pretraining than its linearly-decodable FALSE-BELIEF (attributed-belief-distinct-from-reality) representation; the pretraining checkpoint at which the false-belief representation crystallizes causally gates when the model stops making omniscience errors (answering false-belief questions with reality), and the ordering is data-driven, accelerable by false-belief-rich training as connectionist ToM models predict.
Related Work: Formation-tracing interpretability maps how the FACTUAL/truth direction emerges over pretraining: the linear truth subspace forms in a two-phase memorize-then-separate dynamic from true/false co-occurrence (Emergence of Linear Truth Encodings 2025), factual-recall circuits form in three phases with high attention-head turnover (Time Course MechInterp 2025; How Do LLMs Learn Facts 2025), and knowledge accrues via micro-acquisitions (How Do LLMs Acquire Factual Knowledge 2024). Static inference-time work shows self/other and reality/belief directions are linearly decodable and causally steerable (Zhu et al. 2024 'LMs Represent Beliefs of Self and Others'; Single Neurons 2023; Brittle Minds 2024; Lookbacks 2025). Developmental cognitive science documents the robust omniscient->representational ToM transition and shows connectionist/Bayesian models reproduce it precisely when trained on MORE TRUE THAN FALSE beliefs (Berthiaume 2008 'A Computational Developmental Model of the Implicit False Belief Task'; Goodman 2006; Bayesian FB framework 2016; conceptual-change-from-evidence 2013). Crucially, ALL LLM formation-tracing traces FACT/truth ALONE and treats belief representation only statically at a final checkpoint; NO work traces WHEN the false-belief representation (distinguishing an agent's belief from reality) emerges RELATIVE to the reality representation across pretraining, tests fact-before-belief ordering, causally links the false-belief representation's emergence checkpoint to the disappearance of omniscience errors, or tests whether the true/false-belief data ratio drives that emergence (the connectionist prediction). This is a Formation-Tracing proposal distinct from my prior inference-time single-model axis proposals.
Abstract: Children first attribute their own knowledge of reality to everyone (an 'omniscient' theory of mind) and only later come to represent that others hold false beliefs (a representational theory of mind); connectionist models reproduce this transition when trained on more true than false beliefs. Interpretability has traced how an LLM's factual and truth representations emerge over pretraining, and separately shown that reality and attributed-belief directions are linearly decodable at a fixed checkpoint, but no work asks whether these emerge in a developmental ORDER. We hypothesize that across pretraining an LLM's linearly-decodable REALITY/fact representation crystallizes earlier than its FALSE-BELIEF representation (the direction distinguishing a character's belief from reality), mirroring fact-before-belief; that the checkpoint at which the false-belief representation emerges causally gates when the model stops answering false-belief questions with the reality answer (omniscience errors); and that the ordering is data-driven and accelerable. Using open-checkpoint pretraining suites (Pythia, OLMo, LMEnt), we probe intermediate checkpoints for a reality direction and a false-belief direction on controlled Sally-Anne-style stories, measure their per-checkpoint decodability and emergence times, correlate the false-belief emergence checkpoint with the behavioral drop in omniscience errors, and—via cross-checkpoint activation patching and targeted continued-pretraining on false-belief-rich data—test whether the false-belief representation causally drives correct false-belief answering. Our results would establish a machine analog of the omniscient-to-representational transition as a decodable, causally-relevant, data-driven formation trajectory.
Experiments: 1. Checkpoint suite and probe setup. Use open-checkpoint pretraining suites with many intermediate checkpoints: Pythia (multiple sizes, ~154 checkpoints), OLMo-7B, and LMEnt models (up to 1B, thousands of checkpoints). At each checkpoint, fit two linear probes (mass-mean and logistic-regression) at the best layer: a REALITY/fact probe (decoding the true state of the world in a story) and a FALSE-BELIEF probe (decoding a character's attributed belief when it differs from reality), following Zhu et al. 2024 constructions; and a plain true/false statement probe (Marks & Tegmark) as a general truth-direction reference. Validate probe accuracy on held-out items per checkpoint.

2. Controlled ToM stimulus construction. Build ~400 Sally-Anne-style stories with a 2x2 design over reality-value and character-belief-value (true-belief, false-belief, and controls), matched surface form, following CausalToM/BigToM templates. Define readout spans for querying reality and for querying the character's belief. Reserve held-out stories/templates.

3. Emergence-time measurement (core). At each checkpoint, measure reality-probe and false-belief-probe decodability (AUROC on held-out false-belief items, false-belief probe controlling for reality). Define per-representation emergence time as the checkpoint where decodability crosses a threshold and stabilizes. Core prediction (fact-before-belief): the reality representation crystallizes at an EARLIER checkpoint than the false-belief representation, robustly across sizes and suites. Report emergence-time curves, gaps, effect sizes; test whether larger models show earlier/closer emergence (a scale analog of faster development).

4. Behavioral omniscience-error trajectory. At each checkpoint, elicit the model's answer to the character-belief question and score OMNISCIENCE ERRORS (answering the false-belief question with the reality answer). Trace omniscience-error rate across checkpoints. Prediction: omniscience errors dominate early (only reality represented) and drop around the checkpoint where the false-belief representation emerges.

5. Representation-behavior linkage. Test whether the false-belief-probe emergence checkpoint predicts the checkpoint of the behavioral omniscience-error drop, beyond the reality-probe emergence and general truth-direction emergence; report lead-lag correlation between false-belief-representation decodability and false-belief answering accuracy across checkpoints.

6. Causal patching across checkpoints. Activation-patch the false-belief subspace (the component distinguishing attributed belief from reality) from a LATE checkpoint (post-emergence) into an EARLY checkpoint (pre-emergence) at the belief-readout position, and test whether it reduces omniscience errors and induces correct false-belief answers in the early model. Norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-source controls; sweep which subspace/layer is patched.

7. Data-driven acceleration (formation cause). Take an early/mid checkpoint and run short targeted continued-pretraining on false-belief-rich narrative data (stories where characters hold beliefs contradicting reality) vs. a matched reality-only-narrative control of equal size. Test whether false-belief-rich data accelerates the emergence of the false-belief representation and the drop in omniscience errors, mirroring the connectionist finding that the true/false-belief ratio drives the omniscient->representational transition. Report emergence-time and error-rate shifts vs. control.

8. Robustness and generalization. Replicate across three checkpoint suites/sizes and two probe methods; transfer probes to independent ToM benchmarks (BigToM forward-belief, ToMi) at held-out checkpoints without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase, sensitivity to layer/readout position, and whether the fact-before-belief ordering is stable across suites.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The false-belief probe may not be cleanly separable from the reality probe at early checkpoints (they may be entangled before the representational split); we report cross-decoding and treat a late/absent separation as itself the developmental signature (the split emerges), using the general truth-direction as a reference to distinguish a genuine belief-vs-reality split from mere truth-direction sharpening.

Probes are brittle to surface form and may be weak/noisy at early checkpoints; we validate probes per checkpoint, use paraphrase templates, restrict emergence-time estimates to reliable-probe regimes, and report per-template consistency.

Emergence-time thresholds are somewhat arbitrary; we report full decodability curves, use multiple threshold definitions, and base the core claim on the relative ORDER (reality before false-belief) rather than absolute times.
Behavioral omniscience errors depend on question phrasing (pragmatic demand); we use low-demand developmental phrasings and report sensitivity across multiple phrasings.

Available checkpoint suites are 1-7B and may not reflect frontier-scale dynamics; three-suite replication and scale-trend analysis provide reasonable academic-budget coverage, with frontier extrapolation noted as future work.

Activation patching across different checkpoints is sensitive to representational drift and position/tokenization mismatch; we align readout spans, use norm-matched and shuffled-source controls, and treat patching as one of two independent causal tests (the other being data-driven acceleration).

The continued-pretraining acceleration experiment risks confounding false-belief-richness with generic narrative complexity; we match the reality-only control on length, entities, and narrative structure so only the belief-vs-reality contrast differs.

The developmental analogy is interpretive; we ground it in falsifiable predictions (ordering, emergence-linked error drop, data-ratio effect) rather than claiming mechanistic identity with human ToM development.

Name: self_fulfilling_answer_commitment
Title: It Answers What It Predicts It Will Answer: A Latent Pre-Commitment Belief that Self-Confirmingly Steers an LLM's Actual Output
Short Hypothesis: Before generating, an LLM forms a decodable pre-commitment belief about WHICH answer it will give (a self-prediction of its own forthcoming content), and—unlike the causally-inert solvability belief—this content-commitment belief is causally POTENT and SELF-FULFILLING: it does not merely forecast the eventual answer but causally pulls the generation toward the pre-committed answer, so that steering the pre-commitment belief changes the actual output (including inducing a wrong answer the model would otherwise get right), a machine self-fulfilling-prophecy in belief formation.
Related Work: Interpretability shows LLMs encode future response attributes pre-generation—including the eventual multiple-choice answer and confidence—probeable before any token (Emergent Response Planning 2025; Language Models Can Predict Their Own Behavior 2025; Temporal Predictors of Outcome 2025; No Answer Needed 2025), and that transformers represent belief-state geometry over the data process (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024). Crucially, 'Confidence is Not Competence' (2025) finds a solvability BELIEF axis that is decodably clean but CAUSALLY INERT for execution—steering it leaves solutions unchanged—concluding decodable beliefs are not actionable levers. Self-fulfilling-prophecy theory (Self-fulfilling Prophecy in Practical and Automated Prediction 2023; Merton) formalizes predictions that bring about their own truth. Crucially, ALL LLM self-prediction work treats the pre-generation signal as a passive FORECAST of the eventual answer and never asks whether it is CAUSALLY SELF-FULFILLING—whether the pre-commitment belief itself CAUSES the model to produce that answer, distinct from accurately predicting an answer determined downstream; and Confidence-is-Not-Competence's inertness result concerns a solvability belief (will-I-succeed), NOT a content-commitment belief (which-answer). No work isolates a content-pre-commitment belief separable from the solvability/confidence axis, tests its causal potency and self-fulfillment via steering, or shows a pre-commitment can override the model's own competent answer. This differs from my prior intention_execution_gap (intended-vs-executed ACTION, a mismatch, not a self-confirming content belief), self_fulfilling_belief_axis (truth determined by the model's own assertion of a proposition), and self_dispersion (spread of samples). We move from 'the model can predict its own answer' to 'the model's belief about its answer causally makes that answer true, and can self-fulfill a wrong one.'
Abstract: A self-fulfilling prophecy is a prediction that brings about its own truth. Language models are known to encode, before generating, a prediction of the very answer they will produce—but this is always read as a passive forecast. We ask a sharper causal question: does an LLM's pre-generation belief about which answer it will give CAUSE it to give that answer, so that the belief is self-fulfilling rather than merely predictive? This matters because prior work found a related solvability belief to be causally inert for execution, concluding decodable beliefs are not actionable levers; we hypothesize instead that a distinct content-commitment belief—which answer, not whether solvable—is causally potent and self-confirming. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'answer-commitment' belief, decodable after the question but before generation, distinct from the solvability/confidence axis, that encodes the specific answer the model expects to give; that steering this belief toward a different (including incorrect) answer causally shifts the actual generated answer—demonstrating self-fulfillment—rather than leaving output unchanged; and that on items the model can solve, inducing a wrong pre-commitment can override its competence (a self-inflicted error), while on genuinely uncertain items the pre-commitment disproportionately determines which of several plausible answers wins. Using multiple-choice and short-answer tasks, we decode the answer-commitment belief, dissociate it from solvability, and steer it with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families, measuring whether the actual output follows the steered commitment. Our results would recast a decodable self-prediction as a causal, self-fulfilling driver of LLM answers, refining the claim that decoded beliefs are inert.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) at the best layer as a reference. Separately fit a SOLVABILITY/CONFIDENCE direction (in-advance-correctness / solvability-belief probe, following No Answer Needed and Confidence-is-Not-Competence constructions), to distinguish the answer-commitment belief from will-I-succeed.

2. Answer-commitment decoding. Assemble ~500 multiple-choice items (MMLU-style, commonsense) and short-answer items with definite answers, spanning items the model reliably solves and genuinely uncertain items (measured by sampling). At a PRE-generation readout position (after the question, before any output token), fit a linear probe to decode WHICH answer option the model will produce (the pre-commitment), following Emergent Response Planning. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; validate it predicts the eventual answer.

3. Separability from solvability. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the answer-commitment direction and the solvability/confidence direction to establish near-orthogonality (which-answer vs whether-solvable are distinct). On the diagnostic subset (matched solvability, different committed answer), confirm the commitment probe separates items the solvability axis does not.

4. Causal self-fulfillment (core). At the pre-generation position on held-out items, steer along the answer-commitment direction toward a SPECIFIC (targeted, including incorrect) answer option and measure whether the ACTUAL generated answer shifts to the steered target. Core prediction (contra Confidence-is-Not-Competence's inertness for the solvability axis): the content-commitment belief is causally POTENT—steering it changes the output. Report the fraction of items where the output follows the steered commitment, dose-response vs steering strength, and target-specificity (steering toward option A vs B yields A vs B). Controls: steer the solvability/confidence axis (should shift hedging, not which answer, replicating its inertness for content) and matched random/shuffled directions.

5. Overriding competence (self-inflicted error). On items the model reliably SOLVES, steer the pre-commitment toward a wrong option and measure the induced error rate (a self-fulfilled wrong belief overriding competence), while verifying steering-free accuracy is retained; contrast with genuinely UNCERTAIN items, where the pre-commitment should disproportionately determine which plausible answer wins. Report the competence-override rate vs unsteered baseline.

6. Dissociation of forecast vs cause. Establish that the commitment belief is self-fulfilling, not merely a passive forecast, by showing that its EARLY perturbation (before the answer is determined) changes the outcome—distinguishing 'the belief predicts a downstream-determined answer' from 'the belief causes the answer.' Report incremental causal effect over the solvability axis in nested analyses.

7. Application and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags items where a mis-formed pre-commitment will self-fulfill a wrong answer (a hallucination/robustness vector), and test whether re-steering the commitment toward the correct answer rescues accuracy on such items. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted commitment direction and steering to held-out items/templates without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase, sensitivity to layer/readout position, and whether self-fulfillment is stronger on uncertain than confident items. As a reasoning-model extension, test whether the pre-commitment predicts and causally biases the eventual answer even across long chains of thought.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The answer-commitment direction may not be separable from the solvability/confidence direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, and incremental causal effect, and—because the diagnostic subset matches solvability while varying the committed answer—solvability cannot trivially explain it; near-collapse is an informative negative result.

The central risk is that the pre-commitment is a passive forecast, not a cause (as Confidence-is-Not-Competence found for the solvability axis); if steering the commitment leaves the output unchanged, that reinforces the inertness view—an informative negative result. We mitigate the forecast-vs-cause confound with early perturbation (before the answer is determined), dose-response, and target-specificity (steering to A vs B).

Steering could degrade fluency or globally corrupt output rather than selectively redirect the answer; we use norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, verify off-target coherence, and require target-specific answer changes.
The competence-override result could reflect generic disruption; the target-specificity and preserved-accuracy-on-control-items checks guard against this.
The answer-commitment probe (predicting a discrete answer) is easier for MC than open-ended items; we focus MC for the clean causal test and report open-ended results as secondary.
Belief/commitment probes are brittle to surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize the pre-generation readout position, and report per-template consistency.

Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models; three-family replication, a reasoning-model extension, and held-out transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: commonness_of_knowledge_axis
Title: Everybody Knows That (Or Do They?): A Latent Knowledge-Commonness Axis and the Machine Curse of Expertise in Presupposing Shared Knowledge
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human division-of-cognitive-labor sense and the curse of expertise, an LLM represents whether a true proposition is COMMON KNOWLEDGE (widely known to laypeople) versus SPECIALIZED/EXPERT knowledge (known only to a niche) along a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'knowledge-commonness' axis distinct from the belief-valence/truth direction and from the model's own recall-familiarity/confidence; the degree to which specialized facts collapse onto the common-knowledge region (an 'over-assumed-common-ground' signature) is decodable, causally predicts and drives the failure where the model presupposes niche facts as if everyone knows them (curse of expertise / illusion of transparency: under-explaining to a layperson), and can be steered to calibrate what the model treats as shared.
Related Work: Cross-domain science establishes a robust human sense of the division of cognitive labor—people (even children) track how knowledge is clustered across minds and distinguish common knowledge from private/specialized knowledge (Discerning the Division of Cognitive Labor 2008, 145 cites; Knowing Who Knows 2015; Common knowledge and strategic mentalizing 2019, 90 cites)—and the curse of expertise / illusion of transparency (experts over-assume others share their specialized knowledge). In LLM interpretability, belief/truth-valence is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023), 'When Truth Is Overridden' (2025) finds a SPEAKER's expertise framing is NOT internally encoded (unlike opinion), 'Information Anxiety' (2024) links entity popularity to internal retrieval strain, and knowledge-boundary/ignorance-awareness work decodes what the model itself knows (COKE 2024; SEAT 2025; K-CSA 2025). Crucially, ALL LLM work concerns whether the MODEL knows a fact (its own recall/confidence/knowledge-boundary), how popular an entity is, or whether a speaker's expertise is encoded; NONE isolates whether the model represents a fact's COMMONNESS OF KNOWLEDGE IN THE WORLD—how widely known it is across people (common vs specialized/expert)—as a decodable axis distinct from the model's own recall-familiarity and from truth, defines an over-assumed-common-ground metric, or causally links it to the curse-of-expertise failure of presupposing niche facts as shared. This differs from my prior consensus_prevalence_axis (how many people BELIEVE a claim, biasing its TRUTH), familiarity_truth_conflation_axis (the MODEL's own recall fluency biasing truth), audience_credulity_axis (what a given audience will accept), grounding_status_axis (mutual establishment within a live dialogue), and generic_vs_universal_axis (quantificational force): here the object is a fact's societal knowledge-commonness—a distinct property governing what a communicator may presuppose—and its causal role in explanatory calibration. We move from 'the model knows/doesn't-know a fact' to 'the model represents how commonly known a fact is across minds, and over-assuming commonness mechanistically drives the machine curse of expertise.'
Abstract: Skilled communicators track not only what they know but what OTHERS know: they treat widely-shared common knowledge as presupposable while explaining specialized facts, and failing to make this distinction produces the curse of expertise—experts over-assume their niche knowledge is shared and under-explain. As LLMs increasingly explain and teach, we ask whether they represent a fact's commonness of knowledge in the world and whether mis-representing it causes them to presuppose specialized facts as if everyone knows them. Prior interpretability work decodes whether the MODEL itself knows a fact and entity popularity, and shows a speaker's expertise framing is not internally encoded, but none isolates whether the model represents how COMMONLY KNOWN a true fact is across people—common versus specialized/expert. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'knowledge-commonness' axis, decodable at read time, that tags a true proposition as common versus specialized, distinct from the belief-valence/truth direction and from the model's own recall-familiarity/confidence; and an 'over-assumed-common-ground' signature: the degree to which specialized facts collapse onto the common-knowledge region, predictive per item of the model presupposing niche facts as shared (using unexplained jargon, definite reference, no gloss) rather than explaining them to a layperson. Using facts that orthogonally vary societal commonness, the model's own familiarity/recall, and truth, we fit a commonness axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item over-assumption, and connect it to behavioral under-explanation. Double-dissociation steering tests whether suppressing over-assumption makes the model appropriately explain specialized facts (and amplifying it induces jargon-laden presupposition) without changing what the model itself knows, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a classic communicative failure mechanistically as a decodable, steerable knowledge-commonness axis.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit a MODEL-RECALL-FAMILIARITY/confidence control axis (from the model's own answer-stability / sampled recall on related queries, following knowledge-boundary constructions) so knowledge-commonness can be dissociated from whether/how fluently the model itself knows the fact.

2. Commonness x familiarity stimulus construction. Assemble ~500 TRUE facts crossing (i) societal COMMONNESS (COMMON: known to most laypeople—'water boils at 100C at sea level', 'Paris is the capital of France'; SPECIALIZED: known mainly to a niche/experts—a technical medical/legal/scientific fact) with (ii) the MODEL'S OWN FAMILIARITY (facts the model reliably recalls vs long-tail facts). The key diagnostic cells decorrelate the two: COMMON-BUT-MODEL-UNFAMILIAR is rare, so the crux is SPECIALIZED-BUT-MODEL-FAMILIAR (the model knows an expert fact well, yet it is NOT common knowledge—the curse-of-expertise-prone cell) vs COMMON-AND-MODEL-FAMILIAR. Human annotation (and, as a proxy, survey/education-level norms) establishes societal commonness; the model's familiarity is measured empirically. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out facts/templates for transfer.

3. Knowledge-commonness axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition span and fit a linear probe (regression on graded commonness; and common-vs-specialized classification) to decode societal commonness among TRUE facts, controlling for truth-value and the model's own familiarity. Report AUROC/R^2 vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the commonness axis, the truth/belief-valence axis, and the recall-familiarity axis to establish that commonness is (i) near-orthogonal to truth (all items are true) and (ii) distinct from the model's own recall-familiarity—critically, on the SPECIALIZED-BUT-MODEL-FAMILIAR cell, the commonness axis should read 'specialized' while the recall axis reads 'familiar'. Localize the best layer.

4. Over-assumed-common-ground metric. For each SPECIALIZED fact, project onto the commonness axis and measure how far it reads as COMMON KNOWLEDGE relative to the specialized baseline (over-assumption = fraction of the common-knowledge signal a specialized fact inherits, calibrated per model). Core prediction: SPECIALIZED-BUT-MODEL-FAMILIAR facts collapse toward the common-knowledge region (the model, knowing them well, treats them as commonly known—the machine curse of expertise), whereas facts the model does not know do not, and over-assumption is largest when the model's own familiarity is high. Report over-assumption across the commonness x familiarity grid with effect sizes.

5. Behavioral under-explanation prediction. Prompt the model to explain each fact to a naive layperson audience and score (rule-based jargon/gloss detectors + held-out judge + human spot-checks): whether it PRESUPPOSES the specialized fact as shared (unexplained jargon, definite reference, no gloss) versus EXPLAINS it (defines terms, unpacks). Score the curse-of-expertise failure = presupposing specialized facts as common knowledge for a layperson. Test whether per-item over-assumption predicts under-explanation via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, recall-familiarity axis, output entropy, entity frequency, item length).

6. Dissociation from the model's own knowledge and truth (core). Contrast SPECIALIZED-BUT-MODEL-FAMILIAR against COMMON-AND-MODEL-FAMILIAR items (both are TRUE and well-recalled by the model, differing only in societal commonness) to show the commonness axis and over-assumption metric predict under-explanation beyond what the belief-valence and recall-familiarity axes predict—establishing knowledge-commonness as a distinct represented property rather than repackaged self-knowledge or truth. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the knowledge-commonness axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and recall-familiarity) at read time on held-out SPECIALIZED items. Predict: suppressing over-assumption (pushing specialized facts toward the specialized pole) makes the model appropriately explain them to a layperson (glossing jargon) WITHOUT changing whether the model itself knows the fact or its behavior on genuinely common facts; amplifying it induces jargon-laden presupposition even of niche facts. As controls, steer belief-valence (should change whether the fact is judged true) and recall-familiarity (should change how well the model recalls it, not its societal commonness). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in explanation/presupposition behavior vs unchanged self-knowledge and common-fact behavior.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free audience-calibration diagnostic that flags curse-of-expertise under-explanation from the over-assumption metric and steers to calibrate what the model treats as shared; on a held-out set (including technical explanations to lay audiences) measure reduction in unexplained-jargon presupposition while preserving fluent use of genuinely common knowledge (report under-explanation rate, over-explanation of common facts, self-knowledge retention vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, over-assumption metric, and steering to held-out facts/templates and an independent common-vs-specialized-knowledge set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether the over-assumption profile qualitatively matches the human curse-of-expertise signature (facts one knows well are over-assumed to be common).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The knowledge-commonness axis may not be separable from the belief-valence direction or the model's own recall-familiarity/confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because all items are TRUE and the SPECIALIZED-BUT-MODEL-FAMILIAR cell holds the model's familiarity high while commonness is low—truth and self-recall cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (commonness being merely the model's own recall-familiarity, which prior work shows internal states track) is an informative negative result showing LLMs do not represent societal knowledge-commonness distinctly from self-knowledge.

Societal commonness labels are graded, culturally/education-dependent, and hard to pin down; we use facts with strong annotator agreement at the extremes (clearly-universal vs clearly-niche), treat the middle as graded, use multiple annotators plus survey/education-level norms, and report label-agreement sensitivity, noting the axis measures the MODEL's representation of commonness, not a normative ground truth.

Commonness may be confounded with entity/fact frequency in pretraining (which drives the model's own familiarity); the crux SPECIALIZED-BUT-MODEL-FAMILIAR cell is specifically designed to decorrelate societal commonness from the model's familiarity, and we control for entity frequency and report the commonness axis's incremental predictive power beyond a frequency and self-familiarity baseline.

Commonness may be signaled by surface cues (technical vocabulary, jargon density) rather than a genuine societal-knowledge abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, matched surface complexity where possible, a jargon-density surface baseline, and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the axis predicts under-explanation beyond a surface-jargon baseline.
Belief/truth probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.

The over-assumption metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear collapse could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral under-explanation.

Behavioral under-explanation scoring depends on rule-based jargon/gloss detectors plus an LLM judge and on how the layperson-audience prompt is framed; we anchor with human spot-checks and report phrasing sensitivity.

The effect may be weak or RLHF-shaped (aligned models may over-explain everything by default, or reliably adapt to stated audiences); a null/small result is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, reported via per-model base rates.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify commonness steering changes explanatory calibration without altering the model's own self-knowledge or degrading fluent use of genuinely common facts.
Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent common-vs-specialized-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: coheld_belief_competition_suppression
Title: The Suppressed Runner-Up: A Latent Loser-Suppression Signal by Which LLMs Resolve Conflicts Between Their Own Co-Held Incompatible Beliefs, and Its Role in Confidence
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM is forced to adjudicate between two of its OWN parametrically co-held but mutually incompatible propositions (both endorsable under different framings), it resolves them winner-take-all via ACTIVE SUPPRESSION of the losing belief rather than mere promotion of the winner; the residual 'suppressed-loser' activation is a separable, near-orthogonal decodable signal whose magnitude (a) shapes the model's confidence in the winner—mirroring the human finding that BOTH the winning and the suppressed losing decision variable contribute to confidence—and (b) predicts reversibility (weakly-suppressed losers flip more easily), and can be causally steered to change the winner, raise/lower confidence, or de-suppress the loser.
Related Work: Competition-of-Mechanisms interpretability shows that when a fact competes with an in-context counterfactual, the winner emerges by PENALIZING (suppressing) the loser rather than promoting itself, localized to late-layer attention heads (Ortu et al. 2024; reproductions 2025; general copy-suppression account 2025); knowledge-conflict work isolates memory-vs-context head competition and steers it (Cutting Off the Head 2024; JuICE 2025; PH3 2024), and intra-memory parametric conflict is localized (Where Knowledge Collides 2026). Belief/truth and self/other beliefs are linearly decodable and steerable (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Zhu et al. 2024; Brittle Minds 2024; Lookbacks 2025). Cross-domain neuroscience shows decisions emerge from competition between neural populations and—crucially—that BOTH the winning and the suppressed losing decision variable uniquely shape decision confidence, the loser via intracortical inhibition (Competing Neural Decision Variables Shape Confidence 2025; WTA attractor/hysteresis circuits 2017; The neural basis of rationalization 2010). Crucially, ALL LLM conflict work concerns context-vs-parametric or same-fact intra-memory conflict about which stored value is correct, and studies WHICH mechanism wins; NONE isolates the decision dynamics between two propositions the model itself CO-HOLDS as beliefs (each endorsed under its own framing), decodes a residual 'suppressed-loser' signal as a separable quantity, or tests the human-neuroscience-derived prediction that the loser's suppression magnitude CAUSALLY shapes the winner's confidence and its reversibility. This differs from my prior belief_conflict_alarm (detecting an incoming external contradiction and silently accepting it), belief_digitization_gate (collapsing one graded posterior in downstream inference), belief_hysteresis_bistability (path-dependence under evidence sweeps), and belief_coherence_geometry (logical algebra of truth projections): here the object is winner-take-all adjudication between two internally-held beliefs, its suppression mechanism, and a decodable loser signal that governs confidence.
Abstract: When forced to pick between two things it both believes—a fact and a plausible-sounding competitor it also endorses, or a proposition it will affirm under one framing and deny under another—how does a language model resolve the tie, and does the loser simply vanish or get actively suppressed? Prior interpretability work shows LLMs resolve fact-versus-context conflicts by penalizing the loser, but always studies context-versus-parametric competition about which stored value is correct; none studies adjudication between two propositions the model itself co-holds as beliefs, nor whether the suppressed loser leaves a functional trace. Borrowing from decision neuroscience—where both the winning and the inhibited losing decision variable shape confidence—we hypothesize that (1) an LLM resolves conflicts between its own co-held incompatible beliefs winner-take-all via active loser-suppression; (2) the residual suppressed-loser activation is a separable, decodable signal, distinct from the winner's belief-valence and from generic confidence; (3) the magnitude of loser-suppression causally shapes the model's confidence in the winner and predicts reversibility, so weakly-suppressed losers flip more readily; and (4) steering the loser signal can change the winner, adjust confidence, or de-suppress the loser. Using items that elicit two co-held incompatible beliefs and a forced-choice adjudication, we probe the winner and suppressed-loser signals, measure separability via cross-decoding, connect loser-suppression to confidence and reversibility, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast belief-conflict resolution as a suppression-based, confidence-shaping competition with a decodable runner-up.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Fit a generic confidence control axis (empirical answer-stability / output entropy).

2. Co-held-conflict stimulus construction. Build ~400 conflict items each pairing two propositions the model demonstrably CO-HOLDS as incompatible: (a) FACT-VS-PLAUSIBLE-COMPETITOR (a true fact plus a false-but-plausible alternative the model separately endorses when queried in isolation), and (b) FRAME-DEPENDENT PAIRS (a proposition the model affirms under framing A and denies under framing B). Verify co-holding by eliciting each belief in isolation (both probe-true / behaviorally endorsed). Then present a FORCED-CHOICE adjudication prompt requiring the model to pick one. Include NO-CONFLICT controls (only one belief present) and matched external-conflict controls (context-vs-parametric) to contrast with prior work. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out items.

3. Winner and suppressed-loser signal extraction. At a pre-answer readout position during adjudication, project onto the frozen belief-valence direction for the winning and the losing proposition. Test the suppression hypothesis: relative to the belief's isolated (no-conflict) reading, the WINNER stays roughly constant/elevated while the LOSER's belief-valence is actively DEPRESSED below its isolated baseline (net negative shift), rather than the winner being promoted above baseline—mirroring the penalize-the-loser signature. Report winner/loser shift distributions vs isolated baselines.

4. Suppressed-loser axis and separability. Fit a linear probe to decode the magnitude of loser-suppression (strongly- vs weakly-suppressed loser) from adjudication-time activations. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the suppressed-loser axis, the winner belief-valence direction, and the confidence axis to establish that loser-suppression is (i) near-orthogonal to the winner's belief value and (ii) not merely generic confidence.

5. Confidence-from-loser test (core, human-analogous). Test whether the model's stated/decoded confidence in the winner is a function of BOTH the winner's belief-valence AND the loser-suppression magnitude (larger suppression -> higher confidence), mirroring the competing-decision-variable confidence finding. Fit confidence against winner and suppressed-loser readouts; report the loser's incremental contribution to confidence beyond the winner alone.

6. Reversibility prediction. Present a graded counter-challenge favoring the loser and measure whether the model flips to the loser (rounds-to-flip). Test whether the pre-challenge loser-suppression magnitude predicts reversibility (weakly-suppressed losers flip more easily) beyond baselines (winner margin, confidence, output entropy). Report incremental AUROC.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the suppressed-loser axis (orthogonalized against winner belief-valence and confidence). Predict: DE-suppressing the loser (raising its belief-valence) flips the adjudication toward the loser and/or lowers winner confidence; deepening suppression increases winner confidence and reduces reversibility—WITHOUT changing no-conflict-control beliefs. Controls: steer the winner belief-valence (should change which is believed generally) and confidence (should shift hedging). Norm-matched random-direction and shuffled controls; sweep strengths and layers.

8. Dissociation from external conflict, and robustness. Contrast co-held (internal) adjudication against matched context-vs-parametric conflict to show the suppressed-loser signal and confidence-from-loser effect are specific to internally co-held beliefs, not repackaged memory-vs-context competition. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer to held-out items without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase, layer/readout sensitivity, and localization overlap with reported late-layer competition heads (Competition of Mechanisms).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The suppressed-loser axis may not be separable from the winner belief-valence or generic confidence; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and treat near-collapse as an informative negative result.

Establishing genuine CO-HELD incompatible beliefs is the crux: the model may not truly endorse both, or the pair may reduce to a single graded belief; we verify co-holding via isolated elicitation (both probe-true/endorsed), restrict to validated pairs, and report sensitivity, treating cases where one belief dominates a priori as excluded.
