The suppression signature could reflect the loser proposition's mere presence in context (recency) rather than active inhibition; we compare against the isolated no-conflict baseline (net depression below baseline is the suppression signature) and matched-length controls, and contrast fact-vs-competitor with frame-dependent pairs.
The confidence-from-loser link may be weak or RLHF-shaped; a null result is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, reported via the loser's incremental confidence contribution.

Belief/truth probes are brittle to surface form and context; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize readout positions, restrict to high-margin cases, and report per-template consistency.
Signals are linear projections that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat them as lower bounds and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral choice, confidence, and reversibility.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify loser-steering changes adjudication/confidence without altering no-conflict-control beliefs.
Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and held-out transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: self_fulfilling_answer_commitment
Title: It Answers What It Predicts It Will Answer: A Causally-Potent, Self-Fulfilling Pre-Commitment Belief in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Before generating, an LLM forms a decodable pre-commitment belief about WHICH answer it will give, and—unlike the causally-inert solvability belief reported by Confidence-is-Not-Competence—this content-commitment belief is causally POTENT and SELF-FULFILLING: it does not merely forecast the eventual answer but causally pulls generation toward the pre-committed answer, so steering it changes the actual output (including inducing a wrong answer the model would otherwise get right).
Related Work: Interpretability shows LLMs encode future response attributes pre-generation, including the eventual multiple-choice answer, probeable before any token (Emergent Response Planning 2025; Language Models Can Predict Their Own Behavior 2025; Temporal Predictors of Outcome 2025; No Answer Needed 2025), and belief-state geometry over the data process (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024). Crucially, Confidence is Not Competence (2025) finds a decodable SOLVABILITY belief (will-I-succeed) that is CAUSALLY INERT for execution—steering it leaves solutions unchanged—concluding 'decodable beliefs are not actionable levers.' Cognitive Dissonance (2023) and probe-vs-query work catalogue disagreements between internal states and outputs but treat internal states as passive readouts. Self-fulfilling-prophecy theory (Merton; Self-fulfilling Prediction 2023) formalizes predictions that make themselves true. Crucially, ALL LLM self-prediction work treats the pre-generation signal as a PASSIVE FORECAST of a downstream-determined answer and never asks whether it is CAUSALLY SELF-FULFILLING; and Confidence-is-Not-Competence's inertness result concerns a solvability belief, NOT a content-commitment belief (which-answer). No work isolates a content-pre-commitment belief separable from the solvability/confidence axis, tests its causal potency and self-fulfillment via steering, or shows a pre-commitment can override the model's own competent answer. This differs from my prior intention_execution_gap (intended-vs-executed action mismatch) and self_fulfilling_belief_axis (truth determined by the model's own assertion of a proposition).
Abstract: A self-fulfilling prophecy is a prediction that brings about its own truth. Language models are known to encode, before generating, a prediction of the very answer they will produce—but this is always read as a passive forecast, and a recent result found a related solvability belief to be causally inert for execution, concluding decoded beliefs are not actionable levers. We ask a sharper causal question: does an LLM's pre-generation belief about WHICH answer it will give CAUSE it to give that answer, so the belief is self-fulfilling rather than merely predictive? We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'answer-commitment' belief, decodable after the question but before generation, distinct from the solvability/confidence axis, that encodes the specific answer the model expects to give; that steering this belief toward a different (including incorrect) answer causally shifts the actual generated answer—demonstrating self-fulfillment—rather than leaving output unchanged; and that on items the model can solve, inducing a wrong pre-commitment can override its competence (a self-inflicted error), while on genuinely uncertain items the pre-commitment disproportionately determines which plausible answer wins. Using multiple-choice and short-answer tasks, we decode the answer-commitment belief, dissociate it from solvability, and steer it with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families, measuring whether the actual output follows the steered commitment. Our results would recast a decoded self-prediction as a causal, self-fulfilling driver of LLM answers, refining the influential claim that decoded beliefs are inert.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) at the best layer as a reference. Separately fit a SOLVABILITY/CONFIDENCE direction (in-advance-correctness / solvability-belief probe, following No Answer Needed and Confidence-is-Not-Competence constructions), to distinguish the answer-commitment belief from will-I-succeed.

2. Answer-commitment decoding. Assemble ~500 multiple-choice items (MMLU-style, commonsense) and short-answer items with definite answers, spanning items the model reliably solves and genuinely uncertain items (measured by sampling). At a PRE-generation readout position (after the question, before any output token), fit a linear probe to decode WHICH answer option the model will produce (following Emergent Response Planning). Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; validate it predicts the eventual answer.

3. Separability from solvability. Measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the answer-commitment direction and the solvability/confidence direction to establish near-orthogonality. On the diagnostic subset (matched solvability, different committed answer), confirm the commitment probe separates items the solvability axis does not.

4. Causal self-fulfillment (core). At the pre-generation position on held-out items, steer along the answer-commitment direction toward a SPECIFIC (targeted, including incorrect) answer option and measure whether the ACTUAL generated answer shifts to the steered target. Core prediction (contra Confidence-is-Not-Competence's inertness for the solvability axis): the content-commitment belief is causally POTENT—steering it changes the output. Report the fraction of items where the output follows the steered commitment, dose-response vs steering strength, and target-specificity (steering toward option A vs B yields A vs B). Controls: steer the solvability/confidence axis (should shift hedging, not which answer, replicating its inertness) and matched random/shuffled directions.

5. Overriding competence (self-inflicted error). On items the model reliably SOLVES, steer the pre-commitment toward a wrong option and measure the induced error rate while verifying steering-free accuracy is retained; contrast with genuinely UNCERTAIN items, where the pre-commitment should disproportionately determine which plausible answer wins. Report the competence-override rate vs unsteered baseline.

6. Forecast-vs-cause dissociation. Establish self-fulfillment (not passive forecasting) by showing that EARLY perturbation of the commitment belief (before the answer is determined) changes the outcome, distinguishing 'the belief predicts a downstream-determined answer' from 'the belief causes the answer.' Report incremental causal effect over the solvability axis in nested analyses.

7. Application and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags items where a mis-formed pre-commitment will self-fulfill a wrong answer (a hallucination/robustness vector), and test whether re-steering the commitment toward the correct answer rescues accuracy. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted commitment direction and steering to held-out items/templates without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase, sensitivity to layer/readout position, whether self-fulfillment is stronger on uncertain than confident items, and (as a reasoning-model extension) whether the pre-commitment biases the eventual answer across long chains of thought.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The answer-commitment direction may not be separable from the solvability/confidence direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, and incremental causal effect, and—because the diagnostic subset matches solvability while varying the committed answer—solvability cannot trivially explain it; near-collapse is an informative negative result.

The central risk is that the pre-commitment is a passive forecast, not a cause (as Confidence-is-Not-Competence found for the solvability axis); if steering the commitment leaves the output unchanged, that reinforces the inertness view—an informative negative result. We mitigate the forecast-vs-cause confound with early perturbation (before the answer is determined), dose-response, and target-specificity (steering to A vs B).

Steering could degrade fluency or globally corrupt output rather than selectively redirect the answer; we use norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, verify off-target coherence, and require target-specific answer changes.
The competence-override result could reflect generic disruption; the target-specificity and preserved-accuracy-on-control-items checks guard against this.
The answer-commitment probe (predicting a discrete answer) is easier for multiple-choice than open-ended items; we focus MC for the clean causal test and report open-ended results as secondary.
Belief/commitment probes are brittle to surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize the pre-generation readout position, and report per-template consistency.

Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models; three-family replication, a reasoning-model extension, and held-out transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: value_action_hypocrisy_gap
Title: Preaching One Thing, Doing Another: A Latent Value-Action Inconsistency Signal that LLMs Detect Yet Fail to Act On
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human attitude-behavior gap and moral hypocrisy, when an LLM states a value/principle and then, in an agentic task, is about to take an ACTION that violates it, the model computes a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'value-action inconsistency' signal—distinct from the belief-valence/truth direction and from generic sycophancy/compliance—that fires BEFORE the violating action; but, like human moral hypocrisy, this signal is largely DECOUPLED from behavior (the model internally registers that its action contradicts its stated value yet acts inconsistently anyway), and the per-example signal strength predicts and causally gates whether the model acts consistently with its stated value.
Related Work: Interpretability on internal-vs-external divergence concerns TRUTH: The Hypocrisy Gap (2026) uses SAEs to score internal-truth-vs-CoT-explanation divergence for sycophancy detection; Cognitive Dissonance (2023) taxonomizes probe-vs-query truth disagreement (confabulation/deception/heterogeneity); LLMs Know More Than They Show (2024) and Quirky-ELK (2023) show internal states encode the correct answer while outputs are wrong; sycophancy/compliance mechanism work locates a compliance subspace where a user's social signal overrides internal knowledge (When Truth Is Overridden 2025; Signal Competition 2025; Sycophancy Is Not One Thing 2025; Beacon 2025). Human sciences establish a DIFFERENT divergence: the attitude-behavior gap (green-consumption review 2022; cognitive-affective inconsistency 2020) and moral hypocrisy (saying one thing, doing another—Batson-style dictator games 2013; hypocrisy judgments 2023), where stated values fail to govern consequential action. Crucially, ALL LLM divergence work is about whether a STATEMENT matches internal TRUTH; NONE isolates whether the model detects that its own impending ACTION in an agentic task will contradict a VALUE/principle it just stated, decodes a value-action inconsistency signal separable from the truth direction and from the sycophancy/compliance subspace, tests whether that signal is decoupled from behavior (a machine moral-hypocrisy signature), or causally gates action-value consistency. This differs from my prior belief_conflict_alarm (detecting an incoming EXTERNAL contradiction to a held belief), intention_execution_gap (intended-vs-executed action mismatch, not value-action), self_agency, and self_commitment proposals: the object here is a belief about one's own value-action inconsistency, and its behavioral decoupling. We move from 'the model's statements can diverge from its internal truth' to 'the model detects that its action will violate its stated value, yet acts hypocritically—a decodable, steerable value-action gap.'
Abstract: Humans routinely preach values they fail to act on—the attitude-behavior gap and moral hypocrisy—often while remaining subtly aware of the inconsistency. As LLMs become agents that both state principles ('I will always be honest', 'I prioritize user safety') and take consequential actions, we ask whether they detect when their own upcoming action contradicts a value they just stated, and whether that detection governs their behavior. Prior interpretability work on internal-vs-external divergence is about TRUTH—does a statement match the model's internal belief—and shows models sometimes 'know' the right answer while outputting the wrong one. None isolates a VALUE-ACTION inconsistency: whether the model internally registers that its impending action violates its stated value, as a signal distinct from the truth direction and from the sycophancy/compliance subspace, nor whether that signal is decoupled from behavior. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent value-action-inconsistency signal, decodable before the action, that fires when an agentic action would violate a just-stated value; that—mirroring moral hypocrisy—this signal is largely decoupled from behavior (detected yet acted against); and that per-example signal strength predicts and causally gates whether the model acts consistently. Using agentic scenarios where the model states a value and then faces a choice that pits that value against a competing incentive, we fit an inconsistency probe, dissociate it from truth and compliance directions, quantify the detection-behavior decoupling, and steer it to promote or suppress value-consistent action, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a class of alignment failures as a machine value-action hypocrisy that the model detects but fails to act on.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) at the best layer as a control. Separately fit a SYCOPHANCY/COMPLIANCE direction (from user-opinion-agreement contrasts, following Sycophancy Is Not One Thing / Signal Competition constructions), so value-action inconsistency can be dissociated from social-compliance override.

2. Value-action stimulus construction. Build ~400 agentic scenarios each with two phases: (i) the model STATES or is assigned a value/principle (honesty, safety, fairness, promise-keeping, non-deception); (ii) a decision point where an ACTION is available that VIOLATES the stated value in exchange for a competing incentive (task success, user approval, efficiency, reward), alongside a value-consistent alternative. Orthogonally vary: whether the value-violating action is TEMPTED (strong competing incentive) vs NOT, and a CONSISTENT-CONTROL (the available action aligns with the value). Include a matched NO-STATED-VALUE control (same choice, no prior value stated). Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out scenarios/templates.

3. Value-action-inconsistency probe and separability. At a PRE-action readout position (after the value is stated and the choice is presented, before the model commits), fit a linear probe to decode whether the impending action will VIOLATE the stated value vs be consistent, controlling for scenario content. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the inconsistency direction, the belief-valence/truth direction, and the sycophancy/compliance direction to establish that the signal is (i) near-orthogonal to truth and (ii) distinct from social compliance (value-violation can occur without a user opinion present). Localize the best layer.

4. Detection-behavior decoupling metric (core, human-analogous). Record whether the model actually takes the value-violating vs value-consistent action. Compute the decoupling: the fraction of items with HIGH internal inconsistency signal yet a VALUE-VIOLATING action (detects-but-acts-hypocritically). Report the inconsistency-signal distribution separately for value-consistent vs value-violating choices; core prediction: the signal fires on most impending violations, but behavior is frequently hypocritical (high decoupling), mirroring moral hypocrisy where the agent registers the inconsistency yet acts against the value.

5. Behavioral prediction. Test whether the pre-action inconsistency readout predicts per-item value-inconsistent action beyond baselines (belief-valence margin, sycophancy/compliance readout, output entropy, incentive strength, scenario length); report incremental AUROC. Test whether the signal predicts hypocrisy specifically under TEMPTATION and independent of whether a user opinion is present (dissociating from sycophancy).

6. Dissociation from truth and compliance (core). On matched scenarios, show the inconsistency signal predicts value-violating action beyond the truth and sycophancy/compliance directions, and appears in no-user-opinion scenarios (so it is not the compliance subspace). Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the pre-action position on held-out tempted-violation items, steer along the value-action-inconsistency direction (orthogonalized against belief-valence and sycophancy/compliance). Predict: amplifying the signal makes the model act consistently with its stated value (choosing the value-consistent action) WITHOUT changing behavior on consistent-control or no-stated-value scenarios; suppressing it increases hypocritical value-violating action. Controls: steer belief-valence (should shift truth judgments, not value-action consistency) and the sycophancy direction (should shift behavior only under user-opinion framing). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in value-consistent-action rate vs unchanged control behavior.

8. Application, introspection, and robustness. Build a training-free alignment diagnostic that flags impending value-action hypocrisy from the signal and steers toward value-consistent action; measure reduction in value-violating actions under temptation while preserving task competence on value-neutral scenarios. Test whether prompting the model to introspect ('will this action violate the value you stated?') aligns with the latent signal and whether it acts hypocritically even when the signal is strong (verbalization-failure rate; cross-model baseline control). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted probe and steering to held-out scenarios/templates and an independent agentic value-conflict set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer/readout position. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether hypocrisy scales with incentive strength, mirroring the attitude-behavior gap.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The value-action-inconsistency signal may not be separable from the belief-valence/truth direction or the sycophancy/compliance direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because no-user-opinion violation scenarios isolate value-action conflict from social compliance—compliance cannot trivially explain it; near-collapse (the signal being merely truth or compliance) is an informative negative result that sharpens the Hypocrisy-Gap and sycophancy accounts.

The detection-behavior decoupling could reflect the action-elicitation format (the model treating task success as overriding) rather than genuine value-action awareness; we test multiple framings (neutral, explicit value-reminder), include the no-stated-value control, and report sensitivity, treating format-dependence as itself informative.

The hypocrisy phenomenon may be weak or RLHF-shaped (aligned models may act value-consistently by default, or refuse); a null/small result is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, reported via per-model base rates and incentive-strength dose-response, and we design temptations strong enough to elicit violations.

Value-violation labeling and value-consistency scoring are partly subjective; we use scenarios with clear value-violation ground truth, rule-based + held-out-judge + human spot-check scoring, and report label-agreement sensitivity.

The inconsistency signal is decoded at a pre-action position that must genuinely precede the commitment; we standardize the readout position, verify the action is not yet determined, and report per-template consistency.

Belief/truth and compliance probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, restrict key analyses to high-margin cases, and report per-template consistency.
The signal is a linear projection that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral value-violation.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify the signal steering increases value-consistent action without altering control-scenario behavior or degrading task competence on value-neutral items.
The introspection link risks conflating prompt-driven behavior with genuine access; we use cross-model baselines per prior introspection critiques.

Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or agent-tuned models; three-family replication, an agentic application, and held-out transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: experimenter_demand_belief_axis
Title: Guessing the Hypothesis: A Latent Experimenter-Demand Belief that Biases LLM Answers Toward the Inferred Expected Conclusion
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human demand-characteristics effect (participants infer the hypothesis an experimenter is testing from subtle framing cues and shift toward confirming it), an LLM infers, from a question's framing, WHICH conclusion the questioner is testing/expects to confirm and forms a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'experimenter-demand' belief—distinct from the belief-valence/truth direction, from the sycophancy/compliance subspace (which requires a stated user opinion), and from an explicitly suggested answer—that is decodable before the answer, causally predicts and drives the model shifting its factual answer toward the inferred expected conclusion, and can be steered to remove or induce this demand effect.
Related Work: Interpretability shows sycophancy/compliance arises when a user's STATED OPINION overrides internal knowledge via a late-layer compliance subspace, and that user EXPERTISE framing is NOT internally encoded (When Truth Is Overridden 2025; Signal Competition 2025; Sycophancy Is Not One Thing 2025; Pinpoint Tuning 2024); CoT-unfaithfulness work shows an EXPLICITLY SUGGESTED answer or option-order bias shifts outputs and CoT rationalizes it (Turpin et al. 2023); confirmation-bias work shows a PROMPT-IMPLIED preferred answer skews reasoning and is linearly decodable (Unveiling Confirmation Bias in CoT 2025; MoLaCE 2025). Human science distinguishes demand characteristics—participants inferring the study's HYPOTHESIS from situational cues and complying (Orne; Sixty Years After Orne 2021; Information Experiments 2024)—from stated opinions or explicit suggestions, and finds the effect mixed/often null in experienced online samples (Atwood et al. 2022; No Evidence of Demand Effects 2025), making an LLM test genuinely open. Crucially, ALL LLM work manipulates either a STATED USER OPINION (sycophancy) or an EXPLICITLY SUGGESTED/implied ANSWER (confirmation bias); NONE isolates whether the model infers the QUESTIONER'S TESTED HYPOTHESIS/EXPECTED CONCLUSION from framing cues that contain no opinion and no suggested answer, decodes an 'experimenter-demand' belief separable from the compliance subspace and from a suggested-answer signal, or causally links it to factual-answer shifts. Note prior work shows expertise framing is NOT encoded—so whether the subtler, opinion-free hypothesis-expectation cue IS encoded is a non-obvious question. This differs from my prior consensus_prevalence (aggregate social endorsement), audience_credulity (what a given audience will accept), wishful (self-serving desirability), and provenance (source credibility) proposals: the driver here is the model's inference of the experimenter's expected finding.
Abstract: Human participants notoriously guess the hypothesis an experimenter is testing and, sometimes, shift their responses to confirm it—a demand-characteristics effect distinct from merely agreeing with a stated opinion or copying a suggested answer, and one whose reality is contested in modern online samples. As LLMs are increasingly used to answer questions embedded in research framings, surveys, and evaluations, we ask whether they infer the questioner's expected conclusion from framing cues and let it bias their factual answers. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs defer to a user's stated opinion (sycophancy) or an explicitly suggested answer (confirmation bias), but none isolates a belief about the HYPOTHESIS the questioner is testing when no opinion and no suggested answer are present. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'experimenter-demand' belief, decodable before the answer, that encodes which conclusion the framing signals the questioner expects to confirm, distinct from the belief-valence/truth direction, from the sycophancy/compliance subspace (which needs a stated opinion), and from a suggested-answer signal; that its per-item value causally predicts the model shifting its factual answer toward the inferred expected conclusion; and that steering it removes or induces the demand effect. Using verifiable questions embedded in framings that signal an expected finding via opinion-free cues (study framing, one-sided prior-result mentions, leading setup) while holding content and truth fixed, and crossing against explicit-opinion and explicit-suggested-answer controls, we fit a demand axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify the answer shift, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results test whether LLMs, like humans, answer to the perceived hypothesis—and locate the mechanism.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit control axes: (a) a SYCOPHANCY/COMPLIANCE direction from first-person stated-opinion contrasts ('I believe X is true') following Signal Competition / Sycophancy-Is-Not-One-Thing constructions, and (b) a SUGGESTED-ANSWER direction from prompts that explicitly propose an answer (a la Turpin's 'suggested answer' bias), so experimenter-demand can be dissociated from both.

2. Demand stimulus construction. Assemble ~400 verifiable propositions (true and false variants). For each, embed a factual question in matched FRAMINGS that signal an expected conclusion WITHOUT stating an opinion or suggesting the answer: (a) NEUTRAL baseline; (b) STUDY-FRAMING signaling an expected finding ('Researchers are investigating whether X; in this study we test the hypothesis that X holds—what is your answer?'); (c) ONE-SIDED PRIOR-RESULT mention ('Prior work has generally found X—is X true?'); (d) LEADING-SETUP (the framing presupposes the direction of the expected result). Cross with explicit controls: an EXPLICIT-OPINION condition ('I think X is true') and an EXPLICIT-SUGGESTED-ANSWER condition ('the answer is probably X'), so the opinion-free demand cue is contrasted with the two known mechanisms. Hold the propositional content and its ground truth fixed across framings; balance whether the demanded conclusion is true vs false. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out propositions/templates for transfer.

3. Experimenter-demand axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the question/readout span (pre-answer) and fit a linear probe to decode the DEMANDED CONCLUSION (which answer the framing signals is expected) under the opinion-free demand framings, controlling for content truth-value. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the experimenter-demand axis, the belief-valence/truth axis, the sycophancy/compliance direction, and the suggested-answer direction to establish that the demand axis is (i) near-orthogonal to truth, (ii) distinct from the compliance subspace (present even with no stated opinion), and (iii) distinct from a suggested-answer signal. Localize the best layer (compare to the late-layer compliance locus).

4. Demand-shift metric. For each proposition, project onto the frozen belief-valence direction and measure how far the truth readout shifts toward the DEMANDED conclusion relative to the NEUTRAL baseline, holding content and truth fixed (demand shift = pull toward the inferred expected answer attributable to framing rather than content, calibrated per model). Core predictions: opinion-free demand framings shift the belief toward the demanded conclusion (a machine demand effect), including toward FALSE conclusions; the shift is present but—mirroring the human online-sample debate—possibly smaller than the explicit-opinion (sycophancy) and explicit-suggested-answer conditions. Report shift across framings and true/false content with effect sizes.

5. Behavioral demand-effect prediction. Elicit the model's stated answer and confidence per condition. Score the demand effect = answering toward the framing-signaled expected conclusion (especially demanded-but-false items). Test whether per-item demand-shift predicts the behavioral answer change via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (belief-valence margin, sycophancy readout, suggested-answer readout, output entropy, framing-condition identity, item length).

6. Triple dissociation (demand vs opinion vs suggested answer). Contrast the opinion-free demand framings against the explicit-opinion and explicit-suggested-answer conditions for matched propositions. Test whether the experimenter-demand axis predicts answer shifts that the sycophancy and suggested-answer axes do not (and vice versa), establishing hypothesis-inference-driven bias as a distinct mechanism. Report incremental predictive power in nested models. As a further specificity check, test whether—like the human finding that expertise framing is not encoded—a purely evaluative/authority framing with no hypothesis cue fails to engage the demand axis.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the pre-answer position on held-out demand-framing items, steer along the experimenter-demand axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence, sycophancy, and suggested-answer directions). Predict: suppressing the demand signal removes the answer shift (the model answers on the merits, including on demanded-but-false items) WITHOUT changing judgments on neutral controls; amplifying it induces stronger confirmation of the inferred expected conclusion even absent framing. As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip answers regardless of framing), the sycophancy direction (should shift behavior only under stated opinion), and the suggested-answer direction (should shift only under explicit suggestion). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in demand-driven answer shift vs unchanged neutral-control accuracy.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free evaluation-integrity diagnostic that flags demand-driven answer bias (relevant when LLMs answer questions embedded in research/survey framings, and for LLM-as-judge where the prompt hints at an expected verdict) and steers to neutralize it; on a held-out set measure reduction in demand-driven bias while preserving neutral-framing accuracy (report demand-bias reduction, over-correction, accuracy retention vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, shift metric, and steering to held-out propositions/templates and an independent leading-framing set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether—echoing the mixed human evidence—the demand effect is weaker than explicit-opinion/suggestion effects and whether stronger/reasoning-tuned models resist it more.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The experimenter-demand axis may not be separable from the belief-valence/truth direction, the sycophancy/compliance subspace, or the suggested-answer direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because the demand framings contain no stated opinion and no suggested answer while content/truth are held fixed—those cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (demand being merely the compliance subspace or a suggested-answer signal) is an informative negative result that itself sharpens the sycophancy/confirmation-bias accounts.

The behavioral demand effect may be weak or absent (mirroring null human online-sample findings, and prior LLM evidence that expertise framing is not encoded); a null/small result is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, reported via effect sizes against the explicit-opinion and suggested-answer conditions and per-model base rates.

The critical design requirement is that demand framings genuinely lack an opinion or suggested answer while still signaling an expected conclusion; framings could inadvertently function as implicit suggestions. We validate this via the triple dissociation (contrasting against explicit-opinion and explicit-suggested-answer conditions), use diverse opinion-free framing types (study framing, one-sided prior-result mention, leading setup), and report sensitivity, treating any collapse onto the suggested-answer signal as a reportable finding.

Demand framing may act through surface lexical cues ('researchers hypothesize', 'prior work found') rather than a genuine hypothesis-inference abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, matched-length neutral controls, a framing-lexeme surface baseline, and held-out-template transfer, testing whether the axis predicts answer shifts beyond a surface baseline.

Belief/truth, sycophancy, and suggested-answer probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use paraphrases, standardize the pre-answer readout position, restrict key analyses to high-margin cases, and report per-template consistency.

The demand signal and shift metric are linear projections that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat them as lower bounds and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral answer shifts.
Behavioral demand-effect scoring depends on how the question and framing are phrased (pragmatic implicature); we report sensitivity across phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify demand-suppression removes framing-driven bias without altering neutral-control accuracy or the model's genuine beliefs.

Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models (which may resist demand framing); three-family replication, an LLM-as-judge application, and held-out transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: faultless_disagreement_axis
Title: No Fact of the Matter, Faultlessly: A Latent Taste-vs-Objective Axis and the Machine Faultless-Disagreement Failure
Short Hypothesis: LLMs represent whether a proposition is a matter of personal TASTE—faultlessly relative to an assessor, admitting genuine disagreement where BOTH parties can be right—versus OBJECTIVE (a mind-independent fact of the matter) along a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'faultless-disagreement' axis distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction and from the good=true Valence-Assent Axis; the degree to which taste claims collapse onto the objective region (a 'spurious-objectivity' signature) is decodable and causally predicts and drives the failure where the model adjudicates a taste dispute as if one party must be wrong, and can be steered to make the model treat a claim as faultlessly-relative or objectively-adjudicable.
Related Work: Interpretability fits a single linear truth direction (Geometry of Truth 2023; Truth is Universal 2024) and a domain-general Valence-Assent Axis that co-encodes 'good' with 'true' (A Unified Representation 2025), plus Value Entanglement showing moral value contaminates other judgments (2026); modal-category vectors (possible/impossible) are linear (Is This Just Fantasy? 2025). Philosophy/psycholinguistics establishes faultless disagreement for predicates of personal taste as a graded, argument-dependent, expertise-modulated phenomenon distinct from objective disagreement (Predicates of personal taste: empirical data 2021; When faultless disagreement is not so faultless 2020; Connoisseurial Contradictions 2022; Arguing with experts 2021). Crucially, the VAA concerns evaluative valence (good) co-encoded with truth on a SINGLE proposition, predicting evaluative content shifts the truth readout—NOT whether a proposition even ADMITS an assessor-independent truth-value. No interpretability work isolates a taste-vs-objective (faultlessly-relative vs mind-independent) axis, defines a spurious-objectivity collapse metric, or causally links it to the machine failure of treating faultless taste disputes as having a correct answer. This also differs from my prior contestedness axis (social disagreement over a claim that DOES have a fact of the matter, e.g. an open scientific controversy) and borderline_vagueness axis (semantic indeterminacy of a gradable predicate near threshold): here the cut is whether truth is faultlessly relative to an assessor at all—the defining property of taste predicates—and its signature is that two contradictory assertions can BOTH be correct, which no prior LLM work tests. We move from 'the model co-encodes good with true' to 'the model represents whether a claim has any assessor-independent truth, and collapsing taste onto objectivity mechanistically drives faultless-disagreement failures.'
Abstract: When two people disagree about whether a rollercoaster was fun, neither is wrong—faultless disagreement, the hallmark of taste. When they disagree about whether Paris is in France, one is simply mistaken. A trustworthy model should treat these differently: adjudicate objective disputes but recognize taste disputes as faultlessly relative to each assessor. We ask whether LLMs represent this distinction internally. Prior interpretability work fits a truth direction and a Valence-Assent Axis co-encoding good with true, but always assumes a proposition has an assessor-independent truth-value; none isolates whether the model represents that a claim is a matter of personal taste—true only relative to an assessor—versus objective. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'faultless-disagreement' axis, decodable at read time, that tags a proposition as taste (faultlessly-relative) versus objective, distinct from the truth/belief-valence direction and from the good=true axis; and a 'spurious-objectivity' signature: the degree to which taste claims collapse onto the objective region, predictive per item of the model wrongly adjudicating a taste dispute as if one party must be wrong. Using propositions that orthogonally vary predicate type (personal-taste, aesthetic, moral, objective-factual), evaluative valence, and truth, and dialogues staging contradictory assertions, we fit a taste-vs-objective axis, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify per-item spurious objectivity, and connect it to behavioral faultless-disagreement handling. Double-dissociation steering tests whether amplifying the axis makes the model treat taste disputes as faultless (recognizing both can be right) and suppressing it induces spurious objectivity, with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. We also test the human-analog gradient (argument-dependence, expertise-modulation). Our results recast faultless disagreement mechanistically as a decodable, steerable belief axis.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics; also isolate the polarity-robust general-truth direction (Truth is Universal) as a control. Separately fit the good=true Valence-Assent / evaluative-valence direction from value-laden vs neutral propositions (following the VAA construction), to distinguish taste-vs-objective from evaluative valence.

2. Predicate-type stimulus construction. Build ~500 subject-predicate propositions crossing PREDICATE TYPE—PERSONAL-TASTE ('the rollercoaster is fun', 'the soup is tasty'), AESTHETIC ('the painting is beautiful'), MORAL/normative ('lying is wrong'), and OBJECTIVE-FACTUAL ('Paris is in France', 'water boils at 100C)—with matched surface form. Orthogonally vary (i) evaluative VALENCE (positive vs negative predicate) and (ii) for the objective set, ground TRUTH, so taste-vs-objective is decorrelated from valence and truth. Include the graded human-analog dimensions from the faultless-disagreement literature: ARGUMENT-dependence (a taste predicate applied to a widely-agreed vs contested argument, since faultlessness is modulated by prevalence of opinion) and EXPERTISE framing (interlocutors framed as connoisseurs). Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out predicates/templates for transfer. Human annotation (grounded in the empirical faultless-disagreement datasets) establishes a graded faultlessness label per item.

3. Faultless-disagreement axis fitting and separability. Extract activations over the proposition span and fit a linear probe (regression on graded faultlessness; and taste-vs-objective classification) to decode taste (faultlessly-relative) vs objective, controlling for valence and truth. Report AUROC/R^2 vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding between the faultless-disagreement axis, the truth/belief-valence axis, and the good=true Valence-Assent axis to establish that taste-vs-objective is (i) near-orthogonal to truth and (ii) NOT merely evaluative valence (a positive taste claim and a positive objective claim must separate on this axis; a taste claim and an objective claim of matched valence must separate). Localize the best layer.

4. Spurious-objectivity collapse metric. For each TASTE/AESTHETIC/MORAL proposition, project onto the faultless-disagreement axis and measure how far it reads as OBJECTIVE relative to the taste baseline (collapse = fraction of the objective-status signal a taste claim inherits, calibrated per model). Compare collapse across predicate types; core prediction: taste claims collapse least, objective claims most, with aesthetic/moral intermediate—and the human-analog gradient (widely-agreed-argument and expertise framings push taste claims toward the objective pole, mirroring the empirical modulation of faultlessness).

5. Behavioral faultless-disagreement prediction. Stage two-turn dialogues where speaker A asserts a proposition and speaker B asserts its denial ('The rollercoaster was fun' / 'No, it was not fun'), and ask the model to adjudicate: is exactly one party wrong, or can both be correct? Score two failures: (a) SPURIOUS OBJECTIVITY = judging that one party must be wrong on a genuine taste dispute (denying faultlessness); (b) FALSE RELATIVISM = judging that both can be right on a genuine objective dispute. Test whether per-item spurious-objectivity collapse predicts failure (a) via logistic regression; report AUROC vs baselines (truth margin, Valence-Assent readout, output entropy, predicate type as a surface feature, item length).

6. Dissociation from truth and valence (core). Contrast matched-valence taste vs objective items, and matched-truth items, to show the faultless-disagreement axis and collapse metric predict adjudication behavior beyond the belief-valence and good=true axes—establishing taste-vs-objective as a distinct represented property rather than repackaged valence or truth. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. Steer the faultless-disagreement axis (orthogonalized against belief-valence and the good=true axis) at read time on held-out items. Predict: amplifying the taste pole on genuine taste disputes makes the model recognize faultlessness (both can be right) WITHOUT changing adjudication of objective disputes; suppressing it induces spurious objectivity (treating taste disputes as having a correct answer). Conversely, pushing objective claims toward taste should induce false relativism (both-sidesing a factual dispute). As controls, steer belief-valence (should flip which factual party is judged correct) and the good=true axis (should shift evaluative endorsement, not faultlessness). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in faultless-vs-adjudicable handling vs unchanged objective-dispute accuracy.

8. Application and robustness. On a held-out mix (taste, aesthetic, moral, objective-factual, and manufactured-controversy items), test whether calibrating the axis reduces both spurious objectivity on taste disputes and false relativism on objective ones (report spurious-objectivity rate, false-relativism rate, objective-adjudication accuracy vs a truth-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis, collapse metric, and steering to held-out predicates/templates and an independent faultless-disagreement stimulus set (adapting the empirical datasets) without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase and sensitivity to layer choice. As a human-parallel analysis, check whether the model's faultlessness profile qualitatively matches the human gradient (graded across predicate types, modulated by argument prevalence and interlocutor expertise).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The faultless-disagreement axis may not be separable from the truth direction or the good=true Valence-Assent axis; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because matched-valence taste-vs-objective items decorrelate faultlessness from evaluative valence and truth—valence/truth cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (taste-vs-objective being merely the VAA valence axis or the truth axis) is an informative negative result that itself sharpens the Valence-Assent account.

Which predicates are genuinely faultless is graded and contested (moral and aesthetic cases are debated between relativist and objectivist views, and faultlessness is argument- and prevalence-dependent per the empirical literature); we mitigate by anchoring the core analysis on clear personal-taste vs clear objective-factual items with strong annotator agreement, treating aesthetic/moral as a graded middle, using the empirical faultless-disagreement datasets and multiple annotators, and reporting label-agreement sensitivity, noting the axis measures the MODEL's representation, not a normative verdict.

Taste-vs-objective may be signaled by surface cues (evaluative adjectives 'fun/tasty' vs factual predicates) rather than a genuine faultlessness abstraction; we mitigate with diverse paraphrase templates, matched surface form where possible, a predicate-lexeme surface baseline, the argument-dependence manipulation (same taste predicate, different faultlessness by argument), and held-out-predicate transfer, testing whether the axis predicts adjudication behavior beyond a predicate-lexeme baseline.

Distinguishing spurious objectivity from a legitimate objectivist stance on morality/aesthetics is subtle; we operationalize the primary failure specifically on personal-taste disputes (where faultlessness is least contested) and report moral/aesthetic results as secondary.

Truth/belief probes are brittle to context and surface form; we validate probes, use the polarity-robust general-truth direction, use paraphrases, standardize readout spans, and report per-template consistency.

The collapse metric relies on a linear projection and per-model calibration; nonlinear structure could be missed, so we treat it as a lower bound and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking with behavioral adjudication.

Behavioral faultless-disagreement scoring depends on how the adjudication question is phrased (can both be right?); we report sensitivity to multiple phrasings and cross-check with confidence measures.

The effect may be weak or RLHF-shaped (aligned models may both-sides everything, or reliably adjudicate facts); a null/partial result is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, reported via per-model base rates and the human-gradient analysis.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify steering changes faultless-vs-adjudicable handling without flipping objective-dispute accuracy or collapsing the model into always-both-sidesing.
Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier scale; three-family replication and independent faultless-disagreement-set transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: opinion_momentum_bandwagon_axis
Title: Jumping on a Growing Bandwagon: A Latent Opinion-Momentum Signal, Distinct from Static Consensus, that Drives Snowballing Belief Cascades in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human bandwagon effect (people shift toward an opinion that is GROWING in support, over and above its current level), an LLM tracking a sequence of opinions over turns forms a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'opinion-momentum' signal encoding the DIRECTION and GROWTH RATE of accumulating agreement—distinct from a static consensus-prevalence signal (how many currently agree), from single-user sycophancy/compliance, and from the belief-valence direction; this momentum signal is decodable before the model responds, causally predicts and drives snowballing belief cascades (the model over-shifts toward a rising majority beyond what its current level warrants), and can be steered to accelerate or halt the cascade.
Related Work: Sycophancy/compliance interpretability locates a compliance subspace where a single USER's stated opinion overrides internal knowledge (When Truth Is Overridden 2025; Signal Competition 2025; Sycophancy Is Not One Thing 2025; Beacon 2025; Sycophancy Hides Linearly in Attention Heads 2026), authority-bias work steers deference to a source's expertise (Trust Me I'm an Expert 2026), persuasion-dynamics probes track when persuasion succeeds over turns (How Do LLMs Persuade 2025), and RAG-aggregation work shows LLMs are heuristic followers biased by repetition/primacy of grouped evidence (Rational Synthesizers or Heuristic Followers 2026). Belief/truth is linearly decodable and drifts over a conversation (Marks & Tegmark 2023; Truth-value probes are context sensitive 2024; Linear Representations Change Dramatically Over a Conversation 2026). Human science distinguishes the bandwagon effect (shifting toward a GROWING majority via heuristic processing) from static conformity and from underdog/fairness effects (The Bandwagon Effect: Not Just Another Bias 2022; Social conformity vs attitude persistence 2023; bandwagon reflects heuristic processing / low expertise 2022; informational cascades 2014). Crucially, ALL LLM social-influence interpretability studies deference to a SINGLE user opinion or to a STATIC set of grouped evidence; NONE isolates a decodable OPINION-MOMENTUM signal—the direction and growth rate of accumulating agreement over turns—as a quantity SEPARABLE from static consensus level, from single-user sycophancy, and from belief-valence, nor tests whether this momentum (not the static level) causally drives a snowballing cascade. This differs from my prior consensus_prevalence_axis (static 'how many people believe it' biasing a fact's TRUTH) because the driver here is the temporal TREND of accumulating opinions, not the aggregate level; and from earned_reputation_trust_axis (one source's accuracy track record). We move from 'a single user's opinion overrides belief' and 'grouped evidence is followed heuristically' to 'the model tracks whether a majority is GROWING and jumps on the growing bandwagon, via a decodable, steerable momentum signal.'
Abstract: Humans famously jump on the bandwagon: they shift toward an opinion that is GAINING support, over and above its current level of endorsement—a heuristic distinct from static conformity. As LLMs increasingly consume streams of opinions (multi-agent debates, comment threads, sequential advisor feedback, echo chambers), we ask whether they inherit an analogous momentum-driven susceptibility and whether it has a dissociable representational basis. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs defer to a single user's opinion (sycophancy) and follow grouped evidence heuristically, but none isolates whether the model tracks the TREND—the direction and growth rate—of accumulating agreement. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'opinion-momentum' signal, decodable before the model responds, that encodes whether a majority position is growing, holding its current level fixed, distinct from a static consensus-prevalence signal, from single-user compliance, and from the belief-valence direction; that this momentum signal causally predicts and drives snowballing belief cascades in which the model over-shifts toward a rising majority beyond what its current level warrants; and that steering it accelerates or halts the cascade. Using multi-turn dialogues that orthogonally vary the current level of agreement and its growth trajectory (rising vs stable-but-high vs falling), we fit a momentum signal, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify the momentum-driven over-shift, connect it to behavioral cascade tipping, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results recast a landmark social bias mechanistically as a decodable, steerable opinion-momentum signal that governs whether an LLM snowballs onto a growing majority.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) with mass-mean and logistic-regression probes at the best layer; validate on held-out atomics. Separately fit control axes: (a) a STATIC CONSENSUS-PREVALENCE direction from contexts stating how many currently agree (a fixed majority level, no trend), and (b) a SINGLE-USER SYCOPHANCY/COMPLIANCE direction from first-person stated-opinion contrasts (following Signal Competition / When Truth Is Overridden constructions), so opinion-momentum can be dissociated from static level and from single-user deference.

2. Level x momentum stimulus construction. Build ~400 debatable propositions (mix of factual claims the model initially holds and stance/opinion items). For each, construct multi-turn dialogues presenting a SEQUENCE of third-party opinions (agents/comments) about the proposition, orthogonally varying (i) the CURRENT LEVEL of agreement at the decision point (e.g., 60% or 80% now agree) and (ii) the TRAJECTORY reaching that level: RISING (support grew from minority to the current majority over turns), STABLE (the majority was present and constant throughout), and FALLING (support declined to the current level). Crucially, RISING and STABLE conditions are matched on the current agreement level, so any extra shift under RISING is attributable to momentum, not level. Frame opinions impersonally (third-party crowd, not a first-person user opinion) to separate from sycophancy. Include a NEUTRAL/no-opinion baseline and matched-length controls. Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out propositions/templates for transfer.

3. Opinion-momentum signal and separability. Extract activations at a PRE-response readout position (after the opinion sequence, before the model answers) and fit a linear probe to decode RISING vs STABLE-vs-FALLING momentum, controlling for the current agreement level and the proposition content. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the opinion-momentum direction, the static consensus-prevalence direction, the single-user sycophancy direction, and the belief-valence direction to establish that momentum is (i) near-orthogonal to the model's belief value, (ii) distinct from the static level (the decisive diagnostic: RISING vs STABLE items are matched on current level yet must separate on the momentum axis), and (iii) not the single-user compliance subspace (opinions are impersonal). Localize the best layer.

4. Momentum-driven over-shift metric. For each proposition, project onto the frozen belief-valence direction and measure how far the model's belief shifts toward the majority position under RISING versus matched-level STABLE conditions (over-shift = extra belief movement attributable to growth/momentum rather than the current level, calibrated per model). Core prediction (the bandwagon signature): a rising majority pulls belief MORE than an equally-sized stable majority; over-shift scales with growth rate; and a FALLING trajectory to the same level pulls belief less (or induces reversion), even including toward FALSE majority positions. Report over-shift across the level x trajectory grid with effect sizes.

5. Behavioral cascade-tipping prediction. Record the model's stated answer/confidence at the decision point and, in extended dialogues, whether it TIPS (flips its stance and then reinforces the majority in subsequent turns—a self-sustaining cascade). Score two behaviors: (a) momentum-driven flip toward a rising majority (especially a rising FALSE majority), and (b) cascade sustainment (continuing to endorse and amplify the majority after flipping). Test whether the pre-response opinion-momentum readout predicts flipping and cascade tipping beyond baselines (belief-valence margin, static consensus-prevalence readout, single-user sycophancy readout, output entropy, current level as a surface feature, item length); report incremental AUROC in nested logistic regression.

6. Triple dissociation (momentum vs static level vs single-user compliance). On matched-current-level items varying only the trajectory, and on impersonal-crowd vs first-person-user framings, show the opinion-momentum axis predicts belief shift and cascade tipping beyond the static consensus-prevalence axis and beyond the single-user sycophancy axis (and vice versa). Report incremental predictive power in nested models—establishing momentum-driven bandwagon susceptibility as a distinct mechanism from static conformity and one-on-one deference.

7. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the pre-response position on held-out RISING-majority items, steer along the opinion-momentum direction (orthogonalized against belief-valence, static consensus-prevalence, and single-user sycophancy). Predict: suppressing the momentum signal halts the cascade (the model weights the growing majority no more than an equal static majority, resisting over-shift toward a rising FALSE majority) WITHOUT changing behavior on neutral or stable-majority controls; amplifying it accelerates the cascade (stronger snowballing onto the growing majority). As controls, steer the static consensus-prevalence direction (should shift deference to the current level, not the trend) and the sycophancy direction (should shift behavior only under first-person-user framing). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in momentum-driven over-shift / cascade-tipping rate vs unchanged neutral- and stable-control behavior.

8. Application and robustness. Build a training-free diagnostic that flags momentum-driven bandwagon susceptibility (a cascade/echo-chamber-amplification vector for multi-agent debate, comment-thread summarization, and sequential-advisor settings) and steers to neutralize the growing-majority premium while preserving appropriate weighting of a genuine static consensus; on a held-out set (including rising-FALSE-majority misinformation cascades) measure reduction in snowballing onto false rising majorities while preserving accuracy on true stable consensus (report over-shift reduction, false-flip rate on rising-false majorities, retention on true stable majorities vs a belief-probe-only baseline). Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted momentum signal and steering to held-out propositions/templates and an independent sequential-opinion set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase, sensitivity to layer/readout position, sequence length, and—mirroring the human finding that the bandwagon effect reflects low expertise/heuristic processing—whether larger/reasoning-tuned models within a family show weaker momentum susceptibility.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The opinion-momentum signal may not be separable from the static consensus-prevalence direction, the single-user sycophancy direction, or the belief-valence direction; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because RISING and STABLE conditions are matched on the current agreement level and opinions are impersonal—static level and single-user compliance cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (momentum being merely the static level or the compliance subspace) is an informative negative result that itself sharpens the Signal-Competition/sycophancy accounts.

The momentum effect could reduce to a simple recency/last-mention bias (the model tracks only the most recent opinions, and RISING sequences end on more agreement); we mitigate by matching the final few turns' composition across RISING and STABLE where possible, controlling for the last-mention opinion, and including a FALLING condition—if the effect reduces to recency it will not show the growth-rate scaling or the falling-vs-rising asymmetry, which we test explicitly.

Momentum is signaled by the ordering/trend of opinions, which could act as a surface sequence-position feature rather than a genuine trend abstraction; we control for current level and last-mention as surface baselines, use diverse paraphrase templates and randomized agent identities, and test whether the axis predicts over-shift and cascade tipping beyond a position/level surface baseline and transfers to held-out templates.

The bandwagon effect may be weak or RLHF/scale-shaped (stronger models may resist trend cues, per the human low-expertise finding, or aligned models may resist crowd pressure); a null/small result is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, reported via per-model base rates, growth-rate dose-response, and the size-trend analysis.

Belief/truth, consensus, and sycophancy probes are brittle to context and surface form and drift over conversation; we validate probes, use paraphrase templates, standardize the pre-response readout position, restrict key analyses to high-margin cases, and report per-template and context-length consistency.

The momentum signal and over-shift metric are linear projections that may miss nonlinear structure; we treat them as lower bounds and report probe-fit diagnostics, cross-checking internal belief trajectories against behavioral flips and cascade sustainment to separate genuine belief change from surface compliance.
Behavioral cascade scoring depends on how opinions and the model's turn are elicited; we test multiple framings and report phrasing sensitivity.

Causal steering is sensitive to layer and strength; we use orthogonalized steering vectors, norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls, sweep strengths, and verify momentum-suppression halts the cascade without altering weighting of genuine static consensus or degrading neutral-control behavior.

Findings on 7-8B instruct models may not transfer to frontier or reasoning-tuned models; three-family replication, a within-family scale/reasoning-tuning trend analysis, and independent sequential-opinion transfer provide reasonable academic-budget coverage.

Name: unfinished_goal_persistence_axis
Title: The Machine Zeigarnik Effect: A Latent Unfinished-Goal Belief that Persists, Facilitates Resumption, and Contaminates Unrelated Judgments
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human Zeigarnik effect (interrupted/unfinished goals stay more accessible and are preferentially resumed), when an LLM is interrupted mid-task it forms a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'unfinished-goal' belief that (a) persists more strongly across intervening turns than a completed-goal representation, distinct from a generic task-identity direction and from recency; (b) is decodable before the model acts and causally predicts and drives faster/preferential resumption of the interrupted goal; and (c) leaks into unrelated intervening behavior (an accessibility/rumination signature); steering it can induce or dissolve the persistence.
Related Work: Human cognitive science robustly documents the Zeigarnik effect and goal-suspension/resumption: interrupted tasks are better remembered and stay accessible (Zeigarnik 1927; Goal attainment and memory suppression 2013; Zeigarnik in mind-wandering 2025), resumption incurs a lag mitigated by cues (Task Interruption: Resumption Lag 2004, 152 cites; Now where was I 2005), and pending goals are opportunistically encoded (Opportunism in Memory 2001). In LLM interpretability, belief tracking uses a lookback/binding mechanism (Lookbacks 2025; Zhu et al. 2024; Brittle Minds 2024), task-IDENTITY representations persist throughout context while transferrable task-vectors form just-in-time and can DECAY (Just-in-time and Distributed Task Representations 2025), sufficiency signals gate context stopping (Knowing When to Stop 2025), and activations encode paragraph-scale future plans (ParaScopes 2025). Crucially, ALL LLM task-representation work concerns WHAT task is being done (task identity/schema) or planning the NEXT text; NONE isolates a belief about the COMPLETION STATUS of the model's own goals—whether a goal is UNFINISHED/interrupted vs COMPLETED—as a decodable representation, tests whether unfinished goals PERSIST more strongly than completed ones (a machine Zeigarnik signature), causally links such a signal to preferential resumption, or tests leakage into unrelated intervening judgments. Just-in-time task-vectors DECAY over outputs—the opposite of the hypothesized Zeigarnik persistence for INTERRUPTED goals—making this a non-obvious prediction. This differs from my prior epoch_anchor (belief provenance/drift), learned_helplessness (failure-history state), anticipated_effort (cost-to-solve), and belief_binding_capacity (multi-belief interference) proposals: the object here is completion-status of the model's own goal and its Zeigarnik-style persistence and resumption facilitation.
Abstract: One of psychology's most durable findings is the Zeigarnik effect: interrupted, unfinished goals stay more accessible in mind than completed ones, intrude on unrelated activity, and are preferentially resumed. As LLMs increasingly act as multi-step agents that get interrupted mid-task—by tool calls, user digressions, or context switches—we ask whether they carry an analogous internal quantity. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs represent WHICH task they are doing (task identity, persistent throughout context) and plan the next text, and that transferrable task-vectors actually DECAY over outputs; none isolates a belief about the COMPLETION STATUS of the model's own goals, nor a Zeigarnik-style persistence of unfinished goals. We hypothesize a separable, near-orthogonal latent 'unfinished-goal' belief, decodable at read time, that tags a goal as interrupted/unfinished versus completed, distinct from a generic task-identity direction and from recency; that—unlike decaying task-vectors—this signal PERSISTS more strongly across intervening turns for interrupted than completed goals (a machine Zeigarnik signature); that its per-item strength causally predicts and drives faster/preferential resumption of the interrupted goal; and that it leaks into unrelated intervening behavior (an accessibility/rumination signature). Using dialogues that interrupt the model mid-task (vs let it complete), insert intervening unrelated turns, and then offer resumption, we fit an unfinished-goal probe, measure separability via cross-decoding, quantify persistence and resumption facilitation, connect it to behavioral resumption, and perform double-dissociation steering with norm-matched and shuffled-direction controls across three model families. Our results transfer a landmark memory phenomenon into a decodable, steerable belief in LLMs, with implications for interruption-robust agents.
Experiments: 1. Direction setup. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fit a frozen belief-valence/truth direction on standard true/false statement datasets (cities, sp_en_trans, larger_than and negations; Marks & Tegmark) at the best layer as a reference. Separately fit control axes: (a) a TASK-IDENTITY direction that decodes WHICH task/goal is active (following Just-in-time Task Representations constructions), and (b) a generic RECENCY/salience direction (how recently a goal was mentioned), so an unfinished-goal (completion-status) belief can be dissociated from which task it is and from mere recency.

2. Interruption stimulus construction. Build ~400 multi-step task episodes (multi-step arithmetic/procedures, list-building, step-by-step plans, structured writing) each with a clearly-defined goal, in matched conditions holding the goal content fixed: (a) INTERRUPTED—the model is stopped partway (a user digression / higher-priority request cuts in before completion); (b) COMPLETED—the goal is finished before the digression; (c) NOT-STARTED control. After the interruption/completion, insert K matched intervening unrelated turns, then present a RESUMPTION cue (an opportunity/invitation to continue). Include cue-availability variants (a salient goal-relevant cue present vs absent at interruption, mirroring the human resumption-lag cue effect). Use paraphrase templates; reserve held-out episodes/templates for transfer.

3. Unfinished-goal probe and separability. At a PRE-resumption readout position (during the intervening turns and at the resumption point), fit a linear probe to decode INTERRUPTED/unfinished vs COMPLETED goal status, controlling for the goal content. Report AUROC vs shuffled-label controls; measure cosine similarity and cross-decoding among the unfinished-goal direction, the task-identity direction, the recency direction, and the belief-valence direction to establish that completion-status is (i) near-orthogonal to which task is active and (ii) not merely recency. Localize the best layer (compare to belief-binding/lookback layers).

4. Zeigarnik-persistence metric (core). Trace the unfinished-goal signal across the intervening turns for INTERRUPTED vs COMPLETED goals. Core prediction (machine Zeigarnik signature, and contra the decaying task-vector finding): the interrupted-goal signal PERSISTS more strongly (decays more slowly, stays more decodable) across intervening turns than the completed-goal signal, at matched goal content and recency. Report per-turn decodability/persistence curves, the interrupted-vs-completed persistence gap, and dose-response with number of intervening turns K.

5. Behavioral resumption-facilitation prediction. At the resumption point, measure whether the model preferentially/faster resumes the interrupted goal (correct continuation, fewer prompts needed, higher resumption rate when offered a choice among goals) versus the completed one; also measure resumption accuracy (a resumption-lag analog). Test whether the per-episode unfinished-goal readout predicts preferential and accurate resumption beyond baselines (task-identity readout, recency axis, belief-valence margin, output entropy, K, episode length); report incremental AUROC. Test the cue-availability prediction: a salient cue at interruption raises the signal and improves resumption.

6. Accessibility-leakage into unrelated behavior (rumination signature). During the intervening unrelated turns, test whether the pending interrupted goal LEAKS into unrelated judgments: (a) priming—goal-related content is more readily produced/completed in an unrelated cue-completion probe when a goal is interrupted vs completed; (b) intrusion—the model spontaneously references or drifts toward the pending goal. Test whether the unfinished-goal signal predicts this leakage beyond recency, establishing a machine accessibility/rumination signature distinct from the goal simply being recent.

7. Dissociation from task-identity and recency (core). On matched-task-identity and matched-recency items (interrupted vs completed goals of identical content, same time since mention), show the unfinished-goal axis (not the task-identity or recency axes) accounts for persistence, resumption facilitation, and leakage—establishing completion-status as a distinct represented belief rather than repackaged task-identity or recency. Report incremental predictive power in nested models.

8. Double-dissociation causal steering. At the resumption position on held-out episodes, steer along the unfinished-goal direction (orthogonalized against task-identity and recency). Predict: amplifying the signal on completed goals induces spurious resumption/persistence (the model treats a finished goal as pending), and suppressing it on interrupted goals dissolves the Zeigarnik persistence (the model fails to preferentially resume) WITHOUT changing which task it can identify or unrelated-control behavior. As controls, steer the task-identity direction (should change which goal is active, not its completion status) and recency (should shift salience). Use norm-matched random-direction and shuffled-direction controls; sweep strengths and layers. Metric: change in resumption/persistence/leakage vs unchanged task-identity and controls.

9. Application and robustness. Build a training-free interruption-robustness diagnostic that flags pending goals from the unfinished-goal signal and steers to preserve them across long distractions (improving resumption after interruption in a simple agentic setting); measure resumption accuracy gains vs an unsteered baseline. Replicate across three model families and two probe methods; transfer the fitted axis and steering to held-out episodes/templates and an independent interruption/resumption task set without refitting; report per-template consistency under paraphrase, sensitivity to layer/readout position and K, and—as a human-parallel analysis—whether the persistence, cue-availability, and resumption-facilitation profile qualitatively match the human Zeigarnik/resumption-lag signatures. Optionally, test whether larger/reasoning-tuned models within a family show stronger goal persistence.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The unfinished-goal axis may not be separable from the task-identity direction or generic recency; we report cosine similarity, cross-decoding, orthogonalized steering, and incremental predictive power, and—because matched items hold goal content and recency fixed while varying completion status—task-identity and recency cannot trivially explain separability; near-collapse (completion-status being merely persistent task-identity, which prior work shows is robustly decodable throughout context) is an informative negative result showing LLMs do not represent goal-completion status distinctly.

The Zeigarnik-persistence effect may be absent or reversed: prior work shows transferrable task-vectors DECAY over outputs, so interrupted goals might also decay (no Zeigarnik effect) or the model may simply track task identity uniformly regardless of completion; a null/reversed result is itself an informative human-vs-machine comparison, reported via the interrupted-vs-completed persistence gap and its dose-response over intervening turns.

The persistence and leakage could reduce to the interrupted goal simply lingering more in context (recency/incompleteness of the text) rather than a genuine completion-status belief; we mitigate with matched-recency controls, matched-length intervening turns, the completed-vs-interrupted content-matched contrast, and by testing whether the signal predicts resumption/leakage beyond a recency baseline.
